en: Regarding the *Lengqie zongtong* (The Penetration of the Lanka School) and Dependent Origination: In my year of Jiashen, having returned from Changzhou, I stayed briefly in Jiahe where I met the two monks Daguan and Mizang. It was as if we had a long-standing affinity;
day after day we consulted one another, finding delight in Chan and wandering our minds beyond the mundane world. One night, I dreamed that I was walking upon *tūla* cotton.

In the world of Mian, he beheld the countenance of the Compassionate Honored One (Maitreya), which was most majestic; he prostrated himself with solemn reverence and respectfully received his instructions.

The instruction said: "Discrimination is consciousness (*vijñāna*); non-discrimination is wisdom (*jñāna*). Upon waking, he asked two monks, "From which sutra should these words have originated? They both replied, "They seem like words from the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
He immediately took up the *Laṅkāvatāra* and searched through it everywhere, but could not find them. When he reached the year of Dingyou, the monk Du... [of the local community]... arrived.

Upon entering the capital, he spoke with great enthusiasm and tireless joy regarding the three translations of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, saying, "How might I obtain the brush of Juefan (Fayan Wenyi) to compose a treatise on this?
At that time, Da'an was widely practicing the Way; there were no among the inner scriptures to which he had not attained profound mastery.
I remarked, "Were it not for Da'an, this treatise could not have been completed. Subsequently, Da'an requested leave to return to his hometown, where he heard of Hanshan Deqing.
When the Duke entered Guangdong, he passed through Luochuan and paid his respects to entrust [the manuscript] to me.
I had been at Mount Lei for less than three years when the *Biji* (Notes) appeared. Since my visit to Laoshan in the year of Guisi (1593), our correspondence had been sparse;
yet upon reading these notes, it was as if I were facing him in person once again. Reading them the first time, I felt a sense of refreshing clarity; reading them a second time, the same.
Reading it once, I was skeptical; reading it a second time, I made various revisions until the paper was full. I then took up the three translations for comparison.

The Song translation is elegant and profound, possessing an inexhaustible flavor, and thus it could not be altered. As for the thorny passages and inverted syntax, they would remain unintelligible without reference to the two translations from the Wei and Tang dynasties.
I have recorded these points, dividing them into sections and listing them so clearly that they are as plain as looking at one’s own fingers, to facilitate reading.
It was easy for me to collate and edit; I have frequently consulted it and further refined my own deliberations by harmonizing the old commentary with the three translations.

In some places, I have expressed my own insights—even where predecessors had not spoken—ensuring that the concise and profound passages are fully elucidated so as to avoid the lament that the *Laṅkāvatāra* is difficult to read.
Long ago, the First Patriarch said to the Second Patriarch: "These four fascicles of the *Laṅkāvatāra* can [be used]..."
The transmission of the "Seal of the Mind" (Yinxin) was not frequent; later, it was destined to become a study of names and characteristics (*nāmākāra*). Alas!
Even down to the present day, those who can clearly elucidate names and characteristics are rare; how much more so, then, for the Seal of the Mind?

I venture to reckon that the realization of the self-awakened realm within the Chan school (*zongmen*) and the occasional *dharmaparyāya* (provisional teachings) bestowed therein must surely accord with the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*. Yet, [the masters] erroneously took up the *pith instructions* (*jī*) of the venerable patriarchs...

This appendix is attached to the end of the chapter. Rather than clarifying the Sūtras through the Sūtras—which is merely "Sūtra-accordance" (jìng-tōng)—it is better to clarify the Sūtras through the fundamental principle (zōng), which is "Principle-accordance" (zōng-tōng).

To clarify the Sūtras through the Sūtras is to differentiate based on mere conceptual intention; to clarify the Sūtras through the fundamental principle is to differentiate within that which is non-differentiated.
Differentiation refers to *sūtra-accordance* (shuō-tōng), while non-differentiation refers to *principle-accordance* (zōng-tōng). Thus, there are two types of accordance.
In principle, the mind is the single sutra, and the sutra is the single mind; thus, I hope not to deviate from the meaning of the First Patriarch’s transmission of mind through mind.
As for these four fascicles of the *Buddha-ukta-citta-varga*, their ultimate aim does not lie outside of this.

It has been twenty years since the World-Honored One of Compassion (Maitreya) instructed me in a dream, yet it is only now that I have brought it to fruition based on that dream. Could this also be a matter of destiny?

Was it because he was in a state of meditative concentration that he foresaw these things in advance? Furthermore, the two translations from the Wei and Tang dynasties mostly include the preceding "Chapter on Exhortation" (*Prārthanā-parivarta*) and the final "Chapter on Dhāraṇīs" (*Dhāraṇī-parivarta*);
those I dreamed of were not differentiated [from them]. This is the speech of wisdom, which truly exists within the "Chapter on the Proclamation" (*Saṃcodana-parivarta*).

Therefore, I have recorded them together so as not to forget the intent with which the Compassionate Honored One commanded me. As for the realization of wisdom (*jñāna-sākṣātkriyā*), there is no differentiation between them.

Otherwise, one would remain in a state of vast uncertainty, having made no entry at all. Yet, within the *Gāthā-parivarta*, it is prophesied that Nāgāsena has already attained the first stage (*bhūmi*);

this sutra provides great clarification on this point, concluding that he was ultimately able to be born in the Pure Land. Therefore, those who transmit the patriarchal robe should uphold this scripture;
those who progress through the successive stages should uphold this scripture; and those who seek birth in the Pure Land especially must do so.
How could one not place firm faith in this sutra? I have respectfully recorded its beginning and end and committed it to the carving blocks, so that those with clear eyes may examine it.
Alas! Why speak dream within a dream? This is what I hope from my fellow practitioners.
Preface to the *Lengqie zongtong* (Comprehensive Penetration of the Laṅkāvatāra School), written by Jinjian Zeng Fengyi (style name Shunzheng) of Nanyue Mountain;
calligraphed by Liu Risheng (style name Fusheng) of Luling.
Zeng Shunzheng’s father, who had retired from his post as a Minister of Rites (Yibu Dafu), returned to lie in retirement at Hengyang.

He closed his doors and swept away all worldly concerns, devoting himself solely to the teachings of the Śākya tradition. For nearly twenty years, he tirelessly and extensively translated the karmic encounters of venerable patriarchs, gathering and researching widely while engaging in profound verification.
His diligent labors with brush and inkstone were rarely idle for a single day; his passion lay entirely therein, such that he was unaware of anything else.
Regarding his exhaustion [in scholarship], the *Lengyan Zongtong* and *Jingang Zongtong* he authored were widely circulated during his time; now, he has further compiled the *Lengqie Zongtong*.

Having completed my studies of this work, I observe that he gathered materials from the ancient translations of the Song, Wei, and Tang dynasties, and having synthesized them for the present day, he recorded his notes and unified them through the lens of the school (*zong*).
Is the school truly distinct from the sutra? While the sutras flourished in the West, [the school]...
The Celestial Star (Vimalakīrti) awakened to the Way; the Breaking of the Smile at the Flower constituted the transmission of the Dharma.

These lineages flourished in the East, yet the Gate of Wall-Gazing was perilous and steep, being entrusted solely to the Second Patriarch because this scripture could serve as a seal for the mind. Thus we know that clarifying the essence and clarifying the scripture are neither one nor two.
However, those who cling to the literal meaning of the teachings become obstructed and hindered, resulting in all manner of confusion regarding what to accept and what to reject.

It has caused the scriptures to fall into obscurity and their names and characteristics to become fragmented; even between the two schools of meditation and exegesis, they have become like wedges and axes, or water and fire, clashing against one another as they divide into separate sects—this is solely due to the failure to penetrate the fundamental source.

As for the deluded interpretations of later generations, who clap their hands in joy over the "pleasures of Chan," they follow a collapsing tide and a surging wave, with every cry met by a hundred harmonies that cannot be restrained;
this further leaves those gentlemen who worry for the times with no recourse but to lament the loss of the fundamental source.

To claim that this is a perversion rather than a fault of the school is incorrect; therefore, unless one possesses superior faculties and extraordinary wisdom such that past karmic obstructions have long since been dissolved and all攀緣 (pān-yuan, mental attachments) are utterly purified, to falsely claim the title of a Chan practitioner (*dhyāna*) does nothing but harm the teachings—there is no other possibility.

Alas, the difficulty of articulating the essence of the school has long been known! By nature, I am indolent regarding the various Buddhist scriptures and cannot read them all; thus, I have selected those passages suitable for constant recitation and translation.
At times, there were those who understood my work yet mistakenly claimed it was a mere intellectual exercise;

they sighed over the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, lamenting that its phrasing was so concise and profound that they would invariably stop mid-reading, considering such difficulty a natural consequence of their heavy karmic burden, thinking, "This life is already at an end.

Only after obtaining the *Inverted Phrases and Thorny Sentences* compiled by Master Shunzheng did I finally begin to unravel the text, grasping its structural framework and extracting its essential points. Thus, I became somewhat proficient in its underlying meaning, supplemented by the singular insights of the ancient masters of various schools.

I have collated and verified these principles, and found that this sutra—the Buddha’s words on the Heart—is truly resplendent as the noble wisdom of self-awakened realization, clearly pointing the way as if looking at one's own palm.
As for the fervent teaching that eliminates words and letters, those who are deluded may slander it, yet those who know it regard it as the guidance of a true teacher.
What Shunzheng has compiled is indeed rich; when I examine it, I find it equal to the "Wall Contemplation" (Biqianguan). What do you think of this, Shunzheng? I ask you.

Just as I was about to circulate this compilation to stir up and promote this great matter, Sun Jūn Mòchéng of the Court of Imperial Sacrifices donated several thousand pieces of gold to have it carved into printing blocks at Chánggān.

Pleased by his devotion to the good and his courageous assistance, I gave him these words to entrust to the eminent masters of various quarters and the learned gentlemen of strong resolve, so that they might examine them.
The Lankavatara Sutra: A Compendium of the Essential Meaning, Volume One.
*Lanka* (translated here as "Inaccessible") *Avatara* (translated here as "Unsurpassed") *Ratna Sutra*.
Translated by the Tripitaka Master from India, the Śramaṇa Guṇabhadra (translated here as "Virtuous Merit"), during the Song Dynasty.
Translated anew by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Bodhiruci of Northern India during the Wei Dynasty (translated as "Jue Xi" in Chinese);
translated again by the Tripiṭaka Śramaṇa Śikṣānanda of Khotan during the Tang Dynasty (translated as "Jue Xi" in Chinese);
and translated once more by the Bodhisattva Precept Disciple Zeng Fengyi, Court Gentleman of the Ministry of Sacrifices, and Zongtong of the Ming Dynasty.
Tong asked, "Why is this sutra named *Laṅkā*? Is the name Laṅkā Mountain derived from its designation as 'Jewel' (*ratna*)?
Its form has eight facets, yet it appears perfectly spherical; its substance is extremely solid, such that no worldly jewel surpasses it.
This mountain is situated in the midst of the ocean and is composed entirely of this jewel, constantly emitting radiance; therefore, it is called the Unsurpassed Jewel Mountain."

On the summit of the mountain is a city occupied by flying yakṣas. Whenever there are overcast clouds and dark nights, or when the waves surge tumultuously, the form of the mountain becomes even more distinct and its radiance grows ever more intense; yet when the sky is clear and serene, and the sea and heaven are of one color, the mountain is no longer visible.
It was here that the Buddha preached this sutra, which is named after its location—the Avataṃsaka.
The treatise states: "The World-Honored One preached the Dharma atop Mount Malaya in the southern sea, within the city of Laṅkā.
This mountain is five hundred yojanas high; looking down upon the great ocean, there is no path by which to ascend.

The city is composed of various jewels, its radiance surpassing that of the sun and moon, and it has no gates through which to enter. Only those who have attained supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) are capable of ascending there."
The Dharma-gate of Manifesting the Mind-Ground can only be ascended when there is neither cultivation nor realization.
Formerly, when Dongshan and his senior teacher Mi arrived at Yishan, they saw vegetable leaves floating in a mountain stream. Dongshan said, "This is a deep mountain with no people;
why are there vegetable leaves flowing along? Is there perhaps a practitioner of the Way living here? Thereupon, they cleared the weeds and traveled upstream for five or seven *li*, when suddenly—
Seeing that the Master’s physical form was emaciated and his appearance altered, he set down his luggage and paid his respects. The Master said, "There are no paths on this mountain;
from where have you come, O Kalyāṇamitra? Dōng replied, "Setting aside for a moment the matter of there being no path, from where did you enter, Reverend?
The Master said, "I do not come as a wandering monk. Dōng asked, "How long has it been since the Reverend resided on this mountain? The Master said:
Chongchou did not enter the cave and said, "The Master previously resided on this mountain.
The Master said, "I do not know. Chongchou asked, "Why do you not know? The Master said, "I did not come from the realm of humans or devas.
Chongchou asked, "What principle did the Master realize that you were able to reside on this mountain? The Master said, "I saw two earthen oxen fighting as they entered the sea; it was straight."
Having been without news until now, [the monk] finally prepared his formal attire and prostrated, then asked:
"What is the guest within the host? The Master said, "Green mountains shrouded by white clouds. He asked, "What is the host within the guest?

The Master said, "Never leaving one's door for many years. He asked, "How far apart are guest and host? The Master said, "Waves upon the waters of the long river. He asked, "What is the guest? The Master said, "..."
When the Master and his disciple met, what did they say? The Master said, "The clear breeze brushes the white moon.
Dongshan took his leave. The Master then composed a verse, saying: "I have lived all along in this three-bay thatched hut; A single path of divine light leaves the myriad realms at peace.
Do not bring 'is' and 'is not' to debate with me; In this floating life, forced interpretations are irrelevant. Because of this, he burned his hut and entered [the mountains] once more.
Because no trace of him could be found in the deep mountains, later generations called him Master Yinshan (Hidden Mountain). Furthermore, Dongshan asked Yunju, "From where have you come?
Yunju replied, "I have come from treading upon the mountains. Dongshan said, "Which mountain is fit for dwelling? Yunju said, "Which mountain is unfit for dwelling?
Dongshan said, "If that is so, then the entire country has been occupied by you, Dharma brother. Yunju replied, "Indeed."
Shan said, "Not so. Juzhi said, "If that is so, then you have found a way of entry? Shan said, "There is no way.
Juzhi said, "If there is no way, how could you have met with the Old Monk? Shan said, "If there were a way, you would be separated from the Master by a mountain.
Shan then said, "This fellow will, in the future, be beyond the grasp of thousands or ten thousands of people."
Those who have attained realization should know that the Mountain of Jewels is near; they reach it without taking a single step—why then need they go to Laṅkā?
(In the Tang translation, this is titled "Chapter One: The Exhortation of King Rāvaṇa"; in the Wei translation, it is titled "Chapter One: Inviting the Buddha").

Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was dwelling on Mount Malaya by the shore of the great ocean, in the city of Laṅkā, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus and a great assembly of bodhisattvas.
Those bodhisattva-mahāsattvas had all thoroughly mastered the five dharmas, the three natures, and the selflessness of the various consciousnesses;
they were skilled in knowing that the objects of experience are manifestations of their own minds, and they sported therein.
Possessing immeasurable mastery, samādhis, supernormal powers, and various strengths, they manifest in diverse forms according to the minds of sentient beings to skillfully subdue them;

all Buddhas place their hands upon their crowns, and they have all come from various Buddha-lands to this assembly, with the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati as their leader. At that time, the World-Honored One, at the Sea Dragon...
After seven days had passed since the Buddha preached the Dharma within the royal palace, he emerged from the great ocean.
There, immeasurable billions of Brahmās, Śakras, Lokapālas, devas, nāgas, and others came forth to welcome the Buddha.
At that time, the Tathāgata raised his eyes, beheld Mount Malaya and the great city of Laṅkā, and immediately smiled, saying: "In the past, the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas..."

"In this very city, all have taught the Dharma realized through their own noble wisdom—a realm that is not within the speculative views of the non-Buddhists nor the sphere of practice for those of the two vehicles. I shall now likewise reveal this Dharma to King Rāvaṇa.
At that time, by the Buddha’s spiritual power, the Yakṣa King Rāvaṇa heard the sound of the Buddha’s voice and knew from afar as it truly was.
Emerging from the Dragon Palace, surrounded by Brahmā, Śakra, the World-Protectors, devas, and nāgas, he beheld the waves of the ocean and observed that assembly.

Seeing the great ocean of the *ālayavijñāna* stirred by the winds of objective realms, causing the waves of the *pravṛttivijñānas* to arise, he felt a heart of great joy and cried out in a loud voice within that city:
"I shall go to the Buddha and request entry into this city for myself and all the devas and worldlings."

"O people, you have obtained great benefit during this long night. Having spoken these words, he immediately ascended with his retinue into a palace of flowers and proceeded to the place where the World-Honored One was.
Upon arrival, he descended from the palace, circumambulated the Buddha three times to the right, and performed various musical offerings for the Tathāgata;
the instruments they held were all made of great blue indranīla jewels, lapis lazuli, and other such precious gems interspersed among them.
He wrapped his priceless upper garment around [the drum], and as its sound was exquisite and its rhythm harmonious, he spoke a verse therein in praise of the Buddha, saying:
"The Dharma-treasury of the mind's own nature is selfless and free from the stains of views; it is known by realized wisdom. I pray that the Buddha will proclaim it for us."
"O you who have gathered the wholesome dharmas to realize the body of wisdom, who dwell in constant bliss and possess mastery over transformations, may you enter the city of Laṅkā!
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas of the past have all dwelt in this city; may this assembly of yakṣas listen to the Dharma with a single-minded resolve.
Then, Rāvaṇa, King of Laṅkā, having praised the Buddha with songs in the *duṭaka* meter, further [praised him] with song.
He spoke these verses aloud:
"The World-Honored One stayed for seven days within the ocean of Magadha, and only then emerged from the dragon palace to ascend peacefully to this shore.
I, together with my various celestial maidens and the yakṣa retinue, as well as Sugāra and those of great wisdom among the *sāla* trees..."
By means of their supernatural powers, they all proceeded to where the Tathāgata was; each descended from his flower-palace and paid homage to the World-Honored One.
Then, through the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, they addressed the Buddha by their own names, saying: "I am the Rākṣasa King, Daśagrīva Rāvaṇa.
I have now come to the presence of the Buddha; may the Buddha accept me and all the sentient beings within the city of Laṅkā."
The immeasurable Buddhas of the past all ascended to the summit of the Jewel Mountain and, dwelling within the city of Laṅkā, taught the Dharma they themselves had realized;
the World-Honored One should likewise do so—dwelling upon that Mountain Adorned with Jewels and surrounded by a host of Bodhisattvas—proclaiming the pure Dharma.
On this very day, we and the assembly dwelling in Laṅkā desire with one mind to hear the ineffable Dharma of personal realization.
I recall that in the past and future worlds, immeasurable Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, surrounded by their retinues, have expounded this Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra;
this scripture of the Laṅkāvatāra was praised by the Buddhas of old. I pray that the Buddha will likewise go there, and that you, O Honored One, will also expound it for the sake of the assembly.
Out of compassion for the immeasurable hosts of yakṣas, may the Buddhas enter that city adorned with jewels and preach this sublime Dharma-gate.
This wondrous city of Laṅkā is adorned with various jewels; its walls are not of earth or stone, and its lattices are entirely of precious gems.
This host of yakṣas has in the past made offerings to the Buddhas and practiced the path, becoming free from all faults; they have realized and known the truth with constant clarity.
These yakṣas, both male and female, thirst for and look up to the Mahāyāna; they have confidence in the Mahāyāna themselves and also desire to lead others to have such confidence.
I pray that the Unsurpassed Honored One, together with the hosts of rākṣasas such as Kumbhakarṇa and his retinue, will proceed to Laṅkāpurī.
Having diligently made offerings to the Buddhas of the past, future, and present, I wish to hear the Dharma of self-realization and the ultimate path of the Mahāyāna.
May the Buddha, out of compassion for me and the assembly of yakṣas, enter this city of Laṅkā along with the sons of the Buddhas.
"My palace, my court ladies, and all my precious ornaments, as well as the lovely Aśoka Garden—may the Buddha compassionately accept them.
Regarding the Buddha and the Bodhisattvas, there is nothing I would not relinquish, even my own body; I offer myself in service. I only pray that you will compassionately accept me.
At that time, having heard these words, the World-Honored One immediately addressed him, saying: "Yakṣa King, throughout your past lives..."
The Great Teacher, out of compassion for you all, has accepted your request and gone to the Jewel Mountain to preach the Dharma of his own realization;
future Buddhas shall do likewise. This is the dwelling place of those who practice the profound contemplative discipline and experience the bliss of the present life.
Having spoken these words, he and the various Bodhisattvas, out of compassion for you, have accepted your invitation. Thus it was said.
While [the Buddha] remained there in silence, King Rāvaṇa immediately offered the exquisite Lotus Palace, which he himself rode, as a gift to the Buddha.
The Buddha sat upon it, and the King, along with the various bodhisattvas leading and following him in procession and immeasurable court ladies singing praises, made offerings to the Buddha.
They proceeded toward that city; having arrived at the city, King Rāvaṇa and his retinue...

Furthermore, they performed various kinds of sublime offerings; among the hosts of yakṣas, boys and girls offered jeweled nets to the Buddha, and King Lavana offered precious necklaces to the Buddhas and bodhisattvas to hang around their necks.
At that time, the World-Honored One and the various bodhisattvas, having accepted these offerings, each briefly explained the realm of their own realization.
At that time, when the Dharma of the profound realms was being taught, King Rāvaṇa and his retinue again made offerings to the Bodhisattva Mahamati and entreated him, saying:
"I now request the Great Being to inquire of the World-Honored One regarding the realm of the self-realized wisdom of all Tathāgatas."
I, along with the host of yakṣas and these bodhisattvas, desire to hear this with a single mind; therefore, we all exhort you.

You are the most supreme among those who discourse on the practice of yoga; thus, out of reverence, we urge you to inquire about the Dharma—the Dharma of self-realized purity, which ultimately leads to entry into the Buddha-ground and is free from all faults of the non-Buddhists and the two vehicles.
At that time, by means of his supernormal powers, the World-Honored One further manifested within those mountains immeasurable jewel-mountains,
all adorned with hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of exquisite jewels of the devas. Upon each mountain, the body of a Buddha appeared,
and before each Buddha were King Rāvaṇa and his assembly, as well as all beings from the ten directions.

All lands appear therein; within each land there is a Tathāgata, and before each Buddha stands King Rāvaṇa together with his retinue, the great city of Laṅkā, the Aśoka Garden, and such adornments, all identical and without difference.
In each instance, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati poses questions, and the Buddha provides the exposition.
Having spoken this sutra with hundreds of thousands of sublime voices regarding the realm of self-realized gnosis, the Buddha and all the bodhisattvas vanished from the sky and no longer appeared.
King Rāvaṇa saw only his own body remaining within his palace, and he thought to himself:
"Who was that? Who heard those teachings? And who is it that sees the Buddha and [the assembly]?"
Where now are these things—the kingdom, the city, the various jewels, the mountains, the forests, and so forth? Are they the product of a dream, or the creation of an illusion?
Or are they like a city of the Gandharvas, seen through an optical distortion (*timira*), or deluded by a mirage (*marīci*)?
Are they like a woman giving birth to a son in a dream, or like a whirling circle of fire (*alātacakra*)? Reflect further upon all of this.
The nature of all phenomena is thus: they are solely the objective realms of one's own mind's conceptualization.
Ordinary beings are deluded and cannot comprehend this; there is nothing that can see, nor is there anything seen; there is nothing that can speak, nor is there anything spoken.
Seeing the Buddha and hearing the Dharma are both conceptualizations, like what was previously seen. If one cannot see the Buddha by not giving rise to such conceptualization, then—
Upon seeing this, King Laṅkā immediately attained awakening, became free from all defilements, and realized that [all things] are but his own mind, abiding in non-conceptuality.
By the power of the roots of virtue planted in the past, he attained the vision of all phenomena as they truly are;

no longer relying on the awakening of others, he was able to skillfully observe with his own wisdom, forever leaving behind all speculative conjecture and false interpretations, and dwelling in the Great [Vehicle].
Practitioners, appearing in various forms before their teachers, have well-mastered the illusory wisdom of skillful means;

they manifest the signs of progress through the stages (*bhūmi*), constantly delighting in the distancing from mind, thought, and consciousness, severing the threefold continuity, and abandoning the attachments of non-Buddhists.
Through internal self-awakening, they enter the *tathāgatagarbha* and proceed toward the stage of Buddhahood, hearing [these teachings] within the void and inside the celestial palaces.
They all raised their voices and said: "Excellent, Great King! Those practitioners who study as you do should train in this way and should view all phenomena in this way.
If one views them otherwise, that is the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*). You should forever distance yourself from mind, thought, and consciousness;
you should diligently investigate all phenomena and cultivate internal practice, rather than clinging to external views."
Do not fall into the paths of the two vehicles or the doctrines practiced by non-Buddhists, nor into the objects of their views or the various samādhis they seek to attain.

You should not delight in frivolous debate or idle laughter; you should not give rise to the various views of the Vedas, nor should you be attached to royal power or sovereignty, nor should you dwell within the six meditative concentrations (*ṣaḍ-samāpatti*). If you can act in this way, [you shall succeed].
This is the practice of those who practice according to reality as it is: it can subdue the arguments of others, destroy evil views, and abandon all attachment to the view of a self;
it can transform the foundational consciousness through sublime wisdom, cultivate the Mahāyāna path of the bodhisattvas, and enter the stage of the Tathāgata’s personal realization.
You should thus apply yourself diligently to study and cultivation so that you may attain these dharmas.

To further purify the meaning of practicing samādhi and samāpatti, one must not become attached to the realms of the two vehicles or external paths, taking them for supreme bliss as ordinary practitioners do.
Externalists cling to the view of self, the mark of a self, and real *guṇas*, giving rise to grasping and attachment;
those of the two vehicles perceive ignorance as the condition for formations within the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
Lankā King, this dharma that transcends discursive thought and discrimination is the supreme Mahāyāna path;
it enables the accomplishment of the noble wisdom realized within oneself (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*) and causes one to receive sublime births within the various realms of existence.

Lankā King, this practice of the Mahāyāna shatters the cataracts of ignorance, extinguishes the waves of consciousness, and does not fall into the practices of the various views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Lankā King, such is the practice of the non-Buddhists.
Those who cling to a self and produce various divergent doctrines are unable to expound the two meanings of the nature of consciousness and the view free from clinging.
Excellent, King of Laṅkā! Because you previously beheld the Buddha and contemplated this meaning, such contemplation is itself the beholding of the Buddha.
At that time, King Rāvaṇa again thought to himself: "May I once more be granted the privilege of beholding the Tathāgata."
The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, having transcended the teachings of non-Buddhists through Avalokiteśvara,
is able to expound the realm of self-realized noble wisdom that surpasses all matters of emanation and transformation. Abiding in the Tathāgata-samādhi and entering the bliss of samādhi,

he is therefore called the Great Master of Contemplative Practice and is also named the Great Compassionate One, who can burn away the fuel of afflictions and conceptual discrimination until it is exhausted.
Surrounded by the assembly of all Buddha-sons, universally entering the hearts of all sentient beings, pervading all places, endowed with all-knowledge,
and forever free from all conceptualized phenomena and signs— I now vow to behold again the great supernormal powers of the Tathāgata.
By virtue of this vision, that which was not yet attained shall be attained, and that which has been attained shall not regress, as I depart from all conceptualization.
Abiding in the bliss of samādhi, he increased and fulfilled the stage of Tathāgata wisdom.

At that time, the World-Honored One, knowing that King Laṅkā was about to realize the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), out of compassion manifested his body so that the transformed scene returned to its original state.
Then the ten-headed king saw the immeasurable mountain cities he had previously beheld, all adorned with jewels.
In each and every city, there were likewise those who were perfectly awakened ones (Samyaksaṃbuddhas), their bodies adorned with the thirty-two marks;
he saw his own body before all these Buddhas, surrounded by great-wisdom yakṣas who were expounding the Dharma practiced through self-realized gnosis.
He also saw such things as the Buddha-lands of the ten directions, all of which were without any distinction.
At that time, the World-Honored One surveyed the entire assembly with his eye of wisdom, not with his physical eyes;

like a lion king, he turned his gaze with vigorous majesty and laughed joyfully. From the space between his eyebrows, his thighs, flanks, waist, neck, and shoulders—and from within each and every pore of the *de* (卍) sign upon his chest—he emitted immeasurable rays of wondrous-colored light, trailing like the brilliance of a rainbow.

Like the sun spreading its radiance, or like the fierce, blazing flames of the kalpa-ending fire, when Brahmā, Śakra, and the four heavenly kings saw from afar the Tathāgata sitting atop Mount Laṅkā, which is like Sumeru, they laughed joyfully.
At that time, all the bodhisattvas and the assembly of devas had this thought: "The Tathāgata, the World-Honored One, is sovereign over all dharmas; by what cause and condition [does he laugh]?"
Therefore, he laughed heartily, his body emitting radiance; remaining silent and unmoving, he dwelt in the realm of self-realization and entered the bliss of samādhi.
Like a lion king surveying his surroundings, he looked toward Rāvaṇa and contemplated the Dharma as it truly is.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, having previously received the invitation of King Rāvaṇa and further knowing the assembly of bodhisattvas...
With his mind contemplating that all future sentient beings would delight in and be attached to words and letters,

grasping at meaning according to the phrasing and thereby falling into delusion by adhering to the practices of the two vehicles or external paths— or perhaps thinking, "The World-Honored One has already transcended the realm of all consciousnesses;
for what cause and condition does he smile with such great joy?"— in order to sever their doubts, [the Bodhisattva] questioned him.
The Buddha then addressed him, saying: "Excellent, Mahāmati! Excellent, Mahāmati! You observe the world and take pity on all sentient beings;
because they are entangled by evil views throughout the three periods of time, you ask me in order to bring them to awakening.
Those of great wisdom, for the benefit of themselves and others, are capable of asking such questions. Mahāmati, this King of Laṅkā once asked about the past..."
"I now wish to inquire about the two meanings of all Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas, and these same two meanings will also apply to the future.
The distinct characteristics of these two meanings cannot be fathomed by any of the followers of the Two Vehicles or by any of the non-Buddhists.
At that time, the Tathāgata, knowing that King Laṅkā was wishing to inquire about this meaning, addressed him, saying: "King Laṅkā, you wish..."
"Ask me; you should ask me quickly. I shall analyze and explain it for you, fulfilling your aspirations and causing you joy.
By means of wisdom, you shall be able to contemplate and investigate, becoming free from all conceptual discrimination.
You shall thoroughly understand the various stages (*bhūmi*), practice their respective remedies, realize the true meaning, enter the bliss of samādhi, and abide in the protection of all Tathāgatas."

Delighting in *maitrī* and distancing themselves from the faults of the samādhis of the two vehicles, they dwell upon the Bodhisattva stages of Immovable (*acalā*), Good Intelligence (*sādhumatī*), and Dharma Cloud (*dharmameghā*). Therein, they are able to know the selflessness of all phenomena as it truly is.

They shall receive the consecration of their crown with the water of samādhi amidst a great precious lotus flower, and further, immeasurable lotuses appear surrounding them, within which sit countless bodhisattvas.
Abiding there, you and the assembled multitude gaze upon one another; such a realm is inconceivable.
O King of Laṅkā, arise! Practice the skillful means of the stages of cultivation and dwelling, and further give rise to immeasurable skillful means.
You shall certainly attain the state of the Tathāgata as described above—an inconceivable sphere where you manifest forms in accordance with the needs of beings.
That which was to be attained— never before seen by any of the followers of the two vehicles, nor by the various non-Buddhists, Brahmā, Śakra, or the gods— was then realized. At that time,
having received the Buddha’s permission, the King of Laṅkā rose from his seat atop the mountain peak of pure radiance,
which resembled a great lotus made of jewels, surrounded by a host of celestial maidens, and manifested immeasurable varieties of forms.
There were flowers of various colors and fragrances, powdered incense, ointments, banners, flags, canopies, crowns, pendants, necklaces,
and other various exquisite ornaments never before seen or heard of in the world; furthermore,
he magically created all manner of immeasurable musical instruments belonging to the desire realm, surpassing those of all devas, nāgas, gandharvas, and others.
Furthermore, he magically transformed all that exists in the world into musical instruments such as those he had previously seen in the Buddha-lands of the ten directions;
he also magically created nets that completely covered all the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas.
He further manifested various kinds of exquisite garments and erected banners and pennants as offerings. Having performed these deeds, he immediately ascended into the void.
Seven *tāla* trees high in the air, various clouds of offerings rained down, and musical instruments played as they descended from space.
Then, at that very seat, on the second day, the Radiance of Sunlight, atop the mountain peak of Great Lotus Jewel, joyfully and with reverence spoke these words:
"I now wish to ask the Tathāgata about two matters; regarding these two—"
"I have already asked about this matter to the Tathāgatas, Arhats, Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, and those Blessed Ones have explained it to me.
Now I also wish to ask about this same matter; I only pray that the Tathāgata will explain it for me.
Blessed One, these two meanings are taught by the Nirmāṇa-nirmāṇa-tathāgatas, not by the Mūla-buddha. The Mūla-buddha speaks of the realm of the bliss of samādhi."

"It is well said, Blessed One, that you speak of the sphere of false conceptualization; O Lord who has mastery over all phenomena, out of compassion, we pray that you explain these two meanings, for the hearts of all the sons of the Buddha long to hear them. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the king, saying:
"You should question me, and I shall explain it for you. Then, the Yakṣa King further adorned himself with various jeweled crowns and necklaces.
Adorning his body with ornaments, he spoke these words: "The Tathāgata has taught that even the Dharma should be relinquished, let alone what is not-Dharma (adharma).
How can these two kinds of phenomena be relinquished? What is the Dharma and what is the non-Dharma? If the Dharma should be relinquished, how can there be duality?
It is merely within the realm of conceptual differentiation that there is 'existence' and 'non-existence'; these are not real."
In truth, all these are merely conceptual constructions and cannot comprehend the undifferentiated characteristic of the *ālayavijñāna*.
Just as the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) abides like a net of hair—beyond the sphere of impure cognition—how could it ever be discarded?
At that time, the Buddha addressed the King of Laṅkā, saying: "King of Laṅkā, do you not see that jars and other such things are impermanent and subject to decay?"
Ordinary beings give rise to false conceptualizations regarding this; why do you not now understand the distinguishing characteristics of what is Dharma and what is non-Dharma?
This is what ordinary beings conceptualize, not the vision of the noble ones.
O King of Laṅkā, ordinary beings follow after various signs, whereas the noble ones are like one who has seen a palace, gardens, and forests burned down—seeing them as mere appearances.
The nature of a flame is a single source of light and heat, yet due to the power of the fuel, its length, shortness, size, and magnitude each differ individually.
O King of Laṅkā, how can you not understand the distinct characteristics of dharma and adharma in this way?
Just as a single seed gives rise to an infinite variety of differences—sprouts, stalks, branches, leaves, flowers, and fruit—so it is with external phenomena.

Internal phenomena are likewise: conditioned by clarity (*vidyā*), the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and sense-bases (*āyatana*)—all such phenomena—arise within the three realms, undergoing births in various destinies with their respective distinctions of suffering and pleasure, beauty and ugliness, speech and silence, and movement and stillness.

Furthermore, while the characteristic of the various consciousnesses is one, they exhibit diverse distinctions according to their objects, such as superior, middling, or inferior; defiled or pure; and wholesome or unwholesome.

Lord of Laṅkā, not only are there such distinctions among dharmas as described above, but when practitioners cultivate meditative observation, even that which is traversed by their own wisdom is seen to have marks of distinction;
how much more so for dharma and non-dharma, which lack any such various distinctions?
Lord of Laṅkā, you should know that these marks of distinction between dharma and non-dharma are all merely marks.

"O King of Laṅkā, because of conceptual discrimination, what is meant by 'dharmas'? It refers to the false discriminations of the two vehicles and the various non-Buddhists who claim that things such as 'existence' and 'reality' are the causes of all dharmas. Such dharmas as these should be abandoned and left behind;

one should not engage in conceptual discrimination or grasp at their signs within them. When one perceives the dharma-nature of one's own mind, there is no attachment to any objects whatsoever, such as jars and the like."
That which is grasped by the ignorant has no inherent essence. Those who practice contemplation observe all phenomena as they truly are through *vipaśyanā* and thus relinquish them.
O King of Laṅkā, what is it that is not a phenomenon? It refers to all phenomena being without nature and without marks, forever free from conceptual discrimination.
For one who sees according to reality, such objects as "existence" or "non-existence" do not arise at all.
This is called abandoning what is non-Dharma. Furthermore, there are further non-dharmas, namely: the horns of a rabbit, the son of a barren woman, and so forth.
These all lack intrinsic nature and characteristics and cannot be differentiated; they exist as names only in accordance with worldly convention.

They are not like jars and such things that can be grasped and clung to, for they are not objects apprehended by consciousness. Such conceptualizations should likewise be abandoned; this is called "abandoning."
“Dharma and the abandonment of non-Dharma—O King of Laṅkā, what you previously asked has now been fully explained by me.
O King of Laṅkā, you said that you had already asked about this meaning in the presence of past Tathāgatas, and those Tathāgatas had already explained it to you.
O King of Laṅkā, you said that the past is merely conceptual construction and the future is likewise; I am also the same as they.”
Lokendra, all those Buddha-dharmas are free from conceptual discrimination; they have transcended all conceptualization and proliferation (*prapañca*).
They are not like material forms (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*), but are to be realized only by wisdom (*jñāna*). For the sake of enabling sentient beings to attain peace and happiness, he expounds the Dharma;

through the wisdom of signlessness (*animitta-jñāna*), he is called the Tathāgata. Therefore, the Tathāgata has wisdom as his essence and wisdom as his body; it is for this reason that [he is so named].

It can be distinguished, yet it cannot be distinguished by means of that which is distinguished; it cannot be distinguished by means of the marks of self, person, or sentient being. Why is it impossible to distinguish?
Because consciousness arises from objects and grasps at color and form. Therefore, one is detached from the subject that distinguishes and also detached from the object that is distinguished.
O King of Laṅkā, it is like the beings depicted in a painting on a wall—they do not exist.
One realizes that all sentient beings in the world are likewise without karma and without retribution; all phenomena are also thus, without hearing and without speaking.
Lankāvatāra King, sentient beings in the world are like magical transformations; ordinary people and non-Buddhists cannot comprehend this.
Lankāvatāra King, to be able to see in this way is called right view; to see otherwise is called discriminative view.
Due to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), one grasps at duality.

For example, it is as if a person sees their own reflection in water or a mirror, sees their own form in a lamp or the moon, or hears their own echo in a mountain valley, and thereby gives rise to conceptual construction and develops attachment.
This is also like that: phenomena (*dharma*) and non-phenomena (*adharma*) are merely conceptual constructions; they arise solely from conceptual construction.
Unable to abandon them, they only further increase all manner of false imaginings and fail to attain quiescence.

Quiescence refers to the single object of focus; this single object of focus is the supreme samādhi, from which arises the noble, self-realized wisdom that takes the Tathāgatagarbha as its objective domain.

(Wei says: To see according to reality is called right view; to see otherwise is called wrong view. To engage in conceptual discrimination is called dual grasping—all of which are false and do not attain quiescence. Quiescence is called the one mind; the one mind is called the Tathāgatagarbha.
The Tathāgatagarbha is the realm of wisdom entered within one’s own body, wherein one attains the samādhi of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas.)

Tong said: "The World-Honored One, during the assembly at the Lotus Sūtra, emitted light from his white tuft of hair to illuminate and perceive the various Buddha-activities of the worlds in the eastern direction;

yet the *Lotus Sūtra* has already concluded. This [manifestation] at the assembly of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, wherein Mount Vimalasvabhāva appears along with the various events and Mahāmati’s inquiries regarding the Dharma, has likewise already concluded. Thus one may know that all dharmas are [thus]."
"All these are manifestations of one's own mind. Formerly, King Prasenajit asked: "Within the ultimate truth (paramārtha-satya), does conventional truth (saṃvṛti-satya) exist?
If one says it does not exist, then wisdom should not be twofold; if one says it does exist, then wisdom should not be singular.
What is the meaning of this duality? The Buddha said: "Great King, in the past, under the Dharma of the Buddha Nāgaprabha, you once asked this very question."
Regarding this meaning, I have nothing now to say and you have nothing now to hear; this absence of speaking and hearing is called "one meaning" and "two meanings.
These two questions are briefly similar, yet the reasons for the World-Honored One’s answers are entirely different:

one elucidates the School of Characteristics (Lakṣaṇa-yāna), while the other elucidates the School of Nature (Dharmatā-yāna). Therefore, when elucidating the School of Characteristics, phenomena belong to existence and non-phenomena belong to non-existence.
One should abandon both; even that which is seen as it truly is should be abandoned, let alone what is called "Dharma" and "non-Dharma.
The luminous nature of reality not only transcends conceptual discrimination but also transcends verbal expression.
Where there is neither speaking nor listening, one enters the realm of self-realized noble wisdom, which is known as the quiescent single mind.
Chapter One: The Heart of All Buddha-Speech (In the Wei translation, Chapter Two: Questions and Answers; in the Tang translation, Chapter Two, Part One: Assembling All Dharmas).
It is said that this great scripture consists of one hundred thousand verses, one million phrases, three hundred and sixty thousand words, and one hundred and fifty chapters.
Of those transmitted from the West, only this single chapter remains. This chapter is titled "Heart" (*citta*), signifying the single mind.
The thesis is the *paramārtha-citta* (ultimate mind), which is the purity of self-nature;
for all Buddhas realize this mind, it is called the "Chapter on the Mind of All Buddha-Speech. Master Dharma said to the Second Patriarch:
"I have four fascicles of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, which I also entrust to you. This is the essential gateway to the Tathāgata’s mind-ground."
To reveal, instruct, awaken, and lead all sentient beings [to the truth], Mazu one day said to the assembly:
"All of you, believe that your own mind is the Buddha; this very mind is the Buddha-mind.
The Great Master Bodhidharma came from Southern India to China to transmit the Dharma of the Supreme Vehicle—the single mind—to cause you all to attain awakening. He further cited:

The *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* was composed to seal the minds of sentient beings, fearing that you might fall into delusion and lack self-confidence regarding this Dharma of the single mind which each and every one possesses.
Therefore, the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra* takes the Buddha’s words on the mind as its essence and the "no-gate" (*amukha*) as its Dharma-gate.
Those who seek the Dharma should have nothing to seek; outside the mind there is no other Buddha, and outside the Buddha there is no [other] mind.
A separate mind neither grasps at good nor rejects evil; it relies on neither side of purity or defilement.

It realizes that the nature of offenses is empty, such that they cannot be apprehended in every thought-moment because they lack self-nature. Therefore, the three realms are mind-only, and the myriad phenomena of the universe are all sealed by this single Dharma.
Whatever forms one perceives are all perceptions of the mind; the mind is not the mind itself, for it arises dependent upon form.
Therefore, you may simply speak according to the occasion; whether in matters or in principle, there is no obstruction whatsoever.
The fruit of the Bodhi path is also like this: that which arises in the mind is called form (*rūpa*); because one knows form is empty, arising is non-arising.
If you understand this meaning, you may then dress and eat at the appropriate times to nurture the holy embryo. Rest as you please.
When the time has passed, what further matter is there? You have received my teaching; listen to my verse:
"The mind-ground speaks according to the occasion, and Bodhi is likewise merely tranquility. Both principle and phenomena are without obstruction; that which arises is precisely non-arising.
This single phrase—'that which arises is precisely non-arising'—is sufficient to shatter the false views of the heterodox and the Two Vehicles. This constitutes the entirety of the *Laṅkāvatāra*."
The Eye of the School:

Thus have I heard. At one time the Buddha was dwelling on the peak of Mount Laṅkā by the shore of the southern ocean, adorned with various precious flowers, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus and a multitude of great bodhisattvas, having come from various other buddha-fields.

From [various] buddha-fields, these bodhisattva-mahāsattvas— headed by the bodhisattva-mahāsattva Mahāmati— possessed the power of mastery over immeasurable samādhis and sported with supernatural powers (*abhijñā*).
Tong said: "Because this translation is concise in expression yet profound in meaning, it lacks the *Adhyeṣaṇā-parivarta* at the beginning of the scripture;
for it is not a complete sutra, but merely the single chapter on the 'Essence of the Buddha’s Mind. Wei [the Emperor] stated that 'quiescence is called the One Mind.
Since this Dharma of the One Mind cannot be grasped in its profound essence by anyone other than great Bodhisattvas and great Bhikṣus, [it was entrusted] to Mahāmati."
When those present were ranked as the foremost, they all remarked that this "Great Matter" (mahāntam artham) is not something the Lesser Vehicle can reach.
It is just like the Unsurpassed Jewel Mountain in the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, where Buddhas and Māras dwell together and ordinary beings and sages intersect;
it is utterly devoid of rungs on a ladder and has no gate through which to enter. None but those who possess mastery over samādhi and sport with supernormal powers (*abhijñā*) can [enter].

Regarding the reason why those who came from various different Buddha-fields to hear the Dharma at that time were all seated without their great disciples of the Buddha being arranged in order of seniority— except for the Venerable Piṇḍola,
whose karmic conditions were briefly revealed last: formerly, King Aśoka personally went to serve a midday meal to thirty thousand great Arhats within his inner palace.
When the King saw that there was no one in the first seat of the assembly, he asked for the reason. Venerable Samudrareṇu replied, "This is the seat of Piṇḍola;
this person has recently come from seeing the Buddha. The King asked, "Where is he now? The Venerable said, "Wait but a moment.
As soon as he had finished speaking, Piṇḍola descended from the sky. When the King invited him to take his seat and paid him homage, [Piṇḍola] did not accept.
King Gu saw this and asked, "I have heard that you, Venerable One, personally saw the Buddha come; is this so? Pointing his hand upward toward his eyebrows, he said, "Do you understand?
The King replied, "I do not understand. The Venerable One said, "The Dragon King of Lake Anavatapta once invited the Buddha for a meal, and at that time, I was also included among those present.
Observing how Piṇḍola thus provided this instruction, [the King] greatly marveled at him.
O Monk Bābī, King Aśoka has not yet awakened; he is far removed from the Mountain of Jewels.

All Buddhas shall pour water upon his crown, and he will skillfully understand the meaning of the realms manifested within his own mind—the various forms of sentient beings and their various minds, and the immeasurable gates of liberation appearing universally according to their kind—within the five dharmas, the three self-natures, and the two types of consciousness.
When they had thoroughly realized the ultimate non-self of all phenomena, at that time the Bodhisattva Mahāmati—along with the Bodhisattva Maitreyī (translated here as "Wisdom";
in the Wei translation, "along with all the Great Wisdom Bodhisattvas")—traveled through all the Buddha-fields.

Empowered by the Buddha’s spiritual authority, he rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms in reverence, and praised the Buddha with verses.

The General Manager said: "Because Bodhisattvas such as Mahāmati have already realized Equal Enlightenment (samyak-saṃbodhi) and are about to be invested with the rank of Buddha, all Buddhas personally bestow the consecration upon their crowns.
This is because they have transformed consciousness into wisdom (vijñāna → jñāna) and awakened to the realization that the triple world is mind-only (cittamātra).

Regarding the supernatural transformations manifested in the preceding 'Chapter on Exhortation,' they have thoroughly understood the meaning of the fact that these manifested realms are the manifestations of their own minds."

The various mental factors (*caitta-dharma*) and material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) do not transcend five categories, three natures, eight consciousnesses, and two kinds of selflessness. The five categories are:
(1) name (*nāman*), (2) appearance (*nimitta*), (3) conceptual construction (*parikalpita*), (4) correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*), and (5) suchness (*tathatā*). The three natures are:

(1) the nature of conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), (2) the nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*), and (3) the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). The eight consciousnesses are: the six consciousnesses, the seventh consciousness, and the eighth consciousness. The "two" refers to the two kinds of selflessness.
Non-self refers to both the selflessness of persons and the selflessness of phenomena. The various classes of sentient beings do not transcend dependent origination and deluded conceptualization;
being shrouded by the two selves of person and phenomenon, they have not yet attained liberation.

When one realizes correct wisdom and the suchness of the perfectly accomplished nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), one is able to transcend birth and death. This is the gateway to immeasurable deliverance; one should investigate this thoroughly.

Having thoroughly realized that the universal manifestation of forms according to their kind is merely what is manifested by one's own mind—and that this has been fundamentally unborn from the beginning—it is therefore equal to the awakening of the Buddhas, without any distinction.
Thus, one is able to travel everywhere through Buddha-lands to serve all Buddhas.
Master Lingyin Song said in his hall discourse: "The Buddhas of the ten directions are always before you; do you see them? If you say you see them..."
"It is seen by the will and seen by the eye; therefore it is said: 'All dharmas are neither born nor extinguished.
If one can understand in this way, the Buddhas are ever present before one. Furthermore, it is said: 'When seeing form, one sees the mind.
Now, what do you call 'mind'? Is it the mountains, rivers, and the great earth? The myriad phenomena in their dense array? Or blue, yellow, red, white, male, female, and so forth?"
"Phenomenal marks are mind; they are not mind. If they were mind, why would they instead become objective forms?
If they are not mind, yet you say that upon seeing form one sees mind—do you understand? It is simply because of delusion regarding this that inversions arise, resulting in all manner of differences.
Within that which is neither identical nor different, you forcibly produce identity and difference. Now, right here and now—"
When one accepts this and suddenly realizes the fundamental mind, it is luminously clear and devoid of even a single thing that can be seen or heard.
If one seeks liberation apart from the mind, the ancients called this "searching for the source in the waves"; such a person will find it extremely difficult to achieve awakening.

Therefore, when one reaches ultimate penetration here, one skillfully understands the meaning of the manifestations of the objective realm within one's own mind; yet, if one has not yet departed from delusion, [the task remains].
Conceptual discrimination is precisely delusion; seeking its source does not lead beyond the heterodox views and mistaken understandings of the two vehicles.
When the world is detached from arising and ceasing, it is like flowers in the sky; when wisdom realizes neither existence nor non-existence, one gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
All phenomena are like illusions and are far removed from mind and consciousness; when wisdom realizes neither existence nor non-existence, one gives rise to the mind of great compassion.
Distant from the extremes of annihilation and permanence, the world is always like a dream; through wisdom, one finds neither existence nor non-existence, yet gives rise to great compassion.

Knowing that both persons and phenomena lack self (pudgala-nairātmya and dharma-nairātmya), and that afflictions and their residual impressions (*vāsanā*)—this being the cognitive obscuration (*jñeyāvaraṇa*)—are eternally pure and signless, one gives rise to great compassion.

All things are nirvāṇa, yet there is no nirvāṇa; there is no Buddha, yet there is no non-Buddha; the Buddha does not abide in nirvāṇa. (The Tang translation reads: "The Buddha does not dwell in nirvāṇa.")
The Buddha who dwells not in *parinirvāṇa* is far removed from both the awakening and that which is awakened, whether it be existence or non-existence;

having abandoned both of these, the Muni (here translated as "Silent One") contemplates with tranquility, and thus remains far removed from birth. (The Wei translation says: "If one contemplates the Buddha thus, he is tranquil and free from arising and ceasing.
This is called being untainted by this world or the next. (The Tang translation says: "Such a person is free from attachment in this life and the next, having nothing to grasp.")
Tong said: "This is because the Bodhisattva Mahamati has well understood the meaning of the objective realm as a manifestation of his own mind;
thus, he praises the Buddha with what he himself understands, saying that the Buddha is far removed from all worldly phenomena of arising and ceasing, regarding them as like flowers in the sky.
These flowers originally have no roots, arising only through the pressure of a hand; when observed with right wisdom, they are neither existent nor non-existent."
Thereupon, he gives rise to great compassion in order to deliver sentient beings, causing them likewise to transcend birth and cessation.

As for the dharmas such as mind and consciousness clung to by those of the Two Vehicles, the Buddha remains far removed from them; he views them as like an illusion. Illusory phenomena are not real, yet they arise solely through illusion.
Through the contemplation of right wisdom, one perceives that they neither exist nor do not exist. Thereupon, he gives rise to great compassion in order to deliver them.

The two vehicles cause them to likewise transcend mind and consciousness; the Buddha distances himself from the two views of annihilationism and eternalism held by non-Buddhists, regarding them as like a dream.
Within a dream, all discriminations are unreal; through the contemplation of right wisdom, he perceives that things neither exist nor do not exist.
Thereupon, he gives rise to great compassion to deliver the non-Buddhists, causing them likewise to transcend the views of annihilationism and eternalism.

Furthermore, although the Bodhisattva has realized and known the two kinds of selflessness—of persons and of phenomena—and is thus free from both the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), he still retains the traces of conceptual signs (*nimitta*).

Not yet being a Buddha of signlessness (*animitta*), he regards all the flames of the afflictions as utterly pure and entirely equal; having eliminated even those traces of signs, he gives rise to great compassion (*mahākaruṇā*).
The mind brings the Bodhisattvas across to a state of constant purity and signlessness. Thus, that which the Buddha has realized for himself resides in Nirvana;
yet, he further negates even that Nirvana. There is no Buddha who possesses Nirvana, as he is far removed from the subject of awakening;
there is no Nirvana belonging to a Buddha, as he is far removed from the object of awakening. Therefore, it is called "One."
There is absolutely no nirvana, for originally there was no birth-and-death; how then could there be nirvana? If it exists, it is simply the dharma of birth-and-death;
if it does not exist, it is simply the dharma of nirvana. One must completely depart from both of these, stripping away all skin and flesh until only the one true person remains.

If one contemplates the Buddha in this way, then quiescent extinction manifests before one: it is fundamentally unborn from the very beginning. Thus it is said: "Since it is originally without birth..."

Because they are fundamentally unarisen, one does not grasp at dharmas of arising and ceasing, nor grasp at dharmas of mind and consciousness, nor grasp at dharmas of annihilation or permanence, and so on, up to not grasping at the dharma of nirvāṇa. They are eternally pure and signless;
they are not merely pure in this present life, but are likewise pure when extended to future lives as well. The Tang translation says: "The Dharma-body is like an illusion or a dream."
How can one offer praise? To know that there is no nature and no arising is what is called praising the Buddha.
Since the Buddha has no characteristics of sense-faculties or objects, not seeing is called seeing the Buddha. How could one possibly have praise or blame for the Muni?
Therefore, by observing the four words with the Muni’s tranquility, one praises the Buddha. This is the realm of the Tathāgata’s self-awakening; how could it be accessible to ordinary beings?
The monk Ce asked Baizhang, "What is the essential teaching for the sudden enlightenment of the Mahāyāna?

Baizhang replied, "You must first bring all conditions to rest and cease all affairs. Regarding all dharmas—whether good or evil, mundane or supramundane—do not recall them and do not dwell upon them.
Let go of body and mind so that they are free and at ease, and let the mind be like wood or stone."
When there is no discrimination and the mind has nowhere to go, the ground of the mind is like space and the sun of wisdom appears of its own accord—similar to the sun rising when the clouds part.

Simply by ceasing all攀緣 (pān-yuan, conceptual clinging), and exhausting the afflictions of greed, anger, attachment, grasping, defilement, and purity, one remains unmoved by the five desires and the eight winds;
one is not bound by seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, nor is one constrained by any external objects.
When delusions are naturally perfected as the wondrous function of supernormal powers, such a person of liberation faces all objects with a mind free from stillness or agitation;
neither grasping nor scattering, they pass through all sounds and forms without obstruction. This is called a person of the Way.
They employ neither good nor evil, right nor wrong; they do not cherish a single dharma, nor do they reject a single dharma.

One who is called a follower of the Mahāyāna is not constrained by anything—neither good nor evil, emptiness nor existence, defilement nor purity, the conditioned nor the unconditioned, the mundane nor the supramundane, nor by merit or wisdom. This is called the Buddha-wisdom. It is neither good nor ugly;
it is neither principle nor non-principle. When all cognitions, views, and emotional attachments are exhausted, one cannot be bound; being sovereign everywhere, this is called [liberation].
For the sake of bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds, he immediately ascends to the stage of Buddhahood;
drawing from the vessel of Baizhang, he pours forth several hundred words, each of which accords with the verses of Mahamati—this is called the pure instruction of the non-appropriator.
At that time, after the Bodhisattva Mahāmati had praised the Buddha with verses, he announced his own name: "I am named Mahāmati;
I have attained mastery in the Mahāyāna. Now, with one hundred and eight points of meaning, I respectfully inquire of the Most Honored One, the Supreme among Men, the Knower of the World.
Having heard those spoken verses and observed the entire assembly, he addressed the sons of the Buddhas, saying:
"All you sons of the Buddha, now ask whatever you wish; I shall explain for you the realm of self-realization. [The assembly] replied in unison:
"The Most Honored One" (*bhagavat*) is one of the ten titles [of a Buddha]; "Knower of the World" (*lokavid*) is also one of the ten titles.
These two titles alone are cited because [the Buddha] has severed the worldly mind-consciousness of arising and ceasing, as well as the extremes of permanence and annihilation, and so forth.
All dharmas are that which the Buddha has liberated himself from and is able to remain far removed from; he has transcended the world by a vast distance.
Not only is he the most honored among the multitude, but he is the supreme among the honored.
To say that the realm of self-awakening can only be known by oneself and cannot be spoken of to others is entirely unrelated to the "one hundred and eight meanings. This is one sentence.
The answer is complete. Master Liaoye Panshan said in his ascent to the hall:

"O Zen practitioners, you who study the Way within this school are like the earth upholding a mountain, unaware of the mountain’s towering loftiness; or like a stone containing jade, unaware of the jade’s flawlessness.
Those who act in this manner are called 'those who have left home. Therefore, the Teacher said: 'Dharmas are fundamentally not mutually obstructive; the three periods of time are likewise so.'"
Yet, even those who are non-active and without affairs are still like one bound by golden shackles; thus, the spiritual source shines alone, and the Way is entirely unborn.
Great wisdom is not illumination, and true emptiness leaves no trace. True Suchness—whether ordinary or sagely—is all but a dream-word;
both Buddha and Nirvana are merely superfluous designations. Zen practitioners must look for themselves directly; there is no one who can take your place. If, regarding this...
If one thoroughly penetrates the meaning of the phrase regarding Mount Pan, then the realm of self-realization is truly not something obtained through another.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, having received the Buddha’s permission, prostrated at the Buddha’s feet, joined his palms in reverence,
and questioned him with a verse:
How does one purify mindfulness? How does mindfulness increase? How does one perceive delusion? How does delusion increase? (In the Tang translation:
How does one give rise to conceptual construction? How does one purify conceptual construction? How does one give rise to confusion? How does one purify confusion?)
The Commentary states: "Initial conceptualization (*vitarka*) is itself the affliction of views; therefore, purifying conceptualization is to purify one's mindfulness.
The increase of conceptualization is itself delusion; therefore, the increase of right mindfulness is to purify delusion.
The Tang translation distinguishes between shallow and deep levels to provide their respective remedies, which seems somewhat abrupt; it does not compare with this translation.
Cease deluded thoughts to purify one's mindfulness. How does this mindfulness increase?
Once views and ignorance arise, they are termed "delusion. How does this delusion increase? The words are even more allusive:

within this single thought, confusion and awakening give rise to the various phenomena of the ten realms—the environment and its inhabitants, causes and effects. Among these, there are those that are wholesome.
There are those who possess superior goodness, those who are deluded, and those who are further deluded;
it is unknown from where they arise, for one wishes to exhaustively investigate the source of the arising of the ten realms. Therefore, the Buddha later replied: "The phrase 'pure' is not pure;
the phrase 'deluded' is not deluded. This suddenly reveals the quiescent single mind, wherein not even the slightest trace of delusion or enlightenment can be found. Thus says the sutra.
In the midst of expounding many points, he never departs from this essential principle. Great Master Suizhen ascended the hall and said:
"This nature is originally pure and replete with all virtues; it is only due to the two conditions of defilement and purity that distinctions arise.
Therefore, when the sages awaken to it, they exclusively employ its purity to achieve the Way of Enlightenment; when ordinary beings are deluded by it, they exclusively follow its defilement."

Because its essence is non-dual even as it causes one to sink into the cycle of saṃsāra, the *Prajñāpāramitā* states: "It is without duality, without two parts, without distinction, and without interruption.
Furthermore, Chan Master Cheng of Man-an said in his ascent to the hall: "When a single thought-moment is pure, the Buddha dwells in the Demon King’s palace;
when a single evil thought arises, the Demon King dwells in the Buddha’s palace. Master Huai said: "But..."
To believe in this way is called walking with one’s feet firmly planted on the ground; there is ultimately no other dharma and no other principle.
When I, this old monk, have spoken thus, I fear you all will be like those who release the hawk upon seeing the rabbit, or those who seek the sword by marking the boat.
Why? Because a wise host accepts neither the Goddess of Merit nor the Woman of Darkness. Look!
These two venerable elders, by silently citing the scriptures and revealing their own school’s style in just these few words, have encompassed the entire treasury of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.

Why? Because [the text] speaks of the lands and transformational marks, as well as the various non-Buddhists; why is it called "no-sensation" (*asaṃvedana*) next? And for what reason is it named "no-sensation"?
Why is one called a "Son of the Buddha" (in the Tang translation: "What is meant by Son of the Buddha," and in the Wei translation: "Quiescence and Sequence")? To what state does liberation lead?
Who is bound, and who is liberated?
The general principle is that "no reception" and "no shadow" signify the meaning of quiescence and the absence of all marks (*animitta*).
The subsequent text states: "Successively entering the state of no-marks; successively entering the samādhi-realms from stage to stage. This leads into the following question:
"For what reason do they transcend the various stages? Who arrives at 'no reception'? These points collectively identify this sequence of "no reception."
"Successively entering the state of non-characteristic" refers to those Pratyekabuddhas and Śrāvakas who realize partial emptiness;
"gradually ascending through the various stages until reaching the state of non-apprehension" refers to Bodhisattvas of the ten stages who realize true emptiness.
Although this state of non-apprehension is one and the same when realized...
Because their stations differ, they are distinguished by the spheres of their samādhis.

This question concerns the Tathāgata’s manifestation of physical forms within buddha-fields to guide sentient beings and various non-Buddhists, as well as those ranging from pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas—
whether in training (śaikṣa) or beyond training (aśaikṣa)— who follow the stages of quiescence, and those bodhisattvas who are worthy to be children of the Buddha.

To thoroughly liberate all beings and cause them to enter *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*, yet not knowing who binds and who is liberated—compared to the initial question of who is pure and who is deluded, this is even more profound. Only when one can chew through and break open these words, "Who binds? Who is liberated?
will one realize that Great Wisdom (*mahāprajñā*) was originally the master of the household. Formerly, the Fourth Patriarch Daoxin was... [text fragment ends]
At the beginning, Hui-xin asked the Third Patriarch fourteen questions, saying, “I pray that the Master, out of compassion, will grant me the Dharma-gate of liberation.
The Patriarch said, “Who has bound you? He replied, “No one has bound me. The Patriarch said, “Why then do you seek liberation? At these words, Hui-xin attained great enlightenment.
What are the stages of dhyāna, and how is it that there are three vehicles? We pray only that you will explain this for us. From what do the dependent originations arise?
What is the agent and what is the action? Why are there various differing explanations? How does growth occur? (In the Tang translation: "How do all existences arise?
What are the formless attainments and the meditative absorption of cessation? What is the cessation of perception? By what cause does one awaken from concentration?
What is it that produces birth? (The Wei version asks: How does the cause produce the fruit? What causes the body to move and remain? (The Wei version asks: By what cause does the body go or stay?
How does manifest discrimination arise? How are the various stages produced? (The Wei version asks: How does one observe what is seen, and how does one enter the various stages?)

The Master replied: "Liberation is precisely reaching the other shore; it belongs to the wisdom of *prajñā*, while meditative concentration (*dhyāna-samādhi*) belongs to contemplative practice (*vipaśyanā-caryā*).
Therefore, there are varying degrees of depth and shallowness. As the subsequent text states: 'There are these four kinds:

the dhyāna practiced by fools, the dhyāna of observing characteristics, the dhyāna of contemplating reality as it is, and the Tathāgata’s pure dhyāna. This inquiry concerns only the dependent origination of the Three Vehicles."
This refers to the dhyāna of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, which designates the dhyāna practiced by outsiders and fools as a "deviant teaching.

Furthermore, because their views regarding the agent and the action, the fruit and the cause, or whether there is a cause or no cause, will inevitably lead to saṃsāra and do not constitute right concentration, it is called a deviant teaching.
This applies even up to the increase of the three realms of existence and the attainment of the formless concentrations.

Although they are bound to the karmic fruits of humans and devas, the extinction concentration (nirodha-samāpatti) realized by those in the five non-returner heavens is mostly inhabited by those who have attained the fourth fruit.

Those dull-witted arhats who do not turn their minds toward enlightenment merely realize the meditative absorption of cessation and dwell in the bliss of tranquility, taking no delight in preaching the Dharma.
Conversely, those great arhats who do turn their minds arise from concentration, awaken, and proceed toward the Mahāyāna.
Because superior causes produce superior fruits, this body attains great mastery over going and staying;
