it manifests its form to preach the Dharma, skillfully discerns the sequence of non-reception, and transcends into the various stages (*bhūmi*). "Going forward" means advancing from one stage to the next;
"maintaining the body" means abiding in one position after another. Being able to realize the *manomayakāya* (mind-made body) in all these ways is the Mahāyāna.

The Bodhisattva’s dhyāna encompasses the dhyānas of these three vehicles; yet, in inquiring into the arising of conditions, one seeks the ultimate source of dhyāna and distinguishes the path by which it is entered—not merely for the sake of providing an explanation. As Chan Master Huangbo Yun said:
"The source of returning has no duality; the true nature of ignorance is itself the Buddha-nature. It exists through expedient means."
Regarding the "many gates": Śrāvakas perceive the arising of ignorance and perceive the cessation of ignorance;
Pratyekabuddhas perceive only the cessation of ignorance but do not perceive its arising, realizing quiescence in every thought-moment.

The Buddhas perceive that sentient beings arise throughout the day yet have no arising, and cease throughout the day yet have no cessation. This absence of arising and cessation is the fruit of the Mahāyāna.
Thus it is said: "The fruit of the Way is full and Bodhi is perfected; the flower blooms and the world arises. This may serve as a treatise on the essentials of Chan for the Three Vehicles;
one must first penetrate through and return to the source before this path can be attained.

Who is it that destroys the three realms of existence? (In the Tang translation: "How can there be a son of the Buddha who is able to destroy the three realms of existence? In what place does he dwell, and what is his body like? (The original says: "Where is he, and what is his body?

To what destination does he go after rebirth? What makes him a most excellent son [of the Buddha]? By what cause does he attain supernormal powers (*abhijñā*), mastery (*vaśitā*), and meditative concentration (*samādhi*)—[the latter] being here called "right concentration"? How is the mind of this samādhi so supreme? Tell me this.
He asked: "It may still be understood that Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have not yet left the triple world; however, how is it that Bodhisattvas transcend the triple world?
Having transcended the triple world, where are they reborn? Having cast off this body, what kind of body do they receive? Upon being reborn, to what place do they go?
And by what cause do they attain supernatural powers to travel through the lands of all Buddhas?"
"Entering the Samādhi of Sovereignty, one enters meditative absorption in the east and arises in the west; a man enters absorption and a woman arises.
Possessing this samādhi and the mind of right concentration, what are its characteristics? I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain this for me.
Later in the text it says: "Whatever dharmas of samādhi and supernormal powers (*ṛddhipāda*) the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva discriminates..."
The conduct of these [bodhisattvas] all abides by the two kinds of supernatural power (*ṛddhi-bala*) of the Tathāgata. The verse says: "Supernatural power, Honored One among Men;
Great vows, all completely purified; Samādhi and empowerment; The first stage and the tenth stage. [The Buddha] answered in detail as follows:
"What is the most supreme samādhi-mind? Explain this truly for me. Truly, the Tathāgata opens his mouth [to speak]."
"It cannot be attained. One day, Shitou asked Layman Pang: "Since you first met this old monk, how have you conducted yourself in your daily life?
The Layman replied, "If you ask about my daily activities, there is no opening for me to speak," and he presented a verse:
"In daily affairs there is nothing different; Only I myself am in accord. At every point there is neither grasping nor rejecting; In every place..."

Dizang said, "How can it compare to sowing fields here to earn food for one's meal? Xiu said, "But what about the three realms?
Dizang said, "What do you call the 'three realms'? Tiantong’s Verse: All aspects of the teaching and its exposition are merely forced constructs;
Transmitted through mouth and ear, they become fragmented and confused. Sowing fields to earn food is an ordinary matter— It is not a matter of being satiated.
The practitioner does not know when the practice is complete; though they clearly know there is nothing to seek, Zhang Liang never prized the rank of marquis.
Having forgotten all artifice, he returned to the company of fish and birds, washing his feet in the autumnal mists and waters of the Canglang River.
This is precisely what it means to shatter the three realms of existence; what body could there be, and where could it be?
What is called the "storehouse" (ālaya), what are the "mind" (manas) and "consciousness" (vijñāna)? What are birth and cessation? What is seeing and returning [to the source]?

What is the nature of the lineage (gotra) and the non-lineage? What is the measure of mind (cittamātra)? [In the Tang translation: What is the arising of various views? What is the relinquishing of various views? What is existence and non-existence? What is merely mind?
What is the establishment of characteristics and the meaning of non-self (anātman)? Why is there no sentient being (sattva)? What is the conventional truth (saṃvṛti)?

It is asked: What is meant by the view of annihilationism and the view of eternalism? How are they prevented from arising? How is it that the characteristics of the Buddha and those of non-Buddhists do not contradict one another?
And what will be the various different schools in future ages? (This asks about the distinctions among the eighteen schools of the future).
Tong said: "This speaks from the perspective of the samādhi-mind up to the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. The nature of the Garbha is one and the same;

when realized, it is called True Suchness (tathatā) and the Ultimate Reality (bhūtakoṭi), termed 'True Nature' (bhūtalakṣaṇa). When not realized, it is the seed of birth-and-death, termed the 'Eight Consciousnesses.

Here, 'intention' refers to the seventh consciousness (manas-vijñāna); 'discrimination' refers to the sixth consciousness (mano-vijñāna); and 'self' refers to the storehouse consciousness (ālaya-vijñāna)."
The seven consciousnesses and the six consciousnesses are like waves arising from the ocean; thus they belong to the realm of birth and extinction.

Once the seeing has ceased, it is like the waves subsiding and returning to the ocean. Those of the Three Vehicles possess the seed-nature (*gotra*), while non-Buddhists and those who have abandoned their resolve (*icchantika*) lack the seed-nature.
Furthermore, there are those of indeterminate seed-nature, as explained in detail in the subsequent text: it is solely mind.

Since the various phenomena manifested by valid cognition and produced from a single mind have already been established as the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*), why is it further stated therein that there are no characteristics of self, person, or sentient being? What is the meaning of this?
If it is said that there are no characteristics of self, person, or sentient being, then everything must be empty; why then is the world further described [as existing]?
If the truths are characterized by the existence of the world and are eternally abiding, does this not contradict the meaning of selflessness and the absence of sentient beings?
Those who establish [existence] fall into conventional truth; those who deny it fall into the view of nihilism.
Both these views of annihilation and permanence are those of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). If the views of annihilation and permanence do not arise, then...
The Buddha and the non-Buddhists are equal and non-dual; why then do their characteristics not contradict one another?

To see that [the self] does not arise is itself the vision of having already returned to and entered the ocean-like nature of the Tathāgatagarbha. Since the nature is non-dual, the teaching is likewise non-dual.
How then can the disciples of future generations, following the various scriptural divisions (*sūtra-piṭaka*), adhere exclusively to either Chan, Vinaya, or Sūtra?
Or is it that they debate various differences? A Tripiṭaka Master asked Dazhu, "Does True Suchness undergo change?
Dazhu replied, "It does. The Tripiṭaka Master said, "Zen Master, you are mistaken. Dazhu retorted, "Does the Tripiṭaka Master possess True Suchness? He replied, "I do.
Dazhu said, "If there were no change, you would certainly be an ordinary monk. How could that be?"

It is not that one who has not heard of the *kalyāṇamitra* can transform the three poisons into the three groups of pure precepts, transform the six consciousnesses into the six supernormal powers, transform afflictions into bodhi, or transform ignorance into great wisdom and true suchness (*tathatā*).
If there were no transformation, the Three Piṭakas would truly be the teachings of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Zang said: "If that is so, then true suchness is..."
[The Master] said, "There is change. Huizhu said, "If you hold that True Suchness undergoes change, you are likewise an outsider.
[The Master] said, "Just now the Chan Master spoke of True Suchness undergoing change, yet now he says it does not change; how can this be correct?
Huizhu said, "If one clearly perceives one's nature, it is like a *maṇi* jewel manifesting colors—this is called 'change'."

One may also speak of non-transformation, and one may also speak of transformation. If those who have not seen their nature hear it said that True Suchness undergoes transformation, they will understand it as undergoing transformation;
if they hear it said that it does not undergo transformation, they will understand it as being unchanging.

The *Zang* says: "Therefore, we know that the Southern School is truly unfathomable. Someone asked: "Regarding the similarities and differences among the three teachings of Confucianism, Buddhism, and Daoism, how are they? [The Master] said: "It is like a pearl."
It is said: "Those of great capacity employ it and it is the same; those of small capacity grasp it and it is different.

In essence, function arises from the single nature, yet the distinctions in the perceptions of the faculties result in the three [vehicles]. Delusion and enlightenment depend on the person; they do not reside in whether the teaching is the same or different.

If one examines the point of Great Pearl’s realization until there is not the slightest doubt or obstruction, then as for the characteristics of the Buddha and the non-Buddhists— [The original text ends here.]
That they are not contradictory is also self-evident.
What is emptiness? By what cause? What is a *kṣaṇa* (the *Abhidharmakośa-bhāṣya* says: the smallest unit of time is called a *kṣaṇa*)? Destruction (*bhaṅga*). [The Wei translation asks:
What is called emptiness? What is the non-abiding of thought? What is birth from the womb? Why does the world not move? By what cause is it like an illusion, a dream, and a *gandharva* city?
O Bhāskara, why are the world, the mirage in the heat, and the moon’s reflection in water spoken of as the factors of awakening (bodhyaṅga) and the limbs of enlightenment (bodhipakṣadharma)?
Why is there turmoil in the lands? And why is there the perception of existence (bhava-darśana)? [In the Tang translation: "For what reason is the perception of all existences seen?"]
Tong said: "Within the Tathāgatagarbha there are both the seeing-part (darśana-bhāga) and the image-part (nimitta-bhāga).

When established by means of the remote image-part, it constitutes the insentient world, undergoing the cycle of arising, abiding, decaying, and emptying without end. [The Master asked: By what cause does this become empty?
How does it arise, abide, and decay in each kṣaṇa? When established by means of the proximate image-part, it constitutes the sentient multitudes."

Beings born from the womb undergo birth and death without ceasing; in the worlds from the third dhyāna downward, sentient beings are subject to flux and transition, whereas in the worlds from the fourth dhyāna upward, sentient beings abide eternally and remain unmoving.
This is a general designation for the names and characteristics of the three realms. For what reason does the Tathāgata regard these three realms of existence as being like an illusion or a dream?
The City of Fragrance (Gandharvanagara) is like a mirage in the heat or the moonlight reflected on water; all its phenomenal aspects are unreal.
Furthermore, it speaks of the seven factors of enlightenment (*saptabodhyaṅga*): mindfulness, investigation of phenomena, diligence, joy, pliancy, concentration, and equanimity;

as well as the thirty-seven factors conducive to enlightenment (*saptatriṃśadbodhipākṣikadharma*), such as the four foundations of mindfulness (*catvāri smṛtyupasthānāni*) and the four... [right efforts].
The Right Abandonments (samyak-prahāṇa) are four; the Bases of Spiritual Power (ṛddhi-pāda) are four; the Faculties (indriya) are five; the Powers (bala) are five;

and the Factors of the Noble Eightfold Path (āryāṣṭāṅga-mārga) together with the preceding Seven Factors of Enlightenment (bodhyaṅga) constitute thirty-seven. These are called Right Knowledge (samyag-jñāna), for they serve to eliminate names, signs, and delusive thoughts.
Furthermore, from what do these delusive thoughts arise? Why are the lands in turmoil and the sensory objects so chaotic?
What is the deluded view of existence? One gives rise to false discrimination, wherein the "view of existence" is the subject that deludes and the "land" is the object that is deluded.
Because the subject and object rely upon one another, they eventually constitute the delusion of views; it is no longer the true essence of suchness.
Yaoshan asked the novice Gao: "I have heard that Chang'an is very chaotic. The novice replied, "In my country, all is peaceful. Yaoshan said with delight: [This is the true peace].
Miaoyan said, "I do not obtain it from reading the scriptures, nor do I obtain it from requesting instruction.
Touzi said, "There are many who do not read the scriptures and do not request instruction; why is it that they do not obtain it?
Miaoyan said, "I do not say they cannot obtain it; it is simply that they themselves are unwilling to accept it. Touzi’s verse says: "Rising and falling..."
Clouds depart and clouds arrive; they have no land and are free from dust.
Upon the summit of Mount Sumeru grows a rootless grass that does not receive the spring breeze, yet its flowers bloom spontaneously.

This shows that while within the world there is arising and ceasing, there is that which is inherently neither born nor extinguished. Why must one necessarily sever delusion before realizing suchness?
How is it that the world is neither arising nor ceasing, like a flower in the sky? How does one awaken to the world? How does one speak of being free from words?

(In the Tang translation: How does one know the world? How is one free from characters? How is it like a flower in the sky—neither arising nor ceasing? For one who is free from false conceptualization, what is it to be like space?
(In the Tang translation: How is it like space? How is one free from discrimination?)
Tong said: "The characteristics of the world are themselves signless; they are all merely provisional designations and false names.

In reality, they are free from the characteristic of words and free from the characteristic of speech. They are like flowers in the sky, which are fundamentally unarisen and now likewise unextinguished.
These characteristics, in their own nature, are identical to suchness and are fundamentally not delusive. To give rise to deluded discrimination within them is itself false conceptualization."

Just as within the essence, one is free from the marks of false conceptualization and is perfectly identical to the great void—neither deficient nor superfluous—so too, when compared to space, one perceives neither the arising of delusion nor the ceasing of delusion. This seeing-part is itself suchness (*tathatā*); it is not a delusion either.
When both subject and object are stilled and both arising and ceasing are extinguished, the nature is fundamentally suchness, serene and eternally abiding; this is the supramundane.
The highest of the high wisdom is what is called the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). To view those lands as chaotic or to give rise to views of existence—how great a disparity there is!
Ultimately, who is it that is free from deluded thoughts? These words are profound and well worth chewing over.
Zen Master Xian of Luoshan first asked Shishuang, "When arising and ceasing do not stop, how is it? Shishuang said, "Directly."
"Must become cold ashes and withered wood; leave behind a single thought for ten thousand years;
the lid must meet the box; be purely clear and free from a single speck. When Shan asked Yanhou, "When arising and ceasing do not stop, what then?
Yanhou gave a shout (*tuo*). At this, Shan attained realization. Tiantong’s verse says: "Cut off the old entanglements, strike..."
Tearing down the fox’s den and stripping away the leopard’s mist to reveal its true markings; the dragon mounts the thunder to transform its bones.
Startlingly, it arises and extinguishes all confusion—what thing is this that can penetrate and remove [delusion]? The nun was originally a woman.

How many kinds of *yathābhūta* (reality as it is) are there? How many *pāramitās* are there? By what cause does the mind transcend the stages (*bhūmis*)? Who reaches the state of non-apprehension (*anupalambha*)?

(The Tang translation says: "What are the successive stages? How does one attain the shadowless? What are the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*)? How is the flame purified? How many kinds of wisdom (*jñāna*) are there? How many types of precepts (*śīla*) are there? What is the nature of sentient beings (*sattva-dhātu*)?

Tong said: "True Suchness (tathatā), the Dharma-realm (dharmadhātu), the nature of phenomena (dharmatā), the non-falsehood, the non-alteration, the equality, the departure from birth, the fixed nature of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā), the abiding of phenomena (dharmaniyāmatā), the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi), the realm of empty space (ākāśadhātu), and the inconceivable realm—these are unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma).
Furthermore, there are bodhi, nirvāṇa, true suchness, Buddha-nature, the pure white consciousness, emptiness, and the Tathāgatagarbha."
The Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*) is the general fruit of the seven stages and is never separate from the *tathatā* (suchness) and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Generosity, ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom constitute the six *pāramitās*. In the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*, further expedient means, vows, powers, and wisdom constitute the ten *pāramitās*.

Regarding the ten stages (*bhūmis*): the first is the Joyful (*pramuditā*), the second is the Stainless (*vimalā*), the third is the Luminous (*prabhākārī*), and the fourth is the Radiant (*arciṣmatī*).

The stages are: 1) The Ground of Joy, 2) The Ground of Purity, 3) The Ground of Radiance, 4) The Ground of Blazing Wisdom, 5) The Difficult to Conquer, 6) The Manifest, 7) The Far-Reaching, 8) The Immovable, 9) The Ground of Excellent Wisdom, and 10) the Cloud of Dharma. From the first ground through the seventh, one accomplishes the wisdom of effortful application;
from the eighth to the tenth ground, one accomplishes practice that is effortless. Having transcended these ten grounds and reached the state of non-apprehension, there is no further objective realm.
Having first attained the emptiness of persons and then attained the emptiness of phenomena, one realizes the two kinds of selflessness.

Having first purified the afflictive hindrances and then purified the cognitive hindrances, these are called the purification of the two hindrances. However, the subtle ignorance regarding the cognizable (*jñeyāvaraṇa-mūḍhi*) and the extremely subtle ignorance regarding the cognizable are particularly difficult to uproot; nothing but the true wisdom of *prajñā* can destroy them. This wisdom has many names, namely:

The four wisdoms are said to comprise ten wisdoms; furthermore, there are the subsequently attained wisdom (*pṛṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*), the teacherless wisdom (*aśaikṣa-jñāna*), and so forth, all of which are ultimately not outside the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).

As for the precepts, there are the five precepts, the eight precepts, up to the two hundred and fifty precepts for *bhikṣus*, and when the *bhikṣuṇīs* add their own, they constitute five hundred prohibitions.
All of these are intended to restrain the bodily, verbal, and mental karma of sentient beings.
"Precepts give rise to concentration, and from concentration arises wisdom; these are called the three untainted trainings (*trīṇi śikṣāṇi anāsravāṇi*).

Within them lies right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*). Formerly, the Fourth Patriarch said to Niu-tou Rong: "The hundreds of thousands of Dharma gates all return to the single square inch [of the mind].
The wondrous virtues as numerous as the sands of the Ganges are all gathered within the source of the mind. All gates of precept, concentration, wisdom, and supernormal powers..."
All transformations are fully present within yourself, never departing from your own mind. All afflictions and karmic obstructions are originally empty and still;
all causes and effects are like dreams and illusions. There is no triple world from which to escape, and no Bodhi to be attained.
Humans and non-humans are equal in their essential nature. The Great Way is vast and open, transcending thought and beyond deliberation. Such is...
Dharma, you have now already attained everything and lack nothing; how does this differ from that of a Buddha? There is no other dharma apart from this.
You need only allow the mind to be free and at ease: do not perform contemplative practices, nor clear the mind; do not give rise to greed or anger, nor harbor anxiety or worry.
Be vast and unimpeded, moving freely in all directions, neither performing any good deeds nor committing any evil deeds, whether walking or staying.
Whether sitting or reclining, whatever one encounters through the senses or meets with conditions, it is all the wondrous function of the Buddha;
because it is joyful and free from sorrow, it is called the "Buddha. Within the Gate of the Patriarchs, there is such directness and simplicity, unbound by any phenomena.
The wise should realize this for themselves beyond words.

Who gives rise to the various natures of jewels, such as mani-gems and pearls? Who gives rise to all languages, the various natures of sentient beings, the fields of knowledge (*vidyāsthāna*), and the arts and crafts? By whom are these revealed?
Tong said: "The three realms are mind-only; both the sentient and the insentient are objects within the wondrously luminous true mind.
All transformations that arise are manifestations of the true mind. According to Mahāmati’s inquiry, nothing exists outside the names and marks of the three realms.
How could one not know that the nature of gold, silver, and mani-jewels results from their being firm, luminous, and immovable?"
Do you not know that all languages and written characters are formed through the conjunction of false conceptualizations, turning upon the throat, lips, tongue, teeth, gums, and cheeks?
The fields of knowledge and arts are precisely the five vidyās: first, śabdavidyā, which refers to philology and lexicography;

second, śilpakarmasthānavidyā, which refers to the arts and crafts; third, cikitsāvidyā, the science of medicine; fourth, hetuvidyā, which refers to the investigation and determination of the heterodox and the orthodox; and fifth...
"Inner illumination" refers to the clarity regarding cause and effect within the Buddha Vehicle; the former three are external arts, while the latter two are internal teachings.
How could one not know that worldly conventional language is entirely non-contradictory with the true mark (*dharmatā*)?
Yet, when it is asked "by whom is this revealed?", it is intended to point directly to the ultimate, manifest state of reality. When Dazhu of Yuezhou first visited Mazu...
The Patriarch asked, "Where have you come from? He replied, "From Dàyún Monastery in Yuèzhōu. The Patriarch said, "What do you intend to seek by coming here?
He replied, "I have come to seek the Buddha-dharma. The Patriarch said, "In this place of mine, there is not a single thing; what Buddha-dharma is there to seek?
You possess your own precious treasury, yet you fail to look after it and instead wander away, abandoning your home. What is this? He asked, "Which one is that?"
The Patriarch Huimeng said, "The one who is questioning me right now is your own treasure-trove, fully complete with nothing lacking;
you have mastery over its use, so why would you seek it elsewhere? The pearl is recognized within these words as your own original mind, which does not depend on intellectual cognition.
He leaped for joy and prostrated in gratitude. He served the Master for six years, after which his preceptor grew old.

He immediately returned to serve his parents, thereafter concealing his traces and hiding his capacities while outwardly appearing dull and slow-witted. He himself composed the *One-Scroll Treatise on the Essential Gate for Entering the Way through Sudden Enlightenment*.
His dharma-nephew Xuanyan secretly took it out to the region beyond the Yangtze River to present it to Mazu.

Upon finishing its review, Mazu addressed the assembly, saying: "In Yuezhou there is a Great Pearl—perfectly round and bright, its light penetrating freely, existing in a state of total lack of obstruction."
If one awakens to this jewel, then gold, silver, and *maṇi* gems are not worth calling treasures;
as for worldly arts and crafts, how could they even be mentioned between one's teeth?
How many types of *gāthā* are there? How many types of long verses and short phrases constitute them? What is called a *śāstra*?
(The Tang translation says: "The principles differ in several ways; the explanations have several distinctions. He replied:
"Gāthā" is translated here as "recitation," which refers to verse. There are those that stand alone and those that are in stanzas;
they may be long passages or short phrases, differing in many ways, yet none are not sounds expounding the Dharma, and thus they constitute the Way itself.
The value of what is established by principle lies in its personal practice; those who discourse on this principle merely engage in verbal explanation.
Fayen ascended the hall and cited an ancient saying: "I have one word that pervades heaven and earth.
If people do not understand it, then as for these green waters and blue mountains—what is this 'one word'? [He asked: "What is this 'one word'?"
To understand the speech of the ancients, one must first be thoroughly proficient; if you merely employ words to name words, there will be no point of realization.

This is because only by investigating the very root of all phenomena does one finally comprehend a single word—not a mere word or half-sentence understood through intellectual deliberation, but a "single word" where the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases.
To extinguish the beginning and arrive at the realm of the ancients is not merely closing one's eyes and concealing one's essence while seeing nothing in the dark;
this is called the "severance of the path of words. Do not misunderstand this! The Buddha-dharma is not such a principle. Do you wish to understand it?
Even if one were to speak for kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, there would never have been half a word that reached you, O Venerable Ones.
Though not spoken throughout kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, not even a single half-phrase has ever been lacking; you must understand this thoroughly before it will avail.
If you deliberate upon names and words in such a manner, you will merely exhaust your mental and physical strength to no purpose.
To provide mutual verification for all the venerable elders, those of later generations and beginners must quickly investigate this. I have stood long; take care and understand!
Only when one attains the lineage of the Dharma-eye discourse can one reach authentic realization;
it is not merely a matter of making a livelihood through words and arguments.
How do food and drink arise, and how do various desires arise? What is meant by the names "wheel-turning king" and "lesser king"?
What are the various kinds of devas who protect the nation? What are those called terrestrial constellations, as well as the sun and moon?

The general answer is: because sentient beings subsist by means of four kinds of nutriment, there is no craving more intense than that for food; and it is from this that killing, stealing, and sexual misconduct all arise.
According to the Āgamas, at the beginning of the kalpa, sentient beings all consumed "earth-fat" (pṛthivī-parpaṭaka) and [the essence of] the fields.
When the people of China and America were hungry, they ate; when full, they stopped. Later, some individuals took more than their share, leading to conflict and competition.
Consequently, landowners were established to govern them; these are called *kṣatriyas*, and they are designated as kings. These are merely minor kings who protect wealth.
If one becomes a Wheel-Turning Sage King (*cakravartin rāja*), he possesses the seven treasures and travels through the four continents by flight to transform sentient beings.
To guide sentient beings and instruct them in the methods of protection, there is nothing greater than practicing the ten paths of wholesome action (*daśakuśalakarmapatha*).
If one can practice these ten wholesome actions, one will surely be reborn in the heavens.
Whether it be among the Four Heavenly Kings, or likewise in the Trāyastriṃśa, Tuṣita, the four dhyāna heavens, or the four formless realms, their attachment to desire [is progressively diminished].

The more they diminish [their materiality], the higher their position becomes and the further they depart from the earth. The earth is composed of the great elements (mahābhūta) and is ultimately subject to transformation and decay;
whereas the stars, constellations, sun, and moon are produced by the power of karma (*karman*). When heaven and earth first opened, these bodies were immediately attached to the heavens.
The *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* states that all eighty deities are formed from this brilliant radiance due to the fundamental cause of obstructive conceptualization (*saṃjñā*).
Furthermore, those at the very bottom must rely on the illumination of the sun, moon, and stars;
whereas those above the various heavens do not depend on the power of these three luminaries—these are all designations for realms from the Desire Realm upward. A monk asked Baizhang:
"Nowadays, all śramaṇas say, 'I rely on the Buddha's teachings to study one sutra, one śāstra, one dhyāna, and one vinaya.'"

[The questioner] asked: "If one knows the oneness and understands the integration [of practice], is it possible to receive the fourfold offerings of a donor and thereby eliminate [afflictions]? Dazhu said:

"Simply, as you now apply illumination and function—whether it be a single sound, a single color, a single fragrance, or a single flavor—at every single object among all phenomena, whether existent or non-existent, there is not even a speck of dust of grasping or defilement;
nor do you dwell upon that absence of grasping or defilement, for there is neither grasping nor defilement."
One who does not rely on or dwell in intellectual understanding can digest even ten thousand taels of gold daily; yet, if at this very moment,
when examining all phenomena of existence and non-existence at the gates of the six sense faculties, there is even a hair’s breadth of craving that cannot be scraped away or eliminated—
down to the point where one begs from a donor for a single grain of rice or a single thread of silk— [then such a person cannot digest it].
Each one who wears fur and horns, pulling plows and bearing heavy loads, must repay their debts before they can be considered free;
for the Buddha is one who is unattached, one who seeks nothing, and one who relies on nothing. Now, those who wave about and greedily seek the Buddha have all turned their backs upon him.
The *Kāśyapa Sūtra* says: "First, there is the desire to seek to see future Buddhas; second, there is the desire to seek to turn [the wheel of Dharma]..."

The Wheel-Turning King seeks the great clans of the Kṣatriyas; the four [kings] seek the great clans of the Brāhmaṇas, and so on, up to those who, weary of birth and death, seek Nirvāṇa—such evil desires must first be severed.
At present, any grasping, defilement, or stirring thought is entirely termed an evil desire; it all belongs to the six heavens and is under the jurisdiction of Pāpīyān. Alas! How can this be?
Can one fail to be startled and wakefully mindful when encountering even minor matters of food and drink or slight thoughts of sensual desire?
How many kinds of disciples does one who practices for liberation have, and how many kinds of teachers (ācārya—here translated as *guifanshi*) are there?

Furthermore, how many kinds of Buddhas are there, and how many kinds of births (in the Tang language, the various *jātaka* stories of the Tathāgata) are there? Likewise, how many kinds of Māras are there?
As for the various non-Buddhist practitioners (*tīrthika*), how many kinds of them are there?

The general answer is that while liberation (*vimukti*) is the state of one beyond training (*aśaikṣa*), the practices of those still in training (*śaikṣa*)—such as the śrāvaka disciples—differ in manifold ways, including their wisdom, supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), erudition, and preaching of the Dharma;
these are too numerous to enumerate individually. Furthermore, the Buddha possesses [the knowledge] of the past.
In the present and the future, those who currently preach the Dharma throughout the ten directions each perform various kinds of Buddha-works;
how much more so, then, the deeds performed in his previous lives and former existences—how could they ever be fully recounted?

As for the heavenly demons (*deva-māra*) and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who oppose and contradict the True Dharma, there are approximately ninety-six types of such non-Buddhists, of which twenty or so are listed hereafter.

He thoroughly understood that the various types of nirvana were merely false interpretations; that the Māra Pāpīyas dwells only in the Heaven of Making Use of Others' Transformations, while other species are exceedingly numerous;
and that each of these has made great vows to protect the True Dharma. Huangbo said to Pei Xiu:
"Since Master Bodhidharma arrived in this land, he has spoken only of the One Mind and transmitted only the One Dharma. He transmitted Buddha-to-Buddha and did not speak [of anything else]."
Other Buddhas transmit the Dharma through the Dharma and do not speak of other dharmas;
this Dharma is the ineffable Dharma, and this Buddha is the Buddha who cannot be grasped. This is precisely the fundamentally pure mind. Only this one reality is true;
the other two are not real. Prajñā is wisdom; this wisdom is the formless original mind. Ordinary people do not...

To follow the path while merely indulging the six sense-faculties leads to wandering in the six realms of existence. A practitioner of the Way who, in a single thought-moment, calculates birth and death falls into the path of Māra;
in a single thought-moment, they give rise to various views and fall into the path of externalists. To perceive the existence of rebirth and its cessation falls into the path of the Śrāvaka;
to see no existence of birth but only the existence of cessation falls into the path of the Pratyekabuddha. This is the fundamental nature of dharmas.
Neither arising now nor ceasing, not giving rise to the two views, neither rejoicing nor loathing any phenomena—this is solely the single mind;
only then does one attain the Buddha-vehicle. Ordinary people all pursue objects with their minds, and thus their minds give rise to joy and aversion.
If one wishes to be without objects, one should forget the mind. When the mind is forgotten, the objects become empty; when objects are empty, the mind is empty.
If one does not forget the mind while seeking its cessation, yet merely attempts to eliminate objects, those objects cannot be eliminated; it only serves to increase confusion and turmoil.
Therefore, all phenomena are but the mind, and the mind itself is unattainable—what more is there to seek? These are the words of true liberation from Huangbo;
upon awakening to them, one immediately ascends to the stage of Buddhahood, and the various heterodoxies of demons and outsiders can no longer cause delusion.

What are the natures and what are the minds, and how many distinct types of each are there? (The Tang translation reads: "How many varieties of nature are there, and how many distinctions of mind are there?

What is the measure of conventional designation? (The Tang translation reads: "In what sense is it merely a provisional designation? I pray that the Most Victorious One will explain: what are space, wind, and clouds? And what is mindfulness and intelligence?
Tong said: "Mind and nature are one and the same. According to the later text, there are seven kinds of self-nature and seven kinds of the ultimate mind (*paramārtha-citta*).
It explains that the three realms are like an illusion, and all provisional establishments are merely conventional names (*prajñapti*).
To explain this in detail: since this mind and nature are fundamentally one, how can wind and clouds arise within emptiness? Are they not insentient?
There are such transformations as these. How does intelligence arise within mindfulness?

Sentient beings possess such wisdom that they investigate the origins from which names, marks, and delusive thoughts (*vikalpa*) arise. Later, in the passage concerning dependent origination giving rise to delusive thoughts, this is also answered in detail.
A monk asked Linji, "What is the state where mind and mind are not different? Linji [replied].
To say that you intend to ask [about this] is already mistaken. Nature and characteristics are distinct; followers of the Way, do not err.
All phenomena, both mundane and supramundane, lack self-nature and lack the nature of arising; they possess nothing but empty names, and these names are themselves empty.
To recognize those provisional names as real is a great error. Even if such things exist, they are all merely transformations based on conditions.
Within the objective realm, there is the Bodhi, the Nirvana, the Liberation, the Three Bodies, the correspondence of object and wisdom, the Bodhisattvas, the Buddhas, and you yourself;

yet what thing do you seek within these transformed lands? According to Linji’s insight, even the seven self-natures and the seven primary meanings are merely provisional designations of the mind—how much more so are wind and clouds?
How much less could the intelligent have any inherent nature (svabhāva) that can be apprehended?
What constitutes a forest and trees? What constitutes creeping vines and grasses? What are elephants, horses, and deer?
How are they captured? What is base and lowly? By what cause is one base and lowly? What is meant by the six seasonal divisions? And what is an icchantika?
(Regarding this, it is said that faith is not possessed. How are men, women, and those of indeterminate gender born?

How do they practice and fall away? How do they practice and arise? (In two translations, "practice" is rendered as "progress. By what dharma does the Meditation Master establish [the path], and for what kind of person? (The Tang version says: "How many types of *yogācāra* practitioners are there who cause people to dwell therein?

The Wei version says: "By teaching what kind of person to practice, and causing them to dwell in what dharma? What are the characteristics and what are the likenesses of sentient beings as they are born into the various realms of existence? How is it so?
What is the cause for wealth, and by what cause does one attain great abundance? What is the Śākya clan, and by what cause do the Śākyas exist?

From Mount Sumeru down to the heavens and the asuras, the entirety of his domain is exhausted therein. Furthermore, when one minutely enumerates the liberations, supernormal powers, factors of enlightenment, and the path constituents—such as the dharma of the Buddha-sons regarding meditative absorption and the attainment of cessation—as well as the conceptualizations of the dharmas of the pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas."
The two views of conceptualization and discrimination are like the teachings of non-Buddhists;
even down to the lands of icchantikas where the realm is desolate and chaotic, these constitute the lineage of ordinary beings, yet there is no dharma that is not fully detailed therein.

If one can transform consciousness into wisdom, one becomes one with the Buddha and reaches the other shore. It is only sentient beings who are deluded by consciousness, regarding all objects as [real].
It appears to exist, yet in reality it does not; it is merely because sentient beings are attached to signs (*nimitta*).
Internally there is a mind that grasps, and externally there is an object that is grasped—just as one who captures birds or beasts uses a net for their own sake.
Such analogies are the method of universal application, meaning that both the agent and the action are all attachments to signs, like entering [a net].

Amidst the various forests, one captures birds and beasts; greedily pursuing external objects, one is deluded regarding reality and fails to know the principle of truth, which is simply the single mind.
The manifestations of one's own mind are originally without objective realms and originally do not exist as such.

Since delusion has been thoroughly penetrated, both subject and object are simultaneously transcended; therefore, it is said that "this does not exist. This is precisely the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
In the various stages (*bhūmi*), there is originally a sequential progression from stage to stage; that this is here called "without sequence" refers specifically to the Sudden Teaching (*tunmen*).
The previous question, "How are the various stages produced?"—answering by stating that one enters from the *nirodhasamāpatti*—refers to the gradual method (*jienfa*).
The subsequent question, "How does one traverse the various stages?"—answering by stating that one realizes them through suchness (*yathābhūta*)—refers to the sudden method.

Because one transcends all stages (*bhūmi*), there is no mutual arrival; having realized that the mind-only (*cittamātra*) is non-manifesting, one sees all marks as non-marks, which is precisely seeing the Tathāgata.
Thus, one attains the designation of "transformation of the basis" (*āśrayaparāvṛtti*):
namely, being able to transform afflictions into bodhi and transform birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) into nirvāṇa. Although one dwells amidst the hundred transformations of birth-and-death, yet...
There is nothing that it does not encompass; what is called "neither arising nor ceasing" is sovereign freedom (*svatantra*).

From the Buddha’s various *pāramitās* up to this point, the essential outline of the most secret among the five sciences (*pañcavidyāsthāna*), namely the inner science (*adhyātma-vidyā*), has been largely prepared.
As for the other fields of knowledge—medical prescriptions, arts, crafts, and technical skills—though they belong to worldly external disciplines, if one skillfully integrates them...
All of these are metaphors for the *siddhānta* (established doctrine) achieved through causes. A monk asked Huangbo, "What is diligence?
Huangbo replied, "The non-arising of body and mind is called the foremost, most steadfast diligence.
As soon as the mind arises to seek outwardly, one is like King Kali who loves hunting; when the mind does not wander outward, one is the Immortal of Forbearance."
When both body and mind are absent in a person, that is the Buddha-way. Furthermore, a monk asked, "In the past, when King Kali cut and mangled my body, who was it?
Huangbo said, "The immortal was your own mind; King Kali was merely seeking something.
He did not maintain his royal throne—this is called 'craving for gain. Now, when students do not accumulate merit or cultivate virtue, they see..."
If one were to practice in this way, how would it differ from King Kali? When seeing forms, he destroyed the seer’s eyes;
when hearing sounds, he destroyed the seer’s ears; and even when perceiving through cognition, it was likewise so.
To call this "being dismembered limb by limb" is incorrect; for when the seer was practicing patience, there should have been no further dismembering limb by limb.
"You cannot be patient with one mind while being impatient with another. Huangbo said, "Your view of non-arising and your interpretation of patience as liberation are both injuries.
When the immortal was being cut, did he know the pain? He asked again, "In this state, there is no one who experiences;
who is it that feels the pain? Huangbo said, "Since you do not feel pain, come forth!"
"What is there to seek?"—such phrases are also examples of *hetu-siddhānta* (establishment through cause).
When one examines [these], examples such as gold, silver, *maṇi* jewels, and chaotic lands all belong to the category of metaphors; they are collectively termed the "method of universal bestowal."
How many atoms (*paramāṇu*) are there in the various mountains, Mount Sumeru, the earth, the great oceans, the sun and moon, and the bodies of sentient beings—low, middle, and high?

How many *dhanus* (bows) are there in each atom of every *kṣetra* (field)? [Note: Two *hasta* (cubits) make one *dhanus*; four *dhanus* make one *dhanus* (bow); five *dhanus* make one *daśa* (ten-cubit measure, equivalent to ten *hasta*);

twenty *daśa* make one *krośa* (village-measure, here called *xi*, meaning ten *li*); eighty *krośa* make one *krośa* (here called *ju-lu-she*, equivalent to eight *krośa*); eight *krośa* make one *yojana*. Half a *yojana*... [Note: This section provides the standard Indian measurement conversions used in Buddhist cosmology. ...two half-*yojanas* (this second half-...)

Ten *li* (one *yojana*; these forty *li* are what the Tang dynasty called one *zhu-bu*, reaching ten *li*, twenty *li*, and forty *li*). Seven *paramāṇus* (extremely minute particles) constitute one window-dust particle (*vātāyanaraja*).

Seven window-dust particles constitute one rabbit-hair-tip dust particle (*śaśaraja*). Seven rabbit-hair-tip dust particles constitute one sheep-hair-tip dust particle (*aurabhraraja*). Seven sheep-hair-tip dust particles constitute one cow-hair-tip dust particle (*goraraja*). Seven cow-hair-tip dust particles constitute one nit (*yūka*).

Seven nits constitute one louse (*likṣā*). Seven lice constitute one mustard seed (*sarṣapa*). Seven mustard seeds constitute one large barley grain (*yava*). Seven large barley grains constitute one finger-joint (*aṅguliparvan*). Seven finger-joints constitute half a foot (*vitasti*). Two and a half feet constitute one foot (*hasta*).
*Prastha* (one *śīrṣaka*) is approximately one *dōng*; *āḍhaka* (one *dou*) is approximately one *du*; *droṇa* (one *hu*) is ten *du*;

*lakṣa* (ten thousand) and *koṭi* (one hundred million)—the Tang translation for *prastha* is "half a *dōng*"; the Tang translation for *āḍhaka* is "half a *dou*"; the Tang translation for *droṇa* is "one *hu*" and "ten *hu*";
the Tang translation for *lakṣa* is "one hundred thousand"—these various translations differ slightly. This continues up to *vibhūta* (one trillion), each having its own [measure].
How many [units]—that is, how many barley grains—are there in each? How many *aṇu* (atoms) are called one *sarṣapa* (mustard seed)?
How many *sarṣapa* are called one *liptika* (grass-seed)? How many *liptika* are there in a *māṣa*? [The phrase "how many *māṣa* are there in a *dhāna*" is a redundant interpolation.
Furthermore, how many *liptika* constitute a *māṣa-dhāna* (bean)? And how many *māṣa-dhāna* are called one *dhara*?
How many *nārā* (zhūyě) make one *nārā*? How many *nārā* make one *kāliṣaṇa* (liǎng)? How many *kāliṣaṇa* constitute one *pala* (jīn; translated in the Tang as "mustard seed")?

How many atoms (*paramāṇu*) make one mustard seed? How many mustard seeds make one grain of grass? How many grains of grass make one bean? How many beans make one *zhu*? How many *zhu* make one *liang*? How many *liang* make one *jin*?
As for the accumulation of these quantities, how many *pāramitā-merus* (Mount Sumerus) are there? These are matters that should be requested [of the Buddha]; why must you ask?

Regarding other matters—[the Wei translation says: "In this sequence, etc., how many *jin* (weights) make up Mount Sumeru? The Buddha said: "Why do you not now ask me this? How many [atoms] are there in the bodies of the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, Buddhas, and the Sons of the Victorious One (*jina-putra*) respectively?
Why do you not ask this: how many *aṇus* (atoms) are in this flame; how many *aṇus* are in the wind; how many *aṇus* are in each sense organ (*indriya*);

how many *aṇus* are in the pores; and how many are in the eyebrows? [The Tang translation says: "How many particles are there in fire and wind respectively? How many are in each sense organ? And how many are in the eyebrows?"]
[Question: How many atoms (*paramāṇu*) compose each of the pores? [Answer:
Generally speaking, from the various mountains and Mount Sumeru down to the earth, all of this has not been asked by Mahāmati. Within the three realms (*tridhātu*), there are only two dharmas:
form (*rūpa*) and emptiness (*śūnyatā*). Form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form. Having realized the signless (*animitta*)...
If one merely grasps the principle without exhausting the function of its characteristics, how does it differ from inert emptiness?

Thus, from a minute particle through calculation up to Mount Sumeru, and again from Mount Sumeru dispersing back into minute particles—the quantities, magnitudes, and weights within this interval can only be fully fathomed by Buddha after Buddha;
for the Dharma-body of all Buddhas pervades the entire realm of sand-grains.
These accumulated characteristics, taken as a whole, do not depart from within the Dharmakāya; how could there be anything therein that is unknown?

As for the differences in the magnitude of the Saṃbhogakāya among lower, middle, and superior sentient beings, as well as among Buddhas and the most excellent sons [of the Buddha], these all arise from being composed of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
How many atoms (*paramāṇu*) of each of the two great elements—fire and wind—are there? And how many atoms of the earth element are there in the sense organs and pores?
By knowing the quantity of the water element within one's own body, one can know the quantity of the waters of the great ocean;
by knowing the quantity of the fire and wind elements within one's own body, one can know the magnitude of the sun and moon;
and by knowing the number of sense faculties and pores within one's own body, one can know the extent of the earth and the various mountains. Furthermore—
That which is encountered by the six faculties within the six sense objects is none other than "dust" (viṣaya).
This refers specifically to the dust of form (*rūpa-viṣaya*) to precisely manifest the principle that form and emptiness are non-dual;

yet, if one investigates further, the clarity and turbidity, the high and low of the dust of sound (*śabda-viṣaya*) are beyond measure, as are the refinement and coarseness, the distance and proximity of the dust of fragrance (*gandha-viṣaya*), and the sourness [and other qualities] of the dust of taste (*rasa-viṣaya*).
The saltiness, bitterness, and blandness are inexhaustible; the favorability or unfavorability of the objects of touch, and the resulting suffering or pleasure, are inexhaustible;
the goodness, evil, right, and wrong of the objects of mind (dharmas) are inexhaustible.
Therefore, it is by exhausting the functions of all phenomena that the essence which is without form can be recognized. How could there be something else apart from these phenomena?
This refers to one who is "signless" (animitta): for such a person, both the continuity of signs and their lack of continuity are entirely manifestations of one's own mind.
To say that the "measure of mind" (cittamātra) does not exist is truly what is meant by penetrating the signless.
As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states, the Buddha told Ānanda: "Observe the nature of earth: coarse it is the great earth; subtle it is minute dust, down to the ultimate atom (*paramāṇu*)."
If one analyzes dust to its ultimate limit of subtle form, it is composed of seven parts; if one further analyzes the *paramāṇu* (the infinitesimal), it is simply the nature of actual emptiness.
Wansong should cite the *Xinxin Ming*: "The extremely small is identical to the great, forgetting and transcending all boundaries;
the extremely great is identical to the small, with no visible periphery. If someone were to ask what thing in the world is the greatest, one should say: "Reality."
Why is emptiness said to be "the great being the same as the small"? Because its boundaries and manifestations are not seen.

Or, if someone asks, "What is the smallest thing in the world? one should say, "True Emptiness. Why? Because the extremely small is the same as the great, having forgotten and transcended all realms of experience.
A monk asked Huangbo, "What is it to transcend the three realms? Huangbo replied, "Do not contemplate good or evil at all."
At that very place, one emerges from the three realms. The Tathāgata appears in the world to destroy the three existences (*tribhava*).
If all mental activity is absent, the three realms do not exist either. It is like a single mote of dust divided into a hundred parts:
ninety-nine parts are non-existent, while one part remains existent. The Mahāyāna cannot surpass this; only when even that one part is entirely non-existent does the Mahāyāna truly begin.
It surpasses the teachings of all venerable elders regarding the true meaning of signlessness (*animitta*), and it also employs analogies drawn from even a single atom.
O King, Sovereign Lord of Wealth and Universal Monarch (*cakravartin*): how does a king protect? How is he liberated?
This is explained extensively and in prose (the Chinese term "yúan yún" refers to long-form prose). Regarding what you have asked concerning the various desires and dispositions of sentient beings:
What are the various foods and drinks? What is the Forest of Men and Women? What is the Mountain of Solidity?

What is the analogy of the wild deer’s thirst (a mirage) like an illusion or a dream? What is the Mountain Adorned by Celestial Sages and Gandharvas (in the Tang translation: "What are the various wondrous mountains adorned by sages and gandharvas")?
Where does liberation go? Who is bound and who is liberated? What are the realms of dhyāna, transformations, and the external world?
What is the path? What is action without cause? What is action with cause? What is action both with and without cause, and what is that which is neither with nor without cause?
(These four propositions are added here to supplement the differing views mentioned above. What is that which has already ceased after manifesting? How are all perceptions purified?

How do all perceptions transform, and how do all activities transform? (The purification of mindfulness increases according to such a sequence. How are all conceptualizations severed? How does samādhi arise?
Who is it that destroys the three realms of existence? Where, by what body, and in what manner? How is it that there are no sentient beings, yet one speaks of a self?

How is it that worldly convention speaks [of such things]? I pray you, explain these extensively. What are the characteristics of that which is asked about, and what is the nature of that which is asked about as "not-self"?
What is the embryonic matrix (*garbha*), and what are the various different bodies? What are the views of annihilationism and eternalism? What is it?

How is the mind established in meditative concentration, and what are the expressions and various knowledges? How do the sons of the Buddha, who possess the lineage of ethical discipline, achieve their state?

What is the nature of the teacher and the disciple, and how do these various sentient beings come to be? Furthermore, what constitutes food and drink (whereas "food and drink" previously referred to sensual desire, here it refers to eating meat)?
What is the clever contrivance of Māra (referring to the types of clever Māras and the extent of their contrivances)? And what are the trees and climbing vines?
(Questioned by the Son of the Most Victorious One regarding the various lands: What is this transformation of the land?
How does the immortal practice long asceticism? What constitutes a noble clan? From which teacher does one receive instruction? What is meant by ugliness?

How does a person practice in the desire realm yet fail to awaken to Akaniṣṭha (the Heaven of Ultimate Form)? What is mundane supernatural power (*laukika-abhijñā*)? (The aforementioned mundane discourse refers to conventional truth.)

The five supernormal powers are collectively indicated as not departing from the mundane; therefore, they are not supramundane. What is a bhikṣu? What is a transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*)? What is a recompense Buddha (*vipāka-buddha*)?
What is a *tathatā*-Buddha (the Buddha of the wisdom of equality)? [This briefly enumerates the four equalities, all of which are fully possessed.

What is the Sangha? Son of the Buddha, such questions are as follows: there are seven [categories] concerning the lute, the waist-drum, the flower-adorned land, the separation from light, and the mind-ground.
All that has been asked is according to reality; this and other matters are what many sons of the Buddha should inquire about.

Each point corresponds to its respective characteristic, being free from all views and errors, and transcending verbal expression. I shall now reveal them and establish the phrases in their proper order.
Sons of the Buddha, listen attentively: these one hundred and eight phrases are as taught by all the Buddhas.
The Master said: "This was the World-Honored One’s general response to the questions. If one examines it closely, however, there are indeed specific points;

in essence, they do not go beyond the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*), the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), the middle way truth (*madhyamā-pratipad-satya*), and the truth of the primary meaning (*paramārtha-satya*). Therefore, he concludes by saying:
'There are no words for the *siddhāntas*; I shall now reveal them. First, he mentions the Wheel-Turning King and the minor kings who protect sentient beings."

The Dharma does not go beyond extensively explaining the ten wholesome precepts and various contemplations on desire, observing the groves of men and women to awaken to impermanence, suffering, emptiness, and that all things are like illusions and dreams; this is the path of practice for liberation.
Next, it raises the question of where liberation leads and elucidates the realms of dhyāna in detail, such as the views of existence and non-existence held by non-Buddhists.
The views of both existence and non-existence, as well as the view of neither existence nor non-existence, are the meditations practiced by fools; these are all conventional truths (*saṃvṛti-satya*).

If one purifies all mental constructions (*vitarka*), severs all perceptions (*saṃjñā*), and manifests the entry into samādhi where [perceptions] have already ceased, thereby destroying the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*), this is the meditation on the characteristics of analytical observation (*pratyavekṣaṇa-lakṣaṇa-dhyāna*);
this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). It reaches the state where there are no sentient beings, yet it speaks of a self (*ātman*) and [the aggregates].
The meaning of "non-self" is to remain far removed from the two views of eternalism and nihilism so that the mind attains concentration.

Based on this, one preaches the Dharma for the sake of the multitude, whether through the various arrangements of the categories of precepts and natures, or the prohibition against eating meat. One does not abandon the complexities of conventional discourse, yet the characteristics of the ultimate and the conventional do not conflict;
they are non-dual. This is the meditation that accords with reality by taking suchness as its object; it is the Middle Way Truth. At the end, he cites an analogy.
Having come to this land to transform beings over many kalpas, he formerly practiced asceticism as a rishi;
now, having descended into the Gautama clan, he has truly realized bodhi in the Akaniṣṭha Heaven, being named the Bodhisattva Guoming (Rakṣaprajñā).

When he first practiced asceticism as a rishi, he did not go beyond attaining mundane supernatural powers (*abhijñā*); it was only upon manifesting in the body of a bhikṣu that he finally realized the three [knowledges].
The body possesses four wisdoms and is named the Tathāgata’s pure dhyāna; this is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).

Whether the forms of the buddha-lands contain suns and moons or lack them—as extensively recorded in the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra*—and even including the seven stages of the mind-ground which constitute the realm of reality as it is (*yathābhūta-viṣaya*), all that you have asked shall be further examined and elucidated for you, Mahāmati.
Those who fail to ask such questions are still numerous; yet, from the smallest to the largest, all numerical quantities are the locus of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*).

When these are in correspondence with their characteristics, they manifest their lack of characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*). It is like a human body where the hundred bones and nine apertures are all complete, yet when one searches for the characteristic of a "body," it is ultimately unobtainable.
Only then can one distance oneself from the false and erroneous views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
It surpasses what is spoken by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), for they speak of "signlessness" (*animitta*) while remaining detached from all signs.

To speak of signlessness while being detached from signs is merely a state of inert emptiness (*jaḍa-śūnyatā*). These four types of *siddhānta* take the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) as their final limit;
it is precisely to extensively clarify that the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*) does not truly exist, yet ultimately remains ineffable. Nevertheless, this is not so...
It can be explained and further substantiated through detailed analogies that establish the *siddhānta* (the definitive teaching), just as all Buddhas have taught:
this World-Honored One arose with a heart of great compassion, appearing in the world for the sake of the one great cause and condition, and established this Dharma.
Baizhang said: "The Tathāgata remained silent beneath the Bodhi tree for forty-nine days."
However, when contemplating with wisdom, it is obscure and difficult to explain, beyond all analogy.
To say that sentient beings possess Buddha-nature is to slander the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha; to say that sentient beings lack Buddha-nature is likewise to slander the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha.
To say there is Buddha-nature is called the slander of attachment; to say there is no Buddha-nature is called the slander of falsehood. It is as if one were speaking of the Buddha.
To claim that the Buddha-nature exists is the slander of superimposition; to claim that the Buddha-nature does not exist is the slander of deprecation;

to claim that the Buddha-nature both exists and does not exist is the slander of contradiction; and to claim that the Buddha-nature neither exists nor does not exist is the slander of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Just as one might wish not to say that sentient beings have no prospect of liberation, yet if one were to say so, sentient beings would still give rise to [conceptualizations] following those words.
Because the benefit is slight and the loss is great, it is said: "I would rather not preach the Dharma and quickly enter nirvana.
Yet, looking back toward the past, all Buddhas have preached the Dharma of the Three Vehicles. Subsequently, through provisional verses, they established names;
originally, that was not the Buddha, yet they spoke of it as the Buddha; originally, that was not Bodhi, yet they spoke of it as Bodhi.
Regarding those who understand such things as bodhi, nirvāṇa, and liberation, yet are unable to carry even a hundred-stone load, one should first give them a load of one sheng or one he.
To those who find it difficult to believe the definitive teachings (nītārtha), one should first speak of the non-definitive teachings (neyārtha).
Thus, it is better that wholesome dharmas circulate rather than unwholesome ones; for when the limit of wholesome fruits is exhausted, the fruits of evil will arrive.
If one attains Buddhahood, there must be sentient beings; if one attains nirvana, there must be birth and death; if one attains illumination, there must be darkness.
These are merely the reciprocal cycles of out-flowing causes and effects, where nothing fails to correspond and respond to another.
If you wish to escape these reciprocal transformations, simply sever the dualistic extremes; do not let the mind’s calculations and measurements take hold, and you will no longer be a "non-Buddha."
It is not a sentient being, not a relative, not a stranger; it is neither high nor low, neither level nor uneven, neither coming nor going.

It merely does not cling to words, so that one cannot be caught by either side of the channel. Thus one is freed from the mutual conditioning of suffering and pleasure, and freed from the reciprocal response of light and darkness.
True principle is neither truly real nor unreal, and neither false nor non-false. It is not.
These measures, numbers, and objects are like space, which cannot be cultivated or refined.
If the mind has even the slightest conceptualization, it is immediately governed and bound by measure and number. It is like a divination omen being governed by metal, wood, water, fire, and earth;
or like glue that adheres in five places, allowing the Demon King to seize one and take one home at will. All teachings and words are threefold.
The phrases are connected such that they are good in the beginning, middle, and end. At the outset, one must first teach them to give rise to a wholesome mind;
only after breaking their unwholesome mind can they finally be called a "good" Bodhisattva. One who is not a Bodhisattva is what is called a Bodhisattva.
Dharma is neither dharma nor non-dharma—it is all like this. If one speaks but a single phrase, it causes sentient beings to enter hell; yet if [one speaks] three...
To speak of these phrases all at once is for the person themselves to enter hell; it has nothing to do with the Master’s teaching.
To speak until now—that the mirror-like awareness is one's own Buddha—is the "goodness of the beginning. Not to dwell upon that present mirror-like awareness is the "goodness of the middle.
Furthermore, not to create or dwell upon intellectual understanding is the "goodness of the end. As previously mentioned, this belongs to the time after [meeting] Dīpaṃkara Buddha; it is simply this.
"Neither extraordinary nor holy"—Baizhang’s saying accords with every *siddhānta*.
This single phrase, "neither extraordinary nor holy," has already served as a commentary on all one hundred and eight statements.

The phrase "the non-arising phrase" and "the arising phrase" (translated in the Tang as "the arising phrase and the non-arising phrase," and in the Wei as "the view of arising and the view of non-arising").
It is said in general that taking the non-arising phrase as the primary principle possesses profound significance:
all phenomena arise from non-arising, yet this very arising is non-arising; one simply must not form views of either arising or non-arising. This is the world.
Ordinary beings perceive it as arising, while those of the Two Vehicles and externalists perceive it as non-arising; all such views are false and delusory.
The World-Honored One first spoke to shatter them: whether [it be] arising or non-arising, nirvana and the characteristics of emptiness are in a state of flux and lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Since no intrinsic nature can be found, that which is called "arising" is not so, nor is that which is called "non-arising."

This [position] is also incorrect. In this context, there ought to be two phrases: "the phrase of non-arising" and "the phrase that is not non-arising," and "the phrase of arising" and "the phrase that is not arising.
Only then would it accord with the preceding verse. That which is "not arising" is precisely the non-ordinary; that which is "not non-arising" is precisely the non-sage.
To sit and sever both the ordinary and the sage is to manifest the quiescent single mind. This refutes what Mahāmati previously [asserted].

Question: Since dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) arises from conditions, why is it called a "non-arising phrase"? Answer: Because the views of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) and eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) do not arise, it is called a "non-non-arising phrase.
While it is easy to understand that arising is itself non-arising, as for the statement that non-arising is the manifestation of quiescence (*śānti*), why is it said to be "not like" [that]?
This is because, subsequently, all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are shown to be neither arising nor non-arising.
If one were to establish the thesis that there is something which does not arise, it would be identical to the false views of the non-Buddhists; therefore, this is not permitted.

Formerly, when the Sixth Patriarch entered the room after three knocks on the drum, the Fifth Patriarch lectured him on the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*. Upon reaching the passage, "One should give rise to the mind without dwelling anywhere," he attained sudden and great enlightenment.
The Fifth Patriarch, knowing that he had seen his own original nature, immediately entrusted him with the robe and bowl.
The verse for transmitting the Dharma says: "When sentient beings come to plant seeds, the fruit arises from the ground;

since insentient things have no seeds, they lack nature and thus have no arising. If one minutely examines what the Fifth Patriarch said regarding arising and non-arising, one will know that what the Sixth Patriarch realized was that one should give rise to the mind by dwelling nowhere. Thus, it is a matter of whether there is arising or no arising.
Non-interference is the unsurpassed, subtle, secret, perfectly luminous, and true Treasury of the Eye of the Right Dharma.
It is the phrase of permanence and the phrase of impermanence (the Wei translation says: the view of permanence and the view of impermanence).
The commentary states: "Non-arising is permanence; arising is impermanence. This appears to follow the preceding text.
In summary, since no self-nature can be found, what is called "permanent" is not [true permanence], and what is called "impermanent" is also not [true impermanence].
