Intoxicated and deluded by the two extremes of existence and non-existence, they are warped and confused; they do not recognize that they were originally devoid of wisdom, yet falsely claim to have attained omniscience.
[This is] wisdom. To apply this doctrine of causelessness to all phenomena is like one blind man leading a multitude of blind men;

they pull each other into a pit of fire. Is this not deeply lamentable? When Jiufeng was serving as attendant to Shishuang, after Shishuang passed away, the assembly wished to invite the head seat of the hall to succeed him as abbot. Jiufeng did not consent, saying, "Wait for me..."
Jiawen asked about the transgression. "If you can grasp the meaning of our former master, then serve him as you did when he was alive.
He then asked the Head Seat, "Our former master said: 'Rest! Cease! A single thought for ten thousand years! Cold ashes and withered wood! An incense burner in an ancient temple!
A single length of white silk! Tell me, what matter does this clarify? The Head Seat replied, "It clarifies the realm of uniformity."
Regarding this matter of the "limits," Feng said, "If that is so, then you have not yet understood the meaning of our former teacher. Zuo said, "You do not approve of me.
Bring some incense. Zuo then burned the incense and said, "If I have not understood the meaning of our former teacher, may I not be able to cast off my body at the moment the incense smoke rises.
Having finished speaking, he sat and passed away. Feng then patted his back and said, "Passing away while seated, standing..."
That it is not non-existent when he has passed away—this is something I have not even dreamed of grasping in the intent of my former teacher. Tiantong’s verse says:

"The one lineage of Shishuang was personally transmitted to Jiufeng; once the incense smoke has departed, the true pulse is difficult to penetrate. The crane in its moon-nest makes a dream of a thousand years."

In the snow-covered house, people are lost in the single color; sitting and cutting off the ten directions, one still incurs a mark on the forehead. Moving silently a single step, behold the flying dragon.
Danxia’s verse says: “Horned and hairy, a body of a different species; Cold ashes and withered wood, dust in the eyes.
Though you have not yet grasped the meaning of the former master, How can you avoid this fresh phrase at the moment of departure? It was solely for the sake of the Head Seat.
Because they cling to their own achievements as being worthy of honor, they are suppressed by the Nine Peaks. Mahāmati,
if there are other śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas who perceive that which is devoid of self-nature— like clouds, fire-wheels, *gandharva*-cities, the non-arising,
illusions, mirages, water-moons, and dreams— as being the manifestation of internal and external mind and the delusions of beginningless emptiness...

Falsehoods are not separate from one’s own mind. (The Tang translation says: "Contemplate that all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature, like clouds in the sky, like a whirling firebrand, like a city of Gandharvas, like a magical illusion, like a mirage, like the moon reflected in water, and like what is seen in a dream—all are not separate from one’s own mind.

Due to beginningless false views, they are grasped as being external. When the causes and conditions of deluded thoughts are extinguished, one is free from both the conceptualizer and the conceptualized, as well as the names and meanings grasped by the deluded mind.

(The Tang translation says: "Having made this contemplation, one severs the conditions of discrimination and is also free from the names and meanings grasped by the deluded mind. One contemplates that which is contemplated, and [realizes] the body established through experience.

The storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is not associated with the grasped object or the grasper within the realm of consciousness. It is devoid of any objective realm and is free from arising, abiding, and ceasing.

One should contemplate that it arises from one's own mind and enters into conceptual differentiation; as stated in the Tang translation: "It is devoid of the grasped and the grasper, as well as arising, abiding, and ceasing. Contemplating in this manner, one should dwell constantly without abandoning it.
Wei said: "Thus one contemplates and observes that the self-mind is the cause of birth.
[The Master] replied: "The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) do not realize that the illusory realm is a manifestation of their own minds.

Within the ultimate truth (paramārtha), they perceive both existence and non-existence, thereby formulating dualistic views. This constitutes a false view and is not the correct view (samyag-dṛṣṭi). Furthermore, as for all other..."

Śramaṇas and brāhmaṇas are not devoured by evil views. Within my Dharma, they contemplate all phenomena as being devoid of intrinsic nature, like floating clouds, like a fire-wheel, and like a city of Gandharvas.

They contemplate all phenomena as fundamentally unborn from the beginning, like magical illusions, like a mirage, and like the moon reflected in water. They contemplate all phenomena as being like a dream.
All that is perceived—various kinds of deluded thoughts—does not depart from the manifestation within the internal and external mind.
The internal mind consists of the seeds of beginningless falsehood; the external mind consists of false discrimination and attachment to external objects.

Therefore, it is said that these manifestations of the internal and external mind are like events in a dream. In sum, they are the illusory phenomena manifested by one’s own mind, which can be seen everywhere.

This is to realize that [the object] is false. When one performs this contemplation, it can cause the causes of discursive thought (*vikalpa*) to cease, as well as the objects of discursive thought to cease.

Thus, afflictions (*kleśa*) are extinguished, and the obstacles of phenomena (*dharma-āvaraṇa*) are removed. Furthermore, one becomes free from the conceptualization of mental speech and the names of the objects so described, realizing that their nature is empty.
Moreover, the obstacles of principle (*tattva-āvaraṇa*) are eliminated. Then, by means of one's own mind, one contemplates the object of contemplation.

The eighth ālayavijñāna manifests as objective images (*nimitta-bhāga*). Those that are remote constitute the "establishment of enjoyment," namely the receptacle world, which refers to the objects of the six sense-fields.
Those that are intimate constitute the "establishment of the body," namely the sensory faculties, which refer to the objects of the six sense-organs.
Since the ālayavijñāna is both the subject that observes and the object that is observed within its own sphere, it is said to "observe that which is observed."
Within the sphere of this ālayavijñāna, there is a mind that grasps; this is termed "appropriation" (*parigraha*), which refers to the subtle characteristics of the seven consciousnesses.
That which is the object grasped is termed "appropriation," which refers to the very substance of the eighth consciousness.
Where there is both subject and object, one cannot be separated from arising, abiding, and ceasing. Now, observe the ālayavijñāna.
Regarding the objective sphere (*viṣaya*): one does not perceive a grasper, nor does one perceive that which is grasped. With respect to both the grasper and the grasped, neither is applicable;
there is only the departure from both grasper and grasped. Both person and phenomena are empty, such that there is no shadow, no trace, reaching even the station of nothingness (*ākiṃcanyāyatana*).
Having reached the station of nothingness, one enters the sphere of tranquility, where the flow [of consciousness] is extinguished.
Who is it that undergoes arising, abiding, and ceasing? This storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is a realm that is purely and entirely neither-arising-nor-ceasing.
When one contemplates and observes in this way, constantly abiding within the dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing, it is not a state of mere unilateral desiccation or silence.
Within the inconceivable, the functional activity of dharmas arises spontaneously; because all things are without mind, there arises the stage of "conforming entry" (anupraveśa).
It is different. As stated in the subsequent text: "Entering in accordance with the body of the Tathāgata; entering in accordance with the transformations of Suchness (tathatā);
and entering in accordance with the subtle and minute minds of sentient beings. How could this be compared to the annihilation of evil views? The *Awakening of Faith* states:

"When a Bodhisattva first gives rise to the aspiration for enlightenment, they immediately contemplate the essence of the causal and resultant aspects of the dependent origination of the fundamental consciousness's own nature. If one wishes to enter..."
Regarding the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*): since the nature of consciousness itself has no substantial entity, what is there to be contemplated?
Nevertheless, it takes the conceptualization of mental discourse (*manojalpa*) as its object. This is because all objective spheres have nothing but names and phrases as their essence;

therefore, if one is separated from the conceptualization of mental discourse, nothing exists at all. Formerly, when the Elder Qing of Guoqing Temple on Mount Tiantai first encountered Xuansha’s instruction:
The assembly said, "If you all can for one lifetime act as if you had lost your parents, I guarantee that you will attain thorough penetration.
Jing repeated his previous words and asked, "As it is said in the teachings, 'One must not use a mind of known knowledge to fathom the Tathāgata’s unsurpassed wisdom and vision.
How then should one proceed? Sha replied, "You say you have attained thorough penetration."

As for the mind that knows all objects, can it still be measured and attained? Jing entered the path through faith from this point on. Later, he resided at Tiantai Mountain, where he was revered by those both far and near;
he was commonly called the Venerable Dajing. There were often people who asked him: "Whenever I, your disciple, sit in meditation at night..."
My thoughts are scattered and flying about; I do not yet understand the method for subduing them. I pray that you will deign to grant me instruction. Jing said:
"If, while sitting peacefully at night, your thoughts are scattered and flying about, take this very mind that is scattering and fly away, and investigate the place where it scatters and flies."

When one investigates until there is nowhere to find it, where do these fluttering thoughts remain? If one turns back to investigate the investigating mind itself, where is that very mind capable of investigation?
Furthermore, the wisdom that can illuminate is fundamentally empty, and the objects perceived are likewise quiescent.
That which is quiescent yet not-quiescent is because there is no person who can bring about quiescence; that which illuminates yet does not-illuminate is because there is nothing to be illuminated.
This is the objective realm. When both object and wisdom are quiescent, the mind is at ease. One does not seek out branches externally, nor does one dwell in meditative concentration internally.
Both paths are extinguished, and the single nature is serene. This is the essential path for returning to the source.

Furthermore, having observed the meaning of "illusion" within the teachings, I have composed a verse to pose a question to the various students, saying: "If you say that all dharmas are like illusory existences..."
"Committing various transgressions and evils should entail no blame; how then can the karma one has created not perish? Yet, by relying on the Buddha’s compassion, one is uplifted and guided.
At that time, the Elder Xiaojing replied: "An illusory person creates illusory Mount Cakravāḍa; illusory karma can summon illusory objects of treatment.
Failing to realize the illusion gives rise to all kinds of illusory suffering; when one awakens to the illusion, the illusion is fundamentally unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*)."

Observe this view of the two venerable elders: those who deeply cultivate the contemplation of Consciousness-Only must proceed in this manner before the suffering of the three realms of existence, born of false conceptualization, is extinguished, and the conditions of ignorance, craving, and karma are brought to an end. How could non-Buddhists ever reach such a point?
"Mahāmati, that bodhisattva will before long attain the equality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
Possessing great compassion and skillful means, yet without the exertion of contrived means, Mahāmati, he is able to regard the entire realm of sentient beings as being like an illusion.
Without striving through causes and conditions, he remains detached from internal and external objects; seeing nothing outside the mind, he enters successively into the state of signlessness."

One enters sequentially into the samādhi realms from stage to stage, understanding the three realms as being like an illusion. Through analytical observation, one shall attain the illusion-like samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*).
Having transcended the manifestations of one’s own mind and realized their non-existence, one comes to abide in the *prajñāpāramitā*.
Abandoning the skillful means (*upāya*) employed for that birth, one enters the body of the Tathāgata through the vajra-like samādhi (*vajropama-samādhi*).

He enters accordingly into transformations that accord with suchness (*tathatā*). With his supernatural powers (*abhijñā*) being sovereign and his compassion and skillful means fully adorned, he enters equally into all Buddha-fields and the abodes of externalists (the Weibo edition reads "the places where all sentient beings take delight"). Transcending mind, thought, and consciousness (*manas*, *manovijñāna*), this Bodhisattva gradually effects a transformation of his basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) to attain the body of a Tathāgata.

The Master replied: "When a practitioner of the correct path enters the contemplation of *vijñapti-mātra* (consciousness-only), they attain the two designations of 'transformation of the basis' (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*).
That is to say, they transform the basis of birth-and-death into nirvāṇa, and transform the basis of afflictions into bodhi. In sum, this is the transformation of consciousness into wisdom.

Therefore, within the sphere of consciousness, there is no longer the grasped object nor the grasping subject, nor the arising, abiding, and ceasing. Before long, one shall attain nirvāṇa from birth-and-death."
It is equal and impartial. Through the extinction of the seven consciousnesses, the basis for defilement and purity vanishes;

one perceives neither the marks of birth and death nor the marks of nirvāṇa. Therefore, all things are equal. That which arises from the self-mind enters into conceptual differentiation, yet it does not depart from compassion.
This is the skillful means of great compassion that requires no effortful practice; it is without fabrication.

Skillful means consist solely of the ingenuity of great compassion; therefore, one does not abandon sentient beings. Yet, one regards them as like an illusion, for in reality there is no sentient being who attains parinirvāṇa.
Because there is nothing to be developed, one does not exert effort in the cultivation and realization of causes and conditions.

One remains far removed from internal and external objects; mind and environment are of one suchness. Outside the mind there are no phenomena, and thus there is nothing further to be seen. As for the former, it is internal...
The manifestation of external mind is precisely the causal condition for deluded thought (*vikalpa*). Now, as internal and external objects are detached, there remains only the single true mind.
Therefore, the causal conditions of deluded thought are extinguished. Since there is nothing seen, there is nothing experienced. One sequentially enters the state of non-characteristics (*animitta*).
This is the stage of the first abode (*prathama-bhūmi*) where one shatters the darkness and manifests the *dharmatā*. From here, one sequentially enters...
The samādhi of the ground reaching the ground is the entry into the practice directed toward the grounds (*bhūmi*).

This is the transition from the provisional to the real, wherein one realizes the signless samādhi, which is precisely correct reception (*samyaksamādhi*). Furthermore, from the eighth ground through the tenth ground, one emerges from the real and enters the provisional;
understanding the three realms as being like an illusion, one employs illusory-like wisdom to discern and observe, thereby delivering all sentient beings. This is attainment.
In the Illusion-like Samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*), although its functions arise profusely, it is quiescent and sovereign;

thus one is able to transcend the realm of what is manifested by one's own mind and that which is non-existent. Without falling into biased emptiness, one dwells in the right wisdom of Prajñā and reaches the other shore.
As for the aforementioned realm of non-existence, although it is devoid of arising, abiding, and ceasing, it still pertains to the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas.
That which was formerly shared is now transcended and surpassed; both the person and phenomena are emptied by means of emptiness itself.

Having attained these three kinds of emptiness, it is therefore called the wisdom of *prajñā*. Abiding in this wisdom of *prajñā*, one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and enters the stage of Equal Enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*).
Therein, one abandons the expedient means associated with birth and suddenly severs the seeds of the two obstacles, both innate and acquired.
Just as with the diamond-like concentration (*vajropama-samādhi*), the skillful means employed on the first stage (*bhūmi*) are superseded by those of the second stage;

the skillful means employed on the second stage are superseded by those of the third stage. Upon reaching the final moment of mind preceding the diamond-like concentration, the meditative attainment thus acquired can no longer be superseded;

one immediately transcends into wondrous enlightenment (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). Consequently, one is able to enter accordingly into the vast Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*) of the Tathāgata, entering it in accordance with...
Just as the transformations of the Sublime Awakening are supernormal and characterized by unimpeded, sovereign play, he does not merely attain such powers;
rather, through his compassion and skillful means, he is fully adorned with both merit and wisdom, and does not merely attain such wisdom alone.
He enters equally into all Buddha-fields and realms of Māra without exception, as well as into the realms of non-Buddhists.
The sense bases (*āyatana*) are themselves the realm of Māra and the place where all sentient beings find delight;
this is because one has attained the samādhi of the non-discriminative wisdom that universally perceives the form-body (*rūpakāya*). The *Śraddhotpāda Śāstra* states:

"When the Bodhisattva stages are exhausted and skillful means are fully perfected, there is a single thought-moment of correspondence, and awakening arises for the first time; yet the mind has no initial characteristic, as it is far removed from even the most subtle [delusions]."
Through mindfulness, one attains the vision of the nature of the mind; the mind is then eternally abiding, which is termed ultimate awakening (*atyanta-bodhi*).

It is further stated that by means of such great wisdom of skillful means (*upāya-jñāna*), one eliminates ignorance (*avidyā*) and perceives the fundamental Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*), which is equal to True Suchness (*tathatā*) and pervades all places.

This is precisely the point intended. What is meant by "being detached from mind, thought, and consciousness" (*citta-mano-manovijñāna*) refers not only to being detached from deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

By means of causes and conditions, one eliminates the faults and afflictions of the turbid extreme; likewise, by transforming consciousness into wisdom, one eliminates the faults and afflictions of the pure extreme.
Thus, through analytical observation, one attains the illusion-like samādhi, whereby the six consciousnesses are transformed into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation.
Before long, one shall attain the equality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, whereby the seventh consciousness is transformed into the Wisdom of Equality. One then abandons...

Having abandoned the skillful means of producing those [five consciousnesses], one transforms the preceding five consciousnesses into the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*) and reaches the noble state of self-realization.
Like a mani jewel that reflects various colors, one transforms the eight consciousnesses into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-mahājñāna*).

This is how a bodhisattva gradually transforms their body to attain the body of a Tathāgata; it must begin with the practice of the contemplation of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātratā*). — *Mahāyāna-sūtrālaṃkāra-bhāṣya* (Taishō No. 1604) by Asvabhāva.
Ming’an ascended the hall and said: "Do not travel the path where the mind dwells; do not sit upon the effort of non-existence. Depart from both existence and non-existence;
all is vast and empty, as if heaven and earth were void. These four lines of verse encompass the essential purport of this section.
Mahāmati, therefore, those who wish to attain the body of the Tathāgata’s conformative entry (*anupraveśa-kāya*) should distance themselves from the false imaginings of arising,

abiding, and ceasing— which are produced by the expedient means of causes and conditions involving the mind, as well as the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases— and from all that is deceptive. They should proceed directly by means of "mind-only," observing the beginningless habit-energies of false imaginings and deceptions,
and through the contemplation of the non-existence [of external objects] within the three realms of existence, they shall reach the stage of Buddhahood, which is unborn.
The noble path of self-realization is the attainment of mastery over one’s own mind, reaching the stage of non-effortful practice (in the Tang translation, *anābhoga-caryā*).
Like a mani jewel that reflects various colors, it enters into the subtle minds of sentient beings and manifests emanation bodies according to their mental capacities to measure and guide them.
Thus, the stages (*bhūmi*) are established through gradual succession. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should diligently train yourself in this excellent *siddhānta* [of self-realization].

The Commentary states: This summarizes the preceding text. One should practice and study so as to gradually transform the body beyond mind, thought, and consciousness, thereby attaining the body of a Tathāgata.
Here, "mind" refers to the eighth consciousness; "thought" refers to the seventh consciousness; and "consciousness" refers to the six consciousnesses.
The five aggregates (*skandha*), six sense bases (*āyatana*), and eighteen elements (*dhātu*) do not exist apart from the objects before them;

they are merely the products of the conceptual constructions (*vikalpa*) of the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) acting through causes and conditions. They are established through expedient means as having arising, abiding, and ceasing, yet they are false and unreal.

These belong to the coarse characteristics of the sixth consciousness and the seventh consciousness. To be able to distance oneself from them is for the causes and conditions of such conceptual construction to be extinguished and to become free from conceptual construction.

This is the teaching and that which is taught. Having already awakened to the realization that the objects appearing from one's own mind are like an illusory realm, one dwells solely within the measure of mind (*cittamātra*) and proceeds directly to observe the faults of beginningless falsehood. That which belongs to the subtle characteristics of the seven consciousnesses is the cause of the habitual tendencies of false discrimination;
that which belongs to the seeds of the two obstacles is the entirety of "mind-only," which is the object of observation and the experience of that observation.
The storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) establishes the body. Everything that exists within the three realms is established by the storehouse consciousness.
Both the grasper and the grasped are not dissociated from the storehouse consciousness. Reflecting in this manner, one reaches the realm of nothingness.
These three realms are non-existent; being free from arising, abiding, and ceasing, they are the Tathāgatagarbha, the stage of neither-arising-nor-ceasing.
Therefore, it is said that the Buddha-stage is birthless, yet this does not mean it is absolutely unborn. It is the arrival at the noble realm of self-realization.
The arising of conceptualization that follows from one's own mind is itself the mastery of one's own mind through the absence of effortful causes and conditions;

this leads to effortless practice (*anābhoga-caryā*). It is like a mani jewel that reflects various colors: though it is inherently colorless, various colors appear in accordance with their proximity.

This is precisely the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom entering the body of the Tathāgata. As for what is called "entering in accordance with the transformations of Suchness," it means that by means of this [wisdom], which is like a mani jewel reflecting various colors, one enters the subtle minds of sentient beings and employs transformation bodies to deliver them according to the measure of their mental capacities.
This is as stated in the preceding verse of praise to the Buddha: "Delivering sentient beings so they may transcend birth and cessation."

To deliver the followers of the two vehicles by freeing them from mind and consciousness; to deliver the non-Buddhists by freeing them from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism; to deliver the bodhisattvas by purifying their *jvālā* (blazing flames);

and even to deliver the Tathāgatas by freeing them from the subject and object of awakening—this is what is meant by delivering those in the various stages (*bhūmi*) so that they may realize Mind-Only (*cittamātra*).

It is the gradual transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*) to attain the body of a Tathāgata; it is the dharma-gate of establishing continuity. This is the gift of the Dharma of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
This refers to what is called: "The most excellent of all *siddhāntas* that do not depart from self-nature; the various gates of the Mahāyāna perfections; the foremost heart of all Buddhas;
the *siddhānta* that transcends verbal expression—I shall now reveal it. Is it not fitting, then, to practice and study with diligence? Yangshan ascended the hall and said:
"All of you, each turn the light inward and reflect back upon yourselves; do not take my words as a mere record."
He said: "Since beginningless kalpas, you have turned your back on light and plunged into darkness; the roots of your deluded thoughts are deep-seated and cannot be suddenly uprooted.
Therefore, I have provisionally established skillful means to seize your coarse consciousness, like using yellow leaves to stop a child's crying—what validity is there in such a thing?
It is also like a person who takes a hundred kinds of goods and sets them out as a single shop for sale alongside gold and jewels, intending only—"
The mechanism of responding to the light or heavy [situations] is why it is said that Shitou was a shop of pure gold, whereas here I am a general merchandise shop.
If someone comes seeking mouse droppings, I also pick some up and give it to them; if they come seeking pure gold, I also pick some up and give it to them.
At that time, a monk asked, "I do not want the mouse droppings; I ask for the Master's pure gold. Yangshan said, "Chew! (Niè).
"Even in a donkey's year, one would not understand," [Huangbo] said, as he pointed his finger toward his mouth. The monk had no reply. Yangshan said, "If you call out for it, there is a transaction;
if you do not call out for it, there is none. If I were to speak of the Chan school, I would not even have a single person to accompany me;
how much less could there be five hundred or seven hundred? If I were to speak of this and that, they would all vie for the head."
To come forward and pick it up is like using an empty fist to deceive a small child; there is no reality in it at all. I shall now speak clearly to you:
regarding matters concerning the Sage, do not attempt to grasp them with the mind. Simply practice according to reality within the ocean of your own nature.
You need not seek the three knowledges or six supernatural powers. Why? Because these are merely peripheral matters of the Sage. For now...
Furthermore, you must recognize the mind and penetrate the root. Once you have attained the root, you need not worry about the branches; at some point in the future, they will naturally be present.
If you have not attained the root, even if you apply your emotions and efforts to study, you will still not attain it.
Have you not seen how Master Guishan said: "When the sentiments of ordinary and sage are exhausted, the true permanence is revealed; when phenomena and principle are non-dual, this is [the Way]."
"Suchness-Buddha. This consciousness-mind reaches the root; this is, in fact, the primary meaning of the gradual transformation of the body.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding what has been taught concerning mind, thought, mentation, the five dharmas, and the characteristics of self-nature (the Tang translation says:
'I pray that you will explain for me the five dharmas, the characteristics of self-nature, and all the wondrous Dharma-gates')—these are the practices of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas."
The non-conjunction of the objects of perception with the mind and its views demonstrates all teachings. (The Wei translation states:

"Because the spheres of practice of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are far removed from the conjunction of the objects of their own minds' false views, they are able to shatter the essence and characteristics of all speech and metaphors. This constitutes the mark of reality, the heart of all Buddha-words.
(Tang: "Entering from the mind and objects, departing from the marks of what is traversed; this accords with the true meaning, the core of all Buddha-teachings.

To the great Bodhisattvas dwelling in the mountains and seas of Mount Malaya (here called "Producing Fragrance") in the country of Laṅkā, he spoke of the Dharma-body—the realm of the ocean-like storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*)—which is praised by the Tathāgata.

(The Tang translation says: "I only pray that for the sake of this assembly of bodhisattvas in the mountains, you will expound in accordance with the past Buddhas the realm of the dharmakāya, which is like the waves of the ocean of the *ālayavijñāna*").
The Master replied: "This question concerns the five dharmas, the three natures, and the ālayavijñāna.

Previously, when discussing the ālayavijñāna as the body established through the enjoyment of what is observed, I merely indicated its general outline. Therefore, Mahāmati wishes to obtain a detailed exposition."
All arise from the ālayavijñāna; therefore, it is called the "gateways to all wondrous dharmas.

Because it is capable of giving rise to all phenomena, it is called the "ocean-wave of the ālayavijñāna. Because it is fundamentally without arising or ceasing, it is called the "realm of the dharmakāya.
The five dharmas are: name, appearance, conceptualization, correct wisdom, and suchness. As for the three natures:

It is said that there are false conceptualizations (*parikalpita*), dependent origination (*paratantra*), and perfection (*pariniṣpanna*). These all arise from the transformations of the mind, thought, and consciousness—the sixth, seventh, and eighth consciousnesses.

False conceptualizations and dependent origination chase after names and forms; they are entirely the realm of false conceptualization, like waves surging upon the ocean where the ocean itself is no longer seen.
If false conceptualizations are extinguished and right wisdom (*samyagjñāna*) manifests, the single nature (*ekadhātu*) is perfectly realized.
The essence is suchness itself. When the ocean waves have subsided, it is limpid and transparent to the infinite;
this is the realm of the true Dharmakāya. Thus, one knows that all names and characteristics are the objects of one's own mind’s false views.
To harmonize with them is called delusive conceptualization (*vikalpa*). In the sphere of practice for Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, one does not harmonize with them, yet is able to...
To remain far removed from these is what is called right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*). It is able to shatter all verbal expressions without pursuing names;
it is able to shatter all conceptual characteristics (*ākāra*) without pursuing signs. Yet, it can manifest all teachings, wherein teaching is itself non-teaching.
The perfected true mark is the markless; it is the manifestation of suchness, the perfect realization of self-nature.
This mind of the primary meaning is firm, solid, and unchanging; it is that which has been taught by all Buddhas of the past.

This "Chapter on the Mind of the Buddha’s Words" was spoken for the sake of the great Bodhisattvas on Mount Laṅkā, who lamented that the waves of the ocean-like mind are like the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna).
Therefore, Mahāmati, I pray that the World-Honored One will explain this Dharma-gate once more for the assembly of Bodhisattvas on Mount Laṅkā.
Master Yunfeng Yue, ascending the hall, said: "The root of sentient beings relies upon the ocean of wisdom as its source;
the flow of their containment takes the Dharmakāya as its substance. It is only because emotion arises that wisdom is obstructed, and because conceptualization changes..."

Their substance is distinct. When one reaches the root, emotional attachments vanish; when one knows the mind, its substance merges. Have all you virtuous practitioners of Chan gathered here understood?
"The ancient Buddha intersects with the pillar; the Buddha hall vies with the lantern for prominence.
If you do not understand this, consider the layered interplay described by Yunfeng. This is truly the very essence of this passage. Try to judge for yourself how it is.
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed Mahāmati Bodhisattva, saying: "There are four causes and conditions by which the eye-consciousness arises. What are these four? They are:
the failure to realize that what is grasped is a manifestation of one's own mind; the attachment to the habit-energy of form resulting from beginningless false delusions;

the inherent nature of consciousness itself desiring to see various forms and appearances; and [the fourth]. Mahāmati, these are called the four kinds of causes and conditions, like the place where a stream flows."

The storehouse consciousness gives rise to the waves of the evolving consciousnesses. (As the Tang translation states: first, because of failing to realize that what appears is one's own mind and thus grasping at it; second, because of the false habitual tendencies of attachment to form since beginningless time;

third, because such is the nature of consciousness itself; fourth, because of the delight in seeing various forms and signs. Due to these four conditions, the *ālaya-vijñāna* produces the waves of the evolving consciousnesses, like a flowing torrent.)

Tong said: "The four conditions refer to the condition of the sense organ (*indriya*), the condition of form (*rūpa*), the condition of consciousness (*vijñāna*), and the condition of the desire to see.
Regarding the condition of the sense organ: this refers to the eye-organ and its corresponding object. Both are manifestations of one's own mind;

failing to realize that external objects are merely produced from one's own mind, one gives rise to grasping. As soon as the object arrives, it is seized—this is the condition of the sense organ. Regarding the condition of form: the dust of form is fundamentally empty."
From beginningless time, one has clung to and been attached to form, never forgetting it; this is the condition of form (*rūpa-pratyaya*).

As for the condition of consciousness (*vijñāna-pratyaya*), consciousness has discrimination as its nature; it is able to discriminate each of the five bases, and each possesses its own specific nature;
this is the condition of consciousness. As for the condition of desire to see (*didṛkṣā-pratyaya*), it takes craving for the *ālaya* and delighting in the *ālaya* as its sovereign.
When one perceives various sensory objects, the mind naturally gives rise to craving and attachment; this is the condition for the arising of desire.
Due to these four kinds of causes and conditions, the clarity of the *zhan* (stillness) becomes adhered to, giving rise to cognition; the seeds of habitual tendencies are like a torrential stream.

This is called the "water-flowing-place" *ālayavijñāna*. The waves of the evolving consciousnesses—eight evolving into seven, and seven evolving into six—are like the waters of the great ocean undergoing transformation.
They function as waves; thus, the evolving consciousnesses arise in succession like waves, evolving due to four causal conditions.
Furthermore, when subdivided: the grasping of sense organs and objects constitutes the first five consciousnesses; the habitual attachment to forms constitutes the seventh consciousness;
self-nature discrimination constitutes the sixth consciousness; and the seeds of desire to see constitute the eighth consciousness. This...
The four types of consciousness act as mutual causes and conditions, arising one from another in succession; collectively, they are termed *pravṛtti-vijñāna* (evolving consciousness).
In the *Qingliang Dashi Shu*, the two phrases "the transformation of characteristics and the distinction of essence" and "sentiment arises and wisdom is obstructed" are explained as follows:

For example, consider a person endowed with both merit and wisdom who suddenly dreams of a body afflicted by poverty and disease—this is the "transformation of characteristics. It does not... [text continues].
To see one's own original body is for the essence to be distinct. To grasp and recognize it as "this is my body" is for emotion to arise.

To lack faith in the virtue and upright beauty of one's own body is for wisdom to be obstructed. Many people of later generations mistakenly hold that the transformation of marks (*lakṣaṇa*) constitutes the transformation of thought (*saṃjñā-pariṇāma*);
this is not so. A monk asked Bào Cí: "When emotion arises, wisdom is obstructed; when marks transform, the essence becomes distinct. When emotion has not yet arisen, it is like..."
"What? Cí said. The monk asked, "When emotion has not yet arisen, what is it that is separated? Cí said, "This young fellow has not yet met the right person.
Thus, if one attains awakening, one can recognize the nature even while following the flow of phenomena;
if one does not awaken, then even though emotion has not yet arisen, one remains far removed from the nature. Only those who transform consciousness into wisdom have a subtle understanding of this.
Mahāmati, just as the visual consciousness arises simultaneously with all the sense organs, atoms, and pores, so too does it arise in accordance with its respective objects.
It is like a bright mirror manifesting various forms and images, or like a fierce wind blowing upon the waters of the great ocean.

The winds of external objects cause the ocean of the mind to surge with waves of consciousness that do not cease. Due to the characteristics of their activities—whether distinct or non-distinct—the signs of birth produced by karma combine and one becomes deeply attached to them.
Because one cannot discern the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of form and the other sense-objects, the five groups of consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) evolve.

Mahāmati, you should know that the very cause which accompanies those five bodies of consciousness—the cognition of distinct, segmented characteristics—is the cause of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*).

It functions in dependence upon those bodies, yet it does not form the thought: "I am functioning through mutual causality. Rather, it functions through the attachment to the false imaginings of what is manifested by one's own mind;
and while those various fragmented characteristics function together, it discriminates objects as segmented and differentiated. That is to say, regarding them...

It evolves. (The Tang translation says: "As it is with the visual consciousness, so it is with the others; thus the evolving consciousnesses evolve across all sense organs, atoms, pores, eyes, and so forth. They may arise simultaneously, like a bright mirror manifesting various forms and images;

or they may arise sequentially, like a fierce wind blowing upon the waters of the great ocean. It further states: "Because the characteristics produced by causes are neither identical nor different, karma and the characteristics of birth are deeply bound together.

One cannot discern the self-nature of form and other objects as the five bodies of consciousness evolve. Mahāmati, the mental consciousness arises either concomitant with the five consciousnesses or due to the discrimination of distinct objective marks. Yet those various consciousnesses do not think: 'We arise simultaneously, acting as mutual causes. Nevertheless, they simultaneously give rise to discrimination and attachment toward the objects manifested within one's own mind.)
Without distinction in their characteristics, each cognizes its own object.
It is said in general that the evolving consciousnesses arise like waves; the eye-consciousness arises in this way, and so it is for the other sense organs.

This applies even down to the finest dust motes and pores of the skin. They may arise instantaneously, like images appearing in a bright mirror, or they may arise gradually, like the blowing of the wind.

The ocean water: because consciousness arises simultaneously with the sense organs, it is called "sudden"; this refers to the first five consciousnesses. Because objects are distinguished sequentially, it is called "gradual";
this refers to the sixth consciousness. The winds of external objects toss and surge upon the sea of the mind;

this refers to the inconceivable perfuming and transformation of the preceding six sense-objects. Thus, waves arise from the tranquil sea, and the waves of consciousness continue in succession without interruption. This refers to...

The seven consciousnesses are as follows: the ocean of the mind, which is the *ālayavijñāna*, serves as the cause, while the various evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛttivijñāna*) are its manifested effects.
This is like the great ocean serving as the cause, while the waves are its manifested effects.

The characteristics of these two—whether they are different or not different—are as previously illustrated by the analogy of the lump of clay and its atoms. How is it clarified that they are both different and not different? It is because of what is produced by them.
This karma is the active manifestation of ignorance and pertains to the realm of the six consciousnesses.

The seeds of the habit-energies of false conceptualization are the aspect of arising and pertain to the realm of the eight consciousnesses. These two—the aspect of karma and the aspect of arising—are deeply bound together;
they internally rely upon the eight consciousnesses and externally rely upon the six consciousnesses, penetrating deeply into the field of consciousness where they are clung to and not relinquished.

This pertains to the domain of the seven consciousnesses. Due to this firm attachment to self-love, one fails to realize that the intrinsic nature of form and other objects originally belongs to the *nimitta-bhāga* (objective aspect) of the eight consciousnesses and is, like an illusion, devoid of reality. Consequently, the eyes grasp forms and the ears grasp sounds;
everything is appropriated as belonging to oneself. Thus, the five groups of consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*) evolve, and the five consciousnesses pervade the entire body. So it is said.
Because the transformation of the body has not yet entered the conceptualization of the mental ground (*manobhūmi*), the five consciousnesses can only grasp objects;

they lack deliberative thought and thus belong to direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). The sixth consciousness, however, is able to differentiate characteristics such as beauty or ugliness; it belongs to inference (*anumāna*) and non-valid cognition (*abhāva-pramāṇa*).

That very same mental consciousness, occurring simultaneously with the group of the five sense-consciousnesses, manifests when the object reaches [the senses]; this occurs in a single moment (*kṣaṇa*).
The sequential and distinct characteristics of the five sense-objects that flow into [the mind] are individually cognized;

this is precisely what is called the sixth consciousness (manovijñāna). However, if the five sense-faculties do not apprehend the distinct characteristics of the five sense-objects, then the cognition of discrimination would likewise not arise spontaneously.
Furthermore, these six consciousnesses evolve based upon those five groups of consciousness (pañcavijñānakāya). Those...

The consciousnesses arise through mutual dependence; they are fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature. They are like the waters in a river, rushing and flowing together in a turbulent current, each unaware of the others.
They do not form the thought, "We are arising simultaneously in mutual dependence.

Rather, they are merely the objects manifested by one's own mind within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), resulting from the habitual tendencies of beginningless ignorance and false conceptualization.
Deeply entering into conceptual attachment, one says that the seven consciousnesses are active.

Having given rise to grasping, when the various distinct and differing characteristics of the manifest forms and so forth are simultaneously apprehended, one says that the five consciousnesses are active.

From within this, one discriminates the segmented differences of the past objects of the five sense-fields; thus, one says that the sixth consciousness is active. Consequently, one speaks of the five...

The six and seventh consciousnesses each cognize their own respective objects; within that state of non-differentiation, there is a subtle differentiation which is termed the "evolving consciousnesses" (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*).
If one perceives them as distinct, in reality they are one and the same, like the water of the ocean; therefore, they are not different.
A monk asked Baizhang, "In the face of sensory objects, how can one attain a mind like wood or stone? Baizhang replied, "All dharmas are fundamentally..."
It is said: Emptiness does not speak of itself; form, too, does not speak. Neither defilement nor purity has a mind that binds people.

It is only because people themselves give rise to false delusions and attachments, forming various kinds of interpretations, giving rise to various kinds of knowledge and views, and producing various kinds of craving and fear. One should simply understand that all phenomena do not arise of themselves; they all arise from oneself.
These arise from one's own single thought of deluded inversion and the grasping of signs. Know that the mind and its objects fundamentally do not reach one another;
each and every dharma is liberated in its own place, quiescent in its own place, and a site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) in its own place.
If you grasp the essential meaning of Baizhang, then consciousness will no longer arise of itself; the ocean of awakening will be perfectly clear and limpid—what further matter could there be?
For example, when a practitioner enters the meditative absorption of *dhyāna-samādhi*, subtle habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) continue to evolve;
yet, being unaware of this, they think: "Consciousness has ceased, and only then do I enter meditative absorption. In reality, consciousness does not cease as it enters absorption.

It does not cease because the seeds of habitual tendencies have not been extinguished; it appears to cease because the conditions for its evolution and its grasping are incomplete. (The Tang translation reads: "All practitioners...")

One enters into samādhi; through the power of habitual practice, [the consciousnesses] arise subtly without being perceived. One merely thinks, "I have extinguished all consciousnesses and entered samādhi," yet in reality, one does not extinguish consciousness to enter samādhi. Because the seeds of those habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are not extinguished, it is simply that one does not grasp at objects;
this is what is called the "extinction of consciousness."
The Master said: "The previous passage spoke of the waves of evolving consciousness arising; this passage speaks of the ālayavijñāna as the place where the water flows.
Because the flow is so rapid, it is not seen, appearing instead as if tranquil. This is what is called the subtle *dharmatā-vijñāna*, wherein habitual tendencies form a torrential stream.
When practitioners of dhyāna enter into samādhi and reach the state where birth and death are about to be exhausted, within that interval there is a subtle..."
The arising and ceasing are subtle, like ripples on a windless lake. Thus, the seeds of beginningless habitual tendencies arise subtly from within;
unaware of this oneself, one thinks: "I have extinguished consciousness and entered right samādhi."

In truth, consciousness has never ceased. Not only is its beginningless, continuous flow inherently incapable of cessation, but even when its habitual tendencies and seeds remain latent and unmanifested—like fish trapped within ice—it has, in reality, never ceased from the very start.

Therefore, one cannot say that consciousness has ceased. It is merely because the objects present before one have shifted from existence to non-existence, and the conditions for grasping are incomplete, that it is called the "cessation of consciousness. It is not that the mind which grasps is absent; rather, it is simply that the objects to be grasped are incomplete.
This is merely a temporary state in which the mind does not take an object as its condition. If one perceives this as cessation, it is not the actual cessation of consciousness.
Although it is said that one does not grasp at external objects, one has still not yet departed from the duality of subject and object; how, then, can one lightly speak of quiescent extinction?
When Chan Master Huang first visited the Fifth Patriarch, he built a hermitage and sat in meditation continuously for more than twenty years.
He never displayed a look of indolence. Master Ce traveled to the region north of the Yellow River and heard that Master Huang had once studied under Huineng of Huangmei.

Having lived in a hermitage for many years, Huang claimed to be in a state of *samādhi*. Ce went to visit him and asked, "What are you doing while staying here? Huang replied, "I am entering meditative absorption (*dhyāna*).
Ce asked, "When you say you are entering absorption, is there a mind or is there no mind? If there is a mind... [The text continues: "...then all [phenomena would be...]".
"All moving creatures should attain samādhi. If those without minds were to do so, then all things such as grasses and trees would likewise be able to attain samādhi.
He said: "When I enter samādhi, I do not perceive the existence of a mind characterized by being or non-being. He asked:

"If you do not perceive the existence of a mind characterized by being or non-being, this is constant samādhi; how could there be entering and exiting? If there were entering and exiting," [it would not be constant].
"That would not be the Great Samādhi. Huíng remained silent for a long while, then asked, "Whom does your Master follow? He replied, "My Master is the Sixth Patriarch of Caoxi.
He asked, "What did the Sixth Patriarch take to be meditative concentration? He replied, "My Master said: 'That which is wondrously profound, perfectly still, and quiescent...'"
The essence and its function are suchness. The five aggregates are fundamentally empty; the six sense objects do not exist. There is no exiting or entering, no fixed state and no distraction.
The nature of dhyāna has no abiding; it is the stillness of dhyāna that is free from abiding. The nature of dhyāna is unborn; it is the thought of dhyāna that is free from birth.
The mind is like space, yet it lacks even the measure of space. Having heard these essential points of the Dharma, Huáng went to visit the Sixth Patriarch. The Patriarch said:

This was no different from [the teaching of] Ce. Under these words, Xuanhuang attained a sudden and thorough realization; the mind he had cultivated over the preceding twenty years left not even a trace.
That night, the gentry and commoners of Hebei suddenly heard a voice in the air saying, "Master Chan Huang has attained the Way today.
Later, he returned to Hebei and transformed the fourfold assembly. Indeed, when there is entering and emerging from meditative concentration, it is precisely...

This is not yet the Great Samādhi, because the seeds of habitual tendencies have not been extinguished. Only when one realizes non-arising does birth-and-death cease to be birth-and-death, and the beginningless habitual tendencies are suddenly stilled.

Mahāmati, such is the ultimate limit of this subtle ālayavijñāna; except for the Tathāgatas and those Bodhisattvas dwelling on the stages, no one—including all Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and practitioners of external paths—can fathom or definitively comprehend it through the power of the wisdom obtained from their meditative absorptions (samādhi).
It is [only] through the skillful means of the wisdom regarding the characteristics of the remaining stages that one can analyze and decisively determine the meanings of its phrases. Most...
The supreme and boundless roots of goodness reach maturity. One becomes free from the delusions and falsities of the mental constructions that manifest from one's own mind.

Through lower, middling, and superior cultivation while dwelling in seclusion within mountain forests, one is able to perceive the continuous flow of the mental constructions of one’s own mind. (The Tang translation states: "Only those who practice according to reality, by the power of wisdom, realize the characteristics of the various stages.")

They have thoroughly mastered the meaning of words and phrases; they have extensively gathered roots of goodness under boundless Buddhas; and they are able to know [this] without falsely discriminating what is seen by their own minds.
[The Master] replied: "This explains the difficulty of perceiving subtle habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

The subtle store-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), which is called 'neither-arising-nor-ceasing' because it is in union with that which arises and ceases, is named the *ālaya-vijñāna*. It enters into profound stillness."
When stillness merges, it returns to the limit of consciousness. When stillness enters [consciousness], it is called "consciousness"; when it is true stillness, it is called "wisdom.

Wisdom and consciousness together are termed the "limit of consciousness. Wisdom is the nature of consciousness’s clear knowing; its nature pervades the Dharma-realm, and thus there is no coming or going.
When stillness emerges, it becomes the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*); formations are like flowing water. When stillness enters, consciousness ceases and formations subside.
The aggregate of form (rūpa-skandha): when one enters inwardly into the profound clarity within the source of perception (saṃjñā), there is ultimately nothing to enter.

This limit of consciousness is the most difficult to exhaustively realize, except through the power of samādhi and wisdom attained by the Tathāgatas and the Bodhisattvas dwelling on the stages (bhūmi).

Only then can one ultimately reach the stage of non-delusion. As for the samādhi and wisdom attained by those of the two vehicles or external paths, they do not transcend a state of profound stillness and immovability;
yet this stillness is not the ultimate truth, being like a rapid current that appears tranquil from a distance.
Moment by moment they receive perfuming, ultimately returning to birth and extinction. How could one hope to comprehend the unarisen and undying with a mind of birth and extinction?
Only those remaining who practice according to reality within my Dharma can, through the power of wisdom, [attain this].

Having thoroughly understood the characteristics of the various stages (*bhūmi*) and already attained the rank of a Bodhisattva dwelling in the stages, they first abandon the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*).
They are well able to discern and decisively judge the subtle meanings and phrases at the limits of consciousness and wisdom.

It is not that they have planted roots of goodness under only one, two, three, four, or five Buddhas; rather, they have planted all manner of roots of goodness under immeasurable tens of millions of Buddhas. Well...
The faculties reach maturity and habitual tendencies dissolve. One has already become free from the false conceptualizations manifested by one's own mind;
conceptualization is consciousness (*vijñāna*), while non-conceptualization is wisdom (*jñāna*). Only when one is able to transform consciousness into wisdom can one then discern with that wisdom.
How could this be the result of a single morning or evening? It arises from practicing what is to be abandoned through cultivation while dwelling in mountain forests in meditative seclusion.

It is attained. By cultivating the lower, middle, and upper grades within each of the nine stages of the three realms, one investigates them with subtle discernment until the stage of no-more-learning (*aśaikṣa*) is realized and wisdom manifests before one.
Thus, one is able to perceive the subtle habitual tendencies of the continuous flow of one's own mind’s delusive imaginings.
It is like the rippling waves when there is no wind. That which the followers of the Two Vehicles do not perceive, I am able to know in its every detail.
Such a person is one who truly perceives the nature (*dharmatā*). For those who have not yet seen the nature, the nature resides within consciousness; the nature turns along with consciousness.
Therefore, they are unable to awaken. Only those who perceive the nature (xing) find that this nature transcends consciousness;

since consciousness and nature are separated, one can observe the continuous flow of delusive thoughts (*vikalpa*). Those who enter the samādhi of dhyāna do not perceive this subtle flow and falsely claim that consciousness has ceased;
how could they ever reach the ultimate limit of consciousness? Baizhang said: "The monk Zhao [Sengzhao] spoke of the Way of Bodhi..."
It cannot be schemed or measured; it is high with nothing above it, vast beyond limit, profound with nothing below it, and deep beyond fathom.

To speak of it is like setting up a target only to draw an arrow upon it; even to say that present awareness (*jue*) is [the Way] is still not it. To distinguish the clear from the turbid and allow that present awareness is [the Way] is permissible for the time being;
yet apart from this present awareness, to claim there is anything else is entirely the talk of demons. If one merely clings to it as such...
Now, to claim that present awareness is likewise the teaching of demons is also called the "Natural Heretics.
To say that present awareness is one's own Buddha is a limited statement, a conceptual fabrication; it is like the howling of a jackal and still belongs to the gate of sticky attachment.
From the very beginning, they fail to recognize that self-knowing and self-awakening are their own Buddha, instead rushing outward in pursuit of a Buddha elsewhere.
A good spiritual friend provisionally teaches "self-knowing" and "self-awakening" as medicine to treat the illness of seeking outwardly.
Once the illness of outward-seeking has ceased, the medicine must be discarded. If one clings to self-knowing and self-awakening, this is the illness of *dhyāna*;
it is the ultimate *śrāvaka*. It is like water turning into ice: though the ice is entirely water, it is difficult for that ice to quench thirst.

Wang [Zhe] states: According to Baizhang’s words, as for what the sutras describe—the stream of one's own mind's delusive thoughts—although this is reflective awareness (*jñāna*), one must not cling to it as being correct.
Only by doing so can one transform consciousness into wisdom (*jñāna*).
He has received the empowerment of all Buddhas throughout immeasurable lands; he has attained the power of mastery, the superknowledges (*abhijñā*), and samādhis;

he is surrounded by spiritual friends and the retinue of Buddha-sons. He has completely transcended the realms of the nature of mind as manifested by his own mind—namely, the mental faculty (*manas*), the intellect (*manovijñāna*), and the objects of self-nature—as well as false conceptions, the ocean of birth and death, karma, craving, and ignorance. Therefore, O Great...
Wisdom. All practitioners should draw near to the most excellent spiritual friend.
It is said that one who practices according to reality can perceive the continuous flow of their own mind’s delusive thoughts;
thus, they are no longer driven by the flow of delusive thoughts, but are able to master it, causing the habitual tendencies of falsehood to be cast far away in that very instant.
Being thus detached, one is immediately able to realize and enter the realm of the Dharmakāya, connecting one's vital essence (*prāṇa*) with that of the Tathāgatas of the ten directions.
Consequently, the Buddhas of immeasurable lands bestow empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) upon them, and they are soon to succeed to the rank of Tathāgata.
They attain the power of mastery, supernatural faculties (*abhijñā*), and samādhis, naturally surrounded by a retinue of Buddha-sons. This is truly because, regarding the mind...
The mind and mental consciousness truly understand that what is manifested from one's own mind is the realm of self-nature;

this nature is fundamentally unarisen and fundamentally unceasing. If the conceptualizations of false discrimination sink into the ocean of suffering within the cycle of birth and death in the three realms, they take the six consciousnesses as their cause.
If the karma of defilement and purity relies upon attachment to the conceit of "self-love," it takes...
The seven consciousnesses act as causes. If fundamental ignorance acts as the cause through its habitual tendencies and seeds, it takes the eight consciousnesses as its cause.

Having completely transcended all such causes, when the eight consciousnesses function simultaneously, this is termed "correct wisdom" (*samyagjñāna*). When delusive conceptualization is thus abandoned, [this state is realized].
This is precisely suchness (tathatā). This is what is called the supreme spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra).
The various wondrous Dharma-gates regarding the ocean-like dharmas of the ālayavijñāna and the realm of the Dharmakāya, which were previously explained, reach their ultimate consummation only here.
Therefore, all practitioners should draw near to the supreme spiritual friend to enter the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; they must not [rely on] those of the two vehicles or external paths.
Devoured by evil views, Baizhang said: "The great body is hidden within the formless; the great sound is concealed within the rarefied silence.
It is like fire within wood, or like the resonance of bells and drums; when the conditions have not yet assembled, one cannot speak of its existence or non-existence.
Those born in the intermediate states or in the heavens cast it aside like mucus and spittle. The Bodhisattva’s six perfections and myriad practices are like mounting [a vehicle]."
A corpse has crossed over to the other shore, as if having escaped from a prison or through a latrine hole.
The Buddha’s thirty-two marks are like garments covered in grime and oil; it is also said that to claim the Buddha never at all receives the five aggregates is impossible.
The Buddha is not empty space; how could he never receive them? The Buddha simply comes and goes of his own accord.
Because they differ from ordinary sentient beings, traveling from one celestial realm to another and from one buddha-field to another, it should be known that this is the constant law of all Buddhas:
that these most excellent spiritual friends manifest through the dharma-body, supernatural powers, and samādhis, which are truly inconceivable. Therefore, those in training should draw near to them.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Just as the vast ocean waves arise from the forceful wind, Great billows surge through the dark abyss without ceasing;
The storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is likewise ever-abiding, Stirred by the winds of objective realms, Various waves of consciousness leap forth and arise."
Blue, red, and various other colors; conch shells, milk, and rock honey; subtle flavors and diverse flowers and fruits;
the sun and moon and their radiance—these are neither different nor not different. Just as waves arise from the ocean, so too are the seven consciousnesses.
They arise in conjunction with the mind, just as the ocean transforms into various shifting waves; so too do the seven consciousnesses arise in conjunction with the mind.
Tong said: "This verse describes how external objects cause the ocean of the mind to be tossed about, such that the waves of consciousness do not cease.

This is due to the perceived characteristics being either different or non-different. Blue and red refer to the object-field of visible form; the sound of a conch shell refers to the object-field of sound; and milk and incense refer to the object-fields of smell."
Rock honey represents the taste-object (*rasa-viṣaya*); flowers and fruits represent the dharma-object (*dharma-viṣaya*), which refers to phenomena such as cause and effect.

The sun and moon are metaphors for the essence (*svabhāva*); their radiance is a metaphor for function (*vṛtti*). Just as a lump of clay and its subtle particles are neither different nor non-different, so too the eight consciousnesses constitute the essence and the various [evolving] consciousnesses constitute the function.
Objects arise from consciousness, and consciousness arises from objects; both are manifestations of one's own mind, and are not [independent entities].
They are neither different nor not different. These two phrases apply to the seven consciousnesses as well. They arise in conjunction with the mind (*citta*).

First, the seven consciousnesses arise externally by depending on the six consciousnesses and combining with the marks of the karma they perform. Second, the seven consciousnesses arise internally by depending on the eighth consciousness and combining with the causal marks.
Regarding their dependence on the six consciousnesses: it is like the great ocean water serving as the objective sphere (*viṣaya*).

The wind stirs the waves, which arise in succession, one after another, without interruption. It is just the same with the seven consciousnesses: externally, they harmonize with the six consciousnesses.
As for their reliance upon the eighth consciousness, it is like the seawater, clear and tranquil, eternally abiding;
yet suddenly it surges and transforms. When the first movement of a single thought arises, the various consciousnesses flow forth because of it. The seventh consciousness adheres...
The profound emergence of cognition is likewise thus: it internally harmonizes with the eight consciousnesses. Huangbo said:
"That which is one refined brilliance is divided into six harmonious unions. "One refined brilliance" refers to the One Mind; "six harmonious unions" refers to the six sense faculties.
These six faculties each harmonize with their respective objects: the eye harmonizes with form, the ear with sound, and the nose with...

The nose meets with fragrance; the tongue meets with flavor; the body meets with touch; and the mind meets with mental objects (*dharma*). From their meeting in the interval, the six consciousnesses arise, forming the eighteen realms (*dhātu*).
If one realizes that these eighteen realms are non-existent, one binds these six harmonious combinations into a single refined spirit.
This single refined spirit is precisely the mind. Those who study the Way all know this mind, yet they cannot avoid acting as a single entity.
Being clever and discerning regarding the sixfold harmony of the Sangha, you have instead become bound by the Dharma; thus, you do not accord with your original mind. Alas!
Since you are bound by the Dharma, you are driven by consciousness. How can you hope to behold the ever-abiding countenance of the ocean of the *ālayavijñāna*?

That is to say, within the locus of that storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), various consciousnesses evolve. This means that by means of that mental consciousness (manovijñāna), one contemplates the meanings of various signs;

yet these signs are not destroyed. There are eight [consciousnesses], yet they are signless, and even signlessness is signless. (The Tang translation states: "Mind, thought, and mental consciousness constitute the characteristics of consciousness; therefore, it is said that the eight consciousnesses have no distinct characteristics, for there is neither the characteristic-maker nor the characterized.
Just as waves in the ocean are thus without distinction, so too the various differences among the consciousnesses and the mind cannot be [ultimately] established.

[In the two translations, there is no mention of the "seven consciousnesses being likewise. This is a complex sentence concerning the mind arising in conjunction with its associates. It simply states: "For example, as the ocean water moves and various waves arise, so too do the various consciousnesses arise from the ālayavijñāna."

The commentary states: The preceding verse praises how the waves of the evolving consciousnesses arise and are not non-different; this subsequent section praises that the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) is not different [from them].

Because the storehouse consciousness is caused by inconceivable perfuming and inconceivable transformation, the eight evolving [consciousnesses] arise from it, the seven evolve from the six, and they simultaneously and successively act as causes for one another.
Yet each is unaware of the others; they are fundamentally quiescent from the beginning. Thus, it is said of that storehouse [consciousness]:

Regarding the transformation of various consciousnesses within the sphere of consciousness (*vijñānāyatana*): it is merely that the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) discriminates among them, contemplating the meanings of the characteristics of these various consciousnesses, and designating them as "this is the seventh consciousness," "this is the fifth consciousness," or "this is the sixth consciousness," which is called the arising of various waves of consciousness.
If one perceives them as distinct, in reality there is only the single eighth consciousness; there is nothing else.
Regarding distinct characteristics: there is neither a characteristicizer nor a characterized. For example, various waves are but a single body of great ocean water;
there is no further differentiation. Thus, it would be incorrect to say that small waves and large waves are different from the ocean water.
All consciousnesses and the mind are likewise: though they transform, in reality they do not transform. Therefore, it is said that even difference does not exist.
It can be so understood. Generally speaking, that which is subject to destruction is seen as having distinctions; because there is a perceiving subject and a perceived object, it is destructible.
Now, the eight consciousnesses are far removed from subject and object, and thus they are without marks (*animitta*). Even the mark of being "without mark" is itself non-existent.
It is the essence of pure, wondrous stillness; therefore, it cannot be destroyed. That it is signless (*animitta*) means it is unarisen (*anutpanna*).
That even signlessness is signless means it is undestroyed (*aniruddha*). Because it is neither arisen nor destroyed, it is called the ocean of the *ālayavijñāna*, which abides eternally;
who then could destroy it? Since it is indestructible, it is non-different. Formerly, the Venerable Hārītīputra asked twenty-two [questions].
The Patriarch said, "By what karmic conditions have I moved this flock of cranes? The Patriarch continued, "In the fourth kalpa, you were constantly a bhikṣu.
You were about to attend a gathering at the Dragon Palace, and all your disciples wished to follow you.

You observed that among your five hundred followers, not a single person was capable of receiving such sublime offerings. At that time, your disciples said, 'Master, you constantly preach the Dharma...'"
If one is equal regarding food, one must likewise be equal regarding the Dharma; since this is not the case now, how can you be considered a sage?
You shall go to the assembly yourself. From that time forth, you have abandoned this life to seek rebirth, converting various kingdoms.

As for your five hundred disciples, because their merit was slight and their virtue thin, they were born among the feathered tribes. Now, moved by your kindness, they have come as a flock of cranes to follow you.
[The disciple] asked: "By what skillful means can you cause them to attain liberation? The Patriarch said: "I possess the unsurpassed treasure of the Dharma;

you should listen and receive it so that it may transform beings until the end of time. He then spoke this verse: "The mind turns following the myriad objects; In the place where it turns, it is truly profound.
If, following the flow, one recognizes one's nature, There will be neither joy nor sorrow. Upon hearing the verse, the flock of cranes flew away crying out.
And so they depart. If one realizes the true nature of the place where [consciousness] turns, its essence is profoundly still and naturally suchness (*tathatā*);

how could there be any difference? "Mind" (*citta*) is named for the accumulation of karma; "intellect" (*manas*) is named for the extensive accumulation [of objects]; and "consciousnesses" (*vijñāna*) refer to the various cognitions that perceive manifest objects and so forth—these are called the five [sensory consciousnesses].

(The Wei translation says: "The mind can accumulate all karmas; the intellect can contemplate the accumulated objects; consciousness can discern what is cognized; the five consciousnesses perform present discrimination.")
The Master replied: "The various consciousnesses are fundamentally not different from one another. Why, then, are there different names?
It is simply because when the single thought-moment first moves, there are no lack of gradations of depth; each is given its name based on its predominant function.

When it receives perfuming, maintains seeds, and accumulates both defiled and pure karma—encompassing everything—it is called 'citta' (mind) and is designated as the eighth consciousness. It has not yet flowed [into the other modes].

Regarding the mind (*manas*), it flows into consciousness (*vijñāna*). From its biased attachment to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*), it constantly and critically deliberates, transmitting and entering and exiting, and extensively accumulating various karmas;
thus it is called the "mind" and serves as the seventh consciousness. Although it has not yet entered into [the sensory] consciousnesses, it has already departed from the [pure] mind (*citta*).
While the eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, and other consciousnesses are all forms of consciousness, only the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*) is capable of...
The sixth consciousness is so named because it discriminates the objects perceived by the first five [consciousnesses];

although it can also discern past objects of the five sense-fields, it is called the "present consciousness" (*xiànshí*) because the first five consciousnesses manifest only when facing their respective objects and cease to exist when separated from them.
Regarding the mental consciousness (*yìshí*), its power is the strongest; it is capable of discrimination even regarding the eighth and seventh consciousnesses, not only those of the five senses.

It is simply the preceding five [aggregates]. Although mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*) have three names, when they reside in the mind, they are the mind-as-thought and the mind-as-consciousness;
when they reside in the thought, they are the thought-as-mind and the thought-as-consciousness;
and when they reside in the consciousness, they are the consciousness-as-mind and the consciousness-as-thought. It is just as waves are the waves of the sea and the surges of the sea.
How could one possibly achieve something different? Chan Master Qinglin Jian ascended the hall and said: "Under the gate of the Patriarchs, the bird-path is profound and subtle;

when effort reaches its limit, it must turn back, for if one does not investigate thoroughly, it is difficult to clarify. You all must directly transcend mind, intellect, and consciousness to investigate;
only by learning to emerge from the paths of ordinary and sage can you maintain this realization. If you do not act thus, you are not my true heirs."

Therefore, as long as one has not yet transcended mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*), one does not encounter a single person; this still pertains to the realm of meritorious achievement.
When merit is transformed into its proper station and one no longer traverses the "Bird Path," one is able to transcend both the ordinary and the sage, and roam within the ocean of nature.
At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati asked in verse:
"Blue, red, and all other forms and images cause sentient beings to give rise to various consciousnesses, like the manifold waves of the sea; how is this so? I pray that you will explain it."
At that time, the World-Honored One replied in verse:
"Blue, red, and all various colors—waves do not exist at all. The mind is taught as the accumulation of karma, in order to awaken all ordinary beings."
Those karmas do not exist at all; they are detached from what is grasped by one’s own mind. There is no grasping and nothing to be grasped, which is identical to those waves.

(The Tang translation says: "Various forms such as blue and red cannot be found within the waves; it is said that the mind gives rise to manifold marks to awaken ordinary people, yet they fundamentally do not arise.
