their intrinsic nature is such that one consequently clings to these three unconditioned dharmas as being truly existent entities. This nature is remote from both existence and non-existence, transcending both being and non-being.
Yet, what they conceive of as "remote from existence and non-existence" refers to all dharmas being like the horns of rabbits or horses.
Originally, there is neither existence by means of form nor non-existence by means of formlessness; it is only through the discrimination of existence and non-existence that one perceives them.
Having already departed from existence, people are unable to see this and yet claim for themselves the nature of *nirvāṇa*.
It is like one with cataracts looking into the sky and seeing the illusory spinning of hair, claiming that they alone perceive it.
To see [something] and yet instead blame others for not seeing it, taking this to be a departure from non-existence—this is merely an attachment to existence and non-existence.
It is simply what appears before a cataract-afflicted eye; it is not a true departure from existence and non-existence.

If one were truly departing from existence and non-existence, one would not perceive things like the horns of rabbits or horses as being either existent or nonexistent; one would simply be free from both existence and nonexistence.
The wondrous nature of Nirvāṇa, which is the true essence transcending Nirvāṇa itself, is such that how could it ever be fathomed by non-Buddhists?
Therefore, one should know that the "nature" established by them is not a truly existent nature, but rather the establishment of a conceptual mark (*nimitta*).

When these four [extremes] are established, they constitute the view of eternalism (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*); when these same four are denied, they constitute the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*). All of these—

Fools lack wisdom and do not skillfully examine that all things—the manifestations of one's own mind, the sense organs, the body, and the vessel-world—appear as existing yet are not truly existent; how can they grasp them as being permanent?

Furthermore, since they eventually cease, they are not truly non-existent; how can they grasp them as being annihilated? These are the evil views of permanence and annihilation. They are not [the truth].
"This is the possession of the sages and worthies. You should all turn toward the sages and worthies;
you ought to skillfully observe that which is the manifestation of your own mind, for this will keep you far removed from the two faults.

The Buddha-nature of my son is like a straight hook; from the start he sought only the fish that offered their lives. Seeking the scent and chasing the fragrance, this traveler of clouds and water creates a clamorous and confused distinction.
He unfolds it levelly and spreads it out grandly—do not blame me for being careless at the beginning.
To point out flaws and then reclaim the jade is the way of Lord Qin, who did not recognize Lord Lin Xiangru. If one acts with universal penetration, such things do not occur.

If the Way of the household exists within non-existence, it possesses the path of transcendence at that very moment; once one falls into the duality of existence and non-existence, one becomes estranged from it and is not far from the evil views of external paths.
Furthermore, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva well understands the mind, mentation, consciousness, the five dharmas, and the two natures.
Being free from the mark of self and tending toward the ultimate, they manifest various kinds of forms for the sake of bringing peace to sentient beings,
just as the imagined nature exists based upon dependent origination. For example, like a multicolored wish-fulfilling jewel,
they appear universally in all Buddha-fields and assemblies of all Tathāgatas, wherein they listen to and receive the Buddha-dharma, namely:

All phenomena are like illusions, dreams, reflections, and the moon in water; regarding all phenomena, they are free from arising and ceasing, and free from the extremes of annihilation and permanence, as well as the dharmas of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas.
They attain hundreds of thousands of samādhis, even up to hundreds of thousands of koṭi-nayutas (here meaning ten trillion) of samādhis.
Having attained these samādhis, they travel through the buddha-fields, make offerings to the Buddhas, and are born among the devas.
The King proclaimed the Three Jewels, manifesting the body of a Buddha surrounded by a great assembly of śrāvakas and bodhisattvas.

Measuring and liberating sentient beings through the direct realization of what is manifested by one's own mind (*svacittadṛśyamātra*), he analytically expounded that external natures have no inherent existence (the Tang translation states: "He taught that external objects [and their fruits] are all merely mind").
He caused them all to remain far removed from views such as existence and non-existence. At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

The sons of the Buddha observe that this world is the measure of mind; they manifest various bodies, free from conditioned activity, and achieve mastery over the powers and supernormal faculties (the Tang translation reads:

"The sons of the Buddha are able to observe that the world is a mere manifestation of mind; they display various bodies, and their unimpeded supernormal powers and mastery in all actions are fully accomplished").
The interlocutor asked: "Regarding what was stated in the preceding passage—that one should skillfully observe the direct manifestation (*pratyakṣa*) of one's own mind—what are its details?

This direct manifestation of one's own mind is nothing other than the mind (*citta*), the intellect (*manas*), the consciousness (*vijñāna*), the five dharmas, and the three natures (*trisvabhāva*). All that appears is but the manifestation of *cittamātra* (mind-only).

When following defilement, it constitutes names, signs, and false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), which is the nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*) based on false conceptualization. When conjoined with awakening, it becomes the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*)."

Wisdom that is suchness (tathatā) constitutes its own intrinsic nature; it abandons the prior defiled conditions as the characteristic of the non-self of persons (pudgala-nairātmya), and abandons the subsequent conditions regarding phenomena as the characteristic of the non-self of dharmas (dharma-nairātmya).
By skillfully knowing these characteristics and proceeding toward suchness, one attains ultimate nirvāṇa and realizes the unborn and undying.
For the sake of bringing peace to sentient beings, one manifests various forms according to their capacities.
Transformational guidance arises from the dependent origination of the nature of imagined reality (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), conditioned by the nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*).
It takes the power of compassionate vows as its condition and the non-abandonment of sentient beings as its conceptualization.
Just as a *maṇi* jewel can manifest all colors and change according to objects, it manifests all Buddha-lands and universally enters all assemblies.
One listens to and receives all true dharmas, namely: that all dharmas are like illusions, like dreams, like light, like shadows, and like the moon reflected in water;
they cannot be grasped as existent, nor can they be grasped as non-existent;

one remains far removed from the dharmas of arising and ceasing characteristic of ordinary beings, far removed from the dharmas of annihilation and permanence characteristic of externalists, and free from the biased emptiness of the two vehicles.
This is because those ordinary beings cling to duality and followers of the Two Vehicles cling to emptiness; neither understands that all phenomena are like illusions.

Now, by hearing and receiving the Buddha-dharma, one attains the illusion-like samādhi, thereby immediately obtaining hundreds of thousands of samādhis, even traveling through various Buddha-lands to make offerings to the Tathāgatas, manifesting the body of a Buddha and preaching the Dharma for the sake of the multitude—yet all this is but one’s own mind.
Through direct perception, one realizes that the three realms are the Dharma of Mind-only, thereby liberating sentient beings.
One teaches that external objects—whether non-existent or existent—are all devoid of an obtainable self-nature, being like dreams, illusions, reflections of light, or the moon in water.
To say they exist is incorrect; to say they do not exist is also incorrect. Thus, one remains far removed from views of existence and non-existence.

Merely by being free from the errors of arising and ceasing, or of annihilation and permanence, and further by departing from the faults of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, one brings peace to sentient beings, and thus those beings obtain peace.
How could those of the external paths or the two vehicles—who hold views of existence and non-existence—ever be able to manifest such supernatural transformations? As it is said:
Regarding "the measure of what is manifested by one's own mind," this is further detailed in the verse:

"O Son of the Buddha, because one observes that the world is manifested solely as the measure of mind, one is able to manifest various physical forms and perform various spiritual powers without obstruction.
One attains great mastery such that actions proceed without deliberate effort, for one has ultimately realized the absence of self."

"It is merely that which is accomplished through the Illusion-like Samādhi; it is not a true vision. How could those who see the three realms as being solely mind possibly possess such an auspicious omen?
Master Xianshen of Rendu ascended the hall and said: "The arising of all dharmas is manifested solely by the mind.
Such words are an excellent gateway for entry. Now, I ask you all: when you see all things with your eyes..."
The eyes see all forms; the ears hear all sounds; the nose smells all fragrances; the tongue discerns all flavors;
the body touches all objects of sensation; and the mind discriminates all dharmas.
Now, regarding these objects encountered by the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, and mind—are they your own minds, or are they not your own minds? If you say they are...
If your minds were one with your bodies, why would the objects encountered by them remain outside your eyes,
ears, nose, tongue, and bodies? If you say that the objects encountered by the eyes,
ears, nose, and tongue are not your mind, how can you account for the fact that all phenomena [arise] from it?
Birth is a manifestation of mind-only; as for these words remaining in the world, who would not raise them up?
Do you all understand this statement? If you do not, everyone must apply your minds and deliberate together to learn it.
Be diligent within this and do not grow weary of study; when there is nothing more to do, you may withdraw. Such phrases as these are not mere idle talk.
Once understood, one must rest; only when there is actual realization is there a portion of liberation.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again requested of the Buddha, saying:
"I pray only that the World-Honored One will explain for us and for all other Bodhisattvas the characteristics of the emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and absence of self-nature of all dharmas."

When the multitude has awakened to this emptiness—unborn, non-dual, and free from the marks of intrinsic nature—and has abandoned the conceptual constructions of existence and non-existence, they will swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, saying:
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall now explain it to you in detail."

Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your teaching. The Buddha told Mahāmati, “Mahāmati, that which is called ‘emptiness of emptiness’ (śūnyatā-śūnyatā) is the locus of the imagined nature (parikalpita-svabhāva).
Mahāmati, for those who are attached to the imagined nature, I speak of emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and the characteristic of being devoid of self-nature.”
Tong said: "The Great Wisdom (Mahāmati) was told by the Buddha to remain far removed from views such as existence and non-existence.

That which is called 'all phenomena are like illusions, like dreams, like reflections, and like the moon in water' is precisely the dharma of emptiness, the dharma of non-arising, the dharma of non-duality, and the dharma that is free from the marks of intrinsic nature. By means of all phenomena, one returns to the quiescence of the single mind."

Because directly revealing the emptiness of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-śūnyatā*) is the supreme, correct, and final state of Bodhi, Mahāmati again made this request, and the World-Honored One extensively analyzed and explained it point by point.
He first stated that "emptiness of emptiness" (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*) refers precisely to the locus of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*);
these few words alone may be called a direct pointing to the human mind, whereby one sees one's nature and attains Buddhahood.
That which is "emptiness of emptiness" is empty yet not empty; this is called true emptiness (*bhūta-śūnyatā*).

The entire substance of true emptiness is delusion, and the entire substance of delusion is emptiness. Just as lust, anger, and ignorance are delusions, the nature of lust, anger, and ignorance is true emptiness.
True emptiness fundamentally admits of no verbal expression, yet it is spoken of as empty, unborn, non-dual, and devoid of self-nature.
"Characteristics" refers to what is taught for those who give rise to conceptual attachment toward the nature of imagined existence:

because of attachment to existence, emptiness is taught; because of attachment to arising and ceasing, non-arising is taught; because of attachment to the duality of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa, non-duality is taught;
and because of attachment to the notion that a nature of nirvāṇa can be attained, the absence of intrinsic nature is taught.
The characteristics [of phenomena] are none other than the manifestation of the ultimate truth of true emptiness.

If one can realize that the self-nature of deluded thoughts is fundamentally beyond words and speech, one will immediately realize unsurpassed bodhi. Tian Tong cites the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (the *Complete Enlightenment Sūtra*), saying:
"At all times, do not give rise to deluded thoughts; do not attempt to extinguish the various deluded minds; do not dwell upon delusion."
Do not apply further cognitive awareness to the objects of thought; do not fail to recognize that which lacks cognitive awareness, nor fail to discern the reality.
The verse says: Majestic and grand, towering and vast; thrusting the head into the clamor, planting the feet in stability. When the thread beneath the feet snaps, I am free.
When the clay at the tip of the nose is exhausted, rest where you dwell without carving. Do not move it! It is contained within the ancient paper of a thousand years.
The *Song of Realizing the Way* by Yaowu Jingjia says: "Let go of the four elements; do not grasp at them. Within the nature of quiescent extinction, follow along with eating and drinking.
All conditioned phenomena are impermanent and entirely empty—this is the Tathāgata’s Great Perfect Enlightenment.
The words of these two venerable masters emerge as if from a single mouth; they may truly be called those who have forgotten both the real and the false, and who are refreshingly free.

Mahāmati, briefly stated, there are seven kinds of emptiness: the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of self-nature (*svabhāva-svabhāva-śūnyatā*)—[the Wei translation says:

"the emptiness of the existence and non-existence of all dharmas"]—the emptiness of activity (*kriyā-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of non-activity (*akriyā-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of all dharmas being beyond verbal expression (*sarvadharma-nirabhilāpya-śūnyatā*), the emptiness of the ultimate reality of noble wisdom (*paramārtha-āryajñāna-mahā-śūnyatā*), and the emptiness of this and that (*itaretara-śūnyatā*).

What is the emptiness of characteristics? It means that all natures are empty of both specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), because they are observed to be merely accumulations of successive [causal] aggregations.
Because the self-nature and common characteristics of conceptualized things do not arise from self, other, or both, and because they lack inherent nature, their characteristics do not abide;
therefore, it is said that all natures and characteristics are empty. This is called the emptiness of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*).

Tong said, "According to the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-sūtra*, there are twenty kinds of emptiness, namely: internal emptiness, external emptiness, internal-and-external emptiness, emptiness of emptiness, and so forth.
This [text] merely briefly explains seven kinds of emptiness. However, 'emptiness of characteristics' (*lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā*) is the emptiness of form (*rūpa*);

'emptiness of self-nature' (*svabhāva-śūnyatā*) is the emptiness of sensation (*vedanā*); 'emptiness of activity' (*karma-śūnyatā*) is the emptiness of formations (*saṃskāra*); and 'emptiness of non-activity' (*akarma-śūnyatā*) is the emptiness of consciousness (*vijñāna*)."

Emptiness that transcends verbal expression, the emptiness of conceptualization, and the emptiness of the five aggregates are all the total distancing from the false imaginings of existence and non-existence;
they constitute the Great Emptiness of the ultimate meaning and noble wisdom. Since one is already freed from these five through the preceding [analysis], true nature manifests spontaneously.
As for "mutual emptiness" (*itaretara-śūnyatā*), it is merely the wrong view of the outsiders (*tīrthika*), who seek emptiness only within the context of various existing and non-existing phenomena.
Not knowing the emptiness of intrinsic nature, what is meant by the emptiness of characteristics? It means that all self-characteristics and common characteristics are empty.

By observing the aggregates (*skandhas*), one sees them as a successive accumulation of elements that exist in mutual dependence; when analyzed and investigated, they are ultimately found to lack inherent nature.
Thus, neither self-nature, other-nature, nor their combination can give rise to phenomena. As it is said: "All dharmas do not arise from themselves, nor do they arise from others..."

Because arising from another is not possible, nor is it causeless, it is therefore said that there is no arising. This is because self-nature, other-nature, and both together are all devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If there were self-nature, its own characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) would be perceivable; if there were other-nature, the characteristic of the other would be perceivable;
if there were both natures, the characteristics of both would be perceivable. Now, since it is neither from self, nor from another, nor from both...
Since all things abide by depending upon one another, all phenomena lack intrinsic nature, and their characteristic is emptiness.
This is what is meant by "dependent origination without intrinsic nature" and "arising yet not arising. It is not the same as the heterodox views that conceive of total annihilation.
Tian Tong cites the Sūtra, saying: "If one sees all marks as non-marks, one sees the Tathāgata. Fayuan says: "If one sees all..."
"Phenomena and non-phenomena are such that one does not see the Tathāgata. Tiandong [Tianran] held up his whisk and said:

"The World-Honored One speaks of Tathāgata Chan; Fayan speaks of Patriarchal Chan. Those who understand it find it most extraordinary; those who do not understand it are permitted by the 'Phenomena' (xiang).
Later, Wansong praised himself, saying: "All phenomena whatsoever are empty and illusory. If you see all phenomena as non-phenomena, you will see the eyebrows."
When the hairs on the eyes point upward, the World-Honored One’s Dharma-eye demarcates boundaries and establishes realms through skillful means;
by penetrating these three kinds of discourse, one clearly realizes the true limit where marks are empty.
What is the emptiness of intrinsic nature? It means that the intrinsic nature of itself does not arise; this is called the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.
Therefore, it is said to be the emptiness of intrinsic nature.

The interlocutor said: "The previous statement—that the self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and the common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) do not arise because they lack the nature of being produced from self, other, or both, and thus characteristics do not abide—does not mean that these characteristics do not exist at all.
Rather, characteristics lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); when they would arise, they do not arise. This emptiness of characteristics results from the emptiness of intrinsic nature.
Here, the term 'intrinsic nature' (*svabhāva*) is used in contrast to 'other-nature' (*parabhāva*), meaning that which is grasped as one's own."

To grasp the nature of external phenomena is precisely the aggregate of sensation (*vedanā-skandha*). Whether one is in a state where not a single thought arises—which is called "non-arising"—or whether thoughts repeatedly arise in response to objects, they are inherently non-arising.
Because the self-nature and characteristics of all phenomena are empty of both existence and non-existence, they are termed the "emptiness of things and non-things.
Master Nianchan of Amitāyus said: "When the minds of self and others arise, as for the place of their arising..."
Without trace, the self-mind is forgotten; in this forgetting, there is no mark of extinction.
This passage provides a great revelation regarding the fact that the intrinsic nature of all dharmas is emptiness. Huangbo, ascending the hall, said: "The mind itself is Buddha.
From the Buddhas above down to the wriggling insects and sentient beings below, all possess Buddha-nature; they share the same single mind-body. Therefore, Bodhidharma came from the West...
The Celestial One’s coming was solely to transmit the Dharma of the One Mind, pointing directly that all sentient beings are originally Buddhas without depending on cultivation.
Simply recognize your own mind as it is now and see your own original nature; do not seek anything else.
How does one recognize one's own mind? That which is speaking right now is precisely your mind. If you do not speak, nor...
The essence of the functioning mind is like empty space: it has no characteristics and no location;
yet it is not simply non-existent, for it cannot be seen. As the Patriarch said: "The treasury of the true nature within the mind has neither head nor tail;
responding to conditions to transform beings, it is expediently called 'wisdom. If it does not respond to conditions..."
Time cannot be said to exist or not to exist; even at the very moment it is present, it leaves no trace.
Knowing this to be so, if you now simply dwell within non-existence, that is precisely walking the path of all Buddhas.

What is the emptiness of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra-śūnyatā*)? It refers to the fact that the aggregates (*skandha*) arise through the conjunction of karma and causes, and are produced by means of actions and conditions;

they are devoid of a self (*ātman*) and what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*). This is called the emptiness of conditioned phenomena. (The Tang translation states: "That is to say, the various aggregates arise from the combination of karma and causes; being devoid of a self and what belongs to a self, this is called the emptiness of conditioned phenomena.")

Tong said: "The marks (*lakṣaṇa*) are empty externally and their nature (*svabhāva*) is empty internally; yet that which continues uninterrupted within this interval is the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*).

By what means is it emptied? It is said that the aggregate of formations is empty internally because it is devoid of a self (*ātman*), and empty externally because it is devoid of what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*).
The aggregate of formations is precisely the seven consciousnesses (*vijñāna*); these seven consciousnesses internally rely upon the eighth consciousness."
The grasping at the mark of a self is the cause of the mark of self; it arises through the initial movement of the eight consciousnesses and the expedient means of their conjunction.
Since the seventh consciousness cannot be established without the eighth, it is said to be "accomplished by way of its cause.

As for the external grasping at the mark of what belongs to a self (*mama-kāra*), this "what belongs to me" arises from the conjunction of the marks of defiled and pure karma produced by the six consciousnesses.
Thus, the seven consciousnesses arise and are transmitted, entering and exiting; originally they have no fixed locus.

This "I" and "mine" are fundamentally detached from the nature of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), which is itself empty by nature. Therefore, it is called the "emptiness of formations. Master Kaixian Zhao ascended the hall and said:

"The regulations of the monastic community and the family style of the ancient Buddhas consist of one period of inquiry, one request for instruction, and one meal of gruel and rice. But tell me, what does this clarify?"
What is it like? It is as if the minds of all people do not rest and their thoughts do not abide;

if one can rest where there is no resting and be without thought where there is no abiding, one naturally accords with the principle of non-arising. To speak in such a way is to laugh the mouths of others to pieces. Investigate this;
only when you investigate until you penetrate through will you believe that all conditioned phenomena are fundamentally empty. If, regarding that which does not rest and does not abide—
Mahāmati, the merit of practicing the counteractive measures remains very far off.

It is precisely in this way that one practices the emptiness of non-action (*anabhisamskāra-śūnyatā*); because the self-nature of dependent origination is itself without self-nature, it is called the emptiness of non-action (the Tang translation states:
"That which is called the fact that the aggregates are originally in nirvāṇa and lack all conditioned activities is named the emptiness of non-action").

The Master said: "When these activities have already become empty, one reaches the state of profound stillness (*zhan*), unmoving. When this stillness flows outward, it is called 'various activities' (*zhuxing*);
when this stillness flows inward until there is nowhere for it to enter, it is called 'no-activity' (*wuxing*).

'No-activity' means that the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is originally *nirvāṇa* and possesses no activities; therefore, various activities perfume and form seeds, and these seeds perfume..."

The arising of all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) occurs through successive dependent origination; they do not arise of themselves, but arise from conditions. Their cessation does not occur of itself, but ceases through conditions.

Since their arising and cessation follow conditions, what inherent nature (*svabhāva*) could they possess? Since conditioned phenomena are fundamentally empty, the absence of such phenomena is also empty.
Therefore it is said: "This very emptiness of such conditioned phenomena is called the emptiness of non-phenomena. Thus it is cast forth.

The Master addressed the assembly, saying: "If one discusses this matter, it is like a phoenix soaring into the sky leaving no trace, or a wild goat hanging from a tree branch—how can one seek its tracks?
A golden dragon does not dwell in the cold pool; how could a jade hare nestle within the shadow of the moon?
Should guest and host nevertheless be established, one must shake the head beyond the Path of Voice-Hearer (Vipaśyin), where questions and answers are expressed in words."
Along the dark path, he raises his voice as a chant: "If one can act thus, they are still only halfway there; look further with focused eyes, and there is no need for mutual meeting.
The verse says: The water is clear and the moon is full; the man of the Way feels sorrow. The wondrous reaches its ultimate end; there is nothing to rely upon, nor anything to gather.

Beyond the lands lie the paths of the orthodox and the biased, combined and interwoven. Upon the ungerminating branch, one discerns spring and autumn. But tell me, how does one discern that which has no tracks?
Who is it that is empty?
What is meant by the emptiness of all phenomena being beyond verbal expression? It is because the nature of conceptual construction is beyond verbal expression;
thus, the fact that all phenomena are beyond verbal expression is called the "emptiness of all phenomena being beyond verbal expression."
[The Master] said: "Form, sensation, mental formations, and consciousness can all be described and conceptualized; they do not depart from the aggregate of perception (*saṃjñā-skandha*).
This aggregate of perception is itself false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). That which is the object of false conceptualization can be reached by speech.

However, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of false conceptualization is fundamentally empty and quiescent, beyond the reach of speech. Since that intrinsic nature is non-existent and cannot be described by speech, then all phenomena [are likewise so]."
Being free from intrinsic nature, it is also beyond verbal expression; being without words and without speech, it admits of no deliberation.

Thus, what was previously called the emptiness of marks, the emptiness of self-nature, the emptiness of practice, and the emptiness of non-practice cannot admit even a single word, and are all simultaneously emptied.
This is called the "emptiness beyond verbal expression. Vimalakīrti asked Mañjuśrī: "What..."

[The assembly] thus [entered] the Bodhisattva’s gateway into the non-dual dharma. Mañjuśrī said, "As it occurs to me, regarding all dharmas, there is no speaking, no explaining, no indicating, and no cognition;
being free from all questioning and answering—this is the entrance into the non-dual dharma.
Thereupon, Mañjuśrī addressed Vimalakīrti, saying, "We have each spoken for ourselves..."
"Venerable one, you should speak: what is the bodhisattva’s entry into the Dharma-gate of non-duality?
Vimalakīrti remained silent. A heavenly robe then offered this verse: "It was not long before Vimalakīrti broke his silence; Sitting there to deliberate would have resulted in fault.
The blade that shaves hair emits a cold light from within its scabbard; Heterodox paths and celestial māras are all beheaded. Tiantong offered this verse: "Man..."
The Elder of Vairañjī was specially asked about his illness; the Gate of Non-duality opened. Behold the author: the dross on the surface reveals the purity within—who can appreciate this?
Do not lament past errors or look toward what follows. To cast away a precious jade in the marketplace is the fate of the man who had his kneecaps removed at the court of Chu;

to receive a brilliant pearl in return for a broken snake is the tale of the city of Sui. Cease your挑剔 (picking apart) and cease your fault-finding; let the vulgar air vanish entirely, and then you may compare us.
This is the emptiness beyond verbal expression, which only the Pure Name (Vimalakīrti) has most thoroughly elucidated.

What is meant by the "Great Emptiness of the Ultimate Truth of Noble Wisdom regarding all phenomena"? It refers to attaining the noble wisdom of self-awakening, wherein all views and habitual tendencies are empty;
this is called the Great Emptiness of the Ultimate Truth of Noble Wisdom regarding all phenomena.

Tong said: "The above—nature, characteristics, conduct, consciousness, and verbal expression—are all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). To cling to one's own particular views is itself the fault of seeing.
Only when one is able to see into the nature [of reality] does one attain the self-awakened noble wisdom; this pure wisdom is wondrously perfect, fundamentally empty and quiescent.
Where, then, could all faults, views, and habitual tendencies abide? One need only empty these faults, views, and habitual tendencies, and not..."
The emptiness of the noble wisdom of self-awakening is empty yet not empty; this is true emptiness.
All phenomena are established by the noble wisdom of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). When the noble wisdom of the ultimate truth is empty, all phenomena are empty.
These phenomena of arising and ceasing do not depart from the nature of the single True Suchness (*tathatā*), and the nature of the single True Suchness does not depart from all phenomena.

Because all is empty within a single emptiness, it is called "Great Emptiness. What is termed the "Ultimate Meaning" (paramārtha) is the supramundane, supreme wisdom that transcends all dualistic oppositions.
Because it can only be known by oneself, it is called "the noble wisdom of self-awakening" (pratyātma-āryajñāna).
Long ago, when the Seventh Patriarch, the Venerable Vasuvarman, was traveling to spread the Dharma, he arrived at the kingdom of Kāmala. There, a man of wisdom claimed for himself the name "Buddha."
Nandi wished to debate the meaning of the Dharma with his Master. The Master said, "Virtuous one, if you speak of the meaning, it is not the Dharma; if you speak of the Dharma, it is not the meaning.

If you intend to debate the meaning, in the end it will never be a discourse on the meaning. Nandi realized that his Master’s realization of the Dharma was superior, whereupon he requested ordination.
The Master entrusted him with the Treasury of the True Dharma Eye, speaking this verse: "The mind is identical to the realm of empty space; It manifests dharmas equal to empty space."
When the realization of space is attained, there is neither existence nor non-existence of dharmas. Later, Nandī gave the True Dharma to Puṇyamitra, saying in verse:
"Space has no interior or exterior; the mind and its dharmas are likewise. Because one understands space, one penetrates the principle of Suchness.
Regarding the two verses on the transmission of the Dharma: "All dharmas are the noble wisdom of the Great Emptiness; only the various..."

The Patriarch’s realization is most ultimate. Why is it called "emptiness of this or that" (*itaretara-śūnyatā*)? It means that in a given place, that which is absent makes that place empty; this is called emptiness of this or that.

Mahāmati, for example, in the house of Mṛgāramātṛ there were no elephants, horses, oxen, or sheep; yet it was not because there were no bhikṣus that it was said to be empty of them. It was empty of those [animals], but not empty of the bhikṣu-saṃgha. Therefore, it is called emptiness of this or that.

The emptiness of the nature of the hall is not [the same as] the emptiness of the nature of the bhikṣus; it is not that there are no elephants or horses elsewhere (in the Tang translation: "I say that hall is empty, but it is not that there are no bhikṣus present").

Mahāmati, this does not mean that the hall lacks the self-nature of a hall, nor that the bhikṣus lack the self-nature of bhikṣus, nor that there are no elephants, horses, oxen, or sheep elsewhere. This is called the self-characteristic of all dharmas.

That something is absent from another place—that is called "emptiness of this in that" (*itaretara-śūnyatā*). (In the Tang translation: "All dharmas, both their specific and general characteristics...")

Because that which is sought cannot be found, it is called "emptiness of this and that" (*itaretara-śūnyatā*). These are the seven kinds of emptiness; among them, the emptiness of this and that is the coarsest form of emptiness, and you should distance yourself from it.
The Master said: "What is called 'mutual emptiness' (itaretara-śūnyatā) refers to this: when certain phenomena are absent in a particular location, yet other phenomena are present there;
and when those phenomena are absent, yet others are present. Because they are all mutually empty, it is called 'emptiness.

This merely empties their characteristics (lakṣaṇa) but does not empty their intrinsic nature (svabhāva); it empties only those [specific] things but does not empty the remainder. It is, for example, like Mṛgāramātṛ."
The upāsikā Śakrā deeply revered the Triple Gem and constructed a vihāra, establishing bhikṣus within it and not keeping elephants, horses, or the like there.

In the past, I once preached the Dharma for her, saying that what is called "empty" refers to the absence of elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, and so forth, whereas the presence of bhikṣus and others is called "not empty. I was merely speaking of that hall.

That the hall is empty does not mean the hall itself is empty; rather, the nature of the hall is empty. That the bhikṣu is empty does not mean the bhikṣu himself is empty; rather, the nature of the bhikṣu is empty.

This unites sentient beings with the emptiness of both the conditioned and the unconditioned, such that they are all equally empty. Furthermore, it is not that everything is empty in the sense of being identical to nihilistic annihilation.
Although that house lacks elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep, the nature of the elephants, horses, oxen, and sheep is not [non-existent].

In other places, there is no real non-destruction of worldly characteristics; this is called the self-characteristic of all phenomena being primordially thus—empty yet not empty—because it is free from "this" and "that.
They do not understand this, but merely seek that [non-existence] within those [phenomena];
they seek the self-characteristics and common characteristics within the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, yet they cannot find them. It is precisely within those very characteristics that...
To speak of "emptiness of characteristics" is like saying a house is empty of elephants, horses, oxen, sheep, and so forth;
one perceives their absence within the characteristic, rather than perceiving the absence of their intrinsic nature. Therefore, it is called "emptiness of this and that" (*itaretara-śūnyatā*).

This "emptiness of this and that" is merely able to empty away external objects (*viṣaya*), but cannot empty away the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of those objects; thus, this emptiness is the most coarse and superficial.
If emptiness is that which has nothing to be emptied—such as the Great Emptiness of the First Principle Noble Wisdom—this is the most refined form of emptiness;
you all should practice and study it. As for those various forms of "emptiness of this or that," these are called nihilistic views and should be abandoned.
Sengzhi Chang attended upon the Sixth Patriarch. The Patriarch asked him, "Where have you come from, and what do you seek? He replied:
A student recently went to Baifeng Mountain in Hongzhou to pay respects to Master Dàtōng.

Having received his instruction on the principle of seeing one’s nature to become a Buddha, he remained undecided and full of doubt; thus, he has come from afar to offer his prostrations, hoping that the Master will provide him with guidance.
The Patriarch said, "What did he say? Try to quote it for me. The student replied, "I, Zhichang, went there and stayed for a total of three months, yet—"
Because your instruction for the sake of the Dharma was so earnest, I entered the abbot’s quarters alone one night to inquire:
"What is this person's own original mind and original nature? Daotong replied, "Do you see empty space? I answered, "I see it.
He asked, "Do you see that empty space as having any form or appearance? I answered, "Empty space has no shape; how could it have any appearance? He—
He said: "Your original nature is like empty space, wherein not a single thing can be seen; this is called right view. Not a single thing can be known;

this is called true knowledge. There being no blue, yellow, long, or short—merely seeing the source as pure and the essence of awakening as perfectly luminous—is what is called 'seeing one's nature and attaining Buddhahood,' and it is also called the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision. Thus he taught.

Although the man had heard this teaching, he was still not fully resolved. He requested the Master to provide further instruction. The Patriarch said, "That teacher’s explanation still involves the persistence of cognitive views;
that is why you have not yet attained understanding. I shall now show you a verse. The verse says:
"To not see a single dharma while maintaining the view of non-existence is much like floating clouds obscuring the face of the sun. To be unaware of a single dharma while guarding at emptiness—"
"Knowing is like a flash of lightning arising in the great void; this seeing and knowing arises in an instant, yet you mistakenly take it to be real, never understanding the skillful means.
You should, in a single thought, recognize your own error, and your own numinous light will then constantly manifest.
Having heard these verses, his mind was suddenly enlightened, and he composed a verse himself, saying: "Groundlessly giving rise to seeing and knowing, clinging to appearances to seek Bodhi..."

If you harbor a single thought of awakening, how could you transcend the delusions of former times? The source of self-nature is fundamentally one of awakening, yet by following after illumination, you wander in vain through the flux of samsara.
Failing to enter the chamber of the Patriarchs, you wander aimlessly between two extremes.
Viewed from this perspective, those who cling to emptiness and lack true insight should remain outside the gate.

Mahāmati, [dharmas] do not arise of themselves, yet they are not non-arising; except when abiding in samādhi, this is called "non-arising" (in the Tang translation, "non-arising" means that their own essence is non-arising, yet they are not non-arising).
The interlocutor asked: "If it is said that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are empty, why is it further said that all phenomena are unarisen (*anutpanna*)?

Does this mean that phenomena do not arise from themselves, or does it mean they are not unarisen at all times? [The Master] replied: "It means that while phenomena arise, they are non-arising; they are quiescent in their very essence (*tattva*).
They do not become non-arisen only after being suppressed through deliberate cultivation and practice. [This state] excludes those Bodhisattvas of the eighth stage who abide in the three..."
To realize the principle of non-arising within a state of mental obscurity is that which is attained only after cultivation;
this is because the self-nature of all phenomena is fundamentally non-arising from the beginning, and is therefore called "non-arising. Jin Shan Master asked Xiu Shan Master:

"If you clearly know the nature of arising and non-arising, why are you detained by arising? Xiu replied: "A bamboo shoot must ultimately become a bamboo stalk. He continued: "It is like [a seed becoming a tree]."
Xiu said, "Now that you have made this bamboo matting, can you still get it back? Jin replied, "In the future, you will realize it for yourself.
Xiu said, "I am just like this; what is the meaning of the Elder's intent? Jin replied, "This is the Director’s quarters;
which one is the Head Cook’s quarters? Xiu then bowed. Tiantong’s verse says: Vast and open, without dependence, lofty and at ease.
Unrestrained by home or state, peaceful and settled, when people are few, one’s slight strength may distinguish ranks; yet with a vast and open mind-body, all is free from right and wrong.
When right and wrong are extinguished, one stands alone in the Great Way where there are no tracks or ruts.
Observing it from this perspective, those who dwell in samādhi and realize non-arising are still separated from that which is originally unborn by a single speck of dust.

Being devoid of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) is precisely non-arising. Because all phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature—due to their momentary continuity and the manifestation of diversity—all things are thus devoid of intrinsic nature.

(The Chinese translation states: "To be devoid of intrinsic nature means that because they are unarisen, it is with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*) that all dharmas are said to lack intrinsic nature;
because they do not abide for even a moment and are seen to undergo subsequent transformation, they are called 'without intrinsic nature'").
Tong asked: "Once it has been taught that all phenomena (*dharma*) are empty and unarisen, why is it further said that they are devoid of the characteristic of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*)?

Generally speaking, if there were any characteristic of arising to be found, then an intrinsic nature would be found; now, since all phenomena are unarisen, it is precisely because of this non-arising that it is said that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature.
This does not mean they are simply nothingness; it is spoken with a hidden intention (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*)."
It is said that arising is itself non-arising and that nature is itself the absence of nature; because the substance of this continuous flow has,
from time without beginning, been ever-new and never-abiding moment by moment, such that no inherent nature can ever be found,
at the very instant of a *kṣaṇa*, it flows into another nature, and when that other-nature is perceived, the preceding nature— what was called "self"— undergoes transformation.

Wherein, then, does "nature" reside? It is like the nature of gold, which is solid yet melts when meeting fire; it flows into the nature of water. The nature of water flows yet freezes when meeting cold;

it flows into the nature of earth. All these natures lack any inherent self-nature (*svabhāva*) that can be apprehended, because all things are the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*), which is fundamentally unborn from the beginning. This is called the characteristic of all natures being devoid of self-nature.

Linji said: "O practitioners of the Way, in a single kṣaṇa you enter the Flower Treasury World, enter the land of Vairocana, enter the land of spiritual powers, enter the pure land, enter the dharma-realm, enter the defiled, enter the pure, enter the mundane, and enter the sacred;
yet wherever you search among the realms of hungry ghosts and animals, you find nothing at all."
Birth and death exist only as empty names, like illusions and flowers in the sky; do not labor to grasp them.
Let gain and loss, right and wrong, be cast off all at once. How excellent is this discourse on transcending self-nature!
What is meant by "non-duality"? It refers to all phenomena being like heat and cold, like long and short, or like white and black (the Tang translation says:
like light and shadow, like long and short, like white and black—all are established through mutual dependence; individually, they do not exist).

Mahāmati, all phenomena are non-dual because there is no nirvāṇa apart from saṃsāra, nor is there saṃsāra apart from nirvāṇa, due to the existence of the nature of distinct characteristics as causes (the Wei translation says: because of the characteristics of distinct causes). This is called [non-duality].
Non-dual as in nirvāṇa, so it is with all dharmas, including saṃsāra (the Tang translation states: "Nirvāṇa does not exist apart from saṃsāra, nor does saṃsāra exist apart from nirvāṇa;
there is no characteristic of contradiction between saṃsāra and nirvāṇa").
Tong said: "All phenomena (*dharma*) are empty, unarisen, and devoid of self-nature and characteristics, as detailed above.
Why is it called 'non-duality' (*advaya*)? If spoken of in terms of opposition, there are two; if spoken of in terms of the absence of opposition, there is non-duality.
That all phenomena are non-dual means that within opposition there is no opposition—this is like the sun."
It is cool when in shade and hot when in the sun; it is long in summer and short in winter; it is white by day and black by night—all these exist only in mutual dependence.
In reality, the substance of the sun itself has no darkness or light, length or shortness, nor black or white.
Thus, all phenomena are non-dual: there is no birth-and-death outside of nirvana, and there is no nirvana outside of birth-and-death.

Saṃsāra and nirvāṇa do not possess mutually contradictory characteristics, because they differ from the characteristics of their causes and because they possess natures that differ from the characteristics of their causes.
Whatever possesses characteristics necessarily possesses a nature; since it possesses a nature, it exists by virtue of its characteristics.
Now, nirvāṇa lacks intrinsic nature, and saṃsāra lacks intrinsic nature, just as the shadows of the sun vary in length.
When the characteristics of white and black appear as long, the nature of shortness abides in the white characteristic; when the white characteristic appears, the nature of black abides in it.

Thus, while the characteristics of cause and non-cause differ, the substance of the day remains inherently distinct from the characteristics of the cause. Since it is not the characteristic of the cause, no distinct characteristic can be found.
How then can one speak of the two—nirvana and samsara? When examined in this manner, all things [are seen to be thus].
The Dharma is also like this; therefore, it is said that all dharmas are non-dual. Huangbo said:
"The worlds of the ten directions do not go beyond my single mind; all lands of even the finest dust do not go beyond my single thought.
If this is so, what can be said of "internal" and "external"? It is like the nature of honey being sweet; all honey is thus, and it cannot be otherwise.
It is said that while this honey is sweet, where else could there be such bitterness? Therefore it is said: "Space has no interior;
the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is naturally so. Space has no middle; the nature of phenomena is naturally so.
Thus, sentient beings are Buddhas, and Buddhas are sentient beings; sentient beings and Buddhas are fundamentally one and the same body—birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and nirvana.

The conditioned and the unconditioned are originally of one and the same substance; the mundane and the supramundane, as well as the six realms of existence, the four modes of birth, the mountains, rivers, and the great earth—whether possessing nature or lacking nature—are likewise of one and the same substance.

To say they are "the same" means that names and characteristics are empty, existence is empty, and non-existence is empty. Throughout the entire world-system of the Ganges, there is fundamentally but a single emptiness. Thus spoke Huangbo.
Because it is empty and signless, it is non-dual; this accords with the preceding section.
Therefore, one should practice and study that which corresponds to emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and the absence of intrinsic nature.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
I have always taught that the Dharma of emptiness is far removed from the extremes of annihilationism and eternalism; birth and death are like illusions and dreams, yet karma is not destroyed.
This is also true for both space and nirvāṇa. Fools give rise to false imaginings, while the noble ones are free from existence and non-existence.
Tong said: "The World-Honored One has already extensively analyzed and explained emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and the absence of self-nature and characteristics;

yet, in these verses, he again directly reveals that true emptiness is far removed from the delusions of existence and non-existence, unlike the views of the non-Buddhists or the followers of the Two Vehicles.
This is truly what is called the Unsurpassed Dharma-gate. Since the Dharma of emptiness taught by the World-Honored One is said to be 'non-existent'..."
It is born as emptiness; it is also called non-duality, and is said to be devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). It is not by departing from all phenomena that one takes them to be empty;

rather, being empty yet not empty is what constitutes true emptiness (*bhūta-śūnyatā*). It remains far removed from the two views of annihilationism and eternalism. How can one say it is "far removed"?
When ordinary beings perceive permanence, they take it to be existent, and thus they undergo birth and death without realizing that birth and death are [ultimately empty].

Illusions and dreams are fundamentally non-existent from the beginning; yet, because the karma—whether good or evil—performed within those illusions and dreams perfumes the field of consciousness (*vijñānākṣaya*), the causality remains indestructible, and thus one constantly dwells in birth and death. This is the fault of the view of permanence (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*).
The followers of the Two Vehicles (the *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*) perceive this cessation as if there were a Nirvana to be attained, whether it be like empty space or like Nirvana itself.

If one were to say that the three unconditioned dharmas, such as cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), are all taught as "emptiness" for the sake of the Śrāvaka vehicle, then emptiness would merely be the opposite of reality, and cessation would merely be the opposite of arising.
Such mutual opposition between existence and non-existence ultimately leads back into the ocean of birth and death; even their karma would not be destroyed.
Therefore, it is said that "it is also like this," which refers to the fault of the view of annihilation (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*). Foolish people lack wisdom and do not [understand this].

One who is able to see that the true nature is fundamentally empty and far removed from existence and non-existence, yet still forms such deluded conceptualizations and discriminations regarding the states of existence and non-existence, gives rise to the false views of annihilationism and eternalism; these are the deluded thoughts of existence and non-existence.

When the noble ones attain the holy wisdom of self-awakening, where the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity is exhausted, even these deluded thoughts of existence and non-existence have no basis of their own.
From what source do the two views of annihilationism and eternalism arise? This Dharma of true emptiness is neither existence nor non-existence;
it transcends both existence and non-existence. It is fundamentally unborn and fundamentally non-dual. Being free from self-nature, one should practice and study in accordance with this.
A monk took his leave of Zhaozhou, who asked, "Where are you going? The monk replied, "I am going to various places to study the Buddha-Dharma. Zhaozhou said—
He raised his whisk and said: "Where there is a Buddha, one must not dwell; where there is no Buddha, one must run past with all haste.
Even when meeting people three thousand *li* away, do not raise it mistakenly. "Then you will not go," [the monk] said. The Master said:
"Plucking the willow blossoms, plucking the willow blossoms. Tiantong commented: "To sink into emptiness or linger in traces, to err in hand or wound oneself on the blade—none of these are correct."
A patch-robed monk’s coming and going must not enter the marketplace of human affairs; he does not sit upon another’s bed, yet he corrects them directly;
he does not establish the mysterious nor cling to things. Only then can he hold fast and let go with a measure of freedom.
These venerable masters speak of the subtlest Dharma of emptiness, fully revealing the news that all sages are free from both existence and non-existence.
At that time, the World-Honored One again addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, saying:
"Mahāmati, emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, and the departure from the marks of self-nature universally enter into all the *sūtras* (translated here as 'scriptures') of all Buddhas.
Whatever *sūtras* there may be, they all expound this meaning; all *sūtras* are taught through differentiation according to the inclinations and aspirations of sentient beings."
It manifests their meaning, yet it does not truly exist within verbal expression, just as the mirage of a thirsty deer deceives a herd of deer;
the deer cling to the appearance of water, yet no water exists there. In this same way, all the dharmas taught in the sūtras are for the purpose of inspiring joy in the foolish;
they do not constitute the true noble wisdom that lies beyond verbal expression. (Translated from Chinese)
It does not reveal the true Dharma that is the locus of realization through noble wisdom. Therefore, one should rely upon the meaning and not cling to the words.

[The interlocutor] replied: "The World-Honored One has already finished reciting the verses and further exhorted Mahāmati not to cling to words, stating that self-realized noble wisdom arises from personal awakening and is beyond the reach of verbal expression; thus, what is taught in various sutras may..."

Whether one speaks of emptiness, non-arising, non-duality, or being free from the characteristics of intrinsic nature, there is nothing that does not serve as a cause for sentient beings who aspire to bodhi;
it is merely a provisional manifestation intended to inspire joy and arouse the mind of diligence.
There is no true noble wisdom (āryajñāna) existing within words and speech, just as a thirsty deer pursues a mirage.
When one forms the perception of water in a mirage, it is actually not water; where, then, does the meaning of true noble wisdom reside?
Therefore, one should rely upon the meaning and not merely upon the words. A monk asked Mount Yaoshan, "My own matter is not yet clear; I beg the Master for instruction.
Yaoshan remained silent for a long time and said, "It would not be difficult for me to speak a single phrase for you right now, but only—"

"It would have been better for you to see it immediately upon hearing these words; that would still have left some margin. If you had entered into further deliberation, however, you would have committed an offense against me.

It would have been better to simply keep your mouths shut to avoid implicating one another. Observing how Yaoshan pointed this out in such a manner, one can truly say that those who know the Dharma are fearful.
Chapter Two: The Essence of the Mind of All Buddhas.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying:
"World-Honored One, the Sūtras state that the Tathāgatagarbha is pure by nature, possesses the thirty-two marks, and enters into all sentient beings."
The Tathāgatagarbha, which dwells eternally and unchangingly within the body like a precious gem wrapped in a soiled garment,
is likewise enveloped by the soiled garments of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, and defiled by the dust and toil of unreal conceptualizations—
namely, greed, hatred, and delusion— as taught by all Buddhas. Why, World-Honored One, do you speak of a "self" in the same manner as the non-Buddhists?

“Is there such a thing as the *tathāgatagarbha*, World-Honored One? Non-Buddhists also speak of a permanent creator that is free from *guṇas* (the Wei translation says ‘not dependent on various conditions’), which is all-pervading and indestructible.
World-Honored One, their teaching speaks of a self (*ātman*). The Buddha told Mahāmati: “My teaching of the *tathāgatagarbha* is not the same as the self spoken of by non-Buddhists.
Mahāmati, at other times I have spoken of emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*).”

Having already explained the *tathāgatagarbha* through such phrases as "the reality-limit," "dharma-nature," "dharma-body," "nirvāṇa," "devoid of self-nature," "unborn and undying," "originally quiescent," and "by nature nirvāṇic," the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha,
for the sake of severing the fear of the foolish regarding the phrase "selflessness," taught the *tathāgatagarbha* as a realm free from conceptual construction and devoid of [inherent] existence.
"Mahāmati, future and present bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should not form attachments to the view of self.
It is like a potter who, from a single lump of clay, uses human effort, water, wood, a wheel, and a cord as skillful means to produce various vessels.
In the same way, the Tathāgata likewise, regarding the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), abandons all marks of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) by means of various forms of wisdom."
Those with skillful wisdom and expedient means may speak of the *tathāgatagarbha* or speak of non-self; for these reasons, they speak of the *tathāgatagarbha*.

This is not the same as the "self" spoken of by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). It is called the teaching of the *tathāgatagarbha* because it is intended to attract and lead those non-Buddhists who cling to a self.
By speaking of the *tathāgatagarbha*, one causes them to abandon the false views and delusive imaginings of an unreal self and enter the three liberations.
Desiring to swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi* within the sphere of the gates of liberation, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, has thus spoken:
"The Tathāgatagarbha—if it were not so, it would be identical to the views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Therefore, Mahāmati, in order to avoid the views of the non-Buddhists, you should rely upon the selflessness of the Tathāgatagarbha."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"The person, the continuity, the aggregates (the Wei translation says 'person-self and the aggregates'), conditions, atoms, the Primal Victor, and the Creator—these are but the mind's measure of false conceptualization."

Mahāmati said: "World-Honored One, since you have taught that all noble ones are free from existence and non-existence and have distanced themselves from the views of eternalism and nihilism held by the heterodox, why do various sūtras speak of the Tathāgatagarbha as a permanent, true self?
Is this not the same as the *ātman* (self) spoken of by the heterodox? The Buddhas proclaim that the nature of the Tathāgatagarbha is intrinsically pure."
Endowed with the thirty-two marks, it resides within the bodies of all sentient beings, pervading them without exception;
it is not defiled by the aggregates (*skandha*) or the realms (*dhātu*), nor is it sullied by false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).

It is eternally abiding and unchanging, like a precious jewel of great value that, though wrapped in a soiled garment, has its brilliant luster undiminished. Because it is free from dependence on external conditions, it remains outside [of them].

The Way also speaks of a "spiritual self" (ātman) which has a constant name and is called the "agent"; its permanence is the same [as yours]. Although it exists within the five aggregates, it does not rely on various conditions;
its freedom from defilement is the same [as yours]. It pervades the ten directions, and its essence is without birth or extinction;

its traversing of all realms of existence is the same [as yours]. What difference is there between the "self" they speak of and that of the Buddha? I do not know what the World-Honored One’s [teaching] is.
It is said that "permanence, bliss, self, and purity" take non-self as self; whereas what they call the "divine self" (īśvara-ātman) takes the view of a self (ātmadṛṣṭi) as self.
Therefore, these are fundamentally different. The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma originally does not adhere to any single [fixed] position;
thus, for those attached to the view of existence, he taught the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. This emptiness is the *tathāgatagarbha*. For...
For those attached to the view of non-existence, he teaches that the *tathatā*, the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), the *dharmatā*, and the *dharmakāya* are truly real and not false;

this is the non-empty *tathāgatagarbha*. For those attached to the view of both existence and non-existence, he teaches that *nirvāṇa* is free from intrinsic nature, being fundamentally neither existent nor produced, and fundamentally neither non-existent nor extinguished. For those attached to the view of neither existence nor non-existence...
Those who see it declare that it is primordially quiescent and originally not non-existent by nature, being nirvana itself and originally not non-existent;
it is the supreme, ultimate dharma, this Tathāgatagarbha which is both empty and not empty.

Such phrases as these collectively explain the single Dharma of the Tathāgatagarbha. When has it ever been definitively asserted that there is a self? It has already been done for the sake of all the deluded.

Now, because people hear the phrase "non-self" and consequently give rise to fear, it is taught that the realm free from deluded thoughts and devoid of anything existing is called the "Tathāgatagarbha-gate.
To say it is "free from deluded thoughts" means it is free from the notions of self and what belongs to a self;
to say it is "devoid of all" means both person and phenomena are empty. This Tathāgatagarbha originally does not possess a self; how could it be reckoned through the view of a self?
How can we clarify that there is no self? It is like a potter making various vessels:
sometimes by manual labor, sometimes by water, a staff, or a wheel and cord; through these skillful means, the clay is fashioned into a vessel.
Yet once the vessel is formed, the wheel and the cord cannot claim any share in it, nor can the water or the wood.
Human artifice cannot participate therein; it serves only to manifest one's lack of self (*anātman*). The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is likewise:

within the dharma of selflessness that is free from all conceptual marks (*nimitta*), there is the wisdom of various kinds, which is the fundamental ultimate wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*), and the skillful means, which is the subsequently attained provisional wisdom (*prṣṭhalabdha-jñāna*); thus he may speak of the Tathāgata.
The *Tathāgatagarbha* is sometimes explained through various names and designations, each with its own distinctions;
yet in essence, there is truly no self, and it is fundamentally different from the "self" (*ātman*) propounded by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

The reason it is called the *Tathāgatagarbha* is precisely to attract and guide those non-Buddhists who cling to a substantial soul (*puruṣa*), causing them to abandon their unreal views of self and enter into emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
The spheres of the three gates of liberation—signlessness, wishlessness, and emptiness—are intended so that one may swiftly attain unsurpassed bodhi.
Because the view of self is rootless, it is unreal and ultimately subject to arising and ceasing. As for the three gates of liberation:
the Tathāgatagarbha is intrinsically pure, and thus is called "empty"; it is free from all signs because the twelve links of dependent origination have been extinguished.
It is called "signless" because it is inherently free from aspiration and seeking; it is called "wishless" solely for the purpose of transforming and guiding sentient beings.

This is the true path to unsurpassed bodhi. Therefore, when I speak of the Tathāgatagarbha, I do so precisely by means of non-self in order to refute the "self" of the heterodox schools, ensuring that the Tathāgatagarbha taught by the Tathāgata is not described as being empty and non-existent.

Regarding the three gates of liberation—signlessness, wishlessness, and emptiness—it may be considered acceptable for those such as the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) to view them as being identical [to their own views].
However, because the non-Buddhists have not abandoned the basis of their view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*), they forcibly claim that it is all-pervasive; this constitutes a false view (*mithyā-dṛṣṭi*).
You should distance yourselves from this. If you wish to abandon the non-Buddhist view of self, you must properly rely upon the Tathāgata’s teaching of selflessness (*anātman*).
The *tathāgatagarbha* is something that can be countered and eliminated; how then can you say that the *tathāgatagarbha* is the same as the "self" (*ātman*) spoken of by non-Buddhists?
The World-Honored One spoke again in verse to reveal that the non-Buddhist view of self is precisely what must be abandoned:
"There is a person, there is a self, there are dharmas"—these are the two types of attachment to the view of self and person held by non-Buddhists.
Riding upon the view of the self of dharmas, one perceives this [self] merely through the illustration of the self of persons. The five aggregates combine to form a person;

while the aggregates of form, sensation, and perception are easy to understand, it is only the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) that flows on in continuous succession. Externally, it conditions the six consciousnesses to create karma;
internally, it conditions the eight consciousnesses to dwell in the profound darkness. Non-Buddhists take this to be the "divine self" (*puruṣa-ātman*); this divine self is precisely...
To claim that Primal Nature (Prakṛti) acts as the creator based on this is surely a deluded thought;

furthermore, to assert that the great earth arises from the accumulation of atoms, or that Maheśvara brings forth the world as its creator, is to fail to realize that what they call a "creator" is itself dependent and not truly creative.
These are all "heterogeneous causes," which in essence belong to the realm of mental construction (cittamātra).

This is merely delusive conceptualization (*vikalpa*). When one calculates and speculates in this manner, one is still unable to empty the phenomena of the present aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and so forth;
this is called the view of a person-self (*pudgala-ātman-dṛṣṭi*). Such a view of self is still coarse.

If the followers of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) further empty the five aggregates and the three realms (*tridhātu*), this is called the view of dharma-self (*dharma-ātman-dṛṣṭi*). They would not even dare to hope for the Tathāgatagarbha.
How much less could external paths be compared to or equated with it?
Thus, one can discern that the arising and ceasing of deluded thoughts do not, in their entirety, transcend the ocean of the Tathāgatagarbha;

that these very deluded thoughts are the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*), as expounded by all Buddhas, and that the eternally abiding true self is thus—how could such a matter be lightly discussed? A guest came to visit Changsha.
He summoned the Minister of State, who responded with "Yes. Baoshou said, "That is not the Minister of State; his true name is clearly revealed by using a finger to point at the moon.
The man said, "One cannot depart from this very moment of responding to you; otherwise, there would be a second master, which would fall into the den of the spirit-soul.
Baoshou said, "Can one call the Minister of State 'The Most Honored One' (the Buddha)? Furthermore, give him another [name]."
He pierced through the man’s state again and again, saying: "When you do not respond at all like this, are you perhaps the 'disciple' or the 'host'?
Yet you have fallen back into the realm of 'no-matter'. Guo said: "It is not only a matter of responding or not responding;
since beginningless kalpas, this has been the very root of birth and death. Indeed, it cannot escape the eyes of the clear-sighted."
In the *Guo Sha* there is a verse that says: "Those who study the Way do not recognize the Real; it is only because they have from the beginning recognized the spirit of consciousness.
Since beginningless kalpas, this has been the root of birth and death, yet deluded people call it the 'Original Person. This may serve as a definitive critique of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
Now, practitioners of longevity often cite this to validate their own views; could it be that they take what those [non-Buddhists] call the 'Original'..."
"Does the one who comes here resemble the Tathāgata? [The Buddha] smiled.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, observing future sentient beings, again entreated the World-Honored One, saying:
"I only pray that you will explain for us the uninterrupted practice, such as that of the practicing Bodhisattvas-Mahāsattvas, according to the Great Skillful Means of the Buddhas."
He addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati: "What are the four dharmas by which a practitioner attains great skillful means? What are these four? They are:

(1) skillfully discerning that what appears as external objects is but the manifestation of one's own mind; (2) realizing the non-existence of external natures; (3) being free from views concerning arising, abiding, and ceasing;
and (4) attaining the noble wisdom of self-realization and delighting therein. These are called the four dharmas by which a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attains cultivation."
What is the great skillful means of the practitioner? It is when the bodhisattva-mahāsattva skillfully discriminates that which is manifested from his own mind;

that is to say, he contemplates the three realms as being merely the limit of mind (*cittamātra*), free from "I" and "mine," unmoving, devoid of coming and going, and established through the false imaginings of body and property—which are bound by the various forms and activities of the three realms and perfumed by the habitual tendencies of beginningless delusion.
Entering accordingly into manifestation is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s skillful discernment of the manifestations of his own mind.

It is generally termed "Great Wisdom" (*mahāmati*). Because the Buddha has taught that all phenomena are empty, unarisen, non-dual, and devoid of the marks of intrinsic nature, he has clarified the principle of uninterruptedness.
"Uninterruptedness" means there is not even a hair’s breadth of separation; it is the supreme and foremost.
This is the single-minded intent. Although the principle is clearly manifest, it must be attained through practice.

How does one practice so as to realize unsurpassed bodhi and attain correspondence with the unconditioned? Regarding the various great Bodhisattvas practicing the dharma-gates of great skillful means, the Buddha taught that the accomplishment of these skillful means consists of approximately four dharmas: first, skillfully discerning what is manifested from one’s own mind.
Second, skillfully observing that external natures are neither existent nor non-existent; third, skillfully departing from views of arising, abiding, and ceasing;

fourth, attaining the bliss of the noble wisdom of self-realization. What is termed "skillful" implies that there is a sublime awakening existing within it, which cannot be compared to ordinary modes of contemplation;
furthermore, the bliss of the noble wisdom of self-realization is called "skillful bliss," yet it is not a mere indulgence in stillness.
"Nirvāṇa" means the ultimate limit. Why is it initially called "skillfully discerning the manifestation of one's own mind"?

It is because by contemplating that the three realms are mind-only, one awakens to the boundaries of mind-only, thereby distancing oneself from the two attachments of parikalpita (imagined) and paratantra (dependent), and realizing the nature of pariniṣpanna (perfected).
Internally, one is free from the "self" of the sense-faculties and the body; externally, one is free from the "mine" of the vessel-world. Fundamentally, there is no movement within the three realms.
From what does this arise? Its origin is fundamentally detached from coming and going; how could there be birth and cessation within the triple world?

It is but the one mind, and thus it is called "Mind-Only. Yet, that one cannot avoid the shaking of the marks of coming and going through the notions of "self" and "mine" is because of being perfumed by the false habitual tendencies of beginningless time;
therefore, the various forms, activities, and aggregates of the triple world manifest.
Bound within, it manifests the characteristic of a self (*ātman*) and establishes the body and possessions externally as the characteristic of "mine" (*ātmīya*).

What are termed form (*rūpa*) and formations (*saṃskāra*) have sensation (*vedanā*) and perception (*saṃjñā*) contained therein. Thus, both the objective aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the subjective aspect (*darśanabhāga*) arise from the eight consciousnesses;
the deluded conceptualizations of the six realms within the world follow and enter into these two aspects of appearance and seeing.
Yet, the appearance of movement, coming, and going—the various phenomena of the triple world—all arise from false imagination (*vikalpa*).
False imagination has no root; in reality, it has never existed. Since false imagination does not arise, that which is false is itself the Real (*tattva*).
Where, then, is there anything that is not a manifestation of one's own mind? This is what is meant by "skillfully discerning that which is manifested by one's own mind. (Nan)
Jianquan said to Lu Xunfu, "Master Zhao is truly extraordinary; his understanding of the Way is that heaven and earth share the same root and all things are one body.
Jianquan pointed to the peony in the courtyard and said, "Great Officer, when people of this age see this single flower, it is like seeing a dream.
Tiantong’s verse says: "Illuminating through the subtle and the manifest, the root of creation emerges in profusion."
Not seeing its gate, the spirit wanders beyond the kalpas; when asked what attachments exist, one looks before the body and knows the wondrous presence.
The tiger roars through the rustling crags, the wind becomes the dragon’s cry, and again and again the mountain clouds darken.

When Nanquan pierced through the dreams of the age, one must recognize the majestic Honored One who succeeds to the position. An ancient worthy said: "In every place is Maitreya; there is no gate and no entry."
Sudhana, you should know that it is only through such vision that one can skillfully discern what is manifested from one’s own mind.
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva skillfully contemplate external natures as being without intrinsic nature?

It is by contemplating all natures—such as mirages, dreams, and so forth—as being without beginning, as false constructs born of habitual tendencies of deluded imagination, and as the self-nature of all phenomena; thus does the bodhisattva-mahāsattva practice.

Thus, when one skillfully contemplates that external natures have neither existence nor non-existence (the Tang translation says: "when thus contemplating all dharmas, this is precisely seeking the noble wisdom of self-realization"), this is called a bodhisattva-mahāsattva’s skillful contemplation of the existence and non-existence of external natures.

The Master replied: "The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) contemplate external phenomena as being neither existent nor non-existent; they claim that what exists returns to non-existence and that intrinsic nature (svabhāva) itself is extinguished—this constitutes the view of annihilationism.
