The Bodhisattvas contemplate external phenomena as being neither existent nor non-existent, realizing that they are rootless conceptual constructions (vikalpa), while their own realized noble wisdom (āryajñāna) perceives that the self-nature of all phenomena is fundamentally never extinguished. This is what it means to contemplate correctly, and thus they differ from the non-Buddhists."
The Way [is such that] all external phenomena—like mirages, dreams, illusions, and the like—are fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because they have been perfumed by the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of falsehood since beginningless time, one clings to various deluded thoughts as their cause;
thus, one grasps at a mirage as water and a dream as real. In truth, all phenomena lack self-nature and are from the very beginning...
Non-arising is the observation in this way; it is the exclusive pursuit of the noble wisdom realized within oneself (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*).

This is called the "nature of self-nature" (*svabhāva-svabhāva*), which is the thorough observation that all external phenomena are neither nature nor non-nature. It is merely the cessation of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), not the cessation of observational wisdom (*vipaśyanā-jñāna*).

It is the absence of the seeds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-bīja*), yet not the absence of self-nature. This is called the skillful observation of the nature and non-nature of external things. Long!
Shazen ascended the hall and said: "If I were to exclusively exalt the religious teachings, the grass in the Dharma Hall would surely grow a fathom deep;
since that is not possible, I shall speak to you all: the entire ten directions of the world are the eyes of the śramaṇa;
the entire ten directions of the world are the whole body of the śramaṇa; the entire ten directions of the world are one's own light."
I clarify that the worlds of the ten directions are entirely within one's own radiance;
throughout the worlds of the ten directions, there is not a single person who is not oneself. I have always told you all:
the Buddhas of the three periods, the Dharma-realm, and all sentient beings are the light of Mahāprajñā. Before this light has yet been emitted, where were you all?
To understand this thoroughly: even before light has yet been emitted, there is no Buddha and no sentient beings; from where could mountains, rivers, and lands come?
As Changsha said: "If one can immediately realize noble wisdom for oneself, one will be able to skillfully observe that external natures are non-natures."
How does a bodhisattva-mahāsattva skillfully abandon the views of arising, abiding, and ceasing?

It is by realizing that all natures—whether self-nature, other-nature, or both—are unborn, like illusions and dreams, because they are merely the limits of one's own mind; by seeing that external natures have no reality;

by seeing that consciousness is unborn and that conditions do not accumulate; and by seeing that the triple world, internal and external, arises from the conditions of false discrimination regarding all phenomena.

Being unable to perceive [anything], all views of arising apart from intrinsic nature are extinguished; knowing that all phenomena have an intrinsic nature like an illusion and so forth, one attains the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Having attained the patient acceptance of the non-arising of phenomena, one is free from views of arising, abiding, and ceasing.
This is called the bodhisattva mahāsattva’s skillful discernment and freedom from views of arising, abiding, and ceasing.

The interlocutor said: "One who is skilled at discerning that which appears as the manifestation of one's own mind sees its arising; one who skillfully contemplates that external natures are neither existent nor non-existent sees the cessation of seeing.

It seems, however, that this has not yet departed from the views of arising, abiding, and ceasing. How, then, does one who is truly skilled in departing from the views of arising, abiding, and ceasing effect such a departure?
It is by contemplating all phenomena as being like illusions and dreams—devoid of self-nature and devoid of other-nature."
Because the nature of non-duality is fundamentally unarisen, one immediately attains entry into the realm of the non-arising of one’s own mind;
by thoroughly understanding the limits of one’s own mind, one returns to non-apprehension and thus becomes naturally detached.

Having clarified the limits of one’s own mind, one sees that external natures are neither existent nor non-existent, and thus they are not produced by another. One sees that the various consciousnesses do not arise, and thus they are not self-produced. One sees the external...
Conditions do not accumulate, nor do they arise together through combination; one perceives that the three realms arise from deluded conceptualization and are not born without cause.
Within and without the three realms, all phenomena—including the sense organs, the body, and the physical world—cannot be apprehended;
they are fundamentally unborn from the beginning. One who forms this perception is said to have "seen their nature. However, if this perception still persists, it remains [an obstacle].
It has not yet been abandoned. Although advancing toward it, one perceives that even this perception lacks an inherent nature that can be grasped;
yet, although it is devoid of self-nature, the one who gives rise to this perception still persists, meaning its root has not yet been uprooted.

When advancing further, the innate ignorance that gives rise to perceptions is entirely extinguished, leaving no trace or mark whatsoever. Both subject and object vanish together, realizing the unborn (*anutpāda*). This is not to say—
To claim that there is a "patience toward the non-arising of phenomena" (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti) existing separately from all phenomena is incorrect;

rather, it is by knowing that these very phenomena—such as those likened to illusions—are ungraspable within their own intrinsic nature that one realizes the patience toward the non-arising of phenomena and is said to attain the first stage (bhūmi).

While attaining the non-arising of phenomena is not difficult, attaining the patience toward the non-arising of phenomena is difficult. Once this patience has been attained, one enters [the first stage].

Because of great samādhi, one skillfully discerns and is free from views of arising, abiding, and ceasing; because the mind does not cling to them, it is free from views of arising, abiding, and ceasing, for they do not arise of themselves.
Thus it is said: "Skillfully free. Miaoshan asked Yangshan, "How do you understand arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing?
Yangshan replied, "When a single thought arises, I do not see arising, abiding, changing, or ceasing. The Master said:
“Master, why do you speak of ‘expelling dharmas’? Yang said, “The Master just now asked what. The Master said, “Arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.

Yang said, “Yet you call this ‘expelling dharmas. According to the meaning of Master Muzhou and his son Yangshi in expelling dharmas, was there anything more than simply calling it ‘expelling dharmas’?
This is true skillful discernment, which is free from the views of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing.

What is the noble joy of the self-awakened holy wisdom attained by Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas? It refers to attaining the stage of non-arising dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), entering the eighth Bodhisattva stage, becoming detached from mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-mano-manovijñāna*), the five dharmas, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), and the two kinds of selflessness (*nairātmya*), and thereby attaining the body born of intention (*manomaya-kāya*).
"World-Honored One, for what causes and conditions does one attain the body born of intention? The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The body born of intention..."
This is like the movement of the mind, which is swift and unimpeded; therefore it is called "mind-born.

Just as the mind moves without obstruction through stone walls, so too, across immeasurable *yojanas* (here translated as forty li) in distant lands, one does not forget what was previously seen through the power of mental recollection.
As the flow of one's own mind continues without interruption, this body arises without obstruction. O Mahāmati, it is in this way that the mind-born body is attained.

At that time, the bodies born of the mind of the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas—adorned with the marks of sublime features, possessing mastery over the supernatural powers of the Illusion-like Samādhi, and belonging to the noble lineage—were all born simultaneously. Like those born of the mind, they were without obstruction;
according to their mental intentions and the spheres of their original vows, they attained the sublime bliss of self-realized noble wisdom for the sake of bringing sentient beings to maturity.

(The Tang translation says: For example, when the mind remembers various objects previously seen beyond hundreds of thousands of *yojanas*, it proceeds there with a continuous succession of moments so swiftly that neither the physical body nor mountains, rivers, stones, or walls can obstruct it. The mind-born body (*manomaya-kāya*) is also like this:

through the power of the Illusion-like Samādhi, mastery over supernormal faculties, and the adornments of all marks, because it recalls its original vows to bring sentient beings to maturity, it travels like the mind and is born among all the assemblies of noble ones.
Thus, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva attains the stage of non-arising dharma-patience and enters the eighth stage, the Bodhisattva completely relinquishes the [ordinary] mind.
The mind, the mental consciousness, the five dharmas, the three self-natures, the two kinds of non-self, the marks of the body, and the attainment of the *manomayakāya* (mind-made body),

along with the attainment of the noble wisdom of self-realization and its sublime bliss— these are called the four dharmas accomplished by a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva that constitute the great skillful means of a practitioner;
one should train in this way.
The interlocutor said: "First, one is well-versed in discerning that what appears as one's own mind has not yet transcended the mind;

next, one is well-versed in observing that external natures lack inherent existence, yet remains focused on seeking the self-nature of all phenomena, thus not yet having transcended dharmas. Once one is well-versed in leaving behind views of arising, abiding, and ceasing, one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*).
Since arising and ceasing have been extinguished, quiescence is bliss; therefore, it is called 'attaining the noble self-realization.'"
How could those whose wisdom is well-delighted in bliss be exclusively addicted to quiescence like the śrāvakas?
It is said that they have attained the *anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti* on the eighth bodhisattva stage; although they realize the bliss of samādhi, they do not dwell in attachment to it.

They are detached from both the five dharmas and the three natures, and they have cast aside both the eight consciousnesses and the two forms of selflessness. Thus, they preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, proceeding wherever their will leads them.
Therefore, it is called the "body born of mental mastery" (*manomayakāya*). For what reason is it called the "body born of mind"?

It is like when the mind recollects something previously seen; even though that object is in a different direction many *yojanas* away, the mind reaches it with continuous succession of moments without being obstructed by the body, nor obstructed by stone walls or barriers.
If this is so for the ordinary mind, how much more so for the "body born of mind"?
Is he one who has attained the power of the Illusion-like Samādhi of the Body? Is he one who has attained the power of sovereign supernormal faculties (*abhijñā*)?
He is able to be born simultaneously [with all beings], even more swiftly than thought;
or manifesting wondrous marks, surrounded by all the sages, he travels as he wills, being born among all the assemblies of sages, arising simultaneously without any obstruction.

Investigating their fundamental vows, they find that there is nothing other than the desire to bring sentient beings to fulfillment so that each may awaken to their own nature and attain the noble wisdom of self-awakening and bliss;
thus, they are able to manifest bodies throughout the ten realms, moving and abiding without obstruction.

To manifest bodies throughout the ten realms, preaching the Dharma to save sentient beings, adorning Buddha-lands, serving all Buddhas, and performing great Buddha-deeds constitutes the ninth stage (*navamī-bhūmi*).
Regarding the aforementioned matters, how is it that those dwelling in the eighth stage can suddenly achieve this?

It is because they have transformed consciousness into wisdom (*jñāna*), abandoned the mind, intellect, and mentation (*citta-mano-vijñāna*), and attained the two kinds of selflessness (*anātman*) from among the five dharmas and the three natures (*trisvabhāva*).

Having already realized the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), they abide in the bliss of samādhi; this is called the demarcation of the eighth stage. Now, they further transform that very abandonment.
Advancing further, one abandons even that abandonment and forgets it; this is the turning of wisdom toward compassion to attain the mind-born body (*manomayakāya*).
This occurs by proceeding from the eighth stage toward the ninth, attaining the sublime bliss of self-awakened noble wisdom and being able to skillfully employ it to deliver sentient beings.
This is called the great bodhisattva’s accomplishment of the four dharmas through cultivation.
The practitioner, through great skillful means, directs themselves toward the realization that all phenomena are empty, unarisen, non-dual, and devoid of intrinsic nature and characteristics;
reaching this point, they realize each and every principle of immediate succession and swiftly attain unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment.
Should you not train in this manner? Furthermore, by analyzing in detail, one should skillfully discern that which is manifested by one's own mind.
To realize that these three realms are mind-only and that all phenomena are non-dual is the great gate of skillful means practiced by Maitreya Bodhisattva.
To skillfully observe that external natures have no inherent nature and thus realize that all phenomena are empty is the great gate of skillful means practiced by Ākāśagarbha Bodhisattva.
To skillfully depart from views of arising, abiding, and ceasing is the movement of wind.
To realize that all phenomena are without basis and free from the characteristics of intrinsic nature is the gate of great skillful means practiced by the Dharma Prince Vaidūryaprabha;

to attain the sublime bliss of self-awakened noble wisdom and to manifest universally to realize that all phenomena are unborn is the gate of great skillful means practiced by Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva. These are called [the gates].
The great skillful means of the practitioner is the Mahāyāna Dharma; how could it be matched by inferior vehicles? Master Zhenjing addressed the assembly, saying:
"This day has passed, and life likewise diminishes accordingly. Like a fish in scant water, what joy is there in this?
Only the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas find joy in the quiescence of meditative concentration; this is their 'true joy. But for a Bodhisattva who studies Prajñā..."

To find joy in the Dharma and delight in dhyāna is true happiness; for the Buddhas of the three periods of time, the four immeasurable minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity constitute true happiness. Shishuang Puhui said, "Rest! Cease!
Be cold and still!"—this is the happiness of the extinction of the Two Vehicles. Yunmen said, "All-encompassing wisdom penetrates all."
Without obstruction, he raised his fan and said: "The Old Man Śākyamuni’s coming was for the sake of the joy of Dharma-delight and Chan-joy;
Deshan’s staff and Linji’s shout are the joy of the compassion, pity, sympathetic joy, and equanimity of the Buddhas of the three periods.
Apart from these three kinds of joy, nothing else constitutes joy. Now tell me, where do the assembly at Guizong abide?
"Inside there are three kinds; outside, after a long while, it is said: 'Today the master of the estate has prepared rice porridge and distributed alms money.
After the assembly has retired, everyone is invited into the Sangha hall to drink tea.
He gave a shout and said, "If you understand the intent of Zhenjing, this is called attaining the noble wisdom of self-awakening and true bliss; otherwise, there will be days of weeping."
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again requested of the World-Honored One: "I pray that you will explain for me the characteristics of the causal conditions of all dharmas.

By awakening to the characteristics of these causal conditions, I and the other Bodhisattvas shall be free from the false views of existence and non-existence regarding all natures, and free from the views of conceptualization—namely, the views of gradual or simultaneous arising" (the Tang translation reads: "free from views of existence and non-existence, and not falsely clinging to the gradual or sudden arising of all dharmas").
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "All dharmas have two kinds of causal conditions, namely external and internal.
External conditions refer to the production of a jar through the causal conditions of a lump of clay, a staff, a wheel, a string, water, human effort, and various other skillful means;

likewise, the production of a jar from clay, cloth from thread, a mat from grass, a sprout from a seed, or curd from milk through such skillful causal conditions is also like this. This is called external conditions."
What are the causes and conditions for subsequent rebirth? They refer to phenomena such as ignorance, craving, and karma, which receive the name "conditions.

From these arise the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases, which receive the name "arisen from conditions. These are without distinction, yet they are falsely conceptualized by the ignorant; this is called the internal conditioned phenomenon.

Mahāmati said: "I have understood that one should skillfully observe that external natures are non-natures; namely, that all natures have beginningless false conceptualization and habitual tendencies as their cause.
However, I have not yet fully grasped the characteristics of these causes. Furthermore, I have understood that one should skillfully abandon the views of arising, abiding, and ceasing;
namely, seeing that external natures are non-natures, seeing that consciousness does not arise, and seeing that conditions do not accumulate."

Regarding the "view of conceptualization" (*vikalpa-dṛṣṭi*): because one has not yet fully understood the characteristics of the conditions from which things arise, one desires to cognize the characteristics of those causal conditions.
To be free from the false views of existence and non-existence regarding all natures is what was described above as "the view being free from self-nature" (*svabhāva-vinirmukta-dṛṣṭi*).

Regarding the "view of conceptualization" (*avikalpa-dṛṣṭi*): it refers to the attachment to the notion that phenomena arise either gradually or instantaneously; this is what was described above as the "view of arising" (*utpāda-dṛṣṭi*).

"All is extinguished," [said the disciple]. The World-Honored One first raised two kinds of causal conditions (*pratyaya*) and spoke of them, namely: the external vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) and the internal root-body (*indriya-kāya*).

The external condition is illustrated by the analogy of a clay jar: although there is a lump of clay, it must depend upon the wheel, the cord, water, wood, and human labor as conditions before the jar is formed.
Just as with the clay jar, so too all [products] are formed through the conditions of threads to become cloth.
Grass is woven together to form a mat; seeds are conditioned to produce sprouts; and curd is produced from butter—likewise it is so.
Causes precede and effects follow, arising one after another in succession. This is what is meant by the statement that "all phenomena arise from conditions.
A lump of clay originally lacks the nature of a jar, yet it is produced through various skillful means and conditions; it must depend on conditions to arise, and the conditions themselves...

It has never arisen. Internally, the conditions are the twelve links of dependent origination—from ignorance conditioned by [ignorance] leading to volitional formations, up to craving, grasping, and the karmic actions that bind birth and death—which thus receive the name of "conditions. From those conditions, there arise name-and-form, sensation, and consciousness;
these and other dharmas such as the aggregates, elements, and sense bases all arise through mutual conditioning and thereby obtain the name of "that which arises from conditions. Although...

There is an orderly sequence without differentiation; that which arises from the *nimittabhāga* (objective aspect) is called form (*rūpa*) and the six sense bases (*ṣaḍāyatana*), while that which arises from the *darśanabhāga* (subjective aspect) is called consciousness (*vijñāna*), craving (*tṛṣṇā*), karma, and so forth. In total, these are the objects of the eight consciousnesses, which fundamentally have no differentiation.
Yet, ignorant people do not know that these are manifestations of their own minds; they falsely give rise to discrimination, gathering upon conditions and wavering within.
Various forms of attachment are called internal conditions; internal conditions are delusion, and delusion fundamentally has no root.
Since there is no mind that can grasp, there is naturally no object to be grasped. Thus we know that what arises from conditions is like an illusion.
Chan Master Baoneng of Baimen often cited the "Epitaph for Xuefeng" to question the elder masters: "That which exists through conditions is from beginning to end..."
As for the formation and destruction that do not arise from conditions, let us set aside for a moment their persistence through kalpas and their subsequent decay;
where is Xuefeng today? Fayan spoke differently, saying: "Right now is it formation? Is it destruction?
Because Fayan realized that the three realms are mind-only, he did not give rise to dualistic views.

Mahāmati, those causes are of six kinds: namely, the cause of what is to be (bhaviṣyat-hetu), the cause of continuity (prabandha-hetu), the cause of characteristics (lakṣaṇa-hetu), the cause of activity (kriyā-hetu), the cause of manifestation (saṃdarśana-hetu), and the cause of dependence (apekṣā-hetu).

Regarding the cause of what is to be: once the cause of activity has functioned, internal and external phenomena arise. (The Tang translation states: "That is to say, internal and external phenomena act as causes to produce effects. Regarding the cause of continuity:

once the object of perception (*ālambana*) has been established, internal and external phenomena arise, such as the seeds of the aggregates (*skandha*). Regarding the cause of characteristics: it acts... [text fragmentary].

The immediate cause (*samanantara-hetu*) is that which produces a continuous succession; it performs the function of a sovereign cause (*adhipati-kāraṇa*), like a wheel-turning monarch (the Chinese version says:

"it performs the function of a sovereign cause and gives rise to the fruit"). The manifesting cause (*vijñapti-hetu*) is that which, once the activity of false discrimination has arisen, manifests the appearance of the object as its effect, like a lamp illuminating forms and so forth (the Chinese version says:
"it differentiates what arises and can manifest the characteristics of the object, like a lamp illuminating things"). The dependent cause (*apekṣā-hetu*) is that which acts at the time of cessation.

The continuity of succession is severed because the nature of non-delusive production arises (the Wei translation states: "At the time of cessation, one does not perceive the arising of false dharmas; thus the affairs of continuity are cut off").
It is explained in general that the two aforementioned types of causal characteristics are as follows:

first, it clarifies that conditions do not accumulate, meaning that external conditions arise through skillful means and possess no nature of combination; second, it clarifies that delusive thoughts arise from conditions, meaning internal conditions.

Since ignorance arises from that which is fundamentally rootless, it is now explained through six types of causal characteristics to reveal that beginningless, false, and deluded habitual tendencies serve as its cause;
these are, in total, not separate from the mutual causality of the various consciousnesses.

First is the "cause of what is to be" (*bhaviṣyaddhetu*), which is the immediate cause; this refers to how the eight consciousnesses, since beginningless time, have been able to function as a single...

All things act as causes internally while appearing as the "perceived" (nimitta-bhāga) externally; because all phenomena arise from these acting as causes, their production of effects is inconceivable.

Since they function as causes at that very moment, they are called "causes existing at the time [of the effect]" (*sahabhū-hetu*). Second, the "successive cause" (*samanantara-hetu*) refers to the successive consciousnesses:
internally, the eight consciousnesses serve as the support, and externally, the six consciousnesses take external objects as their objective conditions (*ālambana*). Once this has occurred—
Thus, internal and external dharmas produce the seeds of the resultant aggregates (*skandha*);

the active manifestation (*samudācāra*) perfumes the seeds, and the seeds in turn perfume the active manifestation, whereby the defiled and pure resultant aggregates arise in an uninterrupted succession. Therefore, it is called the "successive cause" (*samanantara-hetu*).
Thirdly, this successive cause is precisely the condition of equal and immediate antecedence (*samanantara-pratyaya*), which produces the subsequent state without interval.

Regarding the characteristic of continuity within the continuity of the fruit: there exists an uninterrupted state between [cause and fruit] that has already departed from the cause but has not yet reached the fruit.
It is called "continuity" precisely because it is uninterrupted; since a characteristic can be apprehended in the interval between cause and fruit, it is termed the "characteristic-cause.
Fourth, the "acting cause" is the sovereign condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*), meaning it performs the function of sovereignty.

The arising of the fruit is like that of a Wheel-Turning King (cakravartin): the physical manifestation of the king is the primary cause (*hetu*), while the flying of the seven treasures through the air is the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*).

Since an object cannot produce a fruit by itself and must necessarily rely on the mind as its dominant condition, the Wheel-Turning King is able to act as the superior cause, for the mind is the dominant condition for the object. Therefore...
It is said that as for the efficient cause (*kāraṇa-hetu*), only the six consciousnesses act as the efficient cause. As for the five [other causes], they are the revealing causes (*vyañjana-hetu*):
this means that once the false conceptualization of the first five consciousnesses has arisen, they are able to manifest the characteristics of objects, just as a lamp illuminates things.

False conceptualization belongs to the category of the efficient cause, while the manifestation of characteristics belongs to the category of the produced effect. In terms of the preceding object, form belongs to the illuminated (the effect), while the conceptualization belongs to the illuminator (the cause).

The treatise states that illumination belongs to the object and the lamp belongs to the subject; therefore, the five consciousnesses and the eighth consciousness coexist like illumination not being separate from a lamp.

Because there is only illuminating cognition (*vijñapti*) without yet entering into conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*), it is called the "cause of manifestation" (*nidarśana-hetu*). Sixth is the "dependent cause" (*apekṣā-hetu*):

this refers to the mutual dependence of arising and ceasing—having arisen, it ceases; having ceased, it arises. This mutual dependence functions as the causal utility, as explained previously in the fifth and sixth [sections].
When the seven consciousnesses arise together, "continuity of arising" refers to the two natures of good and evil;

when these five, six, and seven consciousnesses cease together, "continuity of cessation" refers to the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) nature. Therefore, it is said that the nature of non-delusive thought arises;
"non-delusive thought" is precisely the indeterminate. Whereas previously there was the continuity of delusive thought, here for a time—
At times they cease, waiting for continuity; at times they perish, waiting for birth. To have birth and cessation is not to attain the true nature of non-arising and non-ceasing.
These six evolve and turn in mutual dependence, giving rise to internal and external phenomena that are like dreams and illusions.
That foolish people cling to them as being truly existent is entirely due to their failure to understand the beginningless, false habit-energies.

The vital energy (prāṇa) is stored within the field of the eight consciousnesses like a seed; therefore, it is said that the habitual tendencies of deluded thought (*vikalpa-vāsanā*) serve as the cause.
A monk asked Huangbo, "I, a student, do not understand; how does the Master instruct me?
Huangbo said, "I have nothing at all, and from the beginning I have never given anything to anyone. Since time immemorial, you have simply been..."
If you point to others to seek the *yogic bond* (*yoga*) or seek for realization, is this not a case where both disciple and teacher fall into royal peril?
You need only, in a single thought-moment, not accept anything—this is the body without sensation; in a single thought-moment, not conceive anything—this is the body without perception;
to be definitively free from shifting flux and volitional activity—this is the body without mental formations. Do not engage in deliberation, calculation, or conceptualization.
Separation is precisely the absence of a conscious body. As soon as you now give rise to a single thought, it is like the twelve links of dependent origination:
ignorance conditions volitional formations, which are both cause and effect; and so on, up to old age and death, which are also both cause and effect.
Therefore, when the youth Sudhana sought spiritual friends in one hundred and ten places, he sought them solely within these twelve links of dependent origination.
Finally, you will see Maitreya; Maitreya, in turn, will point you toward seeing Mañjuśrī. Mañjuśrī is none other than your own original ground of ignorance.

If, moment by moment, your mind differs from itself as you seek out spiritual friends (kalyāṇamitra) outwardly, then the very first thought that arises is immediately extinguished, and as soon as it is extinguished, it arises again. For this reason, you bhikṣus are born, age, fall ill, and die.
From the time one has repaid causes and answered effects, there is the arising and ceasing of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*); these five aggregates are the five *skandhas*.
When not a single thought arises, the eighteen realms (*aṣṭādaśa-dhātu*) are empty. Thus, the body is itself Bodhi;

the flower and fruit are the mind itself, which is spiritual wisdom (*jñāna*), also called the "spiritual terrace" (*lingtai*). If there is any dwelling or attachment, then the body is a corpse. It is also said:
If one tastes the words of Huangbo regarding the ghost that guards corpses, then all beginningless, false habitual tendencies originate from a single thought;
once the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault—so how could there be any causes or conditions?

Mahāmati, those marks of one's own false discrimination do not arise gradually nor do they arise simultaneously for the foolish (the Chinese text says: "This is what the foolish discriminate for themselves;

it is neither produced gradually nor produced all at once"). Why is this? If they were to arise simultaneously, there would be no distinction between agent and action, and the characteristic of a cause could not be established.
If they were to arise gradually, the characteristic of a self could not be established; therefore, gradual arising does not occur.

Just as there is no designation of "father" if no son is born (the Wei translation says: "If all dharmas were to arise simultaneously, cause and effect could not be distinguished, because the characteristics of the causal and resultant bodies would not be perceived;

if they were to arise sequentially, one could not speak of sequential arising so long as the characteristics of the body have not been attained—just as how can one be called a father when there is no son?"), Mahāmati, the notion of a gradual arising through the continuity of expedient means is not so, for it is merely a false imagination (*vikalpa*).
This is because that which is produced arises from conditions such as objective referents (*ālambana*), sequential conditions (*anuloma-pratyaya*), and dominant conditions (*adhipati-pratyaya*).
Wisdom arises gradually because of the non-arising of the signs of attachment to the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*). [The Wei translation says:

"Foolish ordinary people, observing the sequential continuity of their own minds, find it inconsistent and thus speak in this way: 'The causal condition (*hetu-pratyaya*), the sequential condition (*anantara-pratyaya*), the objective condition (*ālambana-pratyaya*), and the dominant condition (*adhipati-pratyaya*) can produce all phenomena.

Mahāmati, such a sequence of the production of phenomena does not arise; it is merely the grasping of the essence and characteristics of phenomena through false discrimination (*vikalpa*). [The Tang translation says: "Those who engage in conceptual construction say that what is produced by the causal condition, the objective condition, the immediate condition, and the dominant condition is mutually dependent and arises in succession. This is logically untenable; it is entirely an attachment of deluded sentiment."
Because of attachment to signs, Mahāmati, neither gradual nor simultaneous production arises, for the objects of experience are merely the manifestations of one’s own mind.

Since external natures—whether characterized by specific or common marks—lack intrinsic existence, and because the arising of signs occurs through the failure to realize that they are the delusive imaginings of one’s own mind, one should abandon views of both gradual and simultaneous [production]. (The Tang translation states: "Neither gradual nor sudden production exists; it is merely one's own...")

Because the mind manifests as body and resources, and because external self-characteristics and common characteristics are all devoid of intrinsic nature, Mahāmati, consciousness alone arises as its own conceptualized views; therefore, one should abandon the views of sudden or gradual arising within the signs of causal conditions, karmic effects, and their conjunction.

Tong said: "The 'characteristic of conditions' (*pratyaya-lakṣaṇa*) refers to the conventional teaching of dependent origination; the 'characteristic of causes' (*hetu-lakṣaṇa*) refers to the successive arising from causes.
To say 'conventional' is to mean that conditions lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*); to say 'successive' is to mean that causes lack intrinsic nature.

Since there is no intrinsic nature, there is fundamentally no arising. How, then, could there be gradual arising or sudden arising? It is only those ordinary, deluded beings who conceive of such distinctions."
In another version it says: "It is not that they arise gradually, yet through deluded imagination one clings to them as having a gradual character;
it is not that they arise suddenly, yet through deluded imagination one clings to them as having a sudden character. If they were to arise suddenly, cause and effect would be produced simultaneously;
who then would be the agent and who the object? Since the distinctions between the characteristics of cause and effect could not be established, we know that they do not arise suddenly."

If the fruit were to arise gradually, there would first be the cause and then the fruit; yet, since the characteristic of the fruit cannot be obtained [prior to its arising], how can one speak of the cause producing it?
Just as one cannot be called a father before a son exists, once the son is obtained, the name "father" comes into being.
Since cause and fruit are fully present simultaneously, we know that they do not arise gradually. That which arises through gradual succession is fundamentally non-arising.
The speculative proponents of human discourse claim that there is a continuity [of self] through the conditions of skillful means (*upāya*) and dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*);

however, because this does not correspond with the actual intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena, it cannot be established by reason, and thus they say it is not so. It is merely the deluded conceptual discrimination of fools.
They speak thus: "Causes and conditions" refers to the immediate cause of one's own mind; that which is able to give rise [to phenomena] is called "grasping" (*ālambana*).
"Object-condition" (*ālambana-pratyaya*) refers to the mind's apprehension of external objects and so forth; it is the condition as the object.
"Sequential-condition" (*samanantara-pratyaya*) refers to internal and external phenomena arising in succession one after another without interruption; it is the "equal-and-immediate condition.

"Dominant-condition" (*adhipati-pratyaya*) refers to that which exists externally to the object and externally to the fruit; it is so called because it exerts a superior influence over the immediate causal conditions.
These various conditions are said to be able to produce all phenomena; because these conditions are both the producers and the produced, there is a sequential order of gradual arising.

In reality, this gradual arising is fundamentally non-arising, yet it is all due to the attachment to the self-nature of false imagination, which grasps at the characteristics of the essence of phenomena as having a sequential order.
This is merely a provisional device established for the sake of instruction, even if one were to consider it in a single thought-moment.

If non-arising arises from conditions, since there is no agent of arising, how can there be that which is arisen? Therefore, the claim that things arise by means of various conditions is truly not so.
Since gradual arising is not established, instantaneous arising can already be understood as impossible; thus it is said that neither gradual nor simultaneous arising occurs.

Consequently, the various sense organs, bodies, environments, and spheres of experience currently before one’s eyes— *Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the philosophical argument regarding the impossibility of arising (from either a gradual or instantaneous process) within a Madhyamaka framework.*

From what does this arise? It is because all phenomena are manifested solely by the mind; that is to say, they are manifested by the eight consciousnesses as the perceived aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the perceiving aspect (*darśanabhāga*), and as the self-nature and the objects of enjoyment, just as images appear in a mirror.

Since they originally lack intrinsic nature, each of the aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth possesses its own essence as its specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), while the aggregates and so forth combine to form a person as their common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
All are external objects; the nature of externality is non-nature, fundamentally unborn from the beginning. Therefore, whether arising gradually or arising suddenly, all are unborn.

This is not a case of absolute non-arising that would equate with nihilism. Once one removes what is manifested by one’s own mind and attains non-discriminative vision, arising is itself non-arising, for there is fundamentally no mark.
It is only through the lack of awakening of ignorance that deluded arising occurs.
To hold that there is a sequential arising of distinct entities is the characteristic of the expedient means of causal conditioning;

however, because this arises solely from one's own false imagination, it is incorrect to perceive a gradual arising within the nature of conjunction, and it is likewise incorrect to perceive a sudden arising within the nature of conjunction. Such a person clings to what is not a real nature.
To perceive that there is an intrinsic nature is a false view; therefore, it should be abandoned.

If one perceives that which is devoid of intrinsic nature, even the nature of perception cannot be found—how then could delusion be established? If all arising views are extinguished, even the locus of their arising cannot be found—whence could perception arise?
You Bodhisattvas, being able to skillfully understand these conditions and causes, shall attain the state of non-arising.
Shengfaren Shenhui asked the Sixth Patriarch, "Is it sudden first and gradual later, or gradual first and sudden later?

Without awakening to the distinction between the sudden and the gradual, the human mind remains constantly deluded and distressed. The Patriarch replied, "In the midst of hearing the Dharma there is the gradual;

in the awakening to the Dharma there is the sudden. In the practice of cultivation there is the gradual; in the realization of the fruit there is the sudden. Suddenness and gradualness are constant causes arising from awakening."
In the interim, he was not deluded or distressed. Later, Heze remarked:
"When one perceives the pure essence, the eighty-four thousand gates of the various samādhis and pāramitās all arise simultaneously upon that single perception.
However, when one is in true accord with Suchness, all transformations are stilled; at this time, there is nothing further to be seen, nor any samādhis or pāramitās."

The gates of the pāramitās are likewise simultaneously empty and quiescent, with nothing further to be attained; these few words, however, cause all views regarding arising to be utterly extinguished, which corresponds to Heze’s realization—it cannot be said that he has not awakened.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"All things are entirely without birth, nor do they perish through causes and conditions. Within that birth and perishing, one gives rise to the notion of causes and conditions.
This is not to negate the arising of perishing, nor is it the causal continuity that arises; it is not for the purpose of severing the delusive, false imaginings of the ignorant and foolish."

(As the Tang translation says: "All phenomena are without arising and likewise without cessation. Within those various conditions, one discriminates the marks of arising and ceasing; it is not that the convergence of conditions is being negated. Thus they cease and then arise again, yet this merely halts the false imaginings of the ignorant. Whether existent or non-existent, the dharmas of dependent origination are all entirely without arising. Deluded by habitual tendencies, one revolves through these three realms of existence. In reality, there is no arising, and conditions likewise have no cessation. To contemplate all conditioned things is like flowers in the sky. All dharmas are without arising and likewise without cessation.

Within those various conditions, one discriminates the marks of arising and ceasing; it is not that the convergence of conditions is being negated. Thus they cease and then arise again, yet this merely halts the false imaginings of the ignorant. Whether existent or non-existent, the dharmas of dependent origination are all entirely without arising. Deluded by habitual tendencies, one revolves through these three realms of existence.
In reality, there is no arising, and conditions likewise have no cessation. To contemplate all conditioned things is like flowers in the sky.
Grasping and that which is grasped, the abandonment of delusive views, that which has not yet arisen or will arise, as well as the absence of causes and conditions—
all these are non-existent and entirely beyond verbal expression.
The Master said: "The prose section merely refutes the characteristics of causal conditions (*pratyaya-hetu*) and the views of gradual or simultaneous arising;

it has not yet reached the point of explaining in detail that what is manifested within one's own mind as experience is fundamentally without birth or cessation. Therefore, I shall speak in verse to reveal this:

all internal and external phenomena are fundamentally without arising from causes and conditions, nor do they cease through causes and conditions; they are fundamentally without gradualness or suddenness."
Birth is likewise neither gradual nor sudden. Within those various conditions, one discriminates the characteristics of arising and ceasing;

having discerned that all conceptualizations of those conditions are dharmas of arising and ceasing, one perceives that what has ceased arises again through the causal continuity of dependent origination.

I maintain that this is not [independent] non-conditional origination, for it does not negate the meeting of conditions. When conditions assemble, they themselves arise and cease; without conditions, there is no arising or ceasing. This is the universal principle.
Fools are attached to the conceptualization of conditions and do not understand the meaning of non-arising. I speak of "no causes and conditions" merely to eliminate their delusions;
for while all phenomena exist as either being or non-being, each arises from conditions, yet that arising is fundamentally without birth and immediately returns to quiescence.
Since I am free from discrimination, where could the three realms exist? They are merely illusory habitual tendencies that accumulate and expand through delusion.
The "transforming cause" refers to the mutual arising and ceasing of existence within the realms of desire, form, and formlessness;
from within this, phenomena manifest. If one awakens to the true reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), which is pure and free from even a speck of dust, then originally there is neither birth nor cessation.
One should contemplate all conditioned phenomena manifested by one's own mind as being like flowers blooming in empty space.
How could empty space ever be defiled? It is merely produced by pressing on the eyes; this is called delusion.

To see the pressing as the grasping faculty (*grāhaka-indriya*) and the flower as the grasped object (*grāhya-viṣaya*), when in fact neither exists yet one claims they do—this is why it is called delusion.

If one can truly abandon this seeing and remain far removed from false discrimination, then it is not that the flower has already arisen, nor will it arise in the future; it does not arise through conditions.
The emergence of empty space is not caused by the eyes; it is fundamentally without cause or condition. From where could the flowers arise?
They are seen solely through deluded imagination; in reality, they do not exist at all. To realize that nothing exists is to see that all things are entirely without birth.
Since there is no birth, how can there be conditions, and how can there be names? Thus one knows that these various conditions and conceptions are merely words.
[The Master] spoke of the discrimination of empty flowers as having no true reality. Shenhui asked the Sixth Patriarch: "If one uses arising to extinguish extinction, it is extinction;
if one uses extinction to extinguish arising, it is arising. I do not understand the meaning of arising and extinction; I seem like one who is deaf and blind. The Patriarch said:
"Using arising to extinguish extinction is to cause people not to cling to their nature; using extinction to extinguish arising is to cause people’s minds [to be at peace]."

Detaching from objects does not immediately mean detaching from the two extremes; one must further eliminate the illness of arising and ceasing. Furthermore, a person from Shishan asked Chan Master Guifeng:

"How is it that what is produced through the Buddha's transformation arises in the same manner as that [which is not transformed]? Since the Buddha has no 'arising of arising,' what is the meaning of this?
If you say that when the mind arises, dharmas arise, and when the mind ceases, dharmas cease, how can one attain the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*)?"
Yaśas replied: "Since it is said that 'all is like an illusion,' and an illusion is itself emptiness, and emptiness is non-arising, why question the meaning of arising?

When arising and ceasing have ceased, quiescent extinction is the truth; to accept this dharma as non-arising is called the 'patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas' (anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti).
Combining these two explanations and observing them together, the meaning of dependent origination as non-arising becomes brilliantly complete."
(Chapter Two, Part Three of the *Sarvadharma-saṃgraha-parivarta* of the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*).
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me the *Sūtra on the Mind as the Appearance of Verbal Conceptualization*. World-Honored One, if I and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas thoroughly understand speech..."
The *Sūtra on Explaining the Characteristics of the Mind of Discursive Thought* (also translated as the *Dharma-Gate of the Mind*).

By means of this, one can penetrate the two kinds of meanings—the expression and that which is expressed—and swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Through the purification of the two paths of expression and that which is expressed, all sentient beings are brought to maturity.
The Buddha addressed Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it; I shall explain it for you."

Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, “There are four kinds of conceptualization regarding the characteristics of discourse:
namely, discourse on characteristics, discourse on dreams, discourse on the attachment to false conceptualizations, and discourse on beginningless conceptualization.
Discourse on characteristics arises from attachment to the forms and marks of one’s own conceptualization; discourse on dreams...”
Discourse arising from the recollection of previously experienced objects is produced from the realization that one’s own objects lack intrinsic nature (as stated in the Tang translation:

"it means that discourse arises from recollecting previously experienced objects in a dream upon waking, based on unreal objects"). Discourse arising from the attachment to the errors of false conceptualization is produced from the recollection of actions performed by former enemies.
Discourse arising from beginningless false conceptualization is produced from the error of beginningless attachment to falsehoods.

Arising from the habit-energies of seeds (in the Tang translation: arising from the habit-energies of beginningless false attachments to conceptual proliferation)—this is called the fourfold characteristic of the delusive discrimination of verbal expression.
It is generally said, O Mahāmati, that because the Blessed One has taught that all things are non-existent, these are all merely verbal expressions;

since they arise through the causes and conditions of attachment to verbal expression and are subject to birth and cessation, they are indeed delusive discrimination. However, regarding the supreme primary truth (*paramārtha*), [they are not so].
Since manifestation occurs through verbal expression, and because the conceptualization of verbal expression itself possesses its own gateway to the mind-dharmas,
one who thoroughly masters verbal expression— and thus masters that which is expressed— thoroughly masters the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) that is expressed.

Through this mastery of both the penetration of the principle (*siddhānta-praveśa*) and the penetration of the teaching (*deśanā-praveśa*), one swiftly realizes unsurpassed bodhi without departing from verbal expression or that which is expressed.

The two types of destinies are used to purify sentient beings according to those very destinies, so that all sentient beings shall rely upon the meaning (*artha*) rather than clinging to verbal expression; thus, they attain pure understanding regarding these two meanings.

The Buddha stated that verbal expression is called "delusive conceptualization" (*vikalpa*) because it arises dependent upon consciousness; the five, six, seven, and eight consciousnesses do not transcend this.
Regarding the mind, it is said that the characteristics of deluded thought (*vikalpa*) are explained in the *Cittaviparyāsa-sūtra* by way of approximately four types:
First, there is "discursive speech regarding signs" (*nimitta-vyavahāra*), which refers to the arising of speech through the discrimination of all objective forms by the first five consciousnesses.

Because this is spoken in relation to external objects, it belongs to the first five consciousnesses. Second, there is "dream-like speech," which refers to the sixth consciousness recollecting past objects and speaking of them.
Regarding the statement that "arising is like a dream": once one has awakened from the objects experienced previously, one subsequently recollects them;
because verbal expression arises based on unreal objects, it is said to be "without intrinsic nature. Third, regarding the fault of clinging to conceptual proliferation through verbal expression:
this refers to the seven consciousnesses being the basis for defilement and purity, and the prior clinging to those who were either benefactors or enemies, as well as to the actions performed.

Good and evil karma follow wherever recollection reaches, transmitting and emerging from the six consciousnesses; the recollection of the six consciousnesses is merely vivid and distinct regarding their respective objects.
When the recollection of the seventh consciousness occurs, it becomes bound to and flows forth from the karma of enmity;
therefore, it is called "transgressing the four. Fourth, regarding beginningless deluded conceptualization and speech: this refers to the eighth consciousness containing and storing falsehoods.
In reality, there exist seeds of the habit-energy of non-conceptual proliferation (*aprapañca-vāsanā*), within which false attachments are not relinquished;
these suddenly emerge because one has planted the roots of delusion since beginningless time, thereby giving rise to the marks of verbal conceptualization.
These four kinds of verbal expression arise through the successive interaction of eight, seven, six, and five causes and conditions; therefore, they are so called.
This is a delusion. Linji said: "As for my own way of functioning today, it is truly the play of creation and destruction, the manifestation of spiritual transformations.
Entering all circumstances, I am at ease wherever I am; no circumstance can change me. Whenever someone comes seeking me, I immediately go out to look at them.
If they do not recognize me, I then put on various kinds of robes so that people may develop understanding."
"Directly entering my words and phrases—alas, you blind shaveling! You sightless person, you recognize the blue, yellow, red, and white of the garment I am wearing.
I strip it off and enter the realm of purity; as soon as the student sees this, he gives rise to longing and desire.
I strip it off again, and the student loses his mind, wandering about in frantic confusion, crying out, 'I have no clothes!'"
He immediately turned toward the channel and asked, "Do you recognize the person who is wearing these clothes?
Suddenly, he turned his head back and recognized him, saying, "Virtuous One, do not mistake the clothes for the person. Clothes cannot move; it is the person who wears them.
There is the pure robe, there is the unborn robe, the Bodhi robe, the Nirvana robe, the Patriarch’s robe, and the Buddha robe."
Virtue exists only as sound and name; all words and phrases are merely transformations of clothing.
Stirred up from the ocean of vital energy at the navel wheel, they are formed into the meaning of sentences by the clashing of teeth. Clearly know that these are illusory manifestations.

Great Virtuous One, externally you emit the karma of vocal speech, while internally you express mental factors (*caitta-dharma*); since volition (*cetanā*) and mindfulness (*smṛti*) are entirely [like] clothing, you simply recognize them as such.

He wears the garment of reality as his true liberation; though passing through kalpas as numerous as motes of dust, it is merely the garment that permeates the three realms, circulating and revolving within birth and death.
It is not like meeting someone unexpectedly and failing to recognize them, or conversing without knowing their name.
To truly deliver such discourse is genuine skillful mastery; by means of the two kinds of access—speech and that which is spoken—one attains fulfillment and thoroughly purifies.
"All sentient beings perceive through delusion.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again requested the World-Honored One on this matter, saying:
"World-Honored One, we pray that you will further explain the manifested realms of the conceptualization of speech—where, why, how, and by what cause do they arise for sentient beings?"

"Conceptual proliferation gives rise to verbal expression. (The Wei translation says: "I only pray that you will again explain for me the characteristics of the four kinds of false attachments to language: from where do the speech of sentient beings arise?
How do they arise? By what cause do they arise? The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Speech sounds arise from the conjunction of the head, chest, throat, nose, lips, tongue, palate, and teeth."
The Master replied: "The four kinds of verbal expression arise from the five, six, seven, and eight consciousnesses;
these are the causes of delusion. He asked further: "From where do the perceived objects emerge? Why do they emerge? How do they emerge?
Why and how are they merely a matter of conjunction? [The Master replied: "Because of what cause do they emerge? [He continued: "Because of causes."
Because these four preceding types of false conceptualization serve as causes, the Buddha did not answer; he answered only because that locus was conjoined with them.

From the teeth, throat, tongue, and lips, the five tones emerge, and these are further augmented by the head, chest, and nose—the head being the point of general convergence, the chest being where the vital energy (*prāṇa*) issues forth, and the nose also possessing sound. As for the nose: [it is so called because] it has sound.
If they are blocked, sound is not produced. These eight [vocal organs] are the places from which sound emerges;
it is through their harmonious conjunction and the stimulation of the central breath that sound is formed—this is why speech emerges.

If the Buddha’s preaching of the Dharma possesses sixty-four kinds of Brahma-sounds, how could these eight alone serve as its conditions? Therefore, one knows that even the objects of perception (*ālambana*) are illusory. —Miaoshan.
Wu-feng and Yun-yan were standing in attendance together with Baizhang.
Baizhang asked Shigong Weishan, "If one were to shut off the throat, lips, and mouth, how would you speak? Weishan said, "I beg the Master to speak instead.
Baizhang said, "I am not unwilling to speak for you, but I fear it would cause my descendants to perish later on. Xuedou’s Verse: "I beg the Master to speak instead"—a tiger!
Horns grow upon his head as he emerges from the wild weeds; the spring of the Ten Continents has ended and the flowers wither away.
In the coral groves, the sun shines brightly. Baizhang asked again: "Five Peaks, how do you speak when you have shut up your throat, lips, and mouth?
Five Peaks said, "The Master must also shut yours up. Baizhang said, "In a place where no one is, I shall wring my hands and gaze at you. Xuedou [comments]: "How pitiful!"
The verse says: "Even the Master has been swept away; Watching the strategy in the Dragon-Snake Array, it makes one long remember General Li.
A solitary falcon soars ten thousand miles across the heavens. Baizhang again asked Yunyan, "Having swept away the throat, lips, and mouth, how would you speak?
Yuyan said, "Does the Master have them still? Baizhang said, "You have lost your own descendants."
Yundou’s verse says: "Has the Master attained it yet? The golden-haired lion does not crouch on the ground;

two by two, three by three, they walk the old path. Beneath Mount Daxiong, he snaps his fingers in vain. Such phrases do not consist of verbal expression, yet they are not apart from verbal expression.
One must clarify the profound meaning of what is said—how mysterious and subtle it is!
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “World-Honored One, are verbal expressions and conceptual discrimination different or not different?
The Buddha told Mahāmati, “Verbal expressions and conceptual discrimination are neither different nor not different. Why is this? It is because they arise from the same causal characteristics.

Mahāmati, if verbal expressions were different from conceptual discrimination, then conceptual discrimination would not be their cause. If they were not different, then speech [would be indistinguishable from it].”
Because it manifests meaning through its manifestation, it is neither different nor not different [from the cause].
It is replied: "The conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) arises from the five, six, seven, or eight consciousnesses; this is the cause of verbal expression (*abhilāpa*).

Verbal expression issues forth from the conjunction of the throat, lips, teeth, tongue, and so forth; this is the characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of verbal expression. The characteristic does not arise without the cause."

Therefore, one should know that they are neither different nor non-different. If they were different, speech would have its own independent cause and need not depend on conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) as its cause;
yet, conceptual construction and speech are like roots and sprouts—they are fundamentally not different.

If they were non-different, then speech would be identical to conceptual construction and conceptual construction would be identical to speech; how then could they manifest the meaning of what is expressed?
However, since speech can manifest meaning, speech is certainly the agent and meaning is certainly the object; as the subject and object are distinct, how could they not be different?
To say they are different is to be confined by superficial traces; to say they are neither different nor non-different is to transcend the realm of traces.
This is the inconceivable state—how could it be fathomed through discursive thought?
"Deliverance! A monk asked Master Huanglian, "What is the single phrase before sound? Huanglian said, "Before sound there is no phrase;
ask after the sound. Touzi provided this verse: "In the vast void prior to the empty kalpa, the desolate road is still;
Before sound there is no phrase—those who can believe it are rare. If you wish to exhaust the melody of the white clouds over Canglang, Observe first the stone man revealing himself."
Another monk asked Master Chongfu Zhi, "What is the speech of vast expansiveness? Zhi said, "A person without a tongue can speak it. Touzi’s verse says:
When speaking words of vast expansiveness, the tongue is not offended; The pure breeze and lofty melody drift through the azure clouds.
The stone man greedily talks of the affairs of the Western Peak, Unaware that mist rises from the Eastern Cliff to shroud him. From the *Biyan lu* (Blue Cliff Record).
What was previously stated as being different has never actually been different; what was subsequently stated as being non-different has never actually not been non-different.
To gain faith and entry into this is to be well-versed in the ultimate purport of the First Principle (paramārtha).
Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, is speech itself the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), or is that which is expressed by speech the ultimate truth?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Neither is speech the ultimate truth, nor is that which is expressed by speech the ultimate truth.
Why is this? Because the ultimate truth is the noble bliss (*āryasukha*) that is entered through speech."

Meaning is not words; this is the primary truth (*paramārtha*). (The Tang translation says: "Why? Because the primary truth is the cause for the noble ones' state of bliss; one enters it by means of words, but it is not the words themselves.
The primary truth is that which is attained through the self-awakening of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*); it is not the realm of awakening through the conceptualization of words.
Therefore, the conceptualization of words does not manifest the primary truth. Words arise and perish, they are restless and fluctuating, and they function through successive causes and conditions.
If arising occurs through a succession of causes and conditions, that does not reveal the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), Mahāmati, because it lacks the intrinsic nature of self and other.
Since the characteristics of verbal expression do not reveal the ultimate truth—[the Chinese version states: "The ultimate truth is that which lacks the characteristics of self and other;

language possesses characteristics and thus cannot reveal it"]—furthermore, Mahāmati, because one enters into the manifestation of one's own mind, various characteristics are spoken of as being external, whether they exist or do not exist.
To speak of false conceptualization is not to reveal the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). (The "ultimate truth" here means that all various external appearances are merely one's own mind;
they do not exist at all, and cannot be revealed by verbal discrimination. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should abandon the characteristics of false conceptualization expressed in words.

Tong said: "When Mahāmati hears that the characteristic of arising from causes is neither different [from the cause] nor non-different, it is because it is not different since it can manifest meaning, yet it is not non-different either.
If it were not different, would it not follow that verbal expression is itself the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)?
If it were not non-different, would it not follow that there is nothing that can be expressed as the ultimate truth? Therefore, the ultimate truth is not separate from the subject and object."

The Buddha said: "Neither identity nor difference, neither both nor neither—this is precisely the departure from the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*) and the severance of the hundred negations (*śata-apavāda*).
Only by awakening to this state can one clarify the ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*). How could verbal expression itself be the ultimate meaning?
Nor could that which is expressed be the ultimate meaning. Why say that verbal expression is not the ultimate meaning? Because..."
The single meaning is the realm of sublime bliss of noble wisdom; it is entered through words, yet it is not the words themselves.
It is like using a finger to point at the moon—how could the finger be taken for the moon? Therefore, it is said that what is expressed in words is not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Why is it said that what is spoken is not the ultimate truth? Because the ultimate truth is that which is personally realized by noble wisdom.
This attainment can only be realized within oneself and cannot be expressed in words; it is not a realm reached by the awakening of discursive thought (*vikalpa*).

Because verbal expression takes discursive thought as its cause, and because such conceptualizing consciousness lacks the essence of mind, it cannot manifest the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), for that which is spoken is not the ultimate truth. What is spoken...
Why do you not reveal the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)? Will this not contradict what was previously stated—that language is capable of revealing meaning?
It is simply because that language, being conceptual construction and discrimination, involves arising and ceasing, movement and fluctuation;

it does not transcend the six, five, seven, or eight consciousnesses, which do not abide for even a single thought-moment but arise through the successive conditions of one another. The first [consciousness]...

The ultimate meaning (artha) is neither born nor extinguished; it is fundamentally unmoving, does not belong to the realm of causes and conditions or their conjunction, and exists as the singular state of True Suchness (tathatā).
How could it be manifested by the awakening of those deluded thoughts? This is the first point: consciousness cannot manifest wisdom.
If one were to claim that within the primary truth there is a realm to be attained, then characteristics would still persist. Furthermore—

It can be said that the self-characteristic of the one true reality remaining unchanging and the other-characteristic of the one true reality following conditions are both devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Since they lack such a nature, no characteristics can be apprehended; how then could these be displayed by those who speak of characteristics?
This characteristic cannot manifest the absence of characteristics—this is the second point. If it is claimed that [the ultimate] is exclusively non-existent...
It may also be said that there is a persistence of the signless even when [existence] is identical to annihilation.

Now, what is attained through the self-awakening of noble wisdom enters into the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of one’s own mind; although various external appearances manifest, they are like a phantom person performing illusory deeds—when their intrinsic nature is sought, it is entirely non-existent. This is the direct perception of one’s own mind, which is not only free from delusion.
That which can be attained is also without anything truly attainable; yet through the deluded conceptualization of speech, one forcibly makes distinctions.
How could that which is capable of making distinctions possibly discern that which is non-discernible? This delusion cannot manifest the Truth—this is the third point.
By observing these three points, it is sufficient to know that what is spoken of is not the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). The ultimate truth is neither speech nor that which is spoken of.

It is said: "From the very beginning, you are free from the characteristics of language. You Bodhisattvas who wish to attain unsurpassed bodhi should leave behind the characteristics of all conceptual fabrications of speech.
Where the path of language is cut off and the sphere of mental activity ceases—this is truly attaining the ultimate meaning.
This is sufficient to purify all sentient beings. Master Dayang Ming'an ascended the hall and said:
Aragaki peaks ten thousand fathoms high, where bird-paths are hard to traverse; upon sword-blades and thin ice, who would dare to tread?
The wondrous phrases of the ancestral vehicle are difficult to set forth on the path of words; at the Gate of Non-dual Dharma, Vimalakīrti remained silent.
Thus, when Bodhidharma came from the West, he sat facing the wall for nine years before finally meeting one who understood. Today, Dayang is also most groundlessly reckless—take care! Dan.
The *Xia Song* says: "A single phrase that does not hang upon the lips is extraordinary; sitting coldly at Shaolin is the ultimate compassion.
One must know that this Way is not transmitted through verbal instruction; Huike’s standing in the snow was already an act of forced exertion.
If the path above were something that could be proclaimed in words, it would fall into the second or third stage and could not be called the Ultimate Meaning."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The Buddhas have no self-nature, nor do they possess verbal expression; the profound meaning of emptiness within emptiness cannot be fully understood by the foolish.

All natures and self-natures are like shadows; the Dharma of words and speech is known through the wisdom of self-realization by the sons of wisdom. This is the Reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi) as taught by me."

(The Tang translation says: "All phenomena lack intrinsic nature and are likewise beyond verbal expression; the ignorant do not perceive the meaning of emptiness within emptiness, and thus they wander in saṃsāra. All phenomena are without nature and are free from verbal expression and conceptualization; all existences are like dreams or magical illusions—neither birth-and-death nor nirvāṇa.

Just as a king or a householder, in order to delight his children, first gives them similar objects and later gives them the real ones, so too do I now: first I teach the provisional dharma, and later I shall expound for them the dharma of the personally realized reality-limit)."
Tong said: "This verse in the Song translation appears concise yet encompasses a vast range of meaning.

What is called 'the profound emptiness of emptiness' (śūnyatā-śūnyatā) refers to the meaning of the three non-manifestations mentioned above—namely, that arising and ceasing, and agitation, do not manifest as empty. 'The emptiness of the absence of self-nature in both self and other' refers to emptiness.
'Entering deeply into the direct perception (pratyakṣa) of one’s own mind' refers to the profound emptiness of emptiness. As for the Tang translation..."

Conversely, the first two lines of the [verse on] "redundancy" (*punarukta*), which state that all phenomena are without intrinsic nature and beyond verbal conceptualization, share the same intent as the passage in the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra* that says:

"All conditioned phenomena are like a dream, an illusion, a bubble, a shadow, like dew and likewise like lightning; one should view them in this way. Furthermore, it is similar in meaning to the statement: "The self-nature of all phenomena is not as it is expressed in words."
To perceive the signless (*animitta*) without negating signs is precisely the profound meaning of the emptiness of emptiness (*śūnyatā-śūnyatā*).

If one were to speak of this Dharma abruptly to ordinary people, they would certainly be unable to comprehend it and would instead give rise to disbelief; therefore, the expedient metaphors of the crest-jewel and so forth are established.
These are methods of skillful guidance, similar to the ways a king or a householder leads others; they do not represent the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).
Therefore, when one uses verbal expressions to reveal the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), one first speaks of phenomena that appear similar [to it].
Now, I maintain that what is expressed by verbal discourse is not the ultimate truth; rather, it is the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) realized through self-attestation.

Thus, the teachings of verbal discourse are like shadows; they are not what I have taught. What is attained through the noble wisdom of self-realization is the ground of the principle of the reality-limit.
What I have now spoken is, in truth, a teaching of non-teaching; that which I call the Dharma of the Self is subtle and inconceivable.
In the Tang translation, it is said that there is neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa. Because people fear saṃsāra, nirvāṇa is shown to them as an illustration, like the parable of the conjured city.
When those of the Two Vehicles have transcended saṃsāra, they perceive a nirvāṇa to be desirable, and thus [they settle] in nirvāṇa.
Regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), one no longer seeks further advancement, for within the ultimate truth there is neither saṃsāra nor nirvāṇa;
there is no nirvāṇa apart from the Buddha, and no Buddha apart from nirvāṇa.

This mark of the quiescence of all phenomena can only be personally realized and is beyond the reach of verbal expression; therefore, it can only be discussed with those who possess the noble wisdom of self-awakening.
When Linji arrived at Fenglin, Fenglin asked, "Is there anything you would like to ask? Linji replied, "How could one carve flesh to create a wound?
Fenglin said, "The sea moon is clear and without shadow; the swimming fish alone is deluded. Linji said, "Since the sea moon has no shadow, how can the swimming fish be deluded?
Fenglin said, "Observe the wind and see the waves rise; gaze upon the water and the wild geese fly."

Ji said: "The sail drifts across the river; the solitary wheel shines alone. The mountains and rivers are still; a single long啸 (shout) makes heaven and earth autumn. Lin said: "Let the three-inch radiance be as it will; try saying one phrase on the spot. Ji said:

"When meeting a swordsman on the road, you must present your sword; if you are not a poet, do not offer your poem. Fenglin then desisted. Ji then had [this verse]: Sail drifting, the river flows; Solitary wheel, shining alone. Mountains and rivers are silent; A single long shout, heaven and earth turn autumn. Let the three-inch brilliance be as it may; Try saying one phrase when the moment arrives.
When meeting a swordsman on the road, you must show your sword; If you are no poet, do not offer your verse. Fenglin, you may stop now. Ji then had this:
The Great Way is cut off; let things be as they are, whether heading west or east. Stone-fire cannot catch up; lightning-flash finds no passage.
Miaoshan asked Yangshan, "Stone-fire cannot catch up; lightning-flash finds no passage. What do the sages of the past use to benefit people?
Yangshan said, "What is your intention, Master? Miaoshan said, "As long as there is verbal expression, there is no true meaning."
Yangshan said, "Not so. Muzhou asked, "And what about you, my son? Yangshan replied, "The official does not allow even a needle, yet in private one may pass carts and horses.
These karmic conditions are sufficient to show that while the Dharma of self-realization—the ultimate reality—is fundamentally inexpressible, it has never been the case that it is not expressed;
though he speaks all day long, he has never spoken a word. This is the profound Dharma-gate.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying:
