"World-Honored One, we pray that You will explain for us that which is free from being one or different, both or neither, existent or non-existent, neither existent nor non-existent, permanent or impermanent—that which is not traversed by any externalists, but is the domain of the noble wisdom of self-realization;
that which is free from false conceptualization, transcends both specific and general characteristics, and enters into the supreme reality."
The meaning of this is that the characteristics of the successive stages, which gradually progress toward higher and higher purity, enter into the characteristics of the Tathāgata stage.

Without being produced through effort, by the power of original vows—like the realm of a mani jewel of manifold colors—it universally manifests all boundless realms. All the various characteristics of the divisions of the manifestations of one's own mind are thus revealed.
May I and other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, free from such views of the self-nature and the specific and general characteristics of the imagined nature—
which [the Tang dynasty translation states] "all dharmas (all dharmas are the various manifestations of one's own mind")— quickly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi,
so that all sentient beings may be fully endowed with and replete in peace and happiness.
Mahāmati said: Because of the preceding statement that verbal expressions and conceptual discrimination are neither different nor non-different,

and because that which is entered through verbal expression is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), he asked about that which is free from the four positions of oneness and difference, existence and non-existence, permanence and impermanence—
something not practiced by any outsiders but practiced by the noble wisdom of self-realization, which is the primary reality.

How does the meaning enter? Once it has entered the stage of Dry Wisdom (*śuklavidarśanā-bhūmi*) within the realm of reality, one proceeds through these ten stages in a continuous and gradual progression until entering the stage of the Tathāgata’s Equal and Wondrous Enlightenment.
By the power of effortless original vows, he manifests forms in response to sentient beings to deliver them extensively; it is like a *maṇi* jewel that universally displays all colors.
The immeasurable and boundless realms of practice all appear therein; all phenomena are manifestations of one's own mind, appearing as various differentiated parts like images reflected in a mirror.

Being fundamentally non-existent and free from all deluded thoughts, once one perceives the self-nature and the characteristics of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases—both their individual and common traits—one will swiftly realize unsurpassed Bodhi.
May all sentient beings together obtain peace and happiness, being fully and abundantly endowed with it, never again entering the heterodox views of external paths.
Linji addressed the assembly, saying: "There are times when the person is taken away but not the environment; there are times when the environment is taken away but not the person;
there are times when both person and environment are taken away; and there are times when neither person nor environment is taken away. At that time, a monk asked:
"What is 'taking away the person but not the environment'? Jie said: "The warm sun brings forth life, spreading carpets upon the earth; grandchildren with hair as white as silk.
"What is 'taking away the environment but not the person'? Jie said: "The royal decree has already been issued throughout the world;
the general leaves no dust beyond the frontier. "What is 'taking away both person and environment'? Jie said: [He remained silent.]
Duoji said: "To sever communication with Bing and Fen and dwell alone in one corner—how is this? Linji said:

"When the King ascends the precious throne, the village elder sings his song. These four "selections" (liaojian) of Linji are nothing other than a desire for sentient beings to abide in peace and happiness;
only those with the wondrous understanding of self-awakened noble wisdom can grasp their true meaning.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Excellent, excellent! That you are able to ask me about such a meaning brings great peace and great benefit, out of compassion for all devas and people of the world.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well;
I shall analyze and explain it for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Excellent, World-Honored One!"

"Venerable One, it is so; we accept your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Foolish ordinary beings who do not understand the measure of the mind (cittamātra) grasp at internal and external natures.

Relying on [the concepts of] identity, difference, both, neither, existence, non-existence, neither existence nor non-existence, permanence, and impermanence, they become attached through false discrimination (*vikalpa*) based on the causes of self-nature and habitual tendencies.

(The Wei translation says: 'Ordinary beings cannot awaken to the fact that these are merely what is seen of one's own mind; they cling to various external dharmas and characteristics as being truly existent. Therefore, they engage in false conceptualization. "
Tong said: "One who understands the measure of the mind knows that external natures are not-natures; everything is a manifestation of one's own mind and is fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature.
From where could arguments concerning identity and difference, or existence and non-existence, possibly arise?

It is only because they do not know that these manifestations are produced by the measure of the mind that they give rise to deluded discrimination, grasping at the 'seen-part' manifested by the eight consciousnesses as an internal nature, and grasping at what is manifested by the eight consciousnesses..."
The marks are divided into the external nature; from these two natures arise views such as existence and non-existence, identity and difference, annihilation and permanence.

If there were an inherent self-nature upon which these views could rely, their various differences would all stem from the causes of habitual tendencies accumulated over many lifetimes within the storehouse of the eight consciousnesses.
Because one clings to them and does not relinquish them, they become merely false conceptualizations. [This concludes the] Entry into the Great [Vehicle].

The *Mahāyānasaṃparigraha-śāstra* states: "In Kapilavastu, there are those who calculate [the self] as identical (*ekatva*), asserting that the action and the agent are one, or that the characteristic and the bearer of the characteristic are one;
such views are called the calculation of identity. The *Ulūka-sāṃkhya* calculates them as different;

the *Kāruṇika-gautama* calculates them as both identical and different; the son of Jāti calculates them as neither identical nor different. Furthermore, the *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If not..."
If one attains the skillful means of prajñā and enters Abhidharma, one falls into the extreme of existence; if one enters emptiness, one falls into the extreme of non-existence;

if one enters Prajñapti-śāstra (Kuṇḍala), one falls into the extreme of both existence and non-existence. The *Mūlamadhyamaka-kārikā* states that to cling to "neither existence nor non-existence" is called the "discourse of the deluded.
Therefore, if one studies the four gates of the Mahāyāna without grasping the intent of prajñā, one falls into the four types of false views (catvāro viparyāsāḥ). Existence [is thus a fallacy].

These are the four types of slander: the slander of superimposition (*samāropa*), the slander of denial (*apavāda*), the slander of contradiction (*ubhayatva*), and the slander of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) regarding neither existence nor non-existence.
Through these four propositions, one may multiply them into a hundred negations, yet they all do not transcend the two views of annihilationism and eternalism.
Huangbo said: "In ordinary, uneventful circumstances, do not waste your mind on idle pursuits; do not seek the Truth, but simply let go of your views."
Therefore, both internal views and external views are erroneous; both the Buddha-way and the Mara-way are evil.

This is why Mañjuśrī momentarily gave rise to two views and was banished to the two Iron Ring Mountains. Mañjuśrī is ultimate wisdom (*paramārtha-jñāna*), while Samantabhadra is expedient wisdom (*upāya-jñāna*).
Although these two are used in mutual counteraction, ultimately there is neither expedient nor ultimate wisdom; it is simply the One Mind. Furthermore, this mind is not the Buddha.
Sentient beings do not have a view that is distinct from the view of a Buddha; yet, as soon as there is the view of a Buddha, it immediately becomes the view of sentient beings.
Views of existence and non-existence, views of permanence and annihilation, thus become the two Iron Ring Mountains, for they are obstructed by views.

The Patriarchs point directly to the original mind and original substance of all sentient beings, which are inherently Buddha—not something to be accomplished through cultivation, nor belonging to gradual stages.
Next, it is not brightness, because it is not brightness; it is not ignorance (*avidyā*), because it is not darkness; it is not darkness, because it is not darkness.
Therefore, there is no non-ignorance, nor is there the exhaustion of non-ignorance. You must pay close attention to this when entering my school of thought.
Seeing in this manner is called "seeing the Dharma"; seeing the Dharma is called being a "Buddha. When both Buddha and Dharma are absent, that is called [the ultimate].
To call the Sangha the "unconditioned Sangha" (wuwei seng) is also termed the "Three Jewels as One Body.

If Huangbo can be said to have realized the full extent of the mind (xinliang), then not only is there nothing of the four propositions to be abandoned, but furthermore, there is no sacred wisdom (shengzhi) to be attained; this fully encompasses the essential eye of the school’s doctrine in this chapter.
For example, it is like a herd of deer, driven by thirst, who see a springtime mirage and perceive it as water; they rush toward it in confusion, unaware that it is not water.
In the same way, foolish people—whose minds are scorched by the three poisons and perfumed by false conceptualizations from beginningless time—delight in the realm of forms.
Seeing the arising, abiding, and ceasing of things, they grasp at internal and external natures, falling into the views of identity, difference, both, or neither.
The notions of existence, non-existence, both existence and non-existence, and neither existence nor non-existence, as well as permanence and impermanence, are all subsumed under false views.

[The Buddha] replied: "What was said above regarding the various inconsistencies of attachment to the causes of habitual practice and to deluded thoughts cannot be fully exhausted by a single approach;
it must be clarified through metaphors. Previously, Mahāmati asked: "For what reason are things like illusions, dreams, and [the reflection of] a *gandharva*..."

The city of Gandharvas, the world, the mirage of a hot day, and the moon reflected in water—these are detailed answers that, in sum, do not escape the confines of the five aggregates and the eight consciousnesses.
The coarsest among these is when the three poisons of greed, anger, and delusion burn the mind, causing one to joyfully seek various sensory objects;
within the state of non-arising, one falsely perceives arising and ceasing, and grasps at the root-body.

That city neither exists nor does not exist. All are merely manifestations of the mind, devoid of intrinsic nature and fundamentally unarisen.
It is only because of the delusion of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), due to false conceptualization since beginningless time, that this occurs.

One establishes the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*)—identity and difference, existence and non-existence, permanence and annihilation—only upon that appearance.

This refers to what is confronted by the first five consciousnesses (*pañcavijñāna*).
