Furthermore, Mahāmati, having established the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and the five-membered syllogism (*pañcāvayava-vākya*), one attains the self-realization of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna-svasaṃvedana*).
Yet, one still clings to the false conceptualization of existence regarding phenomena that are free from the two natures (*dvaya-svabhāva*). (The Tang translation says:

"Having established the three means of valid cognition, one gives rise to the discrimination of existence regarding the dharmas realized within noble wisdom that are free from the two natures. The Wei translation says: "And thus speaks: 'There truly exists a dharma realized within by the noble ones, which is free from the two natures and false discrimination. )
The Master said: "The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) cling to existence and thereby establish the view of eternalism; they cling to non-existence and thereby slander with the view of nihilism.
These two views—eternalism and nihilism—both involve deluded conceptualization regarding the dependent origination of the two natures.

Within my own Dharma, there are those who, while able to distance themselves from the false views of the non-Buddhists, nevertheless fail to escape attachment to dharmas. Regarding these three types [of practitioners]..."
In their respective systems of the Five-Part Treatise on Valid Cognition (*Pramāṇapañcaka*), these Śrāvakas establish their positions by taking the words of the Sage as their ultimate standard.

Yet, regarding the inconceivable realm of the inner realization of the Sage’s wisdom—which is free from the imagined and dependent natures—they give rise to false conceptualizations, claiming that there exists a perfectly accomplished nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) to be attained apart from the phenomena of the two natures of conceptual construction and dependent origination. Such are these Śrāvakas.

It is merely based on vocal teachings that one gives rise to false and deluded discriminative views. The three types of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) are: direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), inference (*anumāna*), and authoritative testimony (*āptāgama*).
Direct perception is the cognition of what is manifest; inference is the cognition prior to discrimination and comparison, which is known through analogy;

and authoritative testimony is that which takes the sacred teachings as its standard, such that heterodox or false views cannot be shifted. The five-membered syllogism consists of the thesis (*pakṣa*), the reason (*hetu*), and the example (*dṛṣṭānta*).

The three branches are combined and concluded as five parts: for instance, taking "existence" as the thesis (*pakṣa*), "reality" as the reason (*hetu*), and "mountains, rivers, and the great earth" as the example (*dṛṣṭānta*);
taking "impermanence" as the thesis, "existence" as the reason, and "the physical body" as the example;
taking "true permanence" as the thesis, "non-existence" as the reason, and "empty space" as the example—thus they are combined and concluded.
It merely brings about its completion; this is the manner in which the transformation Buddha preaches the Dharma.

Those of the Two Vehicles practice according to the teaching, distancing themselves from the phenomena of false imagination and dependent origination, and perceive the perfected nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva).

They claim that there is a truly existent dharma realized within by the sages, yet they cannot avoid the notion that a self-nature can be attained; this is precisely to be attached to signs (nimitta-grāha).
Although one realizes nirvana, if one takes this mind of arising and ceasing as the fundamental cause for cultivation, how can it be anything other than deluded thought?
Yangshan asked Shuangfeng, "How is your realization these days, brother? Shuangfeng replied, "According to my realization, there is truly not a single dharma that can be grasped by the mind.
Yangshan said, "Your understanding still remains within the realm of objects. Shuangfeng said, "I am simply like this, elder brother."
Furthermore, Yang said: "How is it that you do not know there is not a single dharma that can be taken as an object of the mind?
When Guishan heard this, he said: "Jizi’s single phrase will leave the people of the world in doubt. Xuangjue said: "The sutras state that truly there is no dharma;
however, when Dīpaṃkara Buddha conferred the prediction upon me, he said 'truly there is not a single dharma that can be taken as an object of the mind. Why is this so?"
If your understanding of the Way still remains within the realm of objects, tell me, where does the point of benefit or harm lie?

If this is so, then one who does not perceive a single dharma has not yet departed from the realm; how much less so for one who gives rise to conceptual discrimination regarding the nature of existence?

Mahāmati, when the mind, mentation, and consciousness undergo transformation, and the various delusions regarding the grasped and the grasper—which are manifestations of one's own mind—are severed, those practitioners who cultivate the noble self-realized wisdom of the Tathāgata stage do not form conceptions of existence or non-existence regarding that state. (The Tang translation states:

"All practitioners transform the mind, mentation, and consciousness; being free from the grasping subject and object, they abide in the Tathāgata stage and the Dharma of self-realized sainthood, giving rise to no conceptions regarding existence or non-existence. Furthermore, if a practitioner is thus...

Regarding those who give rise to the perception of existence and non-existence toward objective spheres (*viṣaya*), they grasp at nourishment and grasp at a self and persons (the Chinese translation says:
"If practitioners of the path give rise to attachments to existence and non-existence regarding objective spheres, they then cling to a self, a person, a sentient being, and a life-span").

Mahāmati, if it is said that their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), self-nature, and all common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) are entirely spoken by a *nirmāṇa-buddha* and not spoken by a *dharma-buddha*, and if all such verbal expressions arise solely from delusion;

Now, regarding those who harbor hopes for rebirth and do not establish themselves in the self-nature of the dharmas that lead to the attainment of noble wisdom and the blissful dwelling of self-realized samādhi—
these are distinguished and explained as follows:
it is said that those followers of the two vehicles, within the internal realization of noble wisdom, conceptualize existence within the state where the two self-natures have been transcended.

This conceptualization based on the clinging to the nature of things arises because one has not yet transformed consciousness into wisdom (*jñāna*) and has not yet abandoned the distinction between the subject that realizes and the object realized;

thus, such a notion is formed. However, when the mind, intellect, mentation, and the five sensory consciousnesses—along with body and mind—all undergo transformation into the four wisdoms, the various delusions of grasping and being grasped, which are manifestations of one’s own mind, are severed, and one abides in the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-realization.

Regarding these noble dharmas, for the practitioner, within that which is manifested in their own mind, there is no characteristic of arising in a single moment and no characteristic of cessation in a single moment;

they do not give rise to the perception of existence or non-existence. Furthermore, if a practitioner grasps at the characteristics of existence and non-existence regarding the realm of being and non-being, and gives rise to attachment toward them, they consider that to be the noble [path].

If one realizes within wisdom that these things truly exist, one immediately becomes attached to the four marks of self, person, sentient being, and life-span, as stated in the *Awakening of Full Enlightenment* (Sūtra on Perfect Enlightenment):
"Because the realization of awakening still retains the four marks, and because the realization has not yet forgotten the duality of subject and object.
Since the fundamental nature cannot tolerate the view of existence, nor can it tolerate the view of non-existence, how [can one perceive it]?

The Tathāgata has always taught that the self-nature of nature, its own-characteristics and common-characteristics, and its unchanging *tathatā* are called "self-characteristic *tathatā*," while its following conditions is called "common-characteristic nature. Since there is already a self-nature that can be pointed out, there must also be self- and common-characteristics established;
how then can it be said that all things are non-existent? The Buddha said: "All these phenomena are merely transformations."
What is taught by the Buddha’s provisional teachings is not the Dharma taught by his ultimate teaching; rather, it is the Dharma spoken by a transformation-body Tathāgata.
He speaks such teachings merely for the sake of sentient beings who, out of ignorance and longing, desire something to be realized.
If he were to speak of no-wisdom and no-attainment, they would give rise to fear; therefore, in accordance with their capacities and conditions, he establishes these words through skillful means.
This is not a separate establishment of a nature for proceeding toward [enlightenment] for the sake of attaining the dwelling in the bliss of samādhi through the noble wisdom of self-realization;
rather, it is a conceptual demonstration for ordinary beings who desire to attain a fruit, provisionally establishing nirvāṇa as a "nature" so that they may know where to direct themselves.
Once one has attained the dwelling in the bliss of samādhi through the noble wisdom of self-realization, this [provisional nature] no longer exists.

Because fools rely on such comparisons, they should abandon the provisional and resort to the real. Where they perceive an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), I consider that no intrinsic nature can be found;
where they perceive the existence of *nirvāṇa*, I consider that no *nirvāṇa* is to be realized.
This causes them to distance themselves from the four marks and personally realize the *dharmakāya*. Although they may attain the bliss of *samādhi*, they do not dwell in or become attached to it.
The Dharma-Buddha’s teaching transcends the characteristics of verbal expression; how could there be any further movement toward a self-natured dharma for him to manifest?
Therefore, followers of the Two Vehicles should not harbor deluded attachments to the notion of an existent nature.
While Yangshan was lying down, a monk asked him, "Does the Dharma-body understand how to preach the Dharma? Yangshan replied, "I cannot say it; another would have to."
There was one person who said, "The one who can explain it—where is that person? Yangshan pushed out his pillow.
When Guishan heard this, he said, "Ji-zi (Yangshan) employs the 'blade-edge' matter. Looking at it from this perspective, when the Dharma-Buddha preaches the Dharma, who is there to hear it?
One must be a member of the family themselves to attain it."
For example, it is like the reflection of a tree appearing in water; that reflection is neither a reflection nor not a reflection, neither the form of a tree nor not the form of a tree.

Likewise, those of external paths—conditioned by habitual tendencies and attached to delusive imaginings based on notions of identity, difference, both, or neither, existence, non-existence, both, or neither, permanence, or impermanence—are unable to know that these are merely the manifestations of their own minds.

The Master said: "The five metaphors below clarify in detail that the nature of objective realms is neither existent nor non-existent; one should not grasp them as having an inherent nature by forming deluded conceptual attachments.
This is because what is manifested by one's own mind—the *pramāṇa*—consists of nothing other than the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) and the object-division (*nimitta-bhāga*).

The seeing-division is the grasper (*grāhaka*), and the object-division is the grasped (*grāhya*). The metaphor of water represents the grasper, while the tree, its shadow, and its form represent the grasped."

The non-conceptual form and the conceptual form differ slightly in their degrees of depth. These [non-conceptual forms] are subsumed under the *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) of the first five consciousnesses;
because they merely distinguish [objects] as distinct and white without yet entering the sphere of mental ideation, they are called *pratyakṣa-pramāṇa* (direct perception).

If the mind, thought, and mentation undergo a transformation of body and mind such that the evolving consciousnesses are transformed into wisdom, then even the reflection of a tree appearing in water—[is no longer perceived as such].

One has never grasped it as existing, nor has one ever grasped it as non-existent. Since that water-body is fundamentally not a tree and fundamentally not a reflection, how can one conceive of it as having the nature of existence?
Yet, because the water can reflect objects, the tree enters into the reflection, and the reflection receives the form of the tree, how can one conceive of it as being without nature?
Because such a realm is neither existent nor non-existent, it is the vision of the outsiders (tīrthikas).
Habitual tendencies, perfumed since beginningless time, involve the perception of objects, their reception, and the false conceptualization and attachment [to them].

One merely forms fourfold conceptualizations—of identity or difference, existence or non-existence, and permanence or annihilation—with respect to objects; yet one does not know that these are the manifestations of one’s own mind.

[These manifestations] are neither identical to the objects nor separate from the objects, and thus cannot be grasped through such conceptualizations. Dongshan took his leave of Yunyan and asked about the hundred-year [lifespan].
Later, someone suddenly asked him, "Did you succeed in capturing the Master’s true likeness? Yunyan remained silent for a long while and said, "Just this.
Sansheng hesitated, and Yunyan said, "Dharma-heir Jia, as you take up this matter, you must be extremely careful and discerning. Sansheng still harbored doubts.
Later, while crossing a stream, he beheld his own reflection and attained great enlightenment regarding the previous teaching. He spoke a verse, saying: "Be most careful not to..."
Seeking from another is a long journey; it distances one from the Self. Now I go alone, and everywhere I encounter Him.
He is precisely me now; I am not He. One must understand it in this way to realize Suchness (*tathatā*).
When Dongshan saw his reflection and realized the True Self, why do people of the world instead grasp at the reflection as being the Self?
For example, just as a bright mirror manifests all forms and images according to conditions yet remains free of conceptual construction—
being neither the image nor not the image, yet appearing as an image— the deluded fool, through the false imagination of "image" and "non-image," conceives of it as such. In the same way,

those of external paths with evil views perceive the images of their own minds appearing through false imagination and become attached to them, relying on notions of identity, difference, both, or neither, existence, non-existence, or neither existence nor non-existence.

It is not that one who holds the view of impermanence cannot see it (as the Wei translation notes: "Because one sees when there is an object-condition and does not see when there is no object-condition," this is indeed correct in attributing this to the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha).
It is universally taught that all things are the manifestation of one's own mind; thus, the body of the *nirmāṇakāya* Buddha is also a manifestation of one's own mind.
Its appearance of forms in response to beings is like an image in a mirror, fully endowed with all the various marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*).
There is no deluded conceptualization. Why? Because that Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom is fundamentally not an image, yet it manifests according to conditions;
nor is it without images, for those images and reflections are not the mirror itself.
Since the mirror is fundamentally unarisen, the manifestation of images is not the arising of images—it is non-arising. Being fundamentally unarisen, what room is there for delusion?
To conceptualize and discriminate is like the ignorant and childlike who, playing with a reflection, claim that this image truly exists.

That sentient beings cling to existence and non-existence is not surprising; rather, it is the evil views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) who, through their false imaginings, calculate the images manifested within their own minds as being one or different, existent or non-existent, permanent or impermanent—these fourfold views (*catuskoṭi*)—and thus perceive them as divisions of their own minds.
To distinguish between the existence and non-existence of the image, one discerns it upon the image itself and not upon the mirror;
as for the statement that "to see all marks as no-marks is to see the Tathāgata," there is clearly something therein that has not been fathomed.
Thus, Linji spoke of this evil view, saying: "In my monastery here, I make no distinction between monk and layperson; whoever comes, I recognize them all."
No matter where they may emerge, all names, reputations, phrases, and sentences are but dreams and illusions.
Yet, one sees the person who rides upon these conditions; this is the profound intent of all Buddhas. The Buddha-realm cannot say of itself, "I am the Buddha-realm.
Is it not this very person of no dependence who emerges riding upon the realm? If someone were to come forth and ask:
When someone asks me about the Buddha, I respond from the realm of purity. When someone asks me about a bodhisattva, I respond from the realm of compassion.
When someone asks me about bodhi, I respond from the realm of sublime purity. When someone asks me about nirvana, I respond from the realm of tranquility.
Though there are ten thousand different ways of distinguishing them, the person remains undifferentiated.
Thus, responding to conditions and manifesting forms is like the moon in water; observe how Linji’s discourse on the manifestation of transformation-buddhas is utterly lucid.
For him, the essence of the dharma-buddha is not distinct from this, for there is no other actual point of landing.

For example, when wind, water, and wood come together, sound is produced; that sound is neither an intrinsic nature nor a non-nature (in the Tang translation: for example, an echo arises from the conjunction of the sounds of wind, water, and people;
it is neither existent nor non-existent, because the hearing of sound is not the sound itself; the Wei translation says: "because of sound one hears sound").

In this same way, the false discriminations of the heterodox views of externalists rely on the notions of unity and difference, bothness and not-bothness, existence and non-existence, neither-existence-nor-non-existence, permanence and impermanence.
Tong said: "The body manifested by a transformation Buddha (nirmāṇakāya) is not truly existent, and the sound of the Dharma it proclaims is likewise not truly existent.

For example, consider an echo: is this sound produced by the convergence of wind, water, and human voices—which answers back—considered truly existent? Or is it considered non-existent because the valley itself originally has no sound?"
An echo is a sound that depends upon sound; since sound has no substantial reality, it is neither existent nor non-existent.
Thus, the echo-sound is neither sound nor non-sound, and speech is neither speech nor non-speech.

Yet, because of the power of the habitual tendencies of the false imaginings of the evil views of externalists, they rely on the science of grammar (*śabda-vidyā*) to establish [the existence of] a single [self].
The heterodox arguments of the four extremes—existence, non-existence, annihilation, and permanence—are but sounds; the arising and ceasing of phenomena are entirely delusive.

To engage in conceptual discrimination regarding them is true ignorance. Huangbo said: "If you can now, before the gates of the six sense-faculties, grasp a single occasion, a single environment, a single sutra, a single teaching, a single age, a single moment, or a single name or character, you will be like a wooden puppet."

"What distinguishes a person? Suppose there were suddenly someone to emerge who does not form conceptual understandings based on names or marks—I say that even if one searched throughout the worlds of the ten directions, such a person could not be found, for there is no second person.
He succeeds to the ancestral seat; he is also called a member of the Śākya clan because he is unadulterated and purely singular. Thus it is said, 'If it is a king...'"
When he attained Buddhahood, the prince also followed him into the monastic life. This meaning is extremely difficult to understand;
it simply teaches you not to seek. If you seek, you lose it immediately. It is like a fool who shouts once on a mountain peak;
as the echo comes from the valley, he runs down the mountain to pursue it, but cannot find it. He shouts again, and as the echo resounds once more, he runs back up.
Throughout thousands of lifetimes and myriad kalpas, you have been nothing but a person chasing sounds and pursuing echoes—a man who lives in vain and dies in delusion.
If there were no sound, there would be no echo; Nirvana is without hearing and without knowing, where sound ceases and all traces and footprints are extinguished.
If you can attain such a state, you will be a neighbor to the Patriarchs.

For example, where there is no grass or trees upon the great earth, a mirage flows like a river with surging waves (the Tang translation notes: "the waves of the water-mirage arise when touched by the rays of the sun").

That is neither a nature nor a non-nature, because it is characterized by both craving and non-craving. In the same way, foolish commoners—perfumed by the false habitual tendencies of beginningless time—cling to delusive thoughts based on arising, abiding, and ceasing;
on identity and difference; on conjunction and disjunction; and on existence, non-existence, and neither existence nor non-existence.

It is not that impermanence lacks the conditions for impermanence; rather, it abides in its own sphere of activity, just as a mirage or a wave [is seen within the gate of the self-realized dharma-nature of noble wisdom—wherein one perceives arising, abiding, and ceasing, identity and difference, existence and non-existence, both and neither].

The messenger replied: "All phenomena are merely manifestations of one's own mind. For example, where there is no vegetation upon the great earth, it is inherently tranquil because nothing exists there;
thus, it is not water. Yet, when the sun’s rays shine upon the dust and soil in springtime, they combine to resemble water.
That which appears as water is originally not real, but is produced merely by a mirage."
It has never been otherwise: when there is flickering movement, flames arise; when the movement ceases, they are extinguished, and thus there is nothing to crave.
When the thirsty deer sees them, it becomes deluded and rushes toward them, craving what is not worthy of craving—how great is its folly!
All non-Buddhists and ignorant ordinary people are likewise so, for they have been permeated by the habitual tendencies of false and frivolous conceptual proliferation since beginningless time.
Within the gateway of the Dharma-nature realized by noble wisdom, there is originally no dharma that arises or ceases, but rather a state of tranquil, eternal abiding.
It is through the deluded conceptualization of dependent origination that one perceives arising, abiding, and ceasing;

yet, based on such notions of unity or difference, existence or non-existence, or both or neither, how does this differ from the false perception of shimmering heat-mirages and surging waves where no water exists? Therefore, know that those four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) are fundamentally non-existent.

To savor these flavors and then become deluded by false conceptualizations and attachments can truly be called folly. Previously, the parable of the thirsty deer illustrated attachment to the realm of forms;
this parable of the mirage illustrates attachment to arising, abiding, and ceasing, as well as the distinctions between the self of persons and the self of phenomena.
Therefore, there is no contradiction in its being presented again. Huangbo said: "If, when a single thought suddenly flashes up, one realizes it is like an illusion and like a transformation..."
Flowing into the past, the Buddhas of the past do not exist; flowing into the future, the Buddhas of the future are not non-existent.
Furthermore, they are not called "Buddhas of the future. In the present, moment after moment, there is no abiding; thus, they are not called "present Buddhas.
When a Buddha arises, one must not attempt to grasp it as being this or that—whether awakened or deluded, good or evil—and must never cling to it.

To obstruct him and sever his continuity is like a single thought flickering up, yet encountering a thousandfold locks that cannot be fastened, or a ten-thousand-fathom rope that cannot hold him. Since this is so, why do you intend to extinguish him or stop him?
I am telling you clearly: you are a *vijñāna* (consciousness) of flames; how can you intend to cut it off? It is like a mirage. You!
The Way is near, yet you seek it throughout the worlds of the ten directions and cannot find it; the Way is far, yet when you look, it is right before your eyes.
When you try to pursue it, it moves further away; when you try to avoid it, it comes chasing after you.
You cannot grasp it, nor can you let it go. Since this is so, know that the nature of all dharmas is inherently thus.
Do not worry or be anxious about this; if you carefully savor these words, you will finally believe that the gate of one's own abiding reality is fundamentally free from arising.
Previously, I was deluded, following the views of arising, abiding, and ceasing, and chasing after the True Suchness like a deer pursuing a mirage.
For example, suppose there were a person who, through incantations and mechanical devices—[the Wei translation says:

"by the power of incantations, one causes a corpse or a wooden automaton to arise, which lacks the substance of a sentient being"]—combines them with the skillful means of a piśāca ghost (which means a "demon that devours vital energy") so that they move and act; yet ordinary, foolish people, out of attachment, calculate this as coming and going.
In the same way, those of external paths with evil views hope for [existence] based on the notions of identity, difference, both, neither, existence, or non-existence.

To falsely establish views of existence and non-existence, permanence and impermanence—clinging to such conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) that lack reality—is collectively termed the "non-Buddhist" (*tīrthika*).
Whether through the four positions of identity and difference, existence and non-existence, all are but proliferating dharmas that ultimately lack substance.
Upon what, then, could they rely to establish these dharmas? They rely upon the *ātman*. Since all dharmas arise from...
The *puruṣa* (spiritual self) emanates [from the primordial cause], yet it is unaware that this *puruṣa* is likewise illusory and originally not substantially existent.
It is like a person who, by the power of incantations, raises a corpse or a wooden automaton to take the form of a sentient being;
though it is not actually reckoned among the number of sentient beings, it merely relies on the skillful means of the master’s incantations and the influence of a possessing spirit.

When these elements combine, they form movement, agitation, and activity; when they are solemnly assembled, one perceives them as a person. When the spirits combine, one thinks they are coming; when they separate, one thinks they are going.
Thus, the coming and going of ghosts is fundamentally illusory and empty. Those without wisdom take this to be real. Now, the non-Buddhists take the "spiritual self" (ātman) as their primary tenet;
they do not transcend the shifting flow of the *saṃskāra-skandha* (the aggregate of formations), and thus they fail to reach the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Furthermore, to recklessly cling to false imaginings as being a supreme capacity capable of producing all things is like regarding a mechanical wooden puppet as a real sentient being; therefore, it is called "establishing what is unreal.
Only when one perceives that the three realms are mind-only and all phenomena are consciousness-only can one speak of reality. One day, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha:
[The monk] said, "Today, upon entering the city, I witnessed a most extraordinary event. The Buddha asked, "What extraordinary event did you witness?
He replied, "When I entered the city, I saw a troupe of musicians performing a dance; when I left the city, I saw that they had all become subject to impermanence.
The Buddha said, "Yesterday, when I entered the city, I too witnessed a most extraordinary event. [The monk] asked, "I do not yet know what extraordinary event you witnessed."
The Buddha said, "When I entered the city, I saw a troupe of musicians performing a dance; when I left the city, I also saw musicians performing a dance.

Based on this, I say that all sentient beings are musicians. Ānanda, by cultivating the perception of impermanence, you see the World-Honored One from beginning to end as a musician; this is precisely the manifestation of the realm of one's own mind."
Mahāmati, therefore, those who wish to attain the reality of the noble wisdom of self-realization should abandon the evil views and false imaginings of arising, abiding, and ceasing;
oneness and otherness; bothness and neitherness; existence and non-existence; being and non-being; permanence and impermanence, and so forth.
Tong said: "There are three different types of non-Buddhists (tīrthika): first, those outside of the Buddha-dharma; second, those who are attached to the Buddha-dharma;
and third, those who study the Buddha-dharma and become non-Buddhists. When the Buddha appeared in the world, there were six teachers among the non-Buddhists:
first, Pūraṇa Kāśyapa, who reckoned that all dharmas are neither born nor extinguished; second, Maskarin Gośālīputra..."
Pūraṇa Kāśyapa held that the suffering and happiness of sentient beings occur spontaneously without causes or conditions;
Śramaṇa Māṭhara held that sentient beings attain the Way when their time has ripened, like the counting of threads on a ball of yarn;
Ajita Keśakambala held that the suffering of karmic retribution is replaced by throwing oneself from cliffs or plucking out one's hair; and Kakuda Kātyāyana—[the fifth].
Kauṭilya Kātyāyana maintains that things both exist and do not exist. The six Nirgrantha Jñātiputras maintain that what is produced by karma is fixed and cannot be altered;
these are non-Buddhist outsiders. Furthermore, the Vātsīputrīyas, reading the Śāriputra-abhidharma, established their own distinct doctrine, asserting:
"The self exists outside the four propositions (catuṣkoṭi) and is within the 'Ineffable Store' (avaktavya-kośa)."

The calculation of the path regarding form as self, the separation from form as self, the self within form, and form within the self—likewise for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness—these together constitute the twentyfold view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*).

It is precisely this that the *Mahāvibhāṣā-śāstra* refutes in order to establish the stage of *srotāpanna*. Now, the Vātsīputrīyas calculate the self as being distinct from the six teachers; furthermore—
All treatises that do not accord with the Buddha-dharma reject this [position], as it is an externalist path attached to the Buddha-dharma.

Why, then, are those who practice the Three Learnings of the Buddha-dharma also called "externalists"? It is because the Hīnayāna clings to the two extremes of the provisional and the real, while the Mahāyāna clings to the two extremes of emptiness and existence;
the Hīnayāna clings to the existence of phenomena external to the mind, while the Mahāyāna negates both *bodhi* and *nirvāṇa*.

Because they are attached to the emptiness of all things, they study the Buddha-dharma only to fall into the views of non-Buddhists; these all do not transcend the views of arising, abiding, and ceasing.

The first seven metaphors refute the external non-Buddhists as well as the four calculations of those who, while ostensibly following the Buddha-dharma, are actually non-Buddhists, thereby revealing that the self-realized noble wisdom is fundamentally free from the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*). The final five metaphors refute those who merely study the Buddha-dharma [without realizing its true essence].
Those who have become outsiders, having realized the quiescence of the one mind, likewise find that no noble wisdom (āryajñāna) can be attained; this clearly reveals the principle of non-arising.
This is the summary: if one wishes to attain the noble wisdom of self-awakening, one must depart from the four propositions and evil views.
These four propositions of conceptual construction differ in various ways; one must examine each one individually so as not to be deluded by them.

Because one is thus able to proceed directly toward the upward-pointing Dharma-gate, when all ordinary sentiments and sagely understandings are simultaneously swept away, this constitutes the ultimate matter of self-awakened noble wisdom.
One day, while Yangshan was lying down, he dreamed that he entered the inner courtyard of Maitreya’s residence.
In the assembly hall, all the seats were occupied except for the second seat, which was empty; Yangshan then took his place there. When he sat down, there was...
The Venerable One struck the gavel and said, "Now, for the second time, the one in the seat shall preach the Dharma.
He raised the gavel and proclaimed, "The Mahāyāna Dharma transcends the four propositions and cuts off the hundred negations; listen closely, listen closely! The assembly then all dispersed.
Upon waking, he related this to Guishan, who said, "You have already entered the rank of the sages. Thereupon, he prostrated himself. Tiantong’s verse says: "A Dream."

Amidst the assembly, he embraces his patched robe and joins the ranks of the venerable elders; the lineage of patriarchs sits solemnly to his right. When it comes to assuming the role of the righteous one, he does not yield;
as the *ghanṭā* resounds, he preaches the Dharma with fearless lion’s roars. His mind is as tranquil as the vast ocean, yet as capacious as a peck-measure.

From the eyes of the shark, tears flow; from the belly of the oyster, pearls are revealed. Who would have known that these delirious words would leak my secret? The elders with their bushy brows must surely laugh at this exposure of our family’s flaws.
Transcending the four propositions and cutting off the hundred negations, the illness of Master Ma and his disciples has been cured;

since Yangshan has already realized the stage of sagehood through preaching the Dharma in a dream, those who wish to attain the matter of self-awakened noble wisdom must pass through the pivot of Yangshan’s gate.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"Like an illusion, a dream, a reflection in water, the shadow of a tree, a mass of hair, a mirage—thus one should contemplate the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*) to ultimately attain liberation.

(The Tang translation says: 'The five aggregates of consciousness are like the forms of trees reflected in water; what is seen is like an illusion or a dream, and should not be falsely discriminated. The three realms are like a mirage, a dream, or the optical illusion of floating hairs; if one can contemplate them thus, one will ultimately attain liberation. "
For example, just as a thirsty deer, its mind agitated and deluded by a mirage, perceives it as water though no actual water exists;
so too, from the movement and stillness of the seeds of consciousness, the false imaginings of the foolish arise when they perceive objects.

Like being obscured by a cataract, they cling to and grasp at the nature of things within beginningless birth and death; yet, just as a wedge is driven out by another wedge, one must abandon this grasping through greed.
Viewing all things as like an illusion, a spell, a machine, a floating cloud, a dream, or a flash of lightning, one attains liberation and forever severs the three continuities;
therein there is no agent, being like a mirage or empty space. To know all phenomena thus is to have nothing further to know.
The commentary states: "In the prose section, twelve metaphors are presented; however, excluding the 'mirage' which appears twice, there are only eleven.
These are: 1. Mirage, 2. Gandharva city, 3. Dream, 4. Painting, 5. Floating hair, 6.
Fire-wheel, 7. Water-bubble, 8. Tree-shadow, 9. Bright mirror, 10. Wind-water sound, and 11. Mechanical wooden man. Now, these are interwoven..."
The summary of this verse is simply that all phenomena are like an illusion; thus, the word "illusion" (māyā) is placed at the beginning.
Furthermore, four additional metaphors—cataracts, a wedge, clouds, and lightning—are added, as these too are like illusory events.

Because foolish people do not understand that things are like illusions, they establish fourfold views based on false attachments, ultimately wandering through the cycle of the three realms and failing to attain liberation. If one understands them to be like illusions...
However, to eternally sever the threefold continuity and directly realize the state of self-realized noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*),

which is the realm of non-existence— this is what constitutes entry into the primary, ultimate meaning. Those heterodox outsiders, through the conceptual discrimination of the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*),
rely on the fourfold propositions (*catuskoṭi*) and fail to understand that the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and consciousness manifest within the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).
The reflection of a tree in water is like what is seen in a phantom or a dream; it has no substantial reality and should not be falsely discriminated.
Since all phenomena of the three realms are like [the appearance of] hair-tufts in the eyes or a mirage, they are fundamentally non-existent.

One who can contemplate them in this way attains the skillful means of practice and achieves ultimate liberation. As for why one is unable [to do so]: *Note: The final phrase "so yi bu neng" (所以不能) appears to be an incomplete sentence or a fragment indicating the reason for failure to attain such realization.*
It is like a thirsty deer chasing a mirage; as the mirage flickers and shifts, it deludes its mind, causing it to perceive water where there is no water.

All this arises from the seeds of the eight consciousnesses, wherein the two divisions of *darśana-bhāga* (perceiving aspect) and *nimitta-bhāga* (perceived aspect) move to form sentient beings and remain still to form the world.
Once the subject and object are established, the objective realm immediately manifests, and the deluded thoughts of the foolish arise. Thus it is.
When a person with diseased eyes is obscured by a cataract, the cataract itself is the obscuration of the false root, and that which is obscured is the false object.

Indeed, since beginningless time, through birth after birth, they have been attached to the grasper and the grasped, delighting in the realm of forms and greedily seizing them until they are shrouded and covered, like a wedge from which one cannot escape.
When the Tathāgata preaches the Dharma, he uses various metaphors of unreality as wedges to drive out [this attachment].
It is like using a wedge to extract a wedge, causing that foolish person to abandon their grasping; fundamentally, not even a single one of the four propositions can be found.
That which grasps is like an illusion, like a spell, or like a mechanical device set in motion; that which is grasped is like an illusion, like a floating cloud, or like a flash of lightning.
Observing in this way, the triple world is fundamentally unborn—this is what is called the "world."
The continuity of the realms, the continuity of sentient beings, and the continuity of karmic fruits—all three are utterly empty and void.
How could there not be liberation? Since the three realms do not exist, who is the creator? It is like a mirage in the sky that arises and ceases in an instant;
the sky is motionless and the mirage lacks the nature of agency, being ultimately non-existent. Such is the illusory nature of reality.
By means of this Dharma, one thoroughly knows that all dharmas are fundamentally unconditioned and fundamentally devoid of any locus.

Since they have no locus, there is nothing to be known; and since even "knowing" does not exist, how could one establish the conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) of the four positions—oneness and difference, existence and non-existence?

The verbal teachings are merely provisional names, and they likewise possess no intrinsic characteristics. Regarding them, one gives rise to deluded imaginings; the aggregates (*skandhas*) and formations are like falling hairs (the Tang translation says:

"the various aggregates are like a mass of floating hairs"). Within these, one falsely discriminates; they are established as mere provisional names. If one seeks their characteristics, they cannot be found.

They are like painted falling hairs, illusions, dreams, the city of the Gandharvas, a whirling firebrand, or a mirage in the heat—appearing though non-existent. Sentient beings [are likewise] eternal or impermanent, identical or different, both or neither.

However, within the beginningless succession of faults—the deluded and false imaginings of ignorant fools—various forms appear in the mirror of wisdom, in water, in the pure eye, and in the wondrous mani-jewel;
yet in reality, no inherent nature exists at all. All manifestations appear like a painting or a mirage in the heat of the sun;
though various forms appear, they are as non-existent as a dream.
The Master said: "In the preceding section, one contemplates the three realms as being like an illusion, concluding that the three realms do not exist;

in this section, one contemplates the five aggregates (*skandhas*) as being like an illusion, concluding that the five aggregates are fundamentally empty. The Tang translation says 'the various aggregates are like a mass of floating hairs,' while this [text] says 'the formations within the aggregates are like hanging strands of hair.
This refers specifically to the *saṃskāra-skandha* (aggregate of formations) among the five aggregates, for it was established by non-Buddhists according to the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*)."
Taking the *puruṣa* (the divine self) as their fundamental tenet, they give rise to deluded conceptualizations regarding it, like seeing floating hairs in the sky due solely to an obscured vision.
Even though verbal teachings establish and designate names for the aggregates (*skandhas*), these are merely provisional names;
if one seeks their actual reality, it is utterly unobtainable. Nevertheless, through the conjunction of the five aggregates, the realm of sentient beings exists.
Within those realms, that which is non-existent appears as if it were real:

like a painting with its high and low relief, like an illusion with its men and women, like a dream with its elephants and horses, like a city of the gandharvas, like a fire-wheel, or like water in a mirage;
all together appearing as the vision of falling hair. Herein, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) establish the notions of identity and difference.
The fourfold false views regarding existence and non-existence, impermanence and permanence, arise because one is bound by the delusive imaginings of beginningless falsehood.
If one can transform consciousness into wisdom, the seeds of beginningless falsehood will be almost entirely dissolved;
its clarity is like a mirror, its purity like water, and its wondrousness like a mani-jewel. Although within it...

The various existing forms appear diverse and uneven; yet when observed with the pure eye, they are found to be truly non-existent. There is nothing within that can obscure, nor anything without that is obscured.
From where could views such as existence or non-existence possibly arise? It is not the case that these are entirely non-existent, for that would be equivalent to nihilism.
This is simply because one has awakened to the fact that all phenomena are the manifestation of one's own mind, and thus knows that all dharmas are but one's own [mind].
The manifestation of nature is like the pigments in a painter’s picture; though they appear, they lack the reality of pigment. It is like a mirage on a spring day;
though it appears as water, there is no actual substance of water. Although various forms manifest, they are like what is seen in a dream and cannot be definitively grasped as existing.
Since they cannot be grasped as existing, who then would take up the matters of a dream to establish the fourfold logical positions (*catuṣkoṭi*)? 4.
Once one is free from phrases, one attains the noble wisdom of self-awakening; is this not what constitutes ultimate liberation?
Linji said: "Followers of the Way, the true Buddha has no form and the true Dharma has no characteristics.

If you merely fashion patterns upon these illusory transformations, even if you were to attain something, it would all be nothing more than a wild fox spirit or a demon—certainly not the true Buddha."

These are the interpretations of the non-Buddhists; however, a true student of the Way does not grasp for Buddhas, nor grasp for Bodhisattvas or Arhats, nor grasp for the sublime excellence of the triple world.
Transcending all, they stand alone and liberated, never conforming to things. Even if heaven and earth were overturned, I would have no further doubts.
When the Buddhas of the ten directions appear before me, I do not harbor a single thought of joy, nor do I feel aversion toward the three miserable realms or the hells.
Suddenly manifesting, there is not a single thought-moment; why would the mind be afraid? Thus I see that all phenomena are empty in their appearance:

if they change, they exist; if they do not change, they do not exist. The three realms are but mind; the myriad dharmas are but consciousness. Therefore, as for dreams, illusions, and flowers in the sky, what need is there to grasp at them?
Only you, O practitioners of the Way—those listening to the Dharma right now before me—even if you were to enter fire, [you would not be moved].
One enters fire without being burned; one enters the waters without drowning; one enters the three miserable realms—the hells—as if strolling through a garden pavilion;
one enters the realms of hungry ghosts and animals without receiving retribution. Why is this so? Because there is no basis for aversion in this Dharma.

If you love the holy and hate the common, you will float and sink within the sea of birth and death. Afflictions exist because of the mind; if there is no mind, what afflictions can constrain you? Do not weary yourself.
If you can discern and grasp the marks, you will naturally attain the Way in an instant;
yet if you attempt to follow others with restless effort to learn it, you will remain within birth and death for three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas.

It is better to do nothing and sit cross-legged at the corner of a bed in a forest thicket—how profound these words! To discern and grasp marks is to ultimately return to birth and death; to see all things...
The mark of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmas*) is precisely the attainment of the Way; in this brief treatise, the essential points are fully prepared.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma is free from these four positions: namely, identity and difference, both and neither, existence and non-existence, and neither existence nor non-existence, as well as permanence and impermanence.
It is free from the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of establishing, denigrating, and discriminating between existence and non-existence.
The Tathāgata’s teaching of the Dharma takes as its primary focus the true nature of dependent origination, the path, cessation, and liberation;
he does not teach that things arise from a primal nature, nor from a sovereign lord, nor without cause, nor from atoms, nor from time, nor from the continuity of self-nature.
The Commentary states: Mahāmati asked about that which is not practiced by any outsiders, but is the domain of the noble wisdom of self-realization;

this is answered in detail as follows: the reason the Tathāgata’s teaching transcends the four extremes and various conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) such as existence, non-existence, establishment, and denial, is that he compiles the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) and points out the path of correct practice solely by relying on that ultimate truth.

The reality of dependent origination, non-arising, and the knowledge and vision of liberation regarding suffering, its origin, its cessation, and the path, are not like the assertions of external paths—namely, that they arise from the Primal Nature (*prakṛti*), the Lord (*īśvara*), no cause, atoms (*paramāṇu*), time (*kāla*), or self-nature (*svabhāva*).

These external paths claim that this continuous succession of self-nature gives rise to existence without end; this very continuity of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) is what the external paths designate as the "Self" (*ātman*).
"If there is a self, there is immediately birth and cessation; how could this differ from the ultimate truth of quiescence by anything less than the distance between heaven and earth?
How, then, can liberation be attained? This is why the practice of the noble wisdom of self-awakening remains far removed from the errors of the non-Buddhists.
A monk asked Huangbo: "If a sage being without mind is a Buddha, then when an ordinary person is without mind, should they not sink into emptiness and stillness?"
Fobai said: "The Dharma has neither ordinary nor sage; it is also without sinking or stillness. Since the Dharma fundamentally does not exist, do not form the view of non-existence;
since the Dharma fundamentally is not non-existent, do not form the view of existence. Existence and non-existence are both merely emotional views, like illusory cataracts.
Thus it is said: 'Seeing and hearing are like illusory cataracts; cognition and awareness are the ancestors of sentient beings. Within the school of the Patriarchs..."
This discourse on ceasing the workings of the mind and forgetting views serves as a guide for entering the meaning of the foremost reality:
that by forgetting the workings of the mind, the Buddha-way flourishes, whereas through discrimination, the armies of Māra blaze forth.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, in order to purify the obscurations of afflictions and cognitive hindrances, it is like a merchant leader who sequentially establishes the one hundred and eight propositions,
skillfully discerning the characteristics of the various vehicles and the various stages.

The General Manager said: "Mahāmati asked about the characteristics of the successive stages of gradual progression and purification, up to the characteristics of the various divisions within the realm of what is manifested by one's own mind regarding all dharmas;

this is a detailed response stating that the Tathāgata established the sequence of his teachings through one hundred and eight propositions, wherein 'nothing exists' refers to these one hundred and eight propositions."

It is not that the one hundred and eight phrases are for the purpose of purifying the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*) of sentient beings and thereby attaining the Bodhisattva’s cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).

Rather, just as a caravan leader guides a multitude to a place of jewels necessarily by means of a sequence, so too, within these one hundred and eight phrases, the distinctions among the various vehicles (*yāna*) and the characteristics of the various stages (*bhūmi*) are analyzed; they are taught as existing in order to eliminate the afflictive obscurations.

The sequential stages of the three vehicles are taught to eliminate the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), yet in reality, the phrases of the three vehicles are not [ultimately] phrases of the three vehicles, and the phrases of the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*) are not [ultimately] phrases of the ten stages. They must ultimately converge upon the state of ultimate peace, security, and tranquility.
It is, for example, like a caravan leader who employs skillful means to cross a perilous path, providing temporary rest stations for the sake of transformation.
The city exists for the purpose of hastening toward the place of treasure; thus, it serves as a skillful guide.
A monk asked Chan Master Guangli Fan, "When the thousand paths are cut off and speech and thought are impassable, what then? Fan said, "You are still a man standing at the foot of the steps.
The monk asked, "What is the man who is on the steps? Fan said, "At the dragon pavilion, he does not raise his hand. He then said, "What is the nature of the noble one?"
Try to say it yourself! Do not merely sit upon your long meditation couch and look down on others when they are unwilling to speak;
for if you are suddenly pressed by one of clear vision, you will try to hide within the Iron Ring Mountains. If you reach the gate of Guangli, you must be able to utter the "First Phrase";
only then shall I open a single thread of the Way to discuss with you, my brothers. At that time, there was—
When a monk came out to pay his respects, Huifan said, "I thought this was the captain of a foreign ship; it turns out he is merely a merchant of this land.
Only when one realizes that the hundred and eight phrases are non-existent can one truly understand the matters of the other shore.

Since one has already realized the singular path of the noble and honored, what need is there to speak of dharmas such as liberation? Thus we know that those who have ascended the steps are naturally distinct.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of dhyāna. What are the four? They are: the dhyāna practiced by fools, the dhyāna that contemplates meanings, the dhyāna that takes suchness as its object, and the Tathāgata-dhyāna. What is the dhyāna practiced by fools?

It refers to the practice of śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and non-Buddhists who contemplate the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*), as well as specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), the skeleton, impermanence, suffering, and so forth.

Taking attachment to the signs of impurity as primary, one contemplates these signs without distinction (the Tang translation says: "one observes them with firm attachment and does not abandon them");

progressing through successive stages without eliminating these signs (the Tang translation says: "gradually advancing until reaching the meditative absorption of non-conception"), this is called the meditation practiced by fools.

The Master replied: "The sequential establishment of the one hundred and eight propositions is for the purpose of purifying the two obstacles—the afflictive and the cognitive—and entering into the meaning of the foremost reality; this must be entered by means of meditative contemplation (*dhyāna*). Previously, Mahāmati asked about the nature of the meditative states and why there are three vehicles; this is now answered in detail. Generally speaking, there are four kinds of meditation. 1. *Śamatha-vipaśyanā-bhāvanā-dhyānam* (Meditation on the cultivation of tranquility and insight). 2. *Lakṣaṇa-vikalpa-abhiniveśa-dhyānam* (Meditation on the attachment to the discrimination of characteristics). 3. *Artha-pravicaya-dhyānam* (Meditation on the investigation of meanings). 4. *Tathatā-lakṣaṇa-svabhāva-avabodha-dhyānam* (Meditation on the awakening to the self-nature of the characteristic of suchness). These are the four types of meditation. Regarding the first, *Śamatha-vipaśyanā-bhāvanā-dhyānam*, it is the meditation that cultivates tranquility and insight. It is called "tranquility" because it pacifies the mind, and "insight" because it illuminates objects. Because these two are cultivated together, they are termed "cultivation. This refers to the stage where one has already attained mastery over the mind through the practice of the five roots and five powers, and is now able to enter the stages (*bhūmi*) of the Bodhisattvas. Within this, there are three further distinctions: First, the meditation of the Bodhisattvas who have not yet attained the stages, which is the practice of tranquility and insight while still abiding in the stage of faith and understanding. Second, the meditation of the Bodhisattvas who have attained the stages, which is the practice of tranquility and insight while abiding in the ten stages from the Joyous (*pramuditā*) up to the Cloud of Dharma (*dharmameghā*). Third, the meditation of the Tathāgatas, which is the practice of tranquility and insight while abiding in the stage of Buddhahood. As for the second, *Lakṣaṇa-vikalpa-abhiniveśa-dhyānam*, it is the meditation that involves attachment to the discrimination of characteristics. It is called "characteristics" because it refers to the various marks of the aggregates, elements, sense-fields, and so forth. It is called "discrimination" because it refers to the mental activity that differentiates between subject and object. It is called "attachment" because it refers to the clinging to those discriminated marks as being real. This refers to the stage where one has not yet attained mastery over the mind, and while practicing the four foundations of mindfulness, one still discriminates and clings to the characteristics of the internal and external. Within this, there are also three distinctions: First, the meditation of ordinary beings, which is the practice of tranquility and insight while still abiding in the stage of ordinary existence. Second, the meditation of Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, which is the practice of tranquility and insight while abiding in their respective paths and fruits. Third, the meditation of Bodhisattvas who have fallen back, which is the practice of tranquility and insight while abiding in the stage of faith and understanding but having regressed from the true path. As for the third, *Artha-pravicaya-dhyānam*, it is the meditation on the investigation of meanings. It is called "meanings" because it refers to the various categories of phenomena such as the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields. It is called "investigation" because it refers to the analytical examination of those meanings. This refers to the stage where one has attained mastery over the mind and is able to discern the specific characteristics of all phenomena. Within this, there are also three distinctions: First, the meditation of Bodhisattvas who have not yet attained the stages, which is the investigation of the characteristics of phenomena while still abiding in the stage of faith and understanding. Second, the meditation of Bodhisattvas who have attained the stages, which is the investigation of the characteristics of phenomena while abiding in the ten stages. Third, the meditation of Tathāgatas, which is the investigation of the characteristics of phenomena while abiding in the stage of Buddhahood. As for the fourth, *Tathatā-lakṣaṇa-svabhāva-avabodha-dhyānam*, it is the meditation on the awakening to the self-nature of the characteristic of suchness. It is called "suchness" because it is the ultimate reality, unchanging and constant. It is called "characteristic" because it is the defining mark of that reality. It is called "self-nature" because it is the intrinsic essence of all things. It is called "awakening" because it refers to the direct realization of that essence. This refers to the stage where one has completely severed all delusions and attained the fruit of Buddhahood. Within this, there are also three distinctions: First, the meditation of Bodhisattvas who have not yet attained the stages, which is the awakening to the principle of suchness while still abiding in the stage of faith and understanding. Second, the meditation of Bodhisattvas who have attained the stages, which is the awakening to the principle of suchness while abiding in the ten stages. Third, the meditation of Tathāgatas, which is the awakening to the principle of suchness while abiding in the stage of Buddhahood. These are the four types of meditation. Among them, the first and the last are the true meditations, while the middle two are considered provisional or inferior. By practicing these four types of meditation, one gradually eliminates the two obstacles and realizes the ultimate truth."
The dhyāna practiced by foolish persons refers to the meditative concentrations cultivated by śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and non-Buddhists.
Entering through the contemplation of antidotes, they first contemplate the nature of the selflessness of persons;

they perceive their own bodies and the bodies of others as bound by afflictions, wherein the five aggregates combine to form human constituents, each possessing its own specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*), while their combination constitutes a common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
The interconnected bones are all marks of impermanence, marks of suffering, and marks of impurity; they are ultimately without self.

Observing in this way, one remains firmly attached and does not relinquish it, gradually progressing until reaching the liberation of the non-percipient and the extinction concentration (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
Because there is still a mark of nirvana to be attained, it is said that "the marks are not eliminated," even though one has realized nirvana.
"Not departing from arising and ceasing is called the dhyāna practiced by fools. Linji said:
"There is a certain class of blind shavelings who, having eaten their fill, sit in meditation and engage in contemplative practice;

they grasp at thoughts and outflows, not allowing them to arise, and loathing clamor while seeking stillness—this is the dharma of externalists. The Patriarch said: "If you apply your mind to observe stillness, as soon as you raise that mind..."
"External illumination penetrating the mind and internal realization concentrating the spirit to enter meditative absorption—such as these are all mere fabrications.
Do you now give rise to such things? How can the person listening to the Dharma intend to cultivate it, realize it, or adorn it?
It is not something to be cultivated; it is not something that can be adorned. If one were to try to adorn it..."
To adorn all things for you is itself to adorn you; do not make a mistake.
If you can comprehend the essential meaning of Linji, then those various contemplative practices are like cutting flesh to create sores upon the True Suchness (tathatā)—is this not called folly?

What is the dhyāna of examining the meaning? It refers to when one has realized that persons lack both self-nature and common characteristics, and that external paths lack the nature of self, other, or both;
having further examined the non-self of phenomena, the meanings of the characteristics of those stages progressively advance—this is called the dhyāna of examining the meaning.
The Master said: "This is the dhyāna cultivated by those of the Bodhisattva Vehicle.

It means that having observed the non-self of persons and known that both specific and general characteristics lack intrinsic nature, one also departs from the heterodox views of self-arising, other-arising, or co-arising natures.
Since neither self nor other arises together, this is the Dharma of non-arising. Thereupon, one contemplates the non-self of phenomena and practices the stages [of the path]."
The sequential observation of the meaning of the marks proceeds in stages of superior advancement;
that is to say, it refers to the elimination, stage by stage, of the conceptualization of the two obstacles and the attachment to non-existence that arises with the Ground of Supreme Joy.

Because these pertain to matters prior to the eighth ground, they are termed the "Dhyāna of Observing Meaning. Formerly, the Great Being Abandoning the Coverings asked the World-Honored One: "Does the secret essence of the gate of dhyāna exist?"
"Is there only one gate, or are there many gates? If there are many, then there would be duality;
if there is only one, how can it accommodate infinite and immeasurable sentient beings without becoming cramped? The World-Honored One said: "This essential gate of dhyāna is neither one nor many.
The nature of all sentient beings is identical to empty space; though they are identical to empty space,"

Each of these [faculties] possesses its own gate of dhyāna within body and mind; indeed, they are not cultivated in common. Why is this? When one ceases speech and remains silent, one merges mysteriously with principle; thus, the mouth becomes a gate of dhyāna.
When the eyes cease their discrimination and merge into a state of total unity, there is no difference; thus, the eye becomes a gate of dhyāna.
Regarding the sounds heard by the ear, one realizes they are empty and false, ultimately quiescent, like the hearing of a deaf person. Thus, the ear becomes a gate of dhyāna.

Regarding the Chan gate, it is even so for the body and mind. Good son, carrying all afflictions (*kleśa*) into the Gate of Non-duality is vast, penetrating, pure, empty, profound, still, and settled. A monk asked Chan Master Da Rong Shu, "What is Chan?
Shu said, "The autumn wind at the ancient ferry; the setting sun is unbearable to hear. The monk said, "I am not asking about that."
This Chan Master Shu said, "If you ask that Chan monk about the Chan of the Patriarchs, I would say:
beneath the pine shade beside the Nanhua Pagoda, drinking dew and chanting in the wind—there is even more to it.
If you can observe within this, what is called the Chan of the Tathāgata and the Chan of the Patriarchs will become clear to you of its own accord."
What is the dhyāna that takes suchness as its object? It refers to the non-arising of conceptual constructions regarding the two kinds of selflessness within the realm of reality as it truly is;

this is called the dhyāna that takes suchness as its object. (The Tang translation states: "If one discriminates the two kinds of selflessness, these are false thoughts; if one knows them as they truly are, those thoughts do not arise. The Wei translation states:
"Not abiding in the mind of discrimination, one attains the state of tranquility; this is called the contemplation of True Suchness.")

Tong said: "The followers of the Two Vehicles and the non-Buddhists realize only the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*); it is only within the stages of a Bodhisattva that one first attains the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*).

Yet, what is called the 'discrimination' of these two forms of selflessness is itself a false conception (*vikalpa*). This is because the two types of self-view, which are the objects to be remedied, are not real;
since the object of treatment is unreal, the remedy itself is also false. If one does not dwell upon this discrimination..."
Within the state of distinguishing from deluded thoughts, one attains partial realization of the tranquil realm of *tathatā* (Suchness).
Because that state of reality is such that deluded thoughts do not arise, it is called "Tathatā-dhyāna of Object-Conditioning.

and Bodhisattvas regard its very substance as empty. When Zen monks see a staff, they call it a staff: when walking, they walk; when sitting, they sit.
If you can clearly penetrate these two kinds of "staff" koans, then you will know.
When one does not give rise to false conceptualization regarding things as they truly are, this is called Tathāgata-dhyāna.

What is meant by Tathāgata-dhyāna? It refers to entering the stage of the Tathāgata, attaining the characteristics of the noble wisdom of self-realization, abiding in the three kinds of bliss, and accomplishing inconceivable deeds for the sake of sentient beings; this is named Tathāgata-dhyāna.
Tong said: "Although the two preceding types of dhyāna are called 'correct practice,' they still belong to gradual cultivation and cannot be described as sudden.

If one suddenly awakens to the fundamental mind, transcending directly into the stage of the Tathāgata, opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision, attaining the noble wisdom of self-awakening, and dwelling in the three kinds of emptiness and the three kinds of bliss—this is what is meant by the Tathāgata’s dhyāna, samādhi, bodhi, and nirvāṇa."
Abiding by this, one accomplishes inconceivable deeds for sentient beings through effortless and wondrous function, as vast and inconceivable as the sands of the Ganges;

because this arises from the four immeasurable minds of loving-kindness, compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity born of wondrous enlightenment, it is called the "Pure Dhyāna of the Tathāgata. Master Ren Chan of Bai Shui gave this instruction: "Within the eye..."
"One cannot put sand in the eyes; one cannot put water in the ears. A monk then asked, "What is 'one cannot put sand in the eyes'?
[The Master] said, "The True Man is peerless. The monk asked, "What is 'one cannot put water in the ears'?
[The Master] said, "Pure and white, free from defilement. Tiantong [Rujing] commented: "The old man Baishui may indeed be called great," and then he added, "But he was not yet free from the dregs."
Without external smallness, yet internally complete with ten thousand transformations; it is simply this bare hand and empty body, receiving not a single drop nor a speck of dust.
It is truly all-pervading to the eyes and ears—do you see it? To stand firmly on the ground of no-interruption, how many people know the mind?
To rely on silence and tread the path without stepping upon it, one can act; the mind relies on non-knowing.
Furthermore, this unfolding illumination can be known only by those who possess the noble wisdom of self-awakening.

By contemplating the selflessness of phenomena, they gradually advance; even though they may still conceptually differentiate between the two types of selflessness, false notions do not arise.
