At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, regarding what you speak of as ‘Parinirvāṇa,’ what dharma do you designate as Nirvāṇa?

The Buddha told Mahāmati: “Mahāmati, the transformation of the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of all intrinsic natures within the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), the mind (*manas*), and the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), is called Nirvāṇa.
The nature of Nirvāṇa for all Buddhas and myself is the realm of the emptiness of all phenomena.”

The realm (in the Tang language: the nature of the habitual tendencies of all consciousnesses, the storehouse consciousness, the mental consciousness, and the views; the transformation of the self and what the Buddhas call nirvāṇa) is precisely the sphere of the emptiness of the intrinsic nature of all phenomena.

The interlocutor said: "Because Mahāmati has attained the three kinds of blissful abidings through self-realized noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*), which is itself nirvāṇa, he asks about parinirvāṇa by means of what dharma one enters Buddhahood.
This means that the transformation of birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) is itself nirvāṇa; it is not that there is a separate nirvāṇa apart from the dharmas of birth-and-death.
All the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the intrinsic nature of the various consciousnesses give rise [to this]."

Regarding the first principle of the nature of death: (1) the habit-energy of the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), which is the eight consciousnesses; (2) the habit-energy of the manas, which is the seventh consciousness;
(3) the habit-energy of the mental consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*), which is the sixth consciousness; and (4) the habit-energy of the views, which is the five sensory consciousnesses.
All these consciousnesses each possess their own intrinsic nature and their own habit-energies; if there were no transformation, they would ultimately [not cease].

Returning to the cycle of arising and ceasing, one is only able to transform the six consciousnesses into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation, the seventh consciousness into the Wisdom of Equality, the five sensory consciousnesses into the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is Done, and the eighth consciousness into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom. Where there is discrimination, it is consciousness;
where there is no discrimination, it is wisdom. By transforming that arising and ceasing, one returns to non-arising and non-ceasing, I and...
The Buddhas declare that what is called *nirvāṇa* is precisely the realm of the emptiness of the nature of all phenomena;
it is simply that the self-nature of all consciousness is empty—namely, that the six objects, the six sense bases, the eighteen elements, and even the seven great elements are all empty.
If one realizes that all phenomena are empty, then birth and death are, in their very essence, *nirvāṇa*. This is the unvarying teaching of all Buddhas of the three periods of time.
Yuan Huangbo said: "Now, those who study the Way through Zen must ensure that the mind does not arise in any circumstance;

one should simply discuss the forgetting of contrivance (*wangji*), for then the Buddha-way flourishes. When there is discrimination, the demonic armies flourish. Ultimately, not even a hair’s breadth of a dharma can be obtained. He was asked:
"The patriarchs transmitted the Dharma from one to another—whom did they entrust it to? He replied: "There is no dharma to give to anyone. He said: [Thus it is].
When the Second Patriarch requested the Master to settle his mind, the Master said: "If you say there is a [mind], then the Second Patriarch ought to have been able to find it;
yet the mind cannot be found. This is why I say I have already settled your mind for you.
If there were anything to be gained, it would entirely fall within the realm of birth and death. To attain ultimate nirvana, you must gain conviction in this; only then can you enter."

Furthermore, Mahāmati, as for nirvāṇa, it is the realm of the self-realization of noble wisdom, free from the false imaginings of annihilation and permanence, and beyond the nature of existence and non-existence.
Why is it not permanent? Because the false imaginings of specific and general characteristics have been severed, it is not permanent. Why is it not annihilated?
Because all noble ones—of the past, future, and present—attain self-realization, it is not annihilated. Mahāmati, nirvāṇa is indestructible.
If the immortal were like nirvāṇa, then one who dies would again undergo birth and continuity;

if it were subject to disintegration, it would fall under the characteristics of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*). Therefore, nirvāṇa is free from disintegration and free from death; thus, it is the refuge for practitioners.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, nirvāṇa is neither abandonment nor attainment, neither cessation nor permanence, neither a single meaning nor a manifold meaning.

It is called *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, Mahāmati, as for the *nirvāṇa* of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, it is the realization that their own-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and common-characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) do not involve proximity to sense objects (in the Tang translation:
"abandoning clamor and bustle"), that their views are non-perverted, and that false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) does not arise;
they perceive this state as *nirvāṇa*.

The Master said: "Since the above has already revealed the true realm of *nirvāṇa* and distinguished between the heterodox and the orthodox to clarify that what is pointed to as *nirvāṇa* by non-Buddhists and those of the two vehicles cannot be compared to this, it is said that this *nirvāṇa* abides in the three dharmas:
*tathatā*, liberation, and *prajñā*. These are like the three dots of the syllable 'I' (*ī*), which constitute the wisdom of the sages."
In the realm of self-realization, one does not form the notion of annihilation nor the notion of permanence.
To perceive that which is permanent as having an intrinsic nature, or to perceive that which is annihilated as lacking intrinsic nature—both are equally false conceptual discriminations.

The sphere of noble wisdom is far removed from these. How is it that [reality] is not permanent? It is because it is free from the individual and common characteristics of the combination of the five aggregates.
When the conceptualizations of all discriminating dharmas have been severed and their existence is no longer perceived, one knows that they are not eternal.
Since they are not eternal, they are said to be annihilated. How then can it be said that they are not annihilated?
It is because all noble wisdom—whether attained in the past, to be attained in the future, or being attained in the present—is this very self-realization.

Furthermore, because there is awareness of the three time periods (past, present, and future) without interruption, one knows that it is not severed. Moreover, that which is called "quiescent extinction" (śānti-nirvāṇa) is termed *nirvāṇa*.
Ordinary fools, failing to understand this, mistake *nirvāṇa* for death; those with the false views of non-Buddhists (tīrthika) claim that *nirvāṇa* is annihilation.
In neither case do they transcend the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*). If the fruit of *nirvāṇa* were death, then one would have to undergo rebirth once again.
If the fruit of nirvana were to perish without ceasing its continuity, it would fall into the category of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) rather than being the essence of quiescence;

it would be merely nirvana that does not undergo future existence and is free from death, yet would not belong to the phenomena of arising, abiding, and ceasing, nor would it be free from destruction.
Because the four virtues—permanence, bliss, self, and purity—are perfectly integrated, it is that which is sought by all practitioners.

Taking refuge means relying solely upon the three types of blissful abodes; the essence of nirvāṇa, which is the distancing from all marks such as annihilation, permanence, existence, and non-existence, is fundamentally like this.
Since nirvāṇa is neither death nor destruction, there are no afflictions to be abandoned and no bodhi to be attained.
Being without grasping or relinquishing, it is neither annihilated nor eternal, and is devoid of "this" and "that."
It is neither one nor many; because the one is identical to all, it is not the meaning of "one," and because all are identical to the one, it is not the meaning of "diversity.
It is profoundly still and eternally quiescent, beyond all discrimination—this is called the true meaning of *nirvāṇa*.
As for the *nirvāṇa* of those śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, they do not escape attachment to signs as they seek it, habitually relying upon suffering, emptiness, and impermanence.
Through the contemplation of non-self and so forth, one realizes that the specific and general characteristics of all phenomena originally lack substantial reality.

Furthermore, one contemplates the twelve links of dependent origination as being impermanent, suffering, selfless, and impure. Seeing these as realms of clamor and distraction, one takes no pleasure in frequenting them;
instead, one is devoted to places of tranquility, steadfastly maintaining clarity and brilliance. With views free from inversion, the mind is extinguished and stilled.
When wisdom is such that false conceptualization does not arise, through this merit one perceives that both birth and extinction have been exhausted, and thus forms the notion of *nirvāṇa*.

Yet, since *nirvāṇa* is itself devoid of conceptualization, to harbor such an awakened thought and hope for the attainment of a fruit implies there are afflictions to be abandoned and a *bodhi* to be attained.
Such a person is unable to transform consciousness into wisdom; rather, they merely look toward that aggregate of consciousness with expectation.
Tianjing held the view that *nirvāṇa* is not the ultimate state. The Sixth Patriarch said:
"The unsurpassed Great *Nirvāṇa* is perfectly luminous, eternally quiescent, and illuminating. The ignorant call it death; externalists cling to it as annihilation;
those of the Two Vehicles regard it as non-action. All these belong to the conceptualizations of the deluded mind—the sixty-two views are fundamentally false."
Establishing provisional names—what is their true meaning? Only those of transcendent capacity penetrate this without grasping or rejecting;

they know that the phenomena of the five aggregates and the "self" within them, as well as the various forms and images manifested externally and each of their vocal characteristics, are all equal, like illusions and dreams.
They do not give rise to views of ordinary beings or sages, nor do they form a conceptual understanding of nirvana. [This is] the third of the two extremes.

At the limit where permanence and annihilation are severed, one should accord with the functions of the sense organs without giving rise to the conceptualization of such functions; one does not give rise to discriminative thoughts regarding any phenomena.
When the kalpa-fire burns the ocean floor and the winds strike the mountains until they clash together, there is the true, eternal, tranquil, and extinguished bliss—the mark of nirvana.
This verse by the Sixth Patriarch encompasses the essential purport of this entire chapter.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, what are the two characteristics of self-nature? They are as follows: the attachment to the characteristic of the self-nature of verbal expression, and the attachment to the characteristic of the self-nature of things.
Attachment to the characteristic of the self-nature of verbal expression arises from the attachment to the habitual tendencies of beginningless false speech.
Attachment to the characteristic of the self-nature of things arises from the failure to realize that [the world] is a manifestation of one's own mind.
[They] arise according to their respective limits. [The Master] replied: "It was stated above that the transformation of all self-natures and habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) is itself nirvana.

Thus, there are two kinds of characteristics of self-nature: first, the characteristic of the self-nature of verbal expression (*abhilāpa-svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*); second, the characteristic of the self-nature of phenomena (*dharma-svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*). Regarding verbal expression..."

Not only do the non-Buddhists have conceptual proliferations regarding existence and non-existence, but even the various explanations that differentiate suchness and so forth arise from attachment to the phenomena produced by the habitual tendencies of beginningless false discourse.

Not only are all dharmas subject to arising and ceasing phenomena, but even the attainment of realization of nirvana is a phenomenon; all of these arise because one is unaware that they are the objective portions manifested by one's own mind.
The seeing-part (*darśana-bhāga*) is solely the one mind that grasps external objects and gives rise to appearances;

through attachment to verbal expressions, it functions as the nature of discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), which further involves attachment to that very nature—this is the characteristic of the six consciousnesses and the seventh consciousness.
Since the Tathāgata clearly knows that sounds are like echoes and that verbal expressions possess no actual substance, he transforms these verbal expressions of self-nature.

(In the Tang language: "The World-Honored One merely speaks of dependent origination under different names; there is no difference in meaning. The World-Honored One, the non-Buddhists also speak of existence and non-existence giving rise to birth.

"Is the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination taught by the World-Honored One merely explained under different names as 'dependent origination,' rather than arising from its own essence? This refers to arising from [conditions].
