The Buddha taught that all phenomena arise from existence and non-existence; yet, all phenomena are fundamentally without arising, merely produced in dependence upon various conditions, and having arisen, they again cease.

Furthermore, they do not depart from existence and non-existence, just as in the Dharma of the twelve links of dependent origination—from ignorance conditioned by formations, up to old age and death—all phenomena arise in dependence upon eye-consciousness and so forth. This is...

The Blessed One established that the doctrine of no-cause, the doctrine of non-causality, and the view that things do not arise from causes—namely, that all things exist simultaneously without priority or sequence—are as follows:
"When this exists, that comes to be; from the arising of this, that arises. That is to say, when ignorance exists, then everything up to old age and death exists;

they all exist simultaneously. When ignorance ceases, then everything up to old age and death ceases; they all cease simultaneously. Thus, because this exists, that exists; it is solely through [the principle of] non-existence [that the reverse occurs].
It clarifies that the cycle of delusion and transmigration has no truly existent dharmas, established through a gradual sequence of arising;

therefore, it is called the "teaching of causelessness. It observes that what the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) proclaim—namely, the Primal Nature (*prakṛti*), the Lord Self (*puruṣa*), the Sovereign Truth (*īśvara-tattva*), and Primordial Darkness (*avyakta*)—is such that from Primordial Darkness arises Intellect (*buddhi*), from Intellect arises the Ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*), from the Ego-sense arise the five sense-objects (*pañca-viṣaya*), and from the five... [the five sensory faculties].
Dust gives rise to the five great elements (*mahābhūta*), and from the five great elements arise the eleven faculties;

these twenty-five factors, with the *puruṣa* (the self) as the supreme nature (*prakṛti*), constitute the cause of production. This is established as a gradual process of arising, unlike the Tathāgata’s teaching of causelessness.
Why is this so? Because those non-Buddhists assert that the supreme nature is the cause, and that it does not arise from anything else.
If all phenomena arise through conditions and flow forth from a primordial darkness, then there must truly be that which is produced.
Now, a cause does not arise from conditions; the cause is itself the cause and does not depend upon an effect. That which is produced truly does not exist;
the effect is itself the effect and does not depend upon a cause. When cause and effect are thus clearly distinguished and fundamentally lack any reciprocal succession, then that—
The claim made by the non-Buddhists that things arise without a cause is not entirely incorrect; however, if the World-Honored One teaches the twelve links of dependent origination—
where ignorance is the cause and volitional formations are the result, and where volitional formations are the cause and consciousness is the result,
continuing down to old age and death as the cause and ignorance as the result— then this very same single dharma acts both as a cause and [as an effect].
If one holds that the effect exists within the cause, or that the cause exists within the effect, such confusion leads to an infinite regress.
Is it not then that something is both cause and effect? Or is it that there is neither cause nor effect? Or is it that an effect arises without a cause?
Why is it that you instead find fault with the externalists' doctrine of causes and conditions? For what reason is this, Mahāmati? It is simply that...

Because they distinguish causes and conditions with respect to objects but do not understand how to contemplate dependent origination with respect to their intrinsic nature, the Blessed One spoke of dependent origination as the unsurpassed path of non-arising.

The causal and non-causal doctrines established by those outsiders also contradict their own words, as they claim that what arises from causes is itself causeless; I do not speak thus of causelessness, for this is what I teach.
All phenomena arise from causes and conditions; they do not arise without causes and conditions, nor are they disordered, nor do they entail the fault of infinite regress.
One should simply awaken to the fact that the arising of all phenomena is a manifestation of the mind alone.

To say "because this exists, that exists" means that internally there is no grasping subject-mind and externally there is no grasped object-field; thus, the grasper and the grasped are fundamentally non-existent.
Lacking intrinsic nature, like images appearing in a mirror, dependent origination is fundamentally unborn; its arising is inherently non-existent.
What can be said of "causelessness"? Since causelessness itself does not exist, how could there be the confusion of causes and conditions?
As for those non-Buddhists who cling to various conceptualizations, because they possess both the grasper and the grasped, they fail to realize that all phenomena are but the mind-only.

The nature of external objects as they appear is fundamentally without intrinsic nature; yet, one clings to external objects as being either existent or non-existent, forming views of existence and non-existence regarding the non-dual Dharma.

This obscuration arises solely from the attachment to the phenomenal characteristics of external objects, imagining them to be truly real due to being perfumed by beginningless false habitual tendencies. Such a fault exists, but it is not mine.
I teach the Dharma of dependent origination: being detached from conditions within conditions, and detached from objects within objects.
Since it is fundamentally free from existence and non-existence, how could there be the fault of subject and object?
Furthermore, the "non-arising" I speak of is not an absolute non-arising identical to annihilationism; I constantly say that all things arise through the harmony of causes and conditions.
Phenomena do not arise without causes; rather, causes necessarily depend upon conditions to arise, for causes do not arise of themselves.

Conditions necessarily depend upon causes to arise, for conditions do not arise of themselves. These phenomena arise from the conjunction of causes and conditions, yet they are fundamentally unarisen from the start.
Because the wisdom of the non-Buddhists does not reach this point, they claim that all things arise without cause and are not produced by [causes and conditions].

Arising occurs through the conjunction of causes and conditions; yet, since that which arises has no cause, who could act as its cause? Since that which is produced lacks conditions, who could act as its effect?
To claim there is neither cause nor effect is clearly a nihilistic view (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*), and not the intent of our teaching on non-arising dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

As stated in the *Bai men yi hai* (The Ocean of Meaning of the Hundred Gates): "One who realizes non-arising perceives that sensory objects are the mind, and that the mind taking objects as conditions is the cause."
When causes and conditions harmonize, illusory appearances arise; because they arise from conditions, they necessarily lack intrinsic nature. Why is this?

Now, objects do not arise independently of the mind, but depend upon the mind; the mind does not exist as a mind in itself, but must depend upon conditions. Because they exist through mutual dependence, there is no fixed essence.
What arises from conditions is called "non-arising. This is not a case of negating arising by means of conditions; rather, it is the arising from conditions that is termed non-arising.
These few words alone are sufficient as evidence for this section.
Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, is it not because speech possesses intrinsic nature that all things possess intrinsic nature?
World-Honored One, if there were no intrinsic nature, speech would not arise; therefore, because speech possesses intrinsic nature, all things possess intrinsic nature. The Buddha told him:
Mahāmati, although there is no intrinsic nature, one employs verbal expression, such as "the horns of a rabbit" or "the hair of a tortoise. These are worldly expressions currently in use, Mahāmati;

they are neither existence nor non-existence, but are merely verbal expressions. If, as you say, verbal expressions possess an intrinsic nature and all things possess an intrinsic nature, then your own treatise is undermined.

(The Tang translation states: "Although all dharmas are non-existent, there are still verbal expressions. Is it not evident that people in the world [speak of] the hair of a tortoise, the horns of a rabbit, a stone ox, a colt, and so forth?")

All these are verbal expressions; they are neither existent nor non-existent, yet there are merely verbal expressions. Mahāmati, as for what you have said—that because there are verbal expressions, all dharmas exist—this argument would then be undermined.
Mahāmati, not all buddha-fields possess verbal expressions; verbal expression is merely a fabrication. There are some buddha-fields where the Dharma is revealed by a mere glance;
some where it is done by gestures; some by raising the eyebrows; some by moving the eyes; some by smiling; some by yawning; and some by clearing the throat.

Mahāmati, some contemplate buddha-fields, while others cause them to tremble; it is like the world of *Candana* (translated in Chinese as the World of the Unblinking Eye) and the world of *Gandhavatī* (the World of Wondrous Fragrance), which is the land of the Tathāgata Samantabhadra.
Therein, by means of a mere glance, he causes all bodhisattvas to attain the realization of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and various supreme samādhis.
Therefore, Mahāmati, it is not that there is an intrinsic nature in words, nor that all things possess such a nature; this is what is seen.
In this world, mosquitoes, gnats, insects, and ants—such sentient beings as these perform their respective tasks without any speech.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke in verse:

Just as with space, a rabbit’s horn, or the son of a barren woman (in two translations rendered as "the son of a stone-woman"), there is speech regarding that which does not exist; likewise, regarding the nature of phenomena—

which arise from the conjunction of causes, conditions, and conceptual construction— fools give rise to false imaginings and are unable to know them as they truly are, thus wandering through the cycle of existence within the house of the three realms of being.
Mahāmati said: "The previous statement that all phenomena arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions clearly reveals the subtle principle of their lack of self-nature (*niḥsvabhāva*).
Yet, you now seem to doubt this, suggesting that if they do not arise without cause, then a real self-nature must be obtainable.
You say that if speech possesses a nature, then all phenomena must likewise possess a nature; if phenomena lacked a real nature, upon what would speech depend?"
Why does this arise? It is said that speech does not arise in vain; there must first be the true nature (*dharmatā*) of phenomena for phenomena to arise.
Furthermore, phenomena do not manifest of themselves; there must first be the true nature of speech for them to be manifested. The World-Honored One then refuted both of these positions:
"In the world, there are also those who produce speech regarding phenomena that lack a true nature—for instance, when one speaks of a rabbit's [horn]."
The fur of a horned tortoise or the daughter of a stone woman—such things do not exist at all, yet these descriptions appear. Viewed from the perspective of actual entities, they do not exist;
viewed from the perspective of verbal expression, they have never failed to exist. Although rabbit horns and the like are non-existent, it does not prevent such speech from being uttered.
Why must this speech necessarily arise because of the existence of various phenomena? Wherein does its necessity lie?
If you claim that all things possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then how could verbal expressions regarding phenomena arise if they did not exist?
Your argument would thus be undermined. Furthermore, although all things in the world truly exist, they do not depend upon verbal expressions;
such expressions are merely the conceptual discriminations of the human mind and are only provisionally established. There are Buddha-lands where one simply gazes directly [at reality].
In some buddha-fields, not blinking is called preaching the Dharma; in some buddha-fields, manifesting extraordinary signs is called preaching the Dharma;
in some buddha-fields, merely moving the eyebrows is called preaching the Dharma; in some buddha-fields, moving only the eyes is called preaching the Dharma;
in some buddha-fields, smiling is called preaching the Dharma; in some buddha-fields, yawning is [called preaching the Dharma].
In some Buddha-lands, preaching the Dharma consists of clearing one's throat;
in some Buddha-lands, it consists of mindfulness; in some Buddha-lands, it consists of bodily movement.
Just as in the world-systems of No-Winking and Exquisite Fragrance, within the Buddha-field of the Tathāgata Samantabhadra, the bodhisattvas observe in this manner.
Upon arrival, with eyes not even blinking for a moment, you attained the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*) and also attained immeasurable, supreme samādhis.
These do not exist by virtue of verbal expression; where could all dharmas abide within verbal expression?

If you claim that verbal expression has an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then the existence of all things would likewise have an intrinsic nature, which is logically untenable. Furthermore, in this world, they are like insects and ants.
Since all these things are without verbal expression and each accomplishes its own function, how can this verbal expression be worthy of esteem?
The verse further clarifies that while space is fundamentally non-existent, there is nonetheless the name "space";

likewise, while rabbit horns and the like are fundamentally non-existent, there are nonetheless names such as "rabbit horns. Although these things do not exist, there is verbal expression regarding them.

Although there is fundamentally no real nature, one calculates that there is an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). By means of such verbal expressions, one engages in false conceptualization regarding this intrinsic nature, claiming that all phenomena are thus.
Within these very dharmas that are merely the confluence of causes and conditions, they are fundamentally unarisen from the beginning and lack any real nature;
yet, ordinary fools give rise to deluded thoughts, asserting that there is truly arising and truly existing.

Because one cannot know, as it truly is, that which arises from the manifestation of one’s own mind—that dependent origination is unborn and beyond the reach of verbal expression—one instead grasps at external objects as being either existent or non-existent, giving rise to false discrimination. That which is thus clung to consists of phenomena subject to arising and ceasing;
ultimately, it does not escape the ocean of birth and death, and one continues to revolve through the three realms without end.
"This fault arises precisely because of attachment to the conceptual characteristics of the intrinsic nature of verbal expression.

Because Yaoshan had not ascended the seat for a long time, the monastery administrator said, "The assembly has long been waiting for your instruction; we pray that the Master will preach the Dharma for the sake of the congregation.

Yaoshan ordered the bell to be struck, and when the assembly had gathered, he ascended the seat. After remaining there for a long while, he descended from the seat and returned to his quarters. The administrator... [proceeded].
Thereupon he asked the Abbot, "Just now you promised to preach the Dharma for the assembly; why have you not uttered a single word?

The Abbot replied, "The Sutras have Sutra masters and the Shastras have Shastra masters; why blame me, this old monk? Tiantong’s Verse says: "The foolish child strives for the coin to stop his crying;
The fine steed pursues the wind, its gaze fixed on the whip's shadow. Clouds sweep across the vast sky; it nests within the moon."

The crane’s cry in the cold penetrates the very bones; one cannot sleep. One clearly understands that the World-Honored One’s teaching of the Dharma was like a coin used to stop a child from crying—it was fundamentally without words to speak.
Yet, for a long while, he looked toward the shadow of the whip and followed it; thus, there has never been a lack of instruction.
It should be known that those who cling to the conceptual characteristics of the self-nature of speech are truly deluded.
At that time, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding the term 'constant sound' (*nitya-śabda*), what does it refer to?

The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It refers to delusive confusion (*bhrānti*). (According to the Tang translation: 'It is spoken based on false dharmas. Because of that delusive confusion, even the Noble Ones (*ārya*) manifest it, yet it is not a perversion.
Mahāmati, it is like a mirage in springtime, a fire-wheel, falling hair, a city of the Gandharvas, an illusion, a dream, or a reflection in a mirror."
"Mahāmati, although such worldly perversions are not the wisdom of the enlightened, it is not that they do not appear.

That delusive confusion manifests in various ways; it is not because of the delusive confusion itself that things are impermanent. Why is this? It is because it is free from both existence and non-existence.
Mahāmati, what is meant by being free from existence and non-existence? It refers to the various objective realms of all foolish common people. (The Tang translation says:)

When false phenomena appear, they manifest in immeasurable varieties; yet they are not impermanent. Why? Because they are free from existence and non-existence. How are they free from existence and non-existence? Because all foolish commoners perceive them through various cognitions.
Just as that Ganges is seen by some and not seen by others—thus it lacks the nature of delusion because it appears to others—and yet it is not non-existent;

likewise, this delusion is constant for the noble ones because they are free from inversion, and thus it is not inverted. Therefore, this delusion is eternal, for its characteristic marks are never destroyed.
Mahāmati, because the various marks of delusion (*bhrānti*) are not destroyed by the marks of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*), delusion is eternal.

(The Tang translation says: "It is like the waters of the Ganges; for hungry ghosts they are unseen, yet one cannot say they do not exist because others see them; nor can one say they do exist because they are not seen by those others. Mahāmati, because the deluded dharmas are free from inverted views, the nature of deluded dharmas is eternal and non-different.

It is not that there are distinct marks among the various deluded dharmas; rather, it is through discrimination (*vikalpa*) that distinctions arise. Therefore, the essence of deluded dharmas is eternal. Mahāmati, how is delusion real? Furthermore...
Regarding these delusive phenomena arising from causes and conditions, the noble ones do not give rise to perverted cognition, nor do they give rise to non-perverted cognition.

Mahāmati, with the exception of the noble ones, those who harbor even the slightest conceptualization regarding these delusive phenomena do not possess the characteristics of the objects of noble wisdom.
Mahāmati, whatever exists as such is a false assertion by the foolish; it is not the speech of the noble ones.

Tong said: "The Great Wisdom (Mahāmati) previously stated that *nirvāṇa* is neither annihilated nor eternal; it is the true eternity (*nitya*). While this eternity cannot be manifested, it is manifested through sound.
Therefore, if one takes this eternity as the verbal teaching (*śabda-śāsana*), upon what basis should it be explained?

If one insists on explaining it by relying on the characteristics of phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*), this is precisely attachment to the self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of phenomena. If one says [it] is apart from..."
To claim that there exists a separate, true permanence apart from phenomenal appearances is the "view of emptiness" characteristic of the Two Vehicles.

Therefore, the Buddha taught that there is no phenomenon outside the mind and no mind outside phenomena; what he called "true permanence" was spoken in reliance upon those very deluded and false dharmas.
Because those false and deluded dharmas are prone to inversion, the Noble Ones perceive only their reality, even as they manifest.
There are delusions that are not erroneous; therefore, the wise and ordinary people do not perceive them as delusions.

Because they grasp at what is non-existent as being real—like a mirage, a whirling firebrand, an illusion, a dream, or a reflection—this is called a worldly, inverted view, and not the wisdom of the wise. Those who possess true knowledge do not call it a delusion.

All objects are entirely non-existent; one merely does not give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding what is manifested within one's own mind, yet does not fail to see those delusive phenomena.
When those delusive, false dharmas appear, they manifest in various distinctions as if they were impermanent;
however, it is not that these false dharmas possess the nature of impermanence or can act as impermanence. Why is this? Because those delusions...
The essence of delusion does not itself say it exists, nor does it say it does not exist; its fundamental nature is free from existence and non-existence.

Since it is already free from existence and non-existence, why further call it a "delusive confusion"? It is simply that all dharmas are fundamentally non-existent, yet foolish people produce various interpretations of them as existing;
all dharmas are fundamentally non-non-existent, yet foolish people produce various interpretations of them as non-existent. Regarding existence and non-existence...
Within the sphere of experience, delusion arises spontaneously; yet because that which is free from existence and non-existence is inherently eternal, it is as follows:
the waters of the Ganges are not fire by nature, yet hungry ghosts perceive them only as fire and do not see them as water.
This nature of delusion manifests only to the hungry ghosts; for those others who are free from such delusion, it does not exist.
That water is not manifest does not mean that the water does not exist; delusive matters are likewise thus.
To give rise to the view of existence regarding various objects is perversion; to not give rise to the view of existence regarding various objects is non-perversion.
The Noble Ones remain far removed from both existence and non-existence; they are free from perversion and also free from [the view of] non-existence.
That which is deluded by the inverted and the foolish is not deluded by the noble ones.
Therefore, this delusion is "constant. It is called "constant" because conceptual discrimination does not arise;

phenomena do not possess distinct characteristics, and characteristics are not destroyed, for one characteristic does not destroy another. Thus, the various characteristics of delusion are merely external appearances.
The characteristic of false conceptualization is the internal characteristic. Because of false conceptualization, various characteristics are destroyed;
thus there arise both perverted views and non-perverted views. If there were no conceptualization, the intrinsic nature of all phenomena would lack differentiated characteristics.
It is neither a destruction of the various characteristics of delusive confusion, nor is it a destruction of the characteristics of false conceptualization.
Since their characteristics do not differ from the myriad phenomena, all are thus; therefore, they are called "perpetual delusion.
That which is termed "perpetual" refers to that which is real, true, and unchanging. How can delusion be identical to reality?

It is because all false dharmas arise through the combination of causes and conditions and are fundamentally unborn from the beginning; thus, the Noble Ones do not give rise to [delusive thoughts] regarding them.
Ordinary beings, through their inverted cognition, cling to things as existing; yet they do not give rise to the non-inverted cognition of the Two Vehicles that clings to them as non-existent.

Because all phenomena are fundamentally characterized by quiescence, one should remain far removed from the two kinds of conceptualization—existence and non-existence—and recognize that delusive confusion itself is the reality. This is so, except for those noble ones who have already realized the truth.
To form conceptions regarding what is delusive is nothing other than the activity of holy wisdom and its phenomenal manifestations.

For any other practitioner, if there arises even a slight conception toward these delusive and false dharmas, and if for even a single thought-moment they stir, they immediately deviate from the essence of reality;
they are far removed from the phenomenal manifestations of holy wisdom. One should know that anyone who possesses even a slight conception is, in fact, a fool.
Now, frivolous discourse (*prapañca*) is not the teaching of the Sages; it is spoken solely based on the characteristics of imagined phenomena (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Clinging to such things as mirages and fire-wheels as being truly existent ultimately belongs to the realm of arising and ceasing, which is impermanent.

If, however, one speaks based on the characteristics of the objects of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), then that which is delusive is itself the reality. Within the dharmas of arising and ceasing, there is neither arising nor ceasing.
Since this sovereign [state] is truly eternal, one knows that the phenomena of deluded thoughts (*vikalpa*) are not eternal, whereas the phenomena of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*) are eternal.
Thus, for those who speak of the eternal, should they not be careful regarding what they rely upon?
Ruoyan asked Yantou, "What is the fundamental principle of eternity? Yantou said, "Movement. Ruoyan asked, "What is it like when there is movement? Yantou—
Yangshan said, "If you do not see the fundamental eternal principle, you will stand gazing at the cliff. Touzi said, "If you accept it, you have not yet shed the root-dust;
if you do not accept it, you will sink forever into birth and death. Yangshan then prostrated himself. Tiantong’s verse says: "The perfect pearl has no hole;

the great uncut jade is not carved. What the man of the Way prizes has no sharp edges or corners. Cast aside the path of 'acceptance' and the root-dust is empty; one is liberated in body, free from all trace."

Relying on this rock face as one’s living desk, because one has attained the most thorough penetration of true permanence, it is said that if one does not consent, one will sink forever into birth and death, remaining seated upon the path of inversion;
if one consents, one has not yet escaped the roots and dust, remaining seated upon the path of non-inversion.
Only then, being entirely without reliance and not rejecting any phenomena, does one attain true permanence and sovereignty.
That delusion consists of the arising of two kinds of natures—namely, the noble nature and the nature of the foolish—due to the occurrence of perverted and non-perverted conceptualizations.
The noble nature is distinguished into three types: the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Buddha vehicle.
How does the conceptualization of the foolish give rise to the Śrāvaka vehicle nature? It arises from clinging to self-characteristics and common characteristics.

Hearing of the vehicle of the Śrāvakas is called the arising of the Śrāvaka-vehicle lineage from delusive conceptualization, O Mahāmati. That very same delusive conceptualization gives rise to the Pratyekabuddha-vehicle lineage;
that is, by not closely adhering to the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) within that same delusion, one gives rise to the Pratyekabuddha-vehicle lineage.
How does the wise person give rise to the Buddha-vehicle lineage from that same delusion? It is said: [by realizing] that very...

Realizing that external objects are merely the manifestations of one’s own mind and are neither existent nor non-existent, and thus not giving rise to the marks of conceptual construction—this is called the Buddha-vehicle lineage arising from that very delusion.
Furthermore, the various natures of diverse phenomena, which give rise to the delusions of ordinary people, are called the lineage of the foolish (the Tang translation says:

"There are various foolish people who differentiate false dharmas; regarding various things and events, they decide they are thus and decide they are not otherwise"—this constitutes the nature of the vehicle of birth and death). These are not [the true lineage].
That which has an object is not without an object; this is called the meaning of *gotra* (lineage/nature).

Mahāmati, that very delusion which is non-conceptual—the transformation of the nature of phenomena arising from the habitual tendencies of the mind, mentation, and consciousness of the noble ones—is what is meant by "thusness" (*tathatā*).
Therefore, when I speak of being "free from the mind," this phrase reveals freedom from conceptualization; it is to say one is free from all conceptualizations.

The messenger said: "As for what was stated above—that the various sages do not give rise to delusion here, and that inverted awakening is not non-inverted awakening—both inverted and non-inverted conceptualizations arise based on delusion.

If one discriminates those delusive phenomena as being either inverted or non-inverted, one will be able to establish two kinds of natures: namely, the nature of the sages and the nature of the foolish."
Now, regarding the lineages and the noble lineages, there are threefold distinctions: namely, the Śrāvaka vehicle, the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, and the Buddha vehicle.
As for the Śrāvaka vehicle, they perceive the phenomena of the five aggregates and so forth—which are but delusive confusion—as having self-characteristics and common characteristics;

thus they give rise to attachment, conceive thoughts of weary detachment, and feel revulsion toward suffering and its origin while rejoicing in the path and its cessation—all of which constitute attachment to these characteristics.

Therefore, those of the lineage of the Śrāvaka vehicle are so named; as for those of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle, because they thoroughly understand that the phenomena of the twelve links of dependent origination and so forth—which are subject to delusion—are all empty, false, and unreal in their specific and general characteristics, they distance themselves from bustle and clamor, take no pleasure in intimacy or association, and do not cling to them;
this is called the lineage of the Pratyekabuddha vehicle. These two are both...
To perceive that there are afflictions to be severed, while not yet having realized that afflictions are themselves awakening (*bodhi*), is not the mark of a wise person.
One who possesses wisdom enters the Buddha’s knowledge and vision through those very delusions;
they realize that everything is a manifestation of one's own mind, seeing that both the seer and the seen are nothing but one's own mind, with no external existence.
Since the nature beyond phenomena is neither existence nor non-existence, from where could false conceptualizations of existence and non-existence arise?
That very delusion is, in its essential substance, True Suchness (Tathatā); therefore, it is called the lineage of the Buddha-vehicle.

These three [categories] are called "sages" because they possess no inverted perceptions regarding various phenomenal characteristics; whereas ordinary beings give rise to delusive confusion regarding various things and objects.
One conceives with the conviction that things are thus, certain, and not otherwise; yet these various dharmas are merely false conceptualizations.
This constitutes the nature of the vehicle of birth-and-death, whereby one wanders through the three realms in delusion without ceasing; therefore, it is called "ignorance.
What is the meaning of "lineage" (*gotra*)? Those confused phenomena are not real entities, being like a mirage and the like.
It cannot be definitively asserted that it exists, nor can it be definitively asserted that it is not a real entity, for its various manifestations are clearly perceived.
As the Pure Name (Vimalakīrti) said: "There is no agent, no creator, and no experiencer; yet the karma of good and evil does not perish.
This is the meaning of the *gotra* (spiritual lineage). This *gotra* is common to both the noble and the foolish; when it is within the bonds of affliction, it is called...

When these eight consciousnesses emerge from their entanglements, they are called the *tathāgatagarbha*. It is no cause for discussion that ordinary fools have not yet been able to transform consciousness, but are instead driven by it;
however, as for the noble ones (*āryas*), even amidst such delusive confusion, they do not engage in false discrimination, nor do they form perverted or non-perverted perceptions.
This is truly because the mental activities of the mind, intellect, and consciousness of these wise noble ones are free from all evils.

Because the self-nature of habitual tendencies undergoes a transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), the basis of arising and ceasing is transformed into nirvāṇa, and the basis of afflictions is transformed into bodhi.
It is precisely this delusion that is called *tathatā* (suchness); therefore, it is said that *tathatā* is free from mind and consciousness.
This does not mean that there is a separate *tathatā* existing outside of mind and consciousness; it simply means being free from the conceptualization of them. This is what I have taught.
The purpose of this grammatical formulation is to reveal that the essence of *tathatā* (suchness) is free from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

This means that within that *tathatā*, there are no dharmas of false discrimination, and it is free from all conceptualizations—not only free from inverted conceptualizations, but also free from non-inverted conceptualizations.
All conceptualizations arise from the mind, mentation, and consciousness, which transform through their own nature (*svabhāva*) into [these various forms].

The mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*) are termed the "mind of habitual tendencies. When this mind, intellect, and consciousness are transformed into wisdom, it is termed *tathatā* (suchness).
Once it is termed *tathatā*, that very mind, intellect, and consciousness are transcended; apart from that mind, intellect, and consciousness, from where could conceptualization arise?
That the various sages do not give rise to deluded conceptualizations is precisely like this. As the *Śraddhotpāda-śāstra* says regarding all phenomena: [all phenomena are...]
It is only through deluded thought that distinctions arise; if one is free from mental ideation, then there are no signs of any objective realms.
Therefore, all phenomena have been, from the very beginning, free from the signs of verbal expression, free from the signs of names and words, and free from the signs of mental objects.
They are ultimately equal, without change or variation, indestructible, and are nothing other than the single mind.
Therefore, it is named "Suchness" (Tathatā); this is precisely the point. Zhao Wenru of Huangshan once composed a verse: "Delusive thoughts are originally and fundamentally true;
To remove them is to raise yet another layer of dust. In speech, thought, movement, and stillness—who provides the power? If you examine closely, there is no one else at all.
One must understand it in this way to be called the realization of Suchness. This is indeed how it should be understood. Only then can it be termed the realization of Suchness.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, is delusion existent or non-existent? The Buddha told Mahāmati, "It is like an illusion, devoid of the characteristics of attachment.

If delusion possessed the characteristics of attachment, then the nature of attachment could not be extinguished, and dependent origination would be like the causal production of dharmas as taught by the non-Buddhists (the Tang translation notes:
because it is like an illusion, it lacks the characteristics of attachment; if the essence of the characteristics of attachment were existent, they should be unchangeable, and thus all conditions..."

[The arising] should be like what the non-Buddhists (tīrthika) say regarding a creator producing [beings]. Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, if delusion (*bhrānti*) is like an illusion (*māyā*), it should further act as a cause for other delusions.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is not so; illusions are not the cause of delusion, because they do not give rise to faults.

Mahāmati, illusions do not give rise to faults, because they are devoid of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). [The Tang translation states: 'It is not that various illusory things are the cause of delusive confusion, because illusions do not produce various evils and faults, and because various illusory things are without discrimination.']"
Mahāmati, an illusion arises from the power of another's knowledge, not from the habit-energy of one's own deluded imaginings;
therefore, it does not give rise to faults. Mahāmati, this is a delusive attachment of the minds of fools, not that of the noble ones.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The Sage does not perceive delusion; nor is there reality in the interval between them.
If delusion were itself reality, then one would abandon all delusion. If any characteristic arises, that too is delusion, as impure as a cataract.
Mahāmati asked again in doubt: "Since one has already departed from all conceptualizations, can one then eliminate all dharmas?

Therefore, he asked whether all delusive dharmas ultimately exist or do not exist. The Buddha replied that these delusive dharmas of confusion cannot be said to exist, nor can they be said not to exist;
they are merely like an illusion. Although an illusion manifests in various ways, [it is devoid of intrinsic nature].
Since characteristics are devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), characteristics are themselves non-characteristics;
because no characteristic of attachment can be apprehended, if delusive phenomena possessed characteristics of conceptual clinging, they would have a substantial reality and could not be transformed.

When the mind, intellect, and consciousness of the noble sages undergo transformation, how could they not be completely integrated and vanish without a trace? It is precisely because they are rootless.

Therefore, it can be transformed; if it were not like an illusion and were impossible to extinguish, then all dependently originated phenomena of delusive confusion would be as the non-Buddhists claim:
that dharmas produced by causes and conditions have a creator as their cause and are ultimately existent, and having existed, they are extinguished and are ultimately non-existent.
One would merely cling to and fail to relinquish the objects of existence and non-existence.
The Dharma of dependent origination taught by the Tathāgata as being like an illusion is certainly not like this. Mahāmati again raised a doubt:

"If delusion is like an illusion and fundamentally lacks intrinsic nature, unlike phenomena produced by causes and conditions, then since other delusions arise incessantly, it must be that illusion serves as their cause. The Buddha said: "It is not that illusory things constitute the delusion."
The cause of delusion is illusion; because it does not give rise to various faults and evils, it does not produce transgressions.
The reason it does not produce transgressions is that illusory phenomena lack the discrimination of sentient consciousness.

The reason there is no sentient consciousness is that they arise based on human effort, ingenuity, and incantations, rather than arising from one's own false imaginings or the habitual tendencies of afflictions. Therefore, they do not give rise to transgressions.
The *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* says: "It is like a skilled magician who conjures various men and women; although their faculties appear to move, they depend on a single mechanism.
When that mechanism ceases, they return to stillness, and all these illusions are found to have no inherent nature.
All delusive and false dharmas are like illusions and lack inherent nature; how could they serve as causes for other delusions? Delusion does not act as a cause for delusion."

How could this possibly delude others? It is only the mind of the foolish man that first becomes deluded by illusory and false objects, clinging to them as real and giving rise to inverted perceptions.

This is produced by the habitual tendencies of discursive thought (*vikalpa-vāsanā*), which give rise to all manner of faults and evils, causing one to revolve within the three realms like a young child playing with a shadow, being deceived by the shadow itself. This does not apply to the noble sages (*ārya*), who are not so deluded.
This is deluded by confusion; it specifically refutes those who cling to the conceptualization of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena.

Failing to realize that these are merely the limits of what is manifested by one's own mind, not only do ordinary beings perceive them through inverted cognition, but even the non-inverted cognition of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*) has not yet transcended signs (*nimitta*).
Therefore, the verse singles out to refute the lineage (*gotra*) of the two vehicles to reveal the supreme [vehicle].
The Dharma-gate of the Single Vehicle refers to the noble ones seeing that delusion is itself non-delusion. Why is this so?
Because within this delusion, no real nature can be found at all. Since its nature is absent, its characteristics are likewise absent;
when both nature and characteristics are extinguished, this very midst of delusion is purely and utterly reality. Being reality, it is...
The false is the true, and the true is the false; one does not see any delusion to be abandoned, nor does one see any reality to be attained.
It is like a clear, pure eye gazing across a vast, empty sky—therefore, no delusion is seen.
If one were to abandon all delusions and perceive the arising of marks of reality, then that very reality would [still be a delusion].
This is called "delusive confusion. Although one is free from the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*), one has not yet abandoned the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*).
Because the cognitive hindrances obstruct wisdom (*prajñā*), wisdom is not liberated; thus, they constitute a defilement on the side of purity and are likewise impure.

It is like a person with cataracts who falsely perceives flowers in the sky, not realizing that in the space between them there is no reality at all. For this reason, both Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are equally termed "noble lineages" (*āryagotra*).
It is not equal to the Buddha-vehicle, which transcends the two vehicles and is the supreme ultimate truth.
Master Pang’s verse says: "If one simply has no mind toward the myriad things, What hindrance can the constant surrounding of those myriad things pose?
The iron ox fears not the lion's roar; It is like a wooden man beholding flowers and birds. When flowers and birds encounter a person, they too are not startled."
The essential nature of the wooden man is inherently insentient; when the mind and its objects are thus as they are, what cause for concern is there that the path to Bodhi will not be accomplished?
This is precisely the subtle meaning of the Sage’s non-perception of delusion.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, it is not because of a lack of resemblance to illusion that all dharmas are seen as being like an illusion. Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One, is it because of attachment to various illusory forms that you say all dharmas are like an illusion?

Or is it because of attachment to their distinct characteristics [the Chinese translation says: 'is it because of attachment to this inverted characteristic based on difference']? Or is it because of attachment to various illusory forms that you say all natures are like an illusion?"
World-Honored One, there is no nature that is not like an illusion. Why is this? It is because the various characteristics of form are not caused by anything;

World-Honored One, it is without cause that the various characteristics of form appear like an illusion. Therefore, World-Honored One, there is no attachment to the similarity of various illusory marks.

(The Wei translation says: "Because of clinging to the illusory marks of all dharmas, they are called 'like an illusion'; because of clinging to the inverted marks of all dharmas, they are said to be 'all... [the text here is fragmentary]).

If phenomena are like an illusion, one who clings to the characteristic of all phenomena being like an illusion cannot say that all phenomena are like the characteristic of an illusion. If one says they are like an illusion because of clinging to the inverted characteristics of phenomena, one cannot say that all phenomena are like an illusion.

Why is this? World-Honored One, because various causal characteristics of form are seen; World-Honored One, there is no other cause for the various characteristics of form to be seen as like an illusion. Therefore, it is said that one must not cling to all phenomena as being like an illusion.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is not because of attachment to the various marks of illusion that all phenomena are said to be like illusions, Mahāmati.

Rather, because all unreal phenomena perish as swiftly as lightning, they are like illusions. Mahāmati, for example, a flash of lightning appears for a mere moment and, having appeared, immediately perishes;
it does not appear to the foolish (the Wei version says 'it appears and perishes at once, yet ordinary people do not see it'; the Tang version says 'the worldly fools and ignorant').”
All these are clearly perceived as being without intrinsic nature when one examines all such natures through the self-imaginations of their own and common characteristics;
they are not the clinging to manifest forms and signs (the Chinese translation states: "because one cannot examine what is non-existent, one falsely clings to various forms and signs").
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Since there is nothing that is not illusion, the nature of phenomena is said to be like an illusion—unreal and as swift as lightning; therefore, it is said to be like an illusion."
Tong said: "The Master previously stated that delusion is itself reality, and that reality is certainly not an illusion.
Why is it that non-illusion is identical to being like an illusion, and being like an illusion is identical to non-illusion? Yet, the true essence of non-illusion has no resemblance;
to say it resembles a single thing is incorrect. This non-illusion is not nothingness, for it can perceive all phenomena."
Just as one who perceives an illusion does not perceive it as non-illusory, it is said that it is "not non-illusory.
However, since all phenomena transcend illusion and are beyond analogy, they are described as being "like an illusion. Mahāmati then asked:

"Is it based on attachment to various illusory appearances that you say all phenomena are like an illusion, or is it based on an attachment to something other than these illusory appearances, namely, perversion?"

When it is said that all phenomena are like illusions, does this mean they are called "inverted" based on inverted characteristics, or are they called "inverted" based on non-inverted characteristics?
For one who clings to distinct characteristics, the illusory characteristic is inherently illusory and the inversion is inherently inverted;
since phenomena are fundamentally distinct by nature, one cannot say they are like illusions. If...

Regarding the attachment to various illusory appearances, those who claim that all phenomena are like illusions fail to recognize that phenomena possess an intrinsic nature that is not like an illusion;
how then can they indiscriminately designate them as being "like an illusion"? To clarify why they are not like illusions:
the various manifest material phenomena all possess causal characteristics; if one were to say they are like illusions, then they would lack causes.

Illusion does not act as a cause for other afflictions; it is impossible for there to be no cause at all while the various characteristics of form nevertheless manifest in such a way that they may be said to be "like an illusion. Yet, these various characteristics of form certainly do have causes.

There is no other cause in the world that allows the various characteristics of form to be visible in a manner like an illusion. Therefore, O Blessed One, it cannot be said that [form] exists in dependence [upon a lack of cause].

Regarding the attachment to various illusory appearances, to say that all phenomena resemble illusions is merely to distinguish characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) by means of characteristics, without knowing how to distinguish characteristics by means of the absence of characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*);
it is merely to distinguish illusion by means of illusion, without knowing how to distinguish illusion by means of the absence of illusion.
Therefore, the Blessed One said: "One does not rely on the attachment to various illusory appearances, whether they have a cause or no cause."
The statement regarding similarity—that all phenomena are like illusions—is made because all phenomena are unreal and perish as swiftly as a clap of thunder;
thus they are said to be like illusions. This is a discourse on the absence of real nature (*svabhāva*), not a discourse on the absence of causal nature (*hetutva*).
If one were to argue for the absence of causes, the reality [of things] would still persist; however, by arguing for the absence of reality, one simultaneously forgets the cause. This is so.
All phenomena are unreal; who then is real? All phenomena perish swiftly; who then does not perish?
Therefore, to see them as like an illusion is to see that which is non-illusory. Why is an illusion unreal? It is like a flash of lightning:
it appears and perishes in an instant; though it arises, it does not arise. The foolish and ignorant do not perceive this.
In this regard, just as one perceives a flash of lightning and grasps it as being a real entity, so too are all phenomena;

for the nature of all phenomena is manifested by the false imaginings of one's own mind. Due to the discrimination of these imaginings, there appear to be self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and common characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) that can be apprehended.

One who skillfully observes that these are merely the manifestations of the measure of one's own mind will find that these very self- and common characteristics— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*
Marks are fundamentally without intrinsic nature, and nature itself is fundamentally not manifest;
being utterly non-existent, what marks or appearances could there be to be conceptually attached to? Furthermore, how can one ask whether they have a cause or no cause?
It is solely because one cannot observe this non-existence that one conceptually clings to various marks and appearances; this constitutes delusive inversion, not a person being deluded by illusion.

Yet people are deluded by illusions, and therefore they are called foolish. Furthermore, as for the fact that all phenomena are unreal and perish rapidly like an illusion, it is not merely a matter of saying they are "like an illusion";
it is precisely to reveal the principle that they are not [ultimately] illusory. This can be discussed only with the wise. As the verse says:
"Illusion has no analogy," because there is nothing in the world of things that resembles it; therefore, it does not exist [as a real entity].

It may be said that all phenomena are like illusions; this does not mean that their various natures and characteristics are similar to illusions, but rather that they are unreal and perish as swiftly as lightning—appearing and then immediately vanishing without any substantial essence—and for this reason they are said to be like illusions.
If one can observe that all phenomena are fundamentally without nature and fundamentally...

It is not that the manifest is no different from a flash of lightning; rather, within that which is like an illusion, it is not the substance of illusion—it is the self-nature of suchness (*tathatā*).
Therefore, I say that delusive confusion is itself reality. Regarding this, a monk asked Caoshan, "What is the truth within form?
Caoshan replied, "Form itself is the truth. The monk asked, "How should one demonstrate this? Caoshan held up his whisk. Furthermore—
Question: "What is the original reality of illusion? Answer: "The original reality of illusion is fundamentally true. Question: "When there is illusion, what is manifested?

Cao Shan said: "Illusion itself is manifestation. Question: "If that is so, then from beginning to end one does not depart from illusion. Cao Shan said: "One cannot find the characteristics of illusion.
Because Cao Shan’s exposition of the Patriarchal Chan accords with this point by point, we know that the First Patriarch [was likewise thus].
"It is truly so that these four fascicles of sutra can serve as proof for the mind’s faith.

Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "Regarding what the World-Honored One has taught—that all natures are unarisen and like illusions—will there not be a contradiction between what the World-Honored One has previously and subsequently stated? You have spoken of unarisen natures being like illusions. The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"O Mahāmati, it is not my teaching that the nature of non-arising is like an illusion, for there would otherwise be the fault of contradiction between what precedes and what follows.

Why is this? It is because the realization of arising and non-arising is the manifestation of one's own mind (*svacittadṛśya-mātra*). Whether existent or non-existent, external natures and non-natures do not exist; non-arising is manifested [in this way]. (The Tang translation says:

'I have realized that arising is itself non-arising, for it is merely what is seen by one's own mind. Whether they are said to exist or not to exist, all external phenomena are seen to be without intrinsic nature, because they are fundamentally unarisen. O Mahāmati, it is not that my [teaching] contradicts itself before and after."
To state that there is the fault of contradiction is to destroy the cause of arising [as held by] the non-Buddhists; therefore, Mahāmati, I teach that all natures are unarisen.
Mahāmati, the foolish masses of non-Buddhists desire that existence and non-existence arise, based on their various attachments to their own false imaginings.
Mahāmati, for me, there is no arising from existence or non-existence; therefore, I speak by means of the teaching of non-arising. Mahāmati, this is what I call the teaching of nature.
This is for the sake of embracing birth and death, and for the sake of destroying the view of non-existence and the view of annihilationism.
Because my disciples embrace various karmas and the places of rebirth, I speak of embracing birth and death by means of the nature of sound (the Táng translation says:

"To speak of all dharmas is to cause disciples to know that they embrace birth and death based upon various karmas, thereby preventing them from holding views of non-existence or annihilation"). Mahāmati, I speak of the characteristics of the self-nature of illusion in order to bring about detachment from [grasping at] self-nature.

Because of signs, they fall into the evil views of foolish people; they do not understand that the appearance of signs is the manifestation of one's own mind, and they are ruined by clinging to the characteristics of self-nature produced by causes and conditions.
They speak of the characteristics of the self-nature of illusions and dreams, asserting that all phenomena are such, so as not to allow foolish people with evil views and desires to cling to them.
Thus, regarding all phenomena—both themselves and others—they fail to see them in their state of reality and instead formulate incorrect doctrines.

(The Tang translation says: "To speak of the characteristics of all dharmas as being like illusions is to cause one to leave behind the marks of the intrinsic nature of all dharmas. For the sake of those ordinary fools who have fallen into evil views and desires and do not know that all dharmas are manifestations of mind-only, [the Buddha] speaks of all dharmas as being like illusions and dreams, so that they may distance themselves from attachment to the marks of arising through causes and conditions.
Those fools, clinging to evil views, deceive themselves and others, and are unable to clearly perceive the true abiding place of all dharmas as they really are.
O Mahāmati, to see all dharmas in their true state means to transcend the measure of what is manifested by one's own mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"Non-arising is the non-existence of action; existence is subsumed within birth-and-death (the Chinese translation says: 'Because there is no action, there is no arising; birth-and-death is explained based on karma').
Observing them as being like illusions and so forth, one does not form false conceptions regarding their marks."
Tong said: "If one says that all natures are produced, one should not say they are unproduced;
if one says they are unproduced, there can be no illusion, so one should not say they are like illusions. This is merely being mired in the contradiction of words and phrases;
it does not realize that saying 'unproduced' does not mean they are absolutely unarisen. It means that the arising of all dharmas is itself non-arising."
I perceive only what is manifested by my own mind; whether existent or non-existent, all external phenomena have never failed to arise.
Yet, when one investigates their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), it is utterly unfindable. Being fundamentally unborn, they manifest as arising through the state of non-arising;
how could this not be like a magical illusion? Therefore, there is no fault of contradiction between the earlier and later statements. However, the reason for this is...
I teach that all phenomena are unborn in order to refute the views of non-Buddhists who hold that things arise from causes;

for the causal principles they establish are inconsistent with reality. Those ignorant multitudes of non-Buddhists claim that all phenomena exist and arise from existing causes, or that they do not exist and arise from non-existent causes; it is not from the seeds of their own deluded imaginings that they speak thus.
Taking various attachments and conceptual discriminations as conditions, there is a distinct and separate cause arising from a creator.
They merely give rise to evil views regarding all phenomena, whether existent or non-existent; I teach that the arising of all phenomena is non-arising, and that there is also non-arising.
How can one say they exist? And how can one say they do not exist, given that they are not non-arising? Therefore, by me—
While teaching non-arising, it is said that there is neither arising from a cause nor arising without a cause;

thus, the claims of those non-Buddhists who wish to establish arising from existence or non-existence are self-contradictory. Now, if one teaches non-arising and yet also says that all dharmas possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), why is this?
It is so that my disciples may know there are two kinds of dharmas: first, those that are subsumed...
Second, because they undergo the karma of birth and death in the world, this [teaching] precludes the view of non-existence and the view of annihilationism.

Non-Buddhists claim that all phenomena do not arise from the conditions of one's own deluded conceptualization and attachment; thus, they fail to realize the existence of birth and death and remain perpetually within it.
If one knows and perceives that the various karmas of habitual tendencies and their accumulations are the causes of birth and death, [one will no longer fall into such views].
Reaching the places of rebirth within the three realms as the fruit of birth and death, one knows that birth and death are sustained by various karmas;
thus, one is able to transcend birth and death. When I say that "all dharmas exist," it is for the purpose of sustaining the world.
Since the world is not non-existent, how can one say it is non-existent? This is precisely to refute the nihilistic view of total non-existence held by the heterodox teachers.
Although it is said that all phenomena exist, they have as their essence only names, phrases, and syllables;
even when spoken through the nature of sound, they are not substantial realities—thus, while they exist, they have never truly existed.

Nevertheless, the reason all phenomena are said to be like illusions is that the nature of illusion and the marks of illusion are fundamentally not real entities, so that foolish people may come to know them as being like illusions and thereby distance themselves from them.
Because they are ignorant of the self-nature and self-characteristics of all phenomena, foolish people fall into the evil views of existence and non-existence, hoping to attain fruits;
they fail to realize that the five aggregates and all phenomena are merely manifestations of one's own mind, fundamentally uncreated and fundamentally unborn.
Thus, they falsely conceive of a creator as the cause of birth and cling to self-nature and self-characteristics as being truly existent.
I have taught that the cause which produces something is not the producer of that which is produced; it is certainly not the case that the produced can produce its own cause.
Furthermore, those who cling to the characteristics of dependent origination as having a real intrinsic nature (svabhāva) are mistaken regarding their objects of perception.
Therefore, I speak of the five aggregates and all phenomena as being dependently originated.
Birth is like an illusion and unreal, like the nature of a dream; its essence is non-essence and its characteristic is non-characteristic. All phenomena are thus;

they do not allow the foolish to falsely conceptualize self-characteristics or other-characteristics, nor to hope for the attainment of fruits, nor to cling to evil views that deceive themselves and others.
Unable to clearly perceive the true abiding place of all phenomena as they really are, they instead [cling] to suchness...
To view the state of reality as an incorrect doctrine—regarding those who cling to signs as correct and those for whom things are like illusions as incorrect—is ignorance.
To see all phenomena as they truly are within the state of reality is to realize that they are the manifestation of one’s own mind;
to transcend the manifestation of one’s own mind, to be free from the marks of essence and self-nature, so that not a single dharma can be apprehended—this alone is the truth.

Because it concerns phenomena subject to arising and ceasing, it is considered a correct discourse; however, as long as one has not yet abandoned the characteristics of self-nature (*svabhāva*), and there remains the perception of self-characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and other-characteristics (*paralakṣaṇa*), such that one has not transcended the measure of the mind (*cittamātra*), this is still a matter within the realm of birth and death and is truly an incorrect discourse.
To refute that incorrect discourse, I rely upon the locus of true thusness (*tathatā*) and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) to teach that all dharmas are like [an illusion].
Since illusion is precisely because it is unarisen, it is said to be like an illusion; since it is precisely because it is like an illusion, it is said to be unarisen.
What contradiction could there possibly be? The verse further clarifies that "unarisen" and "like an illusion" are one and the same meaning.
The heterodox paths claim that all phenomena are unarisen, yet they arise due to a creator; however, as for that which is produced by such a cause, how could it possess the nature of being unarisen?

To say that "there is production" is to slander cause and effect; it is not the correct view according to reality. I teach that there is no production, for [all things] are merely the manifestation of one's own mind (*svacittadṛśyamātra*).

Since there is originally nothing produced, how could there be further production? This is precisely to refute the non-nature of "production by an agent" (*kṛtakatva*) as held by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Furthermore, when I speak of "having nature," it is intended to lead my disciples to accept worldly birth in accordance with their karma.
Death is not simply non-existence; this is precisely for the purpose of refuting the nihilistic views of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Birth is itself non-birth, and existence is itself non-existence. This teaching that there is no birth is precisely why it is said to be "like an illusion.
Because the evil views of the non-Buddhists involve hope and attachment to self-characteristics and other-characteristics, I teach "like an illusion" and so forth to correctly refute them.
Fools give rise to false conceptualizations regarding appearances; if one can observe them as being like illusions, then one will not give rise to discrimination toward any appearances.
When discrimination does not arise, appearances are no longer appearances, and the mind and its objects are stilled—this is non-arising.
Therefore, to speak of them as being "like illusions" is precisely to speak of "non-arising. This is a profoundly deep meaning; how could it be expressed through mere words?
