Chapter Three: The Essence of the Mind of All Buddhas (In the Wei translation: Chapter Four, "The Buddha-Mind"; in the Tang translation: Chapter Three, Part One, "Impermanence").
At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Mahāmati, saying: "I shall now explain the characteristics of the differentiation of the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*).
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well. Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "Excellent, World-Honored One!"
"Venerable One, it is so; we shall receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "There are three kinds of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*). What are the three? They are:
the mind-made body born of the blissful absorption of samādhi; the mind-made body born of the realization of the self-nature of dharmas;

and the mind-made body born of the simultaneous arising of its own kind, which is effortless (in the Tang translation: 'without effortful action'). The practitioner realizes these through the progressively higher stages from the first bhūmi upward."
By advancing through these characteristics, one attains the three bodies (*trikāya*). Generally speaking,

as stated at the beginning of the first two fascicles, the Buddha taught that by accomplishing four dharmas, a practitioner attains great skillful means (*mahopāya*) and reaches the eighth stage (*bhūmi*),

where one becomes detached from mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), as well as from the five dharmas, the three natures (*trisvabhāva*), and the two kinds of selflessness (*dvividha-nairātmya*).
Regarding the "body born of mastery" (*vaśitā-nirmita-kāya*) and the "mind-born body" (*manomaya-kāya*): it is called "mind-born" because it moves as swiftly and without obstruction as thought.

Previously, this was spoken of as being attained only in the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), hence it was termed the "general characteristic. Now, since it is stated that it is attained in every stage, it is termed "specifically distinguished.
Thus, within the general characteristic, there are these three types: first, the "correct reception of the bliss of samādhi" (*samādhi-sukha-samāpatti*).

The mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*) arises based on the six consciousnesses; when one realizes the wisdom of the two emptinesses and witnesses the equality of suchness, this is precisely the transformation of the seventh consciousness into the wisdom of equality (*samatā-jñāna*).
Being unmoving like suchness, it is called "right concentration" (*samyak-samādhi*);

because one takes the bliss of right concentration as its enjoyment, it is said that one attains the mind-made body of the "right reception of the bliss of samādhi. This continues until the abandonment of the third [level].
To obscurely cultivate the vast practice of saving sentient beings in accordance with their nature means to give rise to great utility from the equality of true suchness;

this arises by relying on the wisdom of equality to produce the wisdom of wondrous observation, thereby attaining the illusion-like samādhi and penetrating the self-nature and characteristics of all phenomena.
This is called the mind-made body that realizes the self-nature of dharmas. As for when...

When the Vajra-mind severs the ignorance of the arising-aspect and transforms the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*), then the first five consciousnesses simultaneously transform into the All-Accomplishing Wisdom (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*).

Because these manifest equally based upon the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom, bodies of a thousand kinds and ten thousand varieties appear universally at once; therefore, it is said that "the various types appear together."

The birth-body, the unconditioned-practice body, and the mind-made body—these three types of mind-made bodies are all attained by being free from mind, thought, and consciousness, as well as the five dharmas, the self-nature, and the two forms of selflessness.
Furthermore, the mark of the correct reception of the bliss of samādhi pertains to the stages from the first to the seventh bhūmi;
the mark of the realization of the self-nature of dharmas pertains to the stages from the eighth to the tenth bhūmi.

The characteristics of the successive advancement from the equal [stage] to the sublime and the most sublime—namely, the categories, co-nascence, non-action, and practice—possess their own internal distinctions.
These characteristics of the various aspects of the *manomaya-kāya* (mind-made body) and its pervasive penetration are what practitioners should understand.

If one attempts to correlate this with the three bodies of Dharma, Reward, and Transformation, it is not that they are three separate entities; rather, they are a single essence, the realm of wondrous enlightenment.
"Is there not a sequence of ever-increasing progress? A monk asked Chan Master Yin of Dayuan, "Several patrons have invited you;
I wonder to whose house you will go? Dayuan replied, "The moon reflects in the waters of a thousand rivers; every door has it. Monk Danxia composed a verse on this:
"The wondrous, perfect, and formless one existed before kalpas; He manifests billions of provisional bodies according to types. The moon..."
As soon as the night watchman announces the break of dawn, all six realms encounter spring at first light. Forests and springs are the Way;

they do not speak, yet they contain all phenomena. Where could the myriad spirits fail to express their gratitude for this impartiality? Only by seeing it thus can one realize the three kinds of mind-born bodies.
Mahāmati asked: "What is the mind-made body born of the correct realization of the bliss of samādhi?

It refers to the third, fourth, and fifth stages, wherein, by virtue of the correct realization of the bliss of samādhi, the various waves of consciousness arising from the ocean of the mind are stilled; one abides peacefully, and the marks of consciousness no longer arise.

One realizes that the objects appearing as manifestations of one's own mind are neither existent nor non-existent" (the Tang translation reads: "The ocean of mind does not give rise to the waves of evolving consciousness; one understands that all objects appearing to the mind are entirely non-existent").
This is called the Samādhi of Correct Joy, receiving the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*).
Generally speaking, from the first stage (*bhūmi*) through the seventh stage, because Bodhisattvas incline toward quiescence, their various mental states are tranquil;
this is termed "abiding in the mind. The waves of the ocean-like consciousness do not arise, and they are not [disturbed] by the six [consciousnesses].

When the winds of the objective sphere of consciousness cease their agitation and the waves of the evolving consciousnesses settle in tranquil stillness, one has severed the innate grasping at a self and transformed the seventh consciousness into the Wisdom of Equality.

Having realized that the objects manifested by one's own mind exist and yet are not existent, and since there is no longer an object, where can the mind abide? Since the mind has no basis, it is without support.
This state of profound stillness and clarity takes the bliss of samādhi as its object of enjoyment;

it is similar to that of those of the Two Vehicles who are attached to the bliss of cessation. However, while those of the Two Vehicles take this very state as the realization of nirvāṇa, the Bodhisattvas of the seventh stage are further able to give rise to the mind of saving sentient beings; this is why they differ. [This was addressed] to the attendant Da.
He went to the dwelling of Chan Master Hui of Dongshan. Hui asked, "The *Vajra* Samādhi is such that all things are thus;
when autumn departs and winter arrives, what then? The Master said, "It does not matter, Reverend; you may ask.
Hui said, "That is fine for now, but after you have departed, what then? The Master said, "Who would dare to question me? Hui said, "What about Daoyuan?"
One who has attained this says, "I still require another to examine me. Huì said, "To assist and support the Master is not to abandon one's brilliance.
When the attendant prostrated, it was clear that the adamantine right concentration is not simply a state of total non-existence;
it is fundamentally and immediately distinct from those who dwell in biased emptiness.
Mahāmati asked: "What is the mind-made body that realizes the self-nature of phenomena?
It refers to the eighth stage (*bhūmi*), where one observes and realizes that all phenomena such as illusions are entirely non-existent;

through the transformation of body and mind, one attains the illusion-like samādhi and other gateways of samādhi, along with immeasurable marks, powers, masteries, and clarities (translated in the Tang version as: 'realizing that phenomena are like illusions and are all without marks, the mind transforms its basis and abides in the illusion-like concentration and other samādhis')."

They are able to manifest immeasurable sovereign supernatural powers (*abhijñā*), adorned with exquisite flowers, swift as one’s will, like illusions, dreams, the moon reflected in water, or images in a mirror;
neither created nor created-from-elements, yet possessing all various forms and limbs as if they were created or derived from the elements (the Wei translation says:

"not born of the four great elements, yet appearing to possess the characteristics of the four great elements and complete bodily parts"). Entering into all Buddha-fields and assemblies, they penetrate their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
Because it is based on the Dharma, this is called the "Mind-made Body that Awakens to the Self-nature of Dharmas.
Generally speaking, from the seventh stage and below, one enters the emptiness of nirvana from the conventional reality of birth and death;

from the eighth stage and above, one enters the conventional reality of birth and death from the emptiness of nirvana. This is because, having already realized *tathatā* (suchness), one manifests the functioning of *tathatā*.

Having realized that all phenomena are like illusions—being false in their very essence and thus empty in their very essence—and having already attained the realm of non-existence, if one takes nirvana as a basis, one falls into a biased emptiness.
By giving rise to the mind to deliver sentient beings, one can transform that basis so as not to dwell in emptiness; through the transformation of body and mind, one manifests [various forms].
Because of mastery, one attains the illusion-like samādhi (*māyopama-samādhi*) and various other samādhis, capable of manifesting immeasurable sovereign supernormal powers (*ṛddhi-vidhi*);

this is called the power of signs (*nimitta-bala*), which refers to the spiritual power that manifests signs. What is called "insight" (*vidyā*) refers to the three insights (*trividyā*) and the six supernormal powers (*ṣaḍabhijñā*).
Like a wondrous lotus in full bloom, adorned with all manner of ornaments, one attains such [powers] wherever one goes.
The reason his body is adorned by mastery over the mind is that it is like a phantom person performing illusory deeds,
or like a body in a dream, the moon in water, or a reflection in a mirror; it lacks the solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion that constitute the primary elements (*mahābhūta*),
nor does it possess the derived qualities of form, odor, taste, or touch, yet it appears to have both the primary and derived four elements.
The seeds [of these beings] are such that all physical forms are perfectly complete, and their various bodily parts are adorned through the power of spiritual transformation (*ṛddhi*).
They enter into the great assemblies of all Buddha-fields to serve the Buddhas of the ten directions;
wherever they go as they please, they encounter no obstruction. Their swiftness is due to the power of spiritual transformation.
This swiftness arises precisely from the thorough penetration of the self-nature of phenomena (*dharmas*).
Each phenomenon possesses its own self-nature, which is what is meant by saying that each of the myriad things possesses its own *Taiji* (Supreme Ultimate).

However, the nature of the self-nature of phenomena is solely the single mind, which is what is meant by saying that all things are unified within the single Great *Taiji*. Since one has thoroughly penetrated the fact that everything is created by the mind, [this swiftness occurs].

Such adornment and such swiftness are entirely not outside the miraculous transformations of the *māyopama-samādhi* (illusion-like samādhi), which brings immeasurable benefit and happiness to sentient beings, enters among the great assemblies, and preaches the Dharma in accordance with their capacities;

this is called the "Mind-made Body arising from the nature of the self-nature of phenomena" (*dharmatā-prakṛti-ātmaka-manomaya-kāya*). When the Great Being Aśvaghoṣa was turning the sublime wheel of Dharma in the park of Pāṭaliputra, suddenly an old...

A monk asked Yushan, "When a student intends to return home, what should he do?
Yushan said, "Your parents are lying in a thicket of thorns, their entire bodies covered in festering sores; where would you go upon returning?
The monk said, "In that case, I shall not return. Yushan said, "You must indeed return. If you do return, I will show you a prescription for ceasing the consumption of grain."
The Master said, "I shall ask Mount Shan: 'When ascending the hall for the two daily meals, you must not chew so as to break even a single grain of rice.
One must truly follow the words of Yaoshan: 'Throughout the day one eats, yet never chews upon a single grain of rice,' only then can one sever craving and sever ignorance."
Those latent tendencies (anuśaya) do not manifest, yet like the poison of a rat that erupts, they bring about the ultimate severance of all dharmas; this is called "harming an Arhat.
Generally speaking, when various sutras speak of "destroying the sutras" or "burning images," it is because these acts constitute the destruction of the Dharma-jewel.
Therefore, it is also said that those latent tendencies do not manifest, yet they bring about the ultimate severance of all dharmas—this is the severance of the Dharma.
This is precisely what harms the Arhat. The "various proclivities" (*anuśaya*) refer to the eighty-eight proclivities;

that is, the aforementioned greed, craving, ignorance, and so forth, which are established as the afflictions of the nine grades within the three realms. Through the gradual suppression of these by means of dharmas such as the four foundations of mindfulness, they can be rendered non-manifest;
however, this is merely a temporary non-manifestation. When they encounter conditions, they immediately arise, like a rat gnawing at a person.

Although the ulcer has healed, the poison remains stored within; it erupts immediately upon encountering thunder. These various dharmas involve only the severing of coarse delusions and not the subtle delusions;
they involve only the severing of the fetters and proclivities (*saṃyojana* and *anuśaya*) and not the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*).

Therefore, the dull-witted Arhat who does not turn his mind back, even if he enters the sphere of neither-perception-nor-non-perception (*naivasaṃjñānāsaṃjñāyatana*), will, when eighty thousand kalpas have passed, again undergo subsequent existence. If one can, however, by means of...
Through the ultimate realization of the contemplation of the non-self of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*), those subtle habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are severed one by one and completely eliminated.

While previously one only knew the dharmas to be abandoned through seeing (*darśana-heya*), this now advances to the dharmas to be abandoned through cultivation (*bhāvanā-heya*); therefore, it is called "harming an Arhat.
These latent dispositions (*anuśaya*) do not manifest; this is the dharma of an obtuse Arhat. By ultimately severing them, one approaches the emptiness of phenomena (*dharma-śūnyatā*).

In the past, when Huangbo was traveling to Tiantai, he encountered a monk who appeared to be an old acquaintance. They traveled together until they reached a mountain stream where the water had suddenly surged.
Huangbo leaned on his staff and stood still, while the monk urged him to cross with him. Huangbo said, "I ask that you, brother, go first.
The monk immediately placed his straw hat upon the water and floated across. Huangbo remarked, "I regret that I have been in the company of such a mere boatman."
He struck the monk with a single blow and killed him; then, joining his palms upon the water, he praised him, saying, "Truly a vessel of the Great Vehicle!
This is beyond my reach. One such as Huangbo is truly capable of slaying an Arhat."

What is meant by "schism in the Saṃgha"? It refers to the ultimate severance of the conjunction and accumulation of the various aggregates (skandhas) that possess distinct characteristics; this is called a schism in the Saṃgha.
Generally speaking, the term "Saṃgha" refers to a community of bhikṣus who, being free from the notion of a self (ātman) and the notion of a person (pudgala), have gathered together as one.
Regarding this "breaking of the harmony of the Saṃgha" by the multitude: it refers to the aggregate of form (*rūpa-skandha*) having characteristics. Form does not constitute form by itself;

rather, because it is conjoined with the four other aggregates—feeling (*vedanā*), perception (*saṃjñā*), mental formations (*saṃskāra*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*)—it possesses the characteristic of form. These various aggregates possess distinct characteristics.

It is by means of these non-material [aggregates] that form is truly able to accumulate and thus become form. Thus, while being without [independent] characteristics, they are truly able to harmonize [to produce form].
Though they combine to form appearances, these can be accumulated yet remain without shape; though they harmonize and unite, they remain without substance.
Now, by ultimately severing those [aggregates] of sensation, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, they are successively exhausted and eliminated.

This causes that which harmonizes to disperse and that which accumulates to collapse; not only does one dissolve their appearances, but one also dissolves the very dependent origination that constitutes those appearances.

When there are four aggregates (*skandha*) as conditions, there is a coming together; if there are no conditions, who could come together? Therefore, the destruction of the distinct characteristics of the various aggregates is called "schism in the Saṃgha" (*saṃghabheda*).

Previously, the various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) were not manifest, but now, having ceased sensation and perception (*vedanā-saṃjñā*), one next severs the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*) and gradually eliminates it.
Now, as the eight consciousnesses arise, both the perceived aspect (*nimittabhāga*) and the perceiving aspect (*darśanabhāga*) are due to the seventh consciousness.
The harmony of these [elements] is what constitutes this "harmony-breaker," which precisely breaks the seven consciousnesses and a half, while externally relying upon the six consciousnesses.
Chan Master Lì Fǎhǎi of Chùzhōu, because the imperial court had issued an edict to convert his temple into a Shénxiāo Palace, ascended the seat and said to the assembly:
"It is entirely because one has not yet reached ultimate penetration that one speaks of 'right' and 'wrong.'"
If it is unreal, then distinctions such as "this" and "that" vanish; since even this very body does not exist, what need is there to speak of anything outside the body?

Viewed with the True Eye, it is but a source of laughter. Now, as the Sage Ruler has issued his decree to transform the monasteries into temples of Shenxiao, what harm is there in adding a crown to the head of the Buddha? Today, this mountain monk...

Setting aside the horizontal carrying of the staff and hanging up the alms-bag, he establishes his dwelling within the seamless stupa and settles his life beneath the rootless tree, whistling at the moon and chanting in the wind.
Let the cloud-riding immortals and crane-riding transcendents come as they please to cast spells over water, write talismans, and perform incantations by clapping their teeth;
when he attains the Way in years to come and ascends on a white day, he will be worthy to repay [his debts].
To repay this unrequited kindness by assisting in the transformation of non-action—though I fear it may not be jade;
yet if it were jade, how marvelous! Even so, tell me: how would you express the monk’s turning-about? Do you understand?
[He] cast down his whisk and immediately entered into stillness. This was during the reign of Emperor Wuzong of the Tang, who suppressed the Sangha. But...
One can merely destroy the formal monastic community, but it is not like a Chan master who establishes his life within a seamless stupa,
directly breaking through the five aggregates to emerge— truly one who practices the "uninterrupted" path.
Mahāmati, failing to realize that the seven bodies of consciousness— which are the external self-characteristics and common characteristics appearing as the measure of one's own mind—

are ultimately severed through the three gates of liberation and the absence of outflowing evil thoughts, such a Buddha (the Buddha of the eight bodies of consciousness, as translated in the Tang dynasty) is said to have shed the blood of a Buddha with an evil mind.
The Master said: "All aspects of the perceiving subject (*darśana-bhāga*) and the perceived object (*nimitta-bhāga*) are merely manifestations of one's own mind.

When one eliminates the characteristics of the accumulation and aggregation of the aggregates (*skandha*), if one perceives that there are phenomena external to the mind, this is not ultimate elimination.

It is only because one fails to realize that each of the external phenomena and aggregates possesses its own intrinsic nature as a self-characteristic, and that it is through the aggregation of these aggregates that they constitute a person."
All common characteristics (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*) are merely manifestations of one’s own mind (*svacitta-dṛśya-mātra*).

Although the seven consciousnesses (*sapta-vijñāna-kāya*) themselves are the Buddha-nature (*tathāgata-garbha*), and though both defilement and purity have been extinguished, the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) still persists; therefore, these seeds of consciousness must be severed.

The seventh consciousness is partially subtle and internally dependent upon the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*). [The text] states that one should sever that eighth-consciousness-body, yet the eighth consciousness continues to flow.
The commentary states that those who cannot attain cessation rely solely on the seven consciousnesses as the basis for defilement and purity;
they extensively produce seeds of defilement and purity through perfuming, which depend upon the eighth consciousness.

These must necessarily be eradicated by means of the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and by means of the three untainted dharmas of precept, concentration, and wisdom. This is the power of the Mahāyāna.

When the "evil thought" (āśubha-saṃjñā) is sufficient to strike the seven consciousness-pivots (saptavijñāna-kṣura), the eighth consciousness is the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya, while the seventh consciousness is its flowing blood.

When one ultimately severs the seeds of that seventh consciousness and the innate ignorance (sahaja-avidyā) of the Buddha-nature is completely purified, the ripening [consciousness] (vipāka) becomes entirely empty;
this is therefore called "the evil mind shedding the blood of the Buddha's body. This is precisely what is meant by "regarding it as tranquil."
When the windless, rippling waves of stillness can shatter this kind of consciousness, one is able to transform consciousness into wisdom and realize the Tathāgata’s pure Dharmakāya.
Yunmen cited the World-Honored One’s first appearance in the world:
pointing with one hand toward heaven and with the other toward earth, he walked seven steps and gazed in the four directions, saying, "In the heavens above and on the earth below, only..."
I alone am the Honored One. The Gate says: "If at that time I had seen him, I would have struck him with a single blow and fed him to a dog, merely to ensure peace under heaven.
Later, Changling Zhuo offered this verse: "He took seven steps and proclaimed himself Honored;
How could such family disgrace be allowed out the door? He finished saving beings while still in his mother’s womb; Yet he still required one blow for every person."
The *Huantianmu Lishong* (Verses on Paying Homage at Mount Tiantu) says: "Never having entered the womb of Māyā, with both hands one knows not where he rests;
emerging from her right side, this manifestation in the realm of Māra is fit only for lamentation and unfit for contemplation.
These venerable masters may truly be called those who shed the blood of the Buddha with malicious intent.
If men or women commit these acts of immediate retribution, they are called the five *ānantarya* and are also called "those equal to the immediate" (*ānantaryasama*).

(The Wei translation says: "called those who realize the dharma as it truly is"; the Tang translation says: "immediately attain realization of the true dharma. Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are five external *ānantarya*;
I shall now expound them so that you and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, having heard this meaning, will not fall into delusion in future ages.
What is delusion? There are five types of immediate [attainment]. These refer to the previously mentioned immediacies:
if one practices these, one will not attain the dharma of immediate realization (*abhisamaya*) regarding each of the three liberations.

Excluding these, there are other instances where the power of transformation manifests immediate realization—namely, the power of transformation of Śrāvakas, the power of transformation of Bodhisattvas, and the power of transformation of Tathāgatas—which bring about immediate realization for others.

For those who have committed offenses, the removal of doubt and the confession of transgressions serve as an encouragement; thus, through the manifestation of supernatural transformations such as the Avīci hell, it is shown that there is no one who exclusively commits acts of immediate retribution (*ānantarya*) who fails to attain such realization. This is because they have realized that all is merely the manifestation of their own minds, thereby becoming free from the delusions regarding body and property, and detached from the grasping for "I" and "mine.
Alternatively, by encountering a spiritual friend (*kalyāṇamitra*), they may achieve liberation from the continuity of other realms of existence.
Regarding deluded thoughts:

it is universally taught that the *tathatā* (suchness) of the ultimate reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) is fundamentally without interruption. Now, when the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantaryakarma*) are directed toward suchness, they are called "uninterrupted practice" (*anantarya-caryā*).
Because one realizes this Dharma through this practice, one attains the direct realization (*sākṣātkriyā*) of the *tathatā* of the ultimate reality.
Regarding "attaining immediate realization" (*ānantarya*), this borrows the five external *ānantaryas* as a metaphor for the internal practice of immediate realization;

it possesses only a name, for such a thing does not exist in reality. If the five external *ānantaryas* were to lead to falling [into hell], there would be those who fall, those who do not fall, and those who should have fallen but ultimately did not; their meanings are not uniform. If one were to cling to them as being uniform...
This is precisely falling into delusion. What are the five external *ānantarya* [sins]? They are those previously mentioned:
killing one’s father, killing one’s mother, harming an *arhat*, causing a schism in the Saṃgha, and shedding the blood of a Buddha.
If one truly commits such acts, one will not attain realization of the three gates of liberation; one will not realize emptiness, nor realize the signless, nor realize the wishless.

Even if one attains realization, if one's karmic offenses are profound and heavy and one is bound by afflictions, then despite practicing the three gates of liberation, one will not attain the dharma of immediate realization (abhisamaya) in each case; such a person must repay their karma by entering the Avīci Hell.
Apart from those who have committed such [specific] deeds, there is no doubt that others will enter the Avīci Hell. This is so even for Tathāgatas and great Bodhisattvas.

The Bodhisattvas and the great Śrāvakas, by means of the supernormal power of transformation of the aforementioned three types of mind-made bodies (*manomaya-kāya*), manifest the five deeds of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karman*).
This is for the purpose of exhorting other sentient beings who have committed such deeds to reform their ways, and to demonstrate [the truth] to them so as to dispel their doubts;
through the power of their supernatural faculties (*ṛddhi-bala*), they manifest these same actions to lead those beings [to realization].
The practitioner immediately repented his transgressions, eliminated his doubts, and realized liberation; all of these were manifested transformations and not actual deeds.
There has never been one who committed an uninterrupted (ānantarya) act in reality and yet did not enter the Avīci Hell. Thus, is it that the perpetrator can ultimately never escape?
Only by awakening to the fact that birth-and-death and Nirvāṇa are the mere manifestations of one’s own mind is there an exception.
When one realizes that all things are equal and identical within the state of *parinirvāṇa*, one no longer perceives even the attainment of *abhisamaya*.
This is because internally one is free from the delusions of the view of a self (*satkāyadṛṣṭi*), thereby severing the two root afflictions of craving and ignorance;

externally one is free from the delusions of seeking to acquire dharmas or material wealth, thereby distancing oneself from the various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*). Thus, with all phenomena transcending the combination of the five aggregates, one acts solely through the power of one's own mind.
The self and the five aggregates are a combination of form-dharmas; since there is no "mine," there is neither a grasper nor anything to be grasped.

Thus, the seven types of consciousness are thoroughly demolished. Whether through having planted the conditions for *prajñā* over many lifetimes until they have matured, or by encountering a Tathāgata, a Bodhisattva, or a Śrāvaka, one hears the True Dharma and attains awakening.
When the fundamental mind attains liberation, the various delusive thoughts of the continuous cycle of birth and death across other realms cease to exist.
Since these delusive thoughts are absent, one realizes True Suchness (Tathatā) and attains the dharma of non-interruption within the three gates of liberation.
When there is no longer any birth and death to be found before one’s eyes, how could there be an uninterrupted hell? Beyond this, there are the five other types of uninterrupted [retributions].

The meaning must be distinguished. At the assembly on Vulture Peak, there were five hundred bhikṣus who had attained the four dhyānas and possessed the five supernatural powers, yet they had not yet attained the patience of the Dharma (dharmanidhyānakṣānti).

By means of their supernormal power of recollecting past lives, each saw for himself his past crimes, such as killing his father and harming his mother; thus, within their own minds, each harbored doubts.
Because this profound Dharma cannot be realized through such means, Mañjuśrī, receiving the Buddha’s spiritual power, then grasped a sharp sword in his hand and approached the Tathāgata.
The World-Honored One then said to Mañjuśrī: "Stop! Stop! You must not commit an act of parricide; do not seek to harm me.
Even if I am to be harmed, it is better to be harmed by one who is virtuous. Mañjuśrī, from the very beginning..."
In this coming, there is no self or person; it is only through the internal mind that one perceives a self or person.

When the internal mind arises, the self is inevitably harmed, and thus it is called "harm. Thereupon, the five hundred bhikṣus realized the nature of their own minds as being like a dream and like an illusion.
Within dreams and illusions, there is no self or person, nor even the parents who give birth and those who are born. Thus [they understood].
Five hundred bhikṣus praised him in unison, saying: "Mañjuśrī, the Great Sage of Profound Wisdom, you who have reached the bottom of the deep and far-reaching source of the Dharma!
You hold a sharp sword in your hand and press it against the body of the Tathāgata; yet as the sword is so, the Buddha is likewise. They are of one mark and not two;
they are without marks and without origination. How, then, can there be killing within this? If one examines these lines of scripture in conjunction, [the meaning becomes clear].
Thus, through the Tathāgata’s supernormal power and transformations, those who have committed the crimes of immediate retribution are all enabled to attain liberation,
thereby gaining the conviction that everything is created by the mind.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Craving is called the mother, and ignorance is the father; the consciousness that perceives objects is the Buddha, and the various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) are the Arhats;

the accumulation of the aggregates (*skandha*) is called the Sangha. To sever these in immediate succession is what is meant by the five immediate transgressions (*ānantarya*); such a person does not enter the Avīci Hell.
Tong said: "Regarding the five external acts of immediate retribution (*ānantarya-karma*), these refer to those directed toward parents, the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha;
since these exist externally as identifiable, fixed positions, one who commits such acts will undoubtedly enter the Avīci Hell.
As for the five internal acts of immediate retribution, they consist simply of taking craving as the mother and ignorance as the father, while perceiving the objective realm."

The seven consciousnesses are what the Buddha can sever; the various latent tendencies (*anuśaya*) do not manifest [in him]. The Arhat is so called because he has severed the five aggregates (*skandha*) which were previously a collection and aggregation.
The Sangha is established because within the field of the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*), one clings to the marks of self, person, sentient being, and life-span.
By means of uninterrupted practice, one gradually severs these; thus, there is no longer self, person, sentient being, or life-span.
These individuals realize the true Dharma of the Uninterrupted (ānantarya) through such characteristics.
Those who practice these five acts of immediate retribution do not form a seeking for the Buddha, do not form a seeking for the Dharma, and do not form a seeking for the Sangha.
Since the Buddha, Dharma, and Sangha are non-existent, how could there be an Avīci Hell? If the hell does not exist, who would enter it? This is precisely what I mean.
If men and women commit the five deeds of immediate retribution (*pañcānantarya-karma*) yet do not enter the Avīci Hell, it is because of this [understanding].

When the Sangha asked Linji, "What are the five deeds of immediate retribution? Linji replied: "Killing one's father, harming one's mother, shedding the blood of a Buddha, causing a harmonious Sangha to be divided, and burning sutras and images—these are the five deeds of immediate retribution. [The Sangha asked: "How so?"

Fazu said: "Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the father. When you seek the place where your single thought-moment arises and ceases and cannot find it—like an echo responding to empty space, being without affairs wherever you go—this is called 'killing the father. What is the mother? Fazu said:
'Craving (*tṛṣṇā*) is the mother. When your single thought-moment enters the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), you seek that craving and see only the empty nature of all phenomena."
To be without attachment anywhere is called "harming one's mother. What is meant by "shedding the Buddha’s blood"? The answer is:
if you give rise to even a single thought of conceptual understanding within the pure dharma-realm, you will be in darkness everywhere; this is shedding the Buddha’s blood.
What is meant by "breaking the harmony of the Sangha"? The answer is: when your single thought-moment directly penetrates the afflictions.
The fetters and latent tendencies are like space, having no basis; this is what it means to "destroy the harmony of the Sangha. What does it mean to "incinerate scriptures and images"?

Jie said: "To see that causes and conditions are empty, the mind is empty, and dharmas are empty—to decisively sever them in a single thought, so that there is suddenly nothing remaining—this is what it means to incinerate scriptures and images.
Venerable Sir, if you can penetrate in this way, you will escape being labeled by others as either ordinary or holy."
Is it not the case that Linji, obstructing this path, revealed the five deeds of immediate retribution—that which is called "the mind awakening and transforming the Lotus Sutra"?
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for us the Buddha’s knowledge and realization."
“World-Honored One, what is the awakening of a Buddha? The World-Honored One replied to Mahāmati: “The realization that persons and phenomena lack self-nature;
the thorough knowledge of the two obstacles; the transcendence of the two kinds of death; and the severance of the two afflictions—this is called the awakening of a Buddha.
If Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas attain this dharma, they too are called Buddhas. For these reasons, I speak of the One Vehicle.”
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Thoroughly knowing the two kinds of selflessness, having severed the two obstacles and afflictions, and being forever free from the two kinds of death—this is called the Buddha’s awakening."
Tong said: "The 'Great Cause and Condition' is named the Buddha’s knowledge and vision—the opening, showing, awakening, and entering.
There is only this One Vehicle and no other vehicle; this is the essential purport of the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka*.

This also means that what is called my own vehicle is not [merely] the Great Vehicle, for even Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas cannot easily fathom the Buddha's knowledge and realization. Therefore, I pray that the Buddha will speak."
The Buddha taught that one who awakens to all Buddha-dharmas is called a Perfectly Awakened One (*samyaksambuddha*).
Delusion consists of the two attachments to persons and phenomena; the two emptinesses constitute wisdom. Since the two emptinesses empty those two attachments, there is no obstruction of delusion;
since the wisdom that performs the emptying also vanishes, there is no obstruction of wisdom. However, the obstruction of delusion is further divided.

The root cause of *paricchinna-śarīra-janma-maraṇa* (segmented birth and death) is the obstacle of knowledge (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), while the root cause of *pariṇāmi-śarīra-janma-maraṇa* (transformative birth and death) is the obstacle of affliction (*kleśāvaraṇa*).

Since the effect ceases when the cause is extinguished, one is freed from both segmented and transformative deaths. Regarding the two types of afflictions: first, the delusions of view (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*) are called "discriminative afflictions" (*vikalpa-kleśa*);

second, the delusions of cultivation (*bhāvanā-kleśa*) are called "innate afflictions" (*sahaja-kleśa*). These can only be completely severed upon reaching the ultimate fruit; this is the knowledge of the Buddha.

Awakening is simply the awakening to this; if the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas have not yet forgotten their attachment to dharmas, and the cognitive hindrance (jñeyāvaraṇa) remains, they are not free from the death of transformation (nirmāṇacitta), nor have they severed the innate afflictions (sahaja-kleśa).
If they can awaken to and shatter each and every fault, attaining ultimate detachment identical to the awakening of a Buddha, they are then named Buddhas. For these reasons, I have said:
There is only the One Vehicle and no other vehicle. The verse says: "Skillfully knowing the single word 'good' has its flavor.

The followers of the Two Vehicles know the selflessness of persons; Bodhisattvas know the selflessness of phenomena. Because it requires great exertion of effort, it cannot be called "good" [in the conventional sense].
Although the Great Bodhisattvas are able to sever the two obstacles and the two afflictions, these still belong to the category of remedial counteraction (*pratipakṣa*).

If the Tathāgata has spontaneously severed the afflictions of the two obstacles, while the followers of the Two Vehicles have escaped death by fragmentation but not yet escaped death by transformation, and although Bodhisattvas have escaped these two deaths they have not yet attained eternal liberation—it is only when one has thus investigated and exhausted [all things] that they may be called the awakening-knowledge of a Buddha.
To enter this awakening-knowledge is what is meant by "not my vehicle"; those who ride the Great Vehicle may remain silent.
Baizhang said: "Cognition (vijñāna) is turbid while wisdom (jñāna) is clear; prajñā is clear while cognition is turbid. In the Buddha, it is called 'illumination' (zhào);
in Bodhisattvas, it is called 'wisdom' (zhì); in the stage of the Two Vehicles and ordinary beings, it is called 'cognition' (shí), and is also termed 'affliction' (kleśa).
In the Buddha, it is called the 'cause within the fruit'; in ordinary beings, it is called the 'fruit within the cause. In the Buddha, it is called 'turning the wheel of Dharma'."
What is called the turning of the Dharma wheel among sentient beings is called the ornament of the necklace among Bodhisattvas;

what is called the forest of the five aggregates among sentient beings is called fundamental ignorance (mūla-avidyā) in the Buddha. Because this is ignorance that is itself illumination, it is said that ignorance is the essence of the Way.
This differs from the dark obscuration of ignorance in ordinary sentient beings; [here] ignorance must be luminous, as in the case of Baizhang’s “ignorance is the body of the Way.”
Only after such an explanation can one begin to glimpse that the Buddha’s awareness is not something that can be compared to a mere "brightly shining" or "vividly manifest" consciousness.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, for what reason did the World-Honored One proclaim these words in the midst of the great assembly:
‘I am all the Buddhas of the past,’ and ‘I was [the one who underwent] various births’? At that time, I was Mañjuśrī...”
The *Jātaka-sūtra* (in the Tang translation, the *Śatasāhasrikā-jātaka-kathā*) speaks of such things as King Mahāprabhāsa’s six-tusked elephant,
his parrot, Śakra Devendra, and the seer Sunetra— hundreds of thousands of such past lives.

The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Because of four kinds of equality (the Tang translation says: 'relying on the secret intention of the four equalities'), the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, proclaims these words in the great assembly:
'At that time, I was Krakucchanda, Kanakamuni, and Kāśyapa Buddha. What are the four equalities? They are:
equality of letters, equality of speech, equality of dharma, and equality of body. These are called the four equalities."
Because of four kinds of equality, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, proclaims these words amidst the great assembly:
"What is meant by the equality of syllables? If the syllable that designates me as a Buddha also designates all Buddhas—[as the Tang translation says:
'My name is Buddha, and all Tathāgatas are also named Buddha']—then because the intrinsic nature of those syllables has no distinction, this is the equality of names."
Tong said: "The awakening of the Buddha is precisely the Dharma-body (dharmakāya), and the Dharma-body is one alone. Therefore, it is taught as the One Vehicle (ekayāna).

If one suspects that while the Dharma-body is fundamentally one, the retribution-body (nirmāṇakāya) and transformation-bodies (saṃbhogakāya) are various and different, this merely creates obstacles within oneself regarding appearances.
Viewed through the wisdom of the Buddha, all things are equal; what need is there for hundreds of thousands of Jātaka tales?"

Do not these matters all converge upon one point? The Buddha—having been King Mūrdhaja in the past, Śakra, a rishi, and even an elephant or a parrot, and so forth—taught that this Dharma-body is difficult to believe at once;
therefore, he declared, "All Buddhas of the past are myself," using the equality of names, the equality of words, and the equality of dharmas to demonstrate the equality of the body.
Regarding the fourfold equality, it is spoken with the intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya*) that "equality is indeed the self. What is meant by the equality of syllables?
If those syllables are designated as my name "Buddha," then all Tathāgatas of the past were likewise designated by those same syllables as "Buddha.
There is no difference or distinction in the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the word "Buddha"; where there is this reality, there is this name.
"If there is this name, then there must be these characters. If a bodhisattva were to descend [into this world], he could not avoid having this name;
for name and character to be identical—calling myself 'I' was the same as being one of all the Buddhas of the past—what would be wrong with that?
Yangshan asked Sanxing, "What is your name? Sanxing said, "Huiji. Yangshan said, "Huiji is me. Sanxing said, "My name is Hui."
However, Yangshan laughed heartily, "He-he. Xuedou’s verse on this says: "Both gathering and both releasing—what is the school?
Riding a tiger has always required transcending all merit. Having laughed, one knows not where he has gone; Only the mournful wind shall stir for a thousand ages.
If these two venerable masters had exchanged roles with one another and walked side by side hand-in-hand, it would truly have been unfathomable; they must have reached mutual accord.
Regarding this, those who explain characters and so forth say:
"What are the 'languages and so forth'? It means that my sixty-four kinds of Brahma-voice linguistic expressions arise;
likewise, those Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas also have sixty-four kinds of Brahma-voice linguistic expressions arise, without increase."

There is no decrease and no distinction; the nature of the Brahma-voice of the Kalaviṅka (translated here as "the Bird of Wondrous Sound") is collectively termed the sixty-four kinds of Brahma-sounds, as described in the *Guhyakapūrvayoga Sūtra*. It is said that the Buddha’s voice possesses eight inflections (*vibhakti*), namely: substance, object, instrument, ablative, locative, and vocative. These eight inflections each possess eight qualities, namely: 1. Clarity (*viśada*) 2. Purity (*śuddha*) 3. Distinctness (*vibhakta*) 4. Melodiousness (*madhura*) 5. Pleasantness (*premaṇīya*) 6. Delightfulness (*prahlādana*) 7. Penetratingness (*nipāta*) 8. Resonance (*anuravita*) Furthermore, these eight qualities each possess eight further attributes, making sixty-four in total. These are: 1. Being heard from afar (*dūrāśravaṇa*) 2. Being heard clearly even nearby (*antikāśravaṇa*) 3. Not being confused with other sounds (*asaṃsṛṣṭa*) 4. Not being interrupted by other sounds (*anupahata*) 5. Not being diminished by distance (*adūra*) 6. Not being lost in the midst of a crowd (*anupahata*) 7. Not being obstructed by walls or mountains (*anāvṛta*) 8.

Not being suppressed by other sounds (*anabhibhūta*) And for each of these, there are eight further characteristics: 1. Being easy to understand (*suprajñeya*) 2. Being easy to comprehend (*sugrāhya*) 3. Being not harsh (*akarkaśa*) 4. Being not rough (*aparusa*) 5. Being not agitated (*acapala*) 6. Being not confused (*asambhrānta*) 7. Being consistent (*anuloma*) 8. Being appropriate to the occasion (*yathārha*) Thus, the sixty-four qualities of the Buddha’s voice are fully explained.
The voice is harmonious, soft, clearly articulated, easy to understand, free from error, not weak or feminine, vast, and profound.
These eight qualities, each multiplied by eight, constitute the sixty-four qualities of sound. The arising of speech does not depart from the *brahma-svara* (Brahma-voice);
this is the case for all Buddhas. The *Saddharma-smṛty-upasthāna Sūtra* states that the voice of the *kalaviṅka* [is like this].
He emits a wondrous voice that none among devas, humans, or kinnaras can equal, except for the voice of the Tathāgata.
Thus, when the Buddha expounds the Dharma with a single sound, each according to their kind understands it; could this be so without being endowed with the nature of such a voice?
It is because within the nature of the voice there is neither increase nor decrease, and no differentiation. (6)
The fourteen kinds of Brahma-voice are equal to those of all Buddhas. Nanquan called out to the temple steward; the steward responded.

Nanquan said: "When the Buddha remained in the Trāyastriṃśa Heaven for ninety days preaching the Dharma for his mother, King Udayana, longing for the Buddha, requested Maudgalyāyana to employ his supernatural powers to direct artisans there to carve a statue of the Buddha. Only...
[The Master] asked, "Why can the mark of Brahma’s voice not be carved? Yun said, "It would kill people.
One night, while Yaoshan was walking up and down the mountain, the clouds suddenly parted and he beheld the moon.
He let out a great roar, and the sound echoed for about ninety *li* east of Liyang, such that all the local residents said [it was a dragon].
The neighbors questioned one another in turn about the matter until they reached the disciples of Yaoshan, who said, "Last night, the Master let out a great roar from the summit of the mountain.
Li Ao presented him with a poem which says: "Having chosen a secluded dwelling that accords with my rustic sentiments, Throughout the year there is neither seeing off nor welcoming.
Sometimes I ascend straight to the peak of the solitary mountain, And under the moon, I shed my clouds and let out a single roar."
Thus, it can be known from ninety li away that the voice of the Śrāvaka Yaoshan was like the *kalaviṅka* melody of the Tathāgata pervading the worlds of the ten directions;
this is by no means empty talk.
Why then do you say that your body and so forth are no different from the Dharma-body and the marks and signs of the physical bodies of all Buddhas?

Except for manifesting various differentiated physical bodies (*rūpakāya*) in order to subdue sentient beings of various distinct realms of existence, these are called the "bodies" and so forth. Generally, these are termed the *dharmakāya* and the *rūpakāya*.
As for the marks and signs (*lakṣaṇa-vyañjana*), they refer to the three bodies—the *dharmakāya*, *saṃbhogakāya*, and *nirmāṇakāya*—which are non-different from those of all Buddhas.
However, there is a distinction: the *dharmakāya* is one, while the *saṃbhogakāya* is twofold, namely the self-enjoyment (*svasaṃbhoga*) and the other-enjoyment (*parasaṃbhoga*).

The self-enjoyment refers to that which constantly enjoys the vast dharma-bliss for itself; the other-enjoyment refers to that which causes the assembly of bodhisattvas to enjoy the dharma-bliss of the Mahāyāna.
The *nirmāṇakāya* is threefold, namely the Great Transformation [Body] of ten thousand feet, Vairocana, and...

The infinite marks and signs, as well as the minor transformations such as Śākyamuni in his six-foot form, are manifestations that adapt to the various classes of beings—what are called "various births," such as King Mūrdhaja, Śakra Devendra, the Great Elephant, the Parrot, and so forth, entering everywhere. However, by transforming and extinguishing the three minds, one immediately attains the three bodies:
first, the fundamental mind, which is the eighth consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), transforms to attain the *dharmakāya*; second, the [mind of] reliance...

The original mind is the reward body (*saṃbhogakāya*) attained through the transformation of the seventh consciousness; the three arising minds of activity are the emanation bodies (*nirmāṇakāya*) attained through the transformation of the first six consciousnesses.
Because all Buddhas realize this mind, their bodies and so forth are equal. Shūsan ascended the hall and said:
"Before the Xiantong era, this sick monk realized the matter of the Dharma-body; after the Xiantong era, I realized the Dharma-body itself."
Regarding the matter of transcending [the phenomenal], Yunmen went forth and asked, "What is the matter of the Dharma-body's side?
Deshan said, "A withered tree stump. Yunmen asked, "What is the matter beyond the Dharma-body? Deshan said, "It is not a withered tree stump.
Yunmen said, "Do you permit me to speak of principle? Deshan said, "I do. Yunmen said, "Is a withered tree stump not the manifestation of the Dharma-body's side?"
Shanshan said, "Is this? Mendun said, "It is not. Shanshan said, "Is a withered stump not the matter that transcends the Dharmakāya? Mendun said, "It is.
Mendun asked, "But does the Dharmakāya encompass all things or not? Shanshan said, "The Dharmakāya is all-pervasive; how could it not encompass them?
Mendun pointed to a pure water jar and said, "But does the pure water jar encompass the Dharmakāya?"
Mount [Zhaozhou] said: "Dharma-uncle, do not seek the gate near the pure pitcher," and then bowed. An ancient worthy said: "The long is the Dharma-body;
the short is the Dharma-body. Tiantong [Rujing] took up this case and said: "Tell me, what does the Śūnyatā-deva call the Dharma-body?
After a long silence, he said: "Do you understand? One must not lengthen the duck or shorten the crane, nor level the mountains."
"Filled the valley and departed"—this saying is precisely intended to prevent people from driving stakes into empty space.
What are the "equalities"? It refers to myself and those Buddhas attaining the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment;
briefly stated, the unobstructed wisdom of the Buddha-dharma is called the four equalities. Therefore, the Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha, regarding the Great...
Within the assembly, such words were proclaimed:

"The thirty-seven factors of enlightenment are called the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of awakening, and the eightfold noble path. What are the four [foundations of mindfulness]?"

The foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) refer to the foundation of mindfulness of the body, the foundation of mindfulness of feelings, the foundation of mindfulness of the mind, and the foundation of mindfulness of phenomena.
Regarding the internal body, the external body, and both the internal and external bodies, one does not give rise to discursive thoughts;

possessing right mindfulness and clear comprehension, with the desire to subdue worldly greed and sorrow, one dwells in the contemplation of arising, abiding, and cessation, without any dependence. What are the four right endeavors (samyakprahāṇa)? They refer to [the effort] regarding unarisen evil...
What are the four bases of spiritual power (*ṛddhipāda*)?
They are the concentration of desire, the concentration of effort, the concentration of mind, and the concentration of investigation.

These rely upon seclusion, rely upon detachment, rely upon cessation, and are dedicated toward equanimity. What are the five faculties (*indriya*)? They are the faculty of faith, the faculty of vigor... [and so forth].
What are the faculties of energy, mindfulness, concentration, and wisdom? What are called the five powers?
They are the power of faith, the power of energy, the power of mindfulness, the power of concentration, and the power of wisdom. What are called the seven factors of enlightenment?

They are the factor of enlightenment of mindfulness, the factor of enlightenment of investigation of phenomena, the factor of enlightenment of energy, the factor of enlightenment of joy, the factor of enlightenment of tranquility, and the factor of enlightenment of concentration.
The factors of enlightenment such as equanimity, what is meant by the Eightfold Noble Path?

It refers to right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration—all of which are sublime dharmas for severing afflictions and advancing toward Bodhi.
To summarize, the nature of phenomena (dharmatā) is illustrated through analogy: it is like the earth, while the foundations of mindfulness (smṛtyupasthāna) are like seeds.
Right effort is the planting of the bases of psychic power like drawing forth sprouts; the five faculties are like the growth of roots; the five powers are like the increase of stems and leaves;
the seven factors of enlightenment are like the blossoming of flowers; and the eightfold noble path is like the ripening of fruit. There is no difference in what all Buddhas have realized.
Because all Buddhas use this to transform and guide sentient beings, and I do likewise, it is called the equality of dharmas (dharmasamatā). Thus the Buddha-dharma is reached.
If there were even the slightest obstacle within this [equality], it would not be "equal. I alone have attained unobstructed wisdom regarding the Buddha-dharma;
in the single, true, and equal *dharmadhātu*, there is no distinction between self and other. This is merely a brief explanation of these four types of equality.
If one investigates thoroughly, every phenomenon (*dharma*) is equal—how could it be limited to only four?
It is finished! For this reason, the Tathāgata proclaims these words amidst the great assembly: "I am the awakened realization of all Buddhas of the past.
Since there is no duality in the Buddha's awakening and the three bodies of the Buddha follow the same track, I preach the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*).

Formerly, a monk asked Zhaozhou, "The myriad dharmas return to the One; where does the One return? Zhaozhou said: [He pointed to his staff. (Note: The original text implies the famous response involving the staff.)
"I say that in Qingzhou I made a hempen shirt weighing seven *jin*. Xuedou’s verse comments: "He has thoroughly tested the ancient master;
how many people know the weight of the seven-*jin* shirt? Now it is cast into West Lake; who shall receive this gift of pure breeze?
Furthermore, a monk asked an ancient worthy: "In the deep mountains, on a precipitous cliff, utterly remote and devoid of [disturbance]..."
"Is there Buddha-dharma in a human dwelling or not? An ancient worthy said, "There is. A monk asked, "What is the Buddha-dharma in the deep mountains?
The ancient worthy said, "The stones are large where they are large and small where they are small.
Now tell me, is there Buddha-dharma to be discussed here? If you say there is Buddha-dharma, he never once spoke of mind or nature.
The profound explanation is as wondrous as the Way; though the intent of the Buddha-dharma may seem remote, it has never failed you.
Only when you clearly understand this meaning will you know that you have "loaded down the pure breeze."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
“Kāśyapa, Krakucchanda, and Kanakamuni—these four, including myself, I have taught as my sons.”
The messenger said: "The first honored one of the present Bhadrakalpa is Krakucchanda Buddha, which means 'He Who Should Be Severed.
The second honored one is Kanakamuni, which means 'Golden Silence. The third honored one is Kāśyapa, which means 'Drinker of Light.
The verse spoken by Krakucchanda when teaching the Dharma says: 'To see that the body has no reality is to realize the Buddha-body.'"
The mind is like an illusion; this is the Buddha’s illusion. To thoroughly realize that the fundamental nature of body and mind is empty—how is such a person any different from the Buddha?

Kāśyapa spoke these verses on the Dharma: If the Buddha does not perceive a self-body, he knows he is the Buddha. If there were truly a knowing subject, then apart from that, there would be no Buddha.
The wise are able to know that the nature of sin is empty; They remain serene and unafraid of birth and death. Kāśyapa.
The Buddha spoke a verse on the Dharma, saying: "The nature of all sentient beings is pure; from the beginning they are unborn and cannot be extinguished.
This very body and mind are born of illusion; within this illusory transformation, there is neither sin nor merit.
Śākyamuni—translated here as Nengren (Capable Benevolent One)—is the fourth honored one; yet among the great assembly, he frequently speaks of Kāśyapa and Krakucchanda.
"Kunāḷa, because I have attained the unobstructed wisdom of the Buddha-dharma, my names, words, bodies, and dharmas are equal;
by these four kinds of equality, I am no different from all Buddhas.
This can be spoken of as the path for sons of the Buddha, but it is difficult to explain to the common multitude. While the World-Honored One was walking with Ānanda, he saw...
Upon seeing an ancient Buddha stupa, the World-Honored One paid his respects. Ānanda asked, "Whose stupa is this?
The World-Honored One said, "This is the stupa of the Buddhas of the past. Ānanda asked, "Who were the disciples of the Buddhas of the past?
The World-Honored One said, "They were my disciples. Ānanda said, "It should be so, Baizhang."
In his youth, when he accompanied his mother to a temple to pay homage to the Buddha, he pointed to a sacred image and asked his mother, "What is this?
His mother replied, "This is the Buddha. The boy said, "His appearance is no different from that of a human being; I too shall become like him in the future.
Thus we know that Baizhang possessed the seed-nature of the Tathāgata; how could there be any doubt regarding his succession to and flourishing of the Buddha-dharma?

Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has taught—that from the night I attained supreme perfect enlightenment until the night I enter parinirvāṇa, not even a single syllable was spoken therein, nor has it been spoken, nor will it be spoken;
that which is not spoken is the Buddha’s teaching (the Wei translation says: 'The Buddha's speech is no speech')—World-Honored One, Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksaṃbuddha."
"For what reason do you say that this was not spoken by the Buddha? The Buddha said to Mahāmati: "I speak thus because of two dharmas. What are these two dharmas?
They are the dharma of self-attainment (*pratyātma-adhigama*) and the dharma that has existed from the beginning (*pūrvasthita-dharma*). These are called the two dharmas.
It is because of these two dharmas that I speak in this way. What is the dharma of self-attainment? It is that which is attained by those Tathāgatas."

I, too, have attained this, which neither increases nor decreases; it is the ultimate realm of the Dharma realized within oneself, free from verbal conceptualization and free from the two paths of words (the Tang translation says:
"attained through realized wisdom, free from the marks of speech, free from the marks of discrimination, and free from the marks of names").

Tong said: "The previous statement that the Buddha's awareness is no different from that of all Buddhas—that which is called 'awakening to all Buddha-dharmas'—can indeed be indicated through verbal expression.
However, as for the characteristic of the joy attained through personal realization, it can only be known by oneself and cannot be expressed in words;
therefore, Mahāmati again raised the point that during the forty-nine years [of his teaching], the World-Honored One never spoke of it."
This single word is the path that transcends all; it is beyond the reach of verbal expression. Not speaking is itself the Buddha’s teaching, and the Buddha’s teaching is precisely this non-speaking.
As it was with the Buddhas of the past, so it shall be with the Buddhas of the future. Based on what meaning is such a statement made?
It is because the Buddha [realizes] both the Dharma attained through conditions and the primordially abiding Dharma—neither of these two can be contained within words.
This is because it is spoken of as such. How does one realize the Dharma through self-attainment?

If that Tathāgata recognizes his own fundamental mind and perceives his own original nature, he attains realization within unsurpassed Bodhi; I too have attained realization from within this, without increase or decrease.
Because not a single dharma can be apprehended, there is neither increase nor decrease. If there were anything that could be increased or decreased, then...

There is that which can be spoken of as being simply without increase or decrease; this is the ultimate realm of the Dharma attained by oneself, which is free from the characteristics of verbal expression and cannot be explained through the conceptualization of sound, nor can it be explained through the conceptualization of the absence of sound.
Being free from these two extremes, it can only be known and understood by oneself. Because this is the Dharma attained through its own conditions, it is not [otherwise].
Regarding this, Yunmen said, "The Buddha-dharma is most certainly present; it is simply that the tongue is too short. He then added, "It is also long.
Tiantong took up this point and said, "Although Master Yunmen thus raises himself up and topples himself down, his cart does not run crosswise, and his reasoning is without deviation or break.
Furthermore, Chan Master Lingguan of Wushan said, "If you say, 'I am not saying anything,' [you have already spoken]."
"I would rather have my mouth gagged than speak of my Way; I would rather have my tongue shaved bald than utter it. Juefan said:

"The Buddha-dharma is vast indeed, yet it is simply a toothache. When the venerable masters attain the noble wisdom of self-awakening, they experience such sublime bliss that they are like a mute eating bitter melon—unable to describe it to others.
Thus one knows that the Tathāgata has a 'speaking that is not speaking.'"
What is the primordially abiding dharma? It refers to the ancient path of the sages, such as the intrinsic nature of gold, silver, and so forth, which is eternally present within the *dharmadhātu*.
Whether a Tathāgata appears in the world or does not appear, the *dharmadhātu* remains eternally present, like the road leading to that city.
For example, it is like a man traveling through a wilderness who sees the level, direct road leading toward an old city; he then follows it and enters the city to enjoy his heart’s desire.

"Joy" (translated in the Tang dynasty as 'the nature of phenomena is like gold in its ore'; whether a Buddha appears in the world or not, the dharma abides in its station, and the dharma-realm and the dharma-nature are eternally constant).

For example, it is like a person traveling through a vast wilderness who sees an old city and its level, ancient road, and immediately follows it in to rest and enjoy themselves. "Mahāmati, what do you think? Did that person create this road and the various pleasures within the city?
He replied, "No. (The Wei translation says: "Did that person first create this road and follow it into the city? Did he first create all those various adornments? The Buddha said:
"Mahāmati, it is likewise with the eternal abiding of the dharma-realm (dharmadhātu) realized by myself and all past Buddhas.

Therefore, it is said: 'From the night I attained supreme perfect enlightenment until the night I enter parinirvāṇa, in the interval between these two, I have not uttered a single word, nor have I spoken, nor shall I speak.'"
He spoke thus.

[The Master] replied: "How can the primordially abiding dharma (*mūlasthita-dharma*) not admit of being spoken? It is said that the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is primordially and eternally abiding;

that which is called 'all phenomena from the very beginning are eternally of the mark of quiescence'—this is the abiding of phenomena in their own station (*dharma-sthiti*), the characteristic of the world."
It is eternally abiding, just as gold exists within ore; it does not increase when in the ore, nor does it decrease when extracted from the ore—this is the nature of gold and silver.
Therefore, whether a Buddha appears or not, it neither increases nor decreases; this is the nature of the *dharmadhātu*.
That the *dharmadhātu* is eternally abiding, neither increasing nor decreasing, is the level path traversed by all the sages. Those who follow this path...
One immediately ascends to the other shore and experiences the bliss of *yathābhilaṣita* (as desired); this is due solely to this Path, and not due to initial effort.

Furthermore, the various enjoyments experienced upon entering the city are not produced by initial effort, because they are unconditioned (*anabhisaṃskṛta*). Since there is nothing that can be said to have been created from the beginning, the Great Path is level and its enjoyment is sovereign;
it has been thus since antiquity and does not depend on the present day, being the domain of myself and all Buddhas.
The realization of the eternally abiding *dharmatā* of *tathatā* is likewise so; it exists solely as a matter of personal practice, known through one's own silent resonance.
Since that which is self-attained is identical to the primordially abiding Dharma, neither can be described in words.
Therefore, from beginning to end, not a single word was spoken. A monk asked Chan Master Chonghui of Mount Tianzhu: "Before Bodhidharma came to this land..."
"Is there still the Buddha-dharma in the soil? The Master said, "Setting aside for a moment what is yet to come, how is it with the matter right now?
The monk said, "I do not understand; I beg the Master for instruction. The Master said, "Ten thousand ages of eternal sky, a single day of wind and moon.
The monk was silent. The Master spoke again, "Do you understand, *ācārya*? The monk said, "I do not understand. The Master said, "It is within your own portion."
"What is this? What does it matter whether that Dharma came or did not come? His coming here is much like a fortune-teller;

seeing that you do not understand, he has pierced through the lines for you. As soon as the divination arises, good and bad fortune are entirely within your own sphere—observe all of this for yourself.
A monk asked, "What is one who understands the divination? The Master said, "You."
[The student] said: "As soon as one steps out the door, one does not hit the mark. He asked: "What is the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū? The Master said:
"Throughout vast kalpas, he has never been obstructed or stagnant. If he is not the Buddha Mahābhijñājñānābhibhū, what is he? [The student] asked:
"Why do the Buddhadharma not manifest before me? The Master said: "It is precisely because you do not understand that they do not manifest."
"If you were to go and meet him face-to-face, there would likewise be no Buddha to be realized. The questioner asked, "What have the sages of antiquity said about this?
The Master replied, "What words do you see me uttering right now? Master Guanhui’s various discourses are very much like this commentary on the meaning.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
From the night I attained enlightenment until the night of my parinirvāṇa, throughout this interval, I have not spoken a single word.
Because the Dharma realized within myself abides eternally, I say this: there is no difference whatsoever between those Buddhas and me.
Tong said: "As for what was previously stated regarding words, phrases, bodies, and dharmas—these have never been without explanation.
That which can be explained is simply the awakening to all Buddha-dharmas. As for the mark of the joy attained through one's own conditions, there is no place to open one's mouth.
Therefore, from the beginning at the attainment of enlightenment until the end at *nirvāṇa*, not a single word was spoken in the interval between these two."

The fundamental abiding reality (dharmatā) is inherently quiescent and inherently eternally present. Those who attain this Dharma transcend the characteristics of speech and the characteristics of written words;
because it cannot be reached by verbal expression, there is ultimately nothing to be said. This supreme path admits no verbal discourse;
I and all Buddhas are entirely without distinction, neither having spoken in the past nor speaking in the future.
Because it is said that what is not spoken is the Buddha’s teaching. A monk asked Chan Master Guangdeyi: "An ancient said, 'The path of words is cut off;
it is neither past, future, nor present. What is the meaning of this principle? De replied:
"How many kalpas have passed since Maitreya entered nirvana, yet Huiming has still not descended to Kapilavastu? Danxia’s verse says: "Mysterious, limpid, perfect, and bright—this is the foremost."

When the Sage descended from the heavens, attained enlightenment, and entered nirvana—at Kapilavastu, Magadha, and beneath the twin śāla trees—recognize that from the beginning these were not those places at all.
Do you know the Way of the Forest and Spring? It is where the path of speech is cut off, a place neither past, future, nor present.
In this single hall, the wind is cool and still; through the ages, the meaning remains clear.

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again requested of the World-Honored One: "I pray that you will explain for me the characteristics of existence and non-existence regarding all dharmas, so that I and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas may depart from the characteristics of existence and non-existence and swiftly attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall now explain it for you."
You said that Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: "Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati:

"In this world there are two kinds of reliance, namely reliance on existence and reliance on non-existence. These fall into the views of the nature of things and the non-nature of things, wherein one does not leave behind the perception of [existence] while yet entertaining the notion of having left it behind" (the Wei translation says:
"Because one sees the existence of all dharmas and sees the non-existence of all dharmas, one gives rise to the notion of ultimacy regarding dharmas that are not ultimate").

Tong said: "Because you previously stated that the Buddhas of the past are 'me,' it seems as though there is a mark; yet because you also stated that not a single word was spoken, it seems as though there is no mark.
One must depart from these two marks of existence and non-existence to attain unsurpassed bodhi;

therefore, I pray that the World-Honored One will explain this in detail. As the *Vimalakīrti-nirdeśa-sūtra* says: "The original limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) cannot be apprehended, for both saṃsāra and nirvāṇa [are ungraspable]."

Since the original state is equal and detached from both existence and non-existence, those worldly beings who rely on existence to give rise to views do not emerge from the phenomena of birth and death;
those who rely on non-existence to give rise to views do not emerge from the phenomena of nirvana.

To fall into existence means to hold that this nature truly exists—this is certainly a view born of desire. To fall into non-existence means to hold that what once existed has returned to nothingness, and that everything is non-existent.
By nature, those who hold the view that there is existence (*bhava*) are certainly unable to transcend birth and death;
likewise, those who hold the view that there is non-existence (*vibhava*) are also unable to transcend birth and death.

To falsely claim transcendence regarding what is fundamentally not an ultimate dharma, while conceiving it to be ultimate—this need not be discussed for those who fall into the view of existence, but for those who fall into the view of non-existence, it is a grave error.
This requires discernment. The *Mahāprajñāpāramitā-śāstra* states: "If one enters the Abhidharma without the skillful means of Prajñā, one falls into the view of existence;
if one enters emptiness [without it], one falls into the view of non-existence. Thus, by holding to the True Dharma with inverted attachment, one instead becomes a person of heterodox views.
Since there are indeed those who study the Buddha-dharma yet develop the views of external paths, how can one not discern this deeply? Baizhang said: "Mañjuśrī is..."
The Seventh Buddha, the Patriarch-Teacher, also said that this foremost Bodhisattva of the Sahā world, without cause, conceived the notion of seeing a Buddha and the notion of questioning the Dharma;
because of the Buddha’s awesome spiritual power, he was cast down to the two Iron Ring Mountains.
This was not due to a lack of understanding, but was specifically intended to serve as a model for all students, so that future learners would not act likewise.

To see and hear in this way—merely being free from all dharmas such as existence and non-existence, and all views such as existence and non-existence—and for each and every thing to pass beyond the three propositions:
this is called the Wish-Fulfilling Jewel; this is called the Precious Flower Supporting the Feet.

If one forms a view of Buddha or a view of Dharma, it is merely a view of existence and non-existence; it is called a cataract of the eye, for that which is seen is [merely] what is perceived. Thus it is said.

What is called the entanglement of views (*dṛṣṭi-saṃyojana*), what is called the hindrance of views (*dṛṣṭy-āvaraṇa*), and what is called the thicket of views (*dṛṣṭi-gahana*)—if, right now, every thought-moment, as well as all seeing, hearing, perceiving, and cognizing, along with all defilements, were completely eliminated; if every single particle and every single color were entirely the Buddha;
and if the arising of a single thought were entirely the Buddha—then who could know the five aggregates (*skandha*) of the three periods of time, moment by moment?
This number is called "Buddhas filling the void"; these are called "emanated Buddhas" and "jewel stupas.
One must see them exactly as Bai Zhang described for it to be called the ultimate Dharma.
Mahāmati, what is meant by the world depending on existence? It means that the world arises from causes and conditions;

it is not non-existent. From existence there is birth, not from non-existence. (The Tang translation says: "It means that all dharmas arise from causes and conditions; they are truly not non-existent.
