Truly existent dharmas arise from causes and conditions; it is not that non-existent dharmas arise.
Mahāmati, one who speaks in such a manner is speaking of the world as being without cause.
Tong said: "If one realizes that all worldly dharmas are fundamentally unborn from the beginning, then although they appear to exist, they do not truly exist;

this is called 'wondrous existence' (*prabhāsvara-bhāva*). While they never fail to arise through the conjunction of causes and conditions, because those very causes and conditions are themselves not causes and conditions, one does not cling to their existence.
If, however, those in the world rely on views of existence, they claim that things truly arise from causes and conditions."
All phenomena do not arise without causes and conditions; truly, there are phenomena that arise from causes and conditions, and it is not the case that there are no phenomena.
Those who speak in such a manner claim that the world has a real cause of production, yet I consider this to be a doctrine of causelessness.

It is like the false calculations of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), who take a creator—such as *pradhāna* (primordial matter), the four great elements, time, or other such things—to be the cause of production.
The combination of atoms, the *īśvara* (Lord), and so forth are taken as the fundamental nature of the arising of phenomena;
however, these factors are that which is produced (*kṛta*) rather than that which produces (*kartṛ*), and that which is born (*janya*) rather than that which gives birth (*janaka*).

Since they are fundamentally incapable of producing anything yet are falsely considered causes of production, they are in fact causeless. How could there be anything in the world that arises without a cause? Therefore, one should know this.
The world reckons what is not a cause to be a cause; this is to reckon what does not exist to be existent. One who falls into the view of existence is truly deluded.
The Vinaya Master Faming said to Dazhu, "In the houses of Chan masters, many fall into emptiness. Dazhu replied, "It is all the scholars who fall into emptiness.
Faming was greatly startled and asked, "How can you fall into emptiness? Dazhu said, "The sutras and commentaries are merely paper."
Master Ming said, "Those who rely on written characters all establish names, phrases, and other dharmas upon sounds;
since these are all empty constructs, does the Head Seat not fall into emptiness by clinging to the substance of the teaching? Master Zhu replied, "I do not fall into emptiness.
Master Ming asked, "How is it that you do not fall into emptiness? Master Zhu replied, "Written characters and the like are all..."
When great function manifests from wisdom, how could it fall into emptiness? To know this is to know that for those who rely on existence, there is no cause.

Mahāmati, why do those in the world rely on non-existence? It is because they first experience the nature of greed, anger, and delusion, and only thereafter engage in false conceptualization and attachment.

"Mahāmati, the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion is neither existence nor non-existence. If one does not grasp at the existence of a nature, then the characteristics of that nature are quiescent (the Wei translation says:

'there are no dharmas, because the characteristics of all things are not perceived'). Mahāmati, this means that the Tathāgatas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas do not grasp the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion as being either existent or non-existent.
Mahāmati, what herein constitutes a 'destroyer'? Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One..."
"Venerable One, if one were to grasp the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion and subsequently not grasp [them as] the Buddha," the Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Excellent, excellent!
It is well that you understand it thus. Mahāmati, it is not only the nature or non-nature of greed, hatred, and delusion that is destroyed;
this is also the destruction of the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and even the Buddhas. Why is this? Because both the internal and external are unobtainable. Regarding affliction...
Because the nature of affliction is neither different nor non-different, Mahāmati, greed, anger, and delusion—whether internal or external—cannot be apprehended.
Since the nature of greed, anger, and delusion is without body and without grasping, they are not destroyers; for Buddhas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas are liberated by their very nature.
Since both bondage and the cause of bondage lack intrinsic nature, Mahāmati, if there were any who were bound...
"Mahāmati, that which ought to be bound is the cause of bondage; thus it is said that 'destruction' is characterized by non-existence. [The interlocutor] replied:

"What is meant by those in the world who rely on the view of non-existence? It means that they perceive the nature of greed, anger, and delusion, and knowing that they create various karmas, they realize they cannot escape suffering.
Consequently, they desire to sever that nature of greed, anger, and delusion, as well as their false conceptualizations."

To conceptually discriminate and cling to existence and then its subsequent non-existence, taking all things as empty to be *nirvāṇa*—this is first to accept [existence] and later to sever it; seeing the marks of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) as something to be countered is not the dharma of true tranquility. If one does not grasp at the various marks of worldly existence, one will not see that the natures of greed, hatred, and delusion can be grasped. Thus, [it is said]: "If there is no grasping, there is no nature of greed, hatred, and delusion. This is called *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, the Buddha taught that there are two kinds of *nirvāṇa*: first, the *nirvāṇa* with remainder (*sopadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), which is the cessation of the afflictions (*kleśa*) while the body remains; second, the *nirvāṇa* without remainder (*nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*), which is the cessation of both the afflictions and the body. These are called the two kinds of *nirvāṇa*. Moreover, the Buddha taught that there are three kinds of *nirvāṇa*: first, the *nirvāṇa* of the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā-nirvāṇa*), which is the emptiness of all dharmas; second, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of suffering (*duḥkhanirodha-nirvāṇa*), which is the cessation of the five aggregates (*skandha*) through the exhaustion of karma and afflictions; third, the *nirvāṇa* of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-nirvāṇa*), which is the cessation of all conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). These are called the three kinds of *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, the Buddha taught that there are four kinds of *nirvāṇa*: first, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of the outflows (*āsravakṣaya-nirvāṇa*); second, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of birth and death (*jātimaraṇa-nirvāṇa*); third, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma-nirvāṇa*); fourth, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛtadharma-nirvāṇa*). These are called the four kinds of *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, the Buddha taught that there are five kinds of *nirvāṇa*: first, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of the view of self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*); second, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of the view of sentient beings (*sattva-dṛṣṭi*); third, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of the view of life (*jīva-dṛṣṭi*); fourth, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of the view of person (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*); fifth, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of all views (*sarvadṛṣṭi-nirvāṇa*). These are called the five kinds of *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, the Buddha taught that there are six kinds of *nirvāṇa*: first, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*); second, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of the form realm (*rūpadhātu*); third, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*); fourth, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of the world of transmigration (*saṃsāraloka*); fifth, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of the world of peace (*śāntaloka*); sixth, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of all worlds (*sarvaloka-nirvāṇa*). These are called the six kinds of *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, the Buddha taught that there are seven kinds of *nirvāṇa*: first, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of the view of permanence (*nitya-dṛṣṭi*); second, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*); third, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of the view of existence (*bhava-dṛṣṭi*); fourth, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of the view of non-existence (*vibhava-dṛṣṭi*); fifth, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of the view of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*); sixth, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of the view of what belongs to self (*ātmīya-dṛṣṭi*); seventh, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of all views (*sarvadṛṣṭi-nirvāṇa*). These are called the seven kinds of *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, the Buddha taught that there are eight kinds of *nirvāṇa*: first, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of the view of a self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*); second, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of the view of a sentient being (*sattva-dṛṣṭi*); third, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of the view of a life-force (*jīva-dṛṣṭi*); fourth, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of the view of a person (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*); fifth, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of the view of permanence (*nitya-dṛṣṭi*); sixth, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*); seventh, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of the view of existence (*bhava-dṛṣṭi*); eighth, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of the view of non-existence (*vibhava-dṛṣṭi*). These are called the eight kinds of *nirvāṇa*. Furthermore, the Buddha taught that there are nine kinds of *nirvāṇa*: first, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of the view of a self (*ātman-dṛṣṭi*); second, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of the view of a sentient being (*sattva-dṛṣṭi*); third, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of the view of a life-force (*jīva-dṛṣṭi*); fourth, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of the view of a person (*pudgala-dṛṣṭi*); fifth, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of the view of permanence (*nitya-dṛṣṭi*); sixth, the *nirvāṇa* of the cessation of the view of annihilation (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*); seventh, the
One does not perceive the nature of greed, anger, and delusion as something that can be severed, for their characteristic is suchness, which is inherently quiescent from the very beginning.
Therefore, this dharma of quiescence is not something that can be attained by any ordinary, ignorant person;
it is only the Tathāgatas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas who do not grasp at the nature of worldly greed, anger, and delusion, and because they do not grasp at them, they see that these do exist.
Now, since [the nature] does not exist [as a substantial entity], where could one see its non-existence?

This refers to the fact that the nature of the sages of the Three Vehicles is free from greed, hatred, and delusion; it does not mean that something which previously existed later becomes non-existent.

Nevertheless, the principle of primordial quiescence is fundamentally and abruptly distinct from the nihilistic views of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas); therefore, these two must be distinguished. Thus, Mahāmati, why do you ask?
To "destroy great wisdom" means that one first grasps at desire and so forth, and subsequently no longer grasps at them; this is called "destruction.

Since one first perceives their existence through grasping and later perceives their non-existence through non-grasping, such a person intends to destroy all that exists, and there would be nothing they would not destroy.
Therefore, the Buddha said that such a person does not merely refrain from grasping at desire.
If one holds that the nature of delusion and so forth exists first and then ceases to exist, this constitutes annihilationism;

even the dharmas of non-arising and non-ceasing realized by the noble ones of the three vehicles would likewise be subject to annihilationism, ultimately resulting in the total disappearance of the very names of the three vehicles.
This is because they do not understand that what is realized by the noble ones of the three vehicles is not annihilationism.
What is meant by this? It is because greed, anger, and delusion—both internally within the body and mind and externally as worldly defilements—are entirely unfindable.
Thus, the nature of greed, anger, and delusion is itself affliction (*kleśa*), and the nature of these afflictions is itself awakening (*bodhi*).
This is because ice and water are neither different nor not different. If the nature of greed, anger, and delusion were not present within the internal body...
It cannot be apprehended even within external phenomena, because the nature of greed, hatred, and delusion is fundamentally without substance.
Since it lacks substantiality, there is nothing to be grasped; since there is nothing to be grasped, there is nothing to be destroyed.
Thus, when the Tathāgatas, Śrāvakas, and Pratyekabuddhas awaken to this, they see only that all phenomena are quiescent and fundamentally without anything to be grasped.

One opposes greed, anger, and delusion with the intent to destroy them. Since the noble ones of the Three Vehicles are not destroyers [of these afflictions], how can they be free from greed, anger, and delusion?
Because the *tathatā* (suchness) realized by the noble ones of the Three Vehicles is inherently liberated by its very nature, mind and objects do not encounter one another;
there is liberation right where they arise, and nothing is perceived externally as existing.
Those who are bound do not perceive the cause of bondage within themselves; for both the bondage and its cause are fundamentally non-existent.
Afflictions constitute bondage, yet the nature of afflictions is itself empty. Ignorance is the cause of bondage, yet the nature of ignorance is itself empty.
Since both bondage and its cause are empty, how could one not be liberated? If one perceives the existence of craving...
If the nature of hatred and delusion constitutes bondage, there would have to be five abiding afflictions as the cause of that bondage;

one who wishes to sever such bondage must necessarily sever its cause. Since these bonds of view and their causes possess an existent nature, and because one does not realize whether the nature of the afflictions is different or non-different [from them], one seeks to sever and destroy each one individually, regarding them as non-existent. This is—
That which is fundamentally non-existent is falsely conceptualized as existent; that which is fundamentally non-nonexistent is falsely conceptualized as nonexistent.
To speak thus of "destruction" is to be like a withered sprout or a rotten seed—one who severs the Buddha-nature. This is called the mark of universal non-existence;
it is the worldly person who, relying on the view of nonexistence, grasps at the mark of nothingness. Thus the monk questioned Dazhu.
"How does one obtain the pearl of Great Nirvāṇa? "By not creating the karma of birth and death. "What is the karma of birth and death?
"The seeking of Great Nirvāṇa is the karma of birth and death. Abandoning defilement to grasp purity is the karma of birth and death.
Having attainment and realization is the karma of birth and death. Not being liberated from the gate of antidotes is the karma of birth and death. "What about..."
"How can one immediately attain liberation? He replied: "The pearl is fundamentally without bondage; there is no need to seek its release.
Simply act directly and proceed straightforwardly—this is 'equality with the unequaled. To know this is to know that relying on 'non-existence' is not true nirvana."

For this reason, Mahāmati, I say that it would be better to hold the view of a personal self as large as Mount Sumeru than to give rise to the view of emptiness based on the overweening pride of non-existence.
Mahāmati, this "overweening pride of non-existence" refers to falling into the views of self-characteristics and common characteristics;

it is the failure to understand that all things are merely manifestations of one's own mind (the Tang translation says: "falling into the midst of desires for self and common views, failing to realize that all dharmas are manifested by the mind alone").

To perceive that external natures are impermanent, undergoing moment-to-moment destruction, and that the continuity of the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases flows on and undergoes transformation and cessation—
free from the characteristics of words and conceptualization— is what is called "the destroyer."

Tong said: "The Tang dynasty master said: 'If one explains according to this profound meaning (sandhyābhāṣya), it would be better to give rise to a view of self as large as Mount Sumeru than to give rise to a view of emptiness while harboring overweening pride (adhimāna).

For those who perceive that all things are non-existent and see only a single emptiness—wherein no worldly phenomenon can surpass it—they are already arrogant. Upon hearing of true emptiness (śūnyatā), they are further startled.'"

To claim that the teaching of non-emptiness is inherently quiescent from the outset and that one may simply cast off one's robes and depart without relying on spiritual effort—this is what is called "overweening pride" (*adhimāna*).
Such a view of emptiness is precisely as Yongjia described: "A vast, unbridled emptiness that negates cause and effect;
such reckless wandering invites calamity. Therefore, the World-Honored One spoke with intentional meaning (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*).
"It is better to give rise to the view of a self than to give rise to the view of emptiness"—this is an extreme statement regarding the impossibility of giving rise to the view of emptiness.

To sever and extinguish the view of emptiness is called "destruction"; it falls into a biased emptiness where one grasps at the mark of a nirvāṇa that can be attained, and there exists a self-nature of one who attains nirvāṇa, and for the sake of that, there is a nirvāṇa that is realized.

Their common characteristics are such that they perceive only nirvana as something desirable and seek to attain its fruit through such hope, unaware that all phenomena are manifestations of the mind alone and are inherently quiescent, needing no destruction.
Since they maintain only the view of destruction, what is there that they do not destroy? Thus, they perceive the external vessel-world as being inherently impermanent and momentary.

The continuous transformation and disintegration occurring therein means that externally there is nothing that is not empty. Furthermore, seeing internally that the faculties, the body, the aggregates (*skandha*), the elements (*dhātu*), and the sense bases (*āyatana*) all flow in succession and are subject to change and extinction, means that internally there is nothing that is not empty.
Consequently, one regards the state of being far removed from the characteristics of speech, writing, and the like, as well as from deluded conceptualization and discrimination, as being "one."
To claim that all things are utterly non-existent based on such a void is called "destruction.
Such a person merely perceives that all phenomena arise and then perish, failing to understand the meaning of their original lack of arising and ceasing.
They even seek to extinguish that which has flowed continuously from beginningless time and cannot be extinguished; thus, they destroy the lineage of the Tathāgata, which is the ultimate harm.
For this reason, the Buddha said it is better to give rise to the view of a self than to give rise to the view of emptiness.
The third discourse on "Contemplating the Mind" in the *Yongjia ji* states: "When the mind corresponds with emptiness, what anxiety or joy can there be regarding censure or praise?

When the body corresponds with emptiness, what suffering or pleasure can there be regarding being cut by a blade or smeared with fragrance? When the environment of support corresponds with emptiness, then..."

Regarding giving and plundering, what is gained and what is lost? When the mind corresponds with both emptiness and non-emptiness, attachment and views are entirely forgotten, and one universally rescues others through compassion.
When the body corresponds with both emptiness and non-emptiness, internally it is like withered wood, yet externally it manifests dignified deportment.
When the physical environment corresponds with both emptiness and non-emptiness, craving for possessions is forever severed, yet material resources are provided to sustain others.
When the mind corresponds with emptiness, non-emptiness, neither emptiness nor non-emptiness, the true mark (dharmatā) is first clarified and the Buddha’s knowledge and vision are opened.
When the body corresponds with emptiness, non-emptiness, neither emptiness nor non-emptiness, a single mote of dust enters right concentration while all motes of dust arise as samādhi.
When the environment and its support correspond with emptiness, non-emptiness, neither emptiness nor non-emptiness, [the same occurs].

Thus, the transformation-born beings in the adorned lands of fragrant terraces and jeweled pavilions must pass through each of these stages one by one before they can attain the principle of true emptiness;
how could the mere view of emptiness as non-existence constitute the ultimate?
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Existence and non-existence are the two extremes; even the realm of the mind (in the Tang translation: the sphere of mental activity). Purifying that realm, the mind of equanimity is quiescent.
Without grasping at the nature of objects, extinction is not nothingness; all things are thusness, just as the Thus-Come One is.
This is the realm of the sages.

It is generally said that if one does not grasp at the existence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) in this verse, then because the characteristics of nature are quiescent, the two extremes of existence and non-existence are like having greed and like being without greed; these are external objects which the mind perceives as existing and grasps.
To regard this as having a mind that perceives its own absence and does not grasp it as non-existent is merely the sphere of activity of the mind.

Both of these are delusions collectively termed "impurity. If one purifies these two types of spheres, one not only ceases to be attached to objective phenomena but also no longer maintains them within the mind; then this mind is neither existent nor non-existent.
Suddenly and expansively, one attains equanimity, neither forming views of existence nor views of non-existence; the single mind is profoundly still and perpetually self-extinguished.
This nature of extinction is seen as such simply by not grasping at the realms of existence and non-existence, rather than by asserting that extinction is a state of total nothingness.
If extinction were a state of total nothingness, one would fall into the view of non-existence.
When the realm of marks is realized, all that has phenomenal existence is immediately extinguished; how then could it not be called *tathatā* (suchness)?
All phenomena are entirely *tathatā*; to accord with *tathatā* is for all things to be quiescent.
Now, this nature of equanimous extinction is inherently such as it is (*tathatā*) when there is no activity, and it is likewise such as it is when there is activity.
As for the mind and its objects being thus-tathatā, tranquil and unmoving, it is not necessary to annihilate external objects before one perceives this immobility.

How could such a realm of tathatā be within the reach of ordinary beings? It is a realm spontaneously attained by sages and worthies through the arising of wisdom, a state of sublime bliss wherein, in each and every moment, there is no characteristic of arising and no characteristic of ceasing. This is the fundamental nature.
Because it is inherently unborn, one sees that it has no origin; because it is inherently unceasing, one sees that it has no end.
To be free from both existence and non-existence is what is called the quiescence of nature and characteristics. Master Puming addressed the assembly, saying:
"The mind-dharma of the Patriarchs penetrates the ten directions; it is constant throughout past and present, naturally so, just so. Such is the Dharma."
Without relying on cultivation it is spontaneously accomplished; without relying on attainment it is spontaneously perfected. All manifestations are named the "Unmoving Ground.

It is functioning yet non-existent, non-functioning yet not non-existent. Its wondrous essence is profound and still, eternally constant and unchanging. Its essence merges with its wondrous function, fully embodying the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).
It reflects and manifests boundless forms and appearances in ever-deepening layers. The mind has no self-nature; it is touched [by all things].
The reality is fully manifest within the unmoving site of enlightenment, pervading the worlds of the ten directions.

In such a realm, if one briefly turns the light back [upon itself], yet instead of awakening, turns toward the dust of sensory objects, this becomes a deluded matter like a shadow. The meaning of this is like a great royal highway:
whether one travels upon it or not, the road remains there. What has been discussed thus far is still but a teaching from the gate of transformation.
If one proclaims the essence of the vehicle (*zongsheng*), it is best to disperse at once;

if one awakens to the message of this dispersal, not only will one not be attached to the realms of existence or non-existence, but even the realm of quiescence (*śānti*) will have no place for attachment.
There is no seed, yet there is arising; having arisen, it perishes again. Existence through causes and conditions is neither existent nor non-existent; it does not abide.
My teaching is neither that of external paths, nor is it the Buddha, nor am I, nor is it anything else. How could that which arises from the collection of causes and conditions be non-existent?

Who would hold such a false view, claiming that things arise from causes and conditions and yet asserting they are non-existent? This is merely the conceptual construction of existence and non-existence regarding the nature of phenomena.

If one knows that there is neither arising nor ceasing, and contemplates this as entirely empty and quiescent, being free from both existence and non-existence—this is called the realization that those worldly people who rely on existence and non-existence fail to reach the realm of the sages and worthies.
Those heterodox teachers who claim that things arise without a cause fall into the view of existence; those who claim that what has arisen subsequently perishes fall into the view of non-existence.

Then one falls into the view of non-existence; that which is called "existence" exists in dependence upon causes and conditions, and that which is called "non-existence" does not exist in dependence upon causes and conditions.
Causes and conditions are themselves the dharma of arising and ceasing, and are not the dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing that abides within my teaching.
The quiescent characteristic of my dharma is neither created by external paths nor is it created by the Buddha.
That which is not made by me, nor made by others—these phenomena arise from conditions and these phenomena cease from conditions.
They are originally unborn and fundamentally indestructible; yet that which arises through the gathering and aggregation of causes and conditions has never been non-existent.
However, since each cause and condition lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), who is there to perform this gathering? Who is the cause of this aggregation?
If that which is produced has no basis and nothing to accumulate, then causes and conditions are empty and quiescent in their very substance;

since all phenomena are fundamentally non-existent from the start, why must one further say they are "non-existent"? Therefore, know that those who speak of existence merely argue for the absence of causal production, yet this is inherently a false view;
as for those who claim that what exists returns to non-existence, they falsely calculate that everything undergoes total annihilation.
This also belongs to deluded conceptualization, arising precisely because you do not understand the subtle nature of my teaching—that all things are neither born nor extinguished.

Had you known that all phenomena are merely manifestations of the mind, fundamentally unborn and likewise unextinguished, then with birth and extinction absent, quiescent cessation would have been manifest before you.
By contemplating this self-nature and its own characteristics, which are fundamentally empty and still, there is nothing [to be grasped].
Matters are thus, and the objective realm is likewise; it is eternally suchness (*tathatā*), serene and unmoving.
From where could the dualistic views of existence and non-existence arise? By departing from both existence and non-existence, one swiftly attains unsurpassed *bodhi*.

This is the domain of the noble ones (*ārya*); how could it be something that outsiders (*bāhya*) would dare to hope for? Formerly, the Seventh Patriarch, the Venerable Vasumitra, transmitted [the Dharma]...
The Dharma-Buddha Nandimitra then spoke this verse: "The mind is identical to the realm of empty space; It manifests dharmas equal to empty space.
When one realizes empty space, There is neither 'is' nor 'is not'; At that moment, one enters the Samādhi of Compassionate Mind.
Then Brahmā, Śakra, and the hosts of devas all came together to pay homage and spoke this verse: "Ancestor of the sages of the Bhadrakalpa."
Then the Venerable of the seventh position, out of compassion for me, requested, "Please explain the Buddha-ground.
Rising from samādhi, the Venerable addressed the assembly, saying: "The Dharma I have attained is not existent; if one realizes the Buddha-ground, it is free from both existence and non-existence.
Having spoken, he returned to samādhi and manifested the signs of nirvāṇa. This is because it is detached from both existence and non-existence.
This is the Unsurpassed Mind-Seal (*anuttara-cittamudrā*).

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I only pray that you will explain for me and for all bodhisattvas the characteristics of the penetration of the fundamental principle (*siddhānta-naya*).
If the characteristics of the penetration of the fundamental principle are skillfully distinguished, I and all bodhisattvas shall thoroughly penetrate them."
“Having thoroughly understood these characteristics, one swiftly attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*, without following discursive perceptions or the various māras and external paths.
The Buddha said to Mahāmati, “Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon this; I shall speak for you.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “So be it; we shall receive your instruction. The Buddha said to Mahāmati, “All śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas...”

The Bodhisattva Awakening has two kinds of general characteristics, namely, the penetration of the ultimate meaning (*piṭaka-yukti*) and the penetration of the teaching (*deśanā-yukti*). (The Wei translation says: "The characteristics for establishing the practice of the True Dharma for myself and all bodhisattvas.

The Buddha replied: "There are two kinds of dharmas: first, the characteristic of establishing the True Dharma; second, the characteristic of explaining the establishment of the True Dharma. Mahāmati, as for the penetration of the ultimate meaning, it refers to the characteristic of supreme advancement attained through personal realization, which is free from the delusions of speech, words, and letters;
it is the stage of self-realization leading toward the outflow-free realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*). It is... [self-realization].

To be far removed from all false conceptualizations, to subdue all externalists and hordes of Māras, and to cause the radiance of the path of self-awakening to shine forth—this is called the characteristic of the penetration of the ultimate (zōngtōngxiàng). (The Wei translation says:

"Able to grasp the untainted right precepts, realizing the characteristics of the dharmas practiced across the stages, remaining apart from the false conceptualizations and observations of all externalists and the realms of all Māras, subduing all externalists and Māras, and manifesting the dharma of one's own internal realization. The Tang translation says: "Transcending all improper thoughts and perceptions, subduing Māras and externalists, and generating the light of wisdom.")
Mahāmati said: "The previous statement that 'neither arising nor ceasing, transcending both existence and non-existence' is my teaching and the school of self-nature (*svabhāva*).
If one penetrates this school of self-nature, one is able to establish the True Dharma, does not follow any deluded thoughts or false interpretations, and swiftly realizes Bodhi;
nothing is more essential than this, World-Honored One. Furthermore, regarding the "teaching of penetration" (*sūtra-vyākhyāna*), it is not only... [the Buddha] spoke thus.

"To save oneself while being able to save others" refers to the "pervasion of the source" (*zongtong*). This means that by relying on the principle of one's own self-attained superior progress, one grasps the meaning and forgets the words;
one remains far removed from speech, letters, and conceptual discrimination, such that it can only be known by oneself.
What is the characteristic of this self-attained superior progress? It is the ability to take up untainted right precepts and realize the cultivation of the various stages (*bhūmi*).
The characteristics of the Dharma refer to the three untainted trainings—namely, morality, concentration, and wisdom.

Because morality comes first, one proceeds from the tainted realm to the untainted, reaching the untainted realm. Therein, through a single moment of mental correspondence, one spontaneously attains one's own original mind;

this is called the stage of self-awakening (*svabodha-bhūmi*). One obtains partial realization of *tathatā* (suchness) and, by advancing from this point, attains the ten stages (*daśabhūmi*), which are supreme.
The characteristics of this stage of awakening (*bodhibhūmi*) are its own specific marks, which cannot be known by ordinary persons; therefore, it is said to be "attained by oneself.
There is only one reality, with no further branches or leaves; all illusory perceptions of Māras and externalists have been completely distanced.
Since one has already transcended all improper thoughts and perceptions, one is able to subdue Māras and externalists and give rise to wisdom.
This radiance of wisdom-light is precisely the *prajñā* wisdom; it is the sharp sword that subdues Māras and externalists.
Because it manifests the dharma of internal realization within one's own person through the path of self-awakening, this teacherless wisdom and spontaneous wisdom shines with brilliant light.
Just as when a fire breaks out from the earth, whatever it touches is immediately consumed by flame—what Māra or externalist would it not subdue?

This is what is called "establishing the characteristics of the True Dharma," which is precisely what is meant by the "characteristics of the penetration of the fundamental principle" (*zongtong*). After citing the anecdote of the wild fox, Huangbo then asked: "The ancients were mistaken in their response to a single phrase and fell into the body of a wild fox; how is it that today, when you respond to every turn without error, you do not fall into such a state? Baizhang said, "Come closer, and I will tell you. Huangbo stepped forward. Baizhang said: "I am telling you right now. Huangbo then bowed. Baizhang said, "If you had not bowed just now, you would have fallen into the body of a wild fox. Huangbo then prostrated himself fully and departed. This is the meaning of the "penetration of the fundamental principle. It is not that there is no practice or realization; rather, it is because one has completely severed the root of the mind that one is free from the traces of practice and realization. This is why it is called the "penetration of the fundamental principle. It is like a great king who, having ascended the throne, possesses the power to command all officials; he does not need to follow the specific instructions of each individual official. When the king issues a decree, all officials must obey. If they do not obey, they are considered rebellious. If they do obey, they are considered compliant. The Buddha-Dharma is likewise: once one has attained the Way, one possesses the power to command all dharmas. One does not need to follow the specific instructions of each dharma; when the Way is realized, all dharmas are naturally transformed. If one does not realize the Way, one is subject to the constraints of all dharmas. If one realizes the Way, one is free from the constraints of all dharmas. This is why it is called the "penetration of the fundamental principle. It is also like a great general who, having received his commission, possesses the power to command all soldiers; he does not need to follow the specific instructions of each soldier. When the general issues an order, all soldiers must obey. If they do not obey, they are considered rebellious. If they do obey, they are considered compliant. The Buddha-Dharma is likewise: once one has attained the Way, one possesses the power to command all dharmas. One does not need to follow the specific instructions of each dharma; when the Way is realized, all dharmas are naturally transformed. If one does not realize the Way, one is subject to the constraints of all dharmas. If one realizes the Way, one is free from the constraints of all dharmas. This is why it is called the "penetration of the fundamental principle. Furthermore, it is like a great physician who, having mastered the medical arts, possesses the power to command all medicines; he does not need to follow the specific instructions of each medicine. When the physician prescribes a treatment, all medicines must act according to his intent. If they do not act according to his intent, they are ineffective. If they do act according to his intent, they are effective. The Buddha-Dharma is likewise: once one has attained the Way, one possesses the power to command all dharmas. One does not need to follow the specific instructions of each dharma; when the Way is realized, all dharmas are naturally transformed. If one does not realize the Way, one is subject to the constraints of all dharmas. If one realizes the Way, one is free from the constraints of all dharmas. This is why it is called the "penetration of the fundamental principle. It is also like a great sovereign who, having established his realm, possesses the power to command all subjects; he does not need to follow the specific instructions of each subject. When the sovereign issues a mandate, all subjects must obey. If they do not obey, they are considered rebellious. If they do obey, they are considered compliant. The Buddha-Dharma is likewise: once one has attained the Way, one possesses the power to command all dharmas. One does not need to follow the specific instructions of each dharma; when the Way is realized, all dharmas are naturally transformed. If one does not realize the Way, one is subject to the constraints of all dharmas. If one realizes the Way, one is free from the constraints of all dharmas. This is why it is called the "penetration of the fundamental principle. It is also like a great master of the arts who, having perfected his craft, possesses the power to command all tools; he does not need to follow the specific instructions of each tool. When the master employs them, all tools must function according to his will. If they do not function according to his will, they are useless. If they do function according to his will, they are functional. The Buddha-Dharma is likewise: once one has attained the Way, one possesses the power to command all dharmas. One does not need to follow the specific instructions of each dharma; when the Way is realized, all dharmas are naturally transformed. If one does not realize the Way, one is subject to the constraints of all dharmas. If one realizes the Way, one is free from the constraints of all dharmas. This is why it is called the "penetration of the fundamental principle. It is also like a great leader who, having gained the people's trust, possesses the power to command all followers; he does not need to follow the specific instructions of each follower. When the leader gives a direction, all followers must comply. If they do not comply, they are considered disobedient. If they do comply, they are considered loyal. The Buddha-Dharma is likewise: once one has attained the Way, one possesses the power to command all dharmas. One does not need to follow the specific instructions of each dharma; when the Way is realized, all dharmas are naturally transformed. If one does not realize the Way, one is subject to the constraints of all dharmas. If one realizes the Way, one is free from the constraints of all dharmas. This is why it is called the "penetration of the fundamental principle. It is also like a great commander who, having been appointed to a post, possesses the power to command all troops; he does not need to follow the specific instructions of each soldier. When the commander issues an order, all troops must obey. If they do not obey, they are considered mutinous. If they do obey, they are considered disciplined. The Buddha-Dharma is likewise: once one has attained the Way, one possesses the power to command all dharmas. One does not need to follow the specific instructions of each dharma; when the Way is realized, all dharmas are naturally transformed. If one does not realize the Way, one is subject to the constraints of all dharmas. If one realizes the Way, one is free from the constraints of all dharmas. This is why it is called the "penetration of the fundamental principle. It is also like a great ruler who, having established his authority, possesses the power to command all ministers; he does not need to follow the specific instructions of each minister. When the ruler issues a decree, all ministers must obey. If they do not obey, they are considered traitorous. If they do obey, they are considered faithful. The Buddha-Dharma is likewise: once one has attained the Way, one possesses the power to command all dharmas. One does not need to follow the specific instructions of each dharma; when the Way is realized, all dharmas are naturally transformed. If one does not realize the Way, one is subject to the constraints of all dharmas. If one realizes the Way, one is free from the constraints of all dharmas. This is why it is called the "penetration of the fundamental principle. It is also like a great sage-king who, having ascended the throne, possesses the power to command all states; he does not need to follow the specific instructions of each state. When the king issues a proclamation, all states must submit. If they do not submit, they are considered rebellious. If they do submit, they are considered compliant. The Buddha-Dharma is likewise: once one has attained the Way, one possesses the power to command all dharmas. One does not need to follow the specific instructions of each dharma; when the Way is realized, all dharmas are naturally transformed. If one does not realize the Way, one is subject to the constraints of all dharmas. If one realizes the Way, one is free from the constraints of all dharmas. This is why it is called the "penetration of the fundamental principle. It is also like a great teacher who, having perfected his instruction, possesses the power to command all disciples; he does not need to follow the specific instructions of each disciple. When the teacher imparts wisdom, all disciples must understand. If they do not understand, they are considered ignorant. If they do understand, they are considered enlightened. The Buddha-Dharma is likewise: once one has attained the Way, one possesses the power to command all dharmas. One does not need to follow the specific instructions of each dharma; when the Way is realized, all dharmas are naturally transformed. If one does not realize the Way, one is subject to the constraints of all dharmas. If one realizes the Way, one is free from the constraints of all dharmas. This is why it is called the "penetration of the fundamental principle. It is also like a great master of ceremonies who, having mastered the rites, possesses the power to command all rituals;
Huangbo stepped forward and struck the Master with his palm. Baizhang clapped his hands and laughed, saying, "I thought the beard was red, yet here is a red-bearded barbarian!
Miaoyan brought up this previous story and asked Yangshan, "Huangbo constantly employs this device.
Yangshan said, "It is both innate and acquired from others. Miaoyan said, "Is it also received through the lineage of a teacher? Yangshan replied, "It is also."
Regarding this "self-seal of the school" (*zizongtong*), Guishan said, "Just so, just so. Xuefeng asked Deshan, "In the ancestral school of the Dharma-vehicle, does a student still have a share?
Deshan struck him with a staff and said, "Speak! [Xuefeng] said, "I do not understand. The next day, he requested further instruction.
Deshan said, "My school has no words or phrases; truly, there is not a single dharma to give to anyone. Because of this, Xuefeng attained realization.
When Xing heard of this, he remarked, "The old man Deshan has a backbone as hard as iron that cannot be bent;
nevertheless, even so, he still falls short by a little in the gate of proclaiming the Teaching.
The two preceding cases illustrate the manner of *zongtong* (the penetration of the essence).

What is the characteristic of the penetration of teaching? It refers to the teaching of the various doctrines of the ninefold canon, which is free from characteristics such as difference and non-difference, existence and non-existence, and so forth.

By means of skillful expedients, it accords with sentient beings and teaches the Dharma as appropriate so that they may attain liberation; this is called the characteristic of the penetration of teaching.
Mahāmati, you and the other bodhisattvas should practice and study this.

The interlocutor said: "Among the ninefold and twelvefold divisions of the scriptures, these refer to the ninefold division of the Hīnayāna, which lacks the Vaipulya, the Avyākṛta (unasked self-explanations), and the Vyākaraṇa (prophecies).
As for the ninefold division of the Mahāyāna, it lacks the Nidāna (causes and conditions), the Avadāna (parables), and the Upadeśa (exegesis).
To say 'one who explains this Dharma' does not mean one who is merely skilled at lecturing upon its meaning; the essential point is to realize that [all phenomena] are originally non-existent."

It is taught that by being free from the four propositions (*catuskoṭi*)—such as non-existence, indication, difference, non-difference, existence, and non-existence—and by transcending the hundred negations (*śata-apavāda*), one is thus far removed from verbal expressions, letters, and conceptual proliferation (*vikalpa*).
Yet, through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*), one accords with sentient beings and teaches the Dharma according to their capacities;
all that is taught is the Dharma for attaining one's own superior progress, so as to cause those sentient beings to be free from all [afflictions].
Through the cessation of conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*), one realizes the true nature (*dharmatā*) and attains liberation;

by thoroughly understanding that the characteristics of arising and ceasing are empty and quiescent, one enters my teaching and attains the same realization of the single principle. This is called the "penetration of teaching" (*deśanā-praveśa*).

This penetration of teaching refers to the establishment of the characteristics of the True Dharma, wherein there is no distinction between religious schools or doctrines. It means that the realization of phenomena does not reside in words, and thus one skillfully enters the wordless state.
To be able to manifest speech like an echo throughout the world at the very moment [of realization]—this is it.
A monk asked Wuzu Yan, "What is the matter of Linji? Yan said, "The five heinous crimes heard by thunder.
The monk asked, "What is the matter of Yunmen? Yan said, "A red banner flashing. The monk asked, "What is the matter of Shitou and Yangshan? Yan said, "A broken stele."
Henggulu asked, "What is the matter concerning the Cao-Dong school? Yanyuan said, "The letter was sent, but it did not reach the house. The monk bowed;
Yanyuan said, "Why do you not ask about the matter concerning the Fa-xia school? [The monk] replied, "I leave that for the Master. Yanyuan said, "A patrolman caught at night.
These five houses of the lineage—only when one has thoroughly mastered their essential principles can it be called "mastery of the teaching" (shetong).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:

The fundamental principle (*mūla*), the teaching-vehicle (*deśanā-yāna*), the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), the conditions (*pratyaya*), the self-nature (*svabhāva*), and the teaching (*dharma*)—[the latter two] being what is called "self-realization" (*svasaṃvedana*) and "teaching" (*deśanā*) in the Tang translation—these are well-seen and well-discriminated.

They do not follow the various conceptualizations (*vikalpa*) of the awakened mind; they possess no real nature (*bhūtārtha-svabhāva*). How could the deluded thoughts of foolish people give rise to such false imaginings? Why do they give rise to such imaginings?

The nature is liberation; observing the characteristics of the arising and ceasing of all conditioned phenomena, one sees that they increase through the continuity of the two views and inverted perceptions, such that there is no knowing of anything else—this alone is the true reality, and being free from fault, it is nirvāṇa (in the Tang translation, "nirvāṇa is the departure from mind and consciousness; this single dharma alone is real").
One observes that worldly delusions are like illusions, dreams, and plantain trees; although greed, anger, and ignorance exist, in reality, there is no person.
All aggregates arising from craving and all modes of existence are like illusions and dreams.

Generally speaking, this refers to the dual illumination of both the fundamental principle (*zong*) and the teaching (*shuo*) within the prose section; it is clarified as a synthesis within the verse.

This is called the "fundamental principle" and the "characteristics of the teaching-communication," wherein one attains the Dharma through self-realization and uses it to instruct others. Being able to clearly perceive one's own nature constitutes illumination.
Furthermore, the essential purpose is to skillfully discern all dharmas so as to enable people to attain liberation.

By contemplating even a single virtuous word, one need not rely on discursive thought nor tolerate conjecture; acting in accordance with the true nature (*dharmatā*), one spontaneously attains its wondrousness.
Thus, one is not swayed by various māras or the incorrect perceptions of outsiders. The reason one does not follow such perceptions is that all which I have personally attained is...
In reality, that which is perceived by conceptualization does not possess true existence; truly, there are no external phenomena.

Since ordinary beings engage in various kinds of false imaginings and discriminations, and since these phenomena lack substantial reality and are empty and quiescent in their very essence, how could one give rise to greed, hatred, and delusion within them?
How could one perceive them as existing through conceptualization, and how could one grasp at them?
If one takes greed, hatred, and delusion—which are not of the nature of non-existence—to be liberation, and perceives them as non-existent, consider this:

all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) in the world arise and then cease; having ceased, they arise again. This succession of arising and ceasing, changing and transforming one after another, is not of a true nature.
To see their arising is to take them as existent; to see their ceasing is to... [take them as non-existent].
They consider that which is unborn to be extinguished, and that which is extinguished to be born; thus, external objects increase boundlessly.
Those who rely on existence follow after objects in a state of flux, which is called "inversion" and is fundamentally ignorance.
Those who rely on non-existence are deluded regarding the tainted heavens, taking them to be unconditioned (*asamskrta*); their confused practice is likewise an inversion. These are the two views.
Perversion relies solely upon the mind and consciousness; each person holds their own views, commits various transgressions, and ultimately falls into ruin.
How could this be true nirvana? Nirvana is singular and unique: it consists in being far removed from the mind and consciousness, not forming the two views of existence and non-existence.
Because this one dharma alone is real, it is called the True Truth (*satya*). To realize the True Truth is—

To be free from the karmic obstacles of birth and death is true *nirvāṇa*. Having realized this reality and abiding in the state of suchness, one observes that all worldly deluded thoughts and discriminations are like illusions and dreams, like plantain trees—lacking any true reality.

The metaphors of illusion and dream represent the mind-consciousness and the four aggregates; the metaphor of the plantain tree represents the aggregate of form; both are ultimately without substance.
Once one can realize that this body and mind are not substantial, the grasping at a self is suddenly emptied;

even if the natures of greed, anger, and delusion persist, there is in fact no agent and no experiencer. When both mind and object vanish, the wisdom of the emptiness of persons is attained, and from where could views possibly arise?
Furthermore, these aggregates have, since beginningless time, been rooted in craving, which gives rise to them all.
Because craving for the five aggregates involves arising and ceasing and lacks true reality, although the five aggregates arise, they do not exist as true reality;
they are empty and false in their very place, like an illusion or a dream, and cannot be definitively grasped as existing.
Since they cannot be grasped as existing, why need one strive to sever them so that they become non-existent? By departing from both existence and non-existence, one attains the emptiness of dharmas.
Wisdom relies upon non-existence; since greed, hatred, and delusion are neither intrinsic natures nor liberation, from what could they possibly arise?
When the two views do not arise and one is free from both perversions, this is called the establishment of the True Dharma.
To speak of this establishment of the True Dharma so that people may be without fault and together realize Nirvana is what is meant by "skillful discernment."
The "Patriarchal Transmission" (zōngtōng) and the "Teachings on Exposition" (shuōtōng) appear again later, consisting merely of four-line verses. They do not possess a real, intrinsic nature;
therefore, the following sixteen lines of verse should be read as belonging to the preceding section on "being and non-being, departing from both," for their meaning then naturally coheres.
Linji said: "Students of the Way who do not understand this are attached to names and phrases, and are thus deceived by ordinary people."
The name "holy" implies obstruction; it is because these obstructions hinder the Eye of the Path that one cannot attain clarity.

It is precisely because the twelve divisions of the teachings are all expressions of manifesting [the truth], yet students do not understand this and instead produce interpretations based solely upon the manifest names and phrases, that they remain dependent and fall within cause and effect, unable to escape the birth and death of the triple world. If you wish to be born... [into liberation].

Death, dwelling, liberation, and attachment are all free; recognize right now the person who hears the Dharma—formless, signless, rootless, baseless, and without a place of abode, yet vibrantly alive.
This is precisely the locus for the application of all manner of skillful means, yet it is itself no place.
Therefore, the more one seeks it, the further away it becomes; the more one pursues it, the more it diverges; thus it is called "the secret."
"O practitioner of the Way, do not mistake this dream-like, illusory companion; in the midst of time, it will lead you back to impermanence.
What thing can you seek within this world that constitutes liberation? Only when you see as Linji saw is it called 'good seeing' and only then is it called 'true liberation.'"
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we pray that you will explain for us the characteristics of unreal imagination (*abhūta-parikalpa*).
How does unreal imagination arise? What kind of phenomena are called unreal imagination? And within what kind of phenomena does unreal imagination arise?
(The Tang translation reads: "From what does it arise? By what cause does it arise? By whom is it produced? The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Excellent, excellent!"
"Excellent! It is well that you are able to ask the Tathāgata about such a meaning; it will be of great benefit and bring great peace and happiness to all devas and humans in the world.
Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon it well; I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Excellent, World-Honored One!
We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, "There are various meanings and various [expressions]..."
Mahāmati, from the attachment to false discrimination, discrimination arises; through attachment to the grasped and the grasper, one fails to understand that all is a manifestation of one’s own mind.
Falling into the views of existence and non-existence, one increases the views of the externalists.

Through the attachment to the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of discrimination regarding various external objects, the mind and mental factors give rise to the false discrimination of "I" and "mine. (The Tang translation states: "All sentient beings, regarding various objects, are unable to realize that they are their own mind.")

When various conceptualizations arise based on the false attachment to the manifested objects of grasped and grasper, one falls into views of existence and non-existence, thereby increasing the habitual tendencies of the false views of non-Buddhists.

When the mind and mental factors arise in association, one clings to the notion that external objects exist as variously perceivable things, and one becomes attached to a self and what belongs to a self; for this reason, it is called "false conceptualization."

Tong said: Because it was previously stated that observing worldly delusions as being like dreams, illusions, or plantain trees is the very principle of the lack of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) of delusion, the successive transmission of the former sages does not transcend this. Therefore, Mahāmati asked:
"Since these various characteristics of delusion are clearly known to be unreal, and since they are unreal, they have no root; how then [can they arise]?"
What kind of unreal phenomena do you say are called "unreal imagination"? This is the essence of ultimate imagination.
Within what kind of unreal phenomena does one grasp through imagination? This is the object of ultimate imagination.
World-Honored One, all devas and humans revolve through birth and death due to imagination.
If one knows that things are empty, false, and unreal, one immediately awakens to the principle that deluded thoughts have no inherent nature and attains peace and bliss in that very moment.
Therefore, those who can thoroughly realize this meaning derive the greatest benefit.
All the various worldly meanings that possess names and forms and seem attainable are empty, false, and unreal; it is because all sentient beings [possess] the seven consciousnesses...
By falsely imagining and clinging to various unreal phenomena, the six consciousnesses arise based on such false imaginings.
Why is it said that clinging is false? It is because those who cling perceive a grasper and a grasped;
this arises precisely from not knowing that the internal and external objects of the mind are merely manifestations of one's own mind, appearing like water.
The moon in the center cannot be grasped; yet now one calculates that there is a mind which grasps and an object which is grasped.

To falsely cling to these as real and take them to exist is to fall into the ordinary person’s view of existence (*bhāva-dṛṣṭi*); to empty them and take them to be non-existent is to fall into the two vehicles’ view of non-existence (*abhāva-dṛṣṭi*).
Furthermore, one proceeds to discriminate, thinking they both exist and do not exist, or neither exist nor do not exist.
Thus, the growth of externalist heterodox views arises from the perfuming of deluded imaginings within the field of the eight consciousnesses, forming habitual seeds that have not occurred overnight.
Clinging to external objects and various graspable mental states and mental factors, these arise in conjunction with one another;
yet they do not, in total, depart from the attachment to the sovereign mind of the eight consciousnesses.

Regarding that which is "I" and the fifty-one mental factors as "mine"—this attachment to the various external objects as being merely "I" and "mine" arises from not knowing that the nature of the external world is neither existence nor non-existence, being fundamentally unreal from the beginning.

It is by means of this [realization] that one understands the teaching on the two views of existence and non-existence; the teaching on the increase of these views is called the teaching of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas).
The essence of unreal imagination consists in the mind and mental factors; it is the attachment to "self" and "what belongs to self" that constitutes the locus of unreal imagination as its object.
Unreal imagination arises because of attachment to various external phenomena which lack inherent existence.
If one knows that what appears is merely the manifestation of one's own mind and that external natures have no reality, one immediately realizes [the truth].
Regarding this reality, Guishan asked Yangshan: "Suppose someone were to ask you:
'All sentient beings possess only a vast, wandering karmic consciousness with no fundamental basis to rely upon. How would you test them? Yangshan replied:
"If a monk comes, I would call out to him, 'Sir! When the monk turns his head, I would say, 'What is it? I would wait for him to hesitate before speaking further."
"It is not only that karmic consciousness is vast and boundless, but also that there is no fundamental basis upon which to rely. Mian said, "Excellent! Tiantong’s verse says:
"A single call turns the head back; one recognizes me. The moon through the vines is indistinct, yet already forming a hook.
A child of a thousand-fold wealth, having just fallen into ruin— On this desolate road of poverty, how much sorrow there is! Wansong asked: "For what reason do the Buddhas not [recognize it]?"

"When active wisdom reaches the realm of sentient beings, it is called the karma-consciousness; vast and boundless, one should have known that the lamp was fire long ago, for the rice has already been cooked.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, if there are various meanings and various attachments to unreal false imaginings..."

The arising of conceptualization consists of attachment to the grasped and the grasper, ignorance of the fact that [all things] are merely manifestations of one’s own mind, falling into the views of existence and non-existence, increasing the views and habitual tendencies of externalists, and being attached to various external objects through the conceptualizations of the mind and mental factors, as well as the notions of "I" and "mine.
(This section does not exist in the Tang translation. World-Honored One, if such various external characteristics of objects fall into the characteristics of existence and non-existence...

"World-Honored One, it is free from existence and non-existence, and free from the characteristics of views. The ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is likewise free from the characteristics of means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), sense organs (*indriya*), parts (*avayava*), examples (*dṛṣṭānta*), and reasons (*hetu*).
[In the Tang translation, this is rendered as 'free from all sense organs, means of knowledge, propositions, reasons, and similes.

World-Honored One, for what reason does false discrimination arise through attachment to the various natures of unreal objects in one place, rather than arising through attachment to the characteristics of the ultimate truth? Is it not so, World-Honored One?"

"Does the Blessed One teach a doctrine of false causes? (The Wei translation says 'falling into worldly discourse'; the Tang translation says 'what is said deviates from reason. You speak of one arising and one not arising. The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"It is not a deluded conception of one arising and one not arising. Why is this? It is because the deluded conception of existence and non-existence does not arise.
When one realizes that external appearances—whether as entities or non-entities—are merely the manifestation of one's own mind, the deluded conception does not arise. Mahāmati, this is what I teach."
How do foolish commoners, due to the various characteristics of their own mental constructions (*vikalpa*) regarding objects and activities appearing before them,

give rise to attachment to the nature and characteristics of these various mental constructions? How can such fools become free from the views of attachment to "self" and "mine," transcend the faults of cause,

effect, and conditions, and— realizing that all is but the measure of their own mentally constructed mind (*cittamātra*)— undergo the transformation of body and mind to attain ultimate, clear understanding of all stages (*bhūmi*)?
The Tathāgata’s realm of self-realization is free from the five dharmas, the three natures, things, views, and false imaginings.

For this reason, I say that false imaginings arise from attachment to various unreal objects; by knowing the reality as it is, one attains liberation from the various false imaginings of one's own mind.
Mahāmati said: "Because the World-Honored One has stated that unreal conceptualization arises from clinging to various unreal objects, I now quote those words of the Buddha to ask:

if these various external objective characteristics are seen as 'existent' by ordinary beings and as 'non-existent' by those of the Two Vehicles, then this state of falling into the extremes of existence and non-existence is ultimately unreal and devoid of intrinsic nature."

That which is not of an inherent nature is yet the object of false conceptualization and discrimination; such views are ultimately unreal because they are devoid of both the characteristic of being seen and the characteristic of that which is seen.

Just as various illusory phenomena are not real, so too is conceptual discrimination. If one is thus free from the characteristics of existence and non-existence, this is no different from the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
The reason why the ultimate truth differs from the conventional truth (*saṃvṛti-satya*) is that...
That which is remote from the teachings spoken by the Noble Ones in the Āgamas, remote from the various faculties and the establishment of the three means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*),
and remote from the characteristics of the five-membered syllogism— namely thesis, reason, and example— is therefore called the true ultimate truth (*paramārtha*). If external,

manifold objects and their characteristics are devoid of both existence and non-existence, and are free from the duality of subject and object such that they are no different from the ultimate truth, then...
This equality and non-duality is called the single locus, the locus of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
Since false imagination (*vikalpa*) is fundamentally unarisen, the various conceptual loci of false imagination cannot possibly arise either.

For what reason is it that while attachment to the various characteristics of objects gives rise to false imagination, attachment to the characteristics of the ultimate truth does not give rise to false imagination? World-Honored One, please...
Is it not identical to the heterodox theories of false causes, which claim that in one place there is arising while in another place there is no arising?
This doubt is most subtle: since truth and falsehood fundamentally have no dual substance, why is arising spoken of regarding the false while arising is not spoken of regarding the true?
If you cling to the realm of the false as being arising, then you must also admit arising in the realm of the true; this would cause the World-Honored One to be seen as strange.
It is not appropriate to say that delusive thoughts arise, for the World-Honored One has clearly stated this. The treatise explains that, fundamentally, delusive thoughts do not arise;
it is only for the sake of those fools who do not perceive the fundamental source that one says delusive thoughts arise.

This is intended to lead fools to realize that the fundamental source is itself originally unarisen. How could one ever say that delusive thoughts arise? Therefore, they are called the nature of delusive thoughts.
It is not that they arise in one place and do not arise in another; they are originally quiescent and fundamentally without arising or ceasing.

Why is this so? It is because those phenomena which are fundamentally non-existent yet are imagined to exist do not arise, and those phenomena which are fundamentally non-non-existent yet are imagined to be non-existent do not arise. Such is the object of that imagination.
External objects and various external meanings, though they appear to have names, marks, and natures, are in their very essence non-natures;

their substance is illusory, and one does not perceive any signs of existence or non-existence that can be grasped. One simply realizes that although all phenomena appear to possess various meanings, they are all manifestations of one's own mind, like flowers in a mirror or the moon in water—neither existent nor non-existent.
There is nothing for discrimination to find accommodation in; this is why deluded thoughts do not arise.
When deluded thoughts do not arise, where could one see their arising and call it "arising"? And where could one see their non-arising and call it "non-arising"?
Therefore, it is said that these are not deluded thoughts characterized by either arising or non-arising. This can only be understood with [the wise].
The path belongs only to those with noble wisdom who have realized for themselves;

as for other deluded ordinary people, they give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding all phenomena manifested within their own minds, whereby various marks of false imagination appear. In total, these do not depart from the activities performed before them, following the various discriminations produced by prior moments of mind.
The first five consciousnesses grasp objects, while the sixth consciousness discriminates, and the seventh [consciousness] [clings].

Because consciousness clings to the eight consciousnesses as containing a storehouse, and because each individually grasps at the appearance of marks to give rise to various false imaginings, I say that "false imaginings arise.
This is said because other ignorant people cannot awaken to the fact that these are merely the manifestations of their own minds;
thus, this fault exists. If I were not to speak of this, how could ignorant people ever become free from the false imaginings of clinging to "I" and "mine"?

To perceive and to be free from the causal conditions and faults of wholesome and unwholesome actions—the agent and the acted upon—and to give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding "self" and "what belongs to self" through the realization of things as they truly are, is the mind-measure (*citta-mātra*) of the delusive imagination of the six consciousnesses.
To be attached to "self" and "what belongs to self" is the mind-measure of the delusive imagination of the seventh consciousness. Regarding the cause of the agent and the acted upon...
That which is conditioned (*pratyaya*) refers to the mind-measure (*citta-mātra*) of the conceptualization of the five sensory consciousnesses.

That which contains the seeds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-bīja*) and constitutes the afflictions from time immemorial refers to the mind-measure of the conceptualization of the eighth consciousness.

To realize that the mind-measure of conceptualization is merely the manifestation of one's own mind, and for the body and mind to undergo transformation such that the eight consciousnesses are transmuted into the four wisdoms—this is precisely it.

While still possessing an ordinary body, one realizes the fruit of sainthood and attains ultimate, clear understanding of the stages of the ten bhūmis, reaching the realm of the Tathāgata’s self-awakening.

One becomes detached from both the five dharmas and the three natures; not only is one detached from names, marks, and false conceptualization, but one is also detached from the phenomena of cultivation and realization regarding correct wisdom and suchness.
Furthermore, one is detached not only from the false conceptualization of dependent origination and the nature of things, but [from all such dualistic attachments].
It is already so; thus, the matters of self-nature, cultivation, realization, and views are also transcended.
Not only do conceptualizations that cling to various meanings and marks cease to arise, but even conceptualizations that cling to the realm of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) do not arise.
Such a measure of mind (*cittamātra*) is the very realm of *tathatā* and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*); it is fundamentally unborn and fundamentally liberated.

It is for the sake of guiding and instructing the ignorant through these skillful means that I say: deluded conceptualization arises from the attachment to various external objects and various unrealities;
thus, one does not transcend birth and death—how then could one attain liberation?

If one awakens to the fact that it is merely the measure of one’s own deluded conceptual mind and reaches the realm of the Tathāgata’s self-realization, knowing the meaning of reality as it truly is, then one will know the truth.
When one realizes the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) through non-attainment, one immediately attains liberation from the various deluded thoughts of one's own mind.
One is no longer bound by the clinging to "self" and "what belongs to self," nor afflicted by the faults of the causal conditions of agent and action.
The various phenomenal marks appearing before one are themselves the very essence of Suchness (*tathatā*); what further deluded thought could there be? Deluded thought [is itself Suchness].

Since there is nothing at all, who could be born and who could be unborn? Therefore, when it is said that "delusive thoughts give rise [to phenomena]," it is precisely intended for sentient beings to awaken to the knowledge that delusive thoughts lack inherent nature and thus ultimately converge upon non-arising.
Linji addressed the assembly, saying: "Those today who study the Buddha-dharma must first seek a genuine insight; if one attains genuine insight..."
Having understood birth and death, one is unstained by them and possesses freedom in coming and going; without seeking excellence, excellence arrives of its own accord.

This is the flow of the Way. Just as the former worthies of antiquity all had their ways of entering and exiting—just as when I, this mountain monk, point out the way to others, I simply want you not to be deluded by others;
if you wish to use it, use it immediately without further hesitation. Now, those who study...
This illness does not reside in any particular place; it resides in a lack of self-confidence.

If you cannot trust yourself, you will immediately become lost and bewildered, following after all external objects until you are turned around by those myriad conditions and deprived of your freedom.
If you can bring to rest this mind that incessantly pursues and seeks, you will be no different from the Patriarch. You wish—
Do you recognize the Buddhas and Patriarchs? It is simply this person before you who is listening to the Dharma.
If you lack faith, you will rush outward in search; even if you were to find something, it would all be mere words and superior signs, and you would never attain their living ancestral meaning.
Do not err! Because Linji had reached the realm of the Tathāgata’s self-awakening, his words were so direct and unerring.
Thus it is.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Various causes and conditions give rise to this world; Through false imagination, one clings to the four extremes. They do not know the penetration of my teaching."
The world is neither born from existence nor is it born from non-existence; it is not born from both existence and non-existence, nor is it born from neither existence nor non-existence.

How could causes and conditions give rise to the deluded imaginings of the ignorant? Being neither existent, nor non-existent, nor both existent and non-existent—by observing the world in this way, the mind turns and attains selflessness.
The interlocutor said: "This verse explains the meaning of the transformation of the body and mind through the mental measure (*cittamātra*) of one's own deluded thoughts;

while the prose seems brief, the verse elaborates upon it. When I say that all phenomena arise from causes and conditions to produce the various worlds, my intention is to reveal that all dharmas are fundamentally unarisen;
yet foolish people do not understand this and, instead, rely on causes and conditions to cling to the four logical extremes."
This deluded conceptualization does not understand the meaning of what I have realized.

The meaning of what I have realized is that all worldly phenomena do not arise from existence, nor do they arise from non-existence, nor do they arise from both existence and non-existence together, nor do they arise apart from both existence and non-existence.
Causes and conditions are fundamentally unarisen; worldly phenomena are thus by nature.

How is it that fools, departing from the four propositions, rely on various causes and conditions to engage in false conceptualization and discrimination, thereby falling into views of existence and non-existence?
They do not know that the various natures of this world are fundamentally neither existent nor non-existent, and furthermore, neither neither-existent-nor-non-existent.
