If one can contemplate the dharmas of the world in this way, one will see that they are fundamentally unarisen.
Since delusion has no basis upon which to be established, the mind is not turned by objects, but rather it is able to turn toward them.

When one does not rely on delusion but relies on the truth, and is free from attachment to "I" and "mine," then body and mind undergo transformation, realizing the two forms of selflessness (*nairātmya*).
Transcending the four propositions and cutting off the hundred negations, one attains liberation without departing from the world.

This is the meaning of my doctrine of liberation. Huangbo said: "Being of one and the same rank in study, you must simply be without learning, without ordinary or sage, without purity or defilement, without great or small, without outflows, and without conditioned action.
In this single mind, through skillful means, diligently adorn yourself. Even if you manage to learn the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings, there is still [something more]."
One must completely relinquish all views and interpretations; therefore, having removed everything else, one remains with only a single bed, lying down ill.

This is simply to not give rise to any views, so that not a single dharma can be grasped, one is not obstructed by dharmas, and one penetrates and transcends the realms of both the mundane and the sagely.
Only then can one be called a world-transcending Buddha. Thus it is said: "I prostrate to the Tathāgata..."
Emptiness has no basis and transcends the heterodox paths. Mind is not different from dharmas, nor are dharmas different from mind.
Since mind is unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), dharmas are also unconditioned. All phenomena arise through the transformation of the mind; therefore, because my mind is empty, all dharmas are empty.

The myriad things of a thousand categories are entirely identical, and throughout the empty realms of the ten directions, they share the same single essence of mind. This is the fundamental nature of the mind.
It is not that the Dharma is different, nor is it otherwise; it is simply because your understanding and views differ that you perceive it as such.
Huangbo has indeed attained the wondrous state where body and mind are transformed, and thus his speech naturally stands apart.
All natures are unborn because they arise from conditions; all that is produced by conditions is a product, not an entity existing of itself.
An entity does not arise from itself, for there would be the fault of two entities, whereas there is no such fault of two entities. No existent nature can be apprehended.
I teach that the mind-measure (*cittamātra*)—which observes all conditioned phenomena as being free from the grasper and the grasped—is the mind-measure that is no-mind.

"Measurement" (*pramāṇa*) refers to that which is ultimately and wondrously pure, being free from both self-nature (*svabhāva*) and the nature of objects and conditions; this I call "mind-only" (*cittamātra*).

It is said in response: This verse expresses the principle that the appearance of external objects—whether as existent or non-existent—is the realization that they are merely the manifestation of one's own mind.
Following the preceding statement that all causes and conditions give rise to the world and its karma, why is it so called?
Non-arising: because the nature of all phenomena is fundamentally unarisen, they arise only from conditions; thus, arising is merely the arising from conditions and not self-arising.
Action is merely the action of conditions and not self-action, for everything is produced by conditions.
That which exists in dependence upon conditions is not something produced that possesses an intrinsic nature; therefore, an effect cannot arise of itself.
A fruit does not become a fruit by itself; it must necessarily arise from a flower. If a fruit were not dependent upon a flower, there would be the logical fallacy of having two fruits.
Furthermore, for a fruit to produce another fruit upon itself is an impossibility; thus, the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of that which is produced is utterly unfindable.
Since only the absence of intrinsic nature can be found, this conditionality must depend upon causes and conditions; it does not arise of itself. Therefore, it is dependent.
It must depend upon conditions and causes and does not arise of itself; therefore, it is said that all natures are unarisen.
If one awakens to the fact that all natures are unarisen, then one observes that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) in the world have never failed to arise.

Yet, internally one is detached from the mind that acts as the perceiver, and externally one is detached from the objects that serve as the perceived. When both mind and object have vanished, [one abides in suchness].
Below, there is no mind to be apprehended; this "mind-measurement of no-mind" is precisely the self-manifestation of one's own mind.

It does not enter into conceptual construction and does not fall into spatial location. This measurement is boundless; that which is called "measurement" is the very nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, which is all-pervasive and replete.
Abiding in its quiescent and numinous awareness, it stands forth alone and distinct, wherein the perceiving subject and the perceived object...

Because both conditions are equally removed from this state of self-nature, which is ultimately wondrously pure—being both mundane and yet transcending the mundane, conditioned and yet transcending the conditioned, stained yet unstained—it is called "wondrous purity.
Therefore, I say that what is fundamentally unborn is called the "measure of mind" (*cittamātra*). Regarding this, the Great Zhen said in his formal lecture: "A student of the Way must recognize..."

Among those of our own time, I see many who take merely a raised brow, a blink of an eye, a single word, or a moment of silence to be a sudden seal of realization, regarding this as the essential core of the mind.
This is truly a failure to understand. I shall now speak clearly for you; each of you must listen attentively:
simply eliminate all deluded thoughts and mental constructions, and what is directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*) is itself the true mind.
When this mind has no contact whatsoever with external objects or when one maintains silent stillness, the mind itself is the Buddha;
there is no need for cultivation or refinement. Why is this? It reflects itself spontaneously according to conditions, functioning with a clear, cool independence.

Even if one exhaustively investigates the locus of its functioning, it cannot be found; yet, what is called "wondrous function" is precisely the original mind. These words are extremely clear, yet they... [are] inconsistent with... [the preceding].
This section is elaborated upon in successive layers:
the designation of a "self" in conventional truth lacks any substantial reality; likewise, the designation of the aggregates (*skandha*) as "aggregates" is also without substance.
There are four kinds of equal characteristics, and from the nature of causality arises the third [point], non-self, and fourth, cultivation—the one who cultivates.
Tong said: "The previous statement regarding the ultimate wondrous purity of nature means that the mundane and the supramundane do not depart from dependent origination while realizing non-arising.
How does one attain this wondrous state? It is because those who perceive the worldly conventional designation of 'self' see that, in the ultimate sense, there is no self;
it has no master, and no substantial reality can be found within the aggregates."
Each individual posits their own calculations as "self," yet in the ultimate sense there is no self, no master, and no substantial entity to be found.

There is no conventional self, which means there is no grasping at a personal self (*pudgala-ātman*). There are no aggregates to be posited, such as the twenty types of view of a body (*satkāya-dṛṣṭi*), which means there is no grasping at a phenomenal self (*dharma-ātman*).
When both person and phenomena are extinguished and both internal and external are forgotten, one attains the One.

Regarding the equality in all respects, when briefly categorized, there are four kinds of equality: First, equality of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa-samatā*): Characteristics refer to the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Since the aggregates are empty, characteristics and the absence of characteristics (*alakṣaṇa*) are equal. Second, equality of cause and effect (*hetu-phala-samatā*): "Effect" refers to that which is produced by a cause.
Both the producer and the produced lack self-arising; thus, cause and effect are unified as one. Third, equality of self (*ātman-samatā*)... [text fragment]
When there is no self and both the person-self and the dharma-self are empty, then the co-arising attachments to self are completely dissolved and return together to the Great Void.

Thus, "no-self" (the fourth non-self) is the dharma that is cultivated, while "one who attains no-self through the transformation of the mind" is the person who cultivates it. Upon reaching no-self, there is neither cultivation nor realization.

Thus, both the practice and the practitioner are equal. When one is driven by the five, six, seven, or eight consciousnesses, one is subject to the flux of conventional truth (*saṃvṭi-satya*) and cannot attain equality; nor can it be called pure.

Only when the evolving consciousnesses realize the state of no-mind (*acitta*) do the false and the true become identical, all things are equal, and every place is pure. Therefore, that which was mentioned above—
As for "wondrous purity," it is to perceive purity within equality. Huangbo said: "Practitioners of the Way, do not doubt that the four elements constitute the body;
since the four elements have no self, the self likewise has no master. Therefore, this body is without self and without master. The five aggregates constitute the mind;
since the five aggregates have no self, the mind likewise has no master. Thus, one knows that this mind is without self."
"Furthermore, there is no master; the six sense organs, the six sense objects, and the six consciousnesses arise and perish through their conjunction, and it is likewise with them.
Since the eighteen realms are empty, all things are empty; there is only the fundamental mind, vast and pure.
These few words accord perfectly with this present section.
When the habitual tendencies of false conceptualization (*vikalpa-vāsanā*) revolve, various minds arise and manifest objects externally; this is the conventional measure of mind (*citta-mātra*).
These external manifestations are not truly existent, yet one perceives them as such. I teach that the various constructions regarding the body and possessions are merely the measure of mind.
Being free from all views and free from both the perceiver and the perceived, where there is neither attainment nor arising—this I call the measure of mind.
Neither being nor non-being, completely transcending both being and non-being—this liberation of the mind I call *cittamātra* (mind-only).
Suchness, the limit of emptiness, nirvāṇa, the dharma-realm, and the various types of mind-born bodies—I declare these to be *cittamātra*.

The interlocutor said: "Above, you have already explained in detail the meaning of how the non-arising of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) occurs through the direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) of one's own mind.
Hereafter, you will further explain in detail the reality of the transformation of body and mind, reaching the state of the Tathāgata’s self-awakening.

As for those various marks of false conceptualization within the minds of other deluded people, they all arise from the turning of consciousness; because they cannot turn back consciousness, they remain in false conceptualization."
Discrimination refers to the six consciousnesses; defilement by habitual tendencies refers to the seventh consciousness; containing the seeds refers to the eighth consciousness;

and manifesting toward external objects refers to the five consciousnesses. Because they are driven solely by the fifth, sixth, seventh, and eighth [consciousnesses], the delusive thoughts of the sixth consciousness arise based on the defilement of the seventh consciousness, which in turn gives rise to the eighth consciousness that contains the habitual tendencies.
Through the transformation induced by the perfuming of seeds, various conceptual minds arise, falling either into the view of existence or the view of non-existence;

grasping at external manifest objects as being a real self or real dharmas, various delusive thoughts arise—this is the mental measure (*citta-mātra*) of worldly fools. As for those who possess the noble wisdom of self-awakening, however:

Otherwise, when the eight consciousnesses arise manifesting with objective parts (*nimittabhāga*) and subjective parts (*darśanabhāga*), and the mind’s vision confronts external objects without yet having entered into conceptual discrimination, these are called the first five consciousnesses;
this constitutes direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). For the ignorant, they grasp at externally manifest objects as being real;
for the wise, they do not see any reality in externally manifest objects, but [see that] they are merely one's own mind.
The various manifestations that appear—both the internal body of the faculties and the external resources—are all the manifestations of the eight consciousnesses.
There is no phenomenon outside the mind, and no mind outside phenomena; when subject and object are mutually integrated, their characteristics are equal.
This is the transformation of the first five consciousnesses into the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*). Therefore, I say it is "mind-only" (*cittamātra*), not the world.
This is what is thoroughly penetrated. Up to the sixth consciousness, there is the view of a self among persons and the view of a self among phenomena;

there is the subject that perceives and the object that is perceived—all of which do not depart from the functioning of the six consciousnesses. "View" refers to intellectual afflictions (*dṛṣṭi-kleśa*), while "perception" refers to emotional afflictions (*kleśa*).
When one is detached from both of these afflictions, one attains non-attainment. Not only is there no attainment, but there is fundamentally nothing to be attained.
After arising, there is no fruit to be attained; prior to it, there is no cause capable of producing it. Since both are devoid of intrinsic nature, cause and effect are equal.
This is the transformation of the sixth consciousness into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation.

Therefore, I speak of this as "mind-only" (*cittamātra*), which is not accessible through conventional worldly understanding. The seventh consciousness is the basis for defilement and purity, yet it originally lacks a substantial entity; externally, it is merely...
Based on the six consciousnesses, there is no self-nature in existence; internally, based on the eight consciousnesses, there is no self-nature in non-existence.
Being free from both nature and non-nature means that regarding the former six consciousnesses, all traces are cut off so that existence is not established;
regarding the latter eight consciousnesses, the seeds are washed away so that even non-existence has no basis. Thus, both existence and non-existence are transcended.
When one attains great liberation and the beginningless grasping at a self is almost entirely dissolved, this is identical to non-self;
this is the transformation of the sixth consciousness into the Wisdom of Equality. Therefore, I speak of it as the "mind-measure" (*cittamātra*), which is not accessible to worldly conventions.
Upon reaching the eighth consciousness, which is the Tathāgata-garbha, when it relies upon the cycle of birth and death, it is termed "enmeshed in afflictions."

The Tathāgatagarbha, based upon the unborn and undying, is called the "Tathāgatagarbha beyond entanglement. It is called *tathatā* (suchness) in contrast to transformation; it is called emptiness (*śūnyatā*) in contrast to existence;
it is called the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) in contrast to non-existence; it is called nirvāṇa in contrast to birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*);

it is called the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*) in contrast to the six destinies; and it is called the mind-made body (*manomayakāya*) in contrast to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*). Thus it reaches suchness.
Only by arising from the realm of self-awakening can one clearly exhaust each and every detail;
when cultivation and the cultivator are entirely equal, this is the transformation of the eighth consciousness into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-jñāna*).

Therefore, I speak of it as the "measure of mind" (*cittamātra*), which is not accessible through worldly conventions. When the body and mind undergo such a transformation, both the subject that perceives and the object perceived become one.
That which has already transcended conceptualization is the measure of mind (*cittamātra*), the mundane and supramundane, what is called the ultimate, wondrously pure nature;
one must reach this as the pinnacle. When one awakens to this measure of mind and knows the meaning of reality as it is, how could there be any unreal conceptualization?
Tianning ascended the hall and said: "The Dharma-body is the wondrous principle beyond words."
Mystically and suddenly transcending the afflictions of beginning and end, you worthy ones—does the Dharma-body exist separately outside this illusory body?
Or is the illusory body itself the Dharma-body? If you understand it in such a way, you are entirely relying on others to form interpretations;
your minds are obscured by these two divergent paths, and your Dharma-eye has not yet attained clarity. Have you not seen the monk ask Jia Shan?
"What is the Dharma-body? Shan said, "The Dharma-body is without form. "What is the Dharma-eye? Shan said, "The Dharma-eye is without flaw. Therefore it is said:
Wuye once remarked, "When I was still a student, someone once asked me, 'What is the Dharma-body? and I simply lay down on dry ground. What is the Dharma-eye?
and I simply urinated in a damp place. "What is the Dharma-body? Yang [the sheep] lay down on the dry spot. "What is the Dharma-eye? The donkey urinated on the wet spot.
Furthermore, someone asked: "What is the Dharmakāya? [To which he replied: "Buying hats and measuring heads. He asked: "What is the Dharmacakṣus?
[To which he replied: "Pits, ravines, mounds, and hills. If one examines this closely, it appears that Jiashan’s understanding of the training was not yet clear;
like a commoner's domestic trinkets, he could not let go of them, causing the gate of emotion to remain firmly closed and the locks of consciousness difficult to open.
"Old monk, if I did not manifest this today before you, it would be difficult for those who follow later to know where to turn.
I exhort you all: do not seek the Truth; you need only let go of views.

If all views are extinguished, the mists of delusion will not arise, and the natural wisdom-mirror will shine through with clarity, with nothing else remaining. Gentlemen, do you understand? There is fire within the pearl."
"You must believe this; do not go toward the heavens to ask about the sun. Danxia’s verse says: "When the Way accords with the ordinary, there is no room for heterodoxy;
why need the practitioner undergo hardships? From now on, do not inquire beyond Sun Bin; the tortoise shell has no spirit, so there is no need to drill it.
Speaking from this perspective, the shackles of consciousness are difficult to open; one must thus turn them over again and again until they are completely exhausted.
[This] was first attained.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has taught that a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva should be skilled in words and meanings, what constitutes a Bodhisattva’s skill in words and meanings? What is 'word' (vāk)? What is 'meaning' (artha)?"
The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it; I shall speak for you.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Excellent, World-Honored One! We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, "What is speech?

It refers to the false conceptualization of words and letters in combination, depending on the throat, lips, tongue, teeth, gums, and cheeks, and arising from the false discourse of 'self' and 'other'."
“Mahāmati, that which arises from the clinging to the habitual tendencies of conceptualization is called ‘words. Mahāmati, what is meant by ‘meaning’?
It refers to being free from all marks of false discrimination and the marks of verbal expression; this is called ‘meaning.

Mahāmati, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva dwells alone in a quiet place, through the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, takes as their object the self-realized awakening, and directs themselves toward the city of Nirvāṇa, they transcend the body of habitual tendencies.”

Having undergone transformation, one awakens to the realm of self-realization (the Tang translation states: "By means of the wisdoms of hearing, reflection, and cultivation, one contemplates and observes toward the path to Nirvana; the realm of one's own gnosis transforms all habitual tendencies").
Contemplating the characteristics of the superior progress between each stage is called the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva’s skillfulness in meaning.

The Master said: "Previously, when Mahāmati asked about the non-arising of all natures and the World-Honored One’s statement that all phenomena are like illusions, I spoke of seeing all dharmas as they truly are, which means transcending the manifestation of one's own mind. As the verse says:

'Observing them as equal to illusions, one does not falsely conceptualize their marks; immediately thereafter, one is said to skillfully observe the bodies of names, phrases, and forms, and accordingly enter into the meanings of those phrases.'"
The "Form-body" (rūpakāya) is precisely the purport of the meaning of "well-spoken words" as taught by the World-Honored One.

Next, the verse answering [the question] regarding the departure from the characteristics of existence and non-existence says: "Contemplating all this as empty and quiescent, one departs from both existence and non-existence.

Thereupon, Mahāmati requested an explanation of the characteristics of the *pratyātmagatigocaralakṣaṇa* (the realization of the ultimate truth), and the World-Honored One explained it by means of the *deśanāpāṭha* (the conventional teaching); this too is the purport of the meaning of "well-spoken words" as taught by the World-Honored One.
This is the purport of the meaning of speech. Now, Mahāmati asks again: "What is speech? What is meaning? And what is the excellence of speech and meaning?
World-Honored One, you have previously explained in detail the principle of the conjunction of words and conceptualization (*vikalpa*) regarding the four kinds of verbal conceptualization;
why then do you now speak further of [relying on] the throat, lips, tongue, teeth, gums, cheeks, and jaws?
This refers to the production of vocal sounds through the conjunction of the head, chest, throat, nose, lips, tongue, teeth, and gums.
The differentiation of these—teeth, tongue, throat, and lips—into the musical scales of *śaṅga*, *gāndhāra*, *ṣaḍja*, *madhyama*, and *pañcama* constitutes the "syllable" (*akṣara*).

Because one engages in discourse regarding principles and phenomena by means of the interaction between self and other, it is called "speech" (*vāk*). It takes the seeds of habitual tendencies (*vāsanā-bīja*) from the clinging of false conceptualization as its basis.
It is because of this that speech arises; these words and syllables are formed through the conjunction of conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
These characteristics of verbal expression are not separate from consciousness. As for meaning (*artha*), it pertains to the stage where consciousness is transformed into wisdom (*jñāna*);
thus, it is free from all characteristics of conceptual discrimination. Since conceptualization no longer exists, upon what could speech depend?
That which is called the severance of the path of speech and the cessation of the sphere of mental activity is the supreme primary meaning (*paramārtha*).
Therefore, all bodhisattvas should rely upon this meaning and not cling to verbal expressions;

rather, they should sit alone in a solitary, empty, and quiet place, and through the skillful means of the three types of wisdom—derived from hearing, reflection, and cultivation—they should contemplate and investigate until they attain self-awakening and realization.

Tending toward the path of non-arising and non-ceasing that leads to Nirvana, one transforms all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*), undergoes the transformation of body and mind, and realizes the realm of self-realized wisdom (*svapratyātma-jñāna*).

Contemplating the stages (*bhūmi*) and the intervals between them, one uses the diamond-like wisdom-mind (*vajra-prajñā-citta*) to sever, one by one, the characteristics of the superior progress previously realized in each stage.
This is what is called "the excellence of meaning" (*artha-sampad*), which is precisely what is meant by the "transmission of the principle" (*zong-tong*). Zhaozhou ascended the hall.
Bodhi, nirvana, suchness, and buddha-nature are all but clothes that cling to the body; they are also called the "actual limit" (*bhūtakoṭi*) of afflictions and the ground of principle.
Where could they possibly be placed? When the one mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault.

You need only investigate this principle, sitting and watching for twenty or thirty years. If you do not understand, then take the head of this old monk from me! They are like dreams, illusions, empty flowers.

To laboriously grasp at the mind is futile if the mind does not differ [from its objects]; when the myriad dharmas are of one suchness, since nothing further can be obtained from the outside, why persist in such grasping?
It is like a sheep that randomly picks up things and puts them into its mouth.
When I heard Yaoshan say, "If someone asks you something, simply tell them to shut their dog's mouth," I too would tell them to shut their dog's mouth.
To grasp at "I" is defilement; not grasping at "I" is purity. It is like a hunting dog that desires only to catch and eat its prey—where is the Buddha-dharma in such a state?
Whether there be a thousand or ten thousand people, they are all merely seekers of Buddha. Among them, one who can be called a true man of the Way is hard to find.
If you would be a disciple of the Empty King (the Buddha), do not let the sickness of the mind become most difficult to cure.
One should wear upon oneself the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), which is free from the characteristics of conceptual construction and verbal expression.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva Skillful in Words and Meaning contemplates that words and meaning are neither different nor not different;
his contemplation of meaning and words is likewise. If words were different from meaning, then meaning could not be discerned through words.
Furthermore, entering into meaning through words is like a lamp illuminating forms (the Tang translation says: "for example, it is as if a person holds a lamp to illuminate objects").

Moreover, Mahāmati, regarding non-arising and non-ceasing, intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), nirvāṇa, the three vehicles, the one vehicle, the mind, self-nature (*ātman*), and so forth—due to clinging to the meanings of conventional expressions, one falls into views of superimposition (*samāropa*) and denial (*apavāda*).
One falsely constructs various distinctions based on these divergent conceptualizations, which are like illusions and manifold delusions.
It is like various illusions; ordinary, foolish sentient beings give rise to false conceptualizations, whereas the noble ones do not. (The Tang translation states:

"If there are those who, regarding non-arising and non-ceasing, self-nature nirvāṇa, the three vehicles and the one vehicle, the five dharmas, the various minds, self-nature, and so forth, grasp at the meaning according to the words, they fall into the views of superimposition and denial, because they give rise to discrimination by treating these as something other than they are—just as seeing an illusion and reckoning it to be real is the vision of a fool, not that of a noble one.")

The interlocutor said: "In the previous chapter on the characteristics of false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), it was clearly stated that speech and false conceptualization are neither different nor not different.
The World-Honored One has further stated that that which is entered through speech is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), but that speech itself is not the ultimate truth.
Now, if that which is entered through speech is the ultimate truth, then they are not different; yet you also say that speech is not [the ultimate truth]."
To speak of this ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) is not to say that it is not different [from conventional expression].

Therefore, the Bodhisattva Skillful in the Meaning of Speech contemplates that speech and meaning are neither different nor non-different. If they were different, speech would be speech and meaning would be meaning;
then one could not discern the meaning by means of the sound of speech. Since meaning is understood and distinguished only through speech, one enters into meaning by means of speech.

It is like holding a lamp to illuminate an object; once the object is perceived, one forgets the lamp. Because one sees the object by means of the lamp, one cannot say the object is different from the lamp, nor can one say they are identical.
Therefore, know that because of words, the lamp is used as an entry point to reach the realm of self-realization which transcends speech—a realm that is neither different nor not different.
If one clings to this state of being "neither different nor not different," [one remains bound].

Regarding the statement that "language can differentiate meanings": this refers to the fact that the essence and characteristics of all phenomena are identical to the sounds of speech, and meaning is like the speech, while speech is like the meaning;

they are without distinction. Within this, based on various conditions, one grasps at marks—whether it be the unborn and unceasing, whether it be self-nature nirvana, whether it be the three vehicles or the one vehicle, or whether it be the five dharmas and the three natures.
Those who grasp at meaning based solely on conventional expressions and take all such things to be substantially existent, do so because they exist due to verbal expression;
yet that which exists due to verbal expression also lacks existence when devoid of verbal expression.
Consequently, they fall into the two types of false views—reification and denial. Since they perceive both existence and non-existence, they differ from those [others].

To give rise to discriminative views is called "establishing one thing as different from another" or "discriminating one thing as different from another"; in essence, these are all merely false imaginings (*vikalpa*).
How could it be that the meaning is not identical to the words, and the words are not identical to the meaning? They are equal and without difference.

It is simply that the words manifest the meaning, like a phantom person performing phantom deeds, manifesting various transformations—sometimes speaking of non-arising and non-ceasing, or sometimes speaking of the self...

Whether it be the nature of nirvāṇa, the teaching of the three vehicles or the one vehicle, or the exposition of the five dharmas and the three self-natures—the meaning intended is not illusory, yet the words used to express it are like an illusion.
If noble sages contemplate those words as being like an illusion, they immediately know them to be non-illusory;
they do not give rise to false conceptualizations regarding the discourse, whereas the ignorant masses do.
Those who perceive [phenomena] as non-different from [their essence] grasp them as truly existent; those who perceive them as different grasp them as truly non-existent.

Just as one might perceive various illusory phenomena and reckon them to be real, thereby engaging in various conceptual discriminations regarding their differences, such individuals fall into the deluded imaginings of the foolish and worldly, rather than being sages and noble ones. Sages and noble ones observe things as they truly are.

"Since illusions and the like are equal in their marks and do not give rise to false conceptualization—because they penetrate the ultimate truth—you Bodhisattvas should skillfully understand the meaning of these words.
The monks asked Fengxue, "When speech and silence involve transcendence and subtlety, how can one pass through them without transgression?
Fengxue said, "I always remember that in the third month of Jiangnan, where the partridges cry, the hundred flowers are fragrant. Xuedou commented, "Ripping open his belly."
Wenxintiantong (剜心天童) held up [the case] and said: "Barely exposed, perfectly round—truly without seams or edges.
But tell me, how does Fengxue’s seamlessness compare to Xuedou’s seamlessness? Do you understand? He brings light and stirs trouble, yet he establishes his house with absolute certainty.
Master Zhao’s *Treasury of Jewels* (*Baocang lun*), in the chapter "The Subtlety of the Essence of Departure and Return" (*Limi tiao miao pin*), says: "Its emergence is subtle."
Entering the state of detachment from cognition, one enters the detachment from external objects; there is no basis for cognition. Emerging from the subtle inner mind, there is nothing to be done;
because the inner mind has nothing to be done, various views cannot shift it. Because external objects have no basis, the myriad phenomena cannot bind it.
This is because speech involves the subtle and silence involves detachment; therefore, it is said that "speech and silence involve detachment and subtlety. Speech is...

To slander while remaining silent is called deceptive slander; regarding this, there are generally three levels—single and double instances where no offense is committed—and this is specifically one of those three levels.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
Those who establish all phenomena through the conceptualization of verbal expression fall, because of that establishment, into the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) of the hells.
Therein, there is no self or aggregates (*skandha*), yet it is not that they are not the self; nor is it that there is no self at all. All things possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
If it were as the deluded and foolish imagine, or as they perceive them, then everyone would see the Truth (*satya*).
All phenomena are devoid of intrinsic nature; they are neither pure nor defiled, yet they are not non-existent in the manner that they are perceived, nor are they nothing at all.
Generally speaking, while one speaks of the meaning of wholesome words, one is particularly detailed regarding the establishment [of views] and the refutation [of errors].

This is because, due to the views of externalists and heterodox views—which do not differ from and are not separate from deluded conceptualization—one is unskilled in the meaning of words. If one knows this to be so...
"Neither different nor non-different" means that although one does not rely on the path of language, one likewise does not cling to the state of wordlessness;

thus, these two faults do not exist. Those who establish all dharmas through the conceptualization of speech do so because dharmas are fundamentally free from the characteristics of speech, yet they establish them as existing by means of speech. As long as this speech exists, [the dharma] exists.
When speech perishes, it perishes because one has fallen into the cycle of birth and death by means of the dharma that is neither born nor extinguished;

thus, there is nothing surprising about their transmigration through birth and death. As for those who slander and establish [false views], they create conceptual constructions of difference, such as when they speak of the establishment of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), saying:
"Within the aggregates there is a self," or "The aggregates themselves are the self. They then claim that the aggregates...

Within the aggregates there is no self; the aggregates are not the self. This is like that [teaching] which establishes false conceptualizations to appear as if it were refuting the twenty kinds of *satkāyadṛṣṭi*.
However, regarding the cessation of the consciousness-aggregate (*vijñānaskandha*) such that it cannot be apprehended, this leads to a total annihilation and a lapse into non-existence.

Those who do not know how to differentiate that "no-self" is itself the self—failing to realize that it is precisely because there is no self that one knows it to be non-existent—it is said: [this is the fault].
Furthermore, it is not that there is no self; why then do those with this false view of non-self not fall into the hells?
Because they are possessed by such perverted understanding, they are born in the Heaven of No-Thought (*asaṃjñisattva*), and when their kalpa is exhausted, they must inevitably re-enter saṃsāra.

Moreover, those who establish [this view] claim that everything possesses an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), just as ordinary fools perceive through the conceptualization and discrimination based on the notion of existence.

If words possessed an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), then all verbal expressions would reveal the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*). For instance, when one speaks of *nirvāṇa*, one would immediately perceive *nirvāṇa*;
when one speaks of the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), one would immediately perceive the One Vehicle; and when one speaks of the ultimate truth, the ultimate truth itself would be manifest.

Thus, we know for certain that all verbal expressions are fundamentally without intrinsic nature. Since they are fundamentally without intrinsic nature, how could one possibly hold to them with fixed attachment?
Regarding those slanderers who claim that all dharmas lack intrinsic nature:
they assert that the pure and impure karma perceived by the ignorant through their false conceptualizations ultimately reverts to nothingness, such that no real entity whatsoever can be found;
this, they say, is the nature of annihilationism. If, indeed, there were no intrinsic nature, then the continuous flow of the True and Eternal would have to be severed.

However, since beginningless time, that which is truly indestructible cannot be severed; while the pure and the impure can be severed, that which severs the pure and the impure is itself truly indestructible.

Thus we know that all dharmas are not non-existent. Since they are not non-existent, how could one who perceives them as unreal firmly cling to the view that they are non-existent? To perceive them as existent is likewise not true.

To regard what exists as non-existent is not true non-existence; yet, by knowing this is not the truth and awakening to the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), whether one speaks of existence or non-existence, it does not contradict the nature of reality.
Such a person is skilled in the meaning of words and is oriented toward the path to Nirvana. How could they come to the point of opposing existence and non-existence and thus fail to escape saṃsāra?
A monk asked Baizhang, "What is meant by 'sentient beings have no Buddha-nature' and 'insentient things have Buddha-nature'?
Baizhang replied, "From humans up to Buddhas is the attachment of sacred emotion; from humans down to the hells is the attachment of ordinary emotion.
Right now, simply do not engage in acceptance or rejection regarding these two realms of ordinary and sacred, nor regarding any phenomena of existence or non-existence."
The mind is also devoid of grasping or rejecting, and devoid of conceptual understanding; this is called "insentient things possessing Buddha-nature.
It is simply because they lack the bonds of emotion that they are called "insentient," yet they are not the same as wood or stone.

If you take the insentience of the vast void, yellow flowers, and green bamboo to mean they possess Buddha-nature, and claim it exists, why is it that we do not see them receiving predictions of enlightenment in the sutras?
One who attains Buddhahood is simply one who possesses present-time discernment and awareness, yet is not altered by sentient beings. This is illustrated by the metaphor of emerald bamboo:
there is nothing that does not respond to conditions, and nothing that does not know the proper time, as in the metaphor of the yellow flower. Furthermore, it is said:
"If one has ascended the steps of the Buddha, insentient things possess Buddha-nature; if one has not yet ascended the steps of the Buddha, sentient beings lack Buddha-nature," as Baizhang taught.
To speak of clinging to existence and non-existence is merely a matter of mental construction; how could such things exist within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)?
Furthermore, Mahāmati, I shall now explain the characteristics of wisdom (*jñāna*) and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
If you and the other bodhisattvas can skillfully discern the characteristics of wisdom and consciousness, you will be able to penetrate their nature and swiftly attain *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*.
O Mahāmati, that wisdom of Bodhi is of three kinds: namely, worldly, supramundane, and supra-supramundane. What is worldly wisdom?
It refers to the attachment to existence and non-existence held by all heterodox teachers and ordinary worldlings. What is supramundane wisdom?
It refers to the attachment to the hope for self-characteristics and common characteristics held by all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas. What is [supra-supramundane] wisdom?... [text fragment ends]
The supreme wisdom in the world refers to that of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas who contemplate all dharmas as non-existent;

they perceive neither birth nor cessation, and remain free from the categories of existence and non-existence. This is the stage of the Tathāgata, where great wisdom arises spontaneously through the realization of the selflessness of persons and phenomena.

That which involves arising and ceasing is consciousness (*vijñāna*); that which is without arising or ceasing is wisdom (*jñāna*). Furthermore, it transcends falling into the extremes of appearance and non-appearance, as well as existence and non-existence.

The various characteristics that serve as causes are consciousness; the transcendence of the characteristics of existence and non-existence is wisdom. Furthermore, the characteristic of nourishment is consciousness;

the characteristic of non-nourishment is wisdom. Furthermore, there are three kinds of wisdom: namely, knowing arising and ceasing, knowing specific and general characteristics, and knowing non-arising and non-ceasing.
Furthermore, the unimpeded characteristic is the sphere of wisdom; the various impeded characteristics are consciousness. (Translated by [Tang])

Attachment to the marks of objects is consciousness (*vijñāna*); non-attachment to the marks of objects is wisdom (*jñāna*). Furthermore, the arising of the mark of expedient means through the conjunction of the three factors is consciousness;

the mark of the self-nature of unimpeded expedient means is wisdom. (The Tang translation reads: "The arising of correspondence through the conjunction of the three is consciousness; the mark of the self-nature of unimpeded correspondence is wisdom. Furthermore, the attainment of marks is consciousness;
the non-attainment of marks is wisdom, because one’s own attainment of the realm of noble wisdom is neither emerging nor entering.
It is like the moon in water.

It is said in general that, based on the meaning of the preceding words, when one contemplates that speech and its meaning are neither different nor non-different, this is the characteristic of wisdom (*jñāna-lakṣaṇa*).

However, if one contemplates that speech and its meaning are either different or not different, and thereby gives rise to views such as existence or non-existence, this is the characteristic of consciousness (*vijñāna-lakṣaṇa*).
The World-Honored One said: "I shall now explain the characteristics of knowledge and consciousness. Regarding the characteristics of knowledge, there are three types.

Worldly knowledge belongs to ordinary people and others who are attached to the notion that all phenomena exist, that all phenomena do not exist, or who speculate on the causes of existence and non-existence without departing from the realm of the world; this is called worldly knowledge. Supramundane knowledge is..."

Those of the two vehicles (śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas) know that the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) of birth and death in the world are to be loathed, and they conceive an attachment to *nirvāṇa* as something to be realized, hoping to attain supramundane fruits.
Their false discrimination takes that which realizes [it] to be the specific characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*) and that which is realized to be the common characteristic (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*).
Although they escape cyclic existence (*saṃsāra*), they actually fall into a biased emptiness; this is called supramundane wisdom. If one transcends...
The Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, the supreme among the wise in the world, contemplate that which is originally non-existent;
they perceive the self-nature as neither arising nor ceasing, transcending the categories of existence and non-existence.

They do not fall into the views of worldly outsiders or ordinary beings who perceive arising and ceasing, but rather enter the stage of the Tathāgata where both person and phenomena are empty, and they do not fall into the vehicles of the Two Vehicles.
This wisdom, which has not yet been forgotten, is indeed teacherless wisdom (*asaṃskṛta-jñāna*) and spontaneous wisdom (*svayambhū-jñāna*);

it arises through self-realization by conditions and is not attained through the accumulation of meritorious efforts. Speaking from this perspective, although mundane wisdom and supramundane wisdom both bear the name "wisdom," they have not yet transcended consciousness (*vijñāna*).
One must necessarily reach the supreme supramundane wisdom in order to eliminate emotional views.
Only when both are extinguished can it be called wisdom (*jñāna*). Thus, ordinary worldlings cling to all things as being either existent or non-existent;
these are all phenomena subject to arising and ceasing. Those who cling to such phenomena of arising and ceasing belong to the functioning of the six consciousnesses' discrimination;
this is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*). If the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas contemplate the dharma of non-existence and see that it is originally unarisen, [this is wisdom].

Furthermore, because it is fundamentally non-extinguished and already detached from the spheres of all consciousnesses, it is called "wisdom. Worldly outsiders fall into views of signs and signlessness;

they claim that external phenomena exist and then cease. They merely engage in conceptual discrimination regarding signs and fall into various causal characteristics of existence and non-existence—such as having seeds or being seedless, having causes or being causeless, and having distinct causes.
To take the *puruṣa* (divine self) as the primary agent of action is what is called "consciousness" (*vijñāna*).

When Buddhas and Bodhisattvas contemplate the non-existent nature of all phenomena, having transcended the categories of existence and non-existence, having departed from the four extremes (*catuskoṭi*) and severed the hundred negations, and having surpassed all characteristics such as existence and non-existence, this is called "wisdom" (*jñāna*). All Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, in their realization of Nirvāṇa, do not depart from [these dualistic views].

The mark of a self-sustainer (*jīvadr̥ṣṭi*) merely nourishes itself by accumulating various phenomena; yet, as long as the perception of a self persists, one still remains within the realm of consciousness (*vijñāna*).

When Buddhas and Bodhisattvas contemplate the non-existence of all phenomena and realize entry into the stage of the Tathāgata, where both persons and phenomena are empty and not even a hair’s breadth remains, this is called wisdom (*jñāna*). Although that mark of self-nourishment...
Having attained the non-self of persons but not yet attained the non-self of phenomena, one has not yet reached the mark of "nurturing growth.

When even the self of phenomena is empty and the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñāna-skandha*) is entirely exhausted, this is called true wisdom (*bhūta-jñāna*). The above analysis of the characteristics of wisdom and consciousness may be considered detailed;
furthermore, it is said that there are three kinds of wisdom, namely, the supramundane, supreme wisdom, which encompasses the two preceding types.
Regarding the various types of knowledge, the first two types of knowledge cannot encompass the superior, supreme knowledge.

This means that knowing the phenomena of arising and ceasing pertaining to ordinary beings and non-Buddhists—knowing them merely as such and not reckoning them as having existence or non-existence—is called "all-knowledge" (*sarvajñatā*).

Knowing the specific and general characteristics of the phenomena of the two vehicles—knowing them merely as such and not falling into the aspiration for those specific and general characteristics—is called... [the second type of knowledge].
The knowledge of the aspects of the path (*mārgākārajñatā*) knows that the dharmas of all Buddhas and Bodhisattvas are neither arising nor ceasing;
because it knows this alone, one enters the stage of the Tathāgata—this is called the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*).
Knowing these three is neither mundane knowledge nor supramundane knowledge, but rather the supreme-supreme supramundane knowledge. This is the supreme-supreme supramundane knowledge.
How could there be a so-called "Supreme Vehicle" that exists apart from worldly dharmas and world-transcending dharmas?

It is simply that ordinary beings are attached to the marks of objective realms, calculating existence and non-existence; they do not transcend the discrimination of the six consciousnesses and are thus obstructed by various objects.
Only by not being attached to the marks of objective realms can one transform the sixth consciousness into the wondrous observation [wisdom].

Although wisdom abides within the midst of arising and ceasing, it is not obstructed by arising and ceasing; therefore, that which is obstructed is consciousness (*vijñāna*), while that which is unobstructed is wisdom (*jñāna*).
The non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) cling to a self (*ātman*) as the agent, which is precisely the seven consciousnesses.
Through the conjunction of three factors and the application of skillful means, the three arise. These three factors are: first, the root...
The conditions consist of the eight consciousnesses; the two types of mental attention (*manasikāra*) constitute its own essence; and the seeds are those perfumed by the six consciousnesses.
That which arises through the expedient means of these three harmonious conditions is not a mark of self-nature.

The Buddha told Mahāmati, “Regarding the immeasurable all dharmas, there is a continuous succession of attachment to the characteristics of the meanings as they are expressed” (Tang: regarding all dharmas, grasping at meanings according to the words and becoming attached).

Profound and secret, their number is immeasurable. These are: the continuity of attachment to signs; the continuity of attachment to the conditions of signs; the continuity of attachment to the nature and non-nature of things;
the continuity of attachment to the conceptualization of birth and non-birth; the continuity of attachment to the conceptualization of cessation and non-cessation;
the continuity of attachment to the vehicle and the non-vehicle; the continuity of attachment to the conditioned and the unconditioned; and the continuity of the stages.
The continuity of the attachment to the imagined characteristics of the self-nature of the stages; the continuity of the uninterrupted attachment to one's own imagined thoughts;

the continuity of the attachment to the categories of existence and non-existence by those who rely on the false imaginings of externalists; and the continuity of the uninterrupted attachment to the imagined characteristics of the three vehicles and the one vehicle.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, these and other continuities of the false imaginings of ordinary, ignorant beings are likewise [to be understood].

Because of this continuity, the deluded thoughts of ordinary fools are like a silkworm making a cocoon; they entangle themselves with the threads of their own delusions, clinging to the characteristics of the continuity of existence and non-existence in others.
The interlocutor said: "Because of the previous mention of the nine kinds of transformation, one knows that all dharmas possess the meaning of continuity;

because of the previous mention of the *gandharva-nagara* (city of the gandharvas), one knows that all dharmas possess the meaning of liberation. Continuity is bondage, while non-continuity is liberation.
[The Master] said: "The 'Profound and Secret Meaning' (*Saṃdhinirmocana*) and 'liberation' here refer specifically to the seven consciousnesses and the subtle [ālayavijñāna]."
The subtle flow of continuity must be mastered through skillful means (*upāya*) before one can attain liberation.

To grasp at the literal meaning of words and cling to them as a real self (*ātman*) or real phenomena (*dharma*) is precisely the false discrimination (*vikalpa*) of the seven consciousnesses, which arises anew and incessantly.
If, within this continuity, one attains non-continuity, one will be able to distance oneself from the delusions of language and letters.
When this awakening reaches the point where delusion is exhausted and pure truth remains, it is called "awakened wisdom.

When this awakened wisdom is brought forth and employed, one attains great *dhāraṇī*, universally enters all Buddha-lands, and possesses sovereign spiritual powers for various manifestations and illuminating radiance.

It is precisely through this awakened wisdom that one skillfully abides within the dharma-realm of sentient beings; by means of the ten inexhaustible vows, one achieves self-liberation and liberates others.
Their effortless practice is like the sun and moon, which move spontaneously without support; it is like a *maṇi* gem, manifesting colors according to its surroundings;

and it is like the four great elements, which are pervasive and unimpeded. Abiding in the various stages (*bhūmi*), they employ a profound wisdom that is diamond-like and illusory, remaining free from the marks of self-referential conceptualization and viewing all phenomena as being like illusions and dreams.

Equally realizing and entering the body of Equal and Wondrous Enlightenment, he teaches the Dharma according to the capacities of sentient beings, causing them to see all phenomena as being like illusions and dreams;
thus they do not cling to existence as the delusion of continuity, nor do they cling to non-existence as the delusion of discontinuity.
Both continuity and discontinuity have not yet transcended the grasping at arising and ceasing. Only...
All things are like illusions; thus, one turns away from arising and ceasing and relies upon the non-arising and non-ceasing.
By means of speech, one turns away from the conventional meaning of words and realizes the most supreme *dharmakāya*. As for that body which has become supremely transformed, this is true liberation.
Their attachment to the continuity of grasping at meanings according to the words arises entirely from the seven consciousnesses transmitting [the seeds] into the *ālayavijñāna*.
Consciousness is the seed of arising and ceasing; its attachments are profound and subtle, and their number is immeasurable.

What is called "immeasurable" refers to all marks, such as the marks of the five aggregates (*skandha*) and so forth; all conditions, such as the twelve links of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*) and so forth;

and those not external to the world, such as the dharmas of the five aggregates, six sense bases (*āyatana*), twelve bases (*āyatana*), eighteen elements (*dhātu*), and the seven great elements, or by means of...

To hold that what exists returns to non-existence, or to hold that there is birth where there is no birth, or to hold that there is cessation where there is no cessation—those who take as their realization the absence of birth and cessation consider these to be vehicles (*yāna*), while those who do not take such a realization consider them to be non-vehicles.
Those who rely upon birth and cessation rely on all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*); those who rely upon the absence of birth and cessation rely on the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Although one has entered into the state of non-action (*asamskrta*) for the sake of the Dharma, because one still discriminates and grasps at the specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) of each stage (*bhūmi*), the innate ignorance (*sahaja-avidyā*) remains unsevered; this still belongs to conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

For the most part, it does not depart from one's own conceptual constructions, such as the discrimination of the six consciousnesses (*ṣadvijñāna*) and the uninterrupted conceptual construction of the seventh consciousness (*manas*), wherein various attachments arise.
This nature is neither nature nor non-nature; the categories of existence and non-existence are the tenets of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
Śrāvakas perceive its arising, Pratyekabuddhas perceive its cessation, and Bodhisattvas of the various stages perceive its neither-arising-nor-ceasing—this is called the Three Vehicles.

That which transcends the Three Vehicles is called the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), also termed the "Non-vehicle. The conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) of the non-Buddhists rely upon the six [bases].
The continuous succession of the marks of conceptualization, discrimination, and attachment regarding consciousness, the three vehicles, and unconditioned dharmas—
this continuous succession based on the deep-seated, secret attachment to uninterrupted conceptualization— is of immeasurable kinds.
My own disciples as well as other outsiders and ordinary fools engage in such conceptual discrimination and secretly cling to this continuous succession.
It is like a silkworm making a cocoon; it binds itself with this and likewise binds others. In total, they do not transcend the two kinds of deluded conceptualizations of existence and non-existence.

Because their desire and attachment are firm, dense, and continuous without interruption, they do not escape the two types of death—fragmentary and transformational—and thus revolve in the cycle of birth and death.
How can one hope that such beings will be able to overturn their basis and act as its master?
"Is it the most supreme body? A monk asked National Teacher Shao, "What is 'not realizing the Dharma of Oneness'?
The Master said, "Wait for the words. The monk asked, "What is 'realizing all Dharmas'? The Master said, "Why are you acting like a drunkard? The Master then said:
"Just as I have answered these venerable ones in this way, how do you understand it? Is it not the true reality?"
Is it that at this very moment there is not a single dharma to be realized? Is it that you recognize his place of origin?
Is it that the whole body is fully manifest? Do not misunderstand! Such a view is called "clinging to grass and leaning on wood";
it is worlds apart from the Buddha-dharma. Even if your answers and discernment were as sharp as a hanging scale, [it would still be useless].
If you merely achieve such inverted views, and if you value nothing more than answering questions and engaging in discerning debate, what difficulty could there possibly be?
I only fear that it will be of no benefit to others and, on the contrary, lead to deception and error.

As for the principles you have mastered through your previous studies—your skill in discerning and debating, your ability to answer questions, and your extensive retention of doctrines—for what reason does your doubt not cease? Listen to the ancient sages...
This failure to understand through skillful means is simply due to much emptiness and little substance.

Elder, you would do better to see through it all at once from the very root—look and see what principle this is! How many Dharma gates could possibly serve as objects for your doubts and seeking of resolution?
Only then will you realize that all those things you have studied until now are nothing but the source of birth and death, the *skandhas*.
This is the livelihood within the realms; therefore, the ancients said that when seeing and hearing are not detached, it is like the moon in the water.

Be careful with what you have! Thus, one does not fall into the various successive states as they are described; only when one is no longer covered by the aggregates (*skandha*) and realms (*dhātu*) does one first possess the portion of liberation.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, therein there is neither continuity nor non-continuity, because all phenomena are seen as quiescent and conceptual construction does not arise;
thus, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sees all phenomena as quiescent. (The Tang translation states:

"In this, there truly exist no marks of secrecy or non-secrecy, because the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva sees all phenomena abiding in quiescence and being free from discrimination. Furthermore, Mahāmati, one awakens to the fact that external natures are neither existent nor non-existent.

By observing that the appearances manifested by one's own mind are non-existent, and by conforming to the realization that all phenomena are merely manifestations of one's own mind—thereby seeing the cessation of the continuity of all things characterized by signs—one perceives that in all dharmas there is neither continuity nor discontinuity of signs. (The Tang translation states:

"If one realizes that all dharmas are manifested only by the mind and that no external objects exist, they are all identical to signlessness. By conforming to the observation that whether things exist or do not exist, all subtle attachments of discrimination are seen to be quiescent; therefore, there are no signs of either subtlety or non-subtlety.")

Furthermore, Mahāmati, within that [reality], there is neither bondage nor liberation. Others fall into error because they do not perceive things as they truly are, asserting that there is bondage and liberation.
Why is this? It is because among all phenomena—whether existent or non-existent, being or non-being—no sentient being can be apprehended (as the Tang translation states:
"Whether all phenomena are existent or non-existent, when one seeks their essential nature, it cannot be found").
The Master said: "To be attached to continuity is to be attached to the characteristic of continuity; to be attached to non-continuity is to be attached to the characteristic of non-continuity.
Within that nature of *tathatā*, there is neither the characteristic of continuity nor the characteristic of non-continuity.
All phenomena have been, from the very beginning, characterized by inherent quiescence."
For one who perceives that all phenomena are originally quiescent, conceptual discrimination does not arise at all;

thus, when Bodhisattvas realize and enter the state of Equal and Wondrous Enlightenment, they possess neither the sentiments of ordinary beings nor the intellectual understandings of sages, seeing only the quiescence of all phenomena—how, then, could there be any room for discrimination?
Indeed, while all phenomena appear in their manifold variety, [they remain fundamentally still].
How is it that all things are quiescent? It is because one realizes that all phenomena are manifestations of mind alone, like images appearing in a mirror.
Although various external forms appear, they all lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Since they have no intrinsic nature, they have no characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*);
therefore, the appearances manifested by one's own mind are all equally without characteristics. This "all-quiescence" does not necessarily mean being separated from anything.

Only after severing all external objects does one perceive their tranquility. By simply following external objects to observe the self-manifestation of the mind, one sees that whether things exist or do not exist, all natures and non-natures are devoid of characteristics; thus, there is neither the view of existence nor the view of non-existence.
Yet, while not discriminating between existence and non-existence, one remains secretly attached to them within the continuity of the mental stream.
Because one perceives its tranquility, regarding all phenomena—whether their marks, conditions, nature, or lack of nature;
whether arising and ceasing or non-arising and non-ceasing; whether vehicles or non-vehicles; whether conditioned or unconditioned;

and whether the specific characteristics of each stage—there is neither a perception of continuity nor a perception of non-continuity. Being thus immediately tranquil, one attains the Great [Vehicle].
Liberation is the meaning of continuity and is what is called liberation. However, as for so-called "liberation," there was originally no bondage;
how then could there now be anything to liberate? Within that state, there is truly neither the characteristic of bondage nor the characteristic of liberation.
This is attained only by realizing, in accordance with reality, that all is the manifestation of one's own mind; thus one attains this true liberation. As for the others, those of the two vehicles—

Falling into the error of failing to realize things as they truly are, one relies merely on deluded conceptualization and conjecture, claiming that such a continuity constitutes bondage and that the absence of such continuity constitutes liberation.
To speak of bondage and liberation is not to describe what is primordially quiescent. Why is this so?
Because one perceives the existence of all phenomena and, though emptying them, has yet been unable to forget those phenomena.
Furthermore, when one perceives all sentient beings and seeks to deliver them, one has not yet forgotten those beings;
though it is called "untying the bonds," one has not yet escaped the bonds, and thus cannot be said to have reached the realm of True Suchness (tathatā) and the Ultimate Reality (bhūtakoṭi).
One who awakens to reality as it is does not perceive any phenomena at all, nor does one find any phenomenon to be attained within phenomena, for they are detached from them.
The Dharma is such that all sentient beings do not perceive any sentient being as obtainable; yet within sentient beings, there is the absence of sentient beings.
Because neither existence nor non-existence has an ascertainable essence, one perceives all phenomena as like illusions, dreams, and so forth.
Since the essence of sentient beings cannot be apprehended, one causes them to abide in the realization that all phenomena are like illusions and dreams.
Only Bodhisattvas who perceive all phenomena as quiescent are able, through skillful means, not to fall into deluded conceptualization;
how could this be within the reach of non-Buddhists or those of the Two Vehicles? Huangbo said: "This mind is luminous and pure, like empty space, without a single mark or characteristic.
To give rise to a thought or stir a movement of the mind is to deviate from the essence of the Dharma and constitutes [delusion]."
To manifest signs of attachment since beginningless time while practicing the six perfections and myriad deeds with the desire to seek Buddhahood is the Buddha of Gradual Succession.
Since beginningless time, there has been no Buddha of Gradual Succession; one need only awaken to the single mind, wherein not even the slightest dharma can be attained—this is the True Buddha.
The Buddha and sentient beings are non-different in their single mind, just like empty space.
Without admixture and without decay, it is like the great sun disk illuminating the four continents.
When the sun rises, its light pervades the world, yet the nature of space is never bright; when the sun sets, darkness pervades the world, yet the nature of space is never dark.
The realms of light and darkness mutually supplant one another, while the nature of space remains vast and unchanging. So it is with the Buddha and the assembly.

The arising of the mind is also like this: if one contemplates the Buddha as having the marks of pure radiance and liberation, while contemplating sentient beings as having the marks of defilement, darkness, and the cycle of birth and death, one who forms such conceptions will not attain Bodhi even after passing through kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, because of being attached to marks.
This single mind alone exists; there is not even so much as a speck of dust of a separate dharma to be found.

To realize that the mind itself is Buddha—those who study the Way today fail to awaken to this essence of mind, and thus they give rise to further thoughts upon the mind, seeking Buddha outwardly and practicing with attachment to forms; all such things are evil dharmas and not the path of Bodhi.
Huangbo’s words are extremely refined and subtle; one can see that this passage contains the secret and profound intent regarding the existence of bondage and liberation.
The great void is like the alternating succession of light and darkness appearing before one;
what interference does it have with the essence of quiescence?
Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are three continuities for the foolish: namely, greed, hatred, and delusion, as well as craving for future existence and delight therein.
"Accompanied by craving" (in the Tang translation: "and arising with craving, together with greed and joy")—because of this continuity, there is the continuity of the realms of existence (*gati*).
That which continues is the continuity of the five realms, O Mahāmati. As for the severance of continuity: where there is no continuity, there is no characteristic of non-continuity.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the conditions of the threefold conjunction act as a means of attachment, whereby the characteristics of consciousness continue and arise without interval through the means of attachment.
Thus, when there is the continuity of the threefold conjunction of conditions and consciousness is severed, the three views and all forms of continuity cease; they are liberated.

It is said in general that the eleven preceding continuities—whether in terms of characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), conditions (*pratyaya*), nature (*svabhāva*), or arising and ceasing (*utpāda-vyaya*)—are simply these three types of continuity.
However, it is only ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) who possess them; for the three—greed, hatred, and delusion—are the ignorance that initiates karma and the craving that flows forth.
Regarding the seeds for future births, it is through the conjunction with craving and delight that ignorance moistens rebirth;

by means of these two types of ignorance, the continuity remains unbroken, causing sentient beings to take successive births in the five destinies—namely, humans, asuras, pretas, hell-beings, and animals.
The devas and siddhas are not mentioned because devas and siddhas are free from greed and hatred.
Due to the karma of delusion and so forth, these three are not severed; that is, within the five destinies of saṃsāra, there is the characteristic of the continuity of birth and death.

There are only two kinds of characteristics regarding the continuity of ignorance: for one whose continuity is severed, there is no characteristic of continuity; nor is there a characteristic of non-continuity.
Since both continuity and non-continuity are unattainable, this is true quiescence and true liberation. Furthermore, what [is there]?

Regarding this cycle of birth and death, although it is said that the six consciousnesses perform their functions, it is the seventh consciousness (*manas*) that serves as the medium for their transmission.
The seventh consciousness possesses three kinds of conditions: first, the fundamental condition, which is the eighth consciousness;
second, the attentional condition, which is the locus of mental movement; and third, the seed-condition, which is the basis for both defilement and purity.

Through the attachment to the expedient means of the conjunction of the three conditions, whether transmitted from the external to the internal or from the internal to the external, the various consciousnesses arise in succession, bound closely together in an uninterrupted continuity. It is precisely these that arise;
whether their expedient means are internal or external, they have no fixed location, and it is precisely through this attachment that [they arise].
Whether it be defiled or pure, if there is grasping and non-forgetting, and if one clings to such skillful means, then there will be deep and secret fetters that continue without interruption.

Because this *manas* and the seven consciousnesses both grasp at the two types of coarse and subtle attachments to self and phenomena (*ātma-dharma*), all greed, anger, and delusion arise in succession.
If the consciousness that arises from the threefold conjunction of conditions is severed, then [the three] are seen.

The liberation that is externally non-reliant upon the six consciousnesses is the liberation of purity through skillful means; the liberation that is internally non-reliant upon the eight consciousnesses is the liberation of innate purity;
and the fact that, at that very moment, the self-characteristics of the seventh consciousness are unobtainable is the liberation of perfect purity.
To realize these three liberations is to attain the Mahāyāna Dharma-gates of emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. How could this be...?
However, when the three continuities do not arise for a fool, it means that all eleven continuities do not arise together. How could it be otherwise?
Since the characteristic of continuity has no self-nature and thus does not arise, the characteristic of non-continuity likewise has no self-nature and does not arise.
That all continuities do not arise is what is called Great Liberation; this refers to the meaning of the profoundly esoteric and the meaning of liberation.
At this divine cauldron, Shengding ascended the hall and cited Dongshan, who said: "Greed, anger, and delusion are utterly ignorant; it relies on me today to recognize them.
As soon as they act, I strike; as soon as they sit, I hammer. I entrust them to the Prince of Mind for careful investigation.
For immeasurable kalpas they have failed to attain liberation; I ask you three, do you know? The ancients spoke thus—Shengding."
This is not so. Greed, anger, and delusion are truly non-existent; throughout the twelve periods of the day, let them act as they will.
Whether walking or sitting, simply entrust yourself to the Heart-King (*cittarāja*). What need is there to deliberate? Since beginningless kalpas, you have been fundamentally liberated;

why must you further inquire whether you know or do not know? Relying on the explanations of these two venerable masters, the paths to liberation differ; let those with clear eyes discern and grasp them.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Unreal imagination is said to be the characteristic of continuity. If one knows that true characteristic of continuity, the net of continuity is severed.
Through ignorance regarding all natures, one is grasped by verbal expressions; it is like a silkworm that weaves a cocoon and entangles itself."
Fools are bound by the continuity of false conceptualization and fail to observe it.
That which is universally termed "reality" is thusness (*tathatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), which is primordially quiescent. How could there be delusion?
How could there be conceptualization? Only when one is free from those various discriminations regarding reality is it called "false conceptualization"; it is not real.

This false conceptualization is not limited to coarse notions such as greed, anger, and delusion; even the failure to forget the "dharma-self" throughout the three stages of worthiness and the ten bhūmis is not ultimate reality.
Since all these are equally termed "false," they are collectively described as the characteristic of continuity (*saṃtati-lakṣaṇa*).

If one knows that reality and realizes that all phenomena are merely manifestations of the mind, and that the mind is fundamentally unborn and phenomena likewise [are so], [then one attains liberation].
Since all dharmas are fundamentally unborn and empty, what further room is there for conceptualization? Therefore, it is not necessary to annihilate dharmas before their reality can be revealed.
Within that very continuity of deluded thought, reality is fully present; as delusion is itself truth, the essence is unborn.
If even liberation does not exist, how could there be any secret attachment or the continuity of the net of dust?
