To grasp at the various meanings of words while failing to relinquish them is like a silkworm spinning a cocoon that only serves to entangle itself;
this cognitive obscuration (jñeyāvaraṇa) prevents liberation precisely because of a lack of skillful observation.

All foolish commoners are likewise bound by the delusions of greed, hatred, and ignorance, just as silkworms bind themselves with their own webs; this afflictive obscuration (kleśāvaraṇa) prevents [liberation].
Liberation also arises from not improperly investigating; for if one knows that true nature of the net of continuity, it is severed.
It is only when Bodhisattvas investigate in accordance with the self-manifesting measure (*svacittadṛśyamātra*) that the continuity of the marks of existence and non-existence becomes tranquil.
Thus, regarding all phenomena, there is neither the mark of continuity nor the mark of non-continuity. This is the meaning of continuity and its liberation.
This is the purport of liberation. Baizhang said: "The fundamental nature is not the Buddha; to tell someone it is the Buddha is to bind their essence.
It simply means that right now, do not form conceptual understandings of "Buddha," nor dwell upon such conceptual understandings.

This is called the extinction of bonds, and it is also called True Suchness (*tathatā*), and also called Essential Suchness (*svabhāva-tathatā*). To seek a Buddha or seek Bodhi is merely the manifestation of the mind's intent.

Now, all seeking of any kind is merely what is called the manifestation of body and mind. For example, although seeking Bodhi is a superior seeking, it only increases the accumulation of dust and toil.
Seeking the Buddha is the seeking of the multitude of Buddhas; seeking all dharmas, whether existent or non-existent, is the seeking of the multitude of sentient beings.
It is simply a matter of present-time discernment and awareness, provided one does not rely upon or dwell in any dharmas, whether existent or non-existent.

This does not enter into the reckoning of the multitudes; it is simply that, regarding each and every sound, fragrance, flavor, touch, and mental object (*dharmas*), one does not find them attractive and does not crave them.
Merely being free from the ten kinds of turbid minds is the "cause of realization" (*vijñapti-hetu*) for attaining Buddhahood.

Those who study the words and phrases seeking their interpretation are called those who attain Buddhahood through the "causal condition" (*pratyaya-hetu*). Seeing the Buddha and knowing the Buddha, one then attains the teaching that the Buddha possesses knowledge.
To have views is, in fact, to slander the Buddha. If one says that the Buddha knows, the Buddha sees, the Buddha hears, and the Buddha speaks, then one cannot see fire, yet one can obtain fire;
one can see, yet one cannot obtain it. It is like cutting an object with a knife: one can obtain the object, but one cannot obtain the cut from the knife.
Those who know the Buddha, those who see the Buddha, those who hear the Buddha, and those who speak of the Buddha are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River.
The Buddha knows this, the Buddha sees this, and the Buddha hears this; the Buddha’s teaching is that not one in ten thousand is anything other than oneself.

Because one lacks eyes, one relies on another to act as one's own eyes—this is what is called "inferential cognition" (*anumāna-jñāna*) in the teachings. Now, even one’s current craving for the Buddha’s knowledge and understanding is itself inferential cognition.
By observing this, one knows that following verbal expressions and grasping at them is like a silkworm wrapping itself in its own cocoon; this is the general case.
This is a conditional cause (*pratyaya-hetu*) and not a cause of realization (*pariniṣpatti-hetu*);
one must possess the eye [of wisdom] oneself before it can be attained. *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, Section on the Penetration of the Essence, Volume Five;

The Remainder of the Third Chapter, "The Heart of All Buddha-Speech.
Mahāmati again addressed the Buddha, saying: "As the World-Honored One has said, 'By means of various delusive imaginings, one imagines various natures;

these do not exist as intrinsic natures, but are merely the nature of delusive imagination' (in the Tang translation: 'As the World-Honored One has said, due to various minds, one discriminates all dharmas; they are not...')."

[The opponent says: "If phenomena possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) yet it is merely a false conceptualization (*parikalpita*), then, World-Honored One, if this intrinsic nature exists only as a false conceptualization and not as an actual nature, and if these natures are mutually dependent, would this not contradict the World-Honored One’s teaching that afflictions and purity are without intrinsic nature?

For all phenomena are but the intrinsic nature of false conceptualization and lack [true] nature. [The Wei translation says: "World-Honored One, if it is only the discrimination of one's own mind and not the characteristics of those phenomena, then according to what the World-Honored One has taught, all phenomena should be without defilement or purity. Why is this so? Because the Tathāgata..."
[It is] because it is said that all dharmas are seen through false discrimination and lack substantial reality. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "So it is, so it is, just as you have said.
Mahāmati, it is not as the foolish and ignorant do with their conceptualizations of the self-nature (*svabhāva*) of phenomena as being real.

This imagined self-nature does not possess the characteristics of a real self-nature. (The Tang translation says: "All ordinary fools discriminate among dharmas, yet the nature of these dharmas is not as they exist; this is merely a false attachment to a non-existent nature and characteristic. Mahāmati, just as...
The noble knowledge of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the noble knowledge, the noble vision, and the noble eye of wisdom—such is the knowledge of this intrinsic nature.

It is collectively termed "Great Wisdom" (*mahāmatis*). Previously, when asked about the characteristics of unreal conceptualization (*abhūta-parikalpa*), the Blessed One replied with various meanings:
that various kinds of unreal conceptualization arise from the clinging to conceptualization; these various conceptualizations and discriminations are manifold.
All phenomena are fundamentally devoid of real nature and are merely false conceptualizations.
If that which arises dependently through the nature of mere imagination does not possess its own inherent nature, then all phenomena would be utterly without self-nature.
Is this not what the World-Honored One meant when he said that both the defilements of afflictions and the purity of nirvana are entirely without nature?
If both defilement and purity are entirely destroyed, would this not lead to the fault of falling into nihilism regarding all phenomena? Why is this?
Because the World-Honored One has taught that all phenomena are merely false conceptualizations and discriminations, lacking any substantial reality.
If all phenomena lack substantial reality, does this not result in nihilism? It is precisely because one does not understand that all phenomena lack substantial reality [that such a question arises].
Because it is the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) that is True Suchness (tathatā), the Buddha, through his Great Wisdom, has taught that all dharmas lack intrinsic nature (niḥsvabhāva).
This is not like the false conceptualizations of ordinary beings who take the essence and characteristics of dharmas to be truly existent;
for those dharmas have never actually existed. This is merely the attachment to an imagined intrinsic nature; such a dharma does not exist.
Since both the characteristic of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*) and the characteristic of being perceivable (*upalabdhi-lakṣaṇa*) are absent, there is no substantial entity.
That which ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) grasp as real is not real; your words are indeed correct.

However, while the conceptualizations of ordinary beings ultimately resolve into the void, the non-conceptualizing wisdom of the noble ones (*āryajñāna*) may be called real; it cannot be [defined] by those...
Since phenomena lack intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), one may simultaneously doubt that pure *nirvāṇa* lacks intrinsic nature as well.
Therefore, when noble wisdom knows that all phenomena possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), this is not like the deluded conceptualization and vision of ordinary beings;

rather, it is based on the knowledge of the noble ones, the vision of the noble ones, and seen by the noble eye of wisdom. It perceives their existence in such a way that they exist while not existing, and do not exist while existing.
If one knows the self-nature and characteristics of all phenomena as they truly are, and knows their suchness and intrinsic nature, how could there be the fault of annihilation?
The *Treatise* says: "By means of this or that conceptualization, various things are conceptually constructed; this imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) does not exist.
The dependent nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*) arises from conditions through discrimination. The perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*) [is the absence of the former within the latter]."
He is always far removed from the former nature and the nature of the former foolish person;

that self-nature consists of the two natures of parikalpita (imagined) and paratantra (dependent), which belong to deluded conceptualization and cannot exist [as such]. The latter, the self-nature of noble wisdom, is the pariniṣpanna (perfected) nature;
that which is far removed from the former two natures has never been non-existent. What was previously called "the absence of nature in deluded conceptualization" refers to this.
This is precisely the nature of noble wisdom. Formerly, when the Buddha was in the world, there were three brothers who heard that in the city of Vaiśālī there was a courtesan named Āmrapālī;
in Śrāvastī, there was a courtesan named Sumana; and in Rājagṛha, there was a courtesan named Utpalabhānā—all of whom possessed [great beauty].
He contemplated a beautiful woman day and night, and subsequently dreamed of engaging in sexual union with her.
Upon waking, he thought to himself: "That woman did not come, nor did I go; yet the act of lust was accomplished. From this, he realized: "Are not all phenomena likewise such?
Thereupon, he suddenly attained the realization of Mind-Only (*cittamātra*). If these three types of people can clarify that false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) is non-existent...
If one realizes that nature is precisely *cittamātra* (mind-only), can this not be called possessing the eye of noble wisdom?

Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "If it is as the noble ones do—knowing with noble knowledge, seeing with the noble eye of wisdom, which is neither the divine eye nor the fleshly eye—and if the self-nature of nature is thus, being both suchness and non-suchness, then, World-Honored One, how is it that fools engage in false conceptualization?"
Because they are separated from these false conceptualizations and do not realize the nature of the noble state, O World-Honored One, they are neither inverted nor non-inverted.
Why is this? It is because they do not realize the self-nature of the noble state; they do not perceive it as being apart from the marks of existence and non-existence.
O World-Honored One, the noble ones do not see in such a way, for they do not regard the objects of their own characteristics as being like the false conceptualizations of ordinary beings.
Because they take it as an object, O Blessed One, that [nature] also manifests as the imagined nature of the self-nature of things (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa-vikalpa-svabhāva*).

It is not said to have a cause or no cause, because one would otherwise fall into the view of the characteristics of existence (*bhāva-lakṣaṇa-dṛṣṭi*). (The Tang translation says: "Even the noble ones do not perceive things as the ordinary people discriminate them; thus they attain [the truth].

It is not an object within their own sphere of activity, for it manifests as the nature and characteristics of all phenomena just as they are falsely grasped. It is not said to have a cause or no cause because one falls into the view of the nature and characteristics of all phenomena. This is a different object.
The realms are not like those [others], for there would be the fault of infinite regress; this is because the Blessed One does not perceive the self-nature or the characteristics of phenomena.

(The Wei translation says: "Other people see objects in a manner unlike this; to speak thus [of their view] entails the fault of infinite regress. Why? Because they do not realize that the characteristics of all dharmas lack the characteristic of intrinsic nature.")

The Master said: "Mahāmati, because the Buddha taught that noble wisdom possesses the self-nature of reality (*svabhāva*), one knows this self-nature of reality by means of noble knowledge, noble vision, and the noble eye of wisdom;
it is not known through the divine eye, the fleshly eye, or the deluded conceptualization and discrimination of ordinary people.
It is clear that such deluded conjecture is insufficient to perceive the nature. Why is this so?"

Do fools attain freedom from these false imaginings? It is only by awakening to reality as it truly is—the realm of the sages—that one transforms deluded consciousness and is thus able to distance oneself from the false conceptualizations regarding external objects. Because they do not realize the nature of the sacred reality, they remain inseparable from false imaginings;
and because they are not free from false imaginings, they are unable to know the self-nature of suchness as it is.
Although those ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*) are able to differentiate various phenomena, this is not a non-perverted view;

yet they are unable to transcend these various differentiations, nor is it a non-perverted view. Why is this? Because they cannot perceive the reality (*yathābhūta-dharma*) that is the domain of the noble ones (*ārya*).
The phenomena perceived by the noble ones are far removed from the characteristics of existence and non-existence. How can one say...?
The realm of the Sage is far removed from the characteristics of existence and non-existence. Although the Sage also possesses discrimination, it is not like the discrimination of ordinary beings;
such false conceptualization does not depart from phenomena, which is to be attached to characteristics.
To be attached to characteristics is the realm of ordinary beings; to be unattached to characteristics is the realm of one’s own practice. Therefore, the Sage...
Ordinary people do not regard the realm of their own characteristics as the realm of ordinary beings;

rather, they see that the appearances of the objective realm within their own minds are solely without marks (*animitta*). This essence of marklessness is itself the essence of the Dharma (*dharmatā*).

Yet those sages also perceive the existence of the nature and self-nature of the Dharma-essence, and therein they differentiate the characteristics of phenomena just as ordinary beings do through their deluded imaginings.
The intrinsic nature (svabhāva) manifests in this way, yet it is not said to exist because of a cause, nor is it said to be non-existent because of no cause.
The reason why existence and non-existence are not spoken of is that to speak of existence or non-existence is to fall into the views of the characteristics and natures of phenomena (dharmas).
Only by not falling into such views does one enter the realm of self-characteristics; it is not otherwise.
The realm of ordinary beings and the spheres of other ordinary beings differ from this realm; they do not perceive it thus.
Some perceive it as having a cause and thereby fall into the view of existence (*bhava*), while others perceive it as being without a cause and thereby fall into the view of non-existence (*abhāva*).
To speak in such a manner leads to the fault of infinite regress. Why? Because they fail to realize the characteristics of the self-nature of reality (*dharmatā-svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*).
Since the self-nature of phenomena lacks any intrinsic essence or characteristic, how can one falsely discriminate between existence and non-existence?
This realm of noble wisdom cannot be fathomed by the deluded conceptualizations of ordinary beings. Dongshan asked a monk, "What thing in the world is most painful?
The monk replied, "Hell is the most painful. Dongshan said, "Not so; it is right here beneath this robe."
To clarify that the beginning of this great matter is suffering, Danxia’s verse says: "In how many places are there boiling cauldrons and glowing coals?
The three poisons of hell are not as bitter as this. You must believe the intimate words of Xinfeng; do not be negligent beneath the *kāṣāya*.
From this, one can see that those who fail to realize the nature of the sage commit boundless errors."

"World-Honored One, the nature of self-nature is also not the cause of the nature of imagined existence (the Wei translation says: 'it is not caused by discrimination that there is the characteristic of the substance of dharmas').
How then is it that one knows imagined existence as it truly is—neither as imagined nor non-imagined? World-Honored One, imagined existence is different from the characteristic of self-nature;

Fools do not know things as they truly are. [The Tang translation states: "The nature and characteristics of all dharmas do not arise from discrimination; why then do you say that all dharmas exist because of discrimination? The characteristics of dharmas are different, and the characteristics of false imagination are different. How could all dharmas be produced by discrimination?

Furthermore, for what reason do ordinary fools discriminate in this way, when such things do not truly exist? Nevertheless, in order to cause sentient beings to abandon false imagination, I teach that the characteristics of false imagination do not exist as they truly are.
World-Honored One, for what reason do you negate the views of existence and non-existence in sentient beings?
[The objection: "There is attachment to the intrinsic nature of things and attachment to the sphere of activity of noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*).

Why does one cause sentient beings to leave behind the views of existence and non-existence regarding the phenomena to which they cling, yet again cling to the sphere of noble wisdom and fall into the view of existence? The interlocutor said: "It was stated above that deluded conceptualization cannot know the characteristics of the self-nature of reality, because the self-nature of delusion is not the cause of the self-nature of reality; thus, one cannot attain the characteristics of the self-nature of reality.

That which is non-discriminative is the true reality (*dharmatā*) and the ultimate mark (*lakṣaṇa*).

When one knows and discriminates in this manner regarding the stage of the principle of *tathatā* and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), to perceive various dharmas as having attainable natures and marks is like not yet being free from them.
It is indeed due to deluded imagination (*vikalpa*). However, the characteristics of all phenomena (*dharma-lakṣaṇa*) differ from the characteristics of deluded imagination;

fundamentally, they do not resemble one another. Deluded imagination possesses discrimination, whereas all phenomena are without discrimination. Since they are dissimilar, they cannot serve as causes for one another.

How then can all phenomena exist through the discrimination of deluded imagination? This is because the essential natures and characteristics of those various discriminated phenomena are distinct, and thus there is no causal relationship.

How can it be said that the characteristics of the imagined nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) are not individually discriminated by noble wisdom (*ārya-jñāna*), given that noble wisdom attains knowledge of things as they truly are (*yathābhūta*) precisely through individual discrimination?
If so, why is it that ordinary beings (*pṛthagjana*), despite their individual discrimination, do not know the existence of the self-nature (*svabhāva*) as it truly is?
It is because while such knowledge exists within the discrimination of noble wisdom, it does not exist for the ignorant and deluded.
If conceptualization does not exist as such in reality, how could the nature of false imagination be anything other [than non-existent]?

However, the World-Honored One, wishing to cause sentient beings to abandon false imagination, has spoken thus: that which manifests according to the nature of false attachment is called "resembling false imagination.
It is not that it is not false imagination; rather, because it does not exist as it truly is, it cannot be said to be [anything else].

The ordinary person is fully possessed of the dharmas of an ordinary person, yet the ordinary person does not know it; the sage is fully possessed of the dharmas of a sage, yet the sage does not realize it.

"Having secured Annam, one still worries about the north of the pass. Reaching this point, all matters of complete perfection are cast away at once."

Furthermore, Pei Xiu’s preface to the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* (Yuanjue jing xu) states: "To be in perfect enlightenment all day long yet never having realized perfect enlightenment is the ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*).

those who are perfect enlightenment all day long yet have never experienced perfect enlightenment are Tathāgatas. By examining these two cases together, one can know the sequence of what was perceived first;
the insights [of the two masters] were roughly the same.

The Buddha told Mahāmati: "I do not teach that phenomena are empty, nor do I teach a non-existence that falls into the view of existence; rather, I speak of the reality of the self-nature of noble wisdom.

However, in order to cause sentient beings to abandon phrases that provoke fear—since sentient beings have, from time immemorial, been attached to the characteristics of the self-nature of things and have been attached to the characteristics of the self-nature of the reality of noble wisdom—I speak of the teaching of emptiness. Mahāmati, I...
"Mahāmati, when I speak of the characteristic of self-nature, it means that I abide in the reality of the emptiness attained through personal realization;

I am free from the perception of confused characteristics and free from the view of existence and non-existence regarding what is manifested by one's own mind. Having attained the seal of reality that marks the three liberations, I abide in the observation of self-realization regarding the nature of things, remaining free from the views of existence and non-existence."
The interlocutor said: "What Mahāmati doubts is not that the World-Honored One has fallen into the views of existence or non-existence as perceived by ordinary people or those of the Two Vehicles;

rather, he means that when the World-Honored One speaks of the phenomena of emptiness, one falls into the view of emptiness, and when He speaks of the intrinsic nature of noble wisdom, one falls into the view of characteristics and thus regards it as 'existent. Because this doubt is extremely subtle, the World-Honored One says it is not [the case]."
I teach that dharmas are empty and devoid of intrinsic nature, yet some fall into the view of emptiness;

nor do I teach that the reality of the intrinsic nature of noble wisdom exists, yet others cling to the view of existence. The reason I speak of the reality of the intrinsic nature of noble wisdom as being truly existent is to cause sentient beings to abandon phrases that provoke terror;
for when sentient beings hear of emptiness, they may give rise to fear and dread, imagining it to be annihilation.

Because one wishes to cause them to abandon the provisional nature of false conceptualization and return to the reality of self-nature, it is said that the self-nature and phenomena of noble wisdom are provisional and not real.

The reason for teaching the dharma of emptiness is that sentient beings, from time immemorial, have clung to the characteristics of self-nature and substantiality, calculating that there exists a graspable essence of phenomena;
they thus cling to the self-nature and phenomena of noble wisdom as being truly existent.
Regarding the various marks of self-practice and attainable realms, they can all be summarized as not departing from "viewing.

Therefore, it is said that among the characteristics of the dharmas seen, there is no such dharma that causes one to abandon stubborn emptiness (*tuccha-śūnyatā*) and return to true emptiness (*bhūta-śūnyatā*); this too is provisional and not ultimate.
However, regarding the nature and self-nature as I have explained them, if one understands them thus, there will be no marks of nature or self-nature to be grasped.
What is called the noble knowledge, the noble vision, and the noble eye of wisdom refers exclusively to being unattached to signs; only then is one termed "noble.

I have certainly never spoken of the characteristics of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Yet, when I do not speak of the characteristics of intrinsic nature, it is not that I am saying the essence of phenomena (*dharmatā*) exists or does not exist;
rather, I am merely using conventional discourse to discern the essence of phenomena. I say that my own body is like this.

To realize that phenomena are merely what one has attained for oneself—the emptiness of phenomena as they truly are—and to call this "emptiness according to reality" rather than "not empty," is called "true emptiness.
The Tathāgata eternally abides within this; its self-nature is fundamentally empty, such that not a single dharma can be apprehended.
This can only be realized and attained through self-awakening; it cannot be divided by discursive thought.
The distinction is this: by hearing my Dharma and practicing tranquility, one attains the realm of *tathatā* (suchness) which is free from marks;

one becomes distant from the delusive, confused, and false conceptualizations of ordinary beings, and likewise leaves behind the views of the two vehicles regarding the existence and non-existence of what is manifested by one's own mind.
As for "existence and non-existence," it refers to seeing external phenomena as having existed and then ceasing to exist—all of which are merely false manifestations of one's own mind.

One who can distance themselves from false views attains the three great gates of liberation—emptiness (*śūnyatā*), signlessness (*animitta*), and wishlessness (*apraṇihita*)—which are not comparable to a dull void.
Rather, they are the true seal (*mudrā*) of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and Suchness (*tathatā*). By correctly sealing all phenomena, the mind does not differ from the nature of its own-being;
through the realization of dependent origination and self-awakening, one dwells in the observation of the essence of Suchness.
Self-awakened, self-observing, and abiding by means of the self-nature through the self-nature—one knows thus not by way of deluded conceptual discrimination.
By the transformation of the sixth consciousness into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation, that which is discrimination is non-discrimination;
one thereby departs from delusive and discursive thoughts and does not fall into the views and signs of substantial existence. This is to depart from [clinging to] nature.
It is not that one holds the wrong view of non-existence and thus falls into the characteristic of a nihilistic view;
rather, being free from both "existence" and "non-existence," one is fundamentally quiescent and fundamentally without affairs.

This is called the dharma of emptiness as it truly is, which is the realm of self-awakening—how could there be any characteristics or views therein? I do not speak of the characteristics of intrinsic nature or self-nature.
The Bodhisattva Vajrasama used this as a screen to conceal himself for a thousand years while following the Lord of Māra and his retinue in search of the place where he arose;
yet he could not find it. Suddenly, one day, he saw him and asked, "Upon what do you rely for your dwelling?
For a thousand years I have sought the place of your arising and could not find it. Vajrasama replied, "I do not rely upon any dwelling."
Abiding by not relying on non-abiding, one abides in this manner; because he abides thus, it is known that the Bodhisattva Vajrasama abides in this way.

When the Māra King seeks his point of origin and cannot find it, one knows that the World-Honored One abides in the attainment of the reality of emptiness, having fully realized the realm of the self-nature of the signless naturelessness of phenomena.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, a bodhisattva-mahāsattva should not establish the thesis that "all phenomena are unarisen. Why is this?
Because the thesis [asserts] that all natures are non-natures, and because it speaks of the thesis that all phenomena are unarisen based on the characteristics of arising from causes;
thus, that thesis would be undermined. That thesis—that all phenomena are unarisen—is itself undermined.
Because the thesis arises in dependence [upon other factors], it is replied:
The previous statement "I abide only in the attainment of the dharma of suchness-emptiness" means that both false discrimination and sagely wisdom are empty;
when both the true and the false are discarded, they are fundamentally unborn from the beginning. This does not mean that all dharmas are non-arising.
The claim that "all phenomena are unarisen" is a statement of non-arising made in contrast to the myriad dharmas;

thus, it possesses a sense of relativity and constitutes the false view of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Fearing that this might be confused with the true teaching, the World-Honored One refuted it in detail, stating:
"While the phrase 'all phenomena are unarisen' may superficially resemble the doctrine of non-arising, disciples of the Inner Teaching (*śāsana*) should not take this to be [the ultimate truth]."

What is the reason for their tenets? Those non-Buddhists maintain that all natures and non-natures are unarisen because they see non-arising in the place of cessation—that which exists has returned to non-existence.
Furthermore, they hold that there is a distinct and separate cause capable of producing all phenomena, asserting this to be a creator;
thus, they see non-arising in the place of arising. As for the "creator," it is as explained previously.

To claim that an agent—such as a person (*puruṣa*) or atoms (*paramāṇu*)—is inherently produced rather than a producer, and to take that which cannot produce as the cause of production, is already a false view;
how much more so when one claims that no characteristic of production can be found?
Thus, for one who takes "the non-arising of all phenomena" as their tenet, that very tenet is undermined.
What is meant by "destruction"? It refers to the meaning of their own destruction, which is non-arising.
According to that school, all phenomena—whether existent or non-existent—are said to be non-arising because all dharmas have been extinguished. That school holds that a creator is the cause;
since the creator does not arise, they say there is non-arising. To see non-arising after [the process of] extinction is what is meant by non-arising.
If [a thing] arises only after depending on cessation, then it must depend upon an agent to be seen as non-arising.
Thus, this "non-arising" depends upon an agent to arise; since arising exists by virtue of dependence, the meaning of "non-arising" is not established.
Therefore, to claim that according to your school all phenomena are non-arising is to destroy your own tenet. A monk asked Letan Hui.
"Does the Chan Master know where he was born? The Master said, "Since I have never died, what need is there to discuss birth?
To 'know birth' is precisely the Dharma of non-birth; there is no Dharma of non-birth apart from the Dharma of birth. The Patriarch said, "When there is birth, there is no birth.

[The Patriarch asked,] "Can those who have not seen their nature also be like this? The Master said, "It is not that they do not see their nature; it is simply that they do not see it themselves. It is not that [the Dharma] does not exist.
Why is it that seeing is itself nature? Because there is no nature that can see; consciousness is itself nature, therefore it is called the nature of consciousness.
Awareness is itself nature, thus it is called the nature of awareness. It can give rise to the myriad dharmas, thus it is called the nature of dharmas, and is also named the Dharma-body.
As Aśvaghoṣa said: "That which is called 'Dharma' refers to the mind of sentient beings. Because the mind arises..."
If all phenomena arise, yet the mind is of the nature of non-arising, then phenomena have no source from which they arise, nor do they possess names.
If one establishes the thesis that things are thus non-arisen, then it cannot be subverted.
Furthermore, because that thesis of non-arising enters into all phenomena, its characteristic of non-arising is indestructible; thus, by means of this non-arising, all phenomena are established.
The proponent of the thesis of non-arising has his own position destroyed, Mahāmati.
For the thesis of the non-arising of existence and non-existence enters into all natures, and the marks of existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended therein.

Mahāmati, if that proponent establishes a thesis based on the non-arising of all natures, such that nothing arises, then that very thesis is destroyed, because the marks of the natures of existence and non-existence do not arise; therefore, one should not establish such a thesis.

Because the five-membered syllogism (*pañcāvayava*) involves many fallacies, because its members are mutually different in character, and because it is something produced, one should not establish a thesis (*pakṣa*).
That is to say: "All phenomena are unarisen," "all phenomena are empty," and "all phenomena lack intrinsic nature"—one should not establish these as a thesis.

(The Tang translation says: Furthermore, that thesis itself enters into all phenomena; since the characteristic of non-arising is also unarisen, and furthermore, that thesis is composed of the various members [of the syllogism], and furthermore, that thesis exists...)

The thesis that "all phenomena are non-arising" is itself undermined by this very position, because within all phenomena, both existence and non-existence are non-arising. Therefore, the thesis that "all phenomena are non-arising" collapses of its own accord; it should not be established in such a manner, for it involves many fallacies in its constituent parts and because its successive reasons possess contradictory characteristics.
Just as all phenomena are non-arising, so too are they empty and devoid of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
The interlocutor said: "Following from what was stated above, since the meaning of 'non-arising through dependence' cannot be established in that school, their doctrine is ruined.
Furthermore, they claim that by means of the principle of non-arising, they enter into all phenomena, asserting that all phenomena are entirely unarisen;
yet among all phenomena, there are those with destructible characteristics and those with indestructible characteristics."

Those who hold that what is subject to destruction is called "unborn" might still find their position tenable; however, for those who hold that what is not subject to destruction is called "unborn," how can their view be consistent?

If [you argue] that the beginningless flow which cannot be extinguished is itself its extinction, then even regarding the True Dharma of non-arising and non-extinction, you would likewise treat it as "non-arising. This is because, according to your school, [all things arise] from various...
When divided, the established position that all phenomena (*sarvadharma*) are unarisen is contradicted by its own statement;

because the causes for each of those [phenomena] differ according to the three or five categories of dharmas, the characteristic of arising (*utpāda-lakṣaṇa*) remains manifest. Thus, their own doctrine is self-contradictory and collapses.

That school’s thesis—that there is neither arising nor non-arising—asserts that the characteristic of arising does not arise, and that no existent phenomenon (*bhāva-dharma*) can be apprehended; yet the characteristic of non-arising (*anutpāda-lakṣaṇa*) likewise...
One does not merely see that all non-existent phenomena are unarisen and unattainable within their characteristics;
rather, that school enters into the nature of all phenomena, asserting that the natures of existence and non-existence are unattainable.
Thus, those who speak in this way do not merely negate its characteristics, but negate its very nature as well. If that were the case...

Regarding the thesis [of yours] concerning "non-arising": since you establish the thesis that all natures are non-arising, and both existence and non-existence are unobtainable, upon what basis will you establish that thesis?
In this way, your thesis is undermined because the characteristics of both existence and non-existence are equally non-arising;
therefore, one should not establish a thesis in such a manner. Furthermore, as for that which you establish...

The thesis that all phenomena are unarisen (*sarvadharma-anutpāda*) is established by means of the five members of a syllogism (*pañcāvayava-vākya*): first, the thesis (*pakṣa*); second, the reason (*hetu*);
third, the example (*dṛṣṭānta*); fourth, the application (*upanaya*); and fifth, the conclusion (*nigamana*). Within these, there are many logical fallacies:
nine faults of the thesis, fourteen faults of the reason, five faults of the similar example (*sapakṣa*), and five faults of the dissimilar example (*vipakṣa*), totaling thirty.

The three errors are detailed at length in the *Nyāyapraveśa*; in general, by establishing many produced phenomena through mutual dependence, the claim that "activity" (*kṛti*) is the cause of conditioned impermanence is refuted.
Because the example is not applicable and the dissimilar characteristics are manifest, the doctrine of non-arising is destroyed.
Since that doctrine is already destroyed, one should not establish a thesis (*pakṣa*), just as in the case of the "part" (*avayava*).
Since all phenomena are unarisen, it is impossible to establish a thesis;
thus, the meaning that "all phenomena are empty" is likewise, and the meaning that "all phenomena lack intrinsic nature" is likewise—in neither case should a thesis be established.
As stated previously, because the characteristics of both self-nature and common nature cannot be apprehended, it is said that all phenomena are unarisen. Why, then, is this being stated here?
Regarding the thesis that "all phenomena are unarisen": it was previously stated that all phenomena are devoid of an agent and a cause;
therefore, they are unarisen. This teaching by the Buddha—that all phenomena are unarisen and devoid of an agent and a cause—is the true non-arising.
The non-Buddhists' claim that all phenomena are unarisen does not, however, exclude an agent and a cause. Thus...
Since it pertains to matters on the side of arising and ceasing, one should not establish a formal thesis (*pakṣa*).

That [teaching] merely speaks of emptiness, non-arising, and the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) in relation to all phenomena; it manifests non-arising and non-ceasing in contrast to arising and ceasing, yet it is nothing more than conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*).
Mañjuśrī asked the lady Antavatī: "What is the meaning of 'arising'? The lady replied: "Arising has 'non-arising' as its meaning."

Master Shu asked, "What is the meaning of 'birth'? She replied, "To take non-birth as birth is the meaning of birth. Master Shu asked, "What is the meaning of 'death'? She replied, "Death is... [The text continues: "...to take non-death as death is the meaning of death. Master Shu asked, "How is it that taking non-birth as birth constitutes the meaning of birth? She replied, "If one can clearly know that the four conditions of earth, water, fire, and wind have never attained self-existence and yet are able to harmonize according to what is appropriate, this is the meaning of birth. Master Shu asked, "How is it that taking non-death as death constitutes the meaning of death? She replied, "Death is... Master Shu said, "Excellent! Excellent! He then bowed and withdrew. Master Shu then went to visit Master Xuanze. Master Xuanze asked, "Where have you come from? Master Shu replied, "I have just returned from visiting the nun Miaoxin. Master Xuanze asked, "What did she say? Master Shu recounted their conversation. Master Xuanze said, "She is a woman who has attained the Way; you must go and pay her respects again. Master Shu went to see her once more. "Non-death is the meaning of death; how is this so? What is the meaning of death?

She replied, "If one can clearly know that the four conditions of earth, water, fire, and wind have never been self-acquired and are capable of dispersing according to their natural suitability, this is the meaning of death. The daughter Ātreyī then questioned Mañjuśrī:
If one clearly knows the principle that birth is non-birth, why is one still transmigrated by birth?

It is simply because one's power is not yet sufficient. If even those who clearly know the principle of non-birth cannot avoid transmigration, how much less can those who have not attained the true meaning of non-birth falsely establish their own tenets?

"Mahāmati, it is because Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas teach that all phenomena have the characteristic of appearing and not appearing like illusions and dreams, and because they perceive the faults of [dualistic] cognition, that they should declare all phenomena to be of the nature of illusions and dreams. However, Mahāmati, this is done except for the sake of removing the state of terror from the minds of the foolish;
for the foolish fall into the views of existence and non-existence, and one must not cause them to become terrified and thereby abandon the Great Vehicle."

Regarding the passage [where] Yan (whom the Wei commentary identifies as one who hears that all things are like illusions and dreams and thus gives rise to fear, thereby distancing himself from the Mahāyāna), Tong says:
"One should not establish a thesis that 'all dharmas are non-arising,' for to do so would fall into the view of nihilism and is not the Mahāyāna Dharma.
However, when Mahāyāna Bodhisattvas say that all dharmas are like illusions and dreams, although those illusions and dreams appear..."
Various phenomena arise, yet in reality they have never appeared; nevertheless, sentient beings perceive and cognize them, grasping at them as truly existent.
All of this is a mark of delusion. This confused perception and cognition is the fault of ignorance.
Therefore, a Bodhisattva should teach that all dharmas are of the nature of illusions and dreams, and that the nature of illusions and dreams is itself the true nature. Thus it is said:

That which has never existed has never been non-existent; that which exists yet is not existent, and is non-existent yet is not non-existent, is precisely the Middle Way Truth and is the Mahāyāna Dharma.

When ordinary beings hear it said that things are like illusions and dreams, they fall into views of existence and non-existence and give rise to terror, fearing they will fall into emptiness. It is for the sake of causing these deluded people to be free from such terror.
Because it is a provisional teaching, the self-nature of noble wisdom and the self-nature of phenomena are explained as such so that one may know them;

this causes others to understand how to enter the Mahāyāna without falling into views of existence or non-existence. In reality, the characteristics of the self-nature of phenomena are utterly unobtainable;
they are primordially unborn, yet this does not mean that all phenomena are simply unarisen. Therefore, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) speak of all phenomena [as being eternally existent].
To claim that "non-arising" means that all phenomena must first be annihilated before they can be called non-arising belongs to the view of nihilism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).
When a Bodhisattva says that all phenomena are like illusions and dreams, this means that although all phenomena arise, one perceives their non-arising;
this is the true teaching. If you doubt that the nature of self-nature is not separate from existence and yet claim that all things are empty, [you have not understood].

"Would one not fall into the heterodox views of external paths? This is why the Buddha explained it so thoroughly. A monk asked Master Lishan, "Without passing through the kalpas of a *saṃgha*, one attains the Dharma-body;
I pray that the Master will point this out directly. The Master said, "You inherit your father's profession. The monk asked, "How should I understand this?
The Master said, "Do not apply any further reduction or subtraction. The monk said, "If that is so, then the great assembly has someone to rely upon."
The Master said, "Let us set that aside for a moment; tell me, what is the Dharma-body monk? The monk had no reply.
The Master said, "Ask me and I will tell you. The monk asked, "What is the Dharma-body? The Master replied, "A flower in the sky, a mirage. Now tell me:
when Lishan spoke of the flower in the sky and the mirage, was he speaking of the Dharma-body, or was he not? Consider this point.
Only when you have thoroughly understood and attained liberation can you meet Lishan.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Without self-nature, without speech, without objects, and without continuity—those deluded fools harbor false imaginings like corpses and evil perceptions."
All phenomena are unborn; this is not the tenet of those non-Buddhists who maintain that there is ultimately no nature of arising produced by conditions (the Tang translation states:

"because their so-called arising is not accomplished by conditions"). For the wise, all phenomena are unborn and they do not form conceptualizations regarding them; because those [non-Buddhist] tenets arise from causes, the awakened ones have completely eliminated them.
The Master said: "That all dharmas are non-arising means that all dharmas lack intrinsic nature;
that all dharmas are empty means that because they lack intrinsic nature, they are beyond verbal expression. Because they are empty, there are no phenomenal characteristics.
When there is neither expression nor phenomena, there is no attachment, no continuity, and no locus for the ālayavijñāna."
Those fools, through their deluded conceptualization, claim that the non-arising of all phenomena is equivalent to the beginningless flow [of consciousness] and also describe it as annihilation;
this is a false awakening, like a corpse. For a dead person does not arise, which is the characteristic of annihilation.
To establish the non-arising of all phenomena based on such a view is not the way of the wise; therefore, I speak of the One.
One should not establish the thesis that all phenomena are unarisen; for that which the non-Buddhists take as their thesis is truly incorrect.
They claim that all phenomena are ultimately unarisen, and that whatever phenomena arise cannot be accomplished through causes and conditions, being ultimately unarisen and ultimately unaccomplished.
Thus, they maintain that all phenomena are unarisen, attributing this solely to their own erroneous conceptualization.
The non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) engage in such false conceptualization and discrimination; those possessing wisdom should not form such notions or establish such doctrines.
Because their school asserts that [things] arise from causes, they claim there is a distinct cause acting as a creator.

Since they hold that a creator who does not itself arise can serve as the cause for arising, the very mark of "arising" contradicts the principle of "non-arising. Thus, the characteristic of the cause is inconsistent.
Since their doctrine does not establish this [truth], all that they have established—namely, that all phenomena are unarisen—is merely a product of false awakening.
Those who give rise to such an awakening will all fall into extinction and will sever the lineage of the Buddhas;
therefore, it is called "false awakening. Long ago, Wòlún had a verse which said: "Wòlún has skillful means; he can cut off a hundred..."
When the Sixth Patriarch heard the verse, "Thoughts and objects do not arise in the mind; the Bodhisattva grows day by day," he said that this verse did not clarify the ground of the mind.
He remarked that if one were to practice according to it, it would only serve to increase bondage. To demonstrate this, he spoke a verse:
"Huineng has no clever artifice, Yet I cannot cut off a hundred thoughts. When encountering objects, mental states repeatedly arise; How can Bodhi grow?"
"From this, one can discern the distinction between the heterodox and the orthodox. Tiantong added: "A sunflower turns toward the sun; willow catkins follow the wind.
One must yet possess another pair of eyes before one may truly attain it."
For example, it is like a person with cataracts who, upon seeing, falsely perceives the appearance of falling hairs and becomes attached to their nature;
the nature of things is likewise for the foolish who, through false conceptualization, establish the existence or non-existence of things within the three realms of existence.

By conceptualizing the intrinsic nature of things and reflecting on them, they give rise to the marks of conceptualization and establish verbal teachings that cause the mind to become extremely agitated and trembling. O Son of the Buddha, you are able to transcend and remain far removed from all such conceptualizations.

(The Tang translation states: "The three realms of existence are merely provisional names; there is no real essence to dharmas. Because of these provisional designations, conceptualization and false imaginings regarding provisional names and various phenomena agitate the mind-consciousness. Sons of the Buddha, you have all transcended this and roam in non-conceptuality.")
The Master said: "That which is established by those externalists—the non-arising of all dharmas—is like a person with cataracts who falsely perceives the appearance of floating hairs;
in the sky there is originally no sign of hanging hair, yet because of the cataract in the eye, they perceive that such a sign exists.
The nature of the various conceptual attachments to the existence and non-existence of all dharmas held by these externalists is merely the false fabrication of the ignorant."

When one perceives through delusion and gives rise to conceptual discrimination, claiming that all phenomena are neither produced nor separate from the phenomenal characteristics of the three realms, and thereby engages in speculative calculation such that the phenomenal characteristics of the three realms are taken as truly existent—then what is thus calculated is indeed not false.
However, the three realms of existence are merely provisional designations; there is no further real essence of dharmas that constitutes a substantial entity.
Regarding "nature" (*svabhāva*), one falsely designates it through conventional names and clings to it as a substantial reality, thinking that a self-nature can be apprehended;
thus, through various conceptualizations and deliberations, one may regard it as either nature or non-nature, or as a creator, or as arising without cause.
To speak of all phenomena as unarisen (*anutpanna*) upon these conventionally designated things and characteristics—what is this different from emptiness (*śūnyatā*)?

The "middle wheel" gives rise to false discrimination; the teachings they establish, such as the five-membered syllogism and the like, do not transcend the characteristics of phenomena and are fragmented and diffuse, agitating the consciousness.
Once the mind and intellect are thus disordered, they tremble and find no peace, ultimately resulting in transmigration through the three realms.
Where, then, can that which is called "non-arising" be found? This is why, O Son of the Buddha...
To be able to transcend the triple world is simply to remain far removed from all false conceptualizations. When discrimination does not arise, mind and consciousness are both fused;
they become still and profoundly settled, inherently unborn from the very beginning. Why, then, must it be further said that "all phenomena are unborn"?
O Son of the Buddha, to transcend the three realms of existence is not to engage in false conceptualization within those realms, just as when the sky is clear.
The clear-eyed one sees only emptiness; thus, it is beyond the daring reach of the evil speculations of the non-Buddhists.
Xuefeng ascended the hall and said: "I now ask you all: what matter do you take up? In what world do you establish yourselves and find your livelihood?
Can you discern this? If you cannot discern it, it is just like pressing on the eyes and seeing flowers—seeing things that are not there."

"Have you understood? What you currently see before your eyes—the mountains, rivers, the great earth, forms, emptiness, light, darkness, and all such various things—are all the flower-like manifestations of a weary, deluded mind; they are called inverted perceptions.
Since those who have left the household life recognize the mind and penetrate the source, they are called śramaṇas. You have now already shaved your head and donned the black robes for this purpose."
If the characteristics of a śramaṇa were such that one could immediately benefit oneself and others, then looking at you now, you are all like a vast expanse of black ink;
you cannot even save yourselves, so how can you hope to benefit others? Venerable sirs, the matters concerning the causes and conditions of the Buddha-dharma are of great importance;
do not treat them with indifference, nor gather together to engage in idle chatter and miscellaneous talk, passing your time in vain.
Time and opportunity are difficult to find and truly precious; why, O great man, do you not reflect upon yourself and examine what this matter truly is?
As for the ancestral vehicle of the patriarchs, it is the crown lineage of all Buddhas.
Since you are unable to uphold it, I have used skillful means to exhort you: simply follow the gate of Kāśyapa and proceed directly to transcendence.
This single gate transcends the causes and effects of both mundane and supramundane sages; it transcends the ocean of worlds of Vairocana’s wondrous adornment;
it transcends the expedient gates of other Śākyamunis. Directly beneath you, throughout eternal kalpas, not a single thing has been taught to serve as an eye for you to see.
Why do you not urgently investigate and grasp this for yourself? It is not that I say, "Wait for three or two lifetimes to accumulate pure merit over a long duration."
"Virtuous one, what is the matter of the primary vehicle? It cannot be attained by you through the application of effort and adornment;
it cannot be attained by means of another's mind or past-life recollection. Do you understand? It is simply this:

when Śākyamuni appeared in the world, he performed all these various displays and preached the twelve divisions of the teachings, like pouring water from one vessel into another, creating a great spectacle of Buddha."
When it comes to this gate, not even a single point can be employed; not even a hair’s breadth of artifice will do. Do you understand?
It is like a dream-event, or like words spoken in sleep. A śramaṇa should not show his head;
it is not like a dream-event. Do you understand why? Because one must recognize it. To recognize it is the great liberation, the great penetration—the state of a person who has truly emerged.
Transcending both the mundane and the sacred, you are born beyond birth and death, beyond cause and effect, surpassing Vairocana and exceeding Śākyamuni;
you are not deceived by the causes and effects of the mundane or the sacred. Do you know that nowhere can anyone recognize you?
If you merely remain attached to the net of love for birth and death, you will be bound and carried away by the karma of good and evil, leaving you with no share of freedom.

If you refine yourself until body and mind become like empty space, even if you reach a state of brilliant clarity and profound stillness that does not waver, you have not yet emerged from the *vijñāna-skandha*.
The ancients called this "like a rushing torrent; because the flow is so swift, one is unaware of it and falsely perceives it as tranquility.
If you practice in this way, you will never transcend the boundaries of saṃsāra; you will remain subject to the cycle of birth and death as before.
By means of the Way, one realizes that all conditioned phenomena are impermanent; this is truly the fruit of the three vehicles and is thus to be feared.

If one lacks the eye of the Way, one will not reach ultimate realization. How is it that you ordinary people of today, without expending even a hair’s breadth of effort, can suddenly transcend and attain understanding, saving both mind and energy?
Do you still wish for and delight in this? I urge you to realize it right now, where you stand.
"I will wait until you have mastered it before teaching you how to further refine your practice through cultivation; if things are not like this now, when do you think they will be?

Will you ever agree? With these words, he descended from his seat. This section of tangled discourse is much like a commentary on this verse, truly pointing out that the Son of the Buddha is able to transcend the three realms and accomplish a great matter.
To perceive what is not water as water arises from craving; such is the delusion of the foolish, whereas for the noble ones it is not so.
When the noble ones see the purity born of the three gates of liberation and samādhi, they remain detached from arising and ceasing.

They travel through the state of non-existence, practicing non-existence, which is also neither existence nor non-existence. From this equality of existence and non-existence, the fruits of the noble ones arise.

(The Tang translation says: "Constantly practicing the realm of signlessness, even the practice of the realm of signlessness is itself non-existent; since both existence and non-existence are entirely equal, one gives rise to the fruits of the noble ones.

What is meant by "nature" and "non-nature," and what is meant by "equality"? It means that when the mind does not know the internal or external and is extremely agitated, if one can destroy that [state], the mind will see equality.
The General Commentary states: The first section, which reiterates that all phenomena are unborn and thus no thesis should be established, is concluded.

The following section reiterates that one abides in the self-attained, suchness-like emptiness of dharmas; being free from the delusive view of existence and free from the view of the nature or non-nature of what is manifested by one's own mind, one attains the seal of reality of the three liberations. It is said that it is because of this that fools possess delusion.

Those who are deluded perceive that which is merely a conventional designation within the three realms as being truly existent, just as a thirsty deer pursues a mirage, conceiving it to be water where there is no water.
Because craving arises from extreme thirst, they conceive the notion of water where there is no water;
likewise, it is the same for fools who, arising from craving, give rise to delusion and become greedily attached to the three realms of existence. It is only because...
If one is deluded and confused, one cannot attain purity and will thus sink into the three realms, never escaping birth and death.
The sage is not so; the sage perceives the ground as pure, seeing the three realms as empty and devoid of substance.
Because they have attained the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—they realize meditative concentration therein and obtain the seal of reality (*yathābhūta-mudrā*).
One realizes tranquility by distancing oneself from the phenomena of worldly arising and ceasing; for those whose arising and ceasing do not cease are attached to signs.

Now that one is free from signs, one constantly dwells in the realm of signlessness. To practice in the realm of signlessness is not only to be free from the existence of signs, but also to be free from the non-existence of signs.
When both existence and non-existence have subsided, the nature is naturally equanimous.
This wisdom of equality (*samatājñāna*) is precisely the fruit of the noble ones, arising from the pure vision of the sages.
If the triple world is but a single reality, why do ordinary beings perceive existence and non-existence?

How is it that the continuity of karmic results persists for them, while for the sages everything becomes equal, thereby constituting the fruit of holiness? It is because those deluded beings do not understand that the triple world is *vijñaptimātra* (representation-only).
The mind does not realize that all internal and external phenomena manifested by its own mind are entirely impermanent; it falsely gives rise to conceptual attachments toward them.
Failing to understand internal phenomena, it is moved by what it perceives as internal phenomena;

failing to understand external phenomena, it is moved by what it perceives as external phenomena—just as the waves of the ocean are tossed and driven by the wind and cannot attain tranquility. If one can destroy those [attachments]...
Seeing neither the view of existence nor the view of non-existence, when not a single thought arises, the myriad dharmas are all suchness (*tathatā*).
Like wind stilled and waves subsided so that ripples do not arise—what is this if not equanimity?

The previous statement regarding "attaining the object through self-awakening" refers to observing and abiding in the transformation of the sixth consciousness into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation; here it is called "the mind is thus equanimous."
The transformation of the seventh consciousness into the Wisdom of Equality is possible only because one can transform consciousness into wisdom;
therefore, it is called the noble knowledge, the noble vision, and the noble eye of wisdom—how could it be within the reach of the conceptual discrimination of ordinary consciousness?
Once, Master Guishan pointed to a field and asked Yangshan, "This field: which end is high and which end is low? Yangshan replied, "On the contrary..."

One end was high and the other low. Mian said, "If you do not believe me, stand in the middle and look at both ends. Baoying looked up and said, "There is no need to stand in the middle; do not dwell even in the two ends. Mian said, "If it is thus, look at the water. Baoying said, "The water can level things. Mian said, "The water itself has no fixed nature; it is high where there is high ground and low where there is low ground. Baoying said, "Even water has no constancy; it is high where it is high and level where it is low. Mian said, "It is just as you say. Baoying bowed. Mian said, "You have attained it. Baoying then composed a verse: "Water levels things, yet the water itself has no constancy; The mind levels things, yet the mind itself has no abode. The Dharma is originally without form; How could there be anything to attain? Mian said, "You have truly attained it. Baoying then took leave and went to Mount Nanyue, where he served as head cook for three years. One day, while washing rice, he saw the water flow away and suddenly attained great enlightenment. He then composed another verse: "The rice is washed, and the water flows away; The mind is enlightened, and the body is liberated. I have seen the Buddha of the Western Land; He is none other than this very one. When he finished speaking, he wept. The master of the monastery asked him, "What is the meaning of your weeping? Baoying replied, "I am weeping for all sentient beings. Since beginningless time, they have been wandering through birth and death, seeking something outside themselves. They do not know that their own minds are the Buddha, and they do not realize that their own bodies are the Dharma-body. How pitiful! The master of the monastery said, "Your realization is indeed profound. Baoying then took his staff and departed. He traveled to various places, eventually arriving at Mount Dongshan, where he stayed for several years. Later, he returned to Mount Nanyue and lived in seclusion. When he was about to pass away, he told his disciples, "I have been living here for many years, but I have never once spoken of the Way. Now I must go. He then composed a verse: "I have lived on this mountain for thirty years; I have never once spoken of the Way. Now I depart from this place; Where shall I go? I see the Buddha of the Western Land; He is none other than this very one. Having finished speaking, he passed away. His remains were enshrined in a stupa on Mount Nanyue. It is said that when he first arrived at Mount Nanyue, he met Master Xuefeng Yicun. Xuefeng asked him, "Where have you come from? Baoying replied, "From Mount Nanyue. Xuefeng said, "What is the teaching of Nanyue? Baoying said, "The teaching of Nanyue is like a mirror hanging in a bright room; it reflects everything clearly. Xuefeng said, "Is that so? Baoying said, "Yes. Xuefeng said, "If that is so, then you have already fallen into the secondary. Baoying said, "I have not fallen into the secondary. Xuefeng said, "If you have not fallen into the secondary, then what is it? Baoying remained silent. Xuefeng said, "You have already fallen into the secondary. Baoying then bowed. Xuefeng said, "You have attained it. Baoying then composed a verse: "The mirror is bright, reflecting all forms; The mind is clear, perceiving all things. The Dharma is originally without form; How could there be anything to attain? Xuefeng said, "You have truly attained it. Baoying then took his leave and went to Mount Nanyue. This is the story of how he attained realization.
When Pingshan [Huai] reached this point, he simply ceased speaking. The places of equality taught by the father and son, Poyang Huai and Nanquan Puyuan, are layered with successive locks;
their meaning is inexhaustible. Only when one attains the seal of suchness can one understand the subtlety of what is sealed.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has said: 'Just as when one relies upon an object, wisdom does not apprehend it;
this is the establishment of the measure of conventional designation. It is comprised within the grasping of designations, yet it is not the grasping of intrinsic nature.
Because there is no grasping of intrinsic nature, wisdom does not arise; it is merely a name established by convention. (The Tang translation says: "As the Buddha has taught, if one knows...")

Since objects of perception are merely provisional names and are entirely unattainable, there is nothing to be grasped; because there is nothing to be grasped, there is also no grasper. Since both the grasper and the grasped are absent, the arising of conceptual discrimination ceases, and this is termed "wisdom.

World-Honored One, why is it that wisdom does not attain [its object]? Is it because the self-characteristics and common characteristics of the nature of non-awakening are neither different nor not different?

Or is it because wisdom does not attain them due to the obscuration of the various natures and intrinsic characteristics of self-characteristics and common characteristics? Or is it because of mountains, cliffs, and rocks...?
Is it because of obstructions such as walls, earth, water, fire, or wind that wisdom does not perceive? Or is it because of being too far away or too near that wisdom does not perceive?
Or is it because of old age, youth, blindness, or the impairment of the sense faculties that wisdom does not perceive?

World-Honored One, if wisdom does not perceive because it does not discern whether self-characteristics and common characteristics are different or not different, then one should not speak of "wisdom," but rather of "non-wisdom," for [in such a case] there is none.

If an object cannot be apprehended because it is obscured by its own or shared characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and thus wisdom (*jñāna*) does not attain it, that too is not a lack of wisdom;
it is not that there is no wisdom, O Blessed One, for wisdom arises from the presence of such an objective field (*ālambana*).

Because it accords with that objective field, it is called wisdom (the Tang translation says: "It is called wisdom because it knows the object, not because it does not know"). If it is a mountain, a rock, a cliff, or the ground...

If water, fire, wind, or things extremely distant or near, as well as the aged, children, the blind, and those with impaired faculties, do not perceive something through their wisdom, this is not due to a lack of wisdom;
rather, it is because the object itself cannot be perceived. Thus, it is not a matter of wisdom, but of the absence of wisdom, since the thing in question is unobtainable.

Tong said: "Because of the prior establishment of the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*) and the non-existence of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), the Sage perceives the arising of the three gates of liberation (*vimokṣamukha*) and pure samādhi. As the World-Honored One has taught:

'When the Sage’s wisdom observes the objects before him and conditions various phenomena (*dharmas*), he does not see a single dharma that can be apprehended; it is merely a conventional designation (*prajñapti*)."
Since phenomena are neither graspable nor capable of grasping—because both the grasper and the grasped are absent—wisdom likewise cannot differentiate and grasp them.
The non-arising of differentiation is what is called wisdom; even the name "wisdom" is merely a conventional designation.
Thus, it is said that the non-apprehension of characteristics is wisdom. Now, as for the reason why wisdom does not apprehend characteristics: it is because...
Is it that cognition cannot know its object? Or is it that because the characteristics of the object are obscured, cognition cannot know it?

Are the characteristics of the object—such as mountain crags, rocky walls, and so forth, or those that are extremely distant or extremely near—sufficient to obstruct cognition such that cognition does not apprehend it?
Or is it that due to being old, young, blind, or ignorant, and thus having incomplete sense faculties, one is unable to know them all?
Is it that there is fundamentally nothing capable of knowing, such that because the object cannot be reached by cognition (*jñāna*), cognition does not attain it?

What the Buddha spoke of as "cognition not attaining" must necessarily fall into one of these two cases. If one does not perceive the individual and common characteristics of the aggregates (*skandha*), elements (*dhātu*), and bases (*āyatana*)—whether they are different or not different—and this is called "non-attainment," then one should not say that cognition exists because there is an objective domain.

Yet, because this mind does not illuminate objects, it is not wisdom (*jñāna*). If the self-nature (*svabhāva*) of all phenomena—whether their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) or general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*)—is obscured from my wisdom and thus termed "unattainable," this too is not wisdom. Why?
Because wisdom arises as the capacity to know when there is an object known; it is not that the nature capable of knowing is absent, but rather that it has not encountered [its object].
If one is called "wise" merely because of knowing an object, yet that object does not meet with the mind, it is not truly wisdom.

Even if its specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), its own nature (*svabhāva*), and its characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) are said to be obscured and invisible—like mountain crags, stone walls, or things extremely distant or near—is it not the case that there are nonetheless real objects present before us? As for those external objects themselves...
If one who possesses wisdom cannot perceive something, it is still said that the object obstructs the mind and thus remains unperceived.

However, if it is because of old age and blindness, or childhood and darkness—wherein the sense faculties are deficient and wisdom is incomplete—that one fails to perceive an existing reality, this cannot equally be called "wisdom.
That which is prized as wisdom is its capacity to discern the objects before one.
Furthermore, if one holds that wisdom cannot be attained through wisdom, this is truly something I do not understand; it is precisely what Mahāmati doubts.
It is merely knowing that there is conceptual discrimination (*vikalpa*) which constitutes wisdom, while failing to know that non-conceptualization (*nirvikalpa*) constitutes wisdom.

It is merely taking the conscious awareness of objects as wisdom, while failing to know that being without a mind toward objects constitutes wisdom. This is the spirit of the Magnet Island (*Cakravāḍa*).
Chan Master Zang ascended the hall and said, "To know while being without knowing is not the same as being without knowing and then saying one is without knowing.
He then descended from his seat. Nanquan said, "If one follows the Master’s words in this way, one has only spoken half of it.

Huangbo said, "It was not that Nanquan intended to refute him; he wanted to complete the previous statement. But how would you complete his statement? [The Master] replied, "By saying 'there is nothing'."

To know through non-knowing is not knowing; it is by speaking of knowing that one knows. When this is analyzed with clarity, one attains noble wisdom (*āryajñāna*), noble vision (*āryadarśana*), and the noble eye of insight (*āryaprajñācakṣus*).
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "It is not as you say. Non-wisdom should be wisdom, not non-wisdom. I do not conceal [the truth] in such a manner."

Furthermore, regarding the objects of perception, wisdom does not apprehend them; this is a conventional measure established for the sake of awakening to the fact that all is merely the manifestation of one's own mind.

Whether existence or non-existence, there are no external natures or non-natures; knowing this, one does not apprehend objects. Because they are not apprehended, wisdom does not arise toward such appearances.

Wisdom that accords with the three gates of liberation is likewise unapprehendable. That which is not false imagination is the beginningless nature of neither existence nor non-existence, which is devoid of artifice.

Through the cultivation of wisdom, one attains such knowledge as follows: because one knows that [the other] does not know, one does not sever the false conceptualizations regarding the characteristics, locations, marks, and the existence or non-existence of external objects.
Based on the direct manifestation of one’s own mind (*svacittadṛśya-mātra*), one establishes and explains the grasping and attachment to the marks of "self" and "mine.

[The Chinese text states: "This is truly knowledge; it is not as you say. What I have spoken is not a hidden or concealed teaching. When I speak of 'objects,' they are merely provisional names (*prajñapti*) and are unattainable. This is because one has realized that all external phenomena, whether existent or non-existent, are nothing but what is seen by one's own mind."

Within this, wisdom ultimately has nothing to attain; because there is nothing to attain, no flames of conceptualization arise. One enters the three gates of liberation, and even the substance of wisdom is forgotten. This is not like ordinary people of deluded thought who, since beginningless time, have been perfumed by frivolous proliferation (*prapañca*) and cling to external phenomena as having the characteristics of existence or non-existence.
To know things in such a way is called "not knowing. Failing to realize that these are merely manifestations of one's own mind, one gives rise to false imaginings regarding the flames of wisdom.
Because of these false imaginings, one fails to perceive that external natures lack inherent existence. Thus, one falls into the view of nihilism.
Tong said: "Mahāmati, because he could not apprehend with his wisdom and was unable to know the object, he consequently doubted that it was not wisdom;
thus, he took that which is capable of discrimination to be wisdom. Therefore, the World-Honored One told him: 'It is not so.
You merely know the wisdom of having knowledge, but you do not know the wisdom of non-knowledge. This wisdom is..."
Although birth may appear to be without wisdom, in reality it is wisdom and not non-wisdom. What I have taught is not a hidden or obscured teaching;

rather, it is clearly and plainly revealed, easy to understand. When I say that wisdom cannot be attained through the objects of perception (*ālambana*), this is merely a conventional designation established for the sake of discourse;
in truth, there is not a single dharma that can be apprehended as an object of awakening.

To realize that all external phenomena are merely manifestations of one’s own mind—whether existent or non-existent—is to see that they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), and that this very absence of nature is itself no-nature.
Thus, from the beginning, there has been no arising; such is the knowledge. To know thus is to not-know;
though there is cognitive awareness, the objects of experience are ultimately unobtainable. Since there are no objects to stand in opposition to wisdom, wisdom is [non-dual].
Furthermore, because one cannot discern or grasp [objects], wisdom does not give rise to the "blazing" (*jvālā*) of objects known by that blazing.
Since objects cannot be apprehended, objects do not arise; since the mind cannot be apprehended, wisdom does not arise.
When neither object nor mind arises, one accordingly enters the three gates of liberation. Having entered these, one realizes emptiness.
The wisdom that can know signlessness and wishlessness is itself unattainable; even the substance of this wisdom is forgotten.

This prajñā-wisdom must arise from correct awakening to be known; it is not like the habitual wisdom of ordinary people who, since beginningless time, have clung to external phenomena as having existence or non-existence, form, or appearance, and whose perceptions are false. Thus...
To know this [state] is called "not knowing what is not known," for it is a knowledge of non-knowing that forgets the object within the object; therefore it is said:

"This is knowing, while that is not knowing. When one merely continues to engage in various conceptual discriminations regarding the existence or non-existence of the forms and characteristics of external objects and locations, one fails to establish oneself in what is seen as the manifestation of one's own mind.
To establish that which has no fundamental reality as having a self-nature of phenomena,
