and to likewise establish that which has no self-nature of phenomena as "I" or "mine"— to grasp at and cling to these notions of self and mine,
such that there is an internal mind that grasps and an external object that is grasped, based upon the view of eternalism— this is certainly called a lack of wisdom.

Furthermore, there are those who fail to realize that external objects—whether existent or non-existent—are merely the manifestations of their own minds, being fundamentally empty and quiescent from the beginning, leaving no room for conceptual discrimination.
Consequently, they give rise internally to the cognition of a knowing subject and externally encounter the objects of knowledge, thereby discriminating between them.
They observe that all phenomena and characteristics exist and then cease, ultimately returning to annihilation. Thus do they contemplate.
To think that "not obtaining" [the object] is based on the view of annihilationism is also called non-wisdom (*ajñāna*).
Since this beginningless, false habituated cognition belongs entirely to deluded thought (*vikalpa*), it is not called wisdom.

If wisdom does not obtain [an object] by grasping at phenomena, although it appears as if there were no wisdom, it is in fact correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*); how could it be called non-wisdom? Formerly, in the South...
Quanshi addressed the assembly, saying: "The Buddhas of the three periods do not know it exists; the cat and the white ox, however, do know it exists.
A monk asked Changsha, "Why is it that the Buddhas of the three periods do not know it exists? Changsha said, "Before entering the Deer Park, they were still somewhat close.
The monk asked, "Why is it that the cat and the white ox, however, do know it exists? Changsha said, "..."
"How can you wonder at him? Tian Tong’s verse says: Limping and dragging, with hair all disheveled, Hundred things cannot be grasped;
nothing is fit. In silence, he knows for himself his field is secure; Who would say his belly is so bold?
Pervasively encompassing the Dharma-realm, it is entirely food; With nostrils hanging down, he truly has partaken to satiety. This is knowing that there is.
One should know that the entry into existence or non-existence must proceed from the perspective of both wisdom and ignorance.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"When there are various objects of attachment, if wisdom does not examine them, this is ignorance, not wisdom; such is what those who speak of delusion say."
When wisdom does not discern the non-differentiated nature of phenomena, nor the obstructions, nor the near and far, this is called false wisdom (*mithyājñāna*).
Furthermore, when the faculties of the old and young are obscured and wisdom does not arise, yet there is actually such an appearance (*tad-ālambana*), this too is described as false wisdom.
Tong said: "There are indeed various objects of attachment, yet they do not destroy the characteristics of the mundane world.
Through the observation of wisdom, one does not perceive a single dharma that can be grasped; thus, subject and object do not reach one another. This 'absence of wisdom' is in fact true wisdom.
To claim that this absence of wisdom is not wisdom is merely a doctrine of deluded conceptualization and discrimination; it is a mere intellectual understanding."
Those who possess discrimination take it to be wisdom, yet they do not know that non-discrimination is wisdom.

Since they have already fallen into discrimination, how could they possibly discern that which is non-discriminatory? Therefore, the wisdom that transcends knowing is not something known by those with false imaginings.
If one insists on taking "having knowledge" as wisdom, this is merely the deluded wisdom of the world and is not [true wisdom].

Because it is correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*), when one observes whether [objects] are different or non-different in terms of their specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), one does not encounter obstacles such as mountains or walls, nor does one perceive distance or proximity.
One cannot claim that objects can obstruct the mind and thus prevent it from being wisdom;
even if one is able to see various objective realms, this is called false wisdom (*mithyā-jñāna*) and not correct wisdom, because it is said to pursue external things.
It is heterodox. Furthermore, it is said that those who are old and blind, or young and ignorant, as well as those whose sense faculties are incomplete, lack the wisdom to know for themselves;
yet it is not that there is no object to be known. To claim such people are "unwise" merely describes their heterodox wisdom and does not describe right wisdom;
it implies they take the six sensory functions as the essence of wisdom. This is a worldly false view and is not...
This is the correct discourse. I have always maintained that what you say is not so; one who lacks wisdom should instead be considered wise.

A monk asked Huangbo: "If you say that nature is itself seeing and seeing is itself nature, then since nature is inherently without obstruction and without limit, why is it that one does not see when an object intervenes?
Furthermore, within empty space, why is it that one sees what is near but does not see what is far?"
"How is it when one does not see? The Master said, "This is you generating false and divergent views.

If you say that one does not see because of an intervening object, yet says one sees when there is no object, and thereby claim that the nature possesses obstruction, you are entirely out of touch with the truth.
The nature is neither seeing nor non-seeing; phenomena are likewise neither seeing nor non-seeing. For one who has seen their nature, where is there anything that is not [the nature]?"
My fundamental nature is such that the six realms, the four modes of birth, and the mountains, rivers, and great earth are all, in their entirety, my own body of pure and luminous nature.
Therefore, it is said: "When you see form, you see the mind. Since form and mind are not different, [the delusion arises] solely from grasping at appearances.
If one forms views based on seeing, hearing, sensing, or knowing, and only intends to perceive after removing the preceding object, one falls among those of the Two Vehicles;

this is the perspective of those who rely on supernatural powers (*abhijñā*). To see clearly when near in empty space but not when far away is clearly categorized among the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
The Way is neither internal nor external, neither near nor far. Though near, it is not...
That which can be seen is the nature of all things. If even that which is near cannot be seen, what is the meaning of further saying that that which is distant cannot be seen?
This passage of Huangbo’s discourse is precisely in accord with this verse.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, foolish ordinary people are turned around by the beginningless false impressions and evil habits of delusive discrimination.

While being thus turned around, they do not properly understand the thorough realization of one's own school (svapratyātma-gati) or the communication through teaching (deśanā-gati). Because they are attached to the external characteristics of natures manifested by their own minds, they cling to the provisional teachings.
Consequently, they fail to correctly discern the pure characteristics of the fourfold logical alternatives (catuṣkoṭi) within the thorough realization of their own school.

Tong said: "As for what was stated above regarding that which is not deluded thought: it is because of beginningless nature and non-nature, and the artificial habitual wisdom, that one forms such a cognition.
This is knowing while that is not knowing. Why does that fail to know this knowing?

It is truly because foolish ordinary beings revolve according to the afflictions and deluded thoughts of the conceptual proliferations of existence and non-existence that have persisted since time immemorial."
Because their nature cannot transform objects but is instead transformed by objects, they do not properly understand their own tenets (*sva-siddhānta*) or the teachings of the Dharma.
"Own tenet" refers to the fundamental nature; "teaching" refers to the exposition of that very fundamental nature. One who understands well does not cling to signs nor cling to verbal expressions;
rather, they skillfully discern what is manifested by one's own mind. This is called [the realization of] direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).
These are called the penetration of the source (*zongtong*) and the penetration of the teaching (*shuotong*). Those external paths do not understand this;
they instead cling to the nature and characteristics of external objects manifested by their own minds. Failing to cling to existence, they cling to non-existence.

Having already clung to characteristics, they are far removed from the source of self-nature. Whatever they then speak of is merely a skillful means regarding the nature and characteristics of the manifested external objects.
They speak in this way: some say "it exists," some say "it does not exist," some say "it both exists and does not exist," and some say "it neither exists nor does not exist.
They cling to names, phrases, and verbal expressions, yet they are unable to cultivate right practice regarding the true nature of their own school—the pure dharma that transcends the four extremes.
Because they do not skillfully discern its meaning, their discourse remains far removed from it.

Regarding one's own school: since you are neither proficient in the characteristics of the penetration of one’s own school nor proficient in the characteristics of the penetration of verbal expression, it is said that this demonstrates their ignorance.
Linji said: "In a single thought-moment, you merely give rise to a false understanding based on an empty fist;
within the dharmas of sense-bases and objects, you vainly fabricate monstrosities, becoming self-deprecating and disheartened, claiming 'I am...'"
Ordinary people claim they are sages; bald-headed, they live through many births yet feel no urgency regarding death.
Clad in the skin of a lion, they nevertheless howl like a jackal. Great men do not even possess the breath of a great man.
Unwilling to trust the things within their own house, they merely seek outwardly at the idle names and phrases of the ancients, leaning on the dark while seeking the light.
One cannot penetrate directly; instead, one encounters objects and conditions them, meets with sensory dust and clings to it, and delusion arises wherever contact occurs.
For oneself, there is no fixed standard. Followers of the Way, do not grasp at the words of this mountain monk. Why? Because these words have no foundation;

for a time, they are like painting patterns upon empty space, similar to the metaphor of a painted image. This is the "Pervasion of Principle" and the "Pervasion of Teaching" of the Linji school; therefore, it is excellent.
"One is able to understand and skillfully discern in this way.

Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "It is truly as Your Reverence has taught. I only pray that the World-Honored One will, for my sake, explain the *sūtra-vehicle* (the teaching) and the *principle-vehicle* (the realization).
May I and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas become skilled in these two vehicles, so that in future ages ordinary people and Śrāvakas [may likewise attain understanding]."
The Pratyekabuddhas do not perceive its deficiencies. The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Excellent, excellent! Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it;

I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati replied to the Buddha, "So be it; we shall receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, "The Tathāgatas of the three periods of time possess two kinds of Dharma-attainment:

namely, the attainment of the teaching (*deśanā-prativedha*) and the attainment of one's own realization (*sva-pratipatti-prativedha*). As for the attainment of the teaching, it refers to following..."
To teach various collections of sūtras according to what is appropriate for the minds of sentient beings is called the "communication of teaching" (deśanā-prativedha).

As for the "penetration of one's own school" (sva-siddhānta-prativedha), it means that practitioners leave behind the various false imaginings manifested by their own minds; they do not fall into the categories of identity, difference, both, or neither;
they transcend all mind, thought, and consciousness; they personally realize the realm of the noble ones, and they are free from views based on causal conditions.

[The characteristic of] signs (lakṣaṇa). (The Tang translation says: "the characteristic of seeing that is free from all causal associations. This cannot be known by any heterodox practitioners, śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas who fall into the two extremes.

I declare this to be the Dharma of the ultimate realization of our own school (svaka-siddhānta). Mahāmati, these are the characteristics of the ultimate realization of our own school and the teaching of the conventional (deśanā).
You and the other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice and study them.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"I speak of two kinds of penetration: the penetration of the ultimate principle (*tattvārtha*) and the penetration of verbal expression (*deśanā*). The verbal expression is for the sake of instructing the ignorant; the ultimate principle is for the sake of those who practice."

The Buddha replied: "While it is true that both the *cittamātra-prativedha* (the realization of one's own nature) and the *deśanā-prativedha* (the teaching for others) are not within the knowledge of ordinary beings or those of the two vehicles, if one does not skillfully distinguish between these two types of penetration, they may instead cling to their shortcomings. How then can we ensure that future non-Buddhists and followers of the two vehicles do not fall into false views?
Therefore, Mahāmati, you have again requested an explanation of these two kinds of dharma—the *deśanā-prativedha* and the *cittamātra-prativedha*—for the sake of delivering [beings]."

He is the progenitor of the path of training. Therefore, the Buddha told him that as for "teaching according to circumstances" (sūtra), one should preach whatever dharma is appropriate according to the minds of sentient beings;
thus, he preached various sūtras as skillful means and requisites. In the Sanskrit language, *sūtra* is translated here as "契經" (*qìjīng*).

This means being in accord with principle and in accord with capacity. Being in accord with principle means wondrously conforming to the Middle Way; being in accord with capacity means skillfully reaching those of the three faculties.
Because the sutra contains manifold meanings, it is called "all-encompassing," meaning that there is no principle not included and no capacity not subsumed.

This is what is meant by the "communication of teaching" (*deśanā-prativedha*). As for the "communication of one's own realization" (*svapratyātma-gati-prativedha*), it refers to the practitioner bodhisattva who has departed from their own mind.

Various kinds of discrimination manifest; that is to say, they do not discriminate among the four positions of existence and non-existence, nor among the categories of identity, difference, both, or neither.
These deceptive and evil habitual tendencies of the non-Buddhists all manifest from the mind, the thought, and the consciousness.

Driven by the revolving delusions of existence, non-existence, and so forth, they become attached to the nature and characteristics of external objects and are unable to transcend them; only through spiritual cultivation can one do so.

One who is free from those deluded imaginings immediately transcends the spheres of mind, thought, and consciousness, and realizes entry into the sphere of self-realized noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*).
Now, as for this sphere of self-realized noble wisdom, it is originally suchness (*tathatā*) and originally perfected;
it admits of no deliberation and admits of no contrivance. If one views it through causes and conditions, or if one views it as a self...

However, those views associated with practice that are accomplished through causal effort all remain within the realm of signs; they are not the sphere of the noble wisdom of self-realization (*svapratyātmāryajñāna*).
This sphere of self-realization is far removed from all signs and can only be known by oneself; it is not something known by others.

How much less could those of the various non-Buddhist paths (*tīrthika*) or the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), who have fallen into the dualistic views of existence and non-existence, ever be capable of knowing it?

Do you understand? This is called the Dharma of the Self-Realized Lineage (*svayambhū-gotra*). Previously, Mahāmati asked about the characteristics of the lineage of realization (*siddhānta-naya*) while also mentioning its exposition.
The Buddha stated that for all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas, there are two kinds of realized characteristics.

That which is called the "lineage of realization" refers to the characteristic of supreme progress attained through self-realization, which leads toward the untainted realm (*anāsrava-dhātu*) and the light of the path of self-awakening.
The radiance of clarity emerges; this appears to belong to the gradual [path]. However, that which is apart from mind, thought, and consciousness—the self-realized realm of the sages—is sudden.

What is called the "teaching of the common vehicle" refers to preaching the Dharma in accordance with sentient beings according to their needs, consisting merely of the ninefold teachings (navāṅga-dharma-pravacana).
This [sudden teaching], however, comprises all the various scriptures, leaving nothing unprepared; furthermore, it returns to the three [baskets].
The Tathāgata of the world establishes two kinds of teachings. It is not merely that those of external paths, the two vehicles, and those with false views cannot find fault with them;

rather, they are truly the fixed formulas for preaching the Dharma to benefit sentient beings in future ages. Therefore, the verse further clarifies that the purpose of the "Teaching of the Doctrine" (shōtsū) is to receive those of initial capacity;
this is precisely what constitutes the "Teaching of the Principle" (shūtsū). The purpose of the "Principle of the Principle" (shūtsū) is to serve as...
The practitioner establishes this by asserting that his wandering is "nothingness" and his practice is "nothingness"; thus, he may indeed depart from the characteristics of verbal expression.
Since the penetration of the ultimate principle (zongtong) is beyond the reach of verbal expression, how could it be known by those who engage in deluded conceptualization?
Furthermore, how could they find any deficiency in it? As the preceding verse also says: "The characteristics of the penetration of the ultimate principle and the penetration of the teaching."

Based on oneself and the teachings, one observes them well and discriminates them well; one does not follow various conceptualizations, but merely does not turn in accordance with those conceptualizations.
Thus, one is able to transform the ordinary person who follows conceptualizations. Chan Master Liangsui went to visit Magu.
When Gu saw him coming, he took his hoe and went to weed the grass. When the Master arrived at the weeding site, Gu paid him no mind at all.
He returned to the abbot’s quarters and shut the door. The next day the Master went there again, but Gu shut the door once more. The Master then knocked on the door.
Dagu asked, "Who is it? The Master replied, "Liangsui. As soon as the name was uttered, Liangsui attained sudden enlightenment and said, "Master, do not deceive me.
Had I not come to pay my respects to you, I would have been led astray by the sutras and treatises for the rest of my life.
Dagu then opened the door to meet him. Upon returning to his lecture hall, he said to the assembly, "Where all of you know, Liangsui knows twice as much."

Thus, he understood it all. While others did not know where Liangsui had found this, what was his intention in appearing as the Chan Master Liangsui ten centuries later to serve as the evidentiary proof for this passage of scripture?
(Wei: Chapter Five, on the Lokāyatika).
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One once said:
'One must be careful not to study or associate with the various treatises of the world; if one does so, it will lead to the grasping of desire and not to liberation.'"
“World-Honored One, for what reason do you speak thus? The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“The various phrases and expressions of worldly discourse are adorned with the collection of causes, conditions, and parables; they entice and delude foolish ordinary people.
They do not enter into the true self-realization, nor do they awaken to all dharmas. Through false imagination and inversion, they fall into the two extremes. Such are the ignorant and deluded.”

Deluded, they bring about their own destruction; as the various realms of existence continue in succession, they fail to attain liberation. (The Tang translation states: "They follow the false and deceptive discourses of the world; they do not accord with reality nor correspond to principle.

They cannot realize entry into the realm of ultimate truth, nor can they awaken to the comprehension of all phenomena. They constantly fall into the two extremes, losing the right path for themselves and causing others to lose it as well. They transmigrate through the various realms of existence, never emerging.

[They] are unable to realize that [phenomena] are merely the manifestations of one's own mind, and failing to leave behind external natures and self-natures, they remain attached to false conceptualizations. Therefore, the World-Honored One—

Though they engage in various debates and manifold explanations, they do not escape birth, old age, sickness, death, grief, lamentation, suffering, and affliction; they remain deceived, deluded, and confused.

Generally speaking, regarding what was previously termed the "penetration of the ultimate" (zongtong) and the "penetration of the teaching" (shetong), ordinary people and non-Buddhists fail to grasp their essential points, and thus remain in the world.
Furthermore, the World-Honored One instructed his disciples within the precepts: "Be careful not to study or associate with worldly, unwholesome discourses.
If you study their doctrines or associate with such people, you will only grasp the flavor of worldly desire and fail to grasp the flavor of the supramundane Dharma.
Why was his admonition so strict? The Buddha taught that worldly discourse consists of various forms of eloquence and skillful rhetoric.

These are merely phrases that adorn words for the sake of ornamentation, deceiving the ignorant and foolish. They do not rely on discourse in accordance with the Dharma, nor do they rely on discourse in accordance with the meaning;
rather, they speak of conventional matters solely to follow what the worldly mind delights in.

Consequently, one cannot enter the realm of ultimate reality, is not proficient in the penetration of the essence, cannot awaken to the realization of all phenomena, and is not skilled in the penetration of the teaching.
Relying solely on deluded conceptualization, inverted views, and false speech, they constantly fall into the two extremes of existence and non-existence.
They lose the right path themselves and cause others to lose it as well; not only do they destroy themselves, but they can also destroy others.
Ordinary fools are deluded by them, becoming addicted to the flavors of desire and transmigrating through the various realms of existence without end.
They will never attain liberation; how, then, could there be an opportunity for their release?

This is truly because they are unable to realize that all phenomena are merely manifestations of one’s own mind, free from the marks of existence and non-existence, free from the marks of verbal expression, and devoid of external natures or the lack thereof.
Instead, they cling to external phenomena as being substantially real, becoming attached to various conceptualizations and discursive speech, never departing from them.
External phenomena arise from their own inherent nature and give rise to conceptual discrimination.

Although one may possess skillful eloquence and delight in preaching various dharmas, because one has lost the correct principle, one cannot attain liberation from birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and affliction.

One continues through the succession of various realms of existence, revolving without ceasing. This is merely using various forms of eloquent speech to deceive and delude others, causing mutual confusion.
They cannot attain liberation; this is why I say that those who do not grasp the flavor of the Dharma are like this. National Teacher Shao ascended the hall and said:
"As for the venerable elders of all quarters, their verbal teachings remain in the world like the sands of the Ganges River.
The entire Great Canon of the Tathāgata explains the principles of the Buddha in every fascicle and expresses the Buddha-mind in every sentence. For what reason, then, do they fail to attain it?"

One will indeed understand. If one relies solely on the verbal instructions of the teachings, even a venerable elder might spend kalpas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges without ever attaining thorough penetration.
This is called a perverted view and the intellectual calculations of the conscious mind; it possesses no point of efficacy whatsoever.
This is because the foundation of one's roots is not clear. If one were to exhaustively investigate the source of all Buddhas' Dharma, it is like a river...
The entire Great Canon of the Tripitaka is manifested all at once, lacking not even a hair’s breadth and exceeding not even a hair’s breadth.
The Buddhas constantly appear in the world and constantly preach the Dharma to deliver sentient beings, never ceasing for a moment.

Even the cries of monkeys and birds, and the grasses, trees, and forests, always assist the Elder to trigger his realization; there has never been a single moment when they did not do so for him. It is just like this.

This is a most extraordinary matter. It is truly a pity that the various elders have not investigated this thoroughly so as to cause the Dharma to abide long in the world, to increase the lifespan of humans and devas, and to bring peace and happiness to the king. Take care, and farewell. Viewed from this perspective:
If one does not enter into the true realization of one’s own school (sva-śāsana), then even the Buddha’s teachings are not fit to be practiced or approached, let alone worldly treatises (loka-vāda).
Mahāmati, Śakra Devendra extensively understood various treatises and composed his own work on phonology (śabda-śāstra); yet among those proponents of worldly treatises, there was one—
The disciple, assuming the form of a dragon (in the Tang language: manifesting as a dragon), went to the palace of Śakra-devendra to establish his philosophical tenets.
He made a vow that he would destroy Śakra’s thousand-spoked wheel; should he be defeated, he would cut off one head for each spoke to atone for his humiliation.

Having made this vow, he immediately used the methods of Śakra (in the Tang language: the methods of debate) to subdue him. Śakra fell into defeat and had his chariot destroyed, whereupon [the disciple] returned.

They come into the human world. In this way, Mahāmati, worldly discourse—adorned with causes and analogies—even among animals (the Wei translation says "manifesting in animal forms"), can use various phrases and expressions to delude those gods and asuras who are attached to views of arising and ceasing;
how much more so for humans? Therefore, Mahāmati, one should distance oneself from worldly discourse, as it is capable of bringing about [suffering].

Because they are the cause for the arising of suffering, you must be careful not to associate with them. Mahāmati, those who propound worldly treatises speak only of the body, the senses, and their objects.
Mahāmati, there are hundreds of thousands of such proponents of worldly treatises; however, this will occur only in the future, during the final five hundred years.

It destroys the compilation [of the teachings]. Because evil views are prevalent due to the cause of evil reflections, evil disciples receive them. Thus, Mahāmati, worldly treatises destroy the compilation;
they are adorned with various phrases, expressions, causes, and analogies, speaking of the matters of non-Buddhists.

They are attached to their own causal conditions and lack their own independent realization. Mahāmati, those non-Buddhists have no treatise of their own independent realization; regarding other worldly treatises, they are extensive...
He expounded hundreds of thousands of gateways to the Dharma, yet he possessed no independent realization and was unaware that his own discourse was merely the foolish worldly treatise (*lokāyata*).
It is said: "The evil treatises of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) do not merely destroy themselves and others, leading only to the continuous succession of rebirths in the various realms.
In the past, Śakra Devendra extensively explained various treatises and composed his own work on phonology (*śabda-śāstra*), yet as soon as he uttered a single sound, [he fell from his station].

One may then point out [the error]. Thus, a disciple of the Lokāyata school, manifesting as a dragon through his worldly supernatural powers, went directly to the celestial palace and established the doctrines he had practiced, making this essential declaration: "Kauśika, I shall debate with you."
"If you are not my equal, you shall follow me and destroy your thousand-spoked wheel;
if I am not your equal, I shall rather have my body dismembered limb by limb to atone for my defeat.

Having made this vow before the assembly of gods and humans, he immediately raised objections based on the treatises composed by Śakra. He vanquished Śakra, who, being unable to prevail, destroyed his chariot.
Returning once more to the human realm, such worldly discourse is reasoned in its expression and supported by evidence in its maintenance;
even manifesting in the forms of animals, they can still delude the devas and asuras through various literary expressions,

subduing those masters of *śabda-vidyā* (phonology and logic), bending them and stretching them at will, yet remaining attached to views of arising and ceasing and failing to attain liberation— how much more so [is this true for others]?
Is there anyone among men who is not seduced and deluded by them? For this reason, one should distance oneself from worldly discourse and not associate with it;

for such talk gives rise to a mass of suffering. Since it is the cause that produces suffering and leads to wandering through the various realms of existence, how could one ever study or approach it? Furthermore, that worldly discourse speaks only of the body and sensation.

Regarding their spheres of experience: wherever there is a body, there must be sensation. Tracing this back to its origin, they hold that sensation arises from the primordial darkness (*ādikāra*), gradually extending to the five aggregates (*skandha*), the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), and the twenty-five principles (*tattva*), ultimately culminating in the divine self (*puruṣa*).

For the most part, these do not transcend the description of worldly phenomena based on worldly characteristics; therefore, they are called "Worldly Discourses" (*Lokāyata*). There are hundreds and thousands of such Worldly Discourses.

Adorned with various phrases, at the time when the True Dharma is about to perish during the final five hundred years, he shall establish a system of treatises that will split into many schools, each with different names; through their evil views and divergences, they shall destroy the communal compilation.

My Dharma, consisting of the twelve divisions of the sūtras, will be destroyed by them. Because their evil views will flourish in the world, each will cling to their own causes and uphold their own perspectives.
As these causes and views flourish, their arguments will further intensify, and their evil views will spread.
Their disciples will delight in receiving those teachings; consequently, in future generations, the assembly of the heterodox will collapse, disintegrate, and be divided into factions.
This consists of many sections, adorned with various phrases, expressions, causes, and analogies.

It speaks only of the matters of the heterodox views of outsiders, sometimes asserting existence and sometimes asserting non-existence. Clinging to the characteristics of their own causal conditions, they regard what lacks a cause as being without cause;
in total, they do not transcend the sphere of bodily perception. As for that which is not perceived by the body...
That which is realized through awakening is neither caused by conditions nor produced spontaneously; it can only be personally awakened to and personally understood.
That which cannot be demonstrated to others through verbal discourse—those who have not yet awakened to this certainly do not realize it.

Since those non-Buddhists lack such authentic understanding within their own minds, and since their own doctrines are not penetrating, they do not know the reality of self-awakened noble wisdom, nor do they...
The establishment of the Dharma possesses its own internal logic (*sva-āgama-vāda*). It is by elucidating the principle of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) that one speaks for the sake of others.
However, toward other disciples who practice worldly treatises (*loka-vāda*), one extensively explains hundreds of thousands of categories;

these become fragmented and prolix, moving further and further away from intrinsic nature, and likewise lack any internal logic. Indeed, to fail to penetrate intrinsic nature and instead grasp at external conditions (*ālambana*)—
Regarding those who engage in hundreds of thousands of worldly matters and doctrines, they are called ignorant.
They do not even realize that their own ignorant worldly discourse leads to the fruit of suffering; they remain constantly in a state of arising and ceasing without self-awareness—truly pitiable.
Such are the faults of the evil perceptions of worldly discourse. Therefore, I admonish my disciples: be careful never to associate with or study such things.

Furthermore, when the World-Honored One was about to engage in a debate with the Brahmin Dīrghanakha, he established a preliminary condition, saying, "If my doctrine falls into error, I shall cut off my own head.
The World-Honored One asked, "What is the fundamental tenet of your doctrine? The Brahmin replied, "My tenet is that I accept nothing at all.
The World-Honored One asked, "Is this view itself accepted? Thereupon, the Brahmin shook out his sleeves and departed. Having traveled halfway on his path—
He then reflected and said to his disciples, "I shall return and behead myself to apologize to the World-Honored One.
His disciples said, "Since you were victorious in the presence of the assembly of devas and humans, why should you behead yourself?
Zhi replied, "I would rather behead myself before one who possesses wisdom than achieve victory before one who lacks it. He then sighed and said, "My righteousness lies in both places."
I have incurred defeat. If this view is accepted, my position is defeated at the coarse level; if this view is not accepted, my position is defeated at the subtle level.
No humans, devas, or followers of the two vehicles can know where my meaning falls into defeat; only the World-Honored One and the great Bodhisattvas know where my meaning falls into defeat.
Returning before the World-Honored One, he said: "My meaning has incurred defeat in both respects. Therefore, it must..."
He offered his head as an apology. The World-Honored One said, "In my Dharma, there is no such thing. You should turn your mind toward the Path.
Thereupon, together with his five hundred followers, he simultaneously took refuge in the Buddha, left the household life, and realized arhatship.
Now, that the Brahmin dared to debate the meaning of the Dharma with the World-Honored One—and that he looked upon the one who had bound Śakra—was more than merely excessive.
Thus, while the World-Honored One was ultimately able to subdue the brahmin, Śakra, conversely, was defeated by the worldly discourse (lokāyata).

The evil views of worldly discourse are indeed not easily shattered. In the age of the Final Dharma, how can one find those who deeply understand the intent of the World-Honored One to guide and transform others?
At that time, Mahāmati said to the Buddha: "World-Honored One, if the various phrases, expressions, causes,

and analogies of the worldly discourses of the non-Buddhists lack any self-attained realization or attachment to their own specific objects, then why does the World-Honored One also speak of worldly discourse for the sake of the devas,
humans, and asuras gathered from various regions, extensively explaining immeasurable varieties of phrases and expressions?"
"Is this not my own teaching? Does it not also fall within the category of the wisdom and discourse of all non-Buddhists?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "I do not speak of worldly treatises (*lokāyata*). There is neither coming nor going; I speak only of that which neither comes nor goes.

Mahāmati, 'coming' refers to gathering and arising; 'going' refers to dispersal and destruction. That which neither comes nor goes is that which is neither born nor extinguished. This is what I have taught."

This meaning does not fall within the categories of worldly discourse or false conceptualization. Why is this? It is because one does not cling to the existence or non-existence of external objects, which are merely manifestations of one's own mind.

One cannot be turned by the false conceptualizations of the two extremes. Since the characteristics of objective realms lack inherent nature, when one awakens to them as manifestations of one's own mind, the false conceptualizations of one's own mind do not arise.
When false conceptualizations do not arise, one enters emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness.
The three gates of liberation are called "liberation.

Mahāmati asked in general terms: "If it is the case that non-Buddhists propound various doctrines and cling to their own tenets as being the true Dharma rather than the reality as it is, then does the World-Honored One also extensively teach various [doctrines] to the assemblies gathered from the lands of the ten directions?"

Regarding the phrasing and meaning: [the Buddha] also taught the Dharma using various worldly names, phrases, and metaphors, rather than speaking of the Dharma realized through his own internal wisdom.
If this were so, would it not be the same as the intellectual discourse, terminology, and numerical categories found within the self-systems of the non-Buddhists?
The Buddha replied: "I have extensively expounded various phrases for the sake of the great assembly gathered from all directions."

Taste. I do not speak of the teachings of worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*). Worldly discourse perceives the characteristics of coming and going among humans and devas, yet it does not know that for humans and devas there is in reality neither coming nor going.
I speak only of the Dharma of neither coming nor going. Now, that which "comes" arises through the convergence of conditions;
that which "goes" perishes through the dispersal of conditions. One merely perceives coming and going upon the level of appearances (*nimitta*); such [perception] belongs to birth.
The dharma of cessation. I say that neither coming nor going is precisely the dharma of non-arising and non-cessation.
Regarding the meaning of non-arising and non-cessance as I have explained it: there is nowhere from which it comes, and there is nowhere to which it goes.

It reaches the realm of suchness (*tathatā*) and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and does not fall into the categories of worldly discourse or false conceptualization. Why does it not fall into those categories?
They fail to realize that external entities—whether existent or non-existent—are merely manifestations of their own minds;
thus, they engage in false conceptualization regarding external objects, asserting them to be either existent or non-existent. Driven by these two views, they do not attain liberation.

I, however, do not cling to the existence or non-existence of external objects, but establish and teach that all things are but manifestations of one's own mind. Therefore, the two extremes of existence and non-existence are false.
Conceptual discrimination cannot turn me around; rather, it is I who am turned by what is "mine.
This is because I have understood, as it truly is, that external objects lack intrinsic nature and are merely manifestations of one's own mind, like dreams or illusions.

They cannot be said to exist, nor can they be said not to exist. Therefore, the conceptual discriminations manifested by one's own mind arise without self-nature, [just as] the characteristics of objects [do].

It is not a nature; objects do not arise. Deluded thoughts do not arise; the mind does not arise. When both mind and objects are without arising, one immediately realizes and enters the three gates of liberation—emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness—and becomes far removed from the continuity of birth, death, and the various realms of existence.
This is called liberation. I understand only that the mind and its objects are both empty, being by nature neither born nor extinguished.
Thus, I am able to transform birth and death without being transformed by birth and death; therefore, I do not fall among the categories of worldly discourse and delusive conceptualization.
How could it be that I lack my own realization? The Prefect Yang Xuanzhi questioned the First Patriarch in this manner.
He asked, “In the Five Indias of the Western Heaven, the lineage of masters is taken as the patriarchs. What is their Way?

The Patriarch said, “To clarify the mind-source of the Buddha and to have one’s practice and understanding correspond with each other—this is what is called being a patriarch. He asked again, “What is it like beyond this?

The Patriarch said, “One must clarify the minds of others and know both the present and the past; one does not loathe existence or non-existence, takes nothing from the Dharma, is neither wise nor foolish, and is without delusion.”
“There is no awakening. “If one can understand it in this way, one is therefore called an ancestor (patriarch).

Furthermore, [the disciple] said, “I have turned my heart toward the Triple Gem for many years, yet my wisdom remains clouded and dull, and I am still lost regarding the True Principle. Having just heard your words, Master, I do not know where to apply them.
I pray that you will, out of compassion, reveal the essential tenets. The Ancestor, knowing his sincerity, immediately spoke a verse, saying: “Nor is there...”

One does not give rise to aversion upon seeing evil, nor does one exert oneself in cherishing that which is pleasant. One does not abandon wisdom to draw near to folly, nor cast aside delusion to pursue enlightenment.
To penetrate the Great Way is to transcend all measure; to commune with the Buddha-mind is to go beyond all limits.
Not entangled with either ordinary beings or sages, one who transcends them is called an Ancestor (Zu). Under the gate of an Ancestor, both ordinary beings and sages are left behind;
how could this be the same as the heterodox paths?

Mahāmati, I recall that once, while staying in a certain place, a world-theorizing Brahmin came to me without having first asked for an opportunity. He immediately asked me, "Gautama, is everything created?
I then replied, "To say 'everything is created' is the first kind of world-theory. He asked again, "Is everything uncreated? I then replied...
He said: "To say that 'everything is unconditioned' is the second worldly doctrine (*lokāyata*).
He then asked me: 'Is everything eternal? Is everything impermanent? Is everything born? Is everything unborn? I replied to him:
'These are the six worldly doctrines. Mahāmati, he then asked me: 'Are all things one? Are all things different? Are all things both [one and different]?"

"Are all things not simultaneous? Do all things arise and manifest due to various causes? (The Tang translation says: "Do all things arise and receive birth solely through various causes and conditions?
I then replied to him: "This is the eleventh world-theory, Mahāmati. He asked again: "Are all things indeterminate (*avyākṛta*) or are they determinate (*vyākṛta*)?
Is there a self (*ātman*) or is there no self? Does this world exist or does it not exist? There is...
"Is there another world, or is there no other world? Is there liberation, or is there no liberation?
Are all things momentary (the Wei translation says 'empty'), or are all things non-momentary? Is it space? Is it analytical cessation? Is it nirvāṇa, Gautama?"

"Is it created or uncreated? (The Tang translation states: "Are space, nirvana, and non-analytical cessation created or uncreated? "Is there an intermediate state (*antarābhava*) or is there no intermediate state?
Mahāmati, at that time I replied: "Brahmin, such statements are all merely worldly discourse (*lokavāda*);
they are not what I teach. These are your worldly doctrines. I teach only the various kinds of beginningless, false, and delusive habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*)."

All evils are the causes of the three realms of existence (*tridhātu*). Failing to realize that these are merely the manifestations of one’s own mind, one gives rise to false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) and clings to external natures, as is the case with the doctrines of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

They claim that knowledge arises from the conjunction of the self, the sense faculties, and their objects—as the [Chinese] translation says, "as the non-Buddhists teach, it arises from the harmony of the three:
the self, the faculties, and the objects. I do not hold such a view, O Brahmin. I do not teach a cause, nor do I teach no-cause; I teach only false conceptualization.
The designation of the nature of the grasper and the grasped as dependent origination cannot be realized by you or others who fall into the perception of a self-continuum (*ātma-saṃtati*).

(The Wei translation says: "I speak only of the appearance of objects as graspable and grasper arising from the discrimination of one's own mind. I say that all phenomena arise due to the collection of nominal causes and conditions;

this is not the realm of you Brahmins or others, for you have fallen into the view of a self. Mahāmati, there are not three kinds of nirvāṇa, space, and cessation; it is merely that their enumeration is threefold. (The Tang translation says...)

"Space, nirvāṇa, and non-analytical cessation have only three numerical designations; they originally possess no substantial reality. How much less can one speak of their being produced or unproduced? He replied:
"This is the Blessed One’s extensive elucidation of worldly doctrines (*lokavāda*), intended to ensure that future generations thoroughly understand their falsity and no longer associate with them.
The Brahmins claim that their ancestors were born from the mouth of Brahmā; thus, [they derive] from Brahmā..."

As for their clan, they are sometimes called *brahmins*, belonging to this very category. Each of their lineages possesses its own scriptures and treatises, which they have inherited through generations as their profession;
thus, they are skilled in debate. Relying on their own eloquence, they hastily questioned the World-Honored One whether all phenomena are "conditioned" (*saṃskṛta*) or "unconditioned" (*asaṃskṛta*).
That which is conditioned refers to the phenomena of formative activity (*saṃskṛtadharma*), while that which is unconditioned refers to the phenomena of non-formative activity (*asaṃskṛtadharma*).
In general, these views do not go beyond these two types. When one perceives that there is activity (*saṃskāra*), one regards it as permanent, as arising, as singular, or as co-existent.
When one perceives that there is no activity (*asaṃskāra*), one regards it as annihilated, as ceased, as distinct, or as non-co-existent.
This extends upward to the Brahma-heaven and downward to sentient beings; far back to eighty thousand kalpas, and fine down to...
From among these subtle atoms, they engage in fourfold logical discourses on existence and non-existence. Those who interrogate wisdom thoroughly investigate the causes of birth;
seeing that phenomena arise from various causes and conditions, they claim they are produced by a creator, and thus speak of this world and the next.
That which resembles having signs after the body has perished yet is signless is called the momentary flux of liberation;
that which resembles subsequent conditioned phenomena is called the three unconditioned dharmas—space, nirvāṇa, and cessation not through deliberation.

That which resembles pratyekabuddhas and śrāvakas further raises the question of the conditioned and the unconditioned, thereby revealing its original nature: to engage in "action" (karma) is to be deluded regarding the conditioned.
If one does not act, one enters into non-conceptualization (*asaṃjñā*). Again, he asked about the intermediate state (*antarābhava*) body:

it clearly clings to a conditioned self (*ātman*), yet it does not emerge from the domain of the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*). Those who study the Way do not recognize the Real, solely because they have from the beginning recognized the spirit-self (*vijñāna-ātman*).
Since time without beginning, this has been the root of birth and death; the deluded call this the "original person. This is precisely what it is.

Therefore, the Buddha replied: "Such worldly discourse is not what I teach. Even if you were able to explain various things with great clarity, as long as it does not transcend worldly phenomena, one who has transcended the three realms would never hold such views."
I have taught only that the various evils of beginningless, false, and delusive habitual tendencies are the cause of the three realms.
Since the desire realm, the form realm, and the formless realm differ in their states of defilement and purity, why are they all called "evil"?
When viewing the realm of form from the perspective of the desire realm, the realm of form is considered wholesome.
However, when viewing those who have transcended the three realms from the perspective of the three realms themselves, both the realms of form and formlessness are not yet purely wholesome.

If one cannot realize that all phenomena within the three realms are merely manifestations of one's own mind—that external phenomena lack intrinsic nature and are ultimately unattainable—one will give rise to delusion therein.

Conceptualization discriminates by taking various phenomena as its objects of focus; it may regard them as having agency or as being without agency, just as the various theories of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) maintain, asserting that consciousness arises from the conjunction of the three conditions: the self, the sense faculties, and their respective objects.
Therefore, all phenomena arise from causes and conditions. To claim that they arise from a cause is to say that primordial darkness (*ādikṛta*) gives rise to consciousness (*buddhi*).

To claim that they arise without a cause is to posit some other distinct cause. These are merely attachments to external natures, constructing the dualistic discrimination of existence and non-existence;
they all ultimately amount to frivolous conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*). I do not speak in such a manner. I teach that the various [phenomena] of the three realms...
Phenomena are manifestations of mind alone. Regarding all phenomena, I do not say they have a cause, nor do I say they are without cause;

I only say they are beginningless, false conceptualizations. Seeing the marks of objective realms as consisting of a grasper and a grasped, I declare that this nature of the grasped and the grasper is merely a name, a conventional designation established by the gathering of causes and conditions through which all phenomena arise. Relying upon...
That which arises through conditions is fundamentally rootless. Since its arising is non-arising, how could one perceive it as existing?

How could one perceive it as non-existing? Because one does not perceive it as existing, I do not say there is a cause; because one does not perceive it as non-existing, I do not say there is no cause.
This is not something for you, O Brahmin, nor for the disciples of other worldly philosophers, to fall into or accept from me.
This is knowable only by those who perceive and cling to the continuity of birth and death within a divine self (*ātman*).
You merely grasp at the characteristics of a self and the nature of the grasper and the grasped; you do not depart from the three realms and constantly fall into saṃsāra.

I, however, am simply non-self (*anātman*), free from the grasper and the grasped, and have transcended the three realms. How could you possibly fathom this? Furthermore, it is like space, unconditioned, and nirvāṇa.

The unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and the unconditioned that is cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*) exist within my Dharma; they are merely three in number and fundamentally lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).

How can one speak of their being "produced" or "unproduced"? It may still be permissible to engage in false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) regarding external phenomena by speaking of production and non-production;
however, as for the three unconditioned states, which transcend the characteristics of verbal expression and the characteristics of names and words—how could such [discourse apply]?
To use a mind subject to arising and ceasing to explain the Dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing—how could this be considered wisdom?

Therefore, the Buddha did not speak with him, but spoke instead to Mahāmati. The Third Patriarch’s *Inscription on Faith* says: "The Ultimate Way is not difficult; it only dislikes picking and choosing.
Simply do not harbor hatred or attachment, and all will be transparently clear. A difference of a hair’s breadth results in a gap as vast as heaven and earth. [Desiring...]
Attain manifestation; do not harbor notions of compliance or resistance. For compliance and resistance to contend with one another is a sickness of the mind.
Failing to recognize the profound essence, you labor in vain by merely contemplating stillness. Perfectly identical to the great void, it is neither deficient nor superfluous.

It is only because of grasping and rejecting that things fall short. Do not pursue conditioned objects; do not dwell in the patience of emptiness. With a single state of equanimity, all is obliterated of its own accord. Cease movement.
Returning to rest, the stillness becomes even more restless; one remains stuck in the two extremes, so how can one know the One Kind? If this One Kind is not penetrated, one fails in both places.
To dispel existence and non-existence, follow emptiness until all is empty. Excessive words and excessive deliberations only lead further away from correspondence with reality.
Beyond words and beyond thought, there is nowhere it does not penetrate. To return to the root is to attain the essential meaning; to follow after illumination is to lose the source.
A moment of returning-illumination surpasses the prior emptiness. That prior emptiness underwent transformation entirely due to deluded vision.

Do not seek the truth; you need only cease your views. When these two views do not abide, be careful not to pursue them. As soon as right and wrong arise, one becomes distracted and loses the mind. II.

Because of the one existence, do not seek even that one. When the single mind does not arise, the myriad dharmas are without fault. Where there is no fault, there are no dharmas; where there is no arising, there is no mind.
The capacity [of the mind] ceases because of objects, and objects sink as they follow the capacity. Objects exist because of the capacity, and the capacity exists because of objects.
If you wish to know these two segments, they are fundamentally a single emptiness. This single emptiness is identical to the two, equally containing the myriad phenomena. Do not see them as separate.

Whether refined or coarse, how could there be partiality? The essence of the Great Way is vast; it is neither easy nor difficult. With narrow views and doubt, one becomes increasingly anxious and ever more sluggish.
To grasp it is to lose its measure and inevitably enter a deviant path; to let it be of itself, its essence has neither going nor staying.
To act spontaneously is to accord with the Way; to roam at ease is to transcend affliction. To fixate one's thoughts is to deviate from the Truth;
to be mired in dullness is not good. It is not good to weary the spirit; what use is there for intimacy or estrangement? If you wish to attain the One Vehicle, do not loathe the six sense-objects.

If the six sense-objects are not loathed, they are identical to Perfect Enlightenment. The wise act without contrivance; the foolish bind themselves. The Dharma has no duality; yet in delusion, one clings to it with attachment. Taking...
To employ the mind to observe the mind—is this not a great error? Delusion gives rise to stillness and agitation; awakening is devoid of good and evil.
All dualistic extremes arise from one's own mental deliberations. They are like dreams, illusions, and flowers in the sky—why labor to grasp them?

Let gain and loss, right and wrong, be cast aside all at once. If the eyes do not sleep, all dreams vanish of their own accord. If the mind does not vary, the myriad dharmas are as one. Thus they are one.
The essence is profound and mysterious; in a state of stillness, one forgets all conditions. Viewing the myriad dharmas as equal, one returns to spontaneity.

One dissolves that which is used for comparison, such that nothing can be analogized. In stillness there is no stillness; in movement there is no movement. Since both are not established, how could there be a "one"?
Ultimate and exhaustive, it abides by no rules or regulations; the mind accords with equality, and all that is done ceases.

Doubt is completely purified, and right faith becomes harmonious and upright. Nothing remains; there is nothing to be remembered. It is empty yet luminous, spontaneous, and requires no exertion of mind or strength.
It is not a place for deliberation, difficult for the intellect and emotions to fathom. In the *tathatā* dharma-realm, there is neither other nor self. Essential.
It corresponds with urgency; it is simply called non-duality. Non-duality is universal sameness, encompassing all without exception.

The wise of the ten directions all enter this school. This school is neither constricted nor expansive: in a single thought-moment there are ten thousand years. It is neither here nor not here, yet it is before the eyes of those in the ten directions.
The smallest is identical to the great, as all boundaries and realms are forgotten and severed. The greatest is identical to the small, as no limits or surfaces are seen. Existence is...
This is non-existence. Non-existence is itself existence. If it were not thus, one would certainly have no need to maintain it. One is all; all is one.
If you can simply be like this, why worry that you will not reach completion? The mind of faith is non-dual; non-dual is the mind of faith.
The path of language is cut off; it is neither past, future, nor present. The Third Patriarch’s own transmission of the school pierces the mark with every word.
Much of this consists of words intended to guide the lost and warn against error; were these encountered by non-Buddhists, their very pores would break out in sweat from such false views.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, at that time the Lokāyatika Brahmin again questioned me, saying:
"Is the existence of the three realms of being caused by ignorance, craving, and karma, or is it without cause? I replied to him: "Both of these views are merely worldly discourse."
He asked again: "Do all natures enter into the specific and general characteristics? I replied: "This too is worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*), O Brahmin.
Even the mental stream’s false conceptualization of external objects is all worldly discourse. Furthermore, Mahāmati,"
At that time, the Lokāyatika Brahmin asked me again, "Is there anything that is not a doctrine? I am the master of all non-Buddhist paths;
I speak with various phrases and expressions, adorned with causes, conditions, and parables. I replied to him again, "There is that which does not belong to you.
It is neither a non-doctrine, nor is it something not spoken; yet it is not comprised of those various phrases and expressions."
"Not by means of analogies is it adorned. The brāhmaṇa asked, "What is that which is not worldly discourse, not a non-tenet, and not a non-exposition?
I replied to him, "Brāhmaṇa, there is a discourse that is not worldly, which you followers of the various external paths are unable to know."
Because of clinging to false imaginings regarding the unreality of external natures, one speaks of the non-arising of imagination.
By realizing that existence and non-existence are merely the manifestations of one’s own mind, imagination does not arise, one does not receive external objects, and imagination is forever stilled.
This is called the non-worldly discourse; this is my teaching and not yours, O Brahmin. To briefly explain that consciousness: if it comes...
Whether it be going, dying, or being born; whether it be pleasure or pain; whether it be immersion, seeing, contact, or attachment to various signs;
whether it be conjunction, continuity, craving, or clinging to causes—O Brāhmaṇa, such things as these are your worldly discourses (loka-vāda), not mine.
Mahāmati, the Brāhmaṇas of worldly discourse ask me such questions as: "I..."
He answered thus. The other then remained silent and withdrew without taking leave. (The Tang translation says: "Without questioning me regarding my own school’s true Dharma, he departed in silence.

He pondered his own point of realization and thought to himself: "The śramaṇa son of the Śākyas has strayed outside of my teachings; he speaks of non-arising, signlessness, and causelessness, awakening to the manifestation of signs from his own deluded imaginings.
[Deluded imaginings do not arise. (The Wei translation says: 'The śramaṇa son of the Śākyas is outside my Dharma and is to be pitied; he speaks of all dharmas...')"

There is no cause, no condition, and no characteristic of arising; it is taught that one merely perceives phenomena through the conceptual discrimination of one's own mind. If one can awaken to the fact that these perceived characteristics are but the vision of one's own mind, then such discrimination will not arise.

Mahāmati, this is precisely what you asked me earlier: "For what reason do I say that associating with worldly treatises and various forms of sophistry leads to the grasping of desire and not the grasping of the Dharma?"

The messenger said: "The non-Buddhist asked because the World-Honored One had spoken of the various evils—the causes of the three realms of existence—arising from beginningless false and delusive habitual tendencies.
He then further inquired whether ignorance, craving, and karma act as causes capable of producing the three realms of existence, or if there is, in fact, no cause at all.
He also asked whether all natures enter into the self-characteristics and common characteristics of the five aggregates. He also...
He understands that the various evils of the habitual tendencies of false conceptualization do not transcend the individual and common characteristics of the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).

Ignorance (*avidyā*) and craving (*tṛṣṇā*) are able to give rise to delusion and create karma, serving as the causes for the three realms of existence (*trai-dhātuka*). This is also roughly similar to what the Buddha usually taught.
These are non-Buddhists among those who study the Buddha-dharma; they are unable to abandon views regarding existence and non-existence, or causes and non-causes.

The locus where their views are discriminated is precisely the movement of mind-consciousness falsely calculating external objects. They give rise to discrimination without being separated from external realms.

Even if they speak of the fundamental internal specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa* and *sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), these are likewise the objects of the dharma-sphere (*dharmadhātu*). Therefore, they are all equally categorized [as such].
This is worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*). When the Brahmin’s skillful means were exhausted, he asked whether there existed anything that was not worldly discourse.
His intention was that all the terminology, various phrases, causes, and analogies employed by the various non-Buddhist outsiders (*tīrthika*) without exception emerge from within his own doctrine;
how, then, could there be anything that is not worldly discourse? The World-Honored One said that there is, but—
"It does not belong to you. That which belongs to you does not emerge as the formulation of propositions, reasons, examples, and so forth.
What belongs to me is neither 'doing' nor 'not doing'; it is neither a proposition nor a non-proposition; it is neither spoken nor unspoken.
It is fundamentally beyond verbal expression, yet it has never lacked the adornment of causes and analogies. This is not something that you, followers of external paths, are able to know. You—
The reason why [beings] do not know this is that they falsely conceptualize, cling to, and engage in the discursive proliferation (*prapañca*) of unreal external phenomena.
Therefore, what I call "non-worldly discourse" is that in which all false conceptualization and discrimination do not arise.
What is meant by "the non-arising of false conceptualization" does not refer to the existence of false conceptualization that must be extinguished; rather, it refers to awakening and realization.
All objects, whether present or absent, are manifestations of one’s own mind. There is no phenomenon outside the mind, and no mind outside phenomena.
Thus, truth and delusion are one; delusion and truth are one. Therefore, delusive thoughts do not arise from themselves.

If one perceives external objects as existing, then the mind and its objects stand in opposition, and delusion has not yet been fully extinguished. Only when both mind and object are forgotten does [delusion cease].
Externally, one does not perceive objects; internally, there is no experiencer. Although one may wish to differentiate external objects, fundamentally no external objects can be found.

Upon what, then, could deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*) rely to establish itself? Therefore, deluded conceptualization is forever stilled, abiding in its own place within the realm of quiescence—neither arising nor ceasing.
Thus, that which neither arises nor ceases does not give rise to differentiation; it transcends [all such constructs].
Transcending the three realms—this is called the non-worldly discourse. This is my teaching; it does not belong to you. To state it briefly:
your teaching does not depart from the various consciousnesses, the mind, and the mental factors as they flow on.

Within these, one falsely discriminates regarding coming and going, birth and death, pleasure and pain, sinking and emerging, manifesting and perceiving, or contact with various marks, whether through their combination or otherwise.
The continuity [of existence] does not depart from the seven consciousnesses. If craving and attachment serve as conditions, it does not depart from the six consciousnesses.
If the primordial darkness (*ādikṣaya*) serves as the cause, it briefly approximates the eight consciousnesses.

Your claim that the causes of delusion, craving, and karma—the natures of all things—enter into their own and common characteristics, is thus a thesis established through such inferential discrimination. You maintain the existence of a self (*ātman*) and its transmigration.
"The three realms—this is called worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*). It is not my teaching. Upon hearing this, the Brahmin thought, "This is not the Dharma of worldly discourse;
I must now ask how my own school’s true Dharma is established. He then departed in silence, reflecting on the point where he himself had attained understanding.
However, while he was able to penetrate his ordinary views regarding existence and non-existence, he could not penetrate the state of non-existence.
The intent of this passage is as follows: [The opponent] conversely claims that what the śramaṇa perceives lies outside the scope of my understanding.
He asserts that all dharmas are without cause, without condition, and lack the characteristic of arising; thus, it would follow that everything is non-existent.

Furthermore, he states that when one realizes that the perceived marks are but the manifestations of one's own mind, then conceptual discrimination no longer arises. Yet, if there are already these perceived marks of one's own mind, they are nonetheless "marks."
"This is precisely birth. Furthermore, you say that "delusive conceptualization does not arise"—this is truly something I cannot understand.

Judging by the meaning of these words, it seems you are merely clinging to various phrases and flavors of the false views of existence and non-existence, and are unable to believe in or accept the True Dharma of dependent origination and non-arising.
That you continue through the various realms of existence without attaining liberation is indeed deeply pitiable. Thus it is said.
Therefore, I say that those who habitually study worldly treatises grasp only at desire and do not grasp the Dharma; this is precisely what is meant.
Formerly, the seventeenth patriarch, the Venerable Saṃghanandin, ordained the youth Dharmadatta, changing his name to Gayāśata.
He transmitted the verse of the Eye of the Dharma, which says: "The ground of the mind is fundamentally without birth; the ground arises from conditions. Through conditions, seeds..."
They do not obstruct one another. It is the same with flowers and fruits. Later, the eighteenth patriarch, Gayasata, entrusted the Dharma to Kumārajīva. He spoke in verse:

"When there is a seed and a field of consciousness, Causes and conditions can cause the sprout to emerge. Without hindering one another within these conditions, That which should arise does not arise.
This is the meaning of the non-arising of dependent origination. How could this be something that non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) are capable of [understanding]?
"Profound indeed!
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, what is the meaning of the phrases regarding the grasping of desire and the grasping of the Dharma?
The Buddha told Mahāmati, "Excellent, excellent! You are able, for the sake of future sentient beings, to contemplate and inquire about such phrases."
“Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon this; I shall explain it for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “Yes, I shall receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati:
“That which is called ‘craving’ consists of grasping, rejecting, contact, and savoring (the Chinese text says: that which is called ‘wealth’ can be touched, received, grasped, and savored).
It is being bound by and attached to external objects, falling into the views of the two extremes, and further giving rise to the aggregates of suffering—birth, old age, and sickness.”
Death, sorrow, lamentation, suffering, and despair—all such afflictions arise from craving (*tṛṣṇā*). This is due to associating with worldly treatises and those who follow worldly treatises;
I and all the Buddhas call this "greed. This is what is called "embracing desire and not embracing the Dharma. Mahāmati, what is meant by "embracing the Dharma"?
It means skillfully awakening to the fact that [the world] is merely the manifestation of one's own mind, and perceiving the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*).

Furthermore, when the characteristics of the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) are realized, false conceptualization (*vikalpa*) does not arise. One skillfully knows the progressively higher stages (*uttarottarabhūmi*), transcends mind, thought, and consciousness (*cittamanomanovijñāna*), and receives the empowerment (*abhiṣeka*) of the wisdom of all Buddhas.

Fully possessing and encompassing the ten inexhaustible phrases, one attains mastery over all phenomena without effortful development (as previously stated, this is "mastery of one's own mind through effortless practice"). This is called the Dharma; that is to say, not falling into any [extreme] views.
"Mahāmati, all that is false, all conceptual constructions, all natures, and all dual extremes—many foolish outsiders, Mahāmati, fall into these two extremes of either permanence or annihilation;
they are not wise men. Those who accept the doctrine of causelessness give rise to the view of permanence.
Those who hold that external causes, destructive causes, and conditions lack intrinsic nature give rise to the view of annihilation. Mahāmati, I do not perceive any arising."
Because it abides in cessation, it is called "Dharma. Mahāmati, these are what are termed desire and Dharma;
you and the other Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice and study them.
The Master said: "The World-Honored One has often taught that one must be careful not to study or associate with the various treatises and diverse discourses of the world.
If one does so, it will lead to the grasping of desire and not the grasping of the Dharma. I have already answered this in detail previously.
Now, Mahāmati wishes to further distinguish the meanings of these terms: what is meant by the term 'desire,' and what is meant by the term 'Dharma'? It was not [the case that he did not ask].
Just as non-Buddhists merely contemplate their own conventional systems without consulting the True Dharma, the Buddha commended [the practitioner] for this reason.

He then said: "The greedy person is one who has grasping and abandoning, contact and sensation; they become attached to external objects and give rise to discrimination, falling into the two views of existence and non-existence.
Thus, they lose the right path for themselves, and the succession of various realms of existence continues."
One is not liberated from the aggregate of suffering—birth, old age, sickness, death, sorrow, lamentation, pain, and despair. All such afflictions arise from a single thought of craving (*tṛṣṇā*).

That is to say: ignorance conditions volitional formations (*saṃskāra*); volitional formations condition consciousness (*vijñāna*); consciousness conditions craving, grasping, and clinging, leading even to the suffering of birth, old age, sickness, and death.
This is due to that craving for various phrases and expressions, and the habitual pursuit of worldly treatises along with their associated practices.
Those who associate with the proponents of worldly treatises—myself and all the Buddhas have transcended the world—are said to belong entirely to the realm of greed;

they partake only of the food of desire and not of the food of Dharma. What is called "Dharma" refers to the skillful realization that all phenomena are manifestations of mind alone, that external natures have no inherent existence, and that there is neither grasping nor abandoning.
Contact is without flavor. By realizing the selflessness of persons, one abandons the afflictive obscurations; by realizing the selflessness of phenomena, one abandons the cognitive obscurations.
Not only do the delusory thoughts that conceptualize external objects cease to arise, but even the delusory thoughts that conceptualize internal phenomena cease to arise.
The innate ignorance is gradually severed until it is completely exhausted, whereby one enters from one stage to the next.

In the progressively higher stages (*uttarottara-bhūmi*), one becomes detached from mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), whereby the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are transformed into wisdoms (*jñāna*). Specifically, the first five consciousnesses are transformed into the Wisdom of Accomplishing What Is to Be Done (*kṛtyānuṣṭhāna-jñāna*);
the sixth consciousness is transformed into the Wisdom of Wondrous Observation (*pratyavekṣaṇā-jñāna*); the seventh consciousness is transformed into the Wisdom of Equality (*samatā-jñāna*);
and the eighth consciousness is transformed into the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom (*ādarśa-mahājñāna*). This continues until the attainment of the Great Perfect Mirror Wisdom.
This is the stage of the Dharma-Cloud Empowerment (*dharmameghābhiṣeka*), wherein one possesses all the wisdom of the Buddhas.

The Buddhas personally pour water upon one’s crown; their lights reflecting one another, they confer the rank of Tathāgata. Thus, one becomes fully endowed with the ten inexhaustible phrases (*daśākṣayapada*):

first, the inexhaustibility of the realm of sentient beings; second, the inexhaustibility of the realm of worlds; third, the inexhaustibility of the realm of empty space; fourth, the inexhaustibility of the realm of phenomena (*dharmadhātu*).
1. Exhaustion; 2. the inexhaustibility of the five nirvāṇa realms; 3. the inexhaustibility of the appearance of Buddhas; 4. the inexhaustibility of the Tathāgata’s wisdom;
5. the inexhaustibility of the objects of the mind; 6. the inexhaustibility of that which is entered by Buddha-wisdom; 7. the inexhaustibility of the wisdom that turns the wheel of Dharma.
To encompass all within all phenomena, to possess mastery over one's own mind through effortless practice—this is called [the inexhaustible].

For the sake of the Dharma: if others perceive all views, all falsities, all conceptual constructions (*parikalpita*), all natures (*svabhāva*), and all dualistic extremes as being entirely false and conceptualized appearances from time immemorial—not departing from the transformations of mind, thought, and consciousness—and are able to skillfully awaken to the manifestation of their own mind (*svacittadṛśyamātra*), they themselves will not fall into those various forms of discursive proliferation (*prapañca*). Those outsiders...

The teaching of various dharmas does not go beyond the two views of annihilationism and eternalism. It mostly causes deluded people to fall into these two extremes, whereas those who possess wisdom do not fall into the two extremes.
Only the ignorant accept that nihilistic theory (ahetuvāda), reckoning that the four great elements are not produced from causes;
they claim that things have always been thus, thereby giving rise to the view of eternalism. Or, they may reckon that external derived matter...
