Because they are destroyed and do not arise again, they claim that the nature of causes and conditions is fundamentally non-existent, thereby giving rise to the view of annihilationism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*).

Although their treatises are numerous, they generally do not exceed these two [views]. They perceive only the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing in external phenomena, yet they fail to see that intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is fundamentally without arising or ceasing;
therefore, their teachings cannot be called the True Dharma (*saddharma*). I, however, am merely unattached to...
Regarding marks (*lakṣaṇa*): one does not perceive arising, abiding, change, or cessation as obtainable. From what source could the two views of annihilationism and eternalism arise?
Thus, all awakened understanding does not fall into views; all reality does not fall into falsehood;
all correct reflection does not fall into delusive conceptualization; and all that lacks intrinsic nature does not fall into [the notion of] a nature. All...
The Middle Way does not fall into the two extremes; it is that which has been taught by the Buddhas of the past and is called the "Dharma-food.
This is the meaning of the two terms "desire" and "Dharma. You and the other bodhisattvas should practice and study this.
This is to cause future sentient beings to clearly recognize where the True Dharma resides, so that they will not be deluded by worldly discourses. Huangbo said:
"People of the present day merely desire to acquire much knowledge and understanding, seeking extensively for literary meanings, and call this 'cultivation.

They do not realize that such abundant knowledge and understanding instead result in obstruction; it is like knowing only how to give much fresh butter and milk to a child to eat, without knowing how to digest them."
They do not digest it at all and remain entirely ignorant. All practitioners of the Three Vehicles are of this same nature; they are all called those who cannot digest their food.
That which is known and understood but not digested is entirely poisonous medicine; it is all gathered within the realm of arising and ceasing.
Within True Suchness (Tathatā), such things do not exist at all. Therefore it is said: "Within the treasury of my King, there is no such blade. From before...
All points of conceptual understanding must be entirely set aside, so that there is emptiness without further discrimination;
this is the empty *tathāgatagarbha*. Within the *tathāgatagarbha*, not even a speck of dust can exist; this is the destruction of existence.
When the Dharma King appears in the world, he also says, "At the place of Dīpaṃkara Buddha, I did not obtain even the slightest dharma. This statement...

This is solely to empty your emotional understandings and cognitive measures. Merely by dissolving all emotions within and without until they are exhausted, such that there is no longer any dependence or attachment, one becomes a person of "no affairs.
The teaching-nets of the Three Vehicles are merely medicines prescribed according to individual capacities; what is taught varies according to what is appropriate for each.
If you can simply understand this, you will not be deluded. First, you must not [cling] to a single capacity or a single...
Those who guard the boundaries of the objective realm interpret according to the literal text. Why is this so? Because, in reality, there is no fixed dharma that the Tathāgata can speak of.
In our school, we do not discuss such matters; we simply know that when the mind is stilled, one rests in peace, and there is no further need for retrospective or prospective deliberation.
As Huangbo said: "If even the discussions of the internal teachings (Buddhism) must not be clung to, how much more so the various worldly doctrines?"
Is there anything that does not benefit body and mind?
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"I gather in sentient beings; relying on the precepts, I subdue all evils; through wisdom, I extinguish false views; the three liberations increase. All worldly treatises and the doctrines of external paths are empty."
Those who falsely speak and falsely see regarding the agent and the acted-upon have no school of their own; I alone possess my own school. Free from agent and acted-upon, I teach it to my disciples.
It is far removed from all worldly treatises. The mind-only is invisible; one does not perceive the duality of the grasping subject and the grasped object as having intrinsic nature.
Being free from both extremes of annihilationism and eternalism, this continues until the cessation of the mind’s流转 (pravṛtti). This, then, is...
Regarding those for whom worldly discourse and false conceptualization do not arise: such persons perceive their own mind. That which comes arises as an object;
that which goes does not manifest as an object. Clearly understanding this coming and going, false conceptualization no longer arises.
[Concepts such as] permanence and impermanence, the created and the uncreated, this world and the other world—all these are merely the common currency of worldly discourse.
Tong said: "The World-Honored One stated that those various non-Buddhists have no doctrine of their own; thus, he reiterated his intent in verse, saying:
'I discipline sentient beings; with precepts I subdue all evils, and with wisdom I extinguish all views.'"
This causes the three liberations to flourish; this is the Dharma I have taught.
As for all worldly discourses on existence, non-existence, and so forth, these are all the false and deluded teachings of the outsiders (*tīrthika*).

Because they recklessly speculate that causes and effects possess an agent who acts and an object upon which action is performed, they take only deluded external objects as their tenets; in reality, they have no school of their own.
I alone establish the single mind as my own doctrine. I do not cling to agent or action, and I am free from those false views regarding causes.
For the sake of my disciples, I teach that the worldly discourses of non-Buddhists only provide sustenance for desire and do not provide the sustenance of the Dharma.
You must be careful not to study or associate with them; it is right to distance yourselves from all such worldly discourses. As for those worldly discourses—
"Because there is no self-communication" means that one has not skillfully observed the manifestation within one's own mind—the realm where only mind exists and nothing else does.
Because of the mind that is free from the two extremes, the nature of both grasper and grasped is absent. Thus, one is detached from both nihilism and eternalism;
falling neither into existence nor non-existence, nor into spatial location, this is the very essence of one's own mind. That [essence] is merely...

One perceives the fundamental substance. From the failure to penetrate one's own school’s tenets up to all manner of false conceptualizations, the mind revolves according to objects, wandering without ceasing.
Not only is it called "chasing after things" when it grasps at external natures, but even the conceptualization of the characteristics of phenomena is a flow of the mental faculty;
in the end, it all reverts to worldly discourse (*loka-vāda*). If one can observe that these delusive thoughts lack intrinsic nature, [then...]
Being turned by what is to be transformed, such a person sees that which is the manifestation of their own mind;

it is fundamentally quiescent from the beginning and fundamentally unmoving—this is what is called the "penetration of one's own school" (*svapratyātma-gati*). How could non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) ever possess this?

Yet, why is it that non-Buddhists are turned by false conceptualization (*parikalpita*)? It is because they do not understand the characteristics of arising and ceasing; therefore, those who come perceive causes.
When arising occurs, the departing observer sees the cessation of the fruit; yet they do not realize that all phenomena appear for a moment like lightning and then swiftly perish.

When they depart, they no longer appear, being fundamentally non-existent from the start. If one can thus clearly understand in accordance with reality that the characteristics of coming, going, arising, and ceasing are inherently unborn from the beginning, from where could discrimination possibly arise? When deluded thoughts do not arise, the mind does not undergo transmigration.
This is precisely the dharma that is neither born nor extinguished. That which I have taught as having "the single mind" as its fundamental tenet is this very point.
As for permanence and impermanence, action and non-action, this world and other worlds, and so forth—[all are subsumed therein].
In sum, they do not transcend the two extremes of existence and non-existence; these are merely the characteristics of coming and going within the mundane world.
Yet the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) cling to them as being truly existent. All of these schools establish their tenets based on worldly conventions;

each considers itself to have attained universal understanding, unaware that its views are false and illusory. May the disciples of the Inner Teaching (*ādhyātmika-śāsana*) likewise be cautious regarding what they study! — *Seng* (the Monk)
He asked Huangbo, "What is the conventional truth? Huangbo said, "Why do you engage in such entangling talk? It is fundamentally pure;
what need is there for words, speech, questions, or answers? Simply being without any mind is called untainted wisdom (*anāsrava-jñāna*).
Whether you are walking, standing, sitting, or lying down every day, and in all your speech, do not cling to conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). Even when speaking or blinking an eye..."
All are equally untainted (*anāsrava*). As we move toward the future age of the Dharma’s decay (*mofa*), there will be many who study the Way of Chan;
yet they all remain attached to all sounds and forms. Why do you not let your mind become as empty as space, like withered wood or a stone?
It would only correspond slightly to the analogy of cold ashes from which the fire has departed;
were it otherwise, you would one day be subjected to all the tortures of Old Yama. Alas! To continue through the various realms of existence without attaining liberation is so terrifying.
Why is it that students merely crave the flavor of words?
(Wei: Chapter Six, "Nirvāṇa").
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, regarding what is called 'nirvāṇa,' what dharma do you designate as nirvāṇa?
For the various non-Buddhists each give rise to their own deluded imaginings. The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Listen attentively, listen attentively..."

"Listen well and reflect upon it; I shall explain it for you. Just as the various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) falsely conceptualize nirvāṇa, their conceptualizations do not accord with the true nature of nirvāṇa.

(The Tang translation reads: "Just as the various non-Buddhists differentiate nirvāṇa, none of them accord with the characteristics of nirvāṇa. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Yes, I shall receive your instruction.

The Buddha told Mahāmati, "There are some non-Buddhists who perceive the cessation of the aggregates (skandhas), elements (dhātus), and sense-bases (āyatanas), and the detachment from the realm of desire."
Dharmas are impermanent. The categories of mind and mental factors do not arise; one does not dwell upon objects of the past, future, or present.

All aggregates of sensation are exhausted, like the extinguishing of a lamp or the destruction of a seed; thus, false conceptualization does not arise. Those who perceive this state conceive of it as nirvāṇa.
However, Mahāmati, it is not by the mere destruction of what is seen that one names it nirvāṇa.
Tong said: "In response to this, the Buddha told Mahāmati that nirvana, space, and cessation are not three distinct entities;
it is merely that their enumeration is threefold. He never revealed that nirvana reaches a state of ultimate unity, for he feared it might be confused with the views of non-Buddhist paths."

Therefore, Mahāmati asked what kind of dharma must be present for it to be called *nirvāṇa*. He further inquired whether the various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas), who each give rise to false conceptualizations and discriminations, can attain true *nirvāṇa*.
Those various non-Buddhists' conceptualizations of *nirvāṇa* do not accord with the characteristics of *nirvāṇa*.
Moreover, the true nature of *nirvāṇa* is beyond the reach of their false conceptualizations. Thus, the World-Honored One [spoke as follows].
Each of these is exposed for its faults, while those within my own teaching who designate [the cessation of suffering] as "nirvāṇa" are shown [to be correct].
In general, non-Buddhists lack any self-consistent realization; some non-Buddhists, however, [speak of] the cessation of the five aggregates, the six sense bases, and the eighteen elements.
One is freed from the fetters of the desire realm and does not crave sensory objects. Seeing that all phenomena are impermanent, the mind and its mental factors do not manifest before one.
Maintaining one-pointedness of mind, one perceives no marks of the three periods of time—past, future, or present.
This arises because the aggregates of sensation are exhausted; thus, the fundamental principle is simply non-appropriation of everything. Therefore...
One suppresses and prevents the various desires for the objects of the aggregates, elements, and sense bases from arising.
This is like extinguishing a lamp so that it does not shine again, or like destroying a seed so that it does not sprout again. No grasping arises and no conceptualization is produced;
this is merely the cessation and extinction of all objective spheres, which is termed "non-arising. This is precisely what is meant in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* by "permanently..."
The cessation of dependence is that to which one takes refuge. The teachers of these non-Buddhist schools conceive of this as *nirvāṇa*.
For they take the mere seeing of cessation to be *nirvāṇa*, and thus do not know the wondrous fruit of *nirvāṇa*: the transformation of all arising and ceasing into non-arising and non-ceasing;
wherein in every moment there is no characteristic of arising, and in every moment there is no characteristic of ceasing. All that appears before one—
"All things are quiescent; one does not perceive any mark of cessation that can be apprehended. How could the mere perception of the disintegration of all phenomena be called *nirvāṇa*?
This is the first way in which these non-Buddhists conceptualize *nirvāṇa* and fail to accord with its true nature.
Devaputra’s treatise identifies this as the first of the Small Vehicle (Hīnayāna) and non-Buddhist (Tīrthika) views. Huangbo said:
Ordinary people grasp at objects; practitioners of the Way grasp at the mind. When both mind and objects are forgotten, that is the True Dharma.

Delusory objects are still easy to transcend, but forgetting the mind is most difficult. People do not dare to forget the mind, fearing they will fall into emptiness where there is no place to grasp or seek.
They do not know that emptiness is fundamentally empty and that there is only the single True Dharma-realm. This nature of numinous awareness has, from time without beginning, been...
It shares the same lifespan as empty space; it has never been born and never perished; it has never existed and never been non-existent; it has never been defiled and never been pure;
it has never been clamorous and never been silent; it has never been young and never been old. It has no location and no interior or exterior;
it has no quantity and no form or appearance; it has no color or image and no sound. It cannot be sought and cannot be...
Seek it! It cannot be cognized by wisdom; it cannot be grasped through language; it cannot be encountered through objective phenomena;
it cannot be attained through effort. All Buddhas and Bodhisattvas, as well as all wriggling and moving sentient beings, share this same nature of Great Nirvana.
This nature is the mind; the mind is the Buddha; the Buddha is the Dharma. To depart from this for even a single thought-moment—
All that is truly but deluded thought. One cannot seek mind further through mind; one cannot seek Buddha further through Buddha;
one cannot seek Dharma further through Dharma. Therefore, the practitioner of the Way simply remains directly beneath without mind, attaining realization through silent resonance alone.
If one can penetrate Huangbo’s words, one will immediately know where the true reality of Nirvana resides.

Mahāmati, some consider that moving from one direction to another constitutes liberation; others hold that it is like the ceasing of wind, wherein the perceptions of the body and its objective spheres are extinguished.
Or again, they may consider that the destruction of the vision of the perceiver and the perceived constitutes liberation.

Or they may conceive the notion of liberation regarding the permanent and the impermanent (the Chinese text says: "some say that not seeing the perceiver and the perceived, or that not giving rise to the views of permanence and impermanence, constitutes it"). Or they may see various marks and perceptions as being what brings about [liberation].
Having reflected thus upon the cause of the arising of suffering, they fail to correctly discern that which is the manifestation of their own minds;
fearing signs, they perceive the signless and, developing deep attachment to it, conceive the notion that this is nirvana.
Tong said: "The notion of nirvana held by non-Buddhists does not transcend the view of annihilationism. As the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: 'Some reckon that it is the extinction of the body;

some desire the extinction of craving; some [desire] the extinction of suffering; some [desire] the extinction of ultimate bliss; or the extinction of ultimate equanimity. This is the general outline.
The state described in the preceding section—'separation from desire'—refers to the non-Buddhist path of the extinction of craving. This follows from...

"From direction to direction" refers to the calculation of the extinction of the body, as taught by the second type of non-Buddhist, the Lokāyata teacher. "Not seeing the perceiver and the perceived" is the extinction of ultimate bliss.

"Not giving rise to the conceptualization of permanence or impermanence" is the extinction of ultimate equanimity. "Fearing signs that invite suffering" is the extinction of the exhaustion of suffering.
These are merely presented here in a varied arrangement. "From direction to direction" refers to the discourse of the second non-Buddhist, the Lokāyata teacher. This is the most [extreme].
The first [element] is the various directions (*diś*). From the directions, the people of the world are born; from people, heaven and earth arise.
When heaven and earth perish and vanish, they return to those [directions]. They claim that the directions are eternal and designate them as the cause of *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding the cessation of the perception of the body’s objective sphere, like the stilling of the wind—this is the doctrine of the third non-Buddhist school, the Vāyulakṣaṇa teachers (the Wind-Sage masters). They maintain that wind can produce things and that wind can [dissolve them].
When killing a living being, the body and its objects undergo birth and cessation, yet the wind has no birth or cessation; thus wind is said to be eternal and is the cause of *nirvāṇa*.
Now, when these are unified as one, it is still said that "one abandons birth and moves toward birth," which is merely like the wind momentarily ceasing.

As for the destruction of the perceiver and the perceived, is this not nearly equivalent to the separation from the perceiver and the perceived? That [state] pertains only to the perceiver and the perceived.
Their views are suppressed and do not prevail; they incline toward the bliss of nirvana, unaware that there are characteristics of pleasure or suffering.

This is the extreme of the extinction of non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). According to the arguments of the Vedic masters, many statements such as "the Great Lotus gave birth to Brahmā" are unscriptural and do not accord with this [teaching].
One who does not give rise to conceptual discrimination regarding the views of permanence and impermanence—does this not approximate [the truth]?
Regarding their departure from the views of annihilationism and eternalism: they hold that suffering and pleasure are impermanent, while only equanimity (*upekṣā*) is permanent.
They revere this equanimity and forget [all else], failing to form any discriminative views. This is the extreme abandonment and cessation of the non-Buddhists.

The treatise states that according to the fifth class of non-Buddhist teachers, the followers of Īśvara, the form [of the self] is invisible and pervades all places, and is capable of producing [all things].
That which gives rise to the myriad things is permanent; that which is produced is impermanent.

To think that such [distinctions] approximate the truth regarding various characteristics and perceptions is to differentiate various distinct marks that give rise to all suffering, without realizing that these marks are manifestations of one's own mind.

Thus, they fear conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) while clinging to the signless (*animitta*); they loathe suffering and sever its accumulation (*samudaya*), yet they crave and are biased toward emptiness (*śūnyatā*).
This is the non-Buddhist path of the extinction of suffering (*duḥkhakṣayavyantībhāva*). The *Śāstra* considers this to be the teaching of the naked ascetic (*nirgrantha*) heretical masters.
They practice austerities precisely because they wish to escape from suffering. Their bodies belong to the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), comprising both humans and devas; they are driven by desire.

The total elimination of suffering belongs to the first dhyāna; the inclusion of the complete exhaustion of suffering belongs to the second dhyāna; the inclusion of ultimate bliss belongs to the third dhyāna;
and the inclusion of ultimate equanimity pertains to both the fourth dhyāna and the two formless realms. These practitioners enter the realm of the non-conceptualizing outsiders (*asaṃjñisattva*).
What is called "exhausting the seven limits" means that what appears before them is extinguished; they all regard annihilation after death as *nirvāṇa*. This is based on their own observations.
The locus is also not ordinary; yet, how can one avoid remaining within the triple world? A monk asked Yunmen, "If one does not give rise to a single thought, is there still transgression?
Yunmen said, "Mount Sumeru. Baiyun ended with a verse: "Mount Sumeru fills the universe; Even the Great Compassionate One with a thousand eyes cannot see through it.
Unless one knows how to ride the ox backward by oneself," [The rest of the verse is omitted as per the instruction to provide only the translation.]
Born, one does not cling to following after others. A Celestial Youth’s verse says: "Not giving rise to a single thought is Mount Sumeru.
Shaoyang’s Dharma-giving has no stinginess; if you are willing to come, he hands it over with both hands. If you intend to go, ten thousand fathoms deep, it cannot be grasped.
The vast blue sea is wide; the white clouds are idle. Do not allow even a hair’s breadth of attachment to exist between them.
Even the simulated crowing of a rooster cannot deceive me; I refuse to let you pass through the barrier with such vagueness.

Although those various non-Buddhists may extinguish all thoughts until they reach a state of profound stillness and immovability, this too is merely the simulated crowing of a rooster. How could it be considered true Nirvana?

Some perceive that the internal and external phenomena possess a nature—whether in their specific or general characteristics, whether in the past, future, or present—that is indestructible, and thus conceive the notion of *nirvāṇa*.
Others claim that the self, persons, sentient beings, life-span, and all phenomena are subject to destruction, and thus conceive the notion of *nirvāṇa*.
Or, because their wisdom has been scorched by the evil of non-Buddhist paths (tīrthika), they perceive a distinction between primordial nature (prakṛti) and the person (puruṣa).

They hold that what is produced by the person is called primordial nature. Like those who speculate on the primordial darkness (avyakta), they consider the transformation of the qualities (guṇa-pariṇāma) to be the agent;

they conceive of this as nirvāṇa. Or they say it is the exhaustion of merit and demerit (puṇya-apuṇya)—as the Wei translation notes: "The non-Buddhists say that because such offenses are exhausted, merit is also exhausted, and this is called nirvāṇa. Or they say:
They think that all afflictions are exhausted; some claim it is through wisdom (the Tang translation says: "or they reckon that afflictions are exhausted not by means of wisdom").
Some perceive Īśvara as the true creator of birth and death, and conceive the notion of nirvāṇa. Others claim that birth and death arise from one another in succession and have no other cause.
Thus they are attached to causes, and because of their ignorance, they are unable to realize this; for they do not know.
One forms the conception of *nirvāṇa*.

It is said in general that to perceive that all internal and external phenomena possess an indestructible nature is as described in the *Lengyan jing* (Śūraṅgama Sūtra) regarding the fourfold doctrine of permanence:
internal phenomena, such as the six sense organs, mind, and objects, circulate in a cycle without loss; external phenomena, such as the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), are likewise so. All...

All [of these] take the body as their constant basis, reckoning the subtle atoms (*paramāṇu*) to be eternal and indestructible; this is the "eternalist view" (*śāśvatadṛṣṭi*) of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).

The *Śāstra* maintains that this refers to the seventh school, the Vaiśeṣika masters, who teach: "The self (*ātman*), the person (*pudgala*), sentient beings (*sattva*), and life-span (*jīvita*) all perish.

This is the realization and awakening to the four marks of the exhaustion of cessation. That is to say: seeing suffering (*duḥkha*) and abandoning its origin (*samudaya*); realizing cessation (*nirodha*) and cultivating the path (*mārga*). [This state] abides in cessation.
To have already ceased and no longer advance further is the realization of the śrāvaka of fixed nature; it likewise pertains to a one-sided emptiness and is not true awakening.

The *Śāstra* identifies this as the teaching of the eighth type of practitioner, the "Teacher of Asceticism" (*duḥkha-caryā-vādin*). Alternatively, it refers to those whose wisdom has been scorched and extinguished by the fires of the evil views of non-Buddhists;
this is rooted in the view of self-nature (*svabhāva*) and the view of a self (*ātman*), as well as the notion of a "person" (*pudgala*).
This is the first of the sixteen views. It holds that there is a slight interval between the self-nature (*svabhāva*) and the person (*puruṣa*).
It asserts that the divine self of the person can produce the self-nature; that which is produced by this person is called the self-nature.
This is analogous to the comparison made with the primordial darkness (*avyakta*) giving rise to consciousness (*buddhi*). *Guṇa* refers to atoms (*paramāṇu*) and that which is dependent.

It is the same. This is precisely the view that clings to the existence of a self (ātman) which pervades the ten directions of the world, holding that all sentient beings flow forth as a single class from within one's own body.
The treatise identifies this as the teaching of the ninth non-Buddhist school concerning the retinue of women;
it claims that Maheśvara created eight daughters who gave birth to the devas, nāgas, the eight classes of beings, and so forth, and takes this to be nirvāṇa.
The *pāṣaṇḍas* (heretics) are laughable. Some claim that the exhaustion of merit and non-merit means that both sin and virtue are empty;

this is precisely the denial of cause and effect by the non-Buddhist heretics. The *Śāstra* identifies them as the tenth type of non-Buddhist teacher who propounds the practice of asceticism (*duḥkhacaryā*).

Others claim that because afflictions (*kleśa*) are exhausted by relying on wisdom, [one attains liberation]; [the text] says: "In the Tang [translation], it states that one does not attain the severance of all afflictions through the cultivation of wisdom."
Afflictions are exhausted of themselves. When this correct calculation of the number of thread-balls reaches its ultimate limit, one matures and attains the Way spontaneously.
Affliction and wisdom are mutually dependent. The *Śāstra* considers this to be the teaching of the eleven non-Buddhist masters of the *Viśuddhāloka-śāstra*.
Alternatively, seeing that Maheśvara is able to create sentient beings, they consequently calculate that this deity is the true sovereign who presides over human birth and death.
This is precisely the view that one’s own body and mind flow forth from that [source], and that the empty space of the ten directions all arise from it.

The treatise attributes this to the Mātara-śāstra masters among the twelve non-Buddhist schools, who claim that sentient beings are produced from one another in succession, dying here and being born there in an unceasing cycle of saṃsāra; that for eighty thousand kalpas they have existed without a cause.
Because [they believe] it exists inherently, they claim that birth and death have no other cause. They do not realize that such clinging itself is the cause of birth and death.
Those non-Buddhists, being ignorant and deluded, cannot perceive that ignorance, craving, and karma are its root.
Because they do not know this, they claim that birth and death are causeless; they then point to this lack of cause as being *nirvāṇa*.
The *Lun* (Treatise) attributes this to the teachings of the Nirgrantha masters. These seven types [of views] collectively do not transcend the two views of annihilationism and eternalism;
they cannot be spoken of in terms of the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñānadarśana*). National Teacher Zhong asked a monk, "From where have you come? The monk replied, "From the South.
The Master asked, "How do the teachers of the South instruct people? The monk said, "The teachers of that region simply..."
The following shows that for the student, mind itself is Buddha. "Buddha" has the meaning of awakening. You now fully possess the nature of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
This nature is well able to raise the eyebrows, blink the eyes, and engage in coming and going; it pervades throughout the entire body.
When the head is touched, the head knows; when the foot is touched, the foot knows. Therefore, it is called "Perfect Universal Knowledge" (Samyak-saṃbuddha).
Apart from this, there is no other Buddha. This body is subject to arising and ceasing, yet the nature of the mind has never arisen or ceased since beginningless time.
As for the arising and ceasing of the body, it is like a dragon shedding its bones, a snake sloughing its skin, or a person leaving an old dwelling; thus, the body is impermanent.
"Its nature is eternal. Such is the explanation regarding wood given by those of the south. The Master said:
"If that were so, there would be no distinction between this and the non-Buddhist Śreṇika. He claimed: 'Within this body of mine there is a divine spirit (ātman).
This spirit is capable of knowing pain and itching. When the body perishes, the spirit departs, just as a householder leaves when his house is burning.'"
"Go out! If the hall is impermanent, yet the master of the hall is permanent—if this were truly so, then right and wrong could not be distinguished;
which of these would be correct? In my recent travels, I have frequently seen such appearances.

Recently, Guangsheng has gathered three to five hundred followers, looking up at the Milky Way and claiming that he represents the fundamental tenets of the South. He has altered the *Platform Sutra* and added [to it]..."
To intermingle vulgar talk and excise the sacred intent thereby deluding later followers—how could this constitute the verbal teaching? Alas! Our school is lost.
If seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing were themselves Buddha-nature, then Vimalakīrti should not have said that "the Dharma is apart from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
If one acts through seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, that is merely seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; it is not the seeking of the Dharma.
The monk asked again, "The *Lotus Sūtra* is of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*) and reveals the Buddha’s knowledge and vision (*jñāna-darśana*). How is this so?
The Master said, "It says it reveals the Buddha’s knowledge and vision; it does not say [it reveals those of] Bodhisattvas or followers of the Two Vehicles.

How could the inverted views of sentient beings be the same as the Buddha’s knowledge and vision? From this, one can know that the *nirvāṇa* pointed out by non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) cannot follow [the true path]."
This accords with the characteristics of Nirvana.

Some non-Buddhists claim to have attained the path of True Reality and conceive of it as Nirvana (the Tang translation says: "some reckon that they have realized the Path of Truth, taking their false conceptualizations to be Nirvana").
Or, seeing merit and the arising of merit as being unified, distinct, both, or neither, they conceive of this as Nirvana.

Or, having perceived the nature arising from its own essence—such as the variegated patterns of a peacock’s plumage, various kinds of jewels, and sharp thorns—and having seen these natures, they conceive the notion that this is *nirvāṇa*.

(The Tang translation says: "Or they reckon that all things arise spontaneously; the patterns of a peacock, the sharpness of thorns, and the various jewels produced from jewel-mines—by whom could such things have been made?
Thus they cling to spontaneity (*svabhāva*) as *nirvāṇa*"). Mahāmati, there are some who realize the twenty-five *tattvas*, or those protected by kings.

The kingdom accepts the *Ṣaḍguṇya-śāstra* and conceives the notion that this is *nirvāṇa*. (The Tang translation says: "Some say that by being able to accept the six points and protect sentient beings, one attains *nirvāṇa*").

Or they see time as the creator; those who perceive the world in terms of temporal seasons conceive the notion that this is *nirvāṇa*. Or they speak of nature (*prakṛti*), or they speak of non-nature;

or they speak of knowing both nature and non-nature. (The Wei translation says: "The non-Buddhists say that seeing things, seeing nothing, or seeing both existence and non-existence—such are their discriminations"). Or...

Seeing a distinction between conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) and nirvāṇa, one forms the conception of nirvāṇa [the Tang translation says: or reckoning that all things are no different from nirvāṇa, one forms the conception of nirvāṇa].
Tong said: "To say that one attains the Way of True Reality is the teaching of the fourteenth non-Buddhist school, the Sāṃkhya masters.

They claim that from *prakṛti* (self-nature) arises the Great One (*mahat*); from the Great One arises the mind (*manas*); from the mind arises intellect (*buddhi*); and from intellect arise the five elements."
From the five elements arise the five organs of knowledge; from the five organs of knowledge arise the five organs of action; from the five organs of action arise the five gross elements.
These are called the twenty-five principles (*pañcaviṃśati-tattva*). Primordial Nature (*prakṛti*) is eternal and is able to give rise to all phenomena.

When one returns to primordial nature, one is immediately liberated from all birth and death. This system regards the principle of primordial darkness (*pradhāna*) as the ultimate truth and as *nirvāṇa*.
This refers to those who hold such views. As stated in the *Guṇādi-śāstra* (Treatise on Qualities and so forth), there is the coalescence of the agent (*kartṛ*) and the object (*karma*).
In the Chinese translation, it is said: "Or one calculates that the *guṇa* (quality) and the possessor of the *guṇa* (*guṇin*) coalesce.

These Vaiśeṣika masters postulate six categories (*padārtha*) as the causes for the production of all things: namely, (1) substance (*dravya*), (2) quality (*guṇa*), (3) action (*karman*), (4) generality (*sāmānya*), (5) particularity (*viśeṣa*), and (6) inherence (*samavāya*).

Sixth, regarding similarities and differences: furthermore, from among the categories of substantial entities (*dravya-pada*), they grasp nine factors, namely: earth, water, fire, wind, space, time, direction, conjunction, and disjunction.
Moreover, they calculate that the vessel-world (*bhājana-loka*) is formed by atoms (*paramāṇu*).
What is referred to in the Tang translation as *guṇa* and *guṇin* points to the arising of the world from atoms; the atom is the agent of production, while the world is [the product].
That which is produced is the agent, which is itself merit; that which is produced is that which arises from merit.
It is formed through the conjunction of earth, water, fire, wind, space, and so forth. It cannot be said to be identical, nor can it be said to be different;

it cannot be said to be both identical and different, nor can it be said to be neither identical nor different. This teaching is extremely subtle; the treatise considers it to be the *māyā-śīrṣa* (the head of illusion).
The Master Vasurāta says: "All things arise from Maheśvara and perish into Maheśvara; the three realms are, in their entirety, the single body of Maheśvara.
Much of his discourse is unscriptural, or it appears to originate from the *svabhāva* (intrinsic nature) school.
The treatise considers this to be the teaching of the sixteen non-Buddhist teachers who propound causelessness (*ahetuvāda*). They assert that all things arise without cause and without condition;
for example, the thorns of a thorn bush have no maker, and the various painted patterns on a peacock’s feathers are likewise not made by anyone.
"It exists spontaneously. This refers to what is said in the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra*: "The crow has been black from the beginning; the crane has been white from the beginning.
This is the doctrine of the Naturalists (*Svabhāvavāda*). Alternatively, there are those who perceive the twenty-five principles (*tattva*) as real;

that is, they perceive the primordial matter (*pradhāna*), as calculated by the aforementioned Sāṃkhya masters, as being real. Or there are those who accept the theory of the six qualities (*guṇa*); that is, they accept...

The six categories (ṣaṭpadārtha) postulated by the earlier Vaiśeṣika masters as the causes of arising are able to explain these two dharmas and protect sentient beings, enabling them to attain peace and happiness;
this peace and happiness is precisely nirvāṇa. This section does not appear in the treatise.
This appears to be a redundant repetition. Alternatively, regarding "time" (*kāla*) as the agent:

the treatise records that the proponents of the theory of time among the seventeen non-Buddhist schools (*tīrthika*) assert that time is the cause capable of producing all worldly phenomena; they hold that nothing arises when the time has not arrived, and nothing ceases when the time has not arrived.
They maintain that while all things in the world are impermanent, time itself is eternal. Alternatively, regarding "nature" (*svabhāva*): the treatise treats this as a view.

There is an entity called *nirvāṇa*. This is what is taught by the eighteenth non-Buddhist school, the Ābhāsvara-vādins (Water-Clad Teachers), who claim that water can produce things and water can destroy things, and they assert that water is eternal.

Alternatively, there is the nineteenth non-Buddhist school, the Akriya-vādins (Teachers of the Doctrine of Non-action), who hold the view that there is no such thing as an entity and call this "nirvāṇa. They maintain that space is the [source] of all things.
Regarding causes: all things arise from emptiness and return to extinction within emptiness; thus, empty space is said to be eternal.

Alternatively, there are those who claim that the nature of cognition is non-nature, asserting that the philosophical treatises view the existence or non-existence of things as the cause of *nirvāṇa*.

This is the doctrine of the twenty heretical teachers, such as the master Āṇḍa, who maintain that originally there were no sun, moon, stars, planets, empty space, or earth, but only a great expanse of water.
At that time, Mahānanda was born like a hen’s egg that had split into two parts: the upper portion became heaven, and the lower portion became earth.
Between those two, all sentient beings were born as Brahmās. From Brahmā, they were born and then returned to that place;
this was called Nirvāṇa. These three types [of beings] did not arise apart from earth, water, fire, wind, and space, yet they gave rise to attachment through conceptualization.
One does not emerge from the views of existence, non-existence, or both existence and non-existence. Some perceive a distinction between awakening and nirvāṇa;
others vainly engage in the calculation that all phenomena are no different from nirvāṇa, asserting that the myriad things are merely clamorous agitation.
Nirvana is quiescence; these two are not distinct. Within this, one may differentiate between the refined and the coarse, and resolve upon the true and the false.
If there were an awakening within it, then Nirvana would not be without awakening; yet this state of having awakening is not separate from Nirvana.
The state of neither-perception-nor-non-perception is what is called Nirvana. This one type is missing from Deva’s treatise;
furthermore, neither the Śrāvaka masters nor the non-Buddhist ascetic masters have elucidated it.
When discussing the profound truths of principle, such as they lack; what has been recorded here is merely a brief account of their coarse and superficial views. It seems that this is not [the case].

This is truly what was transmitted by Deva; those with wisdom should be able to illuminate it. A practitioner of the Way asked Dazhu, "Is there any dharma in the world that surpasses spontaneity (*ziran*)?
Dazhu replied, "There is. The practitioner asked, "What dharma can surpass it?
Dazhu said, "The one who is able to know spontaneity. The practitioner asked, "Is primordial qi (*yuánqì*) the Way? Dazhu said, "Primordial qi is simply primordial qi; the Way is..."
Zi Dao said, "If this is so, then there ought to be two people. Baizhang replied, "I know there are not two people. Zi Dao asked again, "What is heterodoxy? What is orthodoxy?
Baizhang said, "The mind pursuing external objects is heterodoxy; objects following the mind is orthodoxy.
With just these few words, the various distinctions between heterodoxy and orthodoxy are revealed beyond the literal meaning.
There are various such delusions spoken by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), which fail to establish what they seek to establish and are rejected by the wise.
Mahāmati, all such [views] fall into the two extremes and are conceived as *nirvāṇa*.

Regarding these delusions of *nirvāṇa* held by the non-Buddhists, there is therein neither arising nor ceasing (the Tang translation says: "therein there is neither abiding nor emerging"). Mahāmati, that one...
Regarding the nirvāṇa of the non-Buddhists as described in their own treatises, when examined with wisdom, nothing whatsoever is established.
Just like their false imaginings, their minds come and go, drifting and racing about; among them, not a single person attains nirvāṇa.
The Master said: "The twenty-one types of *nirvāṇa* mentioned above are merely a brief enumeration of the most prominent ones.
Beyond these, there are over ninety other types of *nirvāṇa* described through various such conceptualizations and delusions.
For the most part, these are explained in treatises based on false and erroneous views; they do not correspond with the true Dharma of reality."
In principle, such assertions are untenable; they are rejected and shunned by the wise. Thus, there are those who assert existence and non-existence, permanence and impermanence;
advancing further, those who assert both existence and non-existence, and both permanence and impermanence;
and advancing yet further, those who assert neither existence nor non-existence, and neither permanence nor impermanence. Altogether, these amount to sixty-two [views].
I see that false conceptualization entirely falls into the two extremes; it does not transcend duality when one conceives of nirvāṇa.
Thus, taking such false conceptualization to be nirvāṇa, there is therein absolutely no abiding in the world.
If there were birth, there would likewise be no entry into nirvāṇa; if there were cessation, all would be annihilated—who then would undergo birth and cessation?
Those various non-Buddhists rely upon their own respective tenets to establish their own treatises.

When these are examined with right knowledge and right wisdom, they are found to contradict correct reasoning and to be self-contradictory. Lacking any suchness-knowledge (*yathābhūta-jñāna*), they have nothing established at all.
Since their doctrines are fragmented and deceptive, they merely misapply their minds and engage in false discrimination, causing their mental states to become agitated.
Scattered, they drift and race back and forth without any rest. Once the mind has flowed out, it does not stop for even a single thought-moment.
Being submerged in the ocean of suffering within birth and death, they continue through the various realms of existence without attaining liberation;
how then could there be anyone who truly attains *nirvāṇa*? Therefore it is said that none among them attain *nirvāṇa*; these non-Buddhists are deluded.
"Calculatingly, all that is not in accord with the characteristics of *nirvāṇa* is not what my Dharma calls *nirvāṇa*.
At Yun’gai Mountain, Master Chan Yuan, having been recommended by Daozheng of Tanzhou to the Prince of Ma, requested to debate the principles of the Dharma.
The Prince invited the Master to ascend the hall for an audience; after tea was served, the Master asked the Prince for his sword, which the Master then grasped.
Jian asked Daozheng, "In your teaching, you speak of 'vague and indistinct, yet within it there is something'; what thing is this? 'Profound and dark, yet within it there is an essence';
what essence is this? Daozheng could not answer; if he had been able to explain the Way, he would have been spared, but as he could not, he was immediately executed.
Daozheng was left bewildered, whereupon he prostrated himself and repented. The Master said to Wang, "Do you recognize this man?"
The King said, "I recognize him. The Master asked, "Who is he? The King said, "Daozheng. The Master said, "It is not he.
If his Way were truly correct, he would have been able to face this mountain monk; instead, he is merely a solitary soul without a master. Because of this, the Daoist no longer made any further fuss.
Even if one were to answer with perfect clarity, it would still not transcend the ultimate truth (míngdì) and would be vastly different from the person of original nature (běnláirén).

"Far removed, Mahāmati! That which I call nirvāṇa means: the thorough realization that [all things] are merely the manifestation of one's own mind; non-attachment to external natures; freedom from the four extremes of conceptualization (*catuskoṭi*);

seeing the state of reality as it is (*yathābhūta*); and not falling into the two extremes of false imagination regarding the manifestations of one's own mind, nor being grasped by the perceived and the perceiver."
Since all that can be apprehended is unattainable and no object of establishment is seen, the foolish do not enter into the various means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and do not cling to reality.
One should not grasp at them; having abandoned them, one attains the noble Dharma of self-realization.

Knowing the two kinds of selflessness, being free from the two afflictions, exhausting the two obstacles, and forever departing from the two deaths, one proceeds through the successive stages up to the stage of the Tathāgata (the Chinese version says: "further cultivating the various stages and entering into...").
The Buddha-ground—characterized by profound samādhis such as those of shadows and illusions—is described as nirvāṇa because it is free from mind, thought, and mental consciousness.
Mahāmati, you and the other bodhisattva-mahāsattvas should practice and study this; you must swiftly distance yourselves from all views of nirvāṇa held by the various non-Buddhist outsiders.

The Master said: "Since it has been established above that none of the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) can attain nirvāṇa, what follows is a detailed explanation of how the nirvāṇa of my own Dharma cannot be fathomed by them.
As I have taught, nirvāṇa means the excellent awakening to the manifestation of one's own mind;
there are no phenomena outside the mind, and no mind outside phenomena. One does not give rise to [discrimination] by clinging to external objects."

Because one discriminates and remains far removed from the fourfold false views of existence, non-existence, identity, difference, both, and neither, and because one attains the true vision of suchness (*tathatā*) and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), which is the state of neither arising nor ceasing, one does not fall into the false views of the two extremes of existence and non-existence as manifested by the discrimination of one's own mind.
Thus, one is able to subsume the mind that grasps; even the "mind-only" (*cittamātra*) becomes unobtainable. Why is this?
It is free from the grasped and the grasper. One sees that all worldly establishments do not transcend the false measurements of conceptual construction;

they are illusory, unreal, and lack any true accomplishment. Because of ignorance, one is deluded regarding the true principle and thus clings to what should not be accepted—the subject and object of apprehension being unfindable.
When one abandons everything and does not grasp at any phenomena, this is called "Reality."
This is indeed the Dharma realized through the direct manifestation of the noble wisdom of self-awakening (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*). What is this realized Dharma?

It is the knowledge of the two kinds of selflessness—of persons and of phenomena—which distances one from both root and secondary afflictions, purifies the two obstructions of delusion and knowledge, eternally transcends the two types of birth and death (the *paricchinna* and the *pariṇāma*), and gradually traverses the stages until reaching the stage of Buddhahood.
To realize that all deep samādhis, such as the "illusion-like" (māyopama), are merely manifestations of one's own mind and are thus like illusions, is not yet the ultimate depth.
To realize that what is illusion is itself reality, and what is reality is itself illusion—that all external objects are eternally and inherently quiescent—is the truly profound samādhi.

Only those who have transformed their evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) into wisdom can realize this; therefore, they transform the mind (*citta*), the intellect (*manas*), and the mental factors (*manovijñāna*).
When the seeds of the arising and ceasing of consciousness are transformed into the wisdom-function of non-arising and non-ceasing, it is then designated as *nirvāṇa*.
The *nirvāṇa* of the three virtues is like the three dots of the syllable *i*; it constitutes the secret treasury of the Tathāgata.
Within this, the self-awakened body of the sage is *tathatā* (suchness); knowing the two kinds of non-self is *prajñā* (wisdom); and being eternally free from the two types of death is...
This liberation is the threefold unity in perfect fusion; therefore, it is called *nirvāṇa*, which is beyond thought and beyond discussion.
Abiding thus, how could it be fathomed by the non-Buddhists? You Bodhisattvas should practice and study, remaining far removed from all non-Buddhist views of *nirvāṇa*.
Seng Zhidao asked the Sixth Patriarch, saying: "When a student first sets out..."
Jia Lan had been studying the *Nirvāṇa Sūtra* for more than ten years without clarifying its essential meaning. He requested that the Master bestow his instruction upon him.
The Patriarch asked, "What is it that you do not understand? Jia Lan replied, "Regarding the passage: 'All conditioned phenomena are impermanent; they are laws of arising and ceasing.
When arising and ceasing have ceased, the extinction of suffering is bliss'—I am confused by this. The Patriarch asked, "How do you doubt it? Jia Lan said, "All sentient beings..."
All beings possess two bodies, namely the form-body (*rūpakāya*) and the dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). The form-body is impermanent, having birth and cessation;

the dharma-body is impermanent [in its manifestation], yet possesses knowledge and awareness. Regarding the sūtra passage which says, "When birth and cessation have ceased, extinction is bliss," I do not yet understand which body attains extinction and which body experiences bliss. If it refers to the form-body, then at the time the form-body ceases, the four...

In great dissolution, everything is entirely suffering and cannot be called bliss. If the Dharma-body were quiescent extinction, it would be identical to grass, trees, tiles, and stones—who then would experience bliss?
Furthermore, the Dharma-nature is the substance of arising and ceasing, while the five aggregates are the function of arising and ceasing.
Substance and function are one; arising and ceasing are constant. When there is arising, the function emerges from the substance; when there is ceasing, [the function returns to] the substance.
Thus, functions are subsumed within the essence. If one allows for rebirth, then the categories of sentient beings are neither interrupted nor extinguished;
if one does not allow for rebirth, then they eternally return to quiescent extinction, becoming identical to insentient things.
If this is so, then all dharmas are constrained and subdued by nirvana such that they cannot even arise—what joy could there be in this?—O Patriarch.
He said: "You are a son of the Śākyas; why do you practice the heterodox views of annihilationism and eternalism to discuss the Supreme Vehicle?
According to what you say, there is a Dharma-body that exists apart from sound and form, separate from birth and death, and seeks quiescence.
Furthermore, you infer the permanence and bliss of Nirvāṇa by claiming the body has sensory enjoyment. This is nothing but clinging to birth and death and being addicted to them."

Worldly happiness, you should now know, is that which the Buddha [diagnoses]: for all deluded beings who mistake the composite of the five aggregates for their own self-nature, and who discriminate all phenomena as external objects;
who are obsessed with birth and loathe death, drifting through the constant flux of every passing thought;
who fail to realize that these are like dreams and illusions, falsely enduring saṃsāra, and thus perceive the eternal bliss of nirvāṇa as a state of suffering.
Throughout the day they run about in pursuit [of it]; out of compassion for them, the Buddha thus reveals the true bliss of *nirvāṇa*.

In a single instant (*kṣaṇa*) there is no characteristic of arising; in a single instant there is no characteristic of ceasing. Since there is further no arising or ceasing to be extinguished, this is the manifestation of quiescent extinction (*śānti*).
At the time of its manifestation, there is also no measure of "manifestation"; this is called eternal bliss. This bliss is without any recipient.
There is likewise no one who does not receive it; how could there be such a thing as "one substance with five functions"?
How much less can one speak of *nirvāṇa* as something that suppresses all dharmas so that they never arise again? This is to slander the Buddha and slander the Dharma. Listen to my verse:
"The unsurpassed Great Nirvāṇa is perfectly luminous, eternally tranquil, and illuminating. The ignorant and foolish call it death; non-Buddhists cling to it as..."
The severing of all seeking by those of the two vehicles is termed "effortless exhaustion. All that belongs to the calculations of the mind consists of the sixty-two views;
these are fundamentally false and established as mere provisional names—what, then, could be called the true meaning?

Only those of transcendent capacity penetrate the state beyond grasping and rejecting, knowing that the dharmas of the five aggregates and the "self" within the aggregates are but external manifestations of various forms and signs.
The characteristic of a single sound is equal and like an illusion or a dream; it does not give rise to views of ordinary beings or sages, nor does it form an understanding of nirvana.
It cuts off the two extremes and the three periods of time, as well as permanence and annihilation. It accords with the functions of all faculties without giving rise to the thought of functioning;

it differentiates all dharmas without forming thoughts of differentiation. Even when the kalpa-fire burns the ocean floor and the wind blows the mountains together in collision, it remains truly constant and tranquil.
The characteristics of Nirvana, which is the extinction of pleasure, are thus; I now speak these words by force so that you may abandon your false views.

Do not follow the literal meaning of my words, but allow yourself to know a small portion of it. With your mind set on the Way, upon hearing this verse you were greatly enlightened; you prostrated and withdrew.
This single verse of the Sixth Patriarch encompasses the wondrous meaning of this entire treatise. The transmission of the Buddha’s Mind-Seal does not reside in speech or written characters.
"Is it so? At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to reiterate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The views of nirvāṇa held by the non-Buddhists are each born of deluded imagination; they arise from the workings of the mind and have no skillful means for liberation."
Fools, bound by their own fetters and devoid of skillful means, conceive the notion of liberation; yet for them, liberation never arises, and their various cognitions lead to divergent destinies.
The views of these various non-Buddhists (tīrthika) all lack liberation, for they are rooted in deluded conceptualization.
Thus, all foolish non-Buddhists, through their false views, engage in debates concerning the existence or non-existence of the agent and the acted-upon; none of them possess liberation.

Ordinary fools delight in false conceptualization and do not hear the words of true wisdom; these are the root of the three kinds of suffering, while true wisdom is the cause for extinguishing suffering.
For example, an image in a mirror appears yet does not exist; likewise, in the mirror of the deluded mind of conceptualization, the foolish perceive duality.

Failing to recognize the mind and its objects, they give rise to the two-fold false conceptualization. Once one understands the mind and its objective realms, false conceptualization will no longer arise.
The mind is the manifestation of various characteristics and the objects characterized; yet it manifests while being non-manifesting, like the false imaginings of the ignorant.
The three realms of existence are merely imagination; external objects do not exist at all. Through various manifestations of imagination, ordinary fools cannot comprehend them.
It is taught in every sutra that imagination never transcends names; if one is separated from verbal expression, there is nothing to be expressed.
The Master said: "This verse concerns the views of nirvāṇa held by the non-Buddhists as previously described in twenty-one ways;
however, these arise solely from the deluded thoughts of their own respective minds.

Since such false discrimination is produced by the movement of mental conceptions, they lack the skillful means for true liberation, and thus the non-Buddhists cling to a nirvāṇa that can be grasped."
Already bound, they further grasp at things with false views; this constitutes their bondage.
Those fools, regarding themselves as the binders, fail to awaken to this truth. Consequently, they distance themselves from the dharmas of skillful means;
though they harbor the notion of liberation, liberation will never arise for them. These various groups of non-Buddhists each produce perverse wisdom and each pursue different paths.
Some perceive permanence and take permanence to be liberation; others perceive annihilation and take annihilation to be liberation.
Based on their own respective understandings, each claims it to be liberation, yet in reality, none possess liberation.
Why is this? Only wisdom can destroy ignorance, and only truth can eliminate delusion. Since they...
The ignorant are bound by fetters and do not depart from deluded thoughts; they drift about and do not depart from falsehood.

Lacking skillful means, how could they attain liberation? Therefore, all foolish non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) with false views regard the agent and the object of action as being either causeless or having a cause, thereby establishing categories of existence and non-existence.

In all the treatises, there is no one who attains liberation; it is only because those foolish ordinary beings delight in false conceptualization and do not hear the wisdom of true liberation that they have reached this state. That false conceptualization does not depart from speech, for language is the root of the three sufferings.
The three sufferings are: the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of conditioned existence (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*).

"Suffering as suffering" (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*) refers to the suffering already present in the three realms; furthermore, within the desire realm (*kāmadhātu*), it specifically refers to the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*).

"Suffering as conditioned existence" (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*) refers to the suffering associated with the destruction of pleasure and so forth. It applies to the three miserable destinies (*durgati*) and to the suffering of the neutral state (*avyākṛta*), which extends throughout the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*).
These three types of suffering do not exist apart from the desire, form, and formless realms. The discourses established by non-Buddhist outsiders do not go beyond these categories.
The arising and ceasing of all phenomena within the three realms are, in reality, the root of the three types of suffering;
how then could one transcend the three realms and attain liberation? One who possesses true wisdom does not form views of existence nor views of non-existence;
fundamentally there is no agent and nothing that is done. Within the limit of reality (*tathatā-bhūtakoṭi*), they do not give rise to a single thought of discrimination.
Since no characteristics of the three realms can be apprehended, from where could the suffering of the three realms arise?
This true wisdom is the actual extinction of the causes of suffering; it is true liberation and true nirvana. Yet they have certainly not heard of this.
As for what is called the extinction of the causes of suffering, does it necessarily require the severance and cessation of all phenomena within the three realms before [it occurs]?
How tragic! It is like an image within a mirror; though it appears, it does not exist.

True Suchness (tathatā) and the limit of reality (bhūtakoṭi) are the mirror, while the phenomena of the triple world are the images. The phenomena of the triple world are manifested solely by one’s own mind;
they cannot be said to exist, nor can they be said to be non-existent. Fools, regarding what is manifested in the mirror of their own minds...
Regarding these marks, through false conceptualization and discrimination, one may see them as existing or see them as non-existing;
to produce these two views is truly due to not recognizing the fundamental substance of one's own mind and external conditioned objects.

Just as with images in a mirror—the images come and go while the mirror neither arises nor ceases—so too do conditions come and go while the mind neither arises nor ceases. Those [who hold such views] do not rely upon the Truth.

Based on reality, yet arising from delusion, one establishes dualistic discrimination through discourse concerning existence and non-existence; thus, one creates the causes of suffering for oneself—this is not to be wondered at.

If one can understand that both mind and objects are the manifestation of one's own mind, and realize that external natures have neither existence nor non-existence—just as images in a mirror appear yet do not exist—how could there be any attachment to these illusory shadows?
How could one give rise to false conceptualization based on such [appearances]? Why is it that false imaginings do not arise?
It is because all phenomena of the triple world are manifested solely by the mind; this mind is itself the manifold variety, and the manifold variety is itself the mind.

The object and the mind are of one suchness, originally quiescent and extinguished, far removed from the characteristics of the grasper and the grasped. Since the grasper and the grasped are both absent, there is no substantial reality.
The various activities of the three realms may manifest, yet they manifest without manifestation;
they cannot be definitively grasped as existing in the way that ordinary, foolish worldlings and non-Buddhists engage in various false imaginings and conceptual discriminations.

Furthermore, all the various phenomena within the three realms do not arise from birth or death, nor do they possess the characteristics of coming and going; they are merely established through false imagination and discrimination.
Abiding in external objects, they grasp them as real entities, not knowing that external natures have no inherent existence and that all shadow-like appearances are originally non-existent.
Because of false imagination (*vikalpa*), various phenomena and various manifestations appear;

yet since these arise from false imagination and false imagination itself has no root, they are fundamentally unarisen. This manifestation of one's own mind (*svacittadṛśyamātra*) is not easily realized.
Kui, all the foolish and ignorant cannot comprehend this; that they transmigrate through the three realms and fail to attain liberation is truly and most piteously lamentable.
It is not merely that the words of non-Buddhists constitute the root of the three sufferings; even these verbal explanations lack any real meaning.
This is precisely as stated in the various sutras regarding "delusive thoughts" (*vikalpa*): it is intended to cause sentient beings to turn back from delusion and return to the truth.
Abiding in nirvāṇa, yet ultimately not departing from names and words; once fallen into names and words, it is no longer the ultimate reality.
If one realizes that the essence of names and words is empty, then while employing verbal expression, one transcends verbal expression.
To intuitively accord with this inconceivable realm, even the Dharma that is taught cannot be apprehended as a single dharma. Only when not a single dharma remains is true reality realized.
This is the meaning of *nirvāṇa* as taught by me; how could it be understood by the ignorant and foolish? A verse from the *Saṃpuṭa-sūtra* says:
"The eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, mind, and all the sense faculties—through these one constantly transmigrates, yet there is no one who transmigrates.
The nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) is fundamentally without birth, yet it manifests with birth. Within this, there is neither one who manifests, nor is there..."
All manifested objects—the eyes, ears, nose, tongue, body, mind, and all the sensory faculties—are entirely empty and devoid of intrinsic nature;

it is only through the discriminating deluded mind that they appear to exist. Thus one should observe that all things are without intrinsic nature. The general purport of this verse is truly no different from the following verse:
"The Master Chanfuben of Qingzhou ascended the hall and, raising his voice, sought to stop the echoes, yet he did not realize [the source]."

Sound is the root of echoes; one who dandles shadows and flees from forms does not know that form is the basis of the shadow. To inquire about the Dharma by means of the Dharma is to not know that the Dharma is fundamentally non-Dharma.
To transmit mind by means of the mind is to not know that the mind is fundamentally no-mind. When one knows that the mind is fundamentally no-mind, one realizes that the mind is like an illusion.
Realizing that dharmas and non-dharmas are like dreams, and that both mind and dharmas are unreal, do not vainly pursue them.
Seeking within dreams, illusions, flowers in the sky, and emptiness—what need is there to grasp at them?

Arriving here, the teachings of the Great Canon of the Buddhas of the three periods, the words of the patriarchs, and the manifest proclamations and entanglements of the old monks throughout the world are all rendered useless. Why is this so?
"Peace itself was brought about by the generals, yet the generals are not permitted to witness the peace. Having said this, he descended from his seat. If...
These discourses are such that, though they contain nothing to be said, one may chew upon them all day long without it being excessive.
*The Sixth Fascicle of the Core Principles of the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*.
The *Treatise on the Nirvāṇa of Non-Buddhists and the Hīnayāna* from within the *Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, explained by Bodhisattva Deva (extracted from the Tibetan Canon for reference).
The *Mani* (卍) edition originally recorded the full text, which is now preserved in the Tripitaka; it is omitted here.
*Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra*, Section on the Penetration of the Essence (*Zongtong*), Volume Seven, Chapter Four:

"The Heart of All Buddha-Speech" (*Yiqiefoyuxin pin*). [In the Wei translation, this is called] Chapter Seven: "The Dharma-Body" (*Fashen pin*); [in the Tang translation, it is called] Chapter Three: "Impermanence" (*Wuchang pin*), Part Two.

At that time, the Bodhisattva Mahāmati addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, we pray that you will explain the Samyak-saṃbuddha (here translated as 'Perfectly Awakened One') for me and the other Bodhisattva-Mahāsattvas, so that we may become skilled in the self-nature of the Tathāgata, awakening ourselves and awakening others.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Ask whatever you desire; I shall explain to you according to your questions. Mahāmati replied:
He addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, does the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, act or not act?
Is he an effect (the Chinese translation says 'fruit') or a cause? Is he a characteristic or that which is characterized?
Is he the speaker or that which is spoken? Is he the awakening or that which is awakened? Are such terms as these different or not different? The Buddha told him:
Mahāmati, for the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, such phrases as these do not refer to a "thing" (bhāva) nor to a "cause" (hetu). Why?
Because both [positions] entail faults. Mahāmati, if the Tathāgata were a "thing," he would either be something produced or impermanent, because of being impermanent;
thus all things would be the Tathāgata, which neither I nor the Buddhas desire. If he were not...
Because that which is created is unattainable, skillful means are empty, being identical to a rabbit’s horn or the son of Baṇḍa (which in this language means "the stone-son").
Because they do not exist, Mahāmati, if there were no phenomena and no causes, then it would be neither existent nor non-existent.
If it were neither existent nor non-existent, it would transcend the four propositions (*cātuṣkoṭi*). These four propositions are worldly discourse; if one transcends them...

As for the four propositions, they do not fall into the four propositions; because they do not fall into the four propositions, the wise should know that all the meanings of the Tathāgatas' words are likewise taken up by the wise.
Tong said: "The Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment, the suchness of self-nature, is precisely the true self of the Dharmakāya.
If one understands this principle well, using it for self-awakening leads to the realm of the noble wisdom of self-realization;

using it to awaken others causes them to turn from delusion toward enlightenment, so that together they may realize Bodhi. This is precisely the World-Honored One’s fundamental intention in delivering sentient beings; therefore, he permitted it."

"Mahāmati, you may ask whatever you wish. However, it is said that the 'Perfectly All-Knowing One' (Samyaksaṃbuddha) knows everything—both the internal nature of the Dharma-body and all external worldly phenomena.
This Perfectly All-Knowing One transcends all things and cannot be fathomed by worldly wisdom.
That which the world calls a 'creator' is a conditioned phenomenon (saṃskṛta-dharma)."

That which is called "non-creation" (akṛta) refers to unconditioned phenomena (asaṃskṛtadharma), whether as cause or fruit, characteristic or that which is characterized, expression or that which is expressed, cognition or that which is cognized; in total, it does not transcend the two categories of the conditioned and the unconditioned.
If one were to claim that the unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment is a distinct Dharma-body apart from these terms and phrases, then...

One cannot say that [the Buddha] has attained universal knowledge. If one were to claim that Unsurpassed Perfectly Complete Enlightenment is not different from these words and phrases—which are identical to all objects of cognition—then it could not be called "Perfect Enlightenment.

How, then, can one transcend difference and non-difference to directly manifest the Dharmakāya? Regarding such words and phrases, the Buddha, through his Perfect Enlightenment, declared them all to be "not so."

Furthermore, because its fruit is not the true fruit and its cause is not the true cause—since both would entail faults when viewed from the perspective of the self-nature of the Dharmakāya—how can it be said that there are no faults?
If one were to say that the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya is a conditioned phenomenon, then it would be identical to that which is produced through effort;
and whatever is produced through effort is impermanent. To take what is impermanent as the Dharmakāya...
All impermanent things in the world are the Tathāgata; this is a law of arising and ceasing which neither I nor the Buddhas permit.
If one says that the Tathāgata is not something produced, then the Dharmakāya would be utterly devoid of any obtainable essence or nature;
even if various skillful means (*upāya*) were established, they would all be empty and useless, identical to [non-existence].
The horns of a rabbit and the son of a barren woman are ultimately non-existent; therefore, this is a doctrine of annihilationism, which neither I nor the Buddhas permit.
Thus it is said that both positions possess faults: to say there is an agent is to fall into existence, and to say there is no agent is to fall into non-existence.
Furthermore, to say there is no fruit and no cause is to be neither existent nor non-existent; this is the Middle Way.

There are those who hold the view that things are neither existent nor non-existent; yet even while they dispel the two extremes of existence and non-existence, they in fact do not depart from the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of the four propositions (*catuṣkoṭi*):
the proposition of existence, the proposition of non-existence, the proposition of both existence and non-existence, and the proposition of neither existence nor non-existence.
These four propositions are merely the deluded speech of worldly outsiders and are not accepted by the wise.
The Way, if it can transcend beyond the four propositions, then one does not fall into the false views of the four propositions;

being free from the four propositions and cutting off the hundred negations, the true and eternal is uniquely revealed and cannot be deluded by heterodox doctrines; therefore, it is what the wise accept.
The meaning of the phrases "I" and "all Tathāgatas" transcends cause and effect, transcends subject and object, and transcends oneness and difference.
"Both together and neither together are likewise thus; one does not fall into the four propositions. Not falling into the four propositions means being free from all faults.
Those who possess the eye of wisdom can distance themselves from all views of existence and non-existence; they shall be able to discern this. Baizhang said:
'To seek a single point of knowledge or a single understanding from a spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitra) is the demonic speech and view of a spiritual friend.'"
Therefore, if one resolves upon the Four Great Vows to deliver all sentient beings before beginning to attain Buddhahood,

this is the Dharma-wisdom of a Bodhisattva; because the vow and the Māra do not abandon one another, if one maintains the fasts and precepts, cultivates dhyāna, and studies wisdom— these being outflowing (sāsrava) virtues—
even if one sits at the site of enlightenment (bodhimaṇḍa) and manifests the attainment of Perfect Enlightenment to deliver beings as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
That several people all realize the fruit of a pratyekabuddha is due to the arising of attachment through the power of roots of goodness;

that one remains entirely free from defilement regarding all phenomena, with the divine principle alone remaining, dwelling in profound meditative concentration (*dhyāna*) without further advancement, is the demon of samādhi due to long-term indulgence;
and that reaching unsurpassed nirvāṇa, which is desireless and tranquil, is the work of Māra.

If one possesses wisdom and is liberated from the various nets of Māra, yet does not abandon [worldly attachments]—even if one has mastered a hundred volumes of the Vedas—all of this is but the dregs of hell.

If one seeks something resembling the Buddha, such a thing is impossible. If, upon hearing the teaching now, one fails to remain unattached to dharmas such as good and evil or existence and non-existence, and instead falls into emptiness without knowing how to discard the superficial for the fundamental, this is precisely a fall.
To seek Buddhahood, Bodhi, or any phenomena such as existence and non-existence within emptiness is to abandon the root and pursue the branches.
It is simply like using coarse food to sustain life, patching rags to ward off the cold, or scooping up water to quench thirst;
beyond these, one should have not even a hair’s breadth of attachment to any phenomena of existence or non-existence. Such a person gradually attains a state of lightness and clarity.
