Distinguishing true spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*): not clinging to existence, not clinging to non-existence, liberated from the ten phrases of demonic speech, uttering words that do not bind people, never claiming oneself to be a teacher in one's speech, speaking like an echo, having words that fill the world without verbal transgression, being worthy of reliance—if one says, "I am able to speak and explain;
I am your preceptor (*upādhyāya*)," [then one is not a true friend].
This disciple’s talk is identical to the teachings of Māra; he speaks pointlessly of "the Way existing before one's eyes," and of whether this is Buddha or not Buddha, Bodhi, Nirvāṇa, or liberation.

He speaks pointlessly of "one knowledge and one understanding," and when a hand is raised or a finger held up, he says, "This is Zen, this is the Way. Such words as these bind people; they have no substance.
While dwelling [in this state], one merely increases the fetters of a bhikṣu; even if one does not speak, there are still verbal transgressions.

It would be better to take the mind as one's teacher rather than the mind being taken as the teacher. Within the teachings of provisional meaning, there are teachers of gods and humans, and there are guiding teachers;

yet within the teachings of definitive meaning, one does not act as a teacher of gods and humans, nor does one take the Dharma as a teacher. One has not yet been able to rely upon and attain profound insight. Furthermore—
If one relies on the teachings of definitive meaning (*nītārtha*), there is still a degree of attachment to signs;
if it were merely a teaching of provisional meaning (*neyārtha*), it would only be fit to be spoken before the deaf and the worldly.

Now, simply by not relying on or dwelling in any phenomena of existence or non-existence, yet neither dwelling in non-reliance nor creating a state of non-reliance—this very understanding is called a "great spiritual friend" (*kalyāṇamitra*). Furthermore...
It is said that the Buddha alone is the Great Good Spiritual Friend (kalyāṇamitra), for there is no second;

all others are termed "outsiders" (tīrthika) and their teachings are called "the speech of Māra. By observing this, one sufficiently knows that the Unsurpassed Perfectly Complete Enlightenment cannot be approximated by any phenomena within the four propositions of existence, non-existence, both, or neither.

Regarding what I have said—that all phenomena (*dharma*) are without self (*anātman*)—you should understand this meaning as follows: the nature of selflessness (*anātmatā*) is what is meant by "without self.

All phenomena possess their own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and do not possess the nature of others, just as [a cow has its own nature and] a horse [has its own]. (The Tang translation says: "Regarding what I have said that all phenomena are without self, it is because there is no nature of self within phenomena that they are called 'without self';

it does not mean that the intrinsic nature of phenomena themselves does not exist. Mahāmati, for example, it is not the case that a cow lacks the nature of a horse, nor that a horse lacks the nature of a cow; in reality...

It is neither existent nor non-existent; it does not lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Thus, [the Tang translation says]: "For example, a cow has no nature of a horse, and a horse has no nature of a cow, yet they do not lack their own intrinsic natures.
All phenomena are likewise. Mahāmati, all phenomena do not lack their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*);

they possess their own specific characteristics, yet this is not something that can be known by the deluded through the notion of a self (*ātman*), because of their false conceptualization (*vikalpa*). In this way, all phenomena are empty, unarisen, and without intrinsic nature.
One should understand the nature [of things] in this way.
It is said that the meaning of the phrases of all Tathāgatas does not fall within the framework of the four propositions;
why, then, must one possess wisdom in order to know them? According to what I have taught, the selflessness of all phenomena does not lead to the error of nihilism.
This refers to the state of "nothingness. One should understand this meaning as follows: all phenomena (*dharma*) lack a sovereign master and are fundamentally devoid of a real nature;
this is called "non-self" (*anātman*). However, this merely excludes the deluded self; it does not exclude the true self.
All phenomena are manifestations of one's own mind, each possessing its own true intrinsic nature, free from the delusions of other-discriminations.
The nature of perception is like this: within the body of another there is no self-nature (*ātmatva*), and within one's own body there is no other-nature (*paratva*);

yet it is not that self-nature does not exist, just as it is with oxen and horses. For example, what is not an ox possesses the nature of a horse, and what is not a horse possesses the nature of an ox.
One cannot say that the nature of a horse exists or does not exist upon the substance of an ox; yet, it is not non-existent.
The nature of an ox cannot be said to exist or not exist upon the body of a horse; yet, it is not that the self-nature of the horse does not exist.
All phenomena are likewise so: to falsely grasp at what is not-self as being self is precisely conceptual discrimination, which is the nature of another.
Within the nature of *tathatā*, no self can be found; thus, there is no discrimination.
Since differentiation is itself intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), all phenomena lack any self-characteristic (*svalakṣaṇa*). That which is not non-existent is existence; it is not non-being.
This true intrinsic nature exists as a reality; this true intrinsic nature is the eternally abiding self-characteristic.
It is simply not subject to annihilation, and it cannot be known by foolish commoners or non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) due to their ignorance of selflessness (*anātman*). For that reason...

To falsely conceptualize and cling to what is not-self as being the self, and even to sever [the self] until reaching the state of non-self, is likewise due to false conceptualization; though there is no self, they still conceive of a self.
Since they thus cling to a delusory self, how could they know the true self? If one can awaken to and know the true characteristic of the self, it is as follows:
That all dharmas are empty is like this; that all dharmas are unarisen is like this;

that all dharmas lack intrinsic nature is precisely what I mean by the principle of non-self. When I speak of emptiness, how could it be a partial emptiness? Because it is true emptiness, it is not empty.
When I speak of the absence of emptiness, how could it be annihilation or non-arising? It is that which is constantly arising is precisely non-arising. When I speak of non-existence...
How could intrinsic nature truly be without nature? It is simply that it lacks extrinsic nature. How could the teaching of non-self truly mean there is no self?
It is simply that there is no deluded self. Only when one clarifies this meaning can one speak of wisdom (*prajñā*);
wisdom should be understood in this way—how could it be something known by the ordinary and the foolish? When the Minister Wen Cao questioned Master Guifeng regarding awakening, he said:
The Master said: "For one who has stilled the mind and ceased delusion, no karma is bound. After the end of this single lifetime, upon what does their spiritual nature rely?
All sentient beings are without exception endowed with the enlightened nature—vividly aware, empty, and still—which is no different from that of a Buddha.
It is only because, since beginningless kalpas, they have never realized this and have falsely clung to the body as the mark of a self, that attachment arises."

Evil thoughts and the like arise according to the mind; following these thoughts, karma is created, and according to that karma, one receives retribution—undergoing birth, old age, sickness, and death, wandering in saṃsāra through long kalpas.
Yet, the enlightened nature within the body has never undergone birth or death;

it is like being driven and enslaved in a dream while the body remains fundamentally at ease, or like water turning to ice while its moist nature remains unchanged. If one can awaken to this nature, it is the Dharmakāya itself.
Since it is inherently unborn, how could there be any dependence or support? It is spiritually lucid and never obscured;
it is clearly and constantly aware. It comes from nowhere and goes nowhere. Yet, through many lifetimes of deluded attachments, habitual tendencies have become one's nature.

Although the subtle flow of joy, anger, sorrow, and pleasure may be suddenly penetrated through the realization of ultimate truth, this refined essence is difficult to eliminate abruptly; one must maintain constant and long-term vigilance.
Diminish it again and again; like the wind suddenly ceasing, the waves gradually subside. How could the practice cultivated in a single lifetime be equal to the power and function of all Buddhas?
One should simply take emptiness and stillness as one's own essence, rather than identifying with the physical body;

and take spiritual awareness as one's own mind, rather than identifying with deluded thoughts. If deluded thoughts arise, do not follow them at all. This is what it means when one faces the end of life.

At the time of death, natural karma can no longer bind them; although they possess an intermediate state (*antarābhava*), their destination is free and spontaneous, allowing them to take up residence at will in the heavens or the human realm.
Once thoughts of love and hatred have been extinguished, they no longer receive a body of segmented birth (*paśyandika-śarīra*).
They are naturally able to transform the short into the long and the coarse into the sublime. When even the subtle, continuous flow [of consciousness] has entirely ceased, all is quiescent.

Only when the great wisdom of the easily awakened one shines forth clearly and remains alone, manifesting thousands of billions of transformation bodies according to the capacities of beings to deliver those with whom they have a karmic affinity,
is one called a Buddha. By contemplating these words of Guifeng, the distinction between the true self and the deluded self will become clear to you of itself.
In this way, the Tathāgata is neither different from nor non-different from the aggregates (*skandha*). If he were not different from the aggregates, he would be impermanent;
if he were different, skillful means (*upāya*) would be empty. If there were both [possibilities], there would have to be a distinction, just as there is a similarity between the horns of a cow.

Yet they are non-different because they belong to the same animal, and different because of distinctions such as length. All phenomena (*dharma*) are likewise, O Mahāmati, just like the right horn of a cow.
The left horn is different from the left horn, and the right horn is different; likewise, length, shortness, and various colors are each distinct.
Mahāmati, in this way, the Tathāgata is neither different nor not different from the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases.

Tong said: "The previous statement that there is no self does not mean there is no self-characteristic; it means there is a self-characteristic, and this self-characteristic is precisely the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.

If one were to claim that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is manifested only after being separated from the five aggregates and the physical body, that would be the heterodox view of a non-Buddhist. Therefore, it is said that the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body and the five aggregates and physical body are neither different nor..."

If they were not different—if the Dharma-body were not different from the five aggregates—then since the five aggregates are conditioned phenomena that undergo transformation and are impermanent, the Dharma-body would also have to be impermanent.

If the Dharma-body were different from the five aggregates, then the Dharma-body would fall into a state of inert emptiness, and all skillful means of cultivation and realization would be rendered useless. This is the relationship between the Dharma-body and the aggregates.

If these were two distinct entities, then the Dharma-body would exist apart from the five aggregates, and the five aggregates would exist apart from the Dharma-body, such that they could not be considered one.
Now, the Dharma-body is right within the five aggregates, and the five aggregates are right within the Dharma-body;
it cannot be said that they are different from this [oneness]. This view of difference and non-difference is like the two horns of an ox.
Because they resemble one another, they are fundamentally not different; yet, because of distinctions such as long and short, they are said to be different.

All phenomena are likewise thus: there should be no characteristic of difference, yet there is the characteristic of difference—just as a cow’s right horn differs from the left, the left horn differs from the right, and so on, up to differences in length and the discrimination of color-forms.
Although there are various differences, they are not distinct in form; there is length and shortness, yet this length and shortness do not exist apart from the horns of the ox.
There is black and white in color, yet this black and white do not exist apart from the horns of the ox.
Just as when a palace or garden is burned, one sees various flames of fire—the nature of which is a single source of light and flame—yet the flames appear long due to the power of the fuel.

Because short and long, large and small, each differ from one another, the characteristics of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body cannot be said to be identical to, nor different from, the five aggregates (skandhas), the six sense bases (āyatanas), and the eighteen elements (dhātus). If it were said to be identical, then identity can only be predicated after there has been duality;
yet since it has never been dual, what need is there to speak of identity? If it were said to be different, then it would not be the same. Thus it is.
The subsequent teaching of "difference" is based on their original identity; what need is there to speak of difference?
Because it is neither different nor not-different, it transcends the reach of verbal discourse and can only be known by the wise themselves. Huangbo said:
"If a student of the Way wishes to know the essential secret, simply do not allow even a single thing to cling to the mind. He spoke of the Buddha’s true Dharmakāya as follows:
If space is used as a metaphor for the Dharmakāya, then space is the Dharmakāya and the Dharmakāya is space.
Ordinary people say that the Dharmakāya pervades the realm of space, yet they do not realize that space contains the Dharmakāya, nor that the Dharmakāya is space and space is the Dharmakāya.
If one definitively asserts that space exists [as a separate entity], then that space is not the Dharmakāya. If...
It is definitively stated that there is a Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*). This Dharma-body is not empty space, yet do not interpret it as being anything other than empty space.
Empty space is the Dharma-body; do not interpret the Dharma-body as being anything other than empty space. Empty space and the Dharma-body have no different characteristics;
Buddhas and sentient beings have no different characteristics; birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*) and nirvāṇa have no different characteristics; and afflictions [have no different characteristics].
Because being free from all marks is no different from bodhi, and that is itself the Buddha;
one does not perceive the horns of an ox by means of length or various colors, for the horns of an ox are simply one.
In this way, the liberation of the Tathāgata is neither different from nor not different from the Tathāgata; it is by means of the name "liberation" that the Tathāgata is spoken of.
If the Tathāgata were different from liberation, he would be constituted by material form (*rūpa-lakṣaṇa*); because he would be constituted by material form, he would be impermanent.
If he were not different, then when a practitioner attains realization, there should be no conceptual differentiation, yet the practitioner perceives such differentiation. Therefore—

Neither different nor not different. (The Wei translation states: "If the Tathāgata’s dharmakāya were not different from liberation, then there would be no distinction between the subject that realizes and the object realized; yet practitioners do perceive both the subject that realizes and the object realized, therefore they are not non-different.")
Tong said: "It was stated above that the Dharma-body and the five aggregates are neither different nor not different; such is the original nature of the Tathāgatagarbha.
Nevertheless, there is a distinction between being enveloped in defilements (*saṃkleśa*) and being free from them. Thus, that which is free from defilements is called liberation (*vimukti*).
This liberation is the practice associated with the Tathāgata; it cannot be said to be one, nor can it be said to be different. It is not yet liberated [from conceptualization]."
When [the afflictions] are present, the Dharma-body is hidden; when liberation is attained, the Dharma-body is manifest.
Thus, based on this liberation, it is called the characteristic of the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body. Why say that it is neither different nor not different?
If one says they are different, then since liberation is the single state of non-existence while the Dharma-body does not depart from existence, there would have to be a Dharma-body that exists.
That which is attained is the Dharma-body; it is not like the conditioned forms produced by the characteristics of form, which are impermanent and ultimately subject to destruction.
Therefore, one cannot say they are different. Yet, if one were to say they are not different, there would be no distinction between the realization and that which is realized.
Consequently, the practitioner who attains the Dharma-body through liberation would have to be without discrimination. However...
The practitioner perceives liberation as the means of realization (the *dharmakāya*) and the *dharmakāya* as the principle to be realized;
these distinctions are clear and distinct, and they have never been anything other than different. Yet, because it is neither different nor non-different, such a distinction cannot be articulated;
therefore, one cannot say they are identical, nor can one say they are different. A monk asked National Teacher Huizhong:
The monk asked, "What is liberation? The Master said, "All dharmas do not reach one another; they are liberated where they stand.
The monk asked, "If that is so, then is it simply cutting them off? The Master said, "I told you that all dharmas do not reach one another;
what is there to cut off? Furthermore, a monk asked, "How does one attain Buddhahood? The Master said, "Drop both Buddha and sentient beings at once, right where you are."
Jietuo asked, "How can one attain resonance? The Master said, "Do not contemplate good or evil, and you will spontaneously see your Buddha-nature.
He asked, "How does one realize the Dharma-body? The Master said, "Transcend the realm of Vairocana.
He asked, "How does one attain the pure Dharma-body? The Master said, "Do not seek it from the Buddha. He asked, "Who is that Buddha?"
The Master said, "The very mind is Buddha. [The student] asked, "Does the mind have afflictions? The Master said, "The nature of afflictions is itself detached.
[The student] asked, "Is it not then severed? The Master said, "One who severs afflictions is called a follower of the Two Vehicles; that afflictions do not arise is called Great Nirvana.
The National Teacher’s various discourses all elucidate that the liberation of the Tathāgata is not something other [than this].
It is not that the object is not distinct [from the cognition]. Likewise, wisdom (*jñāna*) and its manifestation (*jñeyalakṣaṇa*) are neither different nor non-different.

Mahāmati, because wisdom and its manifestation are neither different nor non-different, they are neither eternal nor impermanent, neither the agent nor the acted-upon, neither conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) nor unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*).

Awakening is not that which is awakened to; it is neither characteristic nor that which possesses characteristics; it is neither the aggregates nor distinct from the aggregates; it is neither speech nor that which is spoken;

it is neither identical nor different, neither both nor neither; because it is neither identical nor different, neither both nor neither, it is entirely free from all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).
Being free from all means of valid cognition, it is beyond verbal expression; being beyond verbal expression, it is unborn; and being unborn, it is—
Non-extinction, being non-extinguished, is quiescent extinction; quiescent extinction is the nirvana of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-nirvāṇa*).
The nirvana of intrinsic nature is without objective entity and without cause. Being without objective entity and without cause, it is without cognitive objectification (*ālambana*).
Being without cognitive objectification, it transcends all falsehood. Transcending all falsehood is the Tathāgata; the Tathāgata is the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
Mahāmati, this is called the Buddha of Samyaksaṃbuddha. Mahāmati, the Buddha of Samyaksaṃbuddha is free from all sense-faculties and measures (*pramāṇa*).
Generally speaking, it was said above that the practitioner attains non-conceptualization through correspondence; yet the practitioner perceives [the] division.

Furthermore, that which possesses discrimination is the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness); that which is non-discriminative and corresponds to a single thought-moment is *prajñā-jñāna* (wisdom).

Since this *ālayavijñāna*—here translated as "the object of knowledge"—is neither different nor non-different from the *dharmakāya* and liberation, so too the wisdom of *prajñā* and its objective realm cannot be said to be one, nor can they be said to be [different].
When it is said that they are "different," what is meant by saying they are neither different nor not different? The true wisdom of *prajñā* cannot take any phenomena as its object;
precisely because it cannot take them as objects, it is able to be the known while being free from the known. Precisely because it is the known, one does not perceive any difference within it;
precisely because it is free from the known, one does not perceive any non-difference within it, for not a single dharma can be apprehended.
Therefore, as previously stated by Mahāmati, the meanings of "action" and "non-action" refer to the eternal and the impermanent;

the meanings of "cognition" and "non-cognition" refer to the conditioned and the unconditioned; the meanings of "the characterized" and "the characteristic" refer to the aggregates and what is not the aggregates;

and the meanings of "speaking" and "not speaking" refer to identity, difference, both, and neither. All these various terms and phrases take seeing, hearing, cognition, and knowledge as their respective criteria.
It is taught that all phenomena, in their entirety, do not transcend the measure of the knowable and, in their entirety, do not transcend verbal conceptualization;
in truth, they do not go beyond the four logical alternatives (*catuṣkoṭi*). Within the wisdom of *prajñā*, there is nothing at all;
it is far removed from all mental measures (*cittamātra*) and is not accessible to any mental measure. Thus, it is far removed from all verbal expression and is not any verbal expression whatsoever.
Since that which is spoken of is beyond speech, it is fundamentally without arising. Generally speaking, wherever there is arising, there is cessation;
since there is nothing that arises, there is nothing that ceases. Generally speaking, that which has cessation is brought about by effort;
only that which has no cessation is inherently quiescent from the beginning, not requiring cessation before it becomes ceased. This is quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*).
This is precisely self-nature nirvana, which is neither arising nor ceasing; because it is solely self-nature nirvana, neither arising nor ceasing, it is far removed from birth and death.
All worldly fruits that are realized and causes that are cultivated belong to the realm of arising and ceasing.
This nirvana is like space: it is neither an agent nor an object of action; it is simply non-existence.
Since phenomena cannot be found to have a cause, and since there is neither cause nor effect, upon what could any mental conception depend?
This nirvana is like space; it is neither the subject that perceives nor the object that is perceived. Thus, no deluded conceptualization or dependence can be found.
Since there is no such dependence, one transcends all the falsehoods of the world, which are not seen by those of the non-Buddhist paths or the two vehicles.
This nirvāṇa, which is like space and free from the conceptual proliferation (*prapañca*) of the four extremes, is neither that which speaks nor that which is spoken;
this alone is the one reality, while the other two are not true. Because one realizes this very suchness (*tathatā*) and the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), one is called a Tathāgata.
A Tathāgata is none other than a Buddha, for he has uniquely attained unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment (*anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*).
He is named Samyaksambuddha Buddha. Now, as for the term Samyaksambuddha Buddha:
because he knows all phenomena, both mundane and supramundane, without exception and possesses all-knowledge (*sarvajñatā*), he is called the "Universal Awakened One" (*Samyak-saṃbuddha*).

Because he has awakened himself and possesses the knowledge of all aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*), he is called the "Perfectly Awakened One" (*Buddha*). He causes those who have not yet transcended all... [to do so].

If one falls into all the measures of the sense faculties (*indriya-pramāṇa*), then although the consciousness of radiance (*jvālā-vijñāna*) has not yet been forgotten, one remains far from Prajñā-wisdom.

Only by being able to distance oneself from the various measures of the mind, thought, and mentation (*citta-manas-manovijñāna*), transforming the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) into wisdom, and thereby attaining unimpeded, pervasive awakening, is this true awakening (*samyak-saṃbodhi*). True awakening is itself pervasive awakening; therefore it is said:
Wisdom (*jñāna*) and its radiance (*jvālā*) are neither different nor not different; likewise, the aforementioned *dharmakāya* and liberation (*vimukti*) are neither different nor not different.
This perfect fusion of the three virtues—the *dharmakāya*, *prajñā*, and liberation—is collectively termed "self-nature nirvana" (*svabhāva-nirvāṇa*).
Yongjia said: "The *dharmakāya* being free from doubt is precisely *prajñā*; *prajñā* being free from attachment is precisely liberation."
Liberation and quiescence are the Dharmakāya, like the three dots of the syllable *i* which are neither different nor not different.

The wondrous virtue of Nirvāṇa is likewise; it is not that a Buddha does not realize it. Haoyue Gongfeng asked Changsha Chengyan, "Have the good spiritual friends of the world realized the Nirvāṇa of the Three Virtues? The Master said, "Virtuous One, you ask about the fruition."

Regarding the cause of *nirvāṇa*, it is called *nirvāṇa*. Regarding the *nirvāṇa* of the fruition, a question was asked: "The world’s good spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*) have not yet realized [it];
why have they not yet realized it? The Master said: "Their merit has not yet equalled that of the various sages. [The questioner asked:

"If their merit has not yet equalled that of the various sages, how can they be called 'good spiritual friends'? The Master said: "Because they clearly see the Buddha-nature, they may also be called 'good spiritual friends.'"
The disciple asked, "I do not yet understand by what path their merit becomes equal, such that they are said to have realized Great Nirvāṇa.
The Master showed him this verse: "The Mahāprajñā illuminates liberation; The profound Dharma is the essence of the Dharmakāya’s quiescence. These three are one in principle, perfect and eternal.
If you wish to know where their merit is equal, This is called the Constantly Quiescent Light (Nityaprabhāsvara). It is the fruition of the three virtues of Nirvāṇa, already attained."
To explain how there is nirvana within the cause, the Master said: "Venerable Sir, this sutra speaks of 'non-activity' and 'no-cause.
Changsha spoke of nirvana on the level of the fruit and nirvana within the cause; examine these well—they are neither different nor not different."
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke in verse:

"Completely detached from the measures of the sense-faculties, there is no object and no cause; having already left behind the perceiver and the perceived, one is also detached from the characteristic and the characterized.

Regarding the aggregates, conditions, and so forth, the Perfectly Enlightened One—whether as one or as different—cannot be seen. If there is no seeing," [as the Wei translation says: "The Buddha does not see even a single dharma among all conditions and the five aggregates."]... [there is no seeing].

How, then, is it distinguished? It is neither created nor uncreated, neither an effect nor a cause, neither the aggregates (*skandha*) nor residing within the aggregates, nor is there anything else mixed with them (the Tang translation says:
"neither the aggregates nor non-aggregates, nor separated from other things"; the Wei translation says: "neither the aggregates nor separated from the aggregates, nor located elsewhere").
Nor does it possess any inherent natures as they are perceived through false imagination; yet one should know that it is not that this dharma does not exist, for the dharma is likewise existent.

Therefore, existence exists because of non-existence; if existence were non-existent, it should not be accepted, and if it were existent, it should not be conceptualized. (The Tang translation says: "Since non-existence cannot be grasped, existence also should not be spoken of.

To establish the notions of self and non-self through the measure of verbal expression, to linger and become immersed in the two extremes, and thereby destroying oneself and destroying others—this is liberation from all faults.
To correctly observe that the self is pervasive in this way is called right contemplation.

To disparage the Great Teacher is to say that this general verse describes the Perfectly Enlightened One as being free from all faults; that the sense-faculties (*indriya*) do not depart from the spheres of seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing;
and that by taking the eight consciousnesses as the faculties, the evolving consciousnesses are transformed into wisdom, thereby remaining detached from all phenomena.
The measure of the faculties is precisely the realization of the pure *dharmakāya*. Fundamentally, there is neither the fruit nor the cause of cultivation;
all such things are transcended. Having transcended them, one is also free from the person who perceives and free from the phenomena that are perceived.

How, then, could there still be the characteristics of the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) or the characteristics of the objects perceived by the five aggregates? It is said: "One is free from both characteristics and the characterized. Is this not so?

This is what is meant by "all things being without marks. When one contemplates the five aggregates and all conditions through equal and perfect awakening, they are equal and non-dual with the self-nature *dharmakāya*. One perceives neither their unity nor their difference.
Since neither unity nor difference can be perceived, how could one make distinctions and say they are "neither one nor different," "neither both nor neither"?
Since such conceptual distinctions do not exist, this is neither what is called "action" or "non-action" by those outside the Way, nor is it what the Two Vehicles call "fruit" or "cause.
The inherently pure *dharmakāya* is neither identical to the five aggregates (*pañcaskandha*) nor separate from them;
it is not mixed with other things, yet it never departs from the characteristics of the five aggregates and their conditions.
Nevertheless, regarding these aggregates (*skandha*) and their conditions, those who perceive them as existing grasp them through deluded conceptualization as being existent;

those who perceive them as non-existent grasp them through deluded conceptualization as being non-existent. In reality, they do not possess an intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) such as that which is conceptually discriminated by delusion.
Thus, while one perceives all things as existing, it is not a case of sinking into a void, for that would be like the deluded conceptualizations [of non-existence].
When one discerns all things, there is no such dharma; the nature of dharmas is itself thus: all dharmas are as they are, neither existent nor non-existent, but entirely equal.
This nature of all dharmas has been so from the very beginning. Those false views of existence and non-existence arise through relative opposition:
because something previously existed, one speaks of "non-existence"; because something previously did not exist, one speaks of "existence. If there were no opposition...

Since existence and non-existence are not established even when considered sequentially, one should not grasp at non-existence by asserting that it exists as non-existence, for non-existence likewise lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*).
One should not conceptualize existence by asserting that it exists, for existence likewise lacks intrinsic nature.
Since these two phenomena—existence and non-existence—lack intrinsic nature, then as for what you have spoken regarding "acting," "not acting," and "the fruit": [they are likewise untenable].
Those who associate with causes do not depart from the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*) and the characterized (*lakṣya*); how could they avoid fault?

They are merely deluded within the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), reckoning the self in form (*rūpa*) and form in the self. To claim "the self apart from form" or "form apart from the self" constitutes twenty kinds of views of self (*ātma-dṛṣṭi*).
Failing to realize that the self is not a true self, the ultimate reality (*tattva-artha*) is simply the one True Self.

Those who do not perceive that false self and realize the true self are detached from verbal expression; yet they fail to understand this, clinging instead to words, numbers, and calculations, lingering and refusing to let go.
They become immersed in the two extremes of existence and non-existence, permanence and annihilation; thus they not only ruin themselves but also ruin the world.
Those who fall into the extreme of existence continue through the succession of various realms of rebirth, while those who fall into the extreme of non-existence sever the seeds [of continuity].
If one’s nature possesses such faults, by what means can liberation be attained?

If one can penetrate my teaching—that the Tathāgata’s Dharmakāya is neither different nor not different from the aggregates, elements, and sense-bases—one will not fall into the false views of the two extremes, nor will one fall into the conceptual calculations of the four propositions; thus one is transcendentally liberated, far removed from all falsehood.
This error arises from failing to observe through right mindfulness and thus not attaining the "penetration of one's own school" (*svapravacanadharmatā*).

When one realizes that among all phenomena there is not a single thing that can be found as either identical or different, this is called right observation, this is called right universal awakening, and it is not slandering the Great Dharma Vehicle of the Tathāgata.
Therefore it is said: "Do not disparage the Great Teacher. Baizhang said: "One must distinguish between the host and the guest in speech."
Being stained by craving for all phenomena of existence and non-existence, one’s own mind is deluded by all phenomena of existence and non-existence;

this is the illuminating function of the Demon King, belonging to the realm of Mara. Simply by reflecting and awakening in the present moment, do not rely upon or dwell in any phenomena of existence or non-existence, whether mundane or supramundane; do not even form a conceptual understanding of them, nor rely upon such understanding.

Abiding in non-knowing, understand that one's own mind is the Buddha; its illuminating function is the Bodhisattva-mind. This mind is the sovereign master, while the illuminating function belongs to adventitious dust.
Just as water is described apart from its waves, it illuminates the myriad phenomena without effort. If one can abide in tranquil illumination, there is no need for mysticism;
a hundred things will naturally be threaded through past and present. As it is said: "The Spirit has no function of illuminating; when the ultimate function is reached, it is [the Spirit]."
Because he constantly abides in the ability to act as a teacher in all places, Baizhang possessed such right contemplation, and thus he became a master for a hundred generations.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has said, the sūtras are subsumed [under this]."
Regarding the non-arising and non-ceasing of sensation, the World-Honored One has further stated that "non-arising and non-ceasing" is another name for the Tathāgata.
Why, World-Honored One, do you speak of non-arising and non-ceasing as another name for the Tathāgata on account of the absence of intrinsic nature? [The Chinese version states:

"As explained in the Buddha’s sūtras, one distinguishes and grasps that 'non-arising and non-ceasing' is precisely another name for the Tathāgata. World-Honored One, please explain to me: since this is a non-existent dharma, how can it be called another name for the Tathāgata? As the World-Honored One has said:]
"One should know that to claim all phenomena (*dharma*) are neither arising nor ceasing is to fall into the view of existence and non-existence. The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"I teach that all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing because the categories of existence and non-existence do not manifest. Mahāmati said to the Buddha:
"World-Honored One, if all phenomena are non-arising, then the apprehension of phenomena cannot be found, because all phenomena are non-arising. If there were any phenomenon within names..."
"I only pray that you will explain this for me. The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Excellent, excellent! Listen attentively and listen attentively;
reflect upon it well, and I shall analyze and explain it for you. Mahāmati replied to the Buddha, "Yes, I shall receive the teaching.

The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "I say that the Tathāgata is not without nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), nor is he subsumed under the categories of non-arising or non-ceasing; yet he also does not encompass all phenomena."
Because they depend on conditions, they are neither born nor extinguished, yet this is not without meaning.

Mahāmati, what I call the "mind-born Dharma-body" (manomaya-dharmakāya) is another name for the Tathāgata (the Chinese translation states: "What I call 'non-arising' is precisely the Tathāgata; it is a distinct name for the mind-born Dharma-body").
That which is non-arising is not within the realm of any heterodox teachers, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Bodhisattvas at the seventh stage. Mahāmati, that non-arising is the Tathāgata.

Mahāmati, it is like the various names for Indra—Śakra, Purandara (in Sanskrit, Śakradevendra is translated as "Lord of the Gods," also called "Destroyer of Cities," or "Kauśika"—all of which are alternative names for Indra). In this same way, each of these Buddhas has many individual names;

yet, while there are many names, there is no multiplicity of intrinsic natures, nor is there an absence of self-nature. (In the Tang [Chinese] translation, it says: "For example, Indra, the earth, space, and even hands and feet...")
Each individual thing has many names, yet it does not possess multiple entities on account of those many names, nor is it without an entity.

It is said in response: Since it was previously stated that the Dharmakāya, liberation, and prajñā are of one essence and thus already free from characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), and since at this point one further wishes to be free from names (*nāman*), Mahāmati asks:
"In various places throughout the sūtras spoken by the World-Honored One, it is said that all..."
Regarding the statement that phenomena are neither born nor extinguished, and that the Blessed One further said that "neither born nor extinguished" is another name for the Tathāgata:

does the Blessed One say that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished because they lack intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), or does he say so because he perceives "neither born nor extinguished" as another name for the Tathāgata? If one says that all phenomena are neither born nor extinguished...

Those who hold that "non-existence" (niḥsvabhāva) is a synonym for the Tathāgata fall into the view of non-existence; yet those who further claim it is a synonym for the Tathāgata fall into the view of existence.
Thus, they fall into the views of existence and non-existence. The Buddha taught that all phenomena are neither arising nor ceasing;

this does not refer to the existence or non-existence manifested by worldly views. It is simply that because there is no arising, there is no existence; and because there is no ceasing, [there is no non-existence].
Neither non-existence, nor existence, nor non-non-existence—that which transcends the measure of existence and non-existence is fundamentally neither existent nor non-existent;
therefore, the categories of existence and non-existence do not appear. Mahāmati, because existence and non-existence do not appear, all dharmas are unarisen.
If all dharmas are fundamentally unarisen, then even that which is subsumed within the sūtras cannot be apprehended. Why is this so?
"If all phenomena do not exist as such, who is there to establish their names?
If, within the conventional designations of names, there were some distinct phenomenon that conformed to the meaning of non-arising, I would only wish for you to explain it. The Buddha said:
"The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is not a non-entity; it does not fall into the category of nothingness. Nor is it comprised within the fruits of the path, for it is neither born nor extinguished."

The Dharma is neither arising nor ceasing; it encompasses all dharmas, yet the characteristics of dharmas as having real existence cannot be apprehended, so that one does not fall into the extreme of existence.

Although it is free from existence and non-existence, its non-arising and non-ceasing are not manifested only after conditions for arising and ceasing have been exhausted or existence and non-existence have been transcended.
Because it is fundamentally non-arising and non-ceasing, it has never arisen and never ceased from the very beginning.
Although [the dharmas] have ceased, one still establishes names and so forth for them; this is not a false teaching, because it has the sense that they truly exist.
What is the meaning of this? I say that the mind-born Dharma-body is "unborn yet born" and "born yet unborn"—this is simply another name for the Tathāgata.
That unborn realm is realized as the equality of true reality by those from the eighth stage downward.
Only when one can thus understand that arising is itself non-arising and non-arising is itself arising— wherein no further distinct characteristics can be found—
is it so; for if the cessation realized by all outsiders, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas,

and bodhisattvas of the seventh stage has not yet abandoned the latent store (*ālayavijñāna*) and the characteristics of arising and ceasing still persist, how could they know this true realm of neither arising nor ceasing?
Because it pertains to the realm (*dhātu*), there is the name "unborn" based on the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*); because it accords with the meaning of the unborn, there is the name "Tathāgata.
This does not mean that the true reality is absent; I maintain that "non-arising" is simply another name for the Tathāgata.
For example, Śakra has one name, Śakradevendra; another, Purandara; and another, Kauśika. It is just so.
From the earth and empty space to the hands, feet, and all other things, each possesses many names;
Śakra, so too do these Buddhas. It is not because there are many names that there are many entities; though the names are many, the entity is one.
Nor is it that they lack their own intrinsic nature (svabhāva) such that they eventually lapse into non-existence before being called "non-existent."
If birth itself is non-arising, how can one say that all dharmas are non-arising? Should it not then follow that there should be no different names for them?
Formerly, Nanquan asked a monk, "What sutra are you lecturing on? The monk replied, "The *Sutra of Maitreya’s Descent to Be Born.*" Nanquan said, "When will Maitreya descend to be born?
The monk replied, "He is currently in the heavenly palace; he shall descend to be born in the future. Nanquan said, "There is no Maitreya in heaven, nor is there any on earth."
Dongshan said, "Below there is no Maitreya. Yunju Ying asked, "Above the heavens there is no Maitreya, and below the earth there is no Maitreya;

I wonder who gave him his name? Dongshan was so shaken by this question that his meditation seat trembled, and he said, "Master Ying, when I was at Yunyan, I once asked the Old Man [Nanquan] about this, and my incense burner shook with the answer. Today..."
At these words, Beizi was so overcome that sweat flowed from his entire body. When Dongshan was about to pass away, he said to the assembly, "I have a 'leisurely name' remaining in the world;
who can rid me of it? No one in the assembly could respond. At that time, a novice stepped forward and said, "Please grant me the Dharma-name for the Master.
Dongshan said, "My leisurely name has already been extinguished. Later, Shishuang added a comment, saying: [The text provided ends here.]
"No one has ever been able to get it right," Yunju said. "If there were such a thing as a 'leisurely name,' it would not belong to my late teacher.
Caoshan said, "From antiquity to the present, no one has been able to discern it. Shushan said, "A dragon possesses the power to emerge from the water, yet no one can discern it.
If you can penetrate these words of the various venerable masters, you will know that non-arising is itself the Tathāgata.
Distinct names are themselves non-arising.
Thus, Mahāmati, in this Sahā world (which means "Endurance"), I have three hundred thousand *asaṃkhyeya* names (which means "innumerable").
Fools hear them all and each speaks of my name, yet they do not understand that these are merely different names for me, the Tathāgata.
Mahāmati, there are some sentient beings who know me as the Tathāgata; some who know me as the Omniscient One; some who know me as the Buddha;
some who know me as the Savior of the World; some who know me as the Self-Awakened One; some who know me as the Guide; some who know me as the Universal Guide;
some who know me as the Rishi; some who know me as Brahmā; and some who know me as Viṣṇu.
[This city] is called "Great Power" (Mahābala); some call it "Mastery of Knowledge," some "Supreme Knowledge," some "Kapilavastu" [the city where the Buddha was born],
some "Limit of Reality," some "Moon," some "Sun," some "King," some "Non-arising," some "Non-ceasing," some "Emptiness," some "Suchness," and some "Truth."
Some know the reality-limit (bhūtakoṭi); some know the dharma-nature (dharmatā); some know nirvāṇa; some know the eternal;
some know equality; some know non-duality; some know the signless (animitta); some know liberation; some know the path;
and some know the mind-born (manomaya). Mahāmati, such as these are three hundred thousand asaṃkhyeyas.
My name and title neither increase nor decrease; this world and all other worlds know me entirely as being like the moon reflected in water—neither emerging nor entering.
Yet those foolish people, having fallen into the two extremes, are unable to know me.

Nevertheless, they all pay me respectful homage and make offerings to me, yet they do not skillfully understand the meaning and intent of my words and phrases; they do not discern names, nor do they understand self-realization.
They are attached to various verbal expressions and phrases, conceiving of that which is neither arising nor ceasing as being without intrinsic nature;
they do not understand the distinctions among the Tathāgata’s names— such as Indra, Śakra, and Brahmā— and fail to comprehend their own internal realization,
ultimately adhering to whatever is said regarding all phenomena.

The Master said: "What was stated above—that there is no multiplicity of natures due to a multiplicity of names, yet it is not that there is no intrinsic nature—is further elucidated in detail hereafter.

That the Tathāgata has ten titles means: Tathāgata (Thus-Come One), Arhat (Worthy One), Samyaksaṃbuddha (Perfectly Awakened One), Vidhyācaraṇasaṃpanna (Endowed with Knowledge and Conduct), Sugata (Well-Gone One), Lokavid (Knower of the World), Anuttara (Unsurpassed One), Puruṣadamyasārathi (Charioteer of Men to be Tamed), Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām (Teacher of Gods and Humans), and Buddha Bhagavān (Buddha, the Blessed One)."
The Honored One, the Unsurpassed Knower of the World—his original single title is "Sugata" (the Well-Gone), though this is not the only one; all Buddhas are likewise so.

Their countless hundreds of thousands of names do not go beyond these meanings: they are called "Sun" and "Moon," which refers to the light of the sun and the light of the moon, such as "Solar Face" and "Lunar Face.
In two translations, there are also [epithets] such as "Bull King," "Lion," "Like Water," and "Like Wind."
All of these are explained through metaphors. The "Chapter on the Names" in the *Avataṃsaka* states: "The Tathāgata has four hundred billion and ten thousand names.
The "Chapter on the Lifespan" in the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka* states: "In other lands I act as a Buddha, yet there are further different names;
my clan and surname differ, and my titles are distinguished. Although there are many names, their essence does not differ; it neither increases nor decreases, and it has no coming or going."
There is no coming here or from other worlds; there is no one who knows me in such a way. It is like the moon in water:
it neither emerges from nor enters the water. This is a metaphor for the minds of sentient beings. The moon is a metaphor for the *nirmāṇakāya* (response body) of the Tathāgata.
When the minds of sentient beings are pure, the Tathāgata appears. This is because the *dharmakāya* universally responds to sentient beings and manifests equally, yet without coming or going.
The single moon universally appears in all waters, yet the moon in every body of water is subsumed within that one moon;
it neither emerges nor enters, and thus neither arising nor ceasing can be found. One may call this the "mind-born body," or one may call it "non-arising.
Therefore, it may also be said that non-arising is simply another name for the Tathāgata. Although those foolish people...
Although they hear it being spoken, they do not know that this is another name for the Tathāgata;

because they fall into the two extremes of existence and non-existence through false views, even though they daily revere and make offerings to me, it is as if they do not see the bright moon in turbid water.
They lack skill in understanding the meaning and intent of words and phrases, failing to realize that the various names for the Tathāgata are established based upon their underlying significance.
Meaning is itself the name, and the name is itself the meaning; from the beginning, there is no differentiation between them.
This non-differentiation of names can only be understood by those who penetrate the essential principle of our own school.

Those who merely cling to various words and phrases, and who regard that which transcends existence and non-existence—the dharma of neither arising nor ceasing—as "non-existence," do not truly understand it.
The conceptualization of nature is to differentiate the dharmas that are neither arising nor ceasing by means of the two views of existence and non-existence;

this is precisely not departing from the false views of the two extremes. Since one regards the view of non-arising and non-ceasing as non-existent, yet regards the various names of the Tathāgata as existent, one fails to realize that this very non-arising and non-ceasing is the differentiated manifestation of the Tathāgata.
Names are also like those of Śakra; though there are various different appellations, they are many in name but one in essence.
It is only because they do not understand their own inherent penetration that they cannot decisively reach the ultimate ground where names and reality converge.
This very state of non-arising and non-ceasing is profoundly deep in meaning; fundamentally transcending verbal expression, it pertains to all phenomena.
To grasp the meaning according to the words, while having the meaning obscured by the phrasing—this is like regarding the moon in the water as actually entering or exiting.
Is this not deeply pitiable? Formerly, when the Great Master Mazu was unwell, the head monk asked, "How is your health these days, O Honored One?
The Master replied, "The Buddha of the Sun's Face, the Buddha of the Moon's Face. Xuedou’s verse says: "The Buddha of the Sun's Face..."
"Jade Face and Moon Face—what are these Five Emperors and Three Sovereigns? For twenty years I have labored in earnest for your sake;
how many times have I descended into the Azure Dragon’s cave? These matters are worth recounting; discerning monks, do not treat them with contempt. Tiantong’s verse says:
"Jade Face, Moon Face—stars flow and lightning rolls. Like a mirror facing its reflection, there is no partiality; like a pearl resting on a platter, it is naturally so."
Do you not see? Before the hammer and anvil, gold is refined a hundred times; beneath the knife and ruler, a single thread is guided by a single stroke.
If one clearly realizes this kōan, there will be no name that does not proclaim the title of the Tathāgata, and no object that does not manifest the form of Vairocana;
this is precisely in accord with this profound meaning.
Mahāmati, those deluded people speak thus: "The meaning is identical to the expression; there is no difference between the meaning and the expression.
Why is this? It is because they claim that since meaning has no body, there is no meaning other than the expression itself, and it is merely the expression.
Mahāmati, those of corrupted intelligence do not understand the self-nature of expression, nor do they understand that while expression arises and ceases, meaning does not arise.
Mahāmati, when all verbal expressions are extinguished, one does not fall into the meaning of words;

because one is free from both existence and non-existence, there is neither rebirth nor a body (the Tang translation says: "because one is free from existence and free from non-existence, there is no birth and no substance").

Mahāmati, the Tathāgata does not speak of dharmas that fall into words, for the existence or non-existence of words cannot be apprehended. Mahāmati, except for that which does not fall into words, if there should be any speaking...
When the Tathāgata speaks of "dharmas that fall into words," this is a teaching of falsehood, for dharmas are apart from words.
Therefore, Mahāmati, we Buddhas and all Bodhisattvas do not speak a single word nor answer with a single word. Why is this?
Because dharmas are apart from words. It is not that they lack benefit; rather, what is called "speech" is the conceptual construction of sentient beings.

Therefore, it is generally said: because of the previous statement that one does not understand the meaning and intent of words and phrases, nor distinguish between names and designations—wherein many entities are treated as a single entity—if they are already one, then even though names are of many kinds, there would likewise be no distinction; this constitutes "having parts" (sāvayava).
"Designation" refers to words and phrases; "non-differentiation" refers to the underlying meaning.
Those deluded people who cling to the doctrine that the name is identical to the meaning and the meaning is identical to the name say: "The meaning and its verbal expression are not distinct;
if there are many names, there must be many meanings. Why is this? Because if the meaning had no essence, it could not be expressed through words.
Because it constitutes the very substance [of reality], there is no meaning beyond words and speech; it is merely words and speech themselves.

Those burned by false wisdom do not know the essential nature of words and speech, nor do they know that while words and speech undergo arising and ceasing, their underlying significance (artha) is without arising or ceasing.
Why do words and speech have arising and ceasing? Because they fall into the trap of language and characters.
Furthermore, where there are words and letters, there is the appearance of arising; where there is that which can be seen, there is a determinate essence that can be apprehended.
That which arises must perish, and that which has an essence must decay; these belong to the realm of arising and ceasing and are not the true Dharma.
How then can the meaning take non-arising and non-ceasing as its cause? While it is manifested through words and letters, it does not fall into the trap of the literal expression.
Within the characters, the meaning is fundamentally formless and cannot be said to exist; yet, because there is indeed meaning, it cannot be said not to exist.
Since it belongs neither to existence nor non-existence, it fundamentally does not undergo birth. Since it fundamentally does not undergo birth, it has no self-substance.
Being without birth, it is without cessation; being without substance, it is without decay. Therefore, it is said that the meaning is neither born nor extinguished.
While verbal expression is finite, the meaning is infinite; who then would say that there is no further meaning beyond verbal expression?
Therefore, when the Tathāgata teaches the Dharma, he does not depart from words, yet he does not fall into words. Since it is called "teaching the Dharma," why does he not fall into words?
It is because the Dharma is free from existence and non-existence; thus, the words spoken are likewise [free from them].

To speak while remaining detached from existence and non-existence is silence itself; yet this very silence is speech. When one seeks the characteristics of existence and non-existence, they are utterly unfindable.
Apart from the detachment from existence and non-existence, there is no teaching that does not transcend words. The Tathāgata has constantly said:

"If anyone were to say that the Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma possesses any characteristic of written words that can be apprehended, that person speaks falsely and does not understand all dharmas."
Because it is free from words, the Dharma transcends the realm of words and thus cannot be reached by speech.
Therefore, I have said in my sutras that the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not speak a single word nor answer a single word;
only then does one accord with the fundamental Dharma. As soon as one falls into language, it is no longer the true meaning. Why is this? Because all phenomena...
Because they are free from words and letters, the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas do not fall into the dharma of words and letters.
Nevertheless, for the sake of benefiting all sentient beings, it is not that they do not provide explanations by distinguishing meanings;
they speak only so as to lead back to the meaning, and their speaking is itself non-speaking. Sentient beings, however, do not understand this meaning and take the words themselves to be real.
To speak thus is merely the deluded conceptualization and false views of sentient beings; they do not know that the Dharma transcends words and letters.
Therefore, Yunmen, upon ascending the hall, said: "I have no choice but to tell you all: to say there is 'nothing directly' is already to bury it.
To further desire to step forward, seeking through words and chasing after phrases for understanding, is to go even further astray."

By setting up myriad distinctions and raising extensive objections, one merely wins a victory of verbal dexterity; yet, this only causes the Way to become further removed—when will there ever be a time of rest?
If this matter were to reside within words and phrases, how could the Three Vehicles and the twelve divisions of the teachings lack language?
For what reason, then, is it said that there is a "separate transmission outside the teachings"? If it were to be obtained through scholarly understanding or intellectual acuity...
Even the holy ones of the Ten Stages, whose preaching of the Dharma is like clouds and rain, are still rebuked for their realization of nature as being "like a fine gauze screen.
From this we know that all those with a mind are worlds apart from the enlightened.
Nevertheless, if one has attained the Way, the "fire of the Way" never burns the mouth; though they speak of matters all day long, they never strike against anything.
Lips and teeth have never uttered a single word; all day long one wears clothes and eats rice, yet one has never touched a single grain of rice nor hung a single thread of silk.
Even so, this is still merely talk of the gate and courtyard. One must truly attain it in such a way for it to be so.
If we speak according to the school of the patch-robed monks, presenting the pivot within a phrase requires nothing less than solitary, diligent reflection.
"Even if you can take it up at a single phrase, you are still a drowsy fellow. At that time, a monk asked, "What is this one phrase?
The Master said, "An ancient worthy once said: 'A phrase that does not reveal its wind-bone; before a word is spoken, it is already bestowed.
You advance with your mouth chattering, knowing full well you are utterly at a loss. This extraordinary segment of the School Gate is already contained herein."
Since the Sūtra has almost entirely exhausted its exposition, it would be difficult even for the venerable elders to anticipate this meaning.
Mahāmati, if all dharmas were not taught, the teaching would perish; if the teaching perishes, there would be no Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, or Śrāvakas.
If these did not exist, who would teach and for whom? Therefore, Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva...
Mahāsattva, do not cling to verbal expressions; rather, expound the Dharma through skillful means according to what is appropriate.

Because the aspirations and afflictions of sentient beings are not uniform, I and the Buddhas teach various dharmas for those beings of diverse understandings, so that they may become free from mind, thought, and consciousness.
This is for the sake of attaining the state of the noble wisdom of self-realization, Mahāmati, and not for the sake of [clinging to] the one.
All phenomena are non-existent; they are the manifestation of one's own mind as perceived through direct cognition (*pratyakṣa*), free from the two kinds of false conceptualization.

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas rely on the meaning and not on the words (the Tang translation says: "to cause them to know that all phenomena are manifestations of their own minds, that there are no external objects, and to be free from the two kinds of false conceptualization consisting of the speaker and the spoken").
Tong said: "It was stated above that because the Dharma is detached from words and letters, there should be no Dharma that can be preached;
yet why does the Tathāgata again speak of all dharmas? If he did not speak of all dharmas, the teaching established by the Buddhas since time immemorial would be destroyed.
Once the teaching is destroyed, there would be no Buddhas or Bodhisattvas to serve as witnesses to the Dharma."
Furthermore, there are no pratyekabuddhas or śrāvakas who rely upon the teaching; in total, none exist at all.
Who, then, is the one who preaches the Dharma, and for whom is it preached? This is what is meant by:

"Although one does not rely on the path of language, one likewise does not cling to wordlessness"—this is precisely the essential point. Therefore, Mahāyāna bodhisattvas should bring this to ultimate realization.

Regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), do not cling to verbal expressions; rather, teach all the sūtras and dharmas extensively through skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) as appropriate to the occasion.

This is because among sentient beings there are those who hope to attain the fruit but have not yet abandoned the cognitive obscurations (*jñeyāvaraṇa*), and those who are immersed in the faculties and their objects and have not yet escaped the afflictive obscurations (*kleśāvaraṇa*); since these types are manifold and not uniform, I and the Buddhas act for their sake.
Sentient beings with various differing understandings hear various teachings, yet through the single sound of the Dharma being expounded, each attains understanding according to their own kind;

this causes them to transcend mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). Ordinary people are bound by the sense faculties and objects and do not leave behind the sixth consciousness (*mano-vijñāna*);

non-Buddhists cling to the views of annihilationism and eternalism and do not leave behind the seven consciousnesses; those of the Two Vehicles have realizations and attainments and do not leave behind the eighth consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*).
If one is deluded by consciousness (*vijñāna*), one cannot attain the realm of self-realized noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna-gocara*).
If one can transform consciousness into wisdom and reach the state of self-realized noble wisdom, then one is free from the marks of speech and free from the marks of letters;
for such a person, I do not preach. As it is said: "The Buddha teaches all dharmas to remedy all minds; if there are no minds," [then there is nothing to be taught].
Since the mind functions with respect to all phenomena, it is said that [this teaching] is not for the sake of attaining the state of self-realized noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*).
The reason it is not taught for the sake of attaining self-realized noble wisdom is that such a person has, in accordance with reality, understood that all phenomena are non-existent;
they have realized that the various phenomena of the triple world are merely manifestations of one's own mind and that there are no external objects.
Because it can be attained, there is no external object outside and no internal mind within; thus, one is detached from the two kinds of false conceptualization, namely the speaker and the spoken.
These Mahāyāna bodhisattvas rely solely on the meaning and not on the words;

having already distanced themselves from mind, thought, and consciousness, they have no objective basis regarding the teachings of skillful means, and have already realized the realm of self-awakened noble wisdom.

Furthermore, because it is a ground that cannot be reached by words, the Sage does not establish dharmas as a place for his own personal realization. What about the secret words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs? Rui again remained silent. The Master said, "The secret words of the Buddhas and Patriarchs have been revealed right here. He assented to the Master, saying, "Do you understand? The Master wrote: "I do not understand. The Master said, "If you do not understand, the World-Honored One has secret words;
if you do understand, Kāśyapa does not conceal them. It should be known that the World-Honored One did not preach a Dharma that falls into words and letters;
only one who, like Kāśyapa, does not rely on words and letters is able to believe and accept it."
If good sons or good daughters rely on words and letters, they will destroy the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) themselves and be unable to awaken others;

they fall into a continuity of evil views and preach to the masses, failing to properly comprehend all dharmas, all stages (*bhūmi*), and all characteristics, nor do they understand the phrasing and sentences.

(The Tang translation states: "Those who rely on words and letters fall into evil views and, clinging to their own tenets, give rise to verbal discourse; they cannot skillfully comprehend all [dharmas].")

Since the characteristics of dharmas, their phrasing, and their syntactical structures are themselves corrupted and corrupt [the stages (*bhūmi*)], they cannot cause the minds of people to attain realization.

If one is skilled in all dharmas, all stages, and all common characteristics, and possesses mastery over phrases, meanings, and their inherent nature, then one can delight in the true signless bliss for oneself and establish sentient beings in the equality of the Mahāyāna (the Tang translation says:
"one can also cause others to abide securely in the Mahāyāna’s true signless bliss"). This concludes the section on the Great Wisdom Compendium.
Those who embrace the Mahāyāna embrace all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas;
those who embrace all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas embrace all sentient beings; those who embrace all sentient beings embrace the True Dharma;
those who embrace the True Dharma ensure that the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed; and when the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed—
Then one is able to understand and attain the supreme spheres of rebirth (the Wei translation says "all excellent and sublime places of birth").

Knowing how to attain these supreme spheres of rebirth, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva constantly attains transformation-birth (*upapāduka*), establishes the ten powers of mastery (*vaśitā*) of the Mahāyāna, manifests various physical forms, and thoroughly penetrates the characteristics of sentient beings' appearances, inclinations, and afflictions, preaching the Dharma according to reality. As for "according to reality," it means: [omitted].

That which is "as-it-is" (yathābhūta)—which, according to the Tang translation, means the True Dharma—is without distinction or difference. It is characterized by neither coming nor going, and it is the cessation of all falsity;
this is called "as-it-is. Mahāmati, sons and daughters of good family should not grasp at or adhere to what is said according to conventional expression, for that which is true is beyond words.
Tong said: "The previous statement mentioned that all Bodhisattvas Mahāsattvas rely on the meaning and not on the words. Why do they not rely on the words?
It is because the supreme truth (*paramārtha-satya*) of noble wisdom does not fall within the realm of language and words.
If one relies on words and language, one immediately destroys the ultimate goal of the supreme truth; not only does it destroy it for oneself, it also destroys it for others."
One cannot cause others to attain awakening; why is this? Because their own tenets are not thorough, they fall into a continuous stream of evil views.
Relying solely on the divergent doctrines of their own treatises to preach the Dharma to the masses, they are unable to skillfully comprehend the characteristics of all phenomena.
Since they do not understand the phrasing and terminology, they fail to grasp the characteristics of phenomena, and thus they do not know reality.
If one encounters unwholesome passages and does not know the referents of their terminology, how can one awaken others and cause them to attain the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*)?
If, however, one does not rely on mere words, one will skillfully know all mundane and supramundane dharmas;
skillfully know all the stages (*bhūmi*) and the paths for advancing upward; and skillfully know all conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) and... [unconditioned] phenomena.
To attain mastery over the corresponding characteristics, one must penetrate the words and phrases so that they converge upon their meaning.

When the nature of the meaning is fully realized within the fundamental meaning, and the mind finds delight therein, one is then able to enjoy oneself through the true bliss of signlessness (*animitta-sukha*).
This is the sublime bliss of self-realized noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*), and not the bliss of signs possessed by the two vehicles or external paths. Thus it is said regarding bliss:
That which is signless, neither sorrowful nor joyful, is precisely the mind of equality toward all sentient beings.

Having attained this mind of equality toward all sentient beings, one establishes for them the Dharma of the equal Mahāyāna, causing all sentient beings to dwell securely in the true, signless bliss of the Mahāyāna.
This is the bliss of one’s own nature, fully possessed by every person; I am able [to realize it].
One may delight in it yet be unable to demonstrate it through words; one may attain it yet need not seek it through words.
By relying solely on the meaning, one need not fear an inability to awaken. This is the establishment of the Dharma of the Mahāyāna;
it is the sūtra that accords with principle and accords with capacity, which embraces the Dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing—this is the embracing of the Mahāyāna.
When this teaching is not destroyed, one embraces all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Pratyekabuddhas, and Śrāvakas—those who possess the realized Dharma.

Since there are those who have realized that which is neither born nor extinguished, they embrace all sentient beings, transforming their birth and extinction so that they return to the state of being neither born nor extinguished. Thus, they cause sentient beings to return to that which is unborn.
When the Dharma of cessation is attained, all the deceptive and false phenomena of the world can no longer cause agitation or delusion, and one thereby upholds the True Dharma of the Tathāgata.
Having upheld the True Dharma, one will be able to practice in accordance with the teachings in future lives, so that the lineage of the Buddhas does not become extinct.
Since the lineage of the Buddhas is not severed, one will no longer transmigrate within the three realms.
Furthermore, they do not fall into the void of nihilism, for they are naturally able to discern their superior and wondrous place of birth—

whether it be the Land of Sublime Quiescent Light, the Land of True Reward Adornment, or the Pure Land of Shared Dwelling for Ordinary Beings and Sages— wherein the excellence of its adornments surpasses all else.
Having realized that they have attained such a sublime state of entry, how could these great Bodhisattvas be willing to indulge in the pleasure of mere quiescence?
Yet do you not act for the sake of liberating sentient beings? You constantly manifest the transformation body (*nirmāṇakāya*) to establish the Dharma of the Equal Mahāyāna everywhere;

by means of the ten powers of mastery (*vaśitā*), you manifest various forms and images—namely, the power regarding what is possible and impossible (*sthānāsthāna-jñānabala*), the power of karma, the power of meditative concentration (*dhyāna-bala*), the power of faculties (*indriya-bala*), the power of aspiration (*chanda-bala*), the power of nature (*gotra-bala*), the power of the path leading to all destinations (*sarvatragāminī-pratipad-bala*), the power of recollecting past lives (*pūrvanivāsānusmṛti-bala*), and the power of the divine eye (*divyacakṣus-bala*).
The power of the destruction of outflows (*āsravakṣaya-bala*)—these ten powers are universally manifested in physical forms.
According to the various aspirations, afflictions, and three obstructions of sentient beings, they preach the Dharma as it truly is, in accordance with the time and faculties.

This is the Dharma of the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*) and True Suchness (*tathatā*); because it is neither distinct nor different from all sentient beings, it is called "equality. What is meant by this?
Because the Tathāgata has nowhere from which he comes and nowhere to which he goes, and his essence is suchness (*tathatā*), he is called "Thus" (*Tathā*).
Why is he called "Real"? Because all things possess arising and ceasing, while this alone does not arise or cease;

that which possesses arising and ceasing is false and deceptive, whereas that which is without arising or ceasing is the ultimate reality. Therefore, he is called "Real. These two characters, "Thus-Real" (*Tathāgata*), [express this].
Furthermore, these are merely words and one should not grasp at them; do not become attached to the conceptualizations that follow verbal expression.
One who understands the true meaning should know that as for that which neither comes nor goes, what thing could it be? As for that which is neither born nor extinguished, what form could it have?
Since it is fundamentally free from the characteristics of words, one should not fall into words when preaching the Dharma. — Huangbo.
Now, one who seeks the Dharma does not seek by clinging to the Buddha, does not seek by clinging to the Dharma, and does not seek by clinging to the Sangha;

they should be without seeking. Because they do not seek by clinging to the Buddha, there is no Buddha; because they do not seek by clinging to the Dharma, there is no Dharma; because they do not seek by clinging to the Sangha, there is no Sangha.
[The student] asked: "Venerable Master, you are currently preaching the Dharma; how can you say there is no Sangha and also no Dharma?"
The Master said: "If you see that there is a dharma that can be taught, you are seeking me through sound. If you see a self, this is the dharma of location. Furthermore, there is no dharma;
the dharma is precisely the mind. Therefore, the Patriarch said: 'When this dharma of mind is transmitted, how has any dharma ever been a dharma?
When there is no dharma and no fundamental mind, only then does one understand the mind and the dharma of mind.'"

In reality, there is not a single dharma that can be called "sitting at the site of enlightenment" (*bodhimaṇḍa*). The site of enlightenment is simply the non-arising of all views and the realization that dharmas are fundamentally empty;
it is called the *tathāgatagarbha* of emptiness. Originally there was not a single thing—where, then, could there be any dust?
If one grasps the meaning within this, one wanders freely; what need is there for further discourse? This is precisely the ability to abide in the true bliss of signlessness.
Thus they find their own delight. Xuefeng addressed the assembly, saying: "If I speak of east and west, you will merely seek out my words and chase after my phrases.
If I am like a wild goat hanging from a tree branch, where will you go to grope for me?
A monk asked Baofu, "As for Xuefeng, what teaching did he have that was like a wild goat hanging from a branch? Baofu replied: [The text here implies the master's response to this inquiry].
