"Is it not that you were unable to serve as a junior attendant (xiaoshi) to Xuefeng?
Furthermore, Jingqing asked Xuefeng, "The ancients have said... At this, Xuefeng lay down flat on his back. After a long while, he rose and asked, "What did you ask? Jingqing asked again.
Xuefeng replied, "A man who lives in vain and dies in waves. Touzi’s verse comments: "Ordinarily he loves guests, yet he harbors resentment toward the Tathāgata; when people arrive, he lies down."
"Come, let us stop idle talk and lie together in emptiness; had we known earlier that sleep would not be in vain, these red flames would have fallen into cold ashes.
This was Xuefeng’s teaching according to reality, intended to lead students to rely on the meaning rather than the words;
this is truly the enduring standard left by this sutra.
Mahāmati, it is like a fool who, when pointed at an object by another with a finger, looks only at the finger and does not perceive the actual object.

In this way, such fools grasp at and become attached to the finger of verbal expression; they do not relinquish it until the very end and thus can never attain the supreme reality that transcends words.
Mahāmati, it is as if an infant should eat food that has been thoroughly cooked and should not eat raw food.
If one eats raw food, it causes madness because one does not know the sequential methods for cooking it.
Mahāmati, in this same way, that which is neither born nor extinguished, if not cultivated through skillful means, is unwholesome. Therefore, you should cultivate skillful means well;
do not follow mere words, just as one would not look at the tip of a finger. For this reason, Mahāmati, you should cultivate skillful means regarding the true meaning.
The true meaning is subtle and tranquil; it is the cause of nirvana. Discursive speech is associated with conceptual construction, and conceptual construction is the accumulation of birth and death.
Mahāmati, the true meaning is obtained from those who have heard much. Those who have heard much are those who are skilled in the meaning, not those skilled in discursive speech.
One who is skilled in the meaning does not follow the bodies [of teachings] of any heterodox scriptures or treatises.
Not following it oneself and not causing others to follow it is what is called being a virtuous one of great learning;

therefore, those who seek the true meaning should draw near to such great learning— namely, that which concerns the good meaning— and should distance themselves from its opposite, which is attachment to mere words.
Tong said: "The previous statement that 'good sons and good daughters should not grasp at or adhere to what is spoken as being the reality' was because reality is free from words.
Why then do you say that the primary meaning (paramārtha) is free from the characteristics of words?
It is like using a finger to point at an object for a fool who cannot see it; the object itself is the reality."

The "finger" refers to verbal expression. Those who are foolish do not examine this; they merely look at the finger and fail to grasp the object, or they merely look at the verbal expression and fail to grasp the true meaning.
Such fools take the finger itself to be the object and take the verbal expression itself to be the true meaning.
Following the finger of verbal expression, they grasp it and become attached to it, never ceasing until their death.

If one asks where the object that transcends the finger can be found, or where the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*) that transcends verbal expression resides—it is because one cannot abandon the finger of the written word to grasp the ultimate truth that such a person is called "foolish.
Nevertheless, the teacher of the Dharma must still employ appropriate skillful means (*upāya-kauśalya*) to point it out; for example, as is appropriate for an infant.
Regarding the consumption of cooked food, there are those who do not understand the sequence of maturation; they eat raw food without threshing or boiling it.

If one eats raw things, one will become deranged and confused. Likewise, the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*) is neither born nor extinguished, free from the characteristics of verbal expression and free from the characteristics of written words;
yet if one does not practice through skillful means and stages, it is like eating such raw food.
Infants eat raw food; they do not grasp its essence and thus fail to attain the fully adorned Dharma-body.

Instead, they treat it as unwholesome dharmas, like that foolish person who, not knowing how to cook in spring, consumes grains merely as written characters and fails to obtain the nourishment of their meaning.
For this reason, regarding the true and supreme ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*), O noble sons and daughters...
Women should skillfully cultivate practice so as to find the flavor of the meaning of non-arising and non-ceasing;
they should not cling to words and letters, for it is like looking at the tip of a finger and never knowing what object is being pointed toward.
Regarding the true meaning, one must indeed cultivate through skillful means.
Why is this? It is because that which is called the true ultimate meaning (*paramārtha*) is neither born nor extinguished;
it is silent, tranquil, and most subtle, incomparable to ordinary states of stillness. This is the primary cause for *nirvāṇa* without remainder.
The wondrous virtue of *nirvāṇa*—constancy, bliss, self, and purity—is termed the ground of fruition. Its cultivation and realization must necessarily begin with non-arising.
Because non-extinction is the mind of the causal ground, the meaning of reality should be cultivated through skillful means.
Why is it that one should not cling to verbal expressions? It is because all verbal expressions are conjoined with delusive thoughts (*vikalpa*).
Delusive thoughts arise from falsehood and are extinguished by falsehood; their continuous differentiation is the dharma of birth and death, causing one to circulate within birth and death.
Because one who [clings] cannot attain *nirvāṇa*, it is inappropriate to accept or adhere to verbal expressions.

However, since the meaning of reality (*tattvārtha*) must necessarily be revealed by relying on verbal expressions, would it be possible to exhaustively discard all verbal expressions while seeking the meaning of reality?
This meaning of reality must be cultivated; it is obtained from the "much hearing" (*bahuśruta*) of virtuous spiritual friends (*kalyāṇamitra*). What is called "much hearing" is...

Those who hear this say that it is skillful in the meaning through skillful means regarding the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), rather than being skillful in sound through skillful means regarding various verbal expressions.
They consider it to be skillful in meaning because it truly knows that self-nature (*svabhāva*) is neither born nor extinguished;

whereas all the scriptures and treatises of external paths (tīrthika), whether they posit causes or no causes, ultimately do not transcend the phenomena of birth and extinction, and certainly [do not].
Following his teaching, one neither follows it oneself nor causes others to follow it;

rather, one distances oneself from all evil and burns away [defilements] through wisdom until returning to the ultimate, which is simply the single state of non-arising and non-ceasing. This is what is called "virtuous and learned.
Those who seek the true meaning should indeed draw near to such a learned spiritual friend. Thus he said.
That which is called "good meaning" refers to the skillful means of sequential cultivation that can effectively guide others;
it is not like feeding raw food to an infant. Therefore, one should draw near to and associate with such [teachings].

If one contradicts or opposes this state of being well-versed in the teachings (*bahuśruta*), one may be skilled in mere verbal expression but unskilled in the meaning; such a person remains far removed from *nirvāṇa*.

"One who does not leave birth and death should distance themselves from those whom they might otherwise associate with," said Chan Master Huanglong Weiqing, who had received the seal of mind from Huichang.
He often told people: "The reason students of today have not escaped birth and death is where does their illness lie?
Their illness lies in the fact that their 'thieving mind' has not yet died. Yet this is not their fault; it is the fault of their teachers."
It is also like Emperor Gao of the Han, who deceived and killed Han Xin; though Xin was dead, was his mind truly dead?
Where does the efficacy of the ancient scholars' claim to "transcend birth and death in a single word" lie? It lies in the fact that their "thieving mind" has already died.
Yet this is not something the student can achieve by themselves; it is truly due to the subtle and precise forging of the teacher, as in the case of Emperor Wu of Liang.
When Emperor Wu beheld Hou Jing in the Great Hall, he remained unmoved in voice or expression, yet the heart of Jing was already utterly withered and spent.
What is said by various schools is not without its beauty; however, it is like the flowers painted by Zhao Chang—though they are remarkably lifelike, they are not real flowers.
The scriptural text provides three metaphors for karma; here, three further metaphors are added to complete the set.
The turning of the Dharma is nothing other than causing people to see the moon by means of the finger; do not be deluded by painted flowers.
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva, further empowered by the Buddha’s majestic spiritual authority, addressed the Buddha, saying:

"World-Honored One, there is nothing extraordinary about Your World-Honored One’s manifestation of non-arising and non-ceasing. Why is this? Because even the causal factors of all external paths are likewise [non-arising and non-ceasing]."
The Blessed One has taught that space, cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and the realm of nirvāṇa are neither born nor extinguished.

The Blessed One has also taught that the externalists claim various causes give rise to all worlds, whereas the Blessed One teaches that ignorance, craving, karma, and false discrimination act as conditions for the arising of all worlds;
these are merely differences in names for those causes and conditions. External causal conditions are likewise [taught].

In this way, there is not even a grain of difference between the World-Honored One and the non-Buddhists regarding the nine categories—such as the Supreme Lord (Iśvara), the Sovereign of Beings (Puruṣa), and so forth—which they claim are neither born nor extinguished. The World-Honored One also teaches that all natures are neither born nor extinguished, and that existence and non-existence cannot be apprehended;
likewise, the non-Buddhists also teach that the four great elements are indestructible and that their intrinsic nature is neither born nor extinguished.
"The four great elements are always the four great elements, even as they circulate through the various realms of existence without abandoning their own nature;
the teaching of the World-Honored One is likewise so. Therefore, I say there is nothing extraordinary about it.

I only wish that the World-Honored One would explain its distinctions, for it is by these distinctions that it excels all non-Buddhists; if there were no distinctions, then all non-Buddhists would also be [the Buddha]."
Because [the Buddha] is neither born nor extinguished, the World-Honored One has said that it is impossible for many Buddhas to appear in a single world-system, as previously stated;
for if there were many Buddhas in one world-system, they would be indistinguishable from one another.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "The 'neither-born-nor-extinguished' that I teach is not the same as the 'neither-born-nor-extinguished' of the non-Buddhists."

Why is this? Because those various non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) maintain that there is a self-nature (*svabhāva*) which is unarisen and immutable (in the Tang translation: "The self-nature and characteristics spoken of by the non-Buddhists are real, unarisen, and immutable").
I do not hold such a view, as I fall neither into the category of existence nor non-existence. Mahāmati, my [teaching] is free from the categories of existence and non-existence;

it is free from arising and ceasing; it is neither a nature (*bhāva*) nor a non-nature (*abhāva*). Since it appears like various illusions and dreams, it is not a non-nature. How could it be non-existent?

Because all natures (dharmas) are subsumed by the characteristic of the lack of self-nature (*niḥsvabhāva-lakṣaṇa*)—due to their appearing and not appearing, and due to their being subsumed and not subsumed—all natures are neither non-existent nor not non-existent.

(The Tang translation says: "The Dharma I teach is neither existent nor non-existent, free from arising and free from ceasing. Why is it not non-existent? Because forms are seen in various ways, like illusions and dreams. Why is it not existent?

Because the self-nature of form-characteristics is not existent, and because they are seen and not seen, and grasped and not grasped. Therefore, I say that all dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent. It is merely the awakening to oneself...
When mental direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) arises and conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) ceases, there is peace and happiness, and worldly affairs are forever stilled.
It is said that because the Great Virtuous One has heard much and does not follow any non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*) scriptures or treatises,
he has already implicitly pointed out the subtle and wondrous *nirvāṇa*— the non-arising and non-ceasing that is not the "non-arising" clung to by non-Buddhists.
Regarding "extinction," Mahāmati, by virtue of the Buddha’s majestic spiritual power, has translated this in detail as follows:

it refers to the non-arising and non-extinguishing of the "agent" (kartṛ) postulated by non-Buddhists as the cause of the arising and extinction of all phenomena; this is contrasted with the non-arising and non-extinguishing dharmas taught by the World-Honored One, namely:
space (*ākāśa*), the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*), non-analytical cessation (*apratisaṃkhyā-nirodha*), and the unconditioned state of nirvāṇa (*nirvāṇa-asaṃskṛta*).

There is no difference between these two: namely, that which the non-Buddhists claim—that all sentient beings arise from various causes and conditions—and what the World-Honored One has taught—that the world arises with ignorance, craving, karma, and false discrimination as its conditions. Although the names of these causes and conditions differ, their reality is the same.
This applies even to external objects; for instance, just as lumps of clay or atoms arise from external causes and conditions to produce various phenomena, so too is it with the former case.
Furthermore, there are three such [views]: namely, the non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) who reckon that nine things—
(1) atoms and so forth, (2) the two directions, (3) space, (4) atoms, (5) the four great elements, (6) Mahābrahmā, (7) Śakra, (8) Maheśvara,
and (9) the Lord of Beings (i.e., the Self or Ātman)— are all neither born nor extinguished, and thus they are identical to what the World-Honored One teaches as "one."

The nature of all things is neither born nor extinguished, and there is no difference between them. This refers to the non-Buddhists who calculate that the four great elements are indestructible, circulating through the various realms of existence without abandoning their own nature;

thus they consider this to be "neither born nor extinguished. This is no different from what the World-Honored One has taught: that the nature of the four great elements is truly pervasive throughout the Dharma-realm.
There is nothing whatsoever that is not the path of the non-Buddhists; it has already been said that there is nothing therein that is extraordinary or superior.
Regarding those who surpass the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), if there were no difference [between them], one might ask why the Buddha taught that he is superior.
If the World-Honored One’s teaching were no different from that of the non-Buddhists, then since all non-Buddhists would likewise be Buddhas,
and because the World-Honored One has stated that there are not many Buddhas in a single world-system, it would follow that there must now be many Buddhas, based on what has been taught.
Because the dharma of non-arising and non-ceasing is without distinction, the Buddha said: "My teaching of non-arising and non-ceasing differs from that of the non-Buddhists;
it is also not the same as their theory of non-arising impermanence. Why is this so?

What the non-Buddhists conceive of as non-arising and non-ceasing is the claim that all things possess a real nature and characteristics that do not arise and do not change; however, [they merely]... regarding only... (text fragment ends).

The existence and non-existence of marks have already been distinguished above. One perceives that all phenomena arise and perish in impermanence, yet their intrinsic nature is revealed as neither arising nor perishing, but eternal.
While existence is used to manifest non-existence, this ultimate "non-existence" is merely a discourse on impermanence;
therefore, it falls within the categories of existence and non-existence. I do not speak in such a manner. That which I call the True Self is free from existence.

This teaching that there is no arising or ceasing because all things are devoid of a fundamental basis is neither a doctrine asserting that things possess intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), nor is it a doctrine asserting that they lack intrinsic nature.
Why is it not non-existent? Because forms appear in various ways like illusions and dreams; therefore, they cannot be said to be non-existent. Why is it not existent?
Because the characteristics of illusory and dream-like forms fundamentally lack any intrinsic nature that can be apprehended. Therefore, they cannot be said to be existent.
It may be called "existent," yet it has never been manifest, though in reality it has never failed to manifest;
it has never been encompassed, yet in reality it has never failed to encompass. It exists and yet does not exist; it is non-existent and yet is not non-existent.
Therefore, I say that all dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent, but can be fully realized as being merely manifestations of one's own mind. Thus it is.
The moon in water is like a reflection in a mirror; it is originally non-existent, yet one does not give rise to deluded conceptualization regarding existence.
It is originally not non-existent, yet one does not give rise to deluded conceptualization regarding non-existence. Detached from both existence and non-existence, who could undergo birth and death?
Since birth and death are absent, quiescent extinction is bliss; therefore, one attains stability, peace, and joy that transcend [the mundane].
The worldly affairs of the three realms have forever ceased, and I have attained great liberation. This is precisely what distinguishes me from the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*).
The non-Buddhists do not leave behind worldly affairs; they engage in false discrimination and ultimately fall back into birth and extinction, failing to attain peace and stability.
Because they cling to the existence of marks (*nimitta*), they are not superior. This shall be explained in detail below. What is meant by "World-Honored One" (*bhagavat*)?

Is this not extraordinary? Formerly, Xue Jian asked the Sixth Patriarch: "The virtuous practitioners of Chan in the capital all say that if one wishes to realize the Way, one must practice seated meditation and cultivate concentration;
there has never been anyone who attained liberation without relying on meditation and concentration.
I do not know how the Dharma you teach compares to theirs. The Patriarch replied: "The Way is realized through the mind's awakening; how could it depend on..."
Regarding "sitting," a sutra states: "If one perceives the Tathāgata as either lying down or sitting, this is practicing a deviant path.
Why? Because he comes from nowhere and goes nowhere; being without arising or ceasing is the pure dhyāna of the Tathāgata.
All dharmas are empty and quiescent—this is the pure sitting of the Tathāgata. Since there is ultimately nothing to be realized, how much less is there sitting? Jian said: "My younger brother..."
When the Master returned, the Emperor was certain to ask him; he wished for the Venerable Monk’s compassionate instruction on the essential point of the mind.

The Patriarch said: "The Way has neither light nor darkness; light and darkness are merely the meaning of succession and alternation. That light and darkness are inexhaustible is also a state of exhaustion, for they are names established through mutual dependence.
Therefore, the Sūtra says: 'Dharmas have no peer, for they are without mutual dependence. Jian said: 'Light is a metaphor for wisdom.'"
In dark circumstances, when a person on the path of cultivation does not use wisdom to illuminate and shatter afflictions, by what means can they escape from beginningless birth and death?
The Patriarch said: "Afflictions are themselves bodhi; they are non-dual and without distinction.
To use wisdom to illuminate afflictions is the limited view of the Two Vehicles—the capacity of those with the faculties of sheep and deer. This is not great wisdom."
Those of the highest capacity do not all understand it in this way. [A questioner] asked: "What is the insight and understanding of the Mahāyāna? The Patriarch said:
"Luminosity and ignorance—these two natures are non-dual. This non-dual nature is the true nature (*bhūtalakṣaṇa*).

This true nature does not diminish when dwelling among the ignorant and foolish, nor does it increase when present among sages and worthies; it is not disturbed while abiding in afflictions, nor is it altered while residing in meditative concentration."
It is neither quiescent nor discontinuous, neither eternal nor coming or going, neither in between nor within or without;
its nature and characteristics are suchness (*tathatā*), eternally abiding and unchanging—this is called the Way.

Jian asked, "Master, what distinguishes your teaching of non-arising and non-extinction from that of the non-Buddhists? The Patriarch said, "The non-Buddhists speak of non-arising and non-extinction..."
This means that extinction halts arising, and by means of arising, extinction is revealed; yet even this extinction does not truly extinguish, and this arising is said to be non-arising.
When I speak of non-arising and non-extinction, it is because there was originally no arising, and now there is likewise no extinction. This is why it differs from the heterodox paths.
If you wish to know the essential point of the mind, do not deliberate upon any good or evil whatsoever; you will naturally enter the state of clarity.
The essence of the pure mind is profoundly still and eternally tranquil, yet its wondrous function is as vast as the sands of the Ganges.
Having been briefly instructed by the Master, I attained sudden and great enlightenment. These many doubts and difficulties in this sutra were all made clear by the few words of the Sixth Patriarch.
Those who transmit the Buddha’s Mind-Seal obtain such a perfect correspondence with each instance.
Ignorant ordinary people engage in activities based on false conceptualization, whereas the noble ones do not; such unreal conceptualization is like a city of the Gandharvas or a conjured person.
Mahāmati, just as in a city of the Gandharvas or among conjured people, various beings and merchants may appear to enter and exit;
yet, through the false conceptualization of the ignorant, they are said to truly enter and exit, when in reality there is no one who enters or exits.
It is merely due to their false conceptualization that such great delusion regarding non-arising and non-ceasing arises in ignorant, ordinary people.

For them, there is neither the conditioned nor the unconditioned; they are like a person born from an illusion, who in reality has no arising or ceasing, because their nature is neither existent nor non-existent and is devoid of anything at all.
All phenomena are likewise free from arising and ceasing, yet ignorant, ordinary people [cling to them].

Falling into the false arising of the delusive notions of birth and cessation is not the case for the noble sages; those who do not accord with reality do not hold such views (the Tang translation states: "That which is called false arises contrary to the *dharmatā*, giving rise to inverted views").

Just as the self-nature of phenomena is not different from delusive notions, so too it is not the case that those phenomena are not as they are distinguished by the mind; nor is this an inverted discrimination (the Wei translation states: "As the mind discriminates these phenomena, so they appear;

yet those phenomena are not as they are thus discriminated, nor is this an inverted discrimination"). If one were to differ from these delusive notions, one would be clinging to all things as having a substantial self-nature (*svabhāva*).
One who does not perceive tranquility and does not perceive one who is tranquil never departs from conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).
Therefore, Mahāmati, the vision of signlessness (*animitta*) is superior, not the vision of signs. This is because the vision of signs is the cause for undergoing rebirth and is thus not superior.
Mahāmati, "signless" means that conceptual construction does not arise; it neither originates nor ceases. I call this *nirvāṇa*. Mahāmati, *nirvāṇa* is like the true nature of reality (*tattvārtha*).

When one perceives the departure from the prior conceptualizations of mind and mental factors, and attains the noble wisdom of self-realization of the Tathāgata, I call this Nirvāṇa. It is universally declared:
"I have awakened to the fact that all is merely the manifestation of one's own mind; because conceptualization no longer arises, one is free from existence and free from non-existence."
When birth, separation, and cessation have ceased, there is peace, stability, and happiness, and worldly affairs are forever stilled.
Since one no longer gives rise to deluded thoughts regarding worldly affairs, where could there be birth and cessation? Those foolish outsiders take worldly affairs to be real;
based upon them, they give rise to deluded thoughts, either asserting that things exist or that they do not. They merely engage in false discrimination regarding the activities of existence.
Not perceiving the wondrous reality of non-arising is not the domain of the wisdom of sages and worthies;
they merely cling to unreal things as being real, unaware that these unreal delusions are like the city of the Gandharvas adorned in the sky,
or like illusory beings manifesting various kinds of sentient beings, elephants, and horses.
Regarding such objects as the apparent coming and going of merchants and other activities, the deluded imagine that there truly are signs of coming and going;
in reality, however, there is no one who goes out and no one who enters. It is merely due to the discrimination of their deluded minds that they believe these truly exist.
Thus, what is seen by the ignorant—birth and non-birth, cessation and non-cessation, the conditioned and the unconditioned—is likewise [illusory].
All things are likewise thus: collectively, they do not depart from the realm of illusory transformations, yet one gives rise to delusions of non-arising and non-ceasing therein.

One does not know that in the locus of reality, these conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta*) originally do not exist—as seen by ordinary worldlings—nor do these unconditioned phenomena (*asaṃskṛta*) exist—as seen by those of the Two Vehicles.
It is just like the merchants who enter and exit as created by a magician, or as they might be perceived.
Whether one perceives their arising or their cessation, that illusory person is in fact non-existent;

because all various conceptualizations—whether of arising or cessation, or of having intrinsic nature or lacking intrinsic nature—are entirely absent, it is likewise with all phenomena (*dharmas*) as mere manifestations of one’s own mind: they neither arise nor cease, and they possess neither nature nor [non-nature].
Because the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*) is fundamentally free from arising and ceasing, deluded ordinary beings cling to illusions as real and cling to objects as substantial;
thus they fall into the categories of existence and non-existence within dharmas that are not as they truly are.

Consequently, they give rise to conceptions of arising and ceasing, or conceptions of non-arising and non-ceasing. That which is called "arising and ceasing" is indeed false, whereas that which is called "non-arising" [is the truth].
To say that "extinction" is also false is a delusion; to cling to it as arising and ceasing is certainly an affliction, yet to cling to it as non-arising and non-ceasing is likewise an affliction.
Such inverted discrimination is not that of the noble sages. Those who are noble sages awaken to what is manifested by their own minds and clearly understand it to be like an illusion;
they are not deluded by these illusory transformations, and for this reason it is called wisdom. Others fall into error.

As for "real false discrimination," it is not so; it does not arise in accordance with the dharma-nature, but rather gives rise to inverted views, saying, "This dharma is thus, while that dharma is not thus.
This inverted discrimination is, in fact, not a real inversion, nor is it a non-inversion; there is no actual distinction between them.
The self-nature of true suchness (*tathatā*) is itself false discrimination, and the self-nature of false discrimination is itself true suchness.
Because that which is true is itself delusive, and that which is delusive is itself true, the essence of suchness (*tathatā*) and unreal conceptualization (*abhūta-parikalpa*) are not different.
If one gives rise to divergent views, discriminating and becoming attached to the notion that all phenomena possess a real nature, self-nature, or characteristics—
claiming that suchness is distinct from conceptualization and that suchness exists separately apart from conceptualization— it is as follows:
This attachment arises from not seeing that all phenomena have been quiescent from the very beginning.
Because one does not see the characteristic of the eternal, inherent quiescence of all phenomena, one fails to enter the realm of the reality-limit (*tathatā-bhūtakoṭi*).
Thus, never departing from false conceptualization and clinging to existence as non-existent, one regards this as nirvana; it is merely a total perversion of view. Know this!
One who perceives that which is originally quiescent does not perceive the existence of intrinsic nature or characteristics; this is called the perception of signlessness (*animitta-dṛṣṭi*).
One who clings to all things as having a truly existent essence does not perceive the manifestation of cessation;

this is called the perception of signs (*nimitta-dṛṣṇi*). When comparing these two by weighing them against one another, it is the perception of signlessness that is superior, not the perception of signs.
Those who perceive [characteristics] are said to be inferior, because such perceivers see arising and see cessation;
even if they reach cessation, they will inevitably arise again. Since this becomes the cause for receiving birth, it is not true cessation.

Because arising and ceasing, ceasing and arising, cause them to revolve through the three realms and prevent them from attaining *nirvāṇa*, they are not superior. Those who perceive this signlessness should realize its essence.
In tranquility, one does not perceive existence, and thus the delusion of the conditioned (*saṃskṛta*) does not arise;
one does not perceive non-existence, and thus the delusion of the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) does not arise. Since there is no arising, there is likewise no cessation.
Being fundamentally free from arising and ceasing—this is what I call True Nirvāṇa. That which is called "Nirvāṇa" refers to seeing all phenomena as they truly are.
The true dwelling place is originally quiescent and free from the views of conceptualization and inversion. Regarding all previously mentioned false imaginings of non-Buddhists—
whether they grasp at internal phenomena and name them "mind" (*citta*), or grasp at external phenomena and name them "mental factors" (*caitta*)— their number is not fixed,
yet they do not transcend everything that is produced by the transformations of the six, seven, or eight consciousnesses.

Having distanced oneself from the state where not even a single characteristic can be apprehended, the evolving consciousnesses are transformed into wisdom, and one realizes the realm of the Tathāgata’s noble self-realized wisdom.
This realm of noble wisdom is the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*); it can only be personally realized and awakened to within oneself.
It is fundamentally unborn and unceasing—this is precisely what I call *nirvāṇa*. How could it be something belonging to the non-Buddhists?
How can those who cling to views of having characteristics be discussed in the same breath as this? Xuefeng ascended the hall and said: "The Buddha-way is vast and open, without a fixed path;
it is the gate of liberation that has no gate, the intent of the Way-man that has no intent. Because it does not reside within the three periods of time, it cannot be subject to rising or sinking.
To establish it in opposition to reality is to deviate from the truth; it does not belong to the realm of conditioned construction. To move is to give rise to birth and death."

If you are fundamentally still, you will become intoxicated in the land of dullness; if both movement and stillness are extinguished, you fall into a void. If both movement and stillness are gathered together, it is but a vague, superficial "Buddha-nature.
You must face objects and encounter circumstances like withered wood or cold ashes, applying yourself appropriately at the moment without losing what is fitting.
It is like a mirror reflecting all forms without its radiance being disturbed, or a bird flying through the sky without leaving a trace.
In the emptiness of form, there are no reflections throughout the ten directions; in the three realms, all traces of movement are severed.

One does not fall into the mechanism of coming and going, nor do they dwell in the mind of the intermediate state. Within the bell there is no sound of the drum, and within the drum there is no sound of the bell;
bell and drum do not intersect. In every phrase there is no before or after—like a strong man extending his arm, requiring no external force, like a lion roaming at will.
How could one seek a companion when the Nine Heavens are utterly free of obscuration? Where is there penetration? A single segment of radiance has never been darkened.
If you arrive here, the essence is tranquil and eternally lucid; the sun’s blazing flames are boundless.

Within the sphere of Perfect Enlightenment (*pariniṣpanna-jñāna*), it remains unmoving, swallowing and incinerating heaven and earth while shining forth in total detachment. This is like the words of Xuansha, surpassing all others.
"Having fully realized and entered the realm of the noble wisdom of self-realization, which is characterized by the vision of signlessness and is supremely perfect and wondrous—
could any non-Buddhist possess such extraordinary qualities?
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

To eliminate the doctrine of arising (the Tang translation says: "to remove the attachment to existence"), I establish the meaning of non-arising and teach the Dharma of the Tathāgata (the Wei translation says:
"I teach that dharmas are without cause"). Fools cannot understand that all dharmas are unarisen, without intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*), and non-existent (the Tang translation says:
"nor are they non-dharmas"). Since the *gandharva*-city, illusions, and dreams have no intrinsic nature, they arise without cause; being without self-nature, for what reason would they be empty?

When it is said that because the nature of cognition is not manifest when separated from conjunction, it is empty, unarisen, and without intrinsic nature—I say it is without intrinsic nature (the Tang translation says:

"For this reason, I say it is empty, unarisen, and without nature")—it means that while each individual nature of conjunction appears, it does not exist [independently]. When analyzed, there is no conjunction;
it is not like the views of the non-Buddhists regarding dreams, illusions, falling hairs, mirages, or *gandharva*-cities, nor is it like the worldly [conceptions].
Through various means, they cause those who hold to the doctrine of causes to be subdued by demonstrating that phenomena are without cause;

they expound the meaning of non-arising so that the flow of the Dharma may never be interrupted. By expounding this non-arising, they fiercely confront and terrify all those who advocate for the doctrine of causelessness.
The Master said: "This verse praises the superior vision of signlessness over the vision of signs because the latter is not superior, being the cause for rebirth.
Those with the vision of signs falsely perceive all things as existent and thus give rise to the theory of existence;

they falsely perceive all things as non-existent and thus give rise to the theory of non-existence. These attachments to existence and non-existence both produce [further] theories. Since there is already this taking of birth..."
Because one cannot avoid transmigrating through the three realms, I desire to extinguish those doctrines;

therefore, I establish the principle that is free from existence and free from non-existence, being fundamentally unborn from the beginning. When I speak of such a Dharma, only the noble sages are able to understand it clearly;
it is not something that ordinary, ignorant people can know. That which is called the "non-arising of all dharmas" is not...
Non-existence means that this very non-existence is itself nothing at all, such that one cannot even say it is "non-existent.
It is like a city of Gandharvas appearing in the void, or like the various forms manifested within a dream or illusion; although these appear as manifold phenomena, they truly have no cause.
Therefore, when I speak of "no-cause," it is a synonym for "non-arising. Since there is no arising, [there is no cessation].

If one asks: "Since you have already departed from verbal expression, what is the reason for further stating that all phenomena are empty, that all phenomena are unarisen, and that all phenomena lack intrinsic nature? This is what I shall explain.

The meaning of "non-arising" established by me is fundamentally empty and quiescent, being free from the characteristics of conditioned existence arising from the conjunction of worldly causes and conditions.
Yet the nature of that which perceives and knows does not manifest of itself; though wisdom exists, it cannot be fathomed.

Since it is empty apart from the combination [of conditions], its external object is void, and since there is no perceiving or knowing within, its internal mind is also void. When both interior and exterior are empty, they are fundamentally unarisen.
Therefore, emptiness and non-arising are the teaching of the absence of intrinsic nature (*niḥsvabhāva*); this is what I have called "emptiness."
The meaning of non-arising and the absence of intrinsic nature is fundamentally consistent throughout and admits no divergent explanations.
Furthermore, as for what is called "being apart from all combinations," does one not see that there are indeed various conditions in combination?

This means that all phenomena in the world arise through the combination of individual causes and conditions; although they manifest, they do not exist [independently]. Since they have already manifested...
"What is meant by 'not existing'? It means that when one analyzes each and every phenomenon within this harmony and conjunction, there is nothing that harmonizes and nothing that conjoins;
each lacks intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) and is fundamentally without substance. Thus, harmony and conjunction are themselves non-harmony and non-conjunction.
This is not like the doctrine held by the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), who argue that there was previously harmony and conjunction which now no longer exists. My...

That which has been explained—such as the state of a dream, the transformations of a magical illusion, hair falling from the sky, a mirage, a city of Gandharvas, and so forth—is used as a metaphor for the various things in the world produced through the combination of causes and conditions;
these all appear without a cause and are perceived as existing, yet in reality they have never existed. Thus it is considered.
That which is non-existent is in truth never non-existent; birth is itself non-birth, and manifestation is itself non-manifestation—this is the meaning of "non-arising" established by me.

It is for the purpose of refuting the heterodox theories of "causes of existence," for those proponents of such theories, seeing that all phenomena arise from the combination of causes and conditions, conclude that everything exists.
Seeing that all phenomena perish apart from the combination of causes and conditions, you then claim that there is nothing which does not perish apart from such combinations.
You discriminate between existence and non-existence regarding phenomena that currently appear; though you speak of "causelessness," there is nonetheless a cause.
Since one cannot be free from having a cause, one necessarily undergoes birth and cessation. How could this truly accord with the meaning of the unborn and unceasing? This is my view.

By refuting those opposing treatises, I am precisely elucidating my doctrine of non-arising (*anutpāda*). What I call "non-arising" is the manifestation of quiescence (*śānti*) without severing dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*).

Once this teaching of the meaning of non-arising is fully expounded, the principle of non-arising remains eternally present and the True Dharma (*saddharma*) of the Tathāgata continues without interruption.
How could this be like the so-called "causelessness" (*ahetuka*) of the non-Buddhists?

If one were to sever everything entirely, would that not also sever the lineage of the Tathāgata? Therefore, I teach the doctrine of no-cause (*ahetuvāda*), meaning that there is no cause for arising;
this is to distance oneself from the view that regards such total cessation as the cause for rebirth.
I speak with fervor and without interval so that those non-Buddhists may understand what I have been teaching regarding the doctrines of "having a cause" and "having no cause."
All are for the sake of the theory of birth; having already accepted the causes of birth, they do not depart from birth and death—how could they not know fear?
If they were to recognize this with alarm and dread, they might perhaps change their course and leave behind that mutual perception.

This is what I mean when I say that "non-appearance" is superior to "appearance. Xuan Sha said: "People of the present age do not awaken to the principle within this; they recklessly involve themselves in worldly affairs."

Wandering through the dust of the world, one is stained and attached at every turn and bound by every circumstance. Even if one attains some awakening, the sensory realms remain chaotic and names and forms prove unreal.

Consequently, one intends to settle the mind and withdraw thoughts, to subsume phenomena within emptiness; one closes the eyes and hides the gaze, and as soon as a thought arises, it is immediately destroyed;
as soon as a subtle perception emerges, it is instantly suppressed. Such a view is precisely [the error].
The soul of the outsider who has fallen into emptiness and ruin is that of a dead man whose spirit is not yet dispersed;
dark and obscure, without sensation or cognition, he plugs his ears to steal the bell, deceiving only himself. Here, if one were to see clearly, it would not be so:
it is not a matter of hiding in side doors or back rooms; every word is manifest before one, beyond deliberation, untouched by literary artifice, and fundamentally free from worldly dust.
The objective realm is fundamentally without sequence; it is a provisional name for one who has left the household life. Ultimately, there are no traces.

True Suchness, the stages of ordinary and sagehood, hell-beings, and gods and humans are merely methods used to treat the madness of children. Even empty space undergoes no change; how could the Great Way have rising or sinking?
If you awaken, you move freely in all directions without departing from the fundamental limit. If you reach this point, as for ordinary beings and sages—
There is no place to stand. If you direct your attention toward the words, you will be drowned; if you run outward in pursuit, you fall into the realm of Māra.
Above suchness, there is nothing to be arranged—it is like a furnace of fire that harbors not even a mosquito.
This principle is fundamentally level; what need is there for excavation? Whether moving or still, whether raising an eyebrow or not, this is true understanding.

To speak of "not being strenuous" is a mental fabrication that deviates from the truth. If one reaches this point where not even a hair’s breadth of intentionality is permitted, then any deviation is a failure;
even if a thousand sages were to appear, they could not place a single word there.
Xuan Sha’s extensive entanglements were merely his utmost effort to remind others of the message of formlessness. According to the fundamental state, not even a hair’s breadth of arising is allowed.
"If even [the existence of] a 'Seer' is not permitted to emerge, how much less so the various theories of origination held by the non-Buddhists?
At that time, Mahāmati asked in verse: "What is it?
What is its cause? For what reason does it arise? From where do they combine to form the doctrine of no-cause?"
At that time, the World-Honored One again replied in verse:
"Observing conditioned phenomena, one sees they do not exist without a cause; for those who debate their arising and ceasing, [the view] that there is a cause is thereby extinguished."
The Master replied: "The World-Honored One established the doctrine of non-arising in order to exclude the heterodox theories of arising;
he established the doctrine of 'blazing' causelessness in order to exclude the heterodox views that things have a cause. Mahāmati, you have again asked in verse: 'What is the cause of the heterodox?
For what reason do they establish the theory of arising? If there is a cause for arising, it must depend on conditions.'"

Arising through the conjunction [of conditions], where is that conjunction? It is because they are attached to existence (*bhava*) that the Blessed One propounded the doctrine of causelessness (*ahetuvāda*) to subdue them.

Fearing that they might not understand the intent of causelessness and thus fall into the same position as the causeless theories of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), he posed this question; it was not that they did not know what the Blessed One meant by "causelessness."
This [position] simultaneously negates both those who hold that things have causes and those who hold they are causeless.
The World-Honored One set aside for a moment the question of what the cause is, from whence they arise, and where they combine, in order to await a later answer;

first, he clarified the proponents of the "causeless" theory (*ahetuvāda*), stating that when one observes all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) in the world as being like dreams and illusions, they do not have a cause.
Existence is not something that arises without cause, for it is fundamentally free from the two views of existence and non-existence. Yet, externalists fail to perceive this;
instead, they observe the realm of arising and ceasing and, seeing either its existence or its non-existence, establish theories of "existence with cause" or "non-existence without cause.
Whether one asserts existence with cause or non-existence without cause, neither departs from the realm of arising and ceasing. If one can awaken to this...
The doctrine of causelessness that I have taught is free from existence and free from non-existence; fundamentally, no characteristic of causal conditions can be apprehended.
It is free from arising and free from ceasing; fundamentally, no dharma of arising or ceasing can be apprehended. Thus, false views cease from this point on.
Once false views have ceased, from what could there arise any discourse? Therefore, those who compose treatises on causelessness do so to sever the extremes of existence and non-existence.
To hold this [view] is not the same as the "non-view" (avīkṣā) of those [who deny existence].

Xuan Sha asked about the "pure realm," and an ancient said, "Not seeing a single dharma is a great calamity. "Tell me, what dharma do you not see? Qing pointed to a pillar and said, "Is it not this very dharma?
Xuan Sha said, "In Zhejiang, you may eat clear water and white rice as much as you like, but as for the Buddha-dharma, it is not so."
In a dream, [he saw] Tian Tong [Zhi] picking up [the topic], saying:
"Did Jingqing’s answer at that time and Xuansha’s final statement accord with one another? If so, then Jingqing has long since ceased dreaming of the Buddha-dharma;
he must have been a fellow student of Xuansha to achieve this. According to the meeting between these two venerable masters, is there even any Buddha-dharma?"
How much less could there be the view of non-existence?
At that time, Mahāmati spoke a verse in question:
"What is meant by 'non-arising'? Is it the absence of intrinsic nature, or is it the name 'non-arising' given to phenomena that exist in dependence upon various conditions?"
Names should not be without meaning; they are spoken merely for the sake of conceptual differentiation.
At that time, the World-Honored One again replied with a verse:

"It is not that there is no nature, nor is there non-arising; it is not that one looks to various conditions, nor is there a nature of existence. Yet names are names, and names are not without meaning."
This is not the domain of any outsiders, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or those at the seventh stage; it is called the mark of non-arising (*anutpāda-lakṣaṇa*).
It is far removed from all causes and conditions and detached from all phenomena. There is only the subtle mind abiding in the state where both the perceiver and the perceived are abandoned.
Its body undergoes transformation; I call this "non-arising. It has no external nature or non-nature, nor is there any grasping by the mind.
I declare that the severance of all views is non-arising; thus, one should distinguish between emptiness and the like as being non-empty.
It is called empty because it is non-arising. It is called empty because it is non-arising.
Mahāmati said: "Since I have already understood the meaning of non-arising as a means to eliminate the birth-theories of the heterodox, I now ask again:

For what reason does the Buddha speak of 'non-arising'? Is it because all phenomena lack intrinsic nature and are therefore simply non-existent? Or is it because one observes that things arising from conditions have no self-nature and thus receives this name? Wherein lies the meaning of this? The Buddha replied: [The Buddha said:

"Mahāmati, it is not because all phenomena are simply non-existent that they are called 'non-arising. Rather, it is because one observes that all phenomena arise from conditions and thus have no self-nature that they are designated as such."
To take the absolute absence of nature as non-arising is to fall into emptiness;
to take the non-existence of conditions as non-arising is to pursue external objects, and once those objects depart, there is no non-arising. Therefore, both are erroneous.
One must rely on the meaning of non-arising as inherent within its own essence; this is something that is relinquished only upon reaching the eighth stage.
One is thus able to realize and know that all non-Buddhists, śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and bodhisattvas of the seventh stage do not possess its realm;
it is named as such because therein no characteristic of arising can be found. Why is it said that there is no characteristic of arising?
It is because it is far removed from all worldly causes and conditions and all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*). Furthermore—
Detached from the causes and conditions of cessation, free from all unconditioned phenomena, and transcending both existence and non-existence, there is no agent whatsoever;
it abides eternally in a state of profound stillness, relying solely upon the subtle and tranquil mind. This is called the Immovable Ground (Acalā-bhūmi), and this is called the Abiding Ground.
It is established by the single mind alone; I say that this is "non-arising. Since all dharmas lack causes and conditions, they are thus non-arisen.

When one is free from the conceptualization of existence and non-existence, both the perceiver and the perceived are abandoned, and all mental constructions are extinguished; I call this "non-arising.
When both consciousness and perception are severed, the basis is transformed, the body undergoes a transformation, and one attains the mind-made body (*manomaya-kāya*).
That which was originally unarisen is now born; I call this "non-arising. As for those external objects that are seen, their existence is as follows:
It is neither existent nor non-existent, real nor unreal; the mind has nothing to grasp therein, viewing things as like illusions, dreams, the optical illusion of hair-nets, dry cities, or mirages.
To sever all false conceptualizations and views—this I call "non-arising.
If one considers non-arising to be the absence of intrinsic nature due to various conditions, or if one considers non-arising to be a state of absolute non-existence, [that is not the true meaning].
To generalize that all things are extinguished and do not arise constitutes "non-arising" is to lose the true meaning of the term.
If this were the case, then the previously mentioned phrases such as "lack of intrinsic nature" and "emptiness" would have to be explained through this very discrimination;
for it is because [things] are neither empty nor non-empty that they are said to be "empty," and because [things] neither arise nor do not arise that they are said to be "empty."
Because it exists yet is not existent, it is called "wondrous existence"; because it is non-existent yet not non-existent, it is called "true non-existence.
How could one take the absence of self-nature and categorically equate it with mere nothingness? Huangbo said: "Śrāvakas attain enlightenment by means of sound;
therefore they are called 'Sound-Hearers. However, they do not understand their own minds and instead give rise to interpretations based on verbal teachings or through supernatural powers."

Alternatively, those who rely on auspicious signs, speech, or movement, and hear that there is Bodhi and Nirvana attained through practicing the Buddha-way for three *asaṃkhyeya* kalpas, all belong to the path of the Śrāvakas; this is called the Śrāvaka Buddha.

Only those who directly and suddenly realize that their own mind is fundamentally the Buddha—wherein not a single dharma is to be attained and not a single practice is to be cultivated—this is [the path of] the Unsurpassed [Buddha].
The Superior Path states that this is the True Suchness of the Buddha’s study for those on the Way; one need only fear that a single thought arises, for then one is separated from the Way.
If every thought is signless and every thought is non-active, one is a person beyond study (*aśaikṣa*).
If you wish to attain Buddhahood, you do not need to study any of the Buddha-dharmas at all; you only need to study non-seeking and non-attachment. Non-seeking is the mind itself.
Non-arising and non-attachment mean that the mind does not cease; this non-arising and non-ceasing is itself the Buddha.

The eighty-four thousand Dharma gates correspond to the eighty-four thousand afflictions; they are merely gates for teaching, transforming, and guiding others. Fundamentally, there are no dharmas at all.
To be detached from them is the Dharma; to know this detachment is the Buddha. Simply to be detached from all afflictions is the state of non-existence.
The *Dharma* states: "In this Huangbo, not a single dharma can be obtained; it directly reveals the principle of non-arising.
This truly accords with the present passage:
when the various causes and conditions combine, there is arising and ceasing; apart from these various causes and conditions, there is no separate arising or ceasing.

When one has abandoned the enumeration of causes and conditions, there is no longer any distinct nature. If one speaks of identity or difference, that is the conceptual construction of the non-Buddhists.
The nature of existence and non-existence does not arise; it is neither existent nor non-existent. Apart from the transformation of these enumerations—[as the Tang translation says:

"except for the meeting of various conditions, wherein arising and ceasing are perceived"]—none of these can be found. There are only conventional enumerations that link together like a chain, yet apart from those causes and conditions, [nothing exists].

The meaning of "chain" (śṛṅkhalā) cannot be found as something produced; being without intrinsic nature, it does not arise and is free from the errors of the non-Buddhists. It is merely said that [things] are like a chain of conditions, yet the foolish and ignorant cannot understand this.
It is further stated: "I have taught that which is far removed from all causes and conditions and is also free from all things and a self; I call this 'non-arising'."

What constitutes the causes and conditions, and why is it called "detachment"? The worldly laws of causes and conditions consist of twelve factors, namely those from ignorance (*avidyā*) through old age and death (*jarāmaraṇa*).

If, for even a single moment, ignorance arises and combines with these twelve factors of causes and conditions, there is immediately birth and death, and one does not leave the sea of suffering. However, if for a single moment ignorance ceases—
Apart from the enumeration of the twelve links of dependent origination, there is no other separate dharma capable of undergoing arising and ceasing;

therefore, one can abandon the enumeration of dependent origination at that very moment, which is itself non-arising. The true nature of ignorance is itself Buddha-nature—how could there be any other distinct nature?
If one were to say that "nature" is one thing while the twelve links of dependent origination are another, [it would be a mistake].
Furthermore, the views of identity, difference, both, or neither are all the deluded conceptualizations of externalists.

It is like removing a vessel to observe the space within and asserting that this space is "one. Yet how could that great void ever possess identity or difference? Since it is neither one nor different, it is neither existent nor non-existent.
Therefore, the nature of existence and the nature of non-existence do not give rise to the natures of existence or non-existence. Since these natures do not arise...
If it were obtainable, it would be neither existent nor non-existent, yet it is also unobtainable except through the transformation of numbers when various conditions harmonize.
This arising and ceasing is merely the transformation of numbers; thus, all such notions of unity or difference, existence or non-existence, are entirely unobtainable.
What is called the "transformation of numbers" refers only to worldly conventions that have not yet clarified the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
It is said that there are twelve links of dependent origination, provisionally designated as a chain of mutual arising and ceasing, like hooks or a linked chain that never breaks.
Yet, within the nature of True Suchness (*tathatā*), one is free from those conditions; it is neither existent nor non-existent.

Being fundamentally unbound from the start, why seek liberation? Since this [nature] has no connection whatsoever with the hooks and chains of those conditions, how could there be arising and ceasing?
The meaning of "non-arising" as I have explained it arises from this: if one seeks the meaning of arising apart from causes and conditions, such arising cannot be found.
Arising is thus without meaning; it is the nature of non-arising. Since the nature of arising does not exist, arising is itself non-arising.
This arising lacks self-nature; it is fundamentally unarisen, yet it manifests as non-arising without departing from the phenomena of arising.
Free from all the faults of annihilationism held by the various non-Buddhist paths, I teach that the chain of causes and conditions is, from the very beginning, inherently unborn;
this is not something that can be understood by ordinary, deluded people. Causes do not cause themselves and must depend on conditions;
conditions do not condition themselves and must depend on causes. Both causes and conditions are, in their original nature, unborn.
"This is realized only by noble wisdom; how could externalists ever fathom it? A monk asked Shishuang, "What is the master’s profound depth?
Shishuang replied, "A hairless lock rattles at both ends. Touzi composed a verse on this:
"The moon sets at the third watch, the two mountains shine bright; The ancient road stretches far, moss grows thick. When the golden lock rattles, there is nothing."
Holding the blue waves in hand, the heart-moon hare moves constantly. Furthermore, a monk asked Shishuang, "Does the True Body appear in the world or not?
Shishuang said, "It does not appear. The monk said, "What then of the True Body? Shishuang said, "A glass bottle with its mouth open. Tiantong commented:
"When the whole body is exhausted and one is thoroughly without merit, when one lets go and feels inspired, one follows along."
Do you recognize the old man of Shishuang, who was present yet left no trace in the hall and was never hidden throughout the entire world?
Only by resolving these two cases can one understand the principle that "birth is itself non-birth."
If there were a nature of arising that existed apart from the chain of conditions, then it would follow the doctrine of causelessness and destroy the meaning of the chain of conditions.
Just as a lamp reveals various forms, so too does the chain of conditions manifest;

if this were not the case, then apart from the chain of conditions, there would be no further existence of natures or non-natures, and no arising, being like the self-nature of empty space. Apart from the chain of conditions, wisdom has nothing upon which to discern.

Furthermore, there is another aspect of non-arising, which is the dharma attained by the noble ones (*ārya*): that which arises is itself non-arising; this is the "patience regarding non-arising" (*anutpattika-dharmakṣānti*).
It is said in general that it is merely taught that the chain of conditions is fundamentally non-arising, yet ordinary fools cannot comprehend this.
Because they cling to external conditioned phenomena as being existent or distinct, they claim that causes and conditions give rise to things.
To claim that the dharma of cessation has a separate agent, or that there is a distinct nature of arising apart from the causal chain of dependent origination, is a doctrine of causelessness.
This refers to all those who assert that things arise without cause and are not produced from the conditions of ignorance and false conceptualization;
such views destroy the principle of dependent origination, like the theories of the *paramāṇu* (subtle atoms) or the *pradhāna* (primordial matter).

This is what is meant by saying there is a distinct and different cause. Those people merely see that the chain of causes and conditions (*hetu-pratyaya*) manifests as arising and ceasing, always appearing before their eyes;
yet it is just like a lamp illuminating various images—the lamp is the lamp and the images are the images, and they do not produce one another.
The chain of causes and conditions is like the manifestation of these various images: the images first depend upon the lamp to be seen, yet apart from the images, [the lamp remains].
If the nature of the lamp were something existing separately outside the images, then there would be various natures existing apart from the hook-and-chain [interdependence].
Since these natures would not arise in mutual dependence with the hook-and-chain, they would ultimately lack a cause and be subject to ultimate annihilation.

Therefore, when one observes that all conditions possess no inherent nature and thus names them "non-arising," how could such a position be tenable? Or, some might claim that everything is devoid of nature.
Therefore, there is no essence of arising; its characteristic is like empty space, fundamentally non-existent.
This cannot be realized by immediately detaching from the "hook and chain" (the causal nexus); one must first depart from the hook and chain before its non-arising can be revealed.
This is the view of biased emptiness realized by those of the Two Vehicles and foolish commoners. If one were necessarily to depart from the hook and chain, it would become a mere void.
Although emptiness possesses wisdom, there is nothing to be bestowed upon anyone; how could it give rise to the conceptualization of the meaning of arising and non-arising?

To claim that "lack of intrinsic nature" constitutes "non-arising" is also incorrect. Furthermore, there is another form of non-arising that resembles that of the Two Vehicles but is in fact not the Two Vehicles;
this is the Dharma attained by those of the Three Stages of Worthies and the Ten Stages of Sages. Regarding their [view of] arising...
Yet, non-arising does not depart from the hook and the chain, nor is it bound by the hook and the chain. This is the gradual realization of non-arising:

entering from one stage to the next until the attainment of the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). With the power of this patience firmly established, one no longer gives rise [to further births].
This is what is called "only the subtle mind remaining," wherein both the subject that conceives and the object conceived are entirely abandoned. This is my teaching.
"How could the meaning of non-arising be understood by those ordinary fools? Thus, Cuiyan truly instructed the assembly, saying:
"Not seeing even a single dharma is a great calamity. Mountains, rivers, the great earth, the sun, moon, and stars, form and emptiness, light and darkness—these are not a single dharma.
He raised his staff and said: "When an ordinary person sees this staff, they call it a staff."
When a Śrāvaka sees a staff, he recognizes it as stubborn emptiness and dismisses the staff as non-existent.
When a Bodhisattva sees a staff, has he ever actually used it? When hungry, one eats; when weary, one sleeps; when cold, one turns toward the fire;
when hot, one seeks coolness. It is said that the wisdom of all wisdoms is pure—speaking thus, one laughs until one's face is split.
Tandihui’s nostrils speak of the purity of the wisdom of all-knowledge, of universal quiescence, and of universal non-arising;
yet regarding the upward-pointing root, one still lacks even a speck of dust’s worth of realization. Study this!
If one were to cause all those in the world to observe the "hook-and-chain" (saṃkalana), they would all be freed from the hook-and-chain;

from this, they would attain the samādhi wherein delusion, craving, karma, and so forth are absent. This constitutes the internal hook-and-chain. Drills, fire-sticks, lumps of clay, wheels, seeds, and the like are called external.
If there were a "nature of another" (parabhāva) that arose from causes and conditions, it would not possess the meaning of a hook-and-chain; thus, it would not be established.
If that which arises lacks intrinsic nature, for whom would there be this chain of mutual production? Therefore, one should know the meaning of causes and conditions:

the phenomena of solidity, moisture, heat, and motion give rise to false imaginings in the foolish and ignorant. Apart from these enumerations, there is no other distinct reality; this is what is called "the absence of intrinsic nature.
Just as a physician treats various ailments without proposing a variety of theories—providing diverse remedies according to the differences in the diseases—so too is this teaching.
For the sake of those sentient beings, I destroy their various afflictions and, knowing the superiority or inferiority of their faculties, I preach for them the gate of deliverance.
It is not that there are various dharmas due to differences in afflictions or faculties; rather, I preach only the Dharma of the Single Vehicle, and this is precisely what constitutes the Mahāyāna.

The Master said: "Ordinary people and those outside the Way who destroy the 'hook and chain' do not realize that all things in the world are nothing other than the hook and chain, and thus they truly cannot break them.
The foolish practitioners of the Two Vehicles who seek to leave the hook and chain behind do not realize that one seeks the Dharma by means of the hook and chain;
their minds will never attain stability. If one were to cause the people of the world to rely on the worthy..."
The Dharma attained by the Noble Ones consists in observing the meaning of the "hook and chain" (interdependent connection).
By realizing that the twelve links of dependent origination are fundamentally devoid of intrinsic nature, one finds that everything is free from the hook and chain and is no longer bound by them.
Entering through this, one realizes samādhi and attains the bliss of tranquility; thus, one is not far removed from the noble sages of the past. How does one observe them?

The causal chain of dependent origination has both internal and external aspects. The twelve links of dependent origination—such as ignorance, craving, and so forth—which revolve through the three periods of time, constitute the internal chain.
External causes and conditions include such things as obtaining fire by drilling wood, a lump of clay forming a jar, or a seed producing a sprout;
these each arise through the mutual conditioning of their own specific natures (*svabhāva*). If they were instead to possess the nature of another, [dependent origination would be impossible].
If causes distinct [from those of dependent origination] could serve as the causes and conditions for the phenomena of the world, then a fire-drill could produce sprouts and seeds could form a jar;
furthermore, old age, death, and the suffering of illness would not arise from ignorance, craving, and karma, and this would no longer accord with the principle of the "hook and chain.
If this were so, then all things that do not deviate from the hook and chain would attain samādhi, and such would exist in the world.

For this reason, that doctrine of causelessness is not established. If birth were absolutely annihilated and lacked intrinsic nature, then since there is presently arising and presently ceasing, for whom would there be the chain of bondage from which one could not attain liberation?
Thus, ignorance, delusion, and craving arise successively from one another, producing the cycle of birth and death.
One should know that this ceaseless circulation is the meaning of dependent origination; it is manifest to the ears and eyes, and is truly impossible to destroy.
As for solidity, moisture, warmth, and motion—these are the natures of the four great elements of earth, water, fire, and wind.
Yet, through the deluded thoughts of the ignorant, they imagine there are no seeds and that this body arises from no cause. Thus, they look upon each of these conditions one by one.
There is no intrinsic nature; one does not realize that within these four great elements there is the aspect of intimacy and without them the aspect of externality, all of which arise from ignorance.
Moisture gives rise to water, intense heat gives rise to fire, agitation gives rise to wind, and differentiation gives rise to earth.
Apart from the enumeration of the twelve links of dependent origination, there is no other distinct phenomenon to be designated by a name.
Regarding the condition of form (*rūpa-pratyaya*), earth, water, fire, and wind are all called "form. These merely depend upon all phenomena that are non-existent;

it is said that each lacks its own intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*). Apart from this chain of causes and conditions, it is taught that the four great elements are fundamentally without the nature of arising.
If one speaks in this way of non-arising, then everything is fundamentally non-existent—how, then, could there be illness?
What further need is there for cultivation and purification? Therefore, I say that the essence of causes and conditions is empty and fundamentally unborn;
yet, due to the karmic conditions of sentient beings—like a chain of hooks and locks—worldly affairs do not cease, and they possess various afflictions from which they find no peace or happiness.
It is like a patient whose illnesses differ in their many varieties, for whom a physician provides various remedies.
The essential methods of treatment consist solely in eliminating the disease; there is no room for various false and speculative discourses.
For the sake of sentient beings, I eliminate the diseases of affliction (*kleśa*). There are derivative afflictions and there are root afflictions.
Knowing that their faculties (*indriya*) differ—being either superior or inferior—I preach the teachings of the Great and Small Vehicles (*yāna*) to deliver and liberate them.
It is not that there are various *abhidharma* dharmas because the roots of affliction (*kleśa*) are diverse;

rather, when one does not depart from the hook and chain [of dependent origination], it is affliction, and when one is able to depart from the hook and chain, it is bodhi. It depends entirely upon how sentient beings are able to observe for themselves.
Therefore, although I have taught various gateways to the perfections (*pāramitā*) and established them in manifold ways, they are all...

By preaching the Dharma of the One Vehicle, he causes those sentient beings to awaken to and enter the patience of the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*), opening the Buddha’s knowledge and vision so that they attain immediate liberation, wherein there is absolutely nothing to be grasped as a hook or a chain. This is called: the hook and chain being identical to the absence of hook and chain;
cause and condition being identical to the absence of cause and condition; afflictions being identical to bodhi; and birth-and-death being identical to nirvāṇa. This is named...
This is the Dharma of the Mahāyāna. As the *Saddharmapuṇḍarīka-sūtra* says: "There is only the One Vehicle Dharma; there is neither a second nor a third.
It is only through the Buddha’s skillful means that he speaks [of others], using provisional names merely to guide sentient beings. Entering the Mahāyāna is the fundamental principle.
This is what that refers to. Baizhang said: "It simply means that, at present, one is neither deluded nor distracted regarding each and every object."
Neither angry nor delighted, one scrapes and pares away at the gates of one’s own six sense organs until they are thoroughly cleansed;
such a person of no worldly affairs excels all who possess knowledge and understanding. This ascetic diligence is called the "heavenly eye" and is also called "clear illumination" as the eye;
it is the nature of the Dharma-realm, acting as the carriage that carries cause and effect, and is the Buddha appearing in the world to deliver sentient beings.

When one is born, the preceding thought does not give rise to the succeeding thought, and the preceding thought does not continue into the succeeding thought. When the karma of the preceding thought has passed away, it is called "delivering sentient beings.
If the preceding thought is one of anger, one immediately treats it with the medicine of joy; this is what is meant by saying there is a Buddha who delivers sentient beings.
All verbal teachings are merely for the purpose of treating illnesses; since the illnesses differ, the medicines also differ. Therefore, at times...
To say that there are Buddhas at some times and that there are no Buddhas at others is "true speech" for the purpose of curing illness;
if the illness is cured, every such statement is true speech. If the illness is not cured, every such statement is false speech. "True speech" is [also] "false speech" because it gives rise to views;
"false speech" is [also] "true speech" because it cuts off the delusions of sentient beings. Thus, for the sake of illness, it is false speech.

There is only the illusory appearance of medicine and disease to counteract one another; the appearance of a Buddha in the world to deliver sentient beings is the language of the ninefold teaching, the language of the teachings of provisional meaning.
Hatred and joy, sickness and medicine, are all of one's own self—there are no two separate persons.
Where is there a Buddha appearing in the world? Where are there sentient beings to be delivered? As the sutra says: "In reality, there are no sentient beings."
Those who attain extinction from birth are also said to neither love the Buddha’s Bodhi nor crave or be stained by the dharmas of existence and non-existence;
this is called "delivering others. Furthermore, not remaining attached to oneself is called "delivering oneself. How profound these words are!
When one speaks of both the illness and the medicine, it is all oneself—there is no second person. One must possess the eye of the patriarchal school to realize this.
(Wei: Chapter Eight on Impermanence).
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, all non-Buddhists give rise to the false discrimination of impermanence;
yet the World-Honored One also says that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent and are subject to arising and ceasing. What is the meaning of this?"
"What is meant by the false and the correct? How many kinds of impermanence are there? The Buddha told Mahāmati:
"All non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) maintain seven kinds of impermanence; these do not belong to my teaching. What are the seven? They are:

some say that when an action has been performed and then abandoned, this is called impermanence; some say that the destruction of form and location is called impermanence; some say that form itself is impermanence..."

Some say that the interval during which form undergoes transformation is called impermanence; immediately thereafter, it disintegrates of its own accord, just as in the transformation of milk into curd.
This interval of transformation is invisible, yet impermanence destroys all natures. (The Tang translation states:

"All dharmas continue in an uninterrupted succession, causing them to undergo change and naturally return to extinction.
