Just as milk and curd change from one state to another, although this is invisible, it nonetheless exists within phenomena to destroy all dharmas. Others say that nature itself is impermanent.
Some say that impermanence is the nature of non-existence; some say that all dharmas are unarisen impermanence, which enters into all dharmas.
It is universally said: "The World-Honored One has preached various dharmas to guide sentient beings, to eliminate the diseases of affliction, and to realize non-arising."
Patience has real causes and conditions and real liberation; it is not like the false and delusive discourses of the non-Buddhists.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, you wish for the World-Honored One to clarify the difference between the non-Buddhists' deluded notions of impermanence and the "impermanence of all conditioned phenomena" taught in my teaching—which is a law of arising and ceasing—so that those in the future will not fall into their ways.
These are various heterodox doctrines. World-Honored One, you have briefly cited seven kinds of impermanence held by non-Buddhists;
this is the most refined among them and cannot but be examined. Our teaching asserts that the four great elements do not exist as five aggregates, all of which are empty—this is the correct doctrine.
The non-Buddhists desire to empty the four great elements but lose their true nature; they desire to empty the five aggregates but neglect their reality.

Having partially realized that form, sensation, and perception are empty and exhausted, they reach the stage of the aggregate of formations (*saṃskāra-skandha*), where things arise anew and do not abide;

they then take impermanence itself to be the true essence. Within the aggregate of formations, regarding those subtle and hidden places that cannot be scrutinized, they take them to be the "Dark Principle" (*tattva*) and fall into the view of annihilationism.
Regarding the place within it where the grasping for a self cannot be extinguished, they take it to be a "divine self" (*puruṣa*).
Falling into the view of eternalism, some claim that the transformation and disintegration of form and location is impermanence;

others claim that color and so forth are themselves impermanent, thereby taking the matter derived from the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) to be impermanent. Thus, they are certainly unable to realize the emptiness of the four great elements.
Some claim that the very moment something begins to be produced it is abandoned, and this is called impermanence; others claim that the thing itself is impermanent.
Some say that both existence and non-existence, as well as dharmas and non-dharmas, are all impermanent;

this means there is neither an agent nor an object of action, and furthermore, no four great elements that could be empty. Some say that the non-arising of all dharmas is impermanence, which enters into all dharmas.
Others say that the transformation of form in its intermediate state is called impermanence; this refers to the midst of the dharma of arising and ceasing.
"There is that which does not arise" means that within the transformation of form (*rūpa*), there exists that which does not change; this is indeed close to reason, as the saying goes.
Yet, they merely seek that which does not arise in opposition to arising and ceasing, and seek that which does not change apart from transformation.
All of these are views of existence, non-existence, activity, and permanence that do not depart from external phenomena. (From the *Xiyu ju duo san* [Records of the Third Kuchean Master]).
Zang was a man from India who attained awakening upon hearing the words of the Sixth Patriarch.
Later, while traveling to Mount Wutai, he saw a monk sitting in meditation within a hermitage. Zang asked him, "Master, why do you sit alone? The monk replied, "I am contemplating stillness.
Zang said, "Who is it that contemplates? What is the thing that is still? The monk prostrated himself and asked, "What is the principle of this? Zang said, "You..."
"Why do you not observe yourself and become still? The monk was bewildered. The Master asked, "Whose lineage do you follow? The monk replied, "Master Xiu.
The Master said, "I am one of the lowest seedlings among the heterodox paths of the Western Regions;
I do not fall into such views. To sit blankly and vacantly—what benefit is there for the Path? The monk then asked, "Who is your teacher? The Master replied, "It is I."
"Master Sixth Patriarch, why did you not go quickly to Caoxi to resolve its essential truth?
The monk immediately went to visit the Sixth Patriarch, and the instructions bestowed by the Patriarch coincided perfectly with those of the Master. The monk then attained realization.
Had he not encountered the Third Patriarch’s pointing out, how could he have avoided falling into the views of an outsider?
"Mahāmati, 'the impermanence of the nature of existence and non-existence' refers to the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and their derivatives.

Their specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) perish, and the self-nature (*svabhāva*) of the great elements cannot be apprehended; they do not arise. (The Tang translation says: 'The characteristics of the primary and derivative elements are destroyed; the self-nature of the great elements has never arisen from the beginning.

This 'impermanence of non-arising' is not the impermanence of permanence; it means that all phenomena—whether existent or non-existent, permanent or impermanent, or any such categories of existence and non-existence—are all [non-arisen]."
When analyzed down to the subtlest atom, there is nothing that arises; this is the meaning of non-arising. It is not arising—this is called the characteristic of impermanence as non-arising.
If one does not awaken to this, one falls into the view of all externalists who hold that impermanence consists in the arising of things.
The Master said: "The seven theories of impermanence held by the non-Buddhists do not, in total, go beyond the two views of existence and non-existence, or of annihilationism and eternalism.
The World-Honored One first pointed out and refuted the sixth and seventh of these, which are forms of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).

'Nature' and 'non-nature'—translated in Chinese as 'entity' and 'non-entity'—refer to the four great elements and the derivative matter they produce; both their intrinsic natures and their constituent elements perish. The four great elements are capable of... [text fragment].
Once the derived matter has been produced and its own substance has already perished, that which was derived is no longer the original four great elements, and it likewise perishes along with them.

Just as a seed produces a sprout, both are impermanent. Since there is neither a producer nor a product, the nature of the four great elements cannot be apprehended at all. Being devoid of self-nature, they are fundamentally unarisen. This—

That which is called "the scorched sprout" refers to that which does not perform the function of a sprout, "the broken jar" refers to that which does not perform the function of a jar, and "the severed lineage" refers to that which has been extinguished.
That which is "unborn impermanence" entering into all phenomena does not mean that all phenomena are both permanent and impermanent, or both existent and non-existent;
rather, it means that both are unborn. That [view] takes unborn impermanence as partial...
Abiding within all dharmas, even when analyzing the dharma of arising down to the finest atom, nothing whatsoever is seen.
For this reason, it is called "non-arising. This meaning of non-arising is revealed by means of arising;
it can only be described as "not arising," just as one might say that what existed has returned to non-existence and is no longer as it was before.
Some say: "How can this be called 'non-arising'? This is termed the characteristic of non-arising impermanence;
although one speaks of non-arising, it is actually a theory of arising impermanence.
If my disciples do not awaken to this and instead falsely conceptualize non-arising, thereby falling back into the dharma of arising, they will immediately fall into that [error].
The proponents of the "Arising is Impermanence" theory perceive that all phenomena return to extinction and thus consider them to be unarisen;
they do not realize that arising and ceasing are continuous and that cessation is itself arising. Therefore, for those who take arising to be impermanence, their own argument collapses.
When the practitioner known as Paper-Clothing Daozhe came to visit Caoshan, the Master asked him, "Are you not Paper-Clothing Daozhe? He replied, "I dare not say so."

Shan said, "What is the matter beneath the paper robe? The other replied, "Once a single fur cloak is hung upon the body, all dharmas are fully known. Shan asked, "What is the function beneath the paper robe? The other stepped forward, responded with an "Amen," and stood there as if shedding his skin.

Shan said, "You only know how to go like that; why do you not come like that? Suddenly, [the other] opened his eyes and asked: [Note: This passage describes a dialogue between Master Shan (Shanxian) and a practitioner. The "paper robe" (*zhīyī*) refers to the simple, humble garb of a monk. The phrase "once a single fur cloak is hung upon the body" suggests the realization of the non-dual nature of reality. The practitioner’s response—stepping forward, responding, and standing there—is an expression of direct, non-conceptual action. Shan’s challenge regarding "coming" rather than "going" points toward the necessity of returning to the source of such realization. The sudden opening of the eyes marks a shift in the dynamic of the encounter.]
"A single spiritual true nature does not depend on a womb; how is this so? Shanshan said, "It is not yet wondrous. The monk asked, "What is wondrous?
Shanshan said, "Not borrowing from that which is borrowed.珍重 (Be careful). Having spoken, he descended from the hall and passed away. Shanshan showed a verse, saying:
"The enlightened nature is perfectly luminous, a formless body; Do not mistakenly distance yourself from it through intellectual views. If you harbor thoughts of difference, then..."
The profound essence is obscure and the mind is distracted; thus one does not dwell as a neighbor to the Way. Sentiments divide the myriad dharmas and sink into the realms before one;
consciousness and discernment take many forms, losing the original truth. If you can fully understand this statement, you will clearly see that there is nothing to do—the person of former times.

As for those like the non-Buddhists who divide the myriad dharmas with their sentiments and sink into the realms before them, they truly have nothing worth discussing. Within my Dharma, however, it is consciousness... (Note: The final sentence appears to be incomplete in the source text.)
O Mahāmati, those who fall into various arguments concerning the impermanence of arising—how can they not know how to choose?
That which is the impermanence of the great nature of being is the false discrimination of one's own mind; it is not the nature of impermanence itself. Why is this?
Because the self-nature of impermanence is indestructible. Mahāmati, this is the matter of the impermanence of all things and non-things, excluding [the true nature].
There is no impermanence that can cause all dharmas to become non-existent, just as a staff, tile, or stone destroys various objects.

(The Tang translation states: "They establish impermanence as not itself subject to destruction, yet it can destroy all dharmas. If there were no impermanence to destroy all dharmas, then dharmas would ultimately never perish, resulting in non-existence. It is like a staff, a mallet, a tile, or a stone that can destroy objects while itself remaining undestroyed;
this is also the case here. We see directly that each thing is not different from this nature of impermanence; the phenomenon is not something created by an agent, yet it exists.
If there were no distinction such that "this is impermanent" and "this is the effect produced by a cause," then all natures would be eternal and without cause (the Tang translation says:

because there would be no differentiation, the agent and the acted-upon would both have to be eternal; for one does not see a cause that could bring about the non-existence of dharmas). Mahāmati, that all natures are without nature and yet possess a cause is not something known by the foolish and ignorant.
It is not the case that things arise from non-causes or from dissimilar things; if they were so produced, [all things] would be one.

If all natures were entirely impermanent, this would be a case of dissimilarity: there would be no distinction between the agent and the acted-upon, yet we clearly perceive such distinctions. (The Tang translation says:

"If that which can produce [an effect] were so, then all distinct phenomena should produce one another simultaneously; there should be no distinction between that phenomenon and this phenomenon as producer and produced. Yet we clearly see they are distinct. How could a distinct cause produce a distinct effect?
If nature were impermanent, it would fall into the category of being a causal agent (*kāraka-hetu*). If it falls into that, then all natures would lack ultimate reality.
If all natures were to fall into the category of having the characteristic of being produced by causes, they would themselves be impermanent.

Because they would be impermanent, and because that impermanence itself is impermanent, all natures would not be impermanent; rather, they should be permanent. (The Tang translation states: "If the nature of impermanence is a functional entity, it should be identical to 'that which is produced' and thus itself impermanent.

Because it is itself impermanent, all impermanent phenomena should consequently be permanent. If impermanence were to enter into all natures, it would fall into the three periods of time. That past form and...
Because destruction and the future non-arising of form coexist, present form is inseparable from the characteristic of destruction.

Form is a specific accumulation of the four great elements; since the self-nature of the four great elements and their derivative forms is indestructible, it is neither different nor non-different [from them]. (The Wei translation states:
"Because they are mutually inseparable. Thus, for all non-Buddhists, the four great elements are indestructible, as are the four great elements of all three realms of existence.
Furthermore, regarding derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) existing within the knowable which undergoes arising and ceasing, all non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) contemplate what nature is impermanent?

[They hold that] the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) do not arise, because their self-nature and characteristics are indestructible. (The Tang translation states: "All non-Buddhists reckon that the essential nature of the four great elements is indestructible;

matter is simply a differentiation of the great elements. Since the great elements and derived matter are neither different nor non-different, their self-nature likewise does not perish. O Mahāmati, among the two types of existence, there is nothing—whether the creator or the created—that is not [subject to this].
"Since all things possess the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing, how could there be a separate nature of impermanence that can produce things without itself ceasing?

He replied: "The 'nature of impermanence' spoken of by the non-Buddhists—what the Wei translation calls 'calling it impermanent because there is no thing'—is a false discrimination regarding the state that is neither permanent nor impermanent, wherein they falsely conceive that all phenomena are impermanent."
What is the meaning of "constant nature"? It is because its own-nature (*svabhāva*) is not extinguished.
That which is not extinguished by its own-nature is the constant nature of impermanence; because it is not destroyed, this own-nature is indestructible.

It is capable of destroying all phenomena, and it is that from which the matter of the destruction and impermanence of all these phenomena is established. If one were to exclude this impermanent own-nature, then [destruction] would not exist.
It causes all phenomena, having existed, to return to non-existence and revert to destruction;
just as a staff, a hammer, a stone, or other such things can destroy various objects while their own substance remains undestroyed, this nature of impermanence is likewise.
Because its nature is impermanent, one perceives that all phenomena are impermanent, each distinct from the others, undergoing various transmigrations and various transformations.
The impermanence manifested in these phenomena has this very impermanence as its nature.
This nature of impermanence pervades all things, as the *Śūraṅgama Sūtra* states: "In the nature of all minds, there is no distinction between agent and object.
Even a wise person cannot analyze the myriad phenomena to differentiate within them, saying, "This is impermanent," or "This is..."
To say that the agent is not different from the action performed is erroneous, because there would be no distinction between cause and effect.
If the agent and the action were non-different, then both the agent and the action would be eternal;
one would never perceive a cause capable of causing all phenomena to perish and return to impermanence.
The position that "impermanence" acts as an agent is logically untenable, because all phenomena are without causal nature (*ahetutva*).
Nevertheless, the arising and ceasing of all phenomena—whether characterized by existence or non-existence—do indeed have causes.

This applies regardless of whether one considers the realms of humans and devas, the environment and its inhabitants, or their mutual interdependence; it extends even to the point where a single person resolves their mind to return to the source throughout the ten directions.
Even the simultaneous destruction of all things within space must have a cause; it is simply that this is not something ordinary, foolish people can perceive.

Where there is a cause, there is an effect, and the effect must necessarily resemble its cause. If an effect were to arise from what was originally not its cause and did not resemble it, this would be called a "dissimilar cause.
If a dissimilar cause could produce a dissimilar effect, then all dissimilar phenomena [would arise from one another].

If a plum tree should necessarily produce a plum and a peach tree should necessarily produce a plum, or if a peach tree should necessarily produce a plum and a plum tree should produce a plum, then all would possess an impermanent nature and none would be similar.
In such a case, there would be no distinction between those dharmas—the producer and the produced.
Yet, we currently perceive that all dharmas are distinct, each having its own agent and its own object, with cause and effect clearly evident. How can this be?
Because different causes can produce different effects, it follows that there is a fault in asserting that those [causes] lack causal nature (*ahetutva*).

If one asserts that what is impermanent by nature is a functional entity (*bhāva*), then it must necessarily act; since it necessarily acts as a cause, it possesses the nature of a produced cause (*kṛtakahetu*).

Being thus associated with the nature of a cause and being a product of a causal substance, it falls within the category of conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛtadharma*) and cannot be called "nature" (*svabhāva*). Furthermore...
Furthermore, there is a further error regarding that which is called "nature" (*prakṛti*): it would imply that within a single dharma, all dharmas must be fully present.
If this falls into the category of existence, it consists only of all dharmas subject to arising and ceasing, and cannot ultimately encompass all dharmas that are neither born nor extinguished;
for it would be indistinguishable from the characteristics of all produced causes, effects, and karmic actions. Moreover...
If that which possesses the nature of being an agent were to fall into the category of conditioned activity, it would itself be impermanent;
it should be identical to the impermanence of all produced things, and one could not maintain that the agent is permanent by nature.
Since the agent is impermanent and the produced is impermanent, then all produced phenomena that are impermanent would not be impermanent, but rather identical to the agent.
It is the permanence of indestructibility. Since that which is created cannot be destroyed, how could there be an impermanent nature capable of destroying it?
Furthermore, you claim that the nature of impermanence dwells within all phenomena and yet this nature of impermanence is permanent;
in that case, it should be identical to all phenomena and fall into the three periods of time, ultimately sharing their destruction. Why is this so? If...
If one enters into past form, it has already perished; if one enters into future form, it has not yet arisen;
if one enters into present form, it does not abide, but perishes and changes moment by moment. Since form is subject to destruction, its impermanent nature likewise perishes along with it.
How, then, could it be permanent? Those non-Buddhists falsely calculate that the four great elements are permanent.
The essential nature is indestructible, and the self-nature of derived matter is likewise indestructible;

for that which is "matter" is simply the accumulation of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), appearing as a differentiation of those four great elements. Its essential nature is non-dual, being free from both difference and non-difference.
To treat them as different would mean that the accumulation of the four great elements serves as the cause for the derived matter; thus, they are certainly not different.
One might think that if they were not different, then form would already be a composite whole, yet each part remains distinct;
nor is it the case that they are not different, because each is inseparable from the others.

Thus, all non-Buddhists maintain that the self-nature of the four great elements is indestructible, and that within all phenomena of the three realms of existence, the nature of impermanence is itself eternal.
Since they themselves are not destroyed, one now observes that within the three realms of existence, everything depends upon the four great elements and their derived matter;
in every place, there is nothing that does not possess the characteristics of arising, abiding, and ceasing. Everyone knows that when the four great elements perish, derived matter also perishes.
How could there be any impermanence in the world apart from the four great elements and their derived matter?

If this nature exists apart from the four great elements and derived matter, it would be nothing more than inert emptiness; beyond that, there would be no further dharmas such as the four great elements or the sensory objects.

Upon what basis could the non-Buddhists contemplate and claim that there is a nature that is impermanent, yet whose essence and characteristics are fundamentally unproduced, capable of generating things while its own substance remains eternally indestructible? I maintain that if it were truly impermanent, [it could not be so].
If one enters into all natures, one should fall into the view that they all equally return to destruction throughout the three periods of time.

Since they all equally return to destruction, the thesis you have established—that things are indestructible—collapses. A monk asked Zhaozhou, "When the world is destroyed, this nature is not destroyed.
What is this nature? Zhaozhou said, "The four great elements and the five aggregates. The monk said, "This is still [the realm of]..."
When it is destroyed, how is this nature? The State of Nature (Xingzhou) says: "The four great elements and the five aggregates. Fayuan said: "Is this one, or is it two?
Whether it is destroyed or not destroyed, how do you understand this? You must try to judge for yourself;
you must perceive through this and break through it, only then will you not fall into the heterodox views of external paths."
That which is devoid of initial creation and impermanence is not the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), nor is it something other than them.

Because each of the four great elements has its own distinct characteristics and individual nature, no differentiation can be apprehended; since there is no differentiation among them, they do not further create one another.

One should know that these two skillful means are not produced and shall not be produced. (The Tang translation states: "It is not that the great elements mutually create the great elements, because they are distinct from one another; it is not that they are created by their own characteristics, because they are without difference; nor are they created together, because they are separated.")

To know that this is not the beginning of impermanence: regarding the impermanence of the destruction of form and location, it refers to the four great elements and their derived matter (*bhautika-rūpa*).

They do not perish until the very end; they do not perish even when analyzed down to the subtlest atom (*paramāṇu*). When one observes the destruction of the four great elements and their derived matter, one sees the difference in their forms and locations;
yet, length and shortness cannot be apprehended. It is not that the four great elements themselves perish; rather, it is the destruction of their form and location.

Regarding the statement that "form presently falls into the Sāṃkhya [category]" (translated in the Tang as "this is neither the creator nor the created; it is the destruction of shape, not the substance"): what is its meaning? It means that when form is analyzed down to the subtle atom (*paramāṇu*), only the shapes such as length and shortness are destroyed, while the essential substance of the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*) is not destroyed.

As for the statement that "form is impermanent": if it were meant that form itself is permanent, then only its spatial configuration would be impermanent, and not the four great elements (*mahābhūta*).
If the four great elements were impermanent, that would contradict conventional linguistic expression; yet it is through conventional linguistic expression that they are spoken of.

Those who do not [recognize] the non-nature fall into the worldly view that all natures exist merely as verbal designations. They fail to see that the arising and transformation of self-characteristics constitute impermanence;
they claim that the manifestation of the distinct nature of form is not the manifestation of the four great elements.

Just as when gold is fashioned into an ornament, it is the transformation of the ornament’s appearance that occurs, not the destruction of the gold-nature, but only the destruction of the location of the ornament—so it is with the transformation of other natures and so forth.

It is also thus: when the fire of the various false conceptions of impermanence held by such non-Buddhists as these burns the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) are not burned;
yet, if each of their own specific characteristics were to perish, then the derived matter (*upādāyarūpa*) produced by the four great elements would be annihilated.

(The Tang translation states: "Such various non-Buddhist false discriminations perceive the nature of impermanence. They say: 'Fire cannot burn the specific characteristics of the various great elements; they merely disperse from one another. If they could indeed destroy them, then both the producers and the produced would all be utterly extinguished.")
The interlocutor said: "The three points above exhaustively investigate that the four great elements are non-existent, flowing toward the extreme of annihilation (*uccheda*).

The four points below exhaustively investigate that while the derived matter of the four great elements is impermanent, their intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) is eternal; they have not yet departed from the notion of existence.

'Existence' refers to the act of creating and then abandoning it, whereby one departs from the initial creation to regard it as impermanent. That [previous] explanation concerned the very beginning of initiating an action."
In truth, it has never been the case that they are mutually created, for the four great elements do not create distinct four great elements;

because each possesses its own distinct characteristic, they are not mutually created. If one considers them to be self-created, then since their own characteristics lack any obtainable differentiation, how could they be divided into four?
Thus, they are not self-created. If one considers them to be co-created, then [the other] does not exist.
Because their distinct natures are each mutually exclusive and cannot be harmonized through skillful means, they are unable to create one another;
furthermore, there is no other agent capable of acting as a second means for this. Thus, these four great elements and the rest do not further create one another in common.
From this it follows that originally there is no creator; since there is no initial creation, neither similarity nor difference can be perceived.
One should know that their differences are as follows: first, the notion that what is newly produced is impermanent—that is, the agent who creates is impermanent;

second, the notion that the destruction of shape and location is impermanent, which is the coarsest and shallowest of all explanations, for it claims that while the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) they produce are both indestructible, only their shape and location are destroyed. Upon ultimate analysis of that matter, even down to...

If one examines it down to the level of subtle atoms, who among them is subject to disintegration? One finds that only the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) and the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*)—their shapes, locations, lengths, and transformations—are subject to disintegration;
it is not the essential nature (*svabhāva*) of the four great elements as creators or created that disintegrates. The four great elements do not disintegrate;
rather, it is their shapes and locations that disintegrate, manifesting as different characteristics. This is what the Sāṃkhya non-Buddhists conceive of as the four great elements.
Because their nature circulates through all realms of existence while their essence remains eternally unchanging, the four great elements are said to be "constant.
Third, the view that form is impermanent—that is, the impermanence of its spatial configuration—is not what is meant by the impermanence of the four great elements.
If the four great elements were impermanent, then nothing in the entire world would be impermanent, and thus conventional reality could not be established.
The proponents of the Sāṃkhya discourse on worldly affairs claim that because no worldly affairs can be apprehended,
those worldly affairs discussed through conventional discourse are likewise not truly existent. One should know that such a position falls into the false view of worldly theorizing (*lokāyatika*),
for it asserts that all phenomena exist merely as provisional names and verbal designations, lacking any reality.

There is the view that impermanence arises from its own characteristic; if one perceives it arising from its own characteristic, then form is itself emptiness, and one knows that all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskāra*) are impermanent and subject to arising and ceasing.
This is subsumed within our own doctrine and is not comparable to worldly theories. Fourth is the calculation of transformation, which holds that impermanence exists in the interval [of change];
it asserts that both the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derived matter (*bhautika*) are eternal, and that it is merely the two forms [of color and shape] that change.
In the interim, there exists impermanence which causes the continuity of material phenomena (*rūpa-dharma*) to undergo transformation;

thus, when all material forms manifest as different states, this is called "destruction," yet it is not the destruction of the intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*). It is like gold being fashioned into ornaments:
when the ornaments undergo transformation, this is called "destruction," yet it is not the destruction of the nature of the gold. This applies likewise to other natures.

Transformation is also like this: just as milk is transformed into butter, curd, and so forth, when butter or curd undergoes transformation, it is called "destruction," yet the nature of the milk itself is not destroyed.

In this way, various non-Buddhists engage in false conceptualization and speak of the view of impermanence, claiming that when the four great elements are consumed by fire, the substances of the four elements each disperse individually; however, their own characteristics do not [truly perish].
If fire were able to burn the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), then the derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*) produced by those four elements would necessarily be annihilated;

who then would be the creator and what would be the created? Regarding the four types of false views mentioned above—namely, that the four great elements which possess form will ultimately perish, and that the four great elements which are formless can never be destroyed—one takes what is permanent to be impermanent, and what is non-existent...
To always treat the permanent as permanent is a form of total equivocation; it is the doctrine of "half-arising and half-ceasing, half-neither-arising-nor-ceasing.
Yangshan pointed to a snow lion and asked, "Is there anyone who can pass through this color? Yunmen said, "At that time, he should have pushed it over right then.
Xuedou said, "He only knows how to push it over, but does not know how to lift it up. Wansong said: [The text provided ends here.]
Since it is called "form" (*rūpa*), it must necessarily confront the eye; yet that which is purely white and formless does not confront the eye.
This is why Yunmen said, "At that very moment, I would have pushed him over.

If one recognizes [the state] at the point where the ultimate whiteness is no longer white, one has precisely fallen into the formless realm (*ārūpyadhātu*). Xuedou points out a separate, living path.
Foyan said, "If you try to prop him up right where he has been knocked down, how could there be any sense of order?
Fojue’s verse says: "A single color, nothing surpasses pointing it out to people; Within a world of white silver, one groans in distress.
To transcendently knock him down and then prop him up— How can this compare to the new warmth of the eastern wind and the shining sun?"
The Child’s Verse says: One fall, one rise—the lion in the snowy courtyard. Careful in avoiding transgression yet harboring benevolence; brave in action yet perceiving righteousness.
Clear light shines before the eyes, yet it seems like being lost at home; turning the body toward clarity, one still falls back into the station.
For the monk, there is nothing to rely upon; born together and dying together, what "that" and what "this"? When the warm faith breaks through the plum blossoms, spring arrives.
When cold branches encounter a cool breeze and shed their leaves, autumn clarifies the stagnant waters;
since even the formless limit within the Gate of the Dharma cannot be dwelled upon, how much less could there be any distinct individual characteristics that remain indestructible?
"Mahāmati, the arising of my Dharma is neither eternal nor non-eternal. Why is this? It is because external natures are not determinate [as the Wei translation says:
'I do not say that external objects exist']. I speak only of the subtle mind within the three realms of existence [as the Tang translation says:

'the triple world is mind-only'], and I do not speak of the arising and ceasing of various marks, nor of the combination of the four great elements, nor of the distinctions between the four great elements and their derived forms; for these are both products of false conceptualization."

One should know that the various categories of the grasper and the grasped consist of two kinds of false imagination (*vikalpa*). One is free from the two views of external existence and non-existence (the Chinese translation states this is because no characteristics are taught;

because the various distinctions of the great elements and their natures are neither produced nor extinguished; because they are neither the creator nor the created; because the essential nature of both the grasper and the grasped all arises from discrimination; and because one knows the nature of the two graspings as they truly are).

One who awakens to the fact that false imagination is the manifestation of one’s own mind realizes that it arises through the activity of mental construction and does not arise without such activity. It is free [from the duality of subject and object].
The nature of the mind is devoid of intrinsic nature; the world, the supramundane, and that which is supreme beyond the supramundane—all these phenomena are neither eternal nor non-eternal.
Failing to realize that these are merely the manifestations of one’s own mind, one falls into a continuous succession of evil views regarding the two extremes.

All non-Buddhists fail to realize that these are their own deluded imaginings; such ordinary people lack any fundamental basis for what they call the mundane, the supramundane, or that which transcends them.
The highest [conception] in the world arises from the discourse on false conceptualization (*vikalpa*); it is not something realized by the ignorant and deluded.
It is generally said that these seven kinds of impermanence are all the heterodox views of non-Buddhists and do not belong to my teaching.
What arises within my teaching speaks only of the primary elements (*mahābhūta*) and their objects (*viṣaya*) as being neither permanent nor impermanent; this is called true permanence.

It transcends the mental measure (*cittamātra*) of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*). Why is this? Because the non-Buddhists give rise to views regarding external objects, either asserting they are eternal or asserting they are impermanent; they do not know that external objects are not determinately existent, nor do they realize that there is no self.
Since I do not speak of external objects, I teach that within and without the three realms, there is not a single dharma that does not arise from the subtle, true reality.

The arising of the mind refers only to the statement that the three realms are mind-only, fundamentally devoid of arising and ceasing; it does not refer to the various characteristics that have arising and ceasing,
nor to the distinct characteristics of the conjunction of the four great elements, nor to the primary and derivative forms produced by those four great elements,
because the four great elements are merely a combination of causes and conditions, and are neither the "great" elements themselves nor the objective particles.
Because truly existent dharmas exist, it is said that they are neither produced nor extinguished, and are neither the creator nor the created.
Those non-Buddhists, with their deluded minds, discriminate between the two natures of agent and object;

they perceive the existence of grasping and the grasped, and by clinging to and adhering to all things, they give rise to everything through false discrimination. Therefore, [one should view them] according to reality.
Knowing that both kinds of discrimination are fundamentally illusory, one no longer perceives a grasper or a grasped;

being free from the two views of existence and non-existence regarding external phenomena, one does not grasp at existence because one does not see its presence, nor does one grasp at non-existence because one does not see its absence.
One simply awakens to the fact that all dharmas are the manifestation of one's own mind, like water.

The moon in the center cannot be said to exist, nor can it be said not to exist; therefore, one is able to transcend the views of existence and non-existence and refrain from discrimination regarding the primary elements (*bhūta*) and the derivative elements (*bhautika*), as well as arising and ceasing.

The two kinds of views that arise from false conceptualization among the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are produced by mental activity (*saṃskāra*) based on discursive thought (*vitarka*), giving rise to discrimination.
The characteristics of the objects produced by such activity are called "false conceptualization" (*parikalpita*).
Birth is not called delusive thought (*vikalpa*) unless it involves conceptualization and mental formation;
if one does not give rise to thought and does not produce conceptualization, one is then free from the existence and non-existence manifested by one's own mind.

Having departed from this delusive thought, one is then able to fully comprehend all worldly phenomena (*loka-dharma*), supramundane phenomena (*lokottara-dharma*), and the supreme supramundane phenomena (*lokottara-tama-dharma*).
In reality, this single mind is neither eternal nor non-eternal; because it contains both mundane and supramundane, progressively superior dharmas, it cannot be said to be eternal.
Yet, because one can realize that these are merely the perceptions of one's own mental discrimination, it is not non-eternal.
However, the various non-Buddhists do not realize that these are manifestations of their own minds.
Falling into the continuity of the two extremes of false views, they establish seven types of theories on impermanence.
Because these non-Buddhists do not realize that their own minds are merely false conceptualizations and lack fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*),
whereas the noble ones (*ārya*) do not conceptually construct impermanence because they possess fundamental wisdom, all such non-Buddhists are unable to understand it.
These three kinds of dharmas are: first, the characteristics of worldly dharmas; second, the characteristics of supramundane dharmas;

and third, the characteristics of the most excellent supramundane dharmas. It is said that all these three dharmas rely upon language to manifest various teachings, which consequently become objects of deluded conceptualization and discrimination. One does not realize that all such verbal expressions are ultimately non-existent.
It is eternal, yet it is also said to be non-eternal. How could this be realized by the ignorant and deluded? They simply fail to realize that all is the manifestation of their own minds;
thus they cannot escape the false discrimination of grasper and grasped, nor can they escape the two evil views regarding the existence or non-existence of external phenomena.
Because these evil views continue in succession, they are called "deluded. Yunmen ascended the hall and addressed the assembly: "Venerable brothers..."
“Shangzi, do not engage in false imaginings. Heaven is heaven, earth is earth; mountains are mountains, waters are waters;
monks are monks, laypeople are laypeople. After a long silence, he said, “Bring me the mountain on which the table stands!
A monk then asked, “When a student sees that mountains are mountains and waters are waters, what then? The Master replied, “Why do you ride over the Buddha Hall at the main gate?”
"Pass beyond this," he said. [The monk] asked, "In that case, one does not engage in false conceptualization. The Master said, "Give me back the *huatou* (the critical phrase).
Tell me, how would you explain Yunmen’s 'not engaging in false conceptualization'? You must understand this *kōan* clearly;
only then can it be called having fundamental insight (*jñāna-darśana*).
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"Far removed from what is produced, as well as from differences in form and location; nature and matter are impermanent. The deluded imaginings of the outsiders hold that all natures are indestructible.
Abiding in the great self-nature, the outsiders conceive of impermanence, submerged as they are in various views."
Those various non-Buddhists [claim] that there is neither arising nor ceasing; the nature of the great elements (*mahābhūta*) is itself eternal.

What, then, is meant by the perception of impermanence? (In the Tang translation: "Those various groups of non-Buddhists all [assert] non-arising and non-ceasing; the natures of the great elements are themselves [eternal]. Which, then, is the dharma of impermanence? All is merely the measure of mind (*cittamātra*). Two kinds of mental flow revolve:
the grasper (*grāhaka*) and the grasped (*grāhya*). There is no self (*ātman*) or what belongs to a self (*ātmīya*). Brahmā is the root of the tree; its branches and leaves extend everywhere.
All that I have thus described is merely the measure of that mind (the Wei translation says: "The phenomena of the three realms, high and low—I say they are all mind;
apart from these mental dharmas, nothing else can be found").
The interlocutor said: "In the preceding prose section, the refutation of the seven kinds of impermanence was already complete.
This [section] again summarizes their essential points to refute them: first, 'having acted, one abandons,' meaning that the creator of impermanence is separate from that which is created;
second, 'difference in shape and location'; third, 'impermanence of color,' meaning that the created is impermanent."
Yet they claim that the four great elements (*mahābhūta*) which constitute these [forms] are eternal; this contradicts their initial calculation. Fifth, they hold that nature is impermanent;

sixth, they hold that nature is both non-existent and impermanent, meaning that both the primary elements and the derived forms (*bhautika*) perish together, while within them there exists an impermanent self-nature that does not perish—this contradicts the former calculations. Can these not be called foolish? Fourth, regarding transformation (*pariṇāma*):...
Therein exists an indestructible nature. Seventh, it is said that all phenomena are unborn and pervasively abide within all dharmas;

the self-nature of the four great elements is eternally present and imperishable. Since they are described as both "indestructible" and "eternally present," yet non-Buddhists (tīrthikas) conceive of them as impermanent—taking the permanent to be impermanent and the impermanent to be permanent—they remain submerged [in error].
These various false conceptualizations and views are all untrue, for that which they call "permanent" is not real; moreover, their own words are self-contradictory.
Those non-Buddhists all claim that all phenomena are unarisen, and that things are neither destroyed nor extinguished.
They assert that the four great elements do not destroy one another and that their intrinsic nature is eternally abiding. If this were so, then everything—
This is eternal. Who could perceive that which is an impermanent phenomenon as being impermanent? Therefore, the meaning of what you call the "seven kinds of impermanence" is not established.
As for the Dharma I teach: everything within the three realms is merely the manifestation of one's own mind;
it is both existence and non-existence, yet transcends existence and non-existence; it is both arising and ceasing, yet transcends arising and ceasing; it is fundamentally non-existent.

Regarding the obtainability of subject and object: if those two kinds of conceptual discrimination—subject and object—both arise from the mental engagement that flows forth from one's own mind, then one perceives a grasper and a grasped. If one clings to existence, one regards it as impermanent;
if one clings to non-existence, one likewise regards it as impermanent. In reality, there is no grasper who acts [as such].

Regarding this "self," there is likewise nothing that can be grasped as "mine. It is only because the conscious mind pursues delusions and wanders through saṃsāra that these two kinds of grasping arise. If the mind does not wander, then fundamentally there is no self;
who would be the grasper? Fundamentally there is no "mine"; what would be the grasped? Since the nature of these two graspings is thus detached, where could anything be seen?
Those who perceive existence call it "permanent," while those who perceive non-existence call it "impermanent.

Therefore, what I teach is neither permanent nor impermanent. Furthermore, the non-Buddhists speculate that Mahābrahmā first created sentient beings as the root of all living things, just as a tree trunk gives rise to branches and twigs that pervade the world; such is their teaching.
Those who regard the roots of trees as "I" and the spreading branches and twigs as "mine" possess only the deluded mental constructs (*vikalpa-citta-mātra*) of those outsiders;
they are not included within my Dharma. What I teach is that the three realms, from the highest to the lowest, are but the single mind (*ekacitta*);
apart from the mind, nothing else can be found. To realize that all is a manifestation of the mind alone is [the truth].
There is fundamental wisdom that clearly understands the mundane and supramundane dharmas of the highest order as being neither eternal nor non-eternal.
Those who regard the Brahmā heaven’s supreme and subtle atoms as the creator possess no fundamental wisdom;
they merely engage in various conceptual distinctions and establish seven theories of impermanence based on mere branches and leaves. In total—
It is nothing more than returning to delusion. Chan Master Zhentian of Lantian ascended the hall and said: "A mountain is formed by relying on the first basket of earth;
a long journey is reached by depending on the first step. Venerable One, you have just now come from the side of the hearth—is this the same as the first step, or is it different?
If you say they are the same, you do not understand non-transmigration. If you say they are different, you also do not understand non-transmigration."
"Elder, how do you understand this? Do you understand yet? Here is not there; there is not here.
Tell me, is it one place or two places? Is it shifting or non-shifting? Is it coming and going, or is it not coming and going?
If you can clarify this, then the ancient and the modern will be as one from beginning to end; thereafter, every thought-moment [will be so]."
The impermanent mind and its objects are forever extinguished. Thus it is said: "By observing the direction one knows where another has gone; yet the one who went does not arrive at that direction.

Elder, you have just now come in such a manner, so please depart in such a manner. Contemplate these few words, which reveal that every thought-moment is impermanent and that the mind and its objects are forever extinguished.
Once you realize the state of true non-transmigration, it will accord with the teaching of Mind-Only.
The Essential Meaning in Accordance with the Obscure (Weiyin: Chapter Nine on Entering the Way; Tangyin: Chapter Four on Manifest Realization).
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I only pray that you will explain for all bodhisattvas..."
The sequence of the successive continuity of the cessation-samādhi (*nirodha-samāpatti*) of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas:

if one is skilled in the characteristics of this sequence of the successive continuity of the cessation-samādhi, I and other bodhisattvas will never recklessly abandon the gateway to the bliss of the cessation-samādhi, nor fall into the ignorance of all śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, or non-Buddhists.
The Buddha said, "Mahāmati, listen closely, listen closely, and reflect well upon this."
"I shall explain this for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain it for me.
The Buddha told Mahāmati, "Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the sixth stage, as well as śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas of the seventh stage enter a meditative absorption in every thought-moment that is free from all characteristics of intrinsic nature (*svabhāva-lakṣaṇa*); this is not [the absorption] of the śrāvakas."

Regarding the Pratyekabuddhas: all Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas fall into the meditative attainment (*samāpatti*) that extinguishes the characteristics of the grasper and the grasped within the sphere of conditioned activity.

Therefore, in the seventh stage, there is no meditative attainment of mindfulness. They have not yet attained the non-differentiated characteristic of all phenomena as their own domain; rather, they attain various distinct characteristics and natures.

They attain the meditative attainment that awakens to the characteristics of the wholesome and unwholesome nature of all phenomena. Therefore, in the seventh stage, there is no meditative attainment of wholesome mindfulness.

[The Buddha] said: "Yes. (The Wei translation states: 'In the seventh stage, Bodhisattvas enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*) in every thought-moment. This is because all Bodhisattvas are able to remain far removed from the marks of existence and non-existence regarding all phenomena.

Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cannot enter the meditative absorption of cessation in every thought-moment; they enter it by taking conditioned formations as their object, thereby falling into the sphere of the grasped and the grasper. For this reason, Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cannot enter the meditative absorption of cessation in every thought-moment within the seventh stage.

They enter the meditative absorption of cessation by perceiving the various distinct marks of phenomena—such as existent and non-existent dharmas, wholesome and unwholesome dharmas, as well as common and specific marks. Therefore, due to a lack of skillful means, Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas cannot enter the meditative absorption of cessation in every thought-moment within the seventh stage.'"
[This is] because of the wisdom of skillful means).

He replied: Based on the previous statement that the non-arising and non-ceasing of the heterodox paths (tīrthikas) is no different from that of the Buddha, and since it has been pointed out that the seven kinds of impermanence are dharmas subject to arising and ceasing, the nirvāṇa taught by the heterodox paths is already insufficient to discuss. However...
All Bodhisattvas and those of the two vehicles alike sever the afflictions of the three realms and enter the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).
Yet, there are gradations and distinctions among them; they progress through the stages (*bhūmi*) in succession, each claiming to have attained *nirvāṇa*.

If one thoroughly understands these characteristics, one will know that the bliss of the meditative attainment of cessation within supreme *nirvāṇa* is the true realm, and thus one does not fall [into error].

This is the deluded view of the followers of the two vehicles and the non-Buddhists. The World-Honored One explained this to them in detail, stating that from the first to the sixth bhūmi, bodhisattvas attain the realization of *pudgala-nairātmya* (the selflessness of persons) and enter the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*), which is no different from that of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas;

however, because they still have entry into and emergence from this concentration, they are unable to enter it moment by moment. Upon reaching the seventh bhūmi, they enter it at every thought-moment.

Entering into meditative absorption (*samāpatti*), he thereby transcends all marks of existence and non-existence. Even regarding the mark of the self-nature of the nature of nirvāṇa, he does not grasp at it.
Therefore, this is beyond the reach of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*). Those of the two vehicles contemplate the bliss of meditative absorption;

seeing absorption as something existent, they grasp at it. Relying on conditioned formations (*saṃskāra*) to enter the meditative attainment of cessation (*nirodhasamāpatti*), they fall into the duality of subject and object.
They grasp at objective realms and are unable to enter the *samādhi* of momentary extinction within the seventh stage.

Therefore, in the seventh stage, every thought-moment is both right reception (*samyak-samāpatti*) and non-reception; it is not that they regard right reception as something virtuous and intentionally enter it.

This is because they have attained the realization that all phenomena lack the differentiated characteristics of birth-and-death and nirvana, and this state is not within the scope of the two vehicles.
Furthermore, those followers of the Two Vehicles who fall into the awakening of conditioned activity perceive various characteristics and natures that can be apprehended.

That is to say, they awaken to all phenomena as being existent or non-existent, wholesome or unwholesome, and as having common or distinct characteristics, thereby entering the meditative absorption of cessation (*nirodha-samāpatti*).

They perceive birth and death as something to be loathed and perceive quiescent extinction (*śānti-nirvāṇa*) as something to be delighted in. Because they lack [the realization of] the non-existence of...
The wisdom of skillful means cannot realize nirvana within the context of phenomena subject to arising and ceasing.

Because it regards nirvana as wholesome and takes hold of it, it is properly termed "wholesome mindfulness and right concentration" (*samyak-smṛti-samādhi*), rather than "moment-to-moment right concentration."
At the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), one even forgets the excellence of moment-to-moment meditative absorption (*samādhi*); thus, one attains the non-differentiated characteristic of all phenomena.

How could this be something the followers of the Two Vehicles would dare to hope for? A monk named Siyi asked Yangshan, "What is the essential meaning of entering the gate of sudden enlightenment in the Chan school?
Yangshan replied, "This meaning is extremely difficult. If one is of superior capacity within the lineage of our ancestors..."
"Those of superior wisdom attain great *dhāraṇī* upon hearing it once and awakening to a thousand truths.

But for those whose faculties are dull and whose wisdom is inferior, if they do not settle themselves in the tranquility of meditation, they will be utterly bewildered when they reach this point. The monk asked, "Aside from this one path, is there another way of entry?
Yangshan said, "There is. The monk asked, "What is that? Yangshan asked, "Where are you from? The monk replied, "From Youzhou."
Yang asked the man from the prefecture, "Do you still think of that place? He replied, "I always think of it. Yang said, "That which is able to think is the mind;
that which is thought of is the object. At that place there were multi-storied pavilions, groves, gardens, and crowds of people and horses.
When you turn back to reflect upon what you are thinking of, do you still find all those various things there? He replied, "When I come to this point, I no longer see anything at all. Yang said:
"Is the stage of faith this? Or is it not yet the stage of man? [Tianping] said, "Apart from this, is there another intention?
Yangshan said, "Whether there is something else or nothing else, that is unacceptable. [Tianping] asked, "Having arrived here, how can one be 'this'?
Yangshan said, "Based on your understanding, you have only attained one mystery. Once you have attained the seat and donned the robe, look for yourself later. (Tiantong)
The verse says: Without exterior yet all-encompassing; unobstructed yet profound. Gateways and walls rise tier upon tier;

locks and bolts multiply in layers. Wine is ever full, and guests lie slumbering; rice is plentiful, yet farmers remain prostrate. Suddenly emerging from the void, the wind seizes the wondrous sprouts;
trampling over the blue seas, thunder ushers in the roaming dragons. Those of the Two Vehicles cannot enter; it is the true state of the Seventh Ground.

Receiving [this teaching], they obtain only one mystery. They become intoxicated by the wine of the bliss of samādhi and the nectar of *tathatā* (suchness), as if their bellies were full after a great meal;
how could they possibly break out from the void?

Mahāmati, at the eighth stage, the Bodhisattvas, as well as the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, have the cessation of the delusive appearances of mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*). At the beginning...
Bodhisattva-mahāsattvas from the first stage up to the seventh stage contemplate the extent of the mind, mentation, and consciousness within the triple world.

Free from the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self," they abandon the cultivation of various external characteristics based on their own false imaginings (the Chinese translation says: "they do not see the various characteristics of external dharmas").

Fools, however, perceive two kinds of things within their own minds—the grasper and the grasped—and thus turn toward ignorance, lack of awakening, and the beginningless faults of delusive habitual tendencies.
“Mahāmati, the nirvāṇa of the bodhisattva-mahāsattvas at the eighth stage, as well as that of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas, is maintained by the support of samādhi-awakening.
For this reason, they do not enter parinirvāṇa through the bliss of the gates of samādhi. If they were not so supported, the stage of the Tathāgata would not be fulfilled;
they would abandon all conditioned marks of sentient beings, and thus the lineage of the Buddhas would surely be severed.”
The Buddha, the World-Honored One, has revealed the inconceivable and immeasurable merits of the Tathāgata.

Because Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas are led away by the pleasure obtained through the gates of samādhi, they conceive the notion that it is nirvāṇa. Mahāmati, I have established the seven stages [of the Bodhisattva], in which one skillfully cultivates the characteristics of mind, thought, and consciousness;

skillfully cultivates the notions of "I" and "mine"; and skillfully cultivates the grasping of person and phenomena, as well as selflessness and the arising and ceasing of self-characteristics and common characteristics.
The characteristics of the stages (*bhūmi*) are the sequential continuity of the gates of samādhi through the power of certainty in the four analytical knowledges (*pratisaṃvid*).

They enter the dharmas of the factors of enlightenment (*bodhipākṣika-dharma*), so as not to allow bodhisattva-mahāsattvas to fail to perceive the specific and general characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa-sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) and thus fall into the evil paths of externalists at the seventh stage.
Therefore, the sequence of the stages is established. Mahāmati, in reality there is neither arising nor ceasing, except for what is manifested by one's own mind.
The measure refers to the sequential continuity of the stages (*bhūmi*) and the various activities within the three realms.
That which is not realized by the foolish refers to what I and all the Buddhas teach regarding the sequential continuity of the stages and the various activities within the three realms.

Tong said: "It was stated above that the cessation-equipoise (*nirodha-samāpatti*) of the two vehicles cannot enter the cessation-equipoise of the seventh stage because they are unable to attain the non-differentiated characteristic of all phenomena.
Therefore, upon reaching the eighth stage, one abandons the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*).
Not only do the various characteristics of all phenomena cease, but even the mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-mano-vijñāna*) of the śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas are extinguished."

Discriminative conceptualization is also extinguished. The Wei translation states that in the seventh stage (*bhūmi*), the Bodhisattva transforms and extinguishes the mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-manas-vijñāna*) of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas;

upon reaching the eighth stage, these are transformed and extinguished almost entirely. When the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) is completely exhausted, it is called the Immovable Stage (*Acalā-bhūmi*).
From the first stage through the seventh stage, the contemplative practices cultivated involve seeing all phenomena within the triple world as being solely mind.
The measure manifested by the mind, the intellect, and consciousness is such that the mind is no-mind, the intellect is no-intellect, and consciousness is no-consciousness.
Fundamentally free from the grasping of "I" and "mine," one does not perceive the various marks of external phenomena.
Yet, they give rise to false conceptualizations and delusive habituation within their own minds, perceiving external phenomena as obtainable; thus, they fall into the seeds of external natures.
These are the various characteristics. Furthermore, these foolish outsiders, through two kinds of grasping, perceive with their own minds that which is contained within their own minds;
they see the existence of the subject and object of grasping, and thus claim that all things are annihilated and entirely devoid of cognition.

They fall into the realm of non-conception, failing to realize that this nature of annihilation is merely the result of being permeated by beginningless, false habitual tendencies. This is precisely...
These faults consist of grasping at the grasper and the grasped, not being free from "I" and "mine.
This is the false and deluded conception of nirvana held by non-Buddhists, which is only completely extinguished upon reaching the eighth stage (*bhūmi*). Why is this?

Because the samādhi attained by a bodhisattva in the eighth stage is roughly similar to the nirvana of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*). Nevertheless, within that samādhi, the bodhisattva possesses correct awakening (*samyag-bodhi*).
They are sustained by the empowerment of the power of all Buddhas; thus, although they possess the bliss of samādhi, they do not become attached to it, and therefore do not enter nirvāṇa.

If they were not sustained by the support of the Perfectly Awakened Ones, they would instead find security in the Lesser Vehicle, unable to fulfill the stage of a Tathāgata, abandoning all sentient beings, and failing to proclaim the existence [of the Buddha-nature].
If one were to introduce all dharmas gradually into the Tathāgata’s knowledge and vision, the lineage of the Buddhas would be severed.
For this reason, the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not arise from the samādhi of a Bodhisattva of the eighth stage. They exclaim: "O son of good family! You must arise to deliver sentient beings!
The samādhi you have attained is also attained by those of the two vehicles. Thereupon, they manifest for them the Tathāgata’s unconditioned [compassion].
This compassion flows from the ocean of wondrous enlightenment, producing inconceivable and immeasurable merit.
It causes [beings] to ultimately attain fulfillment and succeed in perpetuating the lineage of the Buddhas; therefore, it does not enter into nirvana.

If śrāvakas and pratyekabuddhas obtain the bliss of the gates of samādhi, they are led away by that bliss and, taking little as sufficient, are unable to turn their minds toward the Great Vehicle to deliver others.

They liberate sentient beings; therefore, they conceive the notion of nirvana therein. For this reason, entering the meditative absorption of cessation prior to the seventh stage is common to both the two vehicles;
thus, one must skillfully establish safeguards. This is why I have divided the stages at the seventh level:
one should skillfully employ expedient means to cultivate the characteristics of mind, thought, and consciousness, remaining far removed from the notions of "self" and "what belongs to self."

Having grasped that there is neither a grasper nor an object of grasping, one attains the wisdom of the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*). Advancing further, one attains the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*), wherein neither specific (*svalakṣaṇa*) nor general (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*) characteristics can be apprehended.
This is because the nirvāṇa realized by the followers of the two vehicles still possesses specific and general characteristics that can be apprehended.

Ultimately, these belong to the realm of arising and ceasing; one should skillfully observe them and remain far removed from them. One should skillfully understand the four kinds of unimpeded eloquence:

namely, unimpededness regarding meaning (*artha-pratisaṃvid*), unimpededness regarding phenomena (*dharma-pratisaṃvid*), unimpededness regarding expression (*nirukti-pratisaṃvid*), and unimpededness regarding joyful exposition (*pratibhāna-pratisaṃvid*).

Having attained the power of certainty within the gates of samādhi, one gains mastery therein. In every thought-moment, one enters correct meditative absorption (*samāpatti*) without the characteristics of entering or emerging. Upon reaching this state, it is purely...

Only through the contemplation of signlessness (*animitta-vipaśyanā*) can one gradually ascend through the stages from the eighth to the tenth, proceeding through the successive stages in continuous succession.
One enters the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (*saptatriṃśad-bodhipakṣa-dharmāḥ*), which are the aids to the path.

The reason I have divided and categorized these dharmas so that they may be well-cultivated is out of concern that bodhisattvas might not skillfully understand specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) and general characteristics (*sāmānyalakṣaṇa*), and might not [skillfully...]
Prior to the seventh stage, the sequence of practice may fall into the heterodox paths of nihilism or eternalism;
therefore, the successive stages are established so that what arises in a preceding stage is extinguished by the succeeding one.
Upon reaching the adamantine path, there is nothing further to be extinguished, and only then does one realize entry into the non-arising, non-ceasing nirvana without remainder. To summarize:
In reality, there is neither arising nor ceasing. All phenomena are but manifestations of the mind; the mind is fundamentally without mind, and manifestation is fundamentally without manifestation.
Apart from the measure of what is manifested by one's own mind, there is originally no arising or ceasing. Only those who possess fundamental wisdom can awaken to this.
This extends to the so-called successive progression through the stages (*bhūmi*) and the severing of the three realms.
The various practices of the nine grades of afflictions are all intended as remedies for the illnesses of sentient beings;
this is something that ignorant, foolish people do not perceive. Why is it that they do not perceive it?

It is because they do not realize that I and the Buddhas have established these dharmas in order to enable sentient beings to realize and enter the nirvana without remainder, which is neither born nor extinguished. Thus it is said:

The absence of the characteristic of speech is itself the signless (*animitta*). It is said that I and all Buddhas speak of the sequential continuity of the stages (*bhūmi*) and speak of the various modes of activity within the triple world (*tridhātu*).
Yet, one merely gives rise to attachment toward these verbal expressions, while fundamentally lacking fundamental wisdom (*mūla-jñāna*).
This refers to how the Tathāgata teaches that all phenomena arise from the conceptualization of verbal expression; this is why it is so called.
[This is] foolishness. A monk asked Mazu, "What is the cultivation of the Way? Mazu said, "The Way does not belong to cultivation.

If one says it is attained through cultivation, then once cultivated, it will still perish, which is the same as the Śrāvakas. If one says there is no cultivation, that is the same as an ordinary person.
He asked again, "By what realization can one attain the Way? Mazu said, "The original nature is inherently complete; it is simply..."

To remain unimpeded amidst good and evil is what is called being a practitioner of the Way. To grasp at goodness and reject evil, or to contemplate emptiness and enter meditative concentration, belongs to the realm of conditioned activity.
If you further seek outwardly, you will become increasingly estranged and distant. Simply exhaust the mental dimensions of the triple world;
a single moment of deluded mind is the very root of birth and death within the triple world. If there is not even a single thought, it is eliminated.
The very root of birth and death is itself the unsurpassed, precious flavor of the Dharma King.

Throughout immeasurable kalpas, the deluded thoughts of ordinary beings—characterized by flattery, crookedness, deceit, falsehood, self-conceit, and arrogance—have coalesced into a single entity. Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"This body is merely composed of various dharmas; when it arises, only dharmas arise; when it ceases, only dharmas cease. When these dharmas arise...

It does not say "I arise," nor does it say "I cease" at the time of cessation. The preceding thought, the subsequent thought, and the middle thought—moment by moment, they do not depend upon one another;
moment by moment, they are quiescent and extinguished. This is called the Ocean-Seal Samādhi (*sāgaramudrā-samādhi*).

It encompasses all phenomena just as hundreds of thousands of diverse streams all return to the great ocean and are collectively termed "ocean water. Abiding in this single flavor, it subsumes all manifold flavors within its dwelling.
In the great ocean, all streams are blended; it is like a person bathing in the great ocean who uses all its waters.

Thus, while the śrāvakas awaken, the ordinary beings are deluded, and while the ordinary beings awaken, the śrāvakas are deluded. The śrāvakas do not know that the Sage’s mind is fundamentally devoid of stages, causes, effects, or hierarchical levels.
They cultivate causes and realize fruits based on mental measures and false imaginings, dwelling for eighty thousand [eons] in the samādhi of emptiness.
For twenty thousand kalpas, although they have already attained awakening, having awakened they fall back into delusion. To the various Bodhisattvas, this state appears as painful as being in hell;
they sink into emptiness and stagnate in stillness, failing to perceive the Buddha-nature.

If these beings of superior capacity suddenly encounter a spiritual friend who points it out to them, they comprehend it in a single word, no longer passing through the successive stages and positions, but attaining sudden awakening to their original nature.
This is the nature of things. Thus, the Sūtra says that ordinary people possess a mind of regression, whereas Śrāvakas do not.

Mazu, despite such complications, attained a transformative awakening through his practice of seated meditation and studying the Buddha. "Grinding a tile cannot produce a mirror; whipping a cart will not make it move.
Once he clarified the essential point of the mind, every word he spoke trampled everyone underfoot.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and those on the eighth stage of the Bodhisattvas are intoxicated by the intoxication of the bliss of the cessation-samādhi (nirodha-samādhi).

They are unskilled in the manifestation of their own minds; they are obstructed by the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of self-characteristics and common characteristics; they fall into the views of grasping at the non-existence of persons and phenomena;
and they conceive of a false nirvana through their deluded thoughts. This is not the awakening of the wisdom of true cessation. Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva perceives...
He delights in the gate of the samādhi of cessation. He has accomplished his original vows through compassion and great pity. He knows the ten inexhaustible phrases that distinguish reality.

He does not falsely conceptualize the notion of nirvāṇa, because for him, false conceptualization regarding nirvāṇa no longer arises (as the Chinese translation states: "because by entering nirvāṇa, the fruit of rebirth no longer arises").

He is free from the false conceptualization of the grasped and the grasper. Having realized that all phenomena are merely the manifestations of his own mind, false conceptualization regarding them no longer arises.
They do not fall into the false discrimination that clings to the external characteristics of the self-nature of mind, thought, and consciousness.

Not being produced from causes other than the Buddha-dharma, they arise in accordance with wisdom and attain the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-realization. It is like a person in a dream who employs skillful means to cross a river;

before he has crossed, he awakens. Having awakened, he reflects upon whether [the crossing] was real or illusory, concluding it was neither real nor illusory—this being due to other beginningless perceptions and auditions.

Awakened consciousness arises from conceptualization (*saṃjñā*). Due to various habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) and various forms and locations, it manifests in dreams according to the presence or absence of thought within the mind, intellect, and consciousness (*citta-manovijñāna*).

Mahāmati, in this way, when a Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva reaches the eighth Bodhisattva stage (*bhūmi*), they perceive the arising of false discrimination (*vikalpa*)—the Wei translation says "perceiving the discriminating mind. Having progressed from the first stage up to the seventh stage, they perceive all phenomena as being like illusions and so forth.

Having employed skillful means to transcend the mental constructions of the grasper and the grasped, one applies the skillful means of the Buddha-dharma so that those who have not yet attained [realization] may attain it.
Mahāmati, this is the indestructible skillful means of the bodhisattva’s nirvāṇa (in the Tang translation, "the nirvāṇa attained is not subject to destruction").

Having transcended mind, thought, and consciousness, one attains the patience regarding the non-arising of dharmas (*anutpattika-dharma-kṣānti*). Mahāmati, in the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is no sequential continuity; thus it is taught.

The dharma of the cessation of all conceptualizations of non-existence (the Tang translation states: "Within the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), there is no sequence and no continuity; it is far removed from all objective spheres and discrimination.
This is what is called the dharma of cessation").
The Master said: "It was stated above that what appears as one's own mind is actually devoid of both arising and ceasing;
all phenomena have been eternally in a state of quiescent extinction from the very beginning. To be able to awaken to this is what is called the awakening of quiescent wisdom.

Those of the two vehicles merely realize the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā) but have not yet realized the emptiness of phenomena (dharma-śūnyatā); they are thus still unable to enter the first [stage]."
How much more so for the gate of the bliss of cessation on the eighth stage? The Buddha taught that there are two kinds of śrāvakayāna practitioners:
