Furthermore, if there is neither awakening nor understanding, nor knowledge or comprehension, this is called "both mother and son having perished. How wonderful is this ultimate discourse! It may serve as the method for a bodhisattva of sharp intelligence to diligently study the Tathāgatagarbha.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:

"The profound Tathāgatagarbha abides together with the seven consciousnesses; it gives rise to the two kinds of grasping. The wise one remains far removed from it, seeing the mind manifest like a reflection in a mirror.
Perfumed by beginningless habitual tendencies, those who observe according to reality find that all phenomena are ultimately without substance."

It is like a fool who, seeing a finger pointing at the moon, looks only at the finger and not at the moon. Those who are attached to names and words do not see that my true mind acts as a stage performer;
the manas is like the director of the troupe, the five consciousnesses are its companions, and deluded thoughts are the audience watching the performance.

Tong said: "To speak of the 'profound Tathāgatagarbha' while taking the fundamental Tathāgatagarbha as the basis means that the 'empty Tathāgatagarbha,' which is free from arising and ceasing, is easily understood by people;

whereas the 'non-empty Tathāgatagarbha,' which does not abandon skillful means and manifests arising and ceasing in conjunction with the seven consciousnesses, is difficult for people to fathom—hence it is called 'profound. It is precisely because..."
It coexists with the seven consciousnesses. Ordinary, ignorant people do not understand that the various conditions of defilement and purity are established based upon it;

seeing the two kinds of grasping—the grasper and the grasped—they fall back into birth and death. The wise, however, thoroughly comprehend that both defilement and purity are neither [real], and that both mind and objects have perished;
thus, the state of grasper and grasped is immediately distanced from them. Emptiness is itself indeterminate.
That which is non-empty is itself empty; because one awakens to and enters the profound *tathāgatagarbha*, it is called "wisdom.
As for what is called "detachment," how could it mean seeking the mind apart from its objects?

All phenomena of the three realms are manifestations of mind alone, like various forms appearing within a mirror—neither existent nor non-existent—due to the two habitual tendencies of defilement and purity from beginningless time.
Because it is that which is perfumed, it merely reflects its image; the mirror remains entirely uninvolved.
If one can truly contemplate the profound Tathāgatagarbha, one will find that coming and going, delusion and awakening, and birth and death are ultimately unobtainable.
All various phenomena are fundamentally without phenomenon; all various marks are fundamentally without mark.
Since beginningless time, habitual tendencies are in fact non-existent; therefore, one is able to remain far removed from grasping.
This profound Tathāgatagarbha is, within phenomena, without phenomenon; within images, without image. One should rely upon the meaning and not rely upon names. As for "name":
Names are like a finger pointing at the moon. When a foolish person sees the finger pointing at the moon, they look only at the finger and do not look at the moon.
Those who are attached to names and fail to see reality are just like this.
One who observes according to reality uses the wisdom of suchness to observe the essence of suchness, and thus does not cling to language or words. Therefore...
One is able to see the meaning of reality. Having seen the meaning of reality, one becomes detached from mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*);

thus, the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*) are transformed into wisdom (*jñāna*). Therefore, it is seen that wisdom is the reality, while consciousness is a provisional designation for the locus.
When observing the *citta*, it appears and transforms according to conditions, like a skilled artisan; when observing the *manas*, it transmits and conveys [objects] in and out.
It is like a musician: when observing the five consciousnesses, they grasp objects and pursue sensory dust, arising together with the consciousness as if they were companions;
when observing the sixth consciousness, its false conceptualization and discrimination cling to things as real, like watching a troupe of performers.

All things are like illusions, fundamentally non-existent. If one clings to the names of mind, thought, and consciousness, one merely grasps at illusory phenomena and fails to perceive the true meaning of the Tathāgatagarbha. As Lord Wang Anshi said in his verse on watching actors:
"Among the actors on the stage, one is noble and another is base; yet the mind knows they are fundamentally the same. What is it that...
Because there is neither longing nor resentment. If this verse may also be called "observing according to reality," Master Wuzu Fayan addressed the assembly, saying:
"Yesterday, when I entered the city, I saw a stage of puppet plays. Unable to resist, I approached to watch.
I saw some that were dignified and extraordinary, and others that were ugly and repulsive; they moved, walked, sat, and were colored blue or yellow."
He saw each of the red and white [forms] clearly. When he looked closely, he realized that there was actually someone inside a blue cloth curtain.
Unable to restrain his amusement, the mountain monk asked the Chancellor his surname. He replied, "Old Monk, if you have seen him, let it be."
"Question: What is your surname? At that single phrase, this mountain monk was left with no words to respond and no principle to uphold.
Is there anyone who can speak for this mountain monk? Yesterday he lost his footing there; today here he uproots the foundation.
If you can understand the news of uprooting the foundation, you will be able to remain far removed from grasping and attachment, and see suchness.
The Nature of the Ālayavijñāna.
*Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, Section on the Penetration of the Essential Principle, Volume Seven;
*Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, Section on the Penetration of the Essential Principle, Volume Eight.
(Chapter Twelve: The Dharma-Gates, according to the Wei translation).

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me the ultimate characteristics of the five dharmas, the self-natures, consciousness, the two kinds of selflessness, and their detailed distinctions, so that I and the other Bodhisattvas-Mahāsattvas may [understand them] within the one..."
"By means of sequential analysis according to the stages of the grounds, one enters into all Buddha-dharmas.
As for entering into all Buddha-dharmas, it extends even to the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-awakening. The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Listen closely, listen closely, and reflect well upon this!
Mahāmati replied to the Buddha, "Yes, I shall receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, "There are five dharmas, three natures, and two kinds of consciousness."
The characteristic of the realm of non-self-discrimination refers to names, signs, and false imaginings; it is right knowledge and suchness.
When a practitioner practices and enters the noble realm of the Tathāgata’s self-realization, they become free from views of annihilation, permanence, existence, and non-existence.

The blissful attainment (*sukha-samādhi*) of the present dharma becomes manifest before them. However, Mahāmati, they do not realize those five dharmas, the natures, the consciousnesses, and the two kinds of non-self.
"The manifestation of external objects within the mind is the deluded imagination (*vikalpa*) of ordinary worldlings (*bāla*), not that of the noble ones (*ārya*).

Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, why does the deluded imagination arise in ordinary worldlings but not in the noble ones? The Buddha told Mahāmati, "Ordinary worldlings cling to conventional designations, names, and signs (*nāma-lakṣaṇa*).
Following after their minds, they scatter; having scattered, they fall into various forms and appearances, and long for views of 'I' and 'mine' (*ahaṃkāra-mamakāra-dṛṣṭi*)."
Expecting and clinging to exquisite forms, and because of that clinging, being shrouded by ignorance, they give rise to defiled attachment.
Once stained by attachment, they accumulate karma born of greed, hatred, and delusion; having accumulated it, they entangle themselves with false imaginings like a silkworm spinning its cocoon.

Thus they fall into the ocean of birth and death and the wilderness of the various realms of existence, like a water-wheel drawing from a well; due to their folly, they cannot understand that this world is like an illusion.

The self-nature of horses, waters, and moons is free from "I" and "mine. It arises from all unreal conceptualizations (*parikalpita*) and is devoid of the characterized (*lakṣya*) and the characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), as well as arising, abiding, and ceasing.
These arise from the conceptualizations of one's own mind; they are not produced by a sovereign creator, time, atoms, or a supreme principle.

Foolish commoners, following after names and signs, [the Tang translation says: "Foolish people do not know that names are provisional designations; their minds follow the flow and perceive various signs, calculating them as 'self'"]...

I am stained by and attached to form, which obscures noble wisdom; giving rise to greed, hatred, and delusion, I perform various karmas. Like a silkworm making a cocoon, I bind myself with my own false imaginings and fall into the great ocean of birth and death across the various realms of existence.

Like a waterwheel drawing from a well, I circulate without end, not knowing that all phenomena are like illusions, like mirages, or like the moon reflected in water—merely what is seen by one's own mind arising from false discrimination. I do not realize that they are free from the grasped and the grasper, as well as arising, abiding, and ceasing, and that they arise from [the notions of] Īśvara, time, atoms, or primordial nature (*pradhāna*), following the flow of names and signs.
The Master replied: "The five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness have already been clearly elucidated by me more than twice before.

That you ask this question again is because you wish to exhaustively discern their respective characteristics, how they mutually encompass one another, and how they interpenetrate, ultimately entering into all Buddha-dharmas so that nothing is excluded."
This may be called the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-awakening; the Buddha then explained it to him in detail, one by one, saying: "The five dharmas encompass all dharmas.
If a practitioner is free from views such as annihilationism, eternalism, existence, or non-existence, they will not fall into names, marks, or false conceptualization.
When the blissful meditative absorption of the present dharma manifests before them, this is the awakening of the various stages."
When the Bodhisattva partially realizes *tathatā* (suchness) and dwells in the stage of Presence (*abhimukhī-bhūmi*), this is called "correct wisdom" (*samyag-jñāna*);

he thereby enters the noble realm of the Tathāgata’s self-realization and realizes *tathatā*. Fools and ignorant ones do not understand the five dharmas, the [three] natures, the various consciousnesses, or selflessness;
they perceive external objects within what is manifested by the mind and give rise to conceptual discrimination, falling into views of permanence, annihilation, existence, or non-existence.
They are not noble ones. Why? Because all names and characteristics are merely provisional designations and are not originally real;
yet foolish people cling to worldly names, and their minds flow along with the arising of phenomena.

Seeing various appearances, they grasp at characteristics based on names, falling into the false views of "self" and "what belongs to self," and thus within their hearts they are fully possessed by these expectations and attachments.
The subtle and wondrous colors of all phenomena are unconsciously entered into the dark and obstructed realm of ignorance;
once there is this defiled attachment, greed arises. Once greed has arisen, one is able to create the karma of greed, anger, and delusion.
Having performed these karmic actions, one cannot stop oneself, like a silkworm spinning its cocoon with a mind of discrimination.

Enshrouded by afflictions, they fall into the great ocean of birth and death within the six realms and various destinies—a perilous and boundless expanse with no limits—circling incessantly like a waterwheel in a well.
They do not realize that the names and characteristics of all phenomena are like illusions, like mirages, or like the moon reflected in water;
though their shadowy forms appear, therein is originally no sovereign who acts as a self.
Furthermore, there is no basis upon which "mine" can be established; since "I" and "mine" do not exist, they are not substantially real.
Their attachment to exquisite forms and the accumulation of various karmas all arise from unreal conceptualizations and discriminations regarding names and signs.
Thus, one fails to know that self-nature is free from "I" and "mine"; once free from these, one is free from the characteristics of the subject and the object. Resting in peace.

The exquisite and virtuous form that is attained is such that, once one is detached from both the visible and the seer, there is no longer any obtainable flow of arising, abiding, changing, and ceasing;
nor is there any accumulation of karma to be found. All these names and characteristics arise from the false discrimination of one's own mind;
they do not arise from Īśvara, time, atoms, or any other supreme principles. This is the case for all ignorant, ordinary beings.

Now, as for these enumerations—namely, that the Lord (Īśvara), time, atoms, the self (ātman), or primordial nature (prakṛti) can produce all things—since they possess names, they must possess characteristics. That which possesses characteristics is something produced; it is not a producer.
To reckon that which is incapable of producing as being productive is a false conceptualization within the midst of phenomena subject to arising and ceasing.
They consider that because all created things are unreal, they are called "false. These deluded people merely follow along with names and appearances;
how could they speak of the noble and wise’s true state of non-arising and non-ceasing?
Formerly, Layman Pang once visited a lecture hall to join in the joy of reciting the *Vajracchedikā Prajñāpāramitā Sūtra*, and upon reaching the passage concerning "no-self" and "no-person," he...
The questioner asked, "Since the Abbot has neither self nor person, who is it that lectures and who is it that listens? The Master replied, "I have no counterpart.
The layman said, "Although I am but a worldly man, I roughly understand and have faith in this. The Master asked, "What is your own understanding, Layman?
The Layman answered with a verse: "No self, and likewise no person; How could there be distance or intimacy? I urge you to cease [this seeking]."
"Passing through these seats, it is not as if one were seeking the true Vajra-prajñā directly; beyond this nature, not even a speck of dust exists.
What I have heard and what I accept with faith are all merely provisional names. Upon hearing this verse, Emperor Chen was delighted and sighed in admiration:
"If a lay practitioner such as you can truly dwell in the bliss of the Dharma in the present, then you have attained what lies before you."

Mahāmati, as for those characteristics: that which is illuminated by visual consciousness is called form; that which is illuminated by auditory, olfactory, gustatory, tactile, and mental consciousnesses is called sound, odor, flavor, tangibility, and phenomena (*dharmas*).
These are what are called "characteristics. Mahāmati, as for those "conceptual constructions" (*vikalpa*):

they are the establishment of various names and the manifestation of various characteristics, such that [the name] is not different from [the characteristic]. (The Tang translation says: "This matter is thus determined and not different. [Examples include: elephant, horse, chariot, infantry, man...
O Mahāmati, what are called "women" and so forth are merely names of false conceptualization. To one who possesses right wisdom, those names and signs are unattainable, being like passing guests.
Thus, the various consciousnesses do not arise; they are neither annihilated nor eternal, and they do not fall into the stages of any externalists, Śrāvakas, or Pratyekabuddhas.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, by means of this right wisdom, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva does not establish names or signs.
Not establishing names and characteristics, abandoning the two views of affirmation and negation, and knowing that names and characteristics do not arise—this is called suchness (*tathatā*).
Mahāmati, the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva who abides in suchness attains the realm of non-existence;
having attained the Bodhisattva’s Stage of Joy (*pramuditā-bhūmi*), he is forever free from all the evils of external paths.

The characteristics of the dharma-realm of the supramundane path toward which one proceeds, the maturation of the discernment of all phenomena such as illusions, the self-realization of the dharma-realm,

and the departure from all false conceptualizations and views of distinct natures (translated in the Tang [Dynasty] as "departure from speculative views")— progressing through these stages up to the Dharma-cloud stage (*dharmameghā-bhūmi*),
wherein the powers of samādhi, mastery, and supernormal knowledges (*abhijñā*) blossom, one attains the stage of the Tathāgata and has already planted [the seeds].

Manifesting various transformations through perfect illumination to bring sentient beings to maturity—like the moon reflected in water—and thoroughly fulfilling the ten inexhaustible phrases for the sake of sentient beings with diverse understandings by teaching the Dharma through analytical distinctions; yet the Dharma-body remains free from mental activity:
this is called the Bodhisattva’s entry into that which is attained as Suchness (*tathatā*).
Tong said: "The preceding discussion on how 'name' is itself 'form' is concluded. Below this, we point out that 'form' also possesses 'name.
What is called 'form' here refers to the various shapes and colors confronted by the eye-consciousness, which are clearly and brightly illuminated; these are all termed 'form' (*rūpa*).
Form inherently possesses the characteristic of shape. As for the sounds confronted by the ear and the fragrances confronted by the nose..."
The objects corresponding to the body of taste and the objects corresponding to touch both possess real entities that can be pointed out, and they also constitute the characteristic of having form.

If the mind and mental consciousness perceive apart from all external objects, internally taking the dharma-relics (*dharmāyatana*) as their condition, these are merely called "provisional form," which is what is meant by the characteristic of being formless.
Within the five dharmas, those called "name" (*nāman*) and "characteristic" (*nimitta*) are like this.
What is called "conceptual construction" (vikalpa) refers to the various provisional designations established upon the aforementioned [objects] and the manifestation of all characteristics;

from within these, one falsely gives rise to discrimination, saying, "This thing is thus," or "This thing is not otherwise," such as the names "elephant," "horse," "chariot," "infantry," "man," or "woman.
These names are established based on characteristics, and characteristics arise following names; both name and characteristic are fundamentally [empty].
Because one falsely clings to this [reality] and gives rise to false discrimination within it, it is called "false conceptualization" (*vikalpa*).

False conceptualization cannot be termed "right knowledge" (*samyagjñāna*); if it were right knowledge, then when one analytically examines those various names and signs established therein, seeking their true nature, they would be found utterly unobtainable, as they arise mutually through dependence upon one another.
Therefore, as they act as mutual guests and arise alternately like travelers passing through, their characteristics are not permanent.
Consequently, the various consciousnesses no longer give rise to false discrimination; this is merely the non-arising of the various consciousnesses, not the annihilation of their characteristics.
Thus, one does not fall into nihilism, nor does one cling to their characteristics, and thus one does not fall into [eternalism].
Because one never falls into the stages of any heterodox paths or the two vehicles, it is called "Right Wisdom" (*samyag-jñāna*).
Those heterodox paths and the two vehicles are also able to bring about the non-arising of the various consciousnesses; however, why is that considered "not right" while this is considered "right"?
It is because they merely know not to establish names and characteristics, desiring to empty everything, yet they remain attached to names in general.
Regarding the two positions of establishing characteristics and engaging in denial, they are both contradictory; how can it be so?

One who possesses correct wisdom does not establish names and characteristics, yet does not fall into the extreme of existence; nor does he ever fail to establish names and characteristics, yet does not fall into the extreme of non-existence.
Since he does not grasp them as existing, he does not give rise to the eternalist view (*śāśvata-dṛṣṭi*); nor does he grasp them as non-existent, [thus avoiding the nihilist view].

First, by severing the two types of false views—namely, the view of nihilism (*ucchedadṛṣṭi*) and the dualistic views of reification and denial—one knows that names and characteristics are fundamentally non-arising, like passing guests that cannot be apprehended;
how then could the various consciousnesses arise of their own accord? Therefore, the non-arising of names and characteristics is the suchness (*tathatā*) of the object;
knowing the non-arising of names and characteristics is the suchness of the mind. This is the suchness of the mind and its objects.

Because it is thus, it is called "Suchness" (tathatā). When a Bodhisattva dwells in Suchness by means of correct wisdom, they illuminate without illuminating, thereby entering the signless and quiescent realm.
Seeing that all signs are non-signs, they immediately attain partial realization of True Suchness and enter the first stage (bhūmi).
Dwelling in the first stage, they realize one hundred gates of the vajra-samādhi of clarity.
Forever free from all twenty-five states of worldly existence and all phenomena subject to arising and ceasing,

they do not dwell in or cling to the nirvāṇa of non-Buddhists or the miserable realms, but correctly abide in the supramundane, non-arising and non-ceasing Dharma— the realm of True Suchness (*tathatā*).
They practice the characteristics of phenomena (*dharmalakṣaṇa*) according to reality until they reach maturity, such that the five dharmas are like an illusion.

In dreams, one is well able to discern that all phenomena are manifested solely from the mind; this is the method of self-awakening to the course of the Dharma and realizing one’s own noble wisdom through practice.
In this way, one gradually distances oneself from false conceptualization and perceives the distinct characteristics of the nature.
For anything perceived as different from the nature involves a degree of speculative conjecture, which creates a discrepancy with the essence of reality; therefore it is said:
Having abandoned conceptual speculation regarding these distinct characteristics, one thus progresses stage by stage through the ten bhūmis.
Throughout this process, it is not that one does not individually attain samādhis and spiritual powers, nor that one does not individually possess sovereign supernormal faculties;
reaching this point, they reach the ultimate of maturation and come into full bloom, like a multitude of flowers blooming in magnificent array.
In the stage of the Tathāgata, having received the consecration of the Tathāgata and being granted the rank of Buddhahood,
he sits upon a lotus palace and emits great radiance; thus, through various transformations that perfectly illuminate the Dharma-realm,
he manifests the *saṃbhogakāya* to bring bodhisattvas to maturity and manifests the *nirmāṇakāya* to bring sentient beings to maturity, just as [reflections appear] in water.
The Moon neither emerges nor enters, yet he is perfectly able to exhaustively realize the ultimate truth (*paramārtha-satya*).
He is clad in the armor of the great vow and has fully perfected the ten inexhaustible phrases (*daśākṣaya-pada*), namely:

the inexhaustibility of the realm of sentient beings, the inexhaustibility of the world-realm, the inexhaustibility of the realm of empty space, the inexhaustibility of the dharma-realm, the inexhaustibility of the realm of nirvāṇa, the inexhaustibility of the appearance of Buddhas, and [the inexhaustibility of] the Tathāgata.
The wisdom of inexhaustible mind has an inexhaustible object; the wisdom of the Buddha’s entry into the inexhaustible turning of the wheel of Dharma is inexhaustible.
For the sake of sentient beings with various inclinations and according to their desires, one discriminates and preaches the Dharma;

though one expounds the Dharma in a single voice, each type of being understands it individually. Although one preaches the Dharma for sentient beings with various inclinations, the Dharma-body itself is self-awakened and detached.
That which is produced by the mind is neither with intention nor without intention, neither with speech nor without speech; it is far removed from mind, thought, and consciousness.

Its very substance is suchness (*tathatā*). This is called the Bodhisattva entering the realm of suchness, attaining within the stage of Buddhahood such and such immeasurable and boundless dharmas—namely: name, mark, conceptualization, correct knowledge, and suchness.
The characteristics of the differentiation of the five dharmas are roughly as follows. The "Appearance" chapter of the *Avataṃsaka Sūtra* states:

"O Sons of the Buddha, there is not a single sentient being who does not possess the wisdom of the Tathāgata; it is only because of delusive thoughts, inversions, and attachments that they do not realize it.
If one is free from delusive thoughts, then all-knowledge, spontaneous knowledge, and teacherless knowledge are attained."

Furthermore, it is said that at that time, the Tathāgata, with his unobstructed and pure eye of wisdom, universally surveyed all sentient beings throughout the entire dharma-realm and spoke these words: "How marvelous! How marvelous!
Why is it that these sentient beings, though possessing the wisdom of the Tathāgata, are deluded by ignorance and folly, neither knowing nor seeing it? I shall instruct them in the right path."
He causes them to forever leave behind delusive thoughts and attachments, so that within their own bodies they may perceive the Tathāgata’s vast wisdom, which is no different from that of the Buddha.
As the Celestial Youth briefly stated: "I now see universally that all sentient beings possess the wisdom, virtues, and marks of the Tathāgata;
it is only because of delusive thoughts and attachments that they do not realize it. The verse says:
The heavens cover it and the earth bears it; formed into a single mass, it pervades the Dharma-realm without limit. When analyzed down to the *paramāṇu*, it has no interior.
Reaching the ultimate subtlety of the profound mystery, who can distinguish front from back? The Buddhas and Patriarchs come to repay the karmic debt of their speech;
let us ask the Elder Master Nanquan: "Everyone eats but a single stalk of vegetables. Thus, these five dharmas are established.
"Only when one repays the debt of verbal karma will one realize suchness; who then would distinguish between front and back?
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva addressed the Buddha, saying, "World-Honored One, how is it that the World-Honored One [teaches] that the three natures enter into the five dharmas?
Are they each possessed of their own specific characteristics (*svalakṣaṇa*) as a school of thought? The Buddha told Mahāmati, "The three natures and the eight..."

"Mahāmati, consciousness enters into the two kinds of selflessness and the five dharmas. Mahāmati, that which consists of name and appearance is the nature of false discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*).
Mahāmati, when the mind and mental factors arise based upon that false discrimination, they arise simultaneously, like the sun and its rays.

They possess various distinct characteristics and maintain their own individual distinctions; this is called the nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*). (In the Tang translation: "Because based upon that discrimination, the mind and mental factors arise simultaneously...")

Arising like the sun and its light is the nature of dependent origination (*pratītyasamutpāda*). Mahāmati, because correct wisdom and suchness (*tathatā*) are indestructible, they are called the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*).

Furthermore, Mahāmati, the false discrimination of what is manifested by one’s own mind consists of eight kinds of conceptualization: namely, the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), the manas, the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the five groups of sensory consciousnesses.
These characteristics are unreal; because they are the false discrimination of characteristics, the two-fold grasping of "self" and "mine" ceases, and thus both [graspings] are non-existent.
I have taught that if one can abandon the two kinds of self-grasping, the wisdom of the two kinds of selflessness will arise and grow.

Therefore, Mahāmati, these five dharmas—the stages of the self-realized noble wisdom of Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Tathāgatas, and their continuous succession—encompass all Buddha-dharmas within them.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, the five dharmas are: characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), names (*nāman*), conceptualization (*vikalpa*), suchness (*tathatā*), and correct wisdom (*samyagjñāna*).

Mahāmati, as for "characteristics" (*nimitta*): when locations, shapes, colors, forms, and so forth appear, these are called characteristics. When something possesses such characteristics, it is designated as a "jar" or the like;
this very thing, and nothing else, is what is called a "name. By establishing various names, one manifests various characteristics.

These mental factors, such as the mind and so forth, which take those names and those characteristics as their objects, are called "conceptual construction" (*vikalpa*). Ultimately, neither those names nor those characteristics can be found.
To attain the state where there is no awakening from beginning to end regarding all phenomena, to be free from mutual succession and unreal conceptualization—this is called *tathatā* (Suchness).

[The Tang translation states: "That name and that mark ultimately do not exist; it is merely the deluded mind's successive discrimination. To observe in this way until awakening ceases is called *tathatā*. This true, definitive, ultimate self-nature is unobtainable;
that is the characteristic of *tathatā*, the point of entry into which I and all Buddhas conform and enter for the universal benefit of all.
To teach, designate, and reveal things to sentient beings as they truly are, to enter into them through right awakening,
and to give rise to neither the notion of annihilation nor eternalism, but to accord with the noble path of self-realization— characteristics that cannot be attained by any outsiders,
śrāvakas, or pratyekabuddhas— is called right knowledge. Mahāmati, this is called the five dharmas, the three natures, the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds [of no-self].

Since all Buddha-dharmas are included within this selflessness, Mahāmati, you should personally study through skillful means and also teach others, rather than following after others. [The interlocutor] said:
Previously, Mahāmati asked about the differentiation of these dharmas and how they enter into all Buddha-dharmas, as well as the knowledge of the five dharmas.
Because it is able to encompass all phenomena exhaustively, he again reiterated his previous request, and the World-Honored One spoke to him in detail once more:

"Those names and characteristics are the objects of conceptual construction (*parikalpita*). If names and characteristics did not exist, how could discrimination arise? This nature of pervasive conceptual construction (*parikalpita-svabhāva*) is included within the five dharmas as 'name' and 'characteristic.
If one relies upon those [names and characteristics], the mind and mental factors (*citta-caitta*) produced by that conceptual construction [arise]."
The dharmas arise simultaneously, like the sun and its light arising at the same time. Here, "the sun" refers to the seven consciousnesses, and "the light" refers to the six consciousnesses.

While the various objects confronted by the first five consciousnesses are distinct from one another, the sixth consciousness discriminates among them, and the seventh consciousness grasps and maintains them from within. Thus, they mutually support one another and arise through mutual conditioning.
The seven consciousnesses are called the dependent nature of origination because they arise simultaneously with the delusive discrimination (*vikalpa*) of the six consciousnesses;
thus, the dependent nature of origination is included within the five dharmas as *vikalpa*.

If one attains true wisdom (*samyagjñāna*) and suchness (*tathatā*), remaining far removed from all delusions and realizing the ultimate reality (*bhūtārtha*), then that delusion is destroyed while the truth remains indestructible. That which is indestructible—
That which is neither born nor extinguished, lacking nothing and having no excess, is precisely the *pariniṣpanna-svabhāva* (perfected nature).

Thus, the *tathāgatagarbha* constitutes the *svabhāva*, and enters into the five dharmas as *samyagjñāna* (correct wisdom) and *tathatā* (suchness). Regarding what is called the three natures all entering into the five dharmas:
the false phenomena manifested by one's own mind are "name" (*nāman*) and "mark" (*nimitta*); to grasp at these is [the imagined nature].

The arising of attachment consists of eight kinds of discrimination, which are precisely what is called "delusive thought" (*vikalpa*). That which is termed the "storehouse consciousness" (*ālayavijñāna*) refers to the eighth consciousness;

the "mind" (*manas*) refers to the seventh consciousness; the "mental consciousness" (*manovijñāna*) refers to the sixth consciousness; and the "five bodies of consciousness" refer to the first five consciousnesses.
These eight distinct characteristics are all unreal; they arise only through the successive production of delusive discrimination.
Because they have not yet been transformed, the evolving consciousnesses are called the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness);
once transformed, they are called the *tathāgatagarbha* (Tathāgata-store), which is precisely right knowledge (*samyagjñāna*). Thus, these eight consciousnesses are included within the five dharmas.

As long as the aggregate of consciousness (*vijñānaskandha*) has not been shattered, one takes the storehouse consciousness to be the self and regards the objects discriminated by that consciousness as "mine. This is what is meant by the "person" (*pudgala*).

Once grasping has been abandoned and the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) relinquished, one takes that which is capable of abandoning as the "self" and that which is realized through such abandonment as "mine.
This is what is called the attachment to dharmas (dharmagrāha). Self and mine are not separate from the two kinds of appropriation (parigraha), which are themselves false conceptualization (vikalpa).
If these two appropriations are extinguished and the two kinds of selflessness (nairātmya) arise, this is right knowledge (samyagjñāna). It is thus.
The two kinds of selflessness—of persons and of phenomena—are also included within these five dharmas.

These five dharmas not only encompass the eight consciousnesses and the two kinds of selflessness, but they also fully subsume all Buddha-dharmas, whether pertaining to Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, Bodhisattvas, or Tathāgatas, and whether in the state of cause or fruit;
they are all unified within the single nature of the Tathāgatagarbha, which has not yet reached the state of Suchness (tathatā).
In the realm of suchness, there are falsely perceived differences of depth and shallowness, and wisdom likewise varies in its degree of ripeness.
Once one reaches *tathatā* (suchness), however, there is only the single true nature, the self-awakened noble wisdom (*svasaṃvedya-āryajñāna*).

Taking this as the ultimate, all the stages (*bhūmi*) are continuous within it, and taking this as their destination, what is there that is not subsumed? Thus concludes the analysis of the five dharmas as they enter into all Buddha-dharmas.

How is it possible to reach the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-awakening? Regarding the essence of the Dharma, one first establishes correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) and subsequently the suchness (*tathatā*);
regarding cultivation and realization, one first realizes suchness and subsequently correct wisdom.
Although without *prajñā* one certainly cannot realize bodhi, yet if one does not perceive the reality of bodhi, it is not called *prajñā*. Therefore, he speaks again:
What are called names, signs, and conceptualization? By "signs" is meant their shapes, colors, and characteristics.
By "names" is meant the designation of the name "vase" based upon the sign of a vase.
By "conceptualization" is meant the manifestation of various unreal signs through the application of provisional names—ranging from those vases and so forth up to the mind and mental factors.

To give rise to false discrimination is this [delusion]. If one finds that those names and those marks are ultimately unattainable, and from beginning to end there is not a single thought of discrimination, then regarding all phenomena there will be no successive discrimination;
one thus departs from unreal conceptualization, and the various consciousnesses do not arise. Even until awakening ceases, there is no external object to be awakened to. This is it.

The object is suchness (*tathatā*); that there is no internal cognizing mind within it is the mind as suchness. Because the object and the mind are one and the same suchness, it is called "suchness-as-suchness" (*tathātathatā*).
This is the ultimate reality of the dharma-nature of self-awakening, which is itself unattainable.

As realized in the tenth stage (*daśabhūmi*), if there were any self-nature to be attained, that would be a mark of difference (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*) and could not be called suchness; it must be definitively non-existent.
If even a single dharma can be apprehended, that would be the characteristic of suchness (*tathatā*).
However, I and all Buddhas, in accordance with the nature of the *tathāgatagarbha*, have realized and entered this state; we reveal and expound it for the sake of all sentient beings.

We also teach that this suchness, the reality-mark (*yathābhūtalakṣaṇa*), is precisely that which is designated by names and signs (*nāmanimitta*) for the purpose of manifestation, yet ultimately cannot be apprehended. It is the departure from names and signs, following along with them.
If one can accord with and awaken to the realm of perfect enlightenment (*samyaksambodhi*), not departing from names and signs (*nāma-nimitta*) to fall into nihilism (*uccheda*),
nor clinging to names and signs to fall into eternalism (*śāśvata*), and thus giving rise to no false conceptualizations of existence or non-existence,

but rather following the noble path of self-realization (*pratyātma-āryagati*), then the objective realm is identical to the mind, and the mind is identical to the objective realm. This is the fundamental nature.
Suchness itself is a characteristic that cannot be attained by any of the non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) or those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).

Those non-Buddhists and followers of the two vehicles do not transcend the mind, thought, and consciousness (*citta-manas-vijñāna*), and as they belong to the faction of evil views, they possess nothing but incorrect knowledge (*ayoniśo-jñāna*).

Because this is the realm of the noble ones' self-realization (*svapratyātma-ārya-gati*), where the mind and consciousness do not reach, it is not something they can attain. It is that which cannot be taken as an object of focus by any deluded conceptualization (*vikalpa*). Thus...

This wisdom of prajñā is called right knowledge; that which is not right knowledge cannot accord with suchness (tathatā), nor can it enter the realm of suchness, and thus it is not called right knowledge.

That which reaches the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-awakening is therefore called the five dharmas, the three natures (trisvabhāva), the eight consciousnesses, and the two kinds of selflessness, which interpenetrate and mutually inform one another.
All Buddha-dharmas are mutually integrated and entirely contained within it; you Bodhisattvas should personally cultivate and study this through skillful means (*upāya*).
If you lack skillful means, you will fall into the nihilistic views of external paths (*tīrthika*) or the partial emptiness of the Two Vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*).
You should also teach others this skillful means, so that they do not follow the false attachments of other external paths or the Two Vehicles. This is due to skillful means.
When right wisdom arises, one realizes suchness through that very wisdom; how could there be any failure to reach the stage of the Tathāgata?
Linji said: "O practitioners of the Way, you must earnestly seek genuine insight so that you may traverse the world freely, avoiding being deluded by these various spirits and demons.
There is nothing more precious than being at ease; yet, to merely engage in artificial contrivances is simply the ordinary."
If you intend to seek it outwardly, you have already gone astray; to seek for "Buddha" is merely to pursue names and phrases.

Do you recognize that which is rushing about in its quest? Even when the Buddhas and Patriarchs of the three periods and ten directions appeared in the world, they did so solely for the sake of seeking the Dharma.
The practitioners of the Way who study today likewise do so solely for the sake of seeking the Dharma; only upon attaining the Dharma is there completion, for until it is attained, there is no end.
Based on the aforementioned five paths of saṃsāra, what is this "Dharma"? Dharma is the mind-Dharma; the mind-Dharma is formless and pervades the ten directions.
It is manifest before one’s eyes, yet people do not believe it; they instead cling to names and cling to phrases, seeking its meaning within words and texts.
This is as far removed from the Buddha-Dharma as heaven is from earth. O practitioners of the Way, when I, this mountain monk, preach the Dharma, I speak...
What dharma is it that, when spoken of as the "Dharma of the Mind-Ground," enables one to enter the ordinary and the holy, the pure and the defiled, the true and the conventional?
It is simply not that your own true and conventional, ordinary and holy can bestow names upon all things true, conventional, ordinary, and holy;
nor can all things true, conventional, ordinary, and holy bestow names upon this person. This is called the flow of the Way.
When one can grasp it and employ it immediately without further attaching names or designations, this is called the "Mysterious Principle" (xuánzhǐ).
This is the true insight of Linji; it is precisely right wisdom that can distance itself from all conventional and sagely names and marks, reaching the stage of the Tathāgata’s self-awakening.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"The five dharmas, the three natures, the eight kinds of consciousness, and the two kinds of selflessness—these entirely encompass the Mahāyāna.
Name and appearance, the nature of false imagination, and the two kinds of characteristics; correct wisdom and suchness—these constitute the perfected nature."

The Master said: "First, the five dharmas encompass the three self-natures; the eight consciousnesses and the two kinds of non-self encompass all Buddha-dharmas, which are collectively subsumed within the Mahāyāna.
This is because the True Wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) and Suchness (*tathatā*) that are taught constitute the supreme ultimate truth (*paramārtha*).
That is to say, by transforming delusion into reality and transforming consciousness into wisdom, until the two kinds of non-self no longer arise, it is all the Great [Vehicle]."
Riding upon the Buddha-dharma is not like the two vehicles (śrāvaka and pratyekabuddha), which practice by clinging to signs and ultimately enter into the Lesser Vehicle.
Next, the verse explains how the five dharmas encompass the three natures, according to the meaning previously stated in the primary response:

namely, that names and signs are false, and to give rise to conceptualization (*saṃjñā*) regarding names and signs is even more falsely unreal; these are the two natures arising from false conceptualization (*vikalpa*).
That which exists therein is empty, false, and unreal, ultimately destined for destruction. If one possesses right wisdom and conforms to suchness (*tathatā*), all things are truly real;
because they are fundamentally unborn from the beginning, they likewise do not perish. Being devoid of destruction, they are primordially perfected.
This is the true characteristic of the perfected nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*). Only by realizing the perfected nature does one reach the state of the Tathāgata.
How could one not practice and study the stage of self-awakening with skillful means? A monk asked Chan Master Huguang Zheng, "What is the original mind?
The Master said, "The rhinoceros develops patterns on its horn from gazing at the moon; the elephant has flowers enter its tusks from being startled by thunder.
Danxia Zhen composed a verse on this: "A three-legged numinous tortoise runs along a desolate path; a single branch of auspicious grass grows wildly."
The peaks hang over Kunlun, and Mount Yu contains moisture; the cool hare conceives in her womb before the moon is known.
These two venerable masters spoke of the original mind, both using metaphors to reveal it. Danxia now extends his own hand and eye, wishing to meet Huguo face-to-face:
"A three-legged numinous tortoise running along a desolate path" refers to the deluded mind; "a single branch of auspicious grass" [growing] in disorder...
The hanging peaks are the primordial mind; the mountain contains jade and naturally moistens its own substance—this is suchness (*tathatā*).

The hare conceives in her womb yet does not yet know its function—this is suchness. Therefore, know that the emergence of patterns on the horns and the entry of blossoms into the tusks are the realm of the hare’s gestation;
they are collectively one inconceivable state, which cannot be known by those who have not personally reached the self-awakening of the Tathāgata.
Regarding the "Stages" (Bhūmi), it is ultimately difficult to speak of this.
(The Wei translation calls this the thirteenth chapter, "The Sands of the Ganges").
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has stated in the passage concerning the past..."
"The Buddhas of the future and present are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges; likewise for those of the past.
How is it, World-Honored One, that you accept this as it is literally stated, or is there another meaning? We only pray that the Tathāgata will compassionately explain this.

The Buddha told Mahāmati: "Do not accept it as it is literally stated. The measure of the Buddhas of the three periods of time is not like the sands of the Ganges. Why is this? Because they transcend the world."
The intervening observation is not a true analogy for what it intends to illustrate; for ordinary, ignorant people and non-Buddhists (the "Tang" translation reads:
"I [say] that the minds of ordinary, ignorant people and various non-Buddhists constantly cling to permanence and impermanence"), nourish evil views, and undergo an endless cycle of birth and death.

Desiring to cause them to weary of and detach from the wheel of birth and death so that they may apply themselves with diligence toward supreme progress, I speak for their sake, saying: "The Buddhas are easy to see; they are not like the *udumbara* flower, which is difficult to encounter."
Because they have attained the vision [of the Buddha], their expedient efforts to seek him cease for a time. Furthermore, when observing those beings to be converted, he speaks thus:
"A Buddha is difficult to encounter, like the udumbara flower. The udumbara flower has never been seen before, is not being seen now, and will not be seen in the future;
yet those who see the Tathāgata see him throughout the world. It is not because he establishes his own realization that he says the Tathāgata appears in the world."
The udumbara flower (translated here as "Auspicious Response Lotus") is something established and understood by Great Wisdom itself;
it transcends worldly expectations and cannot be believed by those ordinary and ignorant people. It is the realm of the noble wisdom of self-realization, for which no analogy can be found.
The true Tathāgata transcends the characteristics perceived by mind, thought, and consciousness, and thus cannot be illustrated by any comparison.
Tong said: "Previously, the five dharmas were used to subsume all phenomena and bring them back to suchness; this suchness is the realm of the Dharma-body (*dharmakāya*).

Because the Dharma-bodies of the Buddhas of the three periods of time are eternally abiding, Mahāmati, wishing to clarify the equality of the Dharma-realm and true suchness (*tathatā*), raised the point that the World-Honored One has often said that the Buddhas of the three periods of time are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and one should regard them as such."
"Is it to be accepted exactly as the Buddha has spoken, or is there another meaning? The Buddha said: 'Do not accept it merely according to the words.
The mind-measure (*cittamātra*) of the Buddhas of the three periods transcends all things and is without equal;
it is not merely like the sands of the Ganges River. Because it transcends the world, it is not of the world; it is to be gazed upon with reverence.'"
How could that which is reached be illustrated by worldly, visible analogies? Therefore, the Sūtra says:
"Among all phenomena within the three realms, whether existent or non-existent, none can serve as an analogy for the Buddha.

Yet, when I speak in this manner, it is for those foolish commoners and non-Buddhists who cling to permanence or impermanence, nourishing evil views and wandering through the cycle of birth and death.

Because those in the intermediate state cannot perceive the realm of True Suchness (*tathatā*), and because I wish to cause them to become weary of birth and death and to give rise to supreme aspiration,
I say that the Buddhas are easy to see and easy to encounter, as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, and not as difficult to see as the *udumbara* flower.
If I were to say that the Buddhas are difficult to encounter, like the *udumbara* flower, they would surely regress.
If one is timid and fails to apply diligent effort, the cessation of that expedient mind seeking the Dharma is not the means to induce progress.
Therefore, I have said that those whose faculties are mature and capable of being transformed are as rare as the sands of the Ganges;

yet at other times, I have also said that a Buddha is difficult to encounter, like the *udumbara* flower, so as to inspire a thirsting longing and cause them to seek with all their might and diligence.
This is also a teaching of skillful means and is not the ultimate reality. The udumbara flower has never been seen in the past, is not seen now, and will not be seen in the future;
yet when a Tathāgata appears in the world, he knows all and sees all—how could he be compared to the udumbara flower?
It is merely said that his appearance is as difficult to encounter as the udumbara flower; it is not spoken of by way of the Tathāgata’s own established realization.
Like the udumbara flower, those who establish and realize the Dharma for themselves dwell in the realm of the Dharma-body of internally realized noble wisdom (*pratyātma-āryajñāna*).
This is peerless in the world; none can look up to it and reach its height, for it is beyond the capacity of ordinary, ignorant people to believe or understand.
Thus, the realm of self-realized noble wisdom transcends all metaphors. Why is this? Because of what exists in the world... [text continues]
That which can be seen is known merely through the conjectures of mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).

Since the Tathāgata has transformed consciousness into wisdom (*jñāna*) and is already far removed from the sphere of mind, thought, and consciousness, how could one use the appearances perceived by worldly mind, thought, and consciousness as a metaphor?
Mind, thought, and consciousness are all unreal, whereas the Tathāgata has realized [the truth].
The state [of reality] is most truly real; since the provisional cannot possibly serve as a metaphor for the real, it is said:

"The measure of the Buddhas of the three periods of time is not like the sands of the Ganges; nothing is more fitting than what is received through teaching. The Third Patriarch’s *Inscription on Faith* says:

"Perfectly identical to the great void, there is neither deficiency nor excess; it is precisely because of grasping and rejecting that one does not accord with Suchness. Thus spoke the Third Patriarch.

It has never been that these cannot serve as metaphors; it is simply that one must not engage in acceptance or rejection. If there were no acceptance or rejection, even the metaphor could not be obtained.
A monk asked Chan Master Zhimen Zu: "What is it like when the lotus flower has not yet emerged from the water?
Zu said, "The lotus flower. The monk asked, "What is it like after it has emerged? Zu said, "The lotus leaf. Tiantong [Zhixian] took up this case:

It is said that the numinous tortoise has no divination marks; its empty shell does not require drilling. Furthermore, a monk asked Chan Master Jingzhong, "What is it like before the lotus has emerged from the water?
Jingzhong replied, "The *han-dan* flowers cover the ground and flow. The monk asked, "What is it like after it has emerged?
Jingzhong replied, "When the leaves fall, one does not know it is autumn. Tongnian commented: "Li Ling held the Han flagstaff."
"Pan Lang riding his donkey backward—this too is one lotus. Even when engaging in extensive discourse with many metaphors, they never fail to correspond with the point of self-realization.
Mahāmati, there is no fault in my using analogies; Mahāmati, it is like the Ganges River.
Just as all fish, turtles, *śuśumāra* (translated as "killing-son fish"), lions, elephants, horses, humans, and beasts may trample upon the sand, yet the sand does not think,
"They are disturbing me," nor does it give rise to false conceptualization; its intrinsic nature is pure and free from all defilements—
so too is the Great River of the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksaṃbuddha, who possesses the self-realized noble wisdom, great power, and mastery of supernormal faculties.
All those who cause disturbance—whether non-Buddhists, humans, or animals—the Tathāgata does not give rise to conceptual thoughts regarding them;

the Tathāgata is tranquil and free from thought and perception. Because the Tathāgata’s original vow is to establish sentient beings in the bliss of samādhi, there is no disturbance whatsoever, remaining as undifferentiated as the sands of the Ganges. Furthermore, this is because he has severed both greed and anger.

The interlocutor said: "If the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is beyond all analogy, why does the Buddha frequently employ analogies—such as saying that the Buddhas of the three periods of time are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges?
There is no fault of self-contradiction here, because there is a distinct meaning [intended].
As for the seven kinds of distinct meanings cited in the following text, first, regarding the Dharma-body as being free from thought: those sands of the Ganges..."

Even if all the fish, turtles, oxen, sheep, elephants, horses, and *śiśumāra* (son-killer) fish in the sands of the Ganges were to trample upon it, it would not give rise to discrimination, nor anger, nor resentment, nor would it even conceive the thought, "They are disturbing me.
Because it is free from false conceptualization and discrimination, it is eternally pure and stainless; the Buddhas and Tathāgatas are likewise so within their own bodies.
Having realized the pure, signless noble wisdom of self-awakening that cannot be traversed by others—
just like the Ganges— it fulfills all powers, supernormal faculties, and sovereign merits, manifesting as numerous as the sands of the Ganges.
Because its power is so great, it can overcome all afflictions, disturbances, and the delusions of all celestial Māras, heterodox teachers, and ignorant beings, who are like fish and turtles.
When the Tathāgata is troubled by a mind of anger and hatred, he remains unmoved and does not give rise to even a single thought of discrimination;

rather, he gathers them in through the samādhi of loving-kindness and compassion. Although he manifests supernatural powers to subdue all Māras, he is always inherently tranquil and free from conceptualization.
This is because the original vow of the Tathāgata desires that all sentient beings enter into nirvāṇa without remainder.
They enter parinirvāṇa through the bliss of samādhi and right reception, establishing sentient beings in peace and security so that they may be fulfilled.

They do not engage in conceptual discrimination, yet they transcend all such discrimination; free from all afflictions and disturbances, they are like the sands of the Ganges, without love or hatred and without distinction.
I say that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, for by their original vows they are universally [present].
Regarding the phrase "settling sentient beings as equal to those as numerous as the sands of the Ganges":

this means they are equal and without marks of difference, having already abandoned attachment to the self and being free from greed and anger. Since greed and anger have been severed, from what could discrimination arise?
Thus, it is said that the Buddhas are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges because they are free from discrimination; this is the first reason why they are without fault.
Huangbo said: "The practitioners of the Way today do not seek awakening within their own minds, but instead fixate on external appearances and grasp at objects;
all such actions turn their backs on the Way. As for the sands of the Ganges, the Buddha said they are merely sand.
When Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, Śakra, Brahmā, and the various devas walk over them, the sands feel no joy; yet when cattle, sheep, insects, and ants trample over them, the sands feel no resentment."
The sand does not resent precious jewels or fragrant scents; the sand does not crave excrement, urine, or foul stench; the sand does not loathe them.
This mind is precisely the mind that is no-mind, free from all marks. There is no further distinction between sentient beings and Buddhas:
simply being able to be without-mind is the ultimate state of a practitioner of the Way. If one does not directly and immediately become without-mind, one will continue to accumulate afflictions.

Even if one practices for kalpas, the Way will not be attained; Huangbo also used the sands of the Ganges to clarify the upward path, which in its entirety does not conflict with the realm of self-awakened noble wisdom.

For example, Mahāmati, the sands of the Ganges are the intrinsic nature of earth; when the kalpa ends and all earth is consumed by fire, that element of earth does not abandon its own nature because it arises simultaneously with the element of fire.
Although other foolish people perceive the thought that "the earth is burning," the earth itself is not burned, for fire is its cause.
In this same way, Mahāmati, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is indestructible like the sands of the Ganges.
Tong said: "The previous statement that 'the self-nature is pure and free from affliction, and even if afflicted, it suffers no loss' was spoken in terms of the indestructibility of the *dharmakāya*.
Those grains of sand in the Ganges have form and resistance; they are the very nature of the earth.
When the kalpas are about to end and the three calamities arise in succession, the great earth is consumed by fire, yet those sands are not lost."
Because its intrinsic nature arises simultaneously with sand and fire, the deluded think that the earth is being burned, yet the earth is not actually burned;
for the earth takes fire as its cause and fire can produce soil, such that earth and fire arise together.
The *dharmakāya* of the Tathāgata is also like this: the deluded will claim that the *dharmakāya* is destroyed when the fire of afflictions burns it, but it is not.
To know that afflictions (*kleśa*) are themselves awakening (*bodhi*)—for without afflictions there would be no way to manifest awakening—is because afflictions and awakening are non-dual in nature;
therefore, the *dharmakāya* is indestructible, just as the sands of the Ganges are indestructible.
A monk asked Daguī: "When the kalpa-fire blazes forth and the great trichiliocosm is utterly destroyed, I wonder: will this [the dharmakāya] be destroyed or not?"

Suí said, "To destroy the Sangha. Yunmen said, "If that is so, then follow him. Suí said, "I follow him. Following the dialogue, he said: "Standing amidst the fires at the end of an eon, one poses a question; even a monk still lingers within two layers of barriers.
How pitiable—a single phrase follows another’s words, as one travels alone across ten thousand miles. Tiantong added to Master Xiu’s dialogue and composed this verse:
"Whether it is destroyed or not, let him go his way. Within the phrase of the great chiliocosm, there is no hook or lock."
The feet of the pivot are mostly obstructed by entanglements; will you not clearly discern this matter?
I have carefully laid bare my heart and brought it forth—do not deliberate! I am superior in the practice of the marketplace;
for the sake of the Great Thousandfold World, a single word serves as both a hammer and a chisel upon this very passage of the sutra.
Mahāmati, just as the sands of the Ganges are without limit, so too is the radiance of the Tathāgata without limit;
for the sake of bringing sentient beings to maturity, it universally illumines all the assemblies of Buddhas.
The Master said: "The Dharma-body is the indestructible essence of True Suchness (*tathatā*). Since there is this essence, there must necessarily be its function;
therefore, it is described in terms of immeasurable radiance. Just as those sands of the Ganges cannot be limited by number or measured by quantity, the radiance of the Tathāgata is likewise so.
The *Awakening of Faith* says: 'That which is called the self-substance exists...'"
Because it is the meaning of the radiance of great wisdom, because it is the meaning of universally illuminating the Dharma-realm,
and for the sake of maturing sentient beings, he uses the radiance of wisdom to universally illuminate the Buddha-lands as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
wherever there are sentient beings whose faculties are about to ripen, he necessarily manifests his body to preach the Dharma for them— a world of infinite radiance.
It is also limitless. Changsha Cen ascended the hall and said: "If I were to exclusively exalt the teachings and the lineage, the weeds in the Dharma Hall would surely grow ten feet deep.
Since that is unavoidable, I shall speak to you all: the entire ten directions of the world are the eyes of the śramaṇa;
the entire ten directions of the world are the whole body of the śramaṇa; the entire ten directions of the world..."
The realms are one's own radiance; the worlds of the ten directions are entirely within this radiance.
Within these worlds of the ten directions, there is not a single person who is not oneself. I have always told you all:
the Buddhas of the three periods of time, the Dharma-realm, and all sentient beings are the light of Mahāprajñā. Before this light has yet been emitted, you all—
Where does a person turn for full understanding? Even before the light has been emitted, there is no news of Buddhas or sentient beings;
from where could mountains, rivers, and lands have come? At that time, a monk asked, "What is the eye of a śramaṇa?

Ceng said, "It is so long that it cannot be brought out. He also said, "Whether one becomes a Buddha or an ancestor, it cannot be brought out; even in the cycle of the six realms of rebirth, it cannot be brought out."
Chushi could not leave. The Master said, "I do not understand what it is that you cannot leave. Chushi said, "By day I see the sun; by night I see the stars.
The Master said, "The student does not understand. Chushi said, "The colors of Mount Miaogao are green and yet green.
This passage of the scripture was further elucidated by Changsha, making its meaning even more clear.
Mahāmati, it is just as when one seeks a sand grain distinct from the sands of the Ganges, it can never be found;
likewise, Mahāmati, for the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, there is no birth or death, nor arising and ceasing, because the causes and conditions [for such] have been severed.

Tong said: "The previous statement regarding the maturation of sentient beings implies that if sentient beings have not yet matured, they still possess the birth-and-death of segmented existence (*paricchinna-jāti-maraṇa*) and the birth-and-death of transformation (*pariṇāma-utpāda-nirodha*), because they have not yet severed the causes and conditions of the three realms of existence (*tri-bhava*). The Tathāgata is not like this;
he is like the sands of the Ganges, which no longer give rise to the characteristic of birth. As for those fine motes of dust, such is the essential nature and characteristic of a mote of dust."

Just as the sands of the Ganges abide in their own nature without alteration or change, never becoming other things or seeking different sands—which can never be found—so too it is with the Tathāgata, the Samyaksaṃbuddha.
He transforms the basis of arising and ceasing into non-arising and non-ceasing;

there is no longer the two kinds of birth-and-death characterized by segmentation and transformation, because he has forever severed the causes of birth-and-death within the three realms of existence.
Within the nature of *tathatā*, coming and going, delusion and awakening, and birth and death cannot be found; it is just as the sands of the Ganges are no different from the sands themselves.
While Jia Shan and Ding Shan were traveling together and conversing, Ding Shan said, "If there is no Buddha within birth and death, then there is no birth and death.
Jia Shan said, "If there is a Buddha within birth and death, then [it is not so]."
Deluded regarding birth and death, the two refused to agree on who would go up [the mountain] together. Da Mei and Jia Shan then raised the question:
"I wonder, between the two of you, whose realization is more intimate? Da Mei said, "One is intimate; the other is distant.
Jia Shan asked again, "Which one is intimate? Da Mei said, "Go for now and come back tomorrow. The next day, Jia Shan went up again and asked Da Mei, "The one who is intimate—"
The questioner was not questioned; after staying at Jia Shan, he himself said, "At that time, I lost one eye," thereby attaining realization through this.
One should know that once ore has become gold, the gold does not revert to ore.
Mahāmati, it is like the sands of the Ganges, whose increase or decrease cannot be perceived.

In the same way, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata’s wisdom matures sentient beings without increasing or decreasing, because it is not a physical phenomenon (*kāyadharma*). Physical phenomena are subject to destruction; the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is not a physical phenomenon.

(The Tang translation states: "For example, it is like the sands of the Ganges: one cannot know them to diminish when taken away, nor see them increase when added. The Buddhas are also like this; through the wisdom of skillful means, they mature sentient beings without decrease and without increase.")
Why is this? Because the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body has no body. [The interlocutor] replied:
"It was stated above that the Tathāgata’s wisdom-light matures sentient beings, ultimately returning to the state of non-arising and non-ceasing by severing the causes and conditions of existence;
yet those causes and conditions of existence inherently possess destruction. However, the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body—"
Why is it not destroyed? It is like the sands of the Ganges: when taken out from the river, one does not see them diminish;
when cast back into the river, one does not see them increase. Nor does the thought arise, "I am entering or exiting the river," because its own substance is immeasurable.
The wisdom of the Tathāgata is also like this; that is, all sentient beings of the ten directions [are likewise].

When one takes up the wisdom of the Tathāgata, the Tathāgata does not diminish; yet all sentient beings of the ten directions have already been brought to maturity, and their Buddha-wisdom is non-dual with his, so the Tathāgata does not increase.
Because the Dharmakāya is signless and not like the physical body which has form, that which has form as its nature can increase or diminish and ultimately undergoes destruction.
The Dharma-body of the Tathāgata is not a physical body; it is devoid of anything that can be increased or diminished, so how could there be any decay?
Lingyun ascended the hall and said: "O worthy ones, all things—whether long or short—are entirely impermanent. Observe the four seasons: the leaves fall and the flowers bloom.
How much more so for the heavens, humans, and the seven realms of existence, as well as earth, water, fire, and wind, throughout kalpas as numerous as dust motes!"

The cycle of formation and destruction and the causes and effects of transmigration are nearing their end; the suffering of the three evil realms does not increase or decrease by so much as a hair’s breadth.

Only the fundamental consciousness remains eternally present. Those of superior capacity who encounter virtuous friends and gain clear understanding will attain liberation on the spot—this is the site of enlightenment (the *bodhimaṇḍa*).
Those of inferior or middling capacity, being dull-witted and ignorant, fail to achieve awakening or illumination; they remain mired in the triple world, wandering through birth and death.
The Buddha Śākyamuni established the teachings for the sake of this heaven and human realm, manifesting and revealing the ultimate Way.
Do you understand? A monk asked: "How can one escape birth, old age, sickness, and death? Yun said: "The green mountains have never moved;
floating clouds come and go as they please. If you can clearly realize the point where Lingyun saw it, not only will the wisdom of the Tathāgata be attained.
Without increase or decrease, the wisdom of sentient beings likewise neither increases nor decreases.

Just as one cannot obtain oil by pressing the sands of the Ganges, even so, although all these sentient beings who are oppressed by extreme suffering press upon the Tathāgata, he does not abandon the Dharma-realm until those sentient beings have attained nirvāṇa; rather, through his own samādhi and vows, he delights in great compassion.
Therefore, [the Wei version says: "The Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, though oppressed by the suffering and afflictions of all sentient beings, cannot find any anger in them"]. The commentary states:
Not only is there no increase or decrease in the number of sentient beings—whether mature or immature—who are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges;
it is also like a person who, wishing to obtain ghee or oil, might press the sands of the Ganges, yet in the end could never obtain any ghee.
Because sentient beings are in the midst of extreme suffering, the Tathāgata, through the power of skillful means, causes them to attain liberation.
Yet, when these sentient beings undergo great anguish and are oppressed by it, the Tathāgata—even until he attains nirvāṇa—should not harbor any resentment;
for the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have long since departed from anger, and anger is ultimately unfindable in them.
Because he does not abandon the vast and boundless characteristics of the *dharmadhātu* due to the bliss of his own *samādhi*,

and because he is sustained by the power of his vow to deliver all sentient beings through that very bliss of his own *samādhi*, having attained the perfection of great loving-kindness and great compassion,
[he thinks]: "If I do not cause all sentient beings to enter *nirvāṇa*, my own body shall likewise not enter [it]."
Because Nirvāṇa does not abandon its original vow to grant happiness to sentient beings, anger cannot be found within samādhi;
it would be like pressing sand to seek oil—it can never be obtained. The Sixth Patriarch said: "If you wish to transform others, you must first possess skillful means;
do not cause them to have doubts, for this is the manifestation of one's own nature. Thus, the Buddha-dharma exists within the world.
Transcending worldly awakening and transcending worldly awakening to bodhi is just like seeking the horns of a rabbit.
What is called right view is termed supramundane, and what is called wrong view is termed mundane. When both right and wrong are completely struck away, the nature of bodhi is manifest as it is.
This is why the True Dharma uproots the extreme suffering of sentient beings; this is why the True Dharma is also struck away, so that one may transcend and enter nirvana. This is of itself...
Awakening oneself and awakening others without encountering resistance means being free from anger and resentment.
Mahāmati, it is like the sands of the Ganges which flow along with the water and do not exist apart from the water;
in the same way, Mahāmati, all dharmas spoken by the Tathāgata flow toward nirvāṇa. Therefore, it is said that they are like the sands of the Ganges. The Tathāgata...
Because "going" has the sense of destruction, it does not follow the flow of various goings; Mahāmati, the original limit of birth and death is unknowable.
Since it is unknowable, how can one speak of "going"? Mahāmati, "going" means cessation, yet the foolish do not understand this.
Tong said: "The Tathāgata’s preaching of the Dharma is like the sands of the Ganges flowing with the water; they never flow against the current. That which causes them to circulate is the water;
for without the water, the sand could not flow of its own accord. Thus, it is not that the water is absent.
Although the Buddhas and Tathāgatas preach the Dharma for sentient beings, though they expound all dharmas, they truly accord with Nirvāṇa."
Just as sand must depend upon water to emerge [from it], and nirvāṇa is like water that does not depart from the sand, so too can it cause all phenomena (*dharma*) to flow through;
yet in reality, it does not follow along with the transmigrations of the various realms (*gati*).

While the various realms involve coming and going—which is the meaning of arising and ceasing—nirvāṇa is the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) of birth and death, free from arising and ceasing, and thus cannot be [subject to] them.
If one uses a knowledge and vision characterized by arising and ceasing to know and perceive, one is incapable of even describing "going";

therefore, the Tathāgata’s teaching follows the flow of *nirvāṇa*. It is not that there is no *nirvāṇa*, for although he abides within the dharmas of arising and ceasing, in reality there is no arising or ceasing.
Just as the Ganges sands follow the water yet the water is not absent, so too the great ocean of *Mahāparinirvāṇa* is the Tathāgata’s wondrous awakening.
The various Bodhisattvas of the realms enter with the current in order to return to the source; the Tathāgata emerges against the current in order to deliver sentient beings.
Although there is entering and emerging, in reality there is neither birth nor extinction.

If one follows the flow through the various realms of existence, one enters into "being" and becomes an ordinary person, certainly not free from birth and extinction. If one enters into "non-being," [one likewise...]
The nirvāṇa spoken of by the non-Buddhists and the followers of the Two Vehicles is not merely devoid of sand; it is also devoid of water, which signifies the meaning of annihilation.
Yet, foolish people stubbornly fail to know or realize that the fundamental limit of birth and death is in truth neither born nor extinguished.
All of the above uses the analogy of the sands of the Ganges, each with its own specific significance; in sum, there is no error in this.
This was a mistake. Once, when Changsha Cen returned from a mountain excursion, he arrived at the gate. The Head Seat asked, "Where have you been, Master?
Changsha said, "I have been on a mountain excursion. The Head Seat asked, "Where did you go?
Changsha said, "At first I followed the fragrant grasses, then I pursued the falling blossoms. The Head Seat said, "That is very much like the spirit of spring. Changsha said, "It is indeed so."
In "The Autumn Dew Dropping on the Lotus," Xuedou provides a comment and a verse in response, saying:
"The great earth is utterly free of even a speck of dust; Who is there whose eyes do not begin to see? First following the fragrant grasses away, Then chasing the falling flowers back.

A weary crane perches on a cold tree; Mad monkeys howl atop the ancient terrace. How boundless is the meaning of Changsha! *Du!* (A shout of realization! These various venerable masters follow [the path]."
"The flow of *nirvāṇa* is truly unfathomable.
Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "World-Honored One, if the original limit of birth and death for sentient beings cannot be known, how can liberation be known?
The Buddha told Mahāmati, "It is through the cessation of the causes of beginningless false delusion, faults, and the habitual tendencies of conceptual construction (*vikalpa-vāsanā*)."
