Knowing that external objects are manifestations of one's own mind, the transformation of the body of false conceptualization is liberation—not its destruction. (The Tang translation states: "To fully know that external realms are manifestations of one's own mind, and that the transformation of discrimination is called liberation, not annihilation.
Therefore, the infinite is not a state of total non-existence; it serves as a synonym for the "infinite" and other such terms used for that false conceptualization.
By examining the internal and external, one becomes free from false conceptualization; there is no difference between sentient beings, wisdom, and *jñeya* (the knowable).

All phenomena are entirely quiescent (the Tang translation says: "free from discriminative thought, there are no separate sentient beings"; by observing with wisdom that all internal and external phenomena, as well as the knower and the known, are entirely extinguished).
Because one does not recognize that they are the false imaginings manifested by one's own mind, false imaginings arise; if one recognizes them, they are extinguished.

Mahāmati asked: "Since the Blessed One has taught that the original limit of birth and death is unknowable, and since it is unknowable, how is it that the Tathāgata attains liberation and causes sentient beings to attain liberation?
Furthermore, can one who attains liberation within the midst of birth and death be known? If it is unknown, what is this so-called 'liberation' that is distinct from [birth and death]?"
All conceptual proliferations (*prapañca*) and afflictions arise from the discriminating mind conditioned by beginningless habituation;

yet, that which is extinguished within due to the cause of beginningless false habitual tendencies is simply the realization of one's own mind as it truly is—that all external phenomena are manifestations of mind alone.
Thus, the discriminating mind that gives rise to the appearance of external objects is nothing other than delusion.
To follow along with delusion and transmigrate is not liberation. When one thoroughly understands the cause of that delusion, the basis of discrimination is overturned;

by overturning the basis of arising and ceasing, one relies upon the non-arising and non-ceasing, which is called liberation. While delusive thoughts may be extinguished, that which knows the delusions is not extinguished;
therefore, liberation is truly not extinguished. Why is it that this cannot be known? Because as long as one has not attained liberation, one remains [in bondage].

Because one is bound by birth and death, there is a limit that can be measured; once liberation is attained and one distances oneself from the realm of birth and death, this is the reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*) of nirvāṇa. It is immeasurable and boundless, difficult to fathom.

Therefore, when it is said that the "original limit" (*pūrvakoṭi*) is boundless and unknowable, this does not mean that everything is utterly non-existent or subject to total annihilation. This is because...
That which cannot be reached by deluded conceptualization is merely designated by such diverse names as "the boundless" and so forth; though the names differ, the substance does not.

Nirvāṇa is precisely the original limit of the birth and death of sentient beings; liberation is precisely sentient beings' clear comprehension of their own minds and their departure from the discriminating mind.
Beyond this, there are no further sentient beings; it is precisely this discrimination that is called [sentient beings].

If sentient beings can observe all internal and external phenomena with wisdom, becoming free from deluded thoughts and non-conceptualizing mind, this non-conceptualization is itself *tathatā* (suchness).
It is not that there exists a separate *tathatā* apart from the deluded thoughts of sentient beings;
fundamentally, it is no different from sentient beings, being non-dual and without distinction. Therefore, this *tathatā* is the primordial limit (*pūrvakoṭi*).
Sentient beings are likewise this suchness (*tathatā*). Because all are thus, both the knower and the known are entirely quiescent.
Having attained this quiescence, there is internally no mind that knows and externally no object that is known; therefore, it is said that the primordial limit (*koṭi*) is unknowable.
It is only because one fails to recognize what is manifested by one’s own mind that one falsely imagines that there are phenomena existing outside of the mind.
Because of discrimination, false conceptualization arises; when false conceptualization arises, one becomes deluded regarding the primordial limit and wanders through birth and death.

If one realizes that all is but mind, then false conceptualization is instantly extinguished. Once false conceptualization is extinguished, all internal and external phenomena are entirely quiescent and extinguished.
This quiescent extinction is itself nirvana. By this, one knows that nirvana and liberation are not [something external].
Regarding the dharma of cessation, Huangbo said: "The Buddhas and all sentient beings are nothing but this one mind; there is no other dharma.
This mind, from time immemorial, has never been born and never ceased. It is neither blue nor yellow, formless and signless.
It does not belong to existence or non-existence; it is reckoned neither new nor old, neither long nor short, neither large nor small."
Transcending all measures, names, words, traces, and oppositions, the very substance [of reality] is such that to stir a thought is to deviate from it.
It is like empty space, without boundaries and immeasurable; this one mind alone is Buddha.
There is no difference whatsoever between Buddha and sentient beings; it is only because sentient beings cling to appearances and seek outwardly that they fail to find it.
If one loses this mind and seeks the Buddha, attempting to grasp the mind with the mind throughout kalpas and for the rest of one’s life, one will ultimately never find it.
One does not know how to still the thoughts or forget discursive虑 (considerations), yet the Buddha manifests before one spontaneously. This very mind is the Buddha, and the Buddha is sentient beings.
When one is a sentient being, this mind does not diminish; when one is a Buddha, this mind does not increase. Thus it continues through the six [realms].
The myriad practices and the sands of the Ganges of merit are inherently complete from the beginning; they require no cultivation or addition.

When conditions arise, they are manifested; when conditions cease, they are quiescent. If one does not resolutely believe that this is Buddha and instead seeks to cultivate with attachment to forms in order to achieve spiritual efficacy, all such efforts are mere delusions that run counter to the Way. Huangbo’s words here truly accord with this sutra.
The profound, subtle, and wondrous meaning.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this significance, spoke in verse:
"Observe all the Teachers, who are like the sands of the Ganges River: they are neither destroyed, nor do they depart, nor are they ultimately finite."

This is the equal observation of all Tathāgatas as being like the sands of the Ganges—completely free from all faults, flowing along with the stream yet eternally constant in nature; this is the perfect awakening of the Buddha.
The Master said: "This verse synthesizes the seven preceding metaphors: like the sands of the Ganges, it cannot be destroyed by fire;
like the sands of the Ganges, it flows along with the current yet does not go away. Ultimate liberation does not reach annihilation.
This is the equal Dharma-body, which neither comes nor goes, neither arises nor ceases. To observe in this manner is called 'seeing all.'"
The True Reality of the Guide is as follows: it is like the sands of the Ganges in its lack of thought, being free from the fault of attachment and aversion;

it is like the sands of the Ganges in its lack of differentiation, being free from the fault of causes and conditions; it is like the sands of the Ganges in its lack of oiliness, being free from the fault of the affliction of suffering.

Its radiance shines universally, and while it expounds the Dharma according to the flow [of beings], its self-nature remains eternally constant. This is the Tathāgata’s perfect enlightenment, which does not follow the cycle of transmigration.
If one observes in this manner, it is called seeing the true substance of all Tathāgatas.

For example, although the sands of the Ganges have various distinct meanings, how could it be said that because they are as numerous as the sands of the Ganges, they are sufficient to match the immeasurable wisdom of the Tathāgata? Huangbo said: "This Dharma is equal; there is no high or low."

What is called Bodhi is precisely this original source, the pure mind, which—along with sentient beings, the Buddhas, the worlds, mountains, and rivers, whether with form or without form—is omnipresent throughout the ten directions, entirely equal and devoid of the marks of "self" and "other.

This original source, the pure mind, is eternally self-perfected, luminous, and universally illuminating; yet worldly people do not realize it, recognizing instead only seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing.
Because one is obscured by mind and by seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing, one does not perceive the essence of brilliant clarity;
yet, if one simply lets go of the mind directly, the essence manifests of itself, like the great sun rising in the void, illuminating the ten directions without further obstruction.
Therefore, those who study the Way should recognize that the activities of seeing, hearing, sensing, knowing, and purposeful action are empty.
Yet, when you turn back to see, hear, perceive, and know, the path of the mind is cut off and there is no place of entry;

simply recognize the original mind within the very state of seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing. However, the original mind does not belong to seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing, nor is it separate from them.
Just do not give rise to views or interpretations regarding seeing, hearing, perceiving, and knowing, and do not stir within them.
Do not depart from mindfulness, nor seek the mind apart from seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing; do not abandon seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing to grasp at dharmas.

Neither identical with nor separate from them, neither dwelling in nor clinging to them—moving freely and at ease in all directions, there is nowhere that is not the site of enlightenment (*bodhimaṇḍa*).
Huangbo’s exposition on the locus of equal and perfect awakening is extremely clear and complete; this verse observes the very essence of the Tathāgata.
This is the meaning.
(The Wei translation designates this as Chapter Fourteen, "The Momentary").
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, I pray that you will explain for me all dharmas."

“World-Honored One, regarding the characteristic of momentary destruction, how is it that all dharmas are momentary? The Buddha told Mahāmati, “Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon this;
I shall explain it for you. The Buddha told Mahāmati, “All dharmas refer to the wholesome, the unwholesome, the indeterminate;
the conditioned and the unconditioned; the mundane and the supramundane; the blameworthy and the blameless; and the out-flowing and the non-out-flowing.”

Mahāmati, in brief, the mind (citta), the intellect (manas), and the consciousness (vijñāna), along with their habitual tendencies (vāsanā), are the cause of the five aggregates of clinging (pañca-upādāna-skandha).
These are nourished by the habitual tendencies of the mind, intellect, and consciousness. Mahāmati, the deluded and ignorant [regard] wholesome and unwholesome conceptualizations as such;
however, the bliss of meditative cultivation, the correct reception of samādhi, and dwelling in the happiness of the present life are what is truly called [liberation].

Regarding what is called "the wise, the noble, the wholesome, the outflow-free, and great wisdom," as well as "the wholesome and unwholesome": this refers to the eight consciousnesses. What are the eight?
They are the Tathāgatagarbha, which is named the Ālayavijñāna; the Manas, the Manovijñāna, and the five bodies of sensory consciousness (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*).

Mahāmati, these five bodies of sensory consciousness, together with the Manas, the Manovijñāna, and the [other] consciousnesses, all possess the characteristics of being wholesome or unwholesome, and they undergo transformation, disintegration, and continuous succession.

The stream flows without interruption; the body arises, and as it arises, it also ceases (the Tang translation says: "there is no distinct substance; having arisen, it immediately ceases"). Not realizing that what appears is one's own mind, there is the successive cessation [of one consciousness] and the arising of another consciousness.
The various distinctions of forms and characteristics are grasped as the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) arises in conjunction with the five sense-consciousnesses.

At the moment of arising, it does not abide for even an instant—this is called a *kṣaṇa* (the Tang translation says: "not understanding that objects are the manifestations of one's own mind, at the time of successive cessation, other consciousnesses arise; the mental consciousness and those five consciousnesses...").
"Taking together various distinct forms and characteristics that do not abide for even a moment—these I call 'momentary phenomena' (kṣaṇadharma).
Mahāmati replied: "World-Honored One, according to the Buddha’s words, the Dharmakāya of the Tathāgata is like the sands of the Ganges—indestructible.
That which is indestructible is without arising or ceasing. Yet the Tathāgata constantly says that all dharmas possess the characteristic of momentary destruction. This must surely be so."
“What are those phenomena that do not abide for even a single moment or instant, but instead revert to arising and ceasing? The Buddha said:
“All phenomena are none other than the mundane and supramundane, the dharmas of ordinary beings and sages.
Taking the three natures—wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate—as conditions, they are conditioned, culpable, and out-flowing; these unwholesome dharmas are termed ‘the mundane.’”
The intermediate state of non-action, which is without fault and without outflows, is a wholesome dharma; this is precisely what is called "transcending the world.

That which is "received" refers to internal dharmas, namely *nirvāṇa*, for it is that which is fully embraced. That which is "not received" refers to external dharmas, as its fundamental principle is the non-acceptance of all things.
These are subsumed under the indeterminate (*avyākṛta*). To state the essential point: they do not go beyond the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), and the five aggregates are based upon the mind.

The meaning of the *skandhas* (aggregates) is that they are accumulated through the various habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the mind and mental consciousness acting as causes for their growth, thereby covering one’s own nature.
When the habitual tendencies are heavy, the covering is deep; when the habitual tendencies are light, the covering is shallow.
As they gradually accumulate and increase, there is the sense of being nurtured and sustained. Ordinary fools are unable to penetrate these aggregates.
Upon emerging [from samādhi], one discriminates between wholesome and unwholesome dharmas within the perfuming of the mind, thought, and consciousness;

to act in accordance with this is to be an ordinary person (*pṛthagjana*), and to give rise to views in accordance with this is to be a non-Buddhist (*tīrthika*). If, moment by moment, one does not abide [in such states], yet remains within the outflows (*āsrava*), one is neither a noble (*ārya*) nor a sage (*ṛṣi*).

However, if the three stages of worthiness (*tri-śaikṣa*) and the ten stages of sainthood (*daśa-ārya*) eliminate the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*) and cultivate the bliss of samādhi, [one attains liberation].
When false conceptualizations are extinguished, one attains samādhi and the meditative absorption of cessation (nirodha-samāpatti).

Within this state, one exercises mastery over experience and takes the realization of the Dharma as joy, abiding in happiness in the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukhavihāra*). This dwelling in happiness does not involve moment-to-moment flux;

it is called a wholesome, untainted (*anāsrava*) dharma. It is not realized by those who are not noble sages (*ārya*), and being unobscured by the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*), one is able to emerge from it.

The world is precisely what is called the noble and the sagely; it is these five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*). If one cultivates them well, they become good; if one does not cultivate them well, they become not-good.
As for what is said regarding their being nourished by the habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*), what are the details thereof?
Those two dharmas—good and not-good, defiled and pure—possess arising and ceasing; what, then, are the so-called eight consciousnesses?

The eight [consciousnesses] are as follows: within the *tathāgatagarbha*, that which arises based on the perfuming of beginningless ignorance and is capable of containing seeds is called the *ālayavijñāna* (storehouse consciousness), which is the eighth consciousness.
That which is capable of transmitting and entering or exiting is called the *manas* (mind), which is the seventh consciousness. That which is capable of discerning...

That which deliberates and calculates is called the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), which is the sixth consciousness. Because it perceives objects as they immediately appear, it is called the five sensory consciousnesses (*pañca-vijñāna*).
Since these five consciousnesses do not depart from the material substance of the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), they are termed the "five consciousness-bodies" (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*).
These aforementioned eight kinds of consciousness all arise from the perfuming and transformation of True Suchness (*tathatā*) by ignorance; thus, they are the Tathāgatagarbha.

Following the conditions of defiled dependent origination, these are termed the eight consciousnesses and possess arising and ceasing. The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the eight consciousnesses nourish the five aggregates (*pañca-skandha*).
This so-called *ālayavijñāna* (the subtle *ādānavijñāna*) consists of habitual tendencies that form a torrential stream; its subtle arising and ceasing occurs moment by moment without abiding.
Because this is not known by those non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*), they are unable to explain it. How, then, is the momentary nature (*kṣaṇikatva*) clarified?

It is not easy to understand. Although those five consciousnesses do not exist apart from the material substance of the four great elements, at the very first moment of their movement when they grasp objects as the seeing-division (*darśana-bhāga*) of the eight consciousnesses, the mind, the intellect, and the mental consciousness all accompany them;
thus, they are able to discern the characteristics of the preceding objects—whether wholesome or unwholesome—as the mind moves, conditions arise, and causes and conditions converge.
The mind undergoes a continuous succession of transformations and disintegrations without interruption. The five consciousnesses clearly transform into the six consciousnesses;
the six consciousnesses differentiate and transform into the seventh consciousness; and the seventh consciousness’s clinging transforms into the seeds of the eighth consciousness.
While the continuity of the seventh consciousness is subject to destruction, the flowing stream of the eighth consciousness is indestructible.

Because the eighth consciousness and the seven consciousnesses do not arise as distinct entities, the former seven undergo successive arising and ceasing, and the eighth consciousness likewise follows along with this law of arising and ceasing.
This is truly because of non-awakening to the fact that all objective realms are manifestations of one's own mind;
they have never arisen and have never ceased. Yet, perceiving these illusory objects, one gives rise to grasping and attachment.
Because they arise and perish as soon as they are grasped, there is a sequential perishing; where there is sequential perishing, other distinct consciousnesses arise.
That which apprehends forms and characteristics is the five consciousnesses; that which cognizes distinctions is the mental consciousness (manovijñāna);

that which grasps and clings is the seventh and eighth consciousnesses. When the five consciousnesses perish, the sixth consciousness arises; when the sixth consciousness perishes, the seventh and eighth consciousnesses [arise].

"Arising" refers to the sequential cessation of one consciousness and the arising of another. However, there is also a simultaneous mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*) that arises together with the five preceding consciousnesses;

the five [sensory] consciousnesses take the sixth as their basis for discernment (*viniścaya-āśraya*), while the sixth takes the five as its gates of clarity (*vyañjana-mukha*), arising in association with them to grasp various distinct forms and characteristics, flowing and transforming from moment to moment.

A *kṣaṇa* does not abide for even a single moment; within the duration of one *kṣaṇa*, there are eighty kinds of arising and ceasing, like eighty strands of thread severed by a single stroke of a blade.
Although there is a slight sequence in the severing of each individual strand, I describe these as "moments" (*kṣaṇa*).
This is not what is taught by the Tīrthikas outside the Tathāgata’s teaching—how could it be easily understood? A monk asked:
A monk asked Zhaozhou, "Does a newborn infant possess the six consciousnesses? Zhaozhou replied, "It is like hitting a ball on fast-flowing water.
The monk then asked Touzi, "What is the meaning of 'hitting a ball on fast-flowing water'? Touzi said, "Thought after thought, there is no lingering. Xuedou commented with this verse:
"The six consciousnesses have no efficacy—extend this one question; The master of the house has shared it together [with you]."
Discerning the source of its arrival is vast and obscure, like a ball struck upon swift water; its point of descent does not linger—who can discern it?

The meaning of Mahamati’s question regarding the characteristic of momentary destruction lies in the destruction of the world. The World-Honored One takes the "moment" (*kṣaṇa*) as time, yet time itself is not something that can be destroyed.
Xuedou says, "Its point of descent does not linger—who can discern it? He likewise takes this non-lagging as [the answer].
The intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*) also accords with the meaning of this section.

Mahāmati, that which is called "momentary" refers to the *ālayavijñāna*, the *tathāgatagarbha* (the Wei translation says: "the *ālayavijñāna* is named *tathāgatagarbha*"). It is the habit-energy (*vāsanā*) of the co-nascent consciousnesses;
while the habit-energy of the untainted (*anāsrava*) is non-momentary, it is not something perceived or grasped as momentary by ordinary, ignorant people.
Because of this [wrong] reasoning, one does not realize that all dharmas are momentary or non-momentary; through the view of annihilation, one destroys unconditioned dharmas.
Mahāmati, the seven consciousnesses do not transmigrate and do not experience suffering or pleasure, nor are they the cause of nirvāṇa.

Mahāmati, the Tathāgatagarbha experiences suffering and pleasure together with their causes, arising and ceasing; it is the ordinary person who is intoxicated by the four stages of abiding and the stage of ignorance.
The ignorant do not realize that momentary perceptions of false conceptualization permeate the mind.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, just as gold, the diamond, and the Buddha’s *śarīra* possess extraordinary characteristics that are never subject to decay, so too, Mahāmati, if there were such a thing as a "moment" (*kṣaṇa*) in the attainment of the unconditioned (the realization of the Dharma), then the noble would cease to be noble;
yet the noble have never ceased to be noble, just as gold and diamonds remain unchanged even after the passage of kalpas.

Regarding the statement that "the measure does not decrease": how is it that ordinary, ignorant people, being unskilled in my teaching of the hidden meaning (*saṃdhyābhāṣita*), conceive of all internal and external phenomena as being momentary? The general response is:
what was described above as "momentary" refers to the non-abiding of every thought-moment (*kṣaṇa-kṣaṇa*) and the grasping at the marks of the wholesome and the unwholesome.
What was previously called the eight consciousnesses is termed the *vijñānālaya* (storehouse consciousness). This *vijñānālaya* is itself the *tathāgatagarbha* (Tathāgata-store);

why, then, does it have arising and ceasing? It is because this *tathāgatagarbha*, together with the seven consciousnesses and the manas, functions as a vehicle for transmission, entering and exiting, giving rise to the *vṛtti-vijñāna* (active consciousness) of discrimination;
thus, seeds perfume the manifest activities, and manifest activities perfume the seeds.
Because they mutually permeate one another, accumulating into habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) that flow incessantly from moment to moment without ceasing, it is called "momentary" (*kṣaṇika*).
However, if one perfumes them with the wholesome, untainted habitual tendencies of samādhi and right reception, then in a single thought-moment they are suddenly stilled;
thus, it is no longer "momentary. This non-momentary state merely severs the thoughts, but does not sever their substance.
The severing of habitual tendencies does not mean the severing of *tathatā* (suchness), yet this is not realized by those ordinary, deluded people.

Those ordinary, deluded people are attached to the false imaginings of good and evil; they cling only to the doctrine of momentary arising and ceasing, failing to realize that all phenomena are neither momentary nor non-momentary, neither arising and ceasing nor non-arising and non-ceasing, but are rather a continuous flow that is fundamentally [empty].
The mark of quiescent extinction is the truly unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

Ordinary fools, failing to realize this, claim that the mark of momentary destruction means that thoughts will not arise again; through their view of annihilation, they destroy the unconditioned dharma.
To say that the unconditioned *nirvāṇa* is "nothing at all" is to destroy the true unconditioned dharma. How can it be understood that they destroy the unconditioned dharma?

Furthermore, those of the two vehicles have already severed the afflictive obstructions (*kleśāvaraṇa*), so that the seven consciousnesses do not circulate—translated here as the "five bodies of consciousness" (*pañca-vijñāna-kāya*)—which indeed do not circulate.
Since the seven consciousnesses do not circulate, there is neither entering nor exiting; since there is neither entering nor exiting, there is neither defilement nor purity;
since there is neither defilement nor purity, there is neither suffering nor pleasure. Although this suffering and pleasure pertain to the five bodies of consciousness, [they are absent here].

Although the seven consciousnesses (*sapta-vijñāna*) serve as the actual cause for experiencing [suffering and pleasure] and for undergoing future existence (*punarbhava*), they are not the primary cause for *nirvāṇa*.

Since *nirvāṇa* is the essence of the *tathāgatagarbha*, which is neither born nor extinguished and cannot be severed or destroyed, it is said that the seven consciousnesses do not transmigrate and are not the cause of *nirvāṇa*. As for the *tathāgatagarbha*:
This [nature] is not separate from anything; all things are suchness (*tathatā*). Although one experiences suffering and pleasure, one is not bound by suffering and pleasure.

Although one is accompanied by the causes of suffering and pleasure, one is not obscured by the causes of habitual conditioning (*vāsanā*). Within the nature of suchness, birth and cessation are utterly non-existent;
those who perceive birth or perceive cessation do so because they are intoxicated by the four kinds of habitual perfuming (*caturvidha-vāsanā*).

Therefore, the ignorance of the four stages of dwelling (*catur-vāsabhūmi-avidyā*) consists of: the ignorance of desire-attachment (*kāma-rāga*), the ignorance of form-attachment (*rūpa-rāga*), the ignorance of existence-attachment (*bhava-rāga*), and the ignorance of attachment to views (*dṛṣṭi-rāga*). These four types of ignorance are obscuring and neutral (*nivṛta-avyākṛta*) and reside within the field of the eight consciousnesses;
thus they are called "stages of dwelling. Intoxicated by the wine of these four kinds of ignorance, one perceives that nirvāṇa can be attained.
Ordinary fools do not realize that within this state there is subtle arising and ceasing, which does not abide for even a single moment; yet, they perceive it as such.
Merely because their minds are defiled by the false conceptualization of *nirvāṇa*, they claim that "the moments [of consciousness] have been severed and no further existence will be received.

Thus, by means of the view of annihilation, they destroy the unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) dharma, failing to recognize that this is not the cause of true *nirvāṇa*. They are those who, having departed from arising and ceasing, realize...
If non-arising and non-ceasing were something existing apart from the mind, it would be called "with interval," and such an interval is not true realization.

If, however, the Tathāgata-garbha is not separate from arising and ceasing, yet one realizes non-arising and non-ceasing—such that there is no dharma outside the mind and no mind outside dharmas—it is called "without interval.
This absence of interval is true realization; it is the realization of the wondrous truth of the Tathāgata-garbha.
That which is like the nature [of things] is like the diamond within gold or the *śarīra* within the Buddha-body;
it attains a marvelous quality that transcends all ordinary objects and is never destroyed. If one realizes the uninterrupted True Dharma of self-awakened noble wisdom, this is Great Nirvāṇa;
at all times and in all places, there is neither arising nor ceasing, yet it is said to exist.
If the characteristic of arising and ceasing in every moment were identical for the Sage and the ordinary person, one could not call him a Sage.
However, while the Sage’s attachment to suffering and pleasure is no different from that of an ordinary person, he has never ceased to be a Sage;
even while within the midst of arising and ceasing, he does not lose his nature of non-arising and non-ceasing, like a body of gold or diamond.
Even if one were to weigh it for successive eons, the portion of the Perfectly Endowed would not diminish; this truly unconditioned dharma cannot be compared to the view of annihilationism.

Why do the foolish and ignorant, being unskilled in my teaching on the concealment of the momentary and the non-momentary, conceive the notion of momentary destruction regarding all internal and external phenomena, while the non-Buddhists grasp at external objects?
Seeing that things exist and then return to non-existence, one claims they perish moment by moment (*kṣaṇabhanga*).

The followers of the Two Vehicles, perceiving that thoughts no longer arise within their internal dharmas, likewise claim they perish moment by moment. All of these fail to understand the subtle and hidden nature of the moment;
how can one discuss with them whether there is perishing or no perishing? Master Chan Zhao, ascending the hall, said: "Originally unborn, now also..."
Non-extinction is the manner of death that cannot be grasped; being born in this very place and extinguished in every place is the pattern for experiencing living birth.
A great man must directly enter the stream of birth and death, lie within the forest of thorns, and—bending, stretching, and moving as he pleases—apply skillful means according to circumstances.
If one can do so, one will adorn the three [realms] with immeasurable expedient means.

The great gates of liberation open wide and clear; yet, were it otherwise, immeasurable afflictions and all manner of worldly toil would stand like mountains before one, blocking the ancient path—this can be known from this very fact.

All habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) are momentary phenomena (*kṣaṇika-dharma*), whereas untainted habitual tendencies (*anāsrava-vāsanā*) are not momentary phenomena; such is the indestructible nature of the vajra.
Only the Noble Ones realize this.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Empty, impermanent, and momentary—these are the false imaginings of the ignorant. Like a river, a lamp, or a seed, they conceive of things as being momentary."
The momentary cessation of turbulence, tranquility, and freedom from activity—wherein all phenomena do not arise—is what I call the meaning of "moment" (*kṣaṇa*).

When a thing arises, it necessarily ceases; this is not taught to the foolish. It is characterized by uninterrupted continuity, perfumed by false conceptualization (*vikalpa*), with ignorance as its cause, and the mind arises from that. Until form has arisen, what interval could there be in between?

[Wei says: "If ignorance (*avidyā*) acts as the cause capable of producing various states of mind, then until form (*rūpa*) has arisen, one must ask: upon what does it depend and abide? When the continuity [of mind] ceases in succession and another mind arises following it, if it does not abide in form at that time, what object of perception (*ālambana*) gives rise to it?
Since it arises from that [preceding state], yet is not produced from a true cause, how can it be known to perish moment by moment (*kṣaṇabhanga*) without having been established?

[Tang says: "If a mind arises conditioned by that [object], then its cause is false; because the cause is false, its essence is not established."* *Note: The passage reflects a debate concerning the nature of mental continuity and the causal basis for the arising of consciousness prior to the formation of material form.*
[Question: "What is the destruction of a moment (*kṣaṇabhanga*)?
[General Reply: It is said that within the prose commentary (*gadya*), the refutation of the characteristics of momentary destruction has not yet been explained in detail; it merely states:
"How is it that fools, being unskilled in my hidden and concealed teachings, [impute] momentariness to all internal and external phenomena?"
Because of that notion, it is explained in detail in the verse: what is called "momentary destruction" by the ignorant refers to the emptiness of all phenomena and the impermanence of all phenomena;
these views are produced by the false conceptualization and discrimination of the ignorant.
I have always taught that they are like a river, like a lamp flame, and like a seed—swiftly shifting and passing away in an instant.
That which does not abide refers merely to the flux of the *saṃskāra-skandha*, where things change and pass away moment by moment;
it does not mean that every thought-moment (*kṣaṇa*) is empty or that every thought-moment is impermanent.

Those fools, failing to realize this, conceive of these moments as being empty or impermanent, ultimately falling into the view of annihilationism and losing the true meaning. Nevertheless, the cessation of a momentary state is not non-existence.

"Meaning" (*artha*) refers to the cessation of those moment-to-moment, non-abiding, agitated conceptualizations, thereby attaining the meditative absorption of *samādhi-samāpatti*, realizing tranquility, and dwelling in the bliss of the present life (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukhavihāra*).
It is the departure from all conditioned phenomena (*saṃskṛta-dharma*) characterized by arising and ceasing, up to the point where all phenomena do not arise;
this is what I call the meaning of the cessation of moments (*kṣaṇa-nirodha*). As for what is called "non-arising," it does not necessarily mean—
It is through cessation that there is subsequently no arising. At the very moment an entity first arises, its cessation is already present; as it arises, it does not arise.
By realizing the state of quiescence without departing from the dharma of arising, one finds that in each instant there is neither instant nor non-instant.
This is my teaching of concealment; it may be spoken only to the wise, but it is not for the foolish. How is this made clear?
That which is about to arise is precisely non-arising. The nature of their continuous succession of arising and ceasing is most subtle;
due to false views, they revolve through the six realms and differentiate the various destinies.
This is called being perfumed by beginningless delusive thoughts and inconceivable influences—yet it is said that these are fundamentally rootless and originally unarisen.
That is to say: can that beginningless ignorance serve as the cause to produce those various momentary minds? This mind does not depart from ignorance;
its nature is to take objects as its conditions. When the object arrives, the mind exists; when the object departs, the mind ceases.
Even when form has not yet arisen—that is, while form is still in the future and the mind has likewise not yet emerged—during this interval, this mind abides.
In what place and with respect to what is there any discrimination? Thus, internally there is nothing upon which it depends; the mind is fundamentally quiescent and has never arisen.

If one were to suppose that there is arising and ceasing within an uninterrupted succession, then at the time when [a preceding moment] is successively extinguished, would this [extinguishing] give rise to that [succeeding moment], such that another mind arises concomitantly with it? Does this arise together with its object? Or...
When objects and consciousness perish together, it is merely said that the mind abides in form. If the mind does not abide in form, then the mind does not take objects as its conditions;
how then could it arise? Thus, there is no external object of cognition, and the mind is fundamentally quiescent, never having arisen.
If it is claimed that the seven consciousnesses circulate because of the discrimination of the six consciousnesses—
When this mind arises, that which takes it as its object and gives rise to it is that very mind’s manifold conceptualizations;

these are originally false and not a nature of true reality. Since the cause is illusory, the substance [of the effect] is truly non-arising, like a woman giving birth to a child from a stone—ultimately there is no accomplishment.
Thus, this characteristic of a moment (kṣaṇa) is fundamentally unaccomplished. How then could a moment have an origin?
Without anything being established, how could one perceive a characteristic of momentary destruction? This is what I mean by "momentary yet not momentary";
only the wise can clearly understand this for themselves, so it truly cannot be discussed with the foolish.
Chan Master Da Ning Kuan ascended the hall and said: "Taking non-thought as the school, taking non-abiding as the foundation, and taking true emptiness as the essence."
The wondrous existence serves as function; thus it is said that the entire earth is true emptiness, and throughout the Dharma-realm is wondrous existence.
Now tell me, who is it that can employ this? The four seasons operate, the sun and moon are ever bright; the Dharma fundamentally does not shift, and the Way has no fixed location.
Following conditions with sovereign ease, one rises and sinks along with things; entering into this land or other lands, and into the realm of ordinary beings.
"Entering the Holy Path" is indeed thus; yet tell me, how do you express the phrase "entering a village, one follows its customs"? After a long silence, he said:

"The Sanskrit of the Western Heaven, the Tang language of this land—because this Great Quiescence is vast and luminous, encompassing the entire earth as true emptiness, one is free and at ease according to conditions.
Since phenomena are fundamentally non-transmigratory, how could there be any mark of momentary destruction?"

The existence of this: how does a practitioner— abiding in the palace of the Light-Sound Heaven (*Ābhāsvara-deva*) through the samādhi of the Vajra-Buddha-relics, dwelling in the indestructible affairs of the world,
established in the True Dharma, possessing the wisdom of the Tathāgata, and having attained the equality of a bhikṣu— perceive the moment (*kṣaṇa*)?
The forms of the gandharvas, illusions, and so forth, do not exist for even a single moment; yet one regards these unreal forms and the like as if they were real.
It is said in general that ordinary fools, shrouded by the five aggregates, fail to realize that all phenomena are neither momentary nor non-momentary;
thus they fall into the wheel of false conceptualization, revolving through birth and death, for which there is no end to discuss. If, however, one practices correctly within my Dharma...

Those who cultivate the bliss of samādhi bring all disturbances to rest and realize the quiescent, eternally abiding true mind, which is ultimately firm and solid like gold, vajra, or the relics of a Buddha.

Even the palaces of the Light-Sound Heaven (*Ābhāsvara-deva*), which neither water nor fire can reach and which abide forever in the world without being destroyed—such extraordinary things as these in the mundane realm are already like this; how much more so [the state of] peace?

Abiding in the True Dharma and dwelling in happiness in the present life, one attains the Tathāgata’s noble wisdom in its full perfection, as well as the bhikṣu’s realization of the equality of true suchness (*tathatā*).

Since afflictions are themselves bodhi and birth-and-death are themselves nirvāṇa, and since the nature of all phenomena is eternally abiding, how could there be any perception of the characteristics of momentary arising and ceasing? Originally, no such thing is seen to exist.
If the characteristic of a moment already exists, how could there be further destruction of that moment?
All those phenomena are like dreams, like illusions, and like cities of the Gandharvas; although they manifest with formal characteristics, no characteristic of a moment can be found.
Why are they not momentary? Because those forms and so forth originally lack real nature; since they lack real nature...
How can it be that derived matter (*upādāya-rūpa*), which is produced by the four great elements (*mahābhūta*), is not real?
Since derived matter is unreal, how is it that ordinary fools regard each of the aggregates (*skandha*), bases (*āyatana*), and elements (*dhātu*)—from unreal forms and so forth—as truly real?
They perceive all phenomena as a continuous flow, asserting they truly have arising and ceasing, yet they see them as having the characteristic of momentary destruction. How can this be? I [ask].

This is precisely what is meant by those ordinary, ignorant people who are unskilled in my teaching of concealment, and who conceive the notion of momentariness regarding all internal and external phenomena.
Chan Master Cairen of Ruiyan ascended the hall and said: "Because heaven is impartial, it constantly covers;
because earth is impartial, it constantly supports; because the sun and moon are impartial, the four seasons are always bright."
Because Nirvana is equal, the noble and the ordinary are not two; because the human mind is equal, there is no contention between high and low.
Holding up his staff and striking once, he said: "O practitioners of Chan! This staff speaks the Dharma-gate of equality for you day and night. Do you hear it?
If you do, I can guarantee that your journey as a wandering monk is complete. If you do not hear it, you must continue your travels.
It is said that even those who do not hear [this] are permitted; for when the eye at the crown of one’s head is upright, why is it that this Dharma is equal, without high or low?
This is called *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. After a long silence, he smiled and said:
"The subsequent text is extensive. Because, according to the perspective of Ruiyan, all things are equal, how could there ever be a single moment (*kṣaṇa*)?"
The characteristic of disintegration can be perceived.

Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, as the World-Honored One has said that one attains perfect enlightenment by fulfilling the six pāramitās, what are these six?
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "There are three kinds of distinctions regarding the pāramitās."
That is to say, regarding worldly, world-transcending, and super-world-transcending great wisdom:

as for the worldly *pāramitās*, because one is attached to and clings to "self" and "mine," and because of the two extremes, for the sake of the pleasures of various places of rebirth—namely, forms, sounds, smells, tastes, and tangibles—one fulfills the *dāna-pāramitā*; the same applies to morality, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.

The supernatural powers of ordinary beings and those born in the Brahma heavens; the supramundane *pāramitās* of great wisdom belonging to *śrāvakas* and *pratyekabuddhas*, which involve falling into the grasping of *nirvāṇa* and practicing the six *pāramitās* out of a desire for their own personal *nirvāṇa*;

and the supreme supramundane *pāramitās*, which consist in awakening to the fact that the measure of one's own mind is a manifestation of false conceptualization, and that it is grasped by the duality of one's own mind.

Therefore, one does not give rise to false conceptualization regarding the various realms of existence, nor does one grasp at the non-corresponding forms and characteristics of one's own mind, nor cling to them as being true happiness.
For the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, one gives rise to the perfection of giving (*dāna-pāramitā*) and initiates the highest of higher skillful means;

thus, the non-arising of false conceptualization with respect to those objects is the perfection of ethical discipline (*śīla-pāramitā*), and the patient acceptance that knows how to restrain that very non-arising of false conceptualization is the perfection of patience (*kṣānti-pāramitā*).

That which is subsumed [by this] is the *kṣānti-pāramitā*. Diligently applying skillful means during the first, middle, and last watches of the night, practicing in accordance with skillful means so that conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) does not arise, is the *vīrya-pāramitā*.
The total cessation of conceptual construction and not falling into the *nirvāṇa* of the Śrāvakas, while embracing [the path], is the *dhyāna-pāramitā*.
Using wisdom to observe that the conceptual constructions of one's own mind have no inherent nature is [the *prajñā-pāramitā*].

Not falling into the two extremes, with the basis of the former body becoming increasingly superior (in the Tang translation: "increasingly purified"), and being indestructible while attaining the noble realization of self-awakening—this is the perfection of wisdom (*prajñāpāramitā*).

Tong said: "The Great Wisdom (Mahāmati) was told by the Buddha that practitioners who attain meditative absorption (samāpatti) obtain the wisdom of the Tathāgata, which is indestructible like the relics of a Buddha made of vajra.
Yet, among those who practice to attain meditative absorption and obtain the wisdom of the Tathāgata, none can reach the other shore like the Six Pāramitās. How does one fulfill the Six Pāramitās?"
The Buddha, having attained perfect enlightenment, distinguishes the *pāramitās* into three types: first, the mundane, which refers to the practices of humans and devas;
second, the supramundane, which refers to the practices of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*); and third, the supreme supramundane, which refers to the practice of the one vehicle (*ekayāna*).
As for the mundane *pāramitās*, they refer to those of ordinary, ignorant people who are attached to the notions of "self" and "what belongs to the self."
Grasping at the two extremes— conceiving "I am able to give" and conceiving that there is an object given— one does not depart from the duality of subject and object.
For the sake of seeking birth in superior realms as a human or deva for oneself, and out of craving and attachment for the pleasures of the five sensory objects such as form,
one practices worldly giving, fulfilling the *dānapāramitā*, and proceeds through the perfections of ethical discipline, patience, diligence, meditative concentration, and wisdom.
Likewise, because one brings about tainted results through tainted causes, one may achieve the five supernormal powers (*pañcābhijñā*) and be born in the Brahma-world.
Although such birth is certain and the supernormal powers allow for entry into purity, they do not transcend the worldly cycle of rebirth;
therefore, they are called "worldly. As Yongjia said: "Giving while dwelling on signs produces heavenly merit, like an upward-pointing arrow shot into the void."
This refers to the saying: "When one's power is exhausted, the arrow falls back; it brings about an unfavorable rebirth in the next life.

As for the supramundane *pāramitās*, this refers to those of the Two Vehicles who, weary of and abandoning birth-and-death (*saṃsāra*), proceed toward *nirvāṇa* by practicing the Dharma of the Four Noble Truths and the Twelve Links of Dependent Origination. These are merely six kinds of inferior untainted practices that seek only [their own] happiness.
They seek only the bliss of their own nirvana and no longer possess the intention to deliver sentient beings;
because they can only save themselves and cannot save others, it is called the Hīnayāna. Although they are able to practice the supramundane pāramitās, this is not ultimate bliss.
As for the supreme-supreme supramundane pāramitās, one awakens to all external...
The nature of dharmas is such that forms, sounds, fragrances, and so forth are all manifestations of one's own mind.

To perceive all internal dharmas—such as grasping at nirvāṇa—is merely the measure of the deluded mind. To take pleasure in what is manifested by one's own mind and firmly grasp it is indeed to create duality with one's own mind;
to delight in one's own nirvāṇa involves both a subject that realizes and an object that is realized, which is likewise to create duality with oneself.
When the mind correctly awakens to both [of these] as being equally false conceptualizations, then discursive thoughts do not arise;

that is, one does not differentiate false conceptualizations. Since the internal dharmas—such as the various realms of existence (*gati*) and what is grasped as nirvana—are fundamentally unrelated to the original self-nature (*prakṛti*), they are said to be "not part of it" (*avibhāga*). How could there be any attachment?
The forms and other phenomena manifested by one's own mind are fundamentally non-arising external dharmas; what, then, is there to crave or cling to?

Nevertheless, for the sake of bringing peace and happiness to all sentient beings, one practices giving—whether through the gift of material wealth or the gift of the Dharma—arousing the most supreme skillful means while perceiving neither giver, nor receiver, nor that which is given.
Although one practices giving, one does not dwell upon signs; this non-dwelling upon signs in giving is identical with one's own mind, and is therefore called "reaching the other shore.
Thus, regarding that giving, one does not give rise to discrimination between all defiled and pure conditions;
this is to accord with the coolness [of nirvana] and constitutes the practice of the *śīla-pāramitā*, wherein there is neither holding nor violating.
The characteristic of the precepts is like space; this is the supreme skillful means of pure morality for reaching the other shore.
That is to say, when neither upholding nor violating arises through the non-arising of even a single thought, one realizes the Dharma of non-arising as it truly is within the mind.
Because the objects of grasping and being grasped are not real and are by nature empty and quiescent, this constitutes [the ultimate purity].
By practicing patience (*kṣānti*), one attains the further shore through the supreme skillful means (*upāya*). There are two kinds of skillful means of diligence (*vīrya*):

first, the specific characteristic (*viśeṣa-lakṣaṇa*), which refers to reciting scriptures and the like; second, the general characteristic (*sāmānya-lakṣaṇa*), which refers to practicing while incorporating the other five perfections (*pāramitā*).

Through diligent cultivation without slackening during the first, middle, and last watches of the night, one accords with the skillful means of practice according to reality (*yathābhūta*) and also severs all [afflictions].

The *Viniścaya-saṃgrahaṇī* states that because one knows the nature of phenomena (*dharmatā*) to be devoid of the characteristics of body and mind, and is thus free from indolence, this constitutes the perfection of vigor (*vīrya-pāramitā*).
It was previously stated that "delusive thoughts do not arise" when one has not yet attained meditative stillness (*dhyāna-śama*);
here, however, delusive thoughts are entirely extinguished, and one attains tranquility by distancing oneself from the delusions of mind (*citta*), thought (*manas*), and consciousness (*vijñāna*).
Through the supreme skillful means of tranquility, although one attains nirvāṇa, one does not realize it as a finality; thus, one does not fall into the nirvāṇa of the śrāvakas.
Because one does not grasp at the realization or the object realized as being the attainment of a fruit, one does not seek further progress.
Since one does not cling to nirvāṇa, one does not dwell upon signs; this is the dhyāna-pāramitā. Within the delusive imaginings of one’s own mind, there is nothing [ultimately existent].
To regard the true nature as a substantial reality and thereby seek to extinguish it is not wisdom.
If one observes with wisdom that there was originally no arising in the past and likewise no cessation in the present, one does not fall into the dualistic views of existence and non-existence.
Having first extinguished birth and death, one realizes *nirvāṇa* and attains a pure body. Reaching this point, one attains the body of wisdom and undergoes transformation.
Surpassing what came before, it does not depart from arising and ceasing, yet realizes non-arising and non-ceasing; in every place, it is indestructible.
This is the attainment of the noble realization of self-awakening, the Dharma-body of the Tathāgata. One seeks the marks of arising and ceasing, yet they are utterly unobtainable.
Like the *vajra* relics of the Buddha, they are ultimately subject to no decay or destruction. This unsurpassed *prajñā* is not ordinary wisdom.
What I can reach is this: what I call the Tathāgata’s perfection of wisdom. One who is thus fulfilled attains *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*;
therefore, it is called the supreme, transcendent *pāramitā*. Chan Master Yunju Ying ascended the hall and said:
"All of you, even if you were to study and master the matters on the Buddha's side, you would still be far from it."
This is a mistaken use of mind; even when the ancients spoke of "celestial flowers falling and stones nodding," it had nothing to do with one's own affairs.

As for everything else, what is this idle fabrication? To take this finite body and mind and apply it toward the infinite is like trying to fit a square block into a round hole—how much confusion and error! If such a thing did not exist, even if you were to...
Gathering blossoms and clustering brocade is likewise of no use; as long as one has not transcended emotional consciousness, one must reach the ultimate exhaustion within all matters right here.

If there is even a hair’s breadth that is not exhausted, one is immediately burdened by worldly dust; how much more so if there is more? To miss it by a hair’s breadth is to fall into a mountain of transgressions.
Have you not seen the ancients say: "The place of study is not mysterious; it is entirely a matter of flowing [into realization]?"
Things of the mundane household cannot be discarded; they all become leaks.
You must, right here, seize the opportunity to go, come, and stay, exhausting every single matter before you can be faultless.

It is like a person who has mastered every head and penetrated every object—they are called merely a "man of affairs," but they are never called "Noble. Know that this is how one recognizes the Noble One.
I have seen only this single path; I have never seen a way that enters through a gate. Know you not that it is not formed by a precious staff?
This should be understood: the first *pāramitā* is most supreme and most noble; without it, the other five perfections can ultimately never reach the other shore.
(Chapter 15 on Transformation according to the Wei translation; Chapter 7 on Metamorphosis according to the Tang translation).

At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva again addressed the Buddha, saying: "World-Honored One, the World-Honored One has prophesied that Arhats shall attain Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi and be no different from all Bodhisattvas. All the assembly...

(First Doubt: If dharmas that arise do not enter nirvāṇa, who then attains the Buddha-way? (Second Doubt: From the initial attainment of Buddhahood until parinirvāṇa, not a single word was spoken in the interim, nor was anything answered;
for the Tathāgata is eternally in samādhi, having neither thought nor reflection, and it is the emanation-Buddha (*nirmāṇabuddha*) that performs the work of a Buddha.
(Third Doubt: For what reason is consciousness said to have the characteristic of momentary, successive disintegration? (Gold)

The Vajrapāṇi spirits constantly follow and attend upon [the Buddha] (the fourth doubt); why did he not provide for the primordial limit (the fifth doubt)? He manifested Māra, the deeds of Māra, and the retribution of evil karma;

the brahmin Cīñcā and the woman Sundarī emerged with empty bowls, and the obstacles of evil karma appeared—how is it that the Tathāgata attained all-knowledge (*sarvākārajñatā*) yet was not free from these faults? (the sixth doubt).

(Tang Dynasty translation: "World-Honored One, Tathāgata, for what reason do you bestow upon Arhats the prediction of *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*? For what reason do you further say that sentient beings who lack the nature for parinirvāṇa attain the Buddha-way?

Furthermore, for what reason do you say that from the initial attainment of Buddhahood until parinirvāṇa, not a single word was spoken in the interim? You also say that the Tathāgata dwells in meditative concentration, without vitarka or vicāra;

that all Buddha-works are merely transformations; that all consciousnesses undergo momentary change and decay; that the Vajra-gods constantly follow and protect him; that the prior limit is unknowable, yet you speak of parinirvāṇa; and that Māras and demonic deeds actually exist; and that there are residual karmic retributions, such as the Brahmin woman Ciñcā-Mānavikā? )

Since the World-Honored One had such karmic obstructions as [the incident with] the female non-Buddhist Tāḍī and returning with an empty bowl, how could he have attained all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*)? And once he had already attained all-encompassing wisdom, why did he not remain free from such faults?

Mahāmati said: "Because the World-Honored One has taught that the practice of the six pāramitās by śrāvakas who have transcended the world and attained the bliss of nirvāṇa is no different from that of bodhisattvas, why have they not received a prediction [of enlightenment]? For this reason, he asked the World-Honored One:
'Why do you grant predictions to śrāvakas, arhats, and others that they shall attain perfect awakening, just like the bodhisattvas?'"
Since they are equal and without distinction, they should all attain nirvāṇa simultaneously. Yet it is further said that the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, do not enter nirvāṇa;
because they desire to lead all sentient beings to enter nirvāṇa, they do not pass into parinirvāṇa.
If, for the sake of all sentient beings, there is no dharma of parinirvāṇa, then they would remain eternally within saṃsāra together with those sentient beings—who then [would be liberated]?

"Does one reach the Buddha-way? Furthermore, World-Honored One, for what reason did you say that from the first moment of attaining Buddhahood, on the very night you realized Great Bodhi, until the night you entered Parinirvāṇa, you did not speak a single word nor give any answer, yet it is manifest that there is a Buddha-way and there is Nirvāṇa? Moreover, you said that the Tathāgata is eternal."

When one abides in meditative concentration (*samādhi*) that is without applied thought (*vitarka*) or sustained thought (*vicāra*), without reflection (*manasikāra*) or investigation (*upalakṣaṇā*), being devoid of both mental deliberation and observation, there is then no speech and no discourse;
one dwells in a non-conceptual concentration (*nirvikalpa-samādhi*). One might argue that such a state should be unable to manifest all the Buddha-activities (*buddhakārya*).
Yet it is said that these Buddha-activities consist entirely of the emanation of various transformations to guide and liberate sentient beings; these are the *nirmāṇabuddhas* (emanation Buddhas).
If the Dharma-Buddha is eternally fixed, then the Transformation-Buddha should likewise be eternally fixed.
Why, then, do you speak of the various consciousnesses as being momentary, not abiding for even a single thought-moment, and characterized by constant change and decay?

Furthermore, regarding the Buddha-work performed by transformations, it is said that Vajrapāṇi constantly follows and guards him. Where, then, is this so-called "eternal fixation"? Since this is the case...
The transformation Buddha preaches the Dharma in accordance with the flow toward Nirvāṇa, yet the original limit (*pūrvakoṭi*) of saṃsāra cannot be known;
this original limit is the very essence of the Dharma-Buddha. Why, then, is the original limit not established?
If one teaches by means of the mind of the ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), how could one further speak of sentient beings attaining liberation and parinirvāṇa? If one enters nirvāṇa...
If *saṃsāra* must have a beginning point (*pūrvakoṭi*), why is it said to be unknowable?
If this beginning point is unknowable, then having transcended the world and being far removed from afflictions (*kleśa*), one would be without enemies;

how then could there currently exist various Māras, the works of Māra, and other matters such as the retribution of evil karma? The Buddha has nine grounds for resentment, namely, the celestial Māras (*devaputra-māra*).

He raised an army, bearing instruments of torture, and advanced toward the Buddha; however, the Buddha, through the samādhi of loving-kindness, encompassed them all, transforming them into lotus flowers—this was his demonic karma.

The Brahmin woman Ciñcā fastened a wooden bowl to her waist and, together with the heretic Sundarī who had killed a girl, falsely slandered the Buddha—this was his evil karma. Furthermore, when the Buddha entered the village of Pāṭaligrāma to beg for alms...

Eating without giving, going out with an empty bowl, eating horse-gram, suffering from headaches and back pains, having one's feet pierced by thorns, Devadatta pushing down a mountain, the attempt to crush the Buddha with a fire pit, the intoxicated elephant, and the poisoned rice—all these were karmic retributions.
Since such karmic obstacles currently exist in the world, how could one attain all-encompassing wisdom (*sarvākārajñatā*)? Now that it has already been attained—
"How is it that the Omniscience of All Aspects (*sarvākārajñatā*) is not free from such faults?
If the Tathāgata is not free from faults, he is not free from afflictions (*kleśa*), and thus he would not be in *nirvāṇa*. Why then do you say that the *nirvāṇa* of the Śrāvakas is not [true]?
This doubt branches out in many ways—divided into six sections in the Song edition and ten in the Tang edition—but in reality, it is merely a single point.
One may doubt that the practitioners of the Two Vehicles who cultivate the six *pāramitās* and attain the bliss of *nirvāṇa* are no different from *arhats*;
why then does the World-Honored One alone bestow predictions upon *arhats* that they can practice the bodhisattva path?
Furthermore, since bodhisattvas and *icchantikas* do not enter *nirvāṇa*, who will realize the Buddha-way? Moreover, the Buddha has also said that there is no speech, no answer, no thought, and no...
If observation always resides in emptiness, for what reason do you further speak of the characteristics of the various consciousnesses as they arise and pass away in succession?
Since these are merely the provisional arrangements of a transformation Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*), why not directly reveal the characteristic of the primordial limit as eternally empty?
As for that which is manifested—various demonic activities and evil karmas—how can these be contrary to *nirvāṇa*? What is meant by the *nirvāṇa* attained by those of the Two Vehicles?
"Is it not the case that [the three vehicles] are false? Therefore, the Buddha answered him by saying that there is only the One Vehicle and no other vehicle. Baizhang said:

"Suppose now there were someone who, with the four requisites of merit and wisdom, made offerings for eighty years to beings of the six destinies and four modes of birth across four million *koṭi* of *asaṃkhyeya* worlds, fulfilling their every desire; after this, they were to think:"
He reflects: "These sentient beings have all already grown old; I shall instruct and guide them with the Buddha-dharma so that they may attain the fruit of *srotāpanna* up to the path of *arhat*.
If the merit of a donor who merely bestows the requisites for happiness upon all sentient beings is already immeasurable, how much more so when they cause them to attain the fruit of *srotāpanna*?"
Even the immeasurable and boundless merit of attaining the path of Arhatship does not equal the merit of the fiftieth person who hears a sutra and rejoices with sympathetic joy (*anumodana*).
The *Bao'en jing* (Sutra on Requiting Kindness) states: "Queen Māyā gave birth to five hundred princes, all of whom attained the fruit of Pratyekabuddhahood and entered parinirvāṇa;
stupas were erected for each of them, and they were individually honored and paid homage."
He sighed, saying: "It is not as good as being born as an only son who attains unsurpassed bodhi, thereby saving my mental and physical strength.
Only now, among hundreds, thousands, and tens of millions of people, does there happen to be one who attains it; its value is equal to that of the three thousandfold great thousandfold world-system.
Therefore, I constantly exhort all people to achieve profound understanding of their own nature. If one's own nature is profoundly realized, one will obtain merit and wisdom."
It is like a nobleman employing the lowly, or like a carriage that does not abide;

if one maintains this as an understanding, it is called the jewel within the topknot, it is called the precious gem of value, it is called bringing in the dung, and it is called carrying out the dung.
The Buddha is simply a person from beyond the realm of birth and death who has come back within the realm of entanglement to act as a Buddha in this way. He is truly such a person.
Those from the other shore of profound transcendence come here to this shore to manifest Buddhahood;
viewed in this light, the transformation Buddhas and their performance of Buddha-works are fundamentally intended only to guide sentient beings toward the attainment of unsurpassed bodhi.
How could they be discussed with those of the Two Vehicles who are addicted to the bliss of nirvana?
The Buddha said to Mahāmati, “Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect well upon it; I shall speak for you. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, “Excellent, World-Honored One!
We shall indeed receive your instruction. The Buddha told Mahāmati, “It is for the sake of *nirvāṇa without remainder* that I speak thus to encourage and advance those who practice as bodhisattvas.
This is because those who cultivate the bodhisattva path in this world and in other worlds delight in sound.”
Hearing that the vehicle of nirvāṇa is intended to cause one to leave the Śrāvaka vehicle and advance toward the Mahāyāna, the transformation Buddha bestows predictions upon the śrāvakas;
it is not the Dharma Buddha. Mahāmati, for this reason, he predicts that the śrāvakas are no different from the bodhisattvas.
Mahāmati, "no different" means that the śrāvakas, pratyekabuddhas, and all Buddhas-Tathāgatas are of one single flavor regarding the severance of the afflictive hindrances and liberation.
The obstacle of wisdom is severed by Great Wisdom; the obstacle of wisdom consists in seeing phenomena as having no inherent nature, which is the supreme purity.

The obstacle of afflictions is severed by prior cultivation of the realization of the non-self of persons, whereby the seven consciousnesses are extinguished. Through liberation from the obstacle of phenomena, the habitual tendencies of the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna) are extinguished, resulting in ultimate purity.
The Master said: "The Buddha appeared in the world for the sake of one great cause and condition—to reveal, awaken to, and enter into the Buddha’s knowledge and vision.

There is only this One Vehicle and no other vehicle. Therefore, for the sake of those śrāvakas who have previously practiced the bodhisattva path, he grants them predictions of enlightenment based on their attainment of nirvana without remainder, thereby inducing and encouraging those timid beings."

Having generated a courageous mind and cultivated the practices of a bodhisattva, [he observes that] in this realm and other directions there are bodhisattvas who have newly resolved their minds [for enlightenment] but who cling to the bliss of the nirvana of the śrāvakas; they do not arise from meditative concentration and lack the intention to deliver sentient beings.

Therefore, in order to cause them to abandon the Lesser Vehicle and advance toward the Great, to practice the Mahāyāna, to attain great bodhi, and to together realize nirvana without remainder, [he acts].
The bestowal of this prediction is that which a transformation Buddha grants to transformed śrāvakas;
it is not something spoken by a Buddha of the dharma-nature (dharmatā-buddha). For this reason, the prediction granted to the arhats and others is no different from that of the bodhisattvas.
This is a secret teaching intended solely to encourage them forward; how could it be said that they will not attain the Buddha-way?

Furthermore, the reason why Śrāvakas are not different from Bodhisattvas is that both the Two Vehicles and the Buddhas, the Tathāgatas, have completely severed the coarse delusions and afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) within the triple world; the resulting pervasive emptiness is termed "liberation.

It is only in this single flavor of sameness that they are identical, but it does not mean that they have also severed the cognitive hindrances (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) and are thus no different from the Buddhas. Wisdom.

Regarding the severance of hindrances: seeing the selflessness of phenomena (*dharmanairātmya*) and thereby attaining liberation from attachment to phenomena is more exceptionally pure than the previously mentioned attainment of the selflessness of persons (*pudgalanairātmya*).
Those who have severed the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) merely practice initially to sever the delusions of the afflictions;
although they attain the emptiness of persons, they have not yet attained the emptiness of phenomena, and thus it is not ultimate purity.
Therefore, the severance of the afflictive hindrances (*kleśāvaraṇa*) consists merely in the transformation of the seven consciousnesses and their cessation;

when the manas-consciousness no longer functions, the grasping at a self (*ātma-grāha*) is suddenly severed, which is called attaining the wisdom of the emptiness of persons (*pudgala-śūnyatā-jñāna*). As for liberation from the hindrance to phenomena (*dharmāvaraṇa*), it occurs through the transformation of the habitual perfumings (*vāsanā*) of the ālayavijñāna;
only when the seeds of ignorance (*avidyā-bīja*) that store these habitual tendencies are completely extinguished is it termed the "pure white consciousness" (*amala-vijñāna*).
This is called attaining the wisdom of the emptiness of phenomena (*dharmasūnyatā*); it is the beginning of ultimate purity.

This is certainly something that the followers of the Two Vehicles cannot reach, yet can it not be said to be no different from that of a Bodhisattva? Chan Master Luopu Yuanshi studied under Linji for a long time as his attendant.
Linji often said: "In the gate of Linji, there is a single arrow; who dares to face its point?"

Nanquan drew a line with his staff and said, "If you can pass over this, then go. Nanquan then shouted; Linji struck him, and Nanquan bowed and departed.
Linji said to others, "In the gate of Linji there is a red-tailed carp that shakes its head and wags its tail as it heads south."
Not knowing whose family’s pickle-jar he would be drowned in, after completing his travels through Luopu, he reached the summit of Jia Shan and pitched a hermitage there, remaining for one year.
Jia Shan, becoming aware of this, sent an attendant monk with a letter to Luopu.
Upon receiving it, Luopu sat down, then extended his hands again and called for the monk; when the monk remained silent, Luopu struck him and said, "Go back and report this to him."

Baofu replied, "I have traveled from afar to seek the wind of your teaching; I beg the Master to grant me an audience."
