Through understanding the transformation of the basis (*āśraya-parāvṛtti*), one knows that unsurpassed *bodhi* is not easily brought to ultimate completion.

Because of the dharma of the primordial abiding (*mūla-sthiti-dharma*), there is no nature of before or after; because of inexhaustible original vows, the Tathāgata expounds the Dharma without deliberation or investigation.
Because he is transformed by right wisdom and his mindfulness is not deluded, he is without deliberation or investigation regarding the four stages of dwelling (*catur-vihāra-bhūmi*).

Because the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of the ground of abiding ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*) are severed, the two afflictions (*kleśa*) are abandoned; one becomes detached from the two kinds of death, realizes the selflessness of persons and phenomena (*pudgala-dharmanairātmya*), and abandons the two obstructions (*āvaraṇa*).

O Mahāmati, because the habit-energies of the seven moments—the mind (*citta*), the intellect (*manas*), the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the six sense-consciousnesses such as the eye-consciousness—are severed by the category of the wholesome and untainted (*anāsrava*), one no longer revolves in saṃsāra. O Mahāmati, the Tathāgatagarbha is the suffering of saṃsāra and nirvāṇa.
The wisdom that takes emptiness as its cause and agitates the mind (in the Tang translation, "delusively attached to emptiness") cannot be realized by foolish ordinary beings.
Generally speaking, the aforementioned bestowal of predictions upon śrāvakas is nothing other than an inducement to practice the bodhisattva path and realize *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa*.
This *anupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* is ultimate purity; it is not merely the attainment of a human [or limited] state.

That which can be realized by those who have no self—namely, the cessation of the seven consciousnesses and the cessation of the habitual tendencies of the storehouse consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*)—is the realization of the Dharma of Non-interruption (*anantara-dharma*), which is the *tathatā* (suchness) of the ultimate limit. This is what is called the true reality (*dharmatā*) of all phenomena:

whether a Buddha exists or not, the *dharmadhātu* is eternally abiding because it is the primordially existing Dharma; thus, the prior and posterior limits are severed, for it has no substantial nature and is therefore non-existent [as a discrete entity].

Regarding the events following the initial attainment of Buddhahood, such as the subsequent preaching of the Dharma—which involves written characters and phrases—it is nonetheless based on the original Dharma;
because such [phenomena] were already fully present from the outset and do not arise anew, it is said that "not even a single word was spoken.

Nevertheless, within that which is ineffable, there is speaking, for the Buddhas and Tathāgatas have, throughout kalpas of cultivating causes, manifested the power to rescue and protect sentient beings.

Because one has given rise to inexhaustible original vows, within the profoundly serene *dharmadhātu*—a mind of constant meditative concentration that is free from deliberation or investigation—one preaches the Dharma in accordance with the capacities of sentient beings.
What is thus preached flows forth from right gnosis (*samyag-jñāna*) in accord with the nature of reality;
it should be known as being like a wish-fulfilling gem, never failing for even a single moment, fundamentally non-delusory, and requiring no further thought or reflection.
This is explained later. The reason why there is neither thought nor deliberation is that the Tathāgata has long since completely severed the ignorance of the four *bhūmi* (stages):
namely, desire-attachment (*kāmarāga*), form-attachment (*rūparāga*), existence-attachment (*bhavarāga*), and view-attachment (*dṛṣṭirāga*).

Because all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) from beginningless time residing in these stages have been severed, and because he is free from these four stages, he is devoid of fundamental afflictions (*mūlakleśa*).

Furthermore, both the primary and secondary afflictions are severed; both the death of the fragmented existence (*paricchinna-janma*) and the death of the transformational existence (*pariṇāmi-janma*) are transcended.

By realizing the selflessness of persons (*pudgala-nairātmya*) and the selflessness of phenomena (*dharma-nairātmya*) as they truly are, both the obstacle of afflictions (*kleśāvaraṇa*) and the obstacle to the knowable (*jñeyāvaraṇa*) are severed.
Since all obstacles are forever eliminated and all delusions are eternally stilled, one abides in a state of constant meditative concentration.
Spontaneously possessing inconceivable karmic functions, one is able to manifest Buddha-activities;
though there is no teaching, there is teaching, and though there is no body, there is manifestation of a body—yet this essential point does not depart from the originally abiding Dharma.

Furthermore, regarding the various consciousnesses said to have the characteristic of momentary, successive disintegration, this refers to the seven types of consciousness—the mind (*citta*), the intellect (*manas*), the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*), and the five sensory consciousnesses—which shift and change from moment to moment.

Because the causes of the flowing moments—which do not abide for even an instant—are the false habitual tendencies stored within the field of the eight consciousnesses, the sovereign mind of the eight consciousnesses likewise arises and ceases simultaneously with the seven consciousnesses;
until the untainted state (*anāsrava*) is attained, it will ultimately continue to revolve in saṃsāra.
When those noble ones cultivate the bliss of samādhi and realize the category of the wholesome and untainted, they are then able to distance themselves from mind (*citta*) and thought (*manas*).
The moments of consciousness cease and no longer revolve; their associated thoughts perish together with them, yet it is not the *tathāgatagarbha* that is extinguished.
Furthermore, the *tathāgatagarbha* neither comes nor goes; it is eternal, constant, and unchanging, and thus cannot be extinguished.
Therefore, this *tathāgatagarbha* is what revolves within the mundane world, and its revolving is likewise [the nature of] suchness (*tathatā*). This is the mundane world and *nirvāṇa*.
The Tathāgatagarbha is suchness, and nirvāṇa is also suchness; the world’s suffering and pleasure arise because of this Tathāgatagarbha, and the causes of suffering and pleasure are also suchness.
Although it coexists with nirvāṇa and the causes of suffering and pleasure, it is not transformed by them.
It is neither arising-and-ceasing nor non-arising-and-ceasing; it is neither momentary nor non-momentary. This is what is hidden.

This teaching on concealment can only be understood by the wise. If those foolish ordinary people and non-Buddhists falsely cling to emptiness and allow their minds to be distracted by it, they may attain the wisdom of emptiness, yet they perceive only its emptiness and fail to realize that it is both empty and not empty.
This meaning of the Tathāgatagarbha—the reality of each moment—is beyond their capacity for realization. If one were to realize it...
The meaning of the Tathāgatagarbha as the reality of each moment is precisely the primordially abiding Dharma;
how, then, could there be any successive marks of decay? Formerly, Cao Shan asked Elder De: "The true Dharmakāya of the Buddha is like empty space;
it manifests forms in response to things, like the moon reflected in water. How do you explain the principle of this 'responding'? De replied:
When Shan said, "It is like a donkey looking into a well," Daode remarked, "That is quite a saying; you have only managed to express eighty percent of it.
Daode asked, "How about you, Master? Shan replied, "It is like a well looking at a donkey. Tiantong’s verse comments: The donkey looks into the well;
the well looks at the donkey. Wisdom encompasses all without limit; purity contains all with abundance. Who can discern the seal behind his elbow? Within the family, no books are stored.
The shuttle-head knows no entanglement with the warp and woof; though the patterns may run wild, the underlying intent remains distinct.

Within the Gate of the Patriarchs, many wondrous feats manifest, yet one does not realize that this sutra has already revealed them long ago. Nevertheless, even when reaching such a state, how easy is it to attain?
Mahāmati, those whom the Vajrapāṇi-guards follow and protect are merely transformation Buddhas (*nirmāṇa-buddha*) and not the true Tathāgata.

Mahāmati, the true Tathāgata is free from all faculties and measures; because he has extinguished all the faculties and measures of ordinary beings, Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and non-Buddhists, and has attained the patience regarding the knowledge of the Dharma that is uninterrupted and abides in the bliss of the present dharma (*dṛṣṭadharma-sukha-vihāra*), he is not [protected by] the Vajrapāṇi-guards.
All emanated Buddhas whom [the Tathāgata] protects are not emanated Buddhas produced from karma; those who are not Buddhas do not depart from the Buddha.

Because they teach the Dharma through signs such as the potter’s wheel created by sentient beings, they do not speak from their own direct realization, but rather from the realm of self-awakened wisdom.

Furthermore, Mahāmati, foolish people give rise to the view of annihilation based on the cessation of the seven consciousnesses; because they do not realize the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), they give rise to it [as non-existent].

Because one constantly perceives them as one's own false imaginings, one does not know the original limit (*pūrvakoṭi*); when the wisdom that realizes they are one's own false imaginings is extinguished, one is liberated from the four stages of abiding (*catur-vihāra-bhūmi*) and, through the severance of the habit-energies (*vāsanā*) of the stage of ignorance (*avidyā-vāsabhūmi*), all faults are severed.

Tong said: "The previous statement that the Tathāgata has no deliberation (*vitarka*) and no investigation (*vicāra*) while expounding the Dharma is because he is transformed by right wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*);

thus, being without deliberation or investigation, he is constantly in meditative concentration (*samādhi*). This Dharma is the essence of the Buddha. The Dharma-Buddha (*dharma-buddha*) does not preach the Dharma;
it is only the Transformation-Buddha (*nirmāṇa-buddha*), transformed by right wisdom, who expounds the Dharma. Therefore, the Vajrapāṇi spirits stand before and behind him."
Those who surround and constantly follow to provide protection are transformation Buddhas (*nirmāṇa-buddha*) and not Dharma-body Buddhas (*dharma-kāya-buddha*).
The Dharma-body Buddha is the Tathāgata of the fundamental reality-limit (*bhūtakoṭi*), who is utterly remote from all faculties, whether large or small, and from all measure and quantity.

All the faculties and measures of ordinary beings, those of the two vehicles (*śrāvaka* and *pratyekabuddha*), and non-Buddhists (*tīrthika*) are completely extinguished therein; it is that which cannot be apprehended by the two vehicles or non-Buddhists.
Knowing that which cannot be seen, one practices according to reality and attains that state of bliss in True Suchness (*tathatā*).
Within this meditative absorption (*samādhi-samāpatti*) of dwelling in happiness in the present life, it is not comparable to ordinary states characterized by interruption;

rather, one abides in the power of the patience of knowledge regarding uninterrupted phenomena (*anantarya-dharma-jñāna-kṣānti*), which is supreme. Having realized this knowledge of uninterrupted phenomena, once this knowledge exists, there is no longer any [interruption].
The patience regarding the knowledge of phenomena (*dharmajñānakṣānti*) within the intermediate state is precisely what is called the Vajra-samādhi.
The Tathāgata always abides in samādhi and does not require protection by the Vajrapāṇis; those whom he protects are merely the *nirmāṇakāya* (emanation) Buddhas.
Furthermore, all *nirmāṇakāya* Buddhas are not born of karmic retribution; they are called "emanations" and are not the true Buddha, yet they arise through causes and conditions.
That which is transformed by correct wisdom (*samyag-jñāna*) is neither separate from the True Buddha, nor is it the Buddha itself, nor is it not the Buddha.
It is, for example, like the vessels produced by a potter; using the wheel, string, clay, and water as causes, various vessels are fashioned to meet the practical needs of sentient beings.
Likewise, the transformation-buddhas (*nirmāṇa-buddha*) created by the Buddha also manifest through the phenomena and characteristics of the activities performed by sentient beings.
Manifesting the thirty-two marks as a cause to preach the Dharma for sentient beings in response to their requests is merely a matter of the physical form, faculties, and dimensions;
it is fundamentally not the realm of self-attained True Suchness or the Limit of Reality (*bhūtakoṭi*).

Rather, it is preaching the Dharma through expedient means according to the capacities of beings, which differs from the true mark. This leads ultimately to the supreme, inwardly realized, self-aware noble wisdom.

The realm of the mind of ultimate meaning (*artha-citta*) is inherently impossible to raise up and show to others; this is precisely why it is said that not a single word is spoken and there is no answer given.
Those deluded beings, relying on the seven consciousnesses which perish moment by moment, give rise to the view of annihilationism (*uccheda-dṛṣṭi*).
Because they see that the seven consciousnesses do not transmit themselves through entry and exit, they claim that all things are severed and impermanent. Furthermore, [they hold this view].
There are those who, failing to perceive the subtle arising and ceasing within the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), give rise to the view of permanence;
they take the tranquil state of the eight consciousnesses to be nirvāṇa, eternally abiding and indestructible.

Both of these views arise from one's own deluded conceptualization and discrimination, such that they do not know the fundamental limit—the true ground of non-arising and non-ceasing. One’s own mind’s discrimination is itself that fundamental limit.
Therefore, one must not conclude that because the beginning of the world cannot be found, it is thus unknowable.

If one can distance oneself from conceptual discrimination, such as the two views of eternalism and nihilism, and eliminate false wisdom, then the evolving consciousnesses will be transformed into gnosis (*jñāna*). One will realize liberation and attain the fruit of *nirvāṇa*.
Because the Buddhas and Tathāgatas have attained liberation, they are far removed from the four stages of abiding (*catur-vāsabhūmi*).
The habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) of the ground of ignorance (*avidyā-āśraya-bhūmi*) permeate the *ālayavijñāna* and are not easily severed;
because craving for existence has not yet been eliminated, it immediately brings forth the fruit of suffering, and thus all faults are difficult to eradicate.

Now, because the habitual tendencies of the ground have been severed, all faults are severed. Although various karmic obstructions manifest as demons or as retributive results, even if they are externally displayed...
If there is nothing within to draw it forth, then even if it exists, it is as non-existent; because the internal lacks its response, the external cannot act.
Therefore, all transgressions are severed at their fundamental limit (*mūlānta*).
When speaking of this fundamental limit, it is neither protected by the Vajrapāṇi spirits nor obstructed by various evil karmas; it is that which is embraced by those of the Two Vehicles.
If one is intoxicated by the ignorance of the four abodes (*catur-vāsa-bhūmi*) within *nirvāṇa*, one cannot leave behind all faults;
how then could such a person be granted a prediction of enlightenment (*vyākaraṇa*) in the same manner as an Arhat? Huangbo said:

"The Patriarch came from the West solely to transmit the Mind-Buddha, pointing directly to you that your own mind is fundamentally Buddha. Because mind and mind do not differ, he is called the Patriarch. If...
"If you see this directly, this very mind immediately transcends all stages of the Three Vehicles;
it is primordially Buddha, not requiring cultivation or achievement. Nanquan said, "If this is so, when the Buddhas appear in the world, what Dharma do they preach?
Baizhang replied, "The Buddhas of the ten directions, appearing in the world, only together preach the Dharma of the One Mind. This is why the Buddha secretly entrusted it to Mahākāśyapa."
This single mind-dharma, its substance exhausting all of space and pervading the entire Dharma-realm, is what is called the "principle of the Buddhas.
How could this dharma be understood by you through words and phrases? Nor can it be seen through any particular stimulus or circumstance.
This meaning can only be attained through silent resonance. This gate is called the unconditioned dharma (*asaṃskṛta-dharma*).

If you wish to realize this, simply know that there is no-mind; if you suddenly awaken, you will attain it immediately. If you apply the mind to study or seek to grasp it, you will only move further away.
If there is no bifurcated path of the mind, and all thoughts of grasping and rejecting are gone, and the mind is like wood or stone, only then do you have the capacity to learn the Way.
As Huangbo said: "A mind without a bifurcated path, a mind without grasping or rejecting, a mind like..."
Even those as insentient as wood or stone can sever the habitual tendencies of ignorance of the four stages of dwelling, distance themselves from the two views of permanence and annihilation,
and easily realize the ultimate limit of nirvana.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
The three vehicles are also not vehicles; the Tathāgata does not pass into extinction (in the Tang translation: "there is no nirvāṇa for the Buddha").

All Buddhas have recorded and taught that [the truth] is free from all faults and evils, and they employ the wisdom of non-interruption (*anantarya-jñāna*) and *nirupadhiśeṣa-nirvāṇa* to entice and advance those of inferior capacity.
Therefore, they speak in a concealed manner. The wisdom arising from all Buddhas is precisely the analytical exposition of the paths and vehicles; these vehicles are not [truly] vehicles.
Thus, it is not Nirvāṇa; yet, regarding desire, form, existence, and views, these are said to be the consciousnesses arising from the four stages of abiding (catur-vyavasthāna-bhūmi).
This is the dwelling place of consciousness, the abode of the mind (manas), and the cessation of the mental consciousness (manovijñāna) and the visual consciousness (cakṣurvijñāna) and so forth.

To speak of impermanence in this way, or to hold the view that Nirvāṇa is permanent, is to be deluded. Because one perceives the impermanence of the mental consciousness, the eye, and so forth, one speaks of annihilationism; being confused by the mental consciousness, one gives rise to false wisdom regarding permanence, claiming it to be Nirvāṇa.

The commentary states: "In the verse, the fact that only the inadequacy of the *nirvāṇa* of the two vehicles (*dvayayāna*) is discerned is sufficient to know that the many doubts and difficulties in the prose section are directed solely toward this single point; they are not mentioned in a general sense.

Therefore, when the Tathāgata constantly speaks of the three vehicles (*triyāna*), it is because these two—the small vehicle (*hīnayāna*) and the bodhisattva’s great vehicle (*mahāyāna*)—cannot be spoken of as the One Vehicle (*ekayāna*), for they are not the Buddha-vehicle."
Furthermore, that which the Tathāgata does not exhaust or annihilate refers to the absence of a person who can realize it and the absence of the principle to be realized;
even the Buddha-vehicle is not [existent]. This is the supreme primary meaning.
Those who awaken to this meaning are prophesied by all Buddhas to certainly become Buddhas, for it is said that all their afflictions have been severed.

This is because they are free from all faults and evils. That very freedom from faults and evils results in the accomplishment of ultimate, uninterrupted wisdom and the realization of *nirvāṇa* without remainder, which is equal to that of all Buddhas and without distinction;
this is the purpose of the prophecy, intended to encourage and lead those timid and inferior beings who are attached to the *nirvāṇa* of the Śrāvakas.

Because they have abandoned the narrow-minded view and are oriented toward the Mahāyāna, he spoke with intentional ambiguity (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*), concealing the truth by saying that there is uninterrupted wisdom and that there is nirvāṇa without remainder; this was merely to cause them to give rise to a mind of diligence.
If, however, one were to speak based on the fundamental, ultimate wisdom realized by all Buddhas—arising from that very realized wisdom—one would speak of the Buddhas of the ten directions.
Within the Dharma, there is only this Single Vehicle (Ekayāna); there is no other vehicle, for all other vehicles are not [ultimately] real.
Therefore, the "Nirvana with remainder" clung to by those of the Two Vehicles ultimately falls within the cycle of arising and ceasing; it is not true Nirvana.
The reason the Nirvana of the Two Vehicles is not permitted is that they are intoxicated by the ignorance of the four abodes of existence and have not yet transcended all [defilements].

"Transcending the four dwelling stages" refers to the dwelling stage of desire-attachment (*kāmarāga-vāsabhūmi*), the dwelling stage of form-attachment (*rūparāga-vāsabhūmi*), the dwelling stage of existence-attachment (*bhavarāga-vāsabhūmi*), and the dwelling stage of all views (*dṛṣṭi-vāsabhūmi*). These four afflictions arise from the mental consciousness (*manovijñāna*);

yet the seventh manas, through internal perfuming by grasping [the ālayavijñāna], causes the eight consciousnesses to remain firmly established as the seeds of birth and death. These seeds are thus contained within [the ālayavijñāna].
Because it resides within the field of the eight consciousnesses, it is called the "abode of consciousness. That which the mind dwells upon is this abode of consciousness;
this constitutes the four grounds of dwelling, namely, innate self-clinging (*ātma-grāha*) and innate clinging to phenomena (*dharma-grāha*), which are not easily extinguished.

Those of the two vehicles perceive the mental consciousness and the six consciousnesses, such as the visual consciousness, and suppress them so that they do not function, [claiming]: *Note: The provided text ends abruptly. The translation reflects the content available.*

This is the doctrine of annihilationism, which is termed "impermanence. Alternatively, being deluded regarding the subtle arising and ceasing within the mental consciousness and the ālaya-vijñāna, they fail to perceive the rapid current of these fluxes;
instead, they regard them as tranquil and thus conceive of them as permanent, forming the notion that this is nirvāṇa.

They do not realize that they are merely intoxicated by the ignorance of the ground (mūla-avidyā), but instead cling to the view of the non-existence of the person (pudgala-nairātmya) as being nirvāṇa, failing to awaken to the [non-existence of] phenomena (dharma).
Because the view of non-self cannot abandon the storehouse-consciousness (*ālayavijñāna*), true *nirvāṇa* remains far off;
thus, it is said that the supreme path has no Buddha in *nirvāṇa*, nor does *nirvāṇa* have a Buddha. How could there be a *nirvāṇa* to be realized?
This is why the Two Vehicles are considered "non-vehicles. A monk asked Chan Master Dongshan Chuan: "Regarding the pure practitioner..."
"When a precept-breaking bhikṣu does not ascend to heaven, nor enter hell, what then? Mount [Shan] said:
"When all have been saved without a single trace remaining, he returns to him beyond nirvāṇa. Danxia’s verse says: "His marks and signs are majestic;
this great man, throughout his life, lacked wisdom and was exactly like a fool. From the beginning, even Buddhas and Patriarchs have found it hard to look upon him; how could hell be empty for him?"
One may rely upon Dongshan’s response, which not only lacks even a shadow of heaven or hell, but moreover leaves no nirvana to be attained;
this is what is called the "unfathomable ultimate limit"— how could it be something that ordinary people can fathom?
(Chapter Sixteen in the Wei Translation: "On Prohibiting the Consumption of Meat"; Chapter Eight in the Tang Translation: "On Abstaining from the Consumption of Meat").
At that time, Mahāmati Bodhisattva asked in verse:
Those bodhisattvas who are resolutely seeking the path of the Buddha—how should they regard alcohol, meat, and onions in their diet?

We pray that the Unsurpassed Honored One will, out of compassion, explain this for us: how can these things, which are foul-smelling and loathsome, objects of craving for fools and a delight for tigers and wolves, be eaten?
For those who eat them, various faults arise; for those who do not eat them, it is meritorious and wholesome.
"I only pray that you will explain to me the merits and faults regarding eating and not eating food.
After the Bodhisattva Mahāmati had spoken this verse of inquiry, he further addressed the Buddha, saying:

"I only pray that the World-Honored One will explain for us the virtues and transgressions of eating and not eating meat, so that I and all other Bodhisattvas may always [abstain from it] in the present and the future."

For those sentient beings who have various desires for meat-eating, he teaches the Dharma through various distinctions so that all sentient beings may direct their hearts toward one another with compassion.

Having attained this compassionate mind, each dwells in their respective stage with purity and clarity. (The Tang translation states: "He causes them to abandon the taste of meat and seek the taste of the Dharma;

to give rise to great compassion for all sentient beings and to love one another as if they were an only child, dwelling in the stage of a Bodhisattva. Thus, Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas swiftly attain ultimate, unsurpassed Bodhi.

Having attained cessation within their own stage, even those heterodox practitioners of evil and false doctrines—who hold the inverted views of nihilism and eternalism and are attached to such perversions—still maintain prohibitions against eating meat.
How much more so for the Tathāgata, the protector of the world, who has perfected the True Dharma; could he possibly eat meat? The Buddha said to Mahāmati, "Excellent, excellent!"
"Listen attentively, listen attentively, and reflect upon this well; I shall speak for your sake. Mahāmati said to the Buddha, "Yes, I shall receive your instruction.
The Buddha told Mahāmati: "There are immeasurable reasons why one should not eat meat, yet I shall now briefly explain them for you.
That is to say, all sentient beings, from the beginningless past, have been related to one another through successive causes and conditions, constantly serving as each other's kin."

One should not eat meat because it is regarded as one's own kin; one should not eat meat because butchers sell it mixed together with the flesh of donkeys, mules, camels, foxes, dogs, oxen, horses, humans, and other beasts;
one should not eat meat because it grows from impure elements and odors;
and one should not eat meat because when sentient beings smell its odor, they all become terrified, just like the *caṇḍālas* (meaning "butchers") and the *tāpasa*s (meaning...).

Meat should not be eaten because when hunters see dogs, they provoke their loathing and alarm, causing them to bark in packs; furthermore, meat should not be eaten because it prevents the arising of a compassionate heart in practitioners;
meat should not be eaten because it is the favorite of the ignorant and foolish, being foul-smelling, impure, and lacking a good reputation;
and meat should not be eaten because it causes various incantations and rituals to fail, due to the taking of life.

Because one perceives the form and gives rise to consciousness, becoming deeply attached to its flavor, one should not eat meat; because those who eat meat are abandoned by the devas, one should not eat meat;
because it causes the breath to smell foul, one should not eat meat; because it results in many evil dreams, one should not eat meat;
because tigers and wolves will scent the odor in empty forests, one should not eat meat; and because it renders food and drink impure...
Because it violates the precepts, one should not eat meat; because it prevents practitioners from developing a sense of revulsion [toward suffering], one should not eat meat.
I have always said that regarding whatever food and drink one consumes, one should conceive of it as the flesh of one's own son or as medicine being taken. Therefore, one should not eat meat;
there is no possibility for those who permit the eating of meat to be my disciples.

Tong said: "In the past, the yakṣa king and his retinue on Mount Laṅkā once welcomed the Buddhas of the past into their city, where they expounded the 'Chapter on the Heart of All Buddha-Speech' concerning the ocean-like dharmakāya. Among them were those who aspired to the path of Buddhahood;
however, the single fact that they consume meat is the result of their karmic retribution and habitual tendencies—what is truly meant by this is..."
"Bhagavān, you have taught that those of the two vehicles are intoxicated by the ignorance residing in the stages (*bhūmi-stha-avidyā*).
For this reason, Mahāmati, even the consumption of meat by yakṣas should be abandoned.

Because they do not understand the presence of merit and fault, or the retribution of wholesome and unwholesome karma, I request the Bhagavān to explain this in detail so that I and the other bodhisattvas may know it."

This meaning is intended to cause those sentient beings of the future and present who have not been perfumed by practice and who eat meat to abandon the taste of meat and seek the taste of the Dharma;
to give rise to great compassion toward all sentient beings and to love one another as if they were an only child;
to dwell on the stages of a bodhisattva and practice according to reality; and to abide in the purity of the stages, clearly understanding the four abodes.

Those who sever [afflictions] on their respective stages and swiftly attain unsurpassed bodhi, and further cause sentient beings to enter the place of rest of the two vehicles—the nirvāṇa realized by themselves—and cause them to cease their attachment to the flavor of the Dharma;
and having themselves rested on their own stage, also quickly achieve unsurpassed bodhi because they cultivate the noble path—such persons should not eat meat. All [beings] are thus.
The non-Buddhists and others preach doctrines of false views, falling into the extremes of nihilism and eternalism, or existence and non-existence;

even they prohibit the eating of meat, neither consuming it themselves nor permitting others to do so. How much more so for the Tathāgata’s pure and correct Dharma, which protects the world by preventing the creation of karma and enabling the accomplishment of the Brahma-faring—how could it permit the eating of meat without any prohibition?
The Buddha briefly explained the faults and perils of eating meat: First, one has previously been a close relative and is now reborn in the bodies of birds, beasts, and so forth;
one should regard them with the compassion of recognizing their shared essence.

If even a rākṣasa, upon hearing this teaching, would give rise to a compassionate heart, how much more should my disciples regard such beings as their own kin? Second, on the roads and in the markets...
First, butchers and those who sell meat may mix the flesh of dogs, horses, humans, or other animals for sale;
how can such filthy and loathsome things be eaten? Second, all meats are composed of impure elements derived from semen and blood;
how can one seeking purity consume them? Third, when people who eat meat are smelled by sentient beings, [they become terrified].
All were struck with terror, like butchers, hunters, fishermen, bird-catchers, dogs barking at a sight that startles them, or beasts fleeing upon seeing [a predator].
When sentient beings saw him from afar, they all thought: "This man will surely kill me. For the sake of protecting their lives, they all fled and avoided him.
It is not fitting for a Bodhisattva who practices loving-kindness and compassion to act in such a way toward sentient beings for the purpose of gathering them in.
Regarding the five reasons for not eating meat: all sentient beings know that the Bodhisattva is a seed of the Tathāgata’s compassionate mind and is able to serve as a place of refuge for them.
If one eats meat, compassion will not arise, and sentient beings will consequently lose all their faith.
Because the Bodhisattva practices compassion in order to protect the faith of sentient beings, one should not eat meat.
The sixth reason for abstaining from meat is to protect the world from slandering the Triple Gem.
If my disciples were to eat meat, they would be like the vulgar and foolish who delight in foul odors and filth, thereby destroying their pure conduct.
This would cause all people in the world to cry out, "Where are there any true śramaṇas or brāhmaṇas practicing pure conduct? Thus, such slander would arise. Therefore, [meat must not be eaten].
Good reputation arises entirely from the faults of those who eat meat; therefore, one should not eat it.

Seventh, noble sons, whether they dwell among burial mounds or in forest groves, or whether they practice incantations, seek liberation, or aspire to the Mahāyāna, because of eating meat, all such endeavors will be obstructed and fail to achieve success.
Therefore, a Bodhisattva who wishes to benefit both self and others [should not eat meat].

Regarding the eighth point on why one should not eat meat: For a long time, sentient beings have eaten meat, and their habituation to the intent to kill has become so ingrained that upon seeing the form and color of an animal, they immediately give rise to a craving for its flavor.

How could a Bodhisattva, who regards all sentient beings with compassion as if they were his own body, look upon them and conceive the thought of eating them? Ninth: [One should not eat meat] because it abandons what is the proper food of the noble ones.
Eating the flesh of sentient beings is like that of a rākṣasa; even the devas keep far away from it, let alone the sages.
Bodhisattvas, seeing the sages, should cultivate compassion and must not eat meat. Tenth, it is like the foul stench of a burning corpse;
how could one smell it and place it in one’s mouth? All meats cause the breath to become foul-smelling.
Eleventh, one should not eat meat: for those who eat meat, sleep is painful and rising from it is also painful;
they frequently see various evils in their dreams, their hair stands on end with terror, and their minds are constantly unsettled; therefore, one should not eat it.
Twelfth, because there is no heart of compassion, one lacks all wholesome powers; this is especially true if one is alone in a secluded place.

Thirteenth, because those who eat meat mostly provide non-humans with the opportunity to seek them out; tigers, wolves, and lions also come to seek and devour their flesh, so that they find no peace and security.
Therefore, one should not eat meat. Furthermore, those who eat meat never know satisfaction in their eating;
they increase their illnesses and are constantly bitten by various insects and all manner of impure creatures.
Fourteenth, because of revulsion, one should not eat: when a bodhisattva practices cultivation seeking liberation from birth and death, they perceive all food and drink as being like pus and blood;
fixing their mindfulness on the Noble Path, they are not moved by craving for flavors and are thus able to receive the offerings of all humans and devas.
If attachment arises, one cannot produce revulsion and detachment, and therefore should not accept [such offerings].

Because it is a gift of faith from the world, one should not eat it; therefore, I have often said that even when an ordinary person consumes pure food for the sake of a pure livelihood, they should regard it with the contemplation of the six relations, as if eating their own child, and with the contemplation of illness, as if taking medicine.
How much more so should one refrain from eating the impure meat of non-noble beings, which gives rise to all manner of sins?
This would ruin all merits as briefly explained above; how then could one permit disciples to eat such food?

If it is pure and delicious food, such as *śāli* rice, wheat, or beans—this is the food permitted by the Buddhas of the past and that which should be obtained by those who have long planted roots of goodness.
There is no possibility that meat-eating would be allowed; this is impossible. (From the *Cibou* [Dense Array]).
A monk asked Caoshan, "What is 'falling into the state of having fur and horns'? Caoshan said, "It is falling into the category.
The monk asked, "What is 'not cutting off sound and form'? Caoshan said, "It is falling into conformity. The monk asked, "What is 'not accepting food'? Caoshan said, "It is falling into nobility.
He then said, "To eat is precisely one's own fundamental matter; it is knowing that there is [this]."
Because of grasping, it is called "falling into nobility. If one clings to the initial mind, thinking that there is a self and a state of sainthood, it is called "falling into categories.

If, at the moment the initial mind recognizes its own affairs and turns the light back upon itself, one casts away form, sound, smell, taste, touch, and phenomena (dharmas) and attains tranquility, this constitutes an achievement;
yet, if one does not cling to these matters of the six sense objects, one remains deluded according to one's capacity.
If you allow it to be as it is, you will be obstructed; thus, the six heterodox teachers are your teachers.
Where those teachers fall, you too will fall. Only then may you take food. This "food" is precisely the food of right livelihood (*samyag-ājīva*).
It is also the seeing, hearing, sensing, and knowing at the gates of the six sense faculties; it is simply not being defiled by them, yet regarding this as falling is not so.
This is the same as previously stated: since one does not even grasp at the fundamental matter of others, how much less so for other matters?
Whenever the Master speaks of "falling" (*duo*), he means that things are mixed and cannot be categorized, or that they are not uniform.

Whenever he speaks of a "beginner," he refers to one who, though awakened, remains the same as one who has not yet awakened. Later, Chan Master Dayang Jingxuan commented on these three kinds of falling, saying: "This..."
One must clearly understand the three phrases and attain the stage of transformation before one can become a water buffalo; this is what is meant by "falling into the same category. The Master said:
"The speech of a śramaṇa’s transformed body belongs to the affairs of a different category. If you do not comprehend this meaning, you will be obstructed.
It simply requires relying on the single thought-moment free from self-interest, and then there is a path for emerging from the body. Second, not accepting food.
The Master Zuiguīduò said: "One must know that after finishing matters on that side, one returns to practice on this side;
if you do not leave this station empty, you will sit fixedly in the 'Noble One' (Zūnguì). The Master Suíduò said:
'Because they do not understand sound and form, they fall everywhere. You must find a way to emerge from within sound and form.'"
"What is the one phrase beyond sound and form? He replied: "Sound is not sound of itself; form is not form of itself.
Therefore it is said: "Do not point to the palm. When one says "point," to what palm would one point?
These two venerable masters spoke of "not receiving food" because they did not take the path of nobility; thus they were able to swiftly achieve unsurpassed *bodhi*, let alone worldly matters.

How could one deign to accept such foul and loathsome food? Furthermore, Mahāmati, in the past there was a king named Siṃhasauvarṇa who ate various kinds of meat until he eventually came to eat human beings. His ministers and subjects, unable to endure this, plotted a rebellion; they cut off his stipends and provided for those who eat meat with [the following]: [The verse: "Meat is like excrement, Like the flesh of one's own son, Like the flesh of one's own child; One should not eat it. Thus, because eating meat brings about such calamities, one should abandon it. Furthermore, Mahāmati, if one eats meat, one will be reborn among the carnivorous Pretas; if one eats meat, one will be reborn among the Piśācas; if one eats meat, one will be reborn among the Kumbhāṇḍas; if one eats meat, one will be reborn among the Rākṣasas; if one eats meat, one will be reborn among the various classes of hell-beings; if one eats meat, one will be reborn among the various classes of animals; if one eats meat, one will be reborn among the various classes of Yakṣas; if one eats meat, one will be reborn among the various classes of Asuras; if one eats meat, one will be reborn among the various classes of Garuḍas; if one eats meat, one will be reborn among the various classes of Kimnaras; if one eats meat, one will be reborn among the various classes of Mahoragas; if one eats meat, one will be reborn among the various classes of Gandharvas; if one eats meat, one will be reborn among the various classes of Devas; if one eats meat, one will be reborn among the various classes of humans. Because eating meat brings about such births, one should abandon it. For these reasons, one should not eat meat. (The Tang translation states: "O Mahāmati, Śakra Devendra, while occupying the position of King of Devas, due to the residual habit of having eaten meat in the past, transformed himself into a hawk and pursued a dove.

At that time, I was a king named Śibi; out of compassion for the dove, I cut flesh from my own body to take its place in death. O Mahāmati, if even the residual habits of Śakra still afflict sentient beings, how much more so those shameless ones who constantly eat meat?

You should know that eating meat afflicts both oneself and others; therefore, a Bodhisattva should not eat meat. O Mahāmati, in the past there was a king who was riding a horse while hunting. The horse became startled and bolted, fleeing into a mountain wilderness where there was no way back and no human habitation. There was a female [deer]...

The Lion, together with his companions, subsequently engaged in wicked conduct and begot offspring; the eldest among them was named Pāda (斑足). Later, he became king and ruled over seven hundred million households. Due to the residual habit of eating meat, he would not eat anything that was not meat. First he ate birds and beasts, and later even humans. All the sons and daughters born to him were *rākṣasas*.

After this body perished, he was reborn among lions, jackals, wolves, tigers, leopards, eagles, vultures, and the like. Even if he sought a human body, it could never be obtained, let alone the path to nirvāṇa beyond birth and death.
Furthermore, Mahāmati, all those who kill for the sake of profit, slaughtering and trafficking living beings—those fools...
O Mahāmati, those deluded beings who eat meat use money as a net to capture various meats.
Those who kill living beings—whether by means of wealth, hooks, or nets—slaughter and trade in various creatures of the air, water, and land for the sake of profit.
Furthermore, O Mahāmati, there are no fish or meats that are not produced through teaching [others to kill], seeking [them], or imagining [them]. For this reason, [meat-eating is not permissible].

"One should not eat meat" (The Wei translation says: "I observe that in the world there is no such meat that does not come from a living being; therefore, I say that the sin of eating meat severs the lineage of the Tathāgata").

Mahāmati, at times I have spoken of prohibiting five kinds of meat, or restricted ten kinds; but now, in this sutra, in every respect and at all times, with the exception of skillful means, all [meat] is completely forbidden.
Mahāmati, even for the Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas, there is nothing... [to be consumed].
As for eating food, let alone eating fish and meat, I do not teach people to act with great compassion as their precursor;

rather, I regard all sentient beings as if they were my only child. Therefore, I do not permit the eating of a child’s flesh. (The Tang translation says: "Śrāvakas, Pratyekabuddhas, and even Bodhisattvas still subsist solely on the food of Dharma;

how much more so the Tathāgata? O Mahāmati, the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body is not a body that consumes mixed food. O Mahāmati, I have already washed away all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*). I have skillfully discerned all mental wisdoms and, through great compassion, regard all sentient beings equally as if they were my only child.")
"How could it be permitted for a śrāvaka disciple to eat the flesh of his own son, let alone eat it himself? There is no such possibility for one who speaks thus.
He replied: "The previous statement regarding the impurity of eating meat and its various faults did not yet address its retribution.
This passage speaks of how Siṃha Sautasa became so addicted to the taste of meat that he eventually ate humans, whereby his kingdom was lost."
This is the retribution for the present life. Furthermore, there was once a king who mated with a female lion and begot a spotted-footed offspring;

at first this creature fed on birds and beasts, but later it even came to eat humans. All its male and female offspring became rākṣasas, and upon rebirth they entered the packs of lions, jackals, and tigers.
This is the retribution for the future life. Even Śakra, due to residual habits, still eats from the bodies of hawks.
To be startled and pursued by a pigeon is a path that has not been easily eliminated since immeasurable past lives. Now, those who eat meat have such immeasurable faults as these;
yet ordinary fools, unaware of such benefits and harms, claim that eating meat does not contribute to the act of killing and therefore incurs no sin.
They fail to consider that most acts of killing are committed for the sake of [eating] meat.
Whether people eat it or do not eat it, there is no act of killing; therefore, eating meat is a crime equal to killing.
Those who kill, though they do not eat the meat themselves, commit various killings for the sake of profit, as money is their flavor.
Those who eat meat, though they do not kill themselves, obtain various kinds of meat for the sake of its flavor.
Money serves as the net; through wealth one obtains flavor, and through the net one obtains wealth. By establishing various skillful means, sentient beings are slaughtered.
Mountains are leveled, land is occupied, rivers are cut, and seas are dammed; whether moving on land, in water, or through the air, there is nothing that is not harmed.
If it is claimed that one does not kill them oneself, nor causes others to kill them, and thus, being free from doubt, they may be eaten—such a thing could never exist in this world.
This meat does not emerge from a command; for what reason, then, do you not permit people to eat it? One may search throughout the world, yet such meat as you describe does not exist.
How could there be fish or meat that is "pure" in the three ways—without being taught to take it, without seeking it out, and without thinking of its flavor—and yet still be present?
Therefore, those who eat meat are no different from those who kill; they harm the lives of sentient beings and sever them.
For this reason, one should not eat [meat] that belongs to the lineage of the Tathāgata.

Furthermore, in other sūtras, I have also prohibited the eating of five kinds of pure meat—namely, meat that has not been seen, heard, or suspected [to have been killed for oneself], or meat left over by birds, or meat from animals that died of themselves—and I have forbidden them so as not to allow their consumption.
Or, I have severed ten kinds of things, namely: humans, snakes, elephants, horses, dragons, foxes, pigs, dogs, lions, and tigers.

The prohibition against eating [meat] for sons, monkeys, and others—which was taught as a gradual restriction intended to lead them toward cultivation through temporary expedient means—is now superseded in this assembly at Laṅkā, where the eating of meat in any form whatsoever is absolutely forbidden.
All those provisional teachings established previously are hereby completely abolished; indeed, the eating of meat is prohibited for all who have left the household life.

If people are entirely impure, and yet claim that the Tathāgata permits the eating of meat and eats it himself, such persons will be ensnared by evil karma and shall inevitably fall forever into states that are not beneficial.
All my noble disciples eat the food of the Dharma and do not eat the food of the physical world; how much more so for the Tathāgatas, the Buddhas, whose food is the Dharma?
The Dharma-abiding body does not subsist on food and drink; it is not a body that dwells upon any kind of food or drink.

Since even ordinary beings do not subsist on the coarse food of *kavaḍīkāra*, how much less could they consume the impure food of fish and meat? Therefore, I teach the noble disciples only the food of the Dharma, and I do not instruct them to eat meat.
By me, all habitual tendencies (*vāsanā*) have been cleansed away, and I am free from all [defilements].

Through skillful discernment and knowledge of the seeking of the necessities of life, existence, and affection, as well as the mind and mental factors, preceded by great compassion, one attains the unshared dharmas.
One universally regards all sentient beings with impartial pity, as if they were an only child.
This is because the Dharma-body transmigrates through the five paths and is called "sentient beings," yet all sentient beings are in fact the Tathāgata’s Dharma-body.
Since [the Buddha’s body] is the very essence [of the Dharma], if one were to eat its flesh, would that not be to wound the Dharma-body and sever the life-force of wisdom?
How, then, could it be permitted for the śrāvaka disciples to eat the flesh of their own children? Therefore, in this sutra, I have opened up skillful means to prohibit all such things entirely.
Since it is not permitted for the śrāvaka disciples to eat meat, how could the King of Laṅkā and others—whose resolve... [be otherwise]?

Those who seek the Buddha-way should not fail to awaken with sudden urgency, reform their hearts and change their thoughts, break through the habits of karmic retribution, and seek birth in a superior realm to realize unsurpassed *bodhi*. The Venerable Xihe of Jingzhao Prefecture was a man of unknown origins;
his life and deeds were quite extraordinary, and he had no fixed dwelling, having received the seal of mind from Dongshan Xuanmi.
In the local dialect of Minchuan, he did not possess monastic requisites nor observe the Vinaya;
throughout winter and summer, he wore only a single cotton robe (*nāṃsa*) and daily gathered shrimp and clams along the riverbanks to fill his belly.

At night, he would stay within the paper-money offerings at the White Horse Temple on Mount Dongshan, leading the local residents to call him "Shrimp-and-Clam Shramana. When Chan Master Jing of Huayan heard of this, he wished to...

To distinguish between the true and the false, [Nanyuan] first hid himself within the paper money. At midnight, when the Master returned, Nanyuan held him firmly and asked, "What is the meaning of the Patriarch’s coming from the West?
The Master immediately replied, "The wine table and dishes before the spirit altar. Nanyuan let go of him and said, "It is not for nothing that you were born of the same root as I.
Later, when Nanyuan went to Chang’an at the summons of Emperor Zhuangzong, the Master also preceded him there.
Daily, he would sing and take selfies, or feign madness as he wandered through the mud and snow, leaving no trace of his coming or going;
his ultimate end was thereafter unknown. This is precisely what the Buddha described regarding the manifestations of Bodhisattvas:

though they may violate the monastic precepts (*vinaya*), it is for the sake of eliminating attachments; though they appear to eat meat, they actually consume nothing. This was the deity encountered by Vinaya Master Daoxuan.
The monks were for the most part like this.
At that time, the World-Honored One, wishing to restate this meaning, spoke these verses:
"Once they were all our own kin; yet now, amidst their loathsome impurity and the growth of various unclean things, the mere scent of them strikes terror into everyone."
One who practices the long-term cultivation of detachment should always distance themselves from all meats, onions, leeks, garlic, and various intoxicants that lead to heedlessness;
likewise, they should always avoid sesame oil and beds with perforated slats, for within them tiny insects dwell in extreme terror.
When food gives rise to heedlessness, heedlessness gives rise to discursive thoughts, and from discursive thoughts arises sensual desire. Therefore, one should not eat such things.
From eating arises craving; this craving deludes and intoxicates the mind. This intoxication increases desire, and one is not liberated from the cycle of birth and death.
To kill sentient beings for profit, using wealth to obtain various meats—both of these are evil karmas, and at death one falls into the Raurava (Crying) Hell.
If there is no instruction, perception, or seeking, then the three kinds of "pure meat" do not exist. Since they do not exist without a cause, one should not eat them.
Because of this, those practitioners are all rebuked by the Buddhas, the World-Honored Ones, of the ten directions;
they will repeatedly devour one another and, after death, fall into the class of tigers, wolves, and other beasts—filthy, loathsome, and always born with dull-wittedness.
They will mostly be born among the Caṇḍālas, hunters, and Taṃbas, or as Dāyinīs (which the Wei translation calls rākṣasīs), and various others.
Carnivorous rākṣasas, cats, wildcats, and the like are born everywhere therein.
Generally speaking, the prose section of the text is concise in its meaning, while the verses further elaborate upon it;
what is called the "brief explanation of the faults of eating meat" is spoken in a general sense for all practitioners, regardless of whether they have previously been one's kin.
One should not eat what is unbearable, vile, impure, unfit for consumption, or mixed with various human or animal remains;
one should not eat animals that are unsuitable to eat because they cause terror, nor should one eat anything unclean. It is not only meat that should not be eaten;
by extension, one should also abstain from onions, leeks, garlic, and alcohol, as these can give rise to heedlessness, since sentient beings are terrified of them.
Therefore, it is not only that eating meat causes dogs to bark in alarm when they are pushed; even in beds with holes bored through them by sesame oil, there are minute insects who are terrified.
One should keep far away from such things. It might be tolerable if food gave rise only to negligence and did not produce various faults;
yet once negligence arises, wrong thoughts (vitarka) arise; once wrong thoughts arise, craving (rāga) arises—thus, [faults] are born from food.
Greed causes the mind to be deluded and intoxicated; it nurtures lust for form and the craving for form, binding one so that one remains long in birth and death.

Revolving in the cycle of birth and death, one cannot attain liberation. With alcohol, onions, and the like acting as auxiliary causes, ignorance increases and one fails to attain liberation from the benefits of the supramundane. How can this not be severed? One must simply...
It might still be tolerable if those who have attained liberation had not yet incurred the retribution for their sins;

however, those who kill living beings do so for the sake of wealth, and those who eat meat do so by using that wealth as a net. Both commit evil karma and fall into the Raurava Hell, where there is no need for further discussion.
If one claims that it is not killed by oneself, not killed by another, and that one has no intention to kill—therefore asserting it to be "pure" in these three respects—[this is likewise untenable].
Regarding meat that is edible, if one has not sought it oneself and no one else offered it, the fault lies with oneself and not with others;
yet in the final analysis, this is the same crime as killing living beings. Therefore, all Tathāgatas of the ten directions universally prohibit it, and practitioners should keep far away from it.
By doing so, one shall escape the sufferings of hell and avoid the necessity of retribution.
That may still be tolerated; however, when they are reborn in the world again, they prey upon one another and fall among the species of tigers and wolves.
While humans possess the nature of tigers and wolves, they become butchers, hunters, and rākṣasīs, never departing from the state of ignorant beasts.
Furthermore, those with the nature of tigers and wolves are born as cats, wildcats, and so forth, being reborn throughout these various classes.
To be free from such foul odors is entirely the retribution for eating meat—a thing loathed by all the Buddhas and Tathāgatas.
How can one not prohibit the eating of meat so that all sentient beings may escape such evil retribution and perhaps find the opportunity for liberation?
Zhaozhou asked the monastery attendant, "Where have you been? The attendant replied, "I went to deliver a birth."
Zhaozhou said, "Why did the crow fly away? The Abbot replied, "It was afraid of me. Zhaozhou said, "You have been the administrative head for ten years;
how can you speak such words? The Abbot then asked, "Why did the crow fly away? Zhaozhou said, "The head of the monastery has no murderous intent.
Zhaozhou picked up his bowl and said, "Thirty years from now, if you see this old monk, keep this to offer him."
If Yang did not see [the Buddha], he would immediately smash [the image] to pieces. Another monk said, "After thirty years, I dare say I have seen the Master.
Then Zhou smashed it as well. Furthermore, a layman asked Chan Master Jue of Guangxiao, "Throughout my life, I have killed oxen;
do I still have sin? The Master said, "There is no sin. The man asked, "Why is there no sin? The Master said, "To kill one..."
One person attained liberation by awakening to the meaning of Zhaozhou’s words “one for each”;
yet if the karmic retribution described in Guangxiao’s response to the layman remains as it was, how can one not stand in awe?

In the *Bandhanamukha-sūtra*, the *Mahāmegha-sūtra*, the *Aṅgulimālīya* (translated into Chinese as *Xiàngxiè* or "Elephant Flank"), the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Aṅgulimālīya* (translated into Chinese by Wei as *Nièpán*), and the *Śrīmālā-sūtra*, as well as in this *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*, I have entirely prohibited the eating of meat.
It is censured by all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and Śrāvakas; those who eat it without shame will always be dull-witted and enshrouded in darkness throughout their lives.
Having previously taught that one must abstain from meat based on what has been seen, heard, or suspected, I have now forbidden all meat.
Because they do not realize it through false conceptualization, they are born in places where meat is consumed.

Just as the fault of lust obstructs noble liberation, so too do wine, meat, onions, leeks, and garlic all serve as obstacles to the Noble Path. In these degenerate ages, sentient beings, out of delusion regarding meat, say:
"This is pure and without fault; the Buddha permitted us to eat it. They should regard eating it as taking medicine, or like eating the flesh of one's own son.

For those who are contented, who have developed renunciation, who practice the alms-round, and who dwell in a mind of loving-kindness—I say that they are always free from fear even when dwelling together with tigers, wolves, and other evil beasts. Those who consume the flesh and blood of sentient beings cause all such beings to be terrified.
Therefore, the practitioner of loving-kindness does not eat meat; one who eats meat lacks compassion and wisdom, and forever turns their back on true liberation.
Furthermore, it contradicts the marks of a noble being; therefore, one should not eat meat.

By abstaining from meat, one will be born into the lineage of Brahmins, into families of practitioners, and into households of wisdom and prosperity—this is why [the Tang translation says: "one will certainly be born among sages and saints, possessing abundant wealth and wisdom"].
The messenger said: "What was stated above regarding the karmic retribution for eating meat is truly terrifying; it was spoken for the sake of the multitude.
However, my Dharma disciples should further honor and uphold the Vinaya, remaining pure and vigilant so as not to transgress it.
As I have at times taught in the *Gajapramardana-sūtra*, the *Mahāmegha-sūtra*, the *Nirvāṇa-sūtra*, the *Aṅgulimālīya-sūtra*, and this *Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra*..."

The sutras strictly prohibit the consumption of meat because all Buddhas, Bodhisattvas, and noble disciples of the sages feel revulsion toward it and reprove it, stating that those who eat it are devoid of shame and remorse, and will thus remain perpetually in the darkness of ignorance throughout birth after birth.

I have previously stated that meat obtained through seeing the killing, hearing of the killing, or suspecting the killing is all unfit for consumption; this already constitutes the total prohibition of all meat.
In this world, how could there be any meat that one might eat without having seen, heard, or suspected it?

It is merely the deluded imaginings of the foolish and ignorant who, failing to realize the underlying intent (*saṃdhāya-bhāṣita*), claim that the Tathāgata permitted the eating of the "three kinds of pure meat.
Thus they give rise to the thought of eating meat, and their minds constantly wander toward the pursuit of flesh; this may truly be called a lack of shame and remorse.

The ultimate consequence is as follows: when sentient beings have their minds intoxicated by greed and nourish their craving and desire, the obstacles of desire become so heavy that they cannot attain liberation.
Such faults arise precisely because alcohol, meat, onions, leeks, garlic, and the like act as auxiliary causes;
all of these are obstacles to the Holy Path. My disciples who wish to seek liberation and realize the state of a sage [must therefore avoid them].

Could the Way possibly be equated with the fault of that greed for desire? Thus, sentient beings of the Final Dharma age, through their deluded thoughts, eat meat and offer foolish explanations, saying that one who eats the "three kinds of pure meat" incurs no sin.
To claim that the Buddha permitted me to eat such things is a failure to observe correctly in the pursuit of liberation. If one truly practices while seeking liberation...
When the liberated one eats pure food, they maintain the mental impression of it being like taking medicine;

viewing it as identical to the Dharma-body and regarding it as food for a child, they should immediately be content and give rise to renunciation, no longer craving or seeking. Relying solely on the Tathāgata’s method of practice, they wander for alms.
Being equanimous toward food, they are likewise equanimous toward the Dharma, dwelling in a mind of loving-kindness and maintaining mindfulness.

One should contemplate the Noble Path and not crave the taste of food as I have taught; one should always give rise to a mind of weary detachment toward all sustenance, receiving food and drink as if applying ointment to a festering ulcer.
Having distanced oneself from meat, there will be no foul odor; even if one were to roam with tigers, wolves, and other wicked beasts, they would not be repelled.
If one eats various kinds of flesh and blood, dogs will bark upon smelling it and wild animals will flee upon seeing it.

How could fearfulness toward sentient beings be appropriate for a practitioner? Therefore, one who practices to seek noble liberation should abide in a mind of loving-kindness (*maitrī*) and must not eat meat.
If one eats meat, one does not contemplate the fact that all beings share the same essence and thus engages in various forms of killing;
this is a lack of loving-kindness. When loving-kindness does not arise, right knowledge and vision (*samyag-jñāna-darśana*) are absent. How [could such a person attain liberation]?
If one possesses wisdom yet that wisdom does not arise, how can one be liberated from the bonds of false perceptions?
Since there is no liberation, one revolves through birth and death; such a person is merely a commoner. How could there be a noble one?
That which is esteemed as the mark of a noble one is their possession of the dharma of compassion, or their protective conduct and deportment capable of delivering sentient beings to [liberation].
Only by serving as a model for sentient beings on the further shore can one be called a noble one (*ārya*);
since eating meat now stands in great contradiction to the liberation of the noble ones, practitioners should not eat it.
By not eating meat, one remains free from impurity, gains birth within the lineage of the *brahmins*, and is able to accord with the Dharma teachings, being constantly born [in such states].
In the place of practice, because one abandons delusion, wisdom arises; because one is able to nurture and sustain sentient beings, one is born into a family of wealth and nobility.
This results from not eating meat, such that in birth after birth and life after life, one is always born among the sages and worthies.
Since such a practitioner possesses such great merit in both their present and future retributions, what need is there for further [worldly] action?
Why then do you not prohibit the eating of meat? Those who can abstain from the meat they eat are born into families of wealth, nobility, and wisdom;

how could it be said that their enjoyment of worldly blessings is all they receive? Possessing both merit and wisdom, they are able to advance toward unsurpassed Bodhi, being born into the family of the Tathāgata and perpetuating the lineage of the Buddhas—all of which has this abstinence from eating meat as its foundation.
Is this not indeed the urgent task for a practitioner? When Venerable Yan-yang asked Zhaozhou, "When one brings nothing at all, what then?
Zhaozhou said, "Set it down. Yan-yang said, "If I bring nothing at all, what is there to set down?
Zhaozhou said, "Then carry it away. At these words, Yan-yang attained great enlightenment. Hereafter...
He lived among one snake and one tiger, feeding them from his own hands; thus people called him "The Honored One. The *Huanglong Song* says:
"If you bring not a single thing, you cannot lift it upon your two shoulders. In an instant, he realized his error beneath these words, and within his heart there was boundless joy.
Having cast away all malice and hatred, the snake and the tiger became his intimates. For a clear and vast thousand years, he remained pure.
The wind had not yet ceased when the Celestial Boy offered this verse: "Failing to guard minor conduct, one yields the first move; Self-aware of a coarse mind, one feels shame for the head-blow.
The game is over as the axe-handle rots at the waist; Washing away mundane bones, one wanders with the immortals.
This may indeed be called "tigers, wolves, and all manner of evil beasts—these can always be shared in dwelling and movement. A monk asked Huangbo, "How is it?"
To attain non-falling through the stages, Huangbo said: "Throughout the entire day one eats rice, yet never chews a single grain;
throughout the entire day one walks, yet never treads upon a single patch of ground. At such a time, there is no person and no mark of self;
being never separated from all phenomena throughout the day, yet not being deluded by various conditions—only then is one called a person of mastery, moment after moment.

Do not perceive any signs; do not recognize the three periods of time—past, present, and future. In the past there was no going, in the present there is no abiding, and in the future there will be no coming.
Sit serenely and upright, allowing things to proceed naturally without constraint; this alone is called liberation. Strive! Strive!
Within this gate, among thousands and tens of thousands of people, only three or five might attain it, if they do not take this as their primary concern.
Since the day for receiving retribution is already at hand, it is said that one must exert effort in this present life to bring matters to a conclusion;
who could afford to let residual calamities persist through successive kalpas? When Huangbo spoke to this point, could he still have entertained the thought of eating meat?
The End of Volume Eight of the *Lengqie abatuo luo bao jing Zongtong* (The Penetration of the Essence of the Laṅkāvatāra-sūtra-ratna).
Postscript to the *Lengqie Zongtong*:
In the past, this unworthy one served as a member of the Directorate of Reception. Looking back upon my own meager and shallow abilities, how could they suffice to attract the worthies of the realm?

The noble elder is one who shines light upon those below to provide them relief, and I have privately been graced by the kindness of the venerable Elder Liu, whose vision has returned to clarity and whose teeth have regained their luster.
Before long after receiving his instruction, the Elder accepted a simple imperial mandate to oversee the administration of the Imperial Stables at Chuyang; for Chuyang is indeed my own [home region].

This is the place where the Holy Ancestor first established his foundation. His rise was achieved by means of the horse, yet the completion of his great merit was compared to the legendary taming of horses at Mount Hua.

Examining the *Jingming* (The Official Post of the Horse Master), one sees that he carefully regulated his attendants and servants to assist the Son of Heaven in upholding the constitutional laws modeled after Heaven;
thus, the Tianfang Bureau has long been held in high esteem as the imperial seat. However, as for the current administration of the pastures and herds...

The system was changed to a tax-in-kind, and the Office of the Imperial Stables (Jiǒngshù) in the region south of the Yangtze (Jiāngtǎo) consequently became known as a place for leisurely cultivation of one’s reputation.

There, the *shùzǐ* (attendant scholars) of Lángyá presented their finest talents amidst the lush greenery of towering ancient paulownias and elm trees, whose verdant foliage formed thousands of columns.

Whenever the nocturnal air gave rise to freshness and the warblers sang their hundred trills, one’s spirit would be suddenly awakened; at such times, the vulgar ears were as if washed clean, and the mundane world was instantly transcended.

Suddenly, there is this expression of not wishing to fly through the air to drink the *xiangxai* vapors and breathe in the purple clarity—a phrase that has not often been encountered even among the Golden Grain [Sūtras]!
It is only fitting that my elder brother, with such grace, has found resonance in a manner that transcends the trap and the snare.

While my elder brother was inspecting the seals for three circuits, he dispatched a letter from across the river; his noble intention is to ensure the dissemination of the *Lengqie* school’s profound teachings. My elder brother’s...
The Preface states: "Formerly, Master Jinjian labored over this with great care and composed several prefaces. Is it that the world lacks those capable of composing the *Fengsu sheng*?

It is simply that there is no one like Huangfu Mi. To carve this into woodblocks and circulate it depends entirely upon you. (Shan) Xie replied, "Yes, yes," yet due to his busy schedule, he could only finish reading it at leisure.
Indeed, when Zhang Wen-ding of the Song dynasty stayed in a monk’s quarters in Langye, he suddenly recognized it as [the work of] [Huangfu] Mi.
This was recorded by the former abbot. Since Master Weng arrived in Chu, he has searched out the old sites and constructed the Scripture-Reading Terrace;

furthermore, he contemplated how to ensure that the Heart-Seal of more than several hundred years would not perish, and looked down with favor upon this unworthy one to join him in propagating the ancestral style.
Thus, this unworthy one has fortunately received the Master's grace, being permitted to follow in his footsteps so as not to let [the tradition] fall into obscurity.

Regarding those who have passed away, the scholars of successive generations have for the most part been constrained by delusions, falsely claiming that the principles of Chan offer no benefit for saving the world.
Yet Wen Ding flourished during the Xiping era of the Song dynasty and was renowned as a great minister of his time;
even today, Master Jinjian has collated [his works] and my father has brought them to light. My father was a man of profound virtue and magnificent reputation.
Within the realm, the Sīnan Yunge and Lingyan pavilions have yet to reach their full potential;
unless one possesses a profound mastery of the world beyond the dust—a vision as vast as the mountains and rivers of the great earth—how could one manage the lofty and exalted compositions?

It is precisely for this reason that those who investigate and realize the Pure Principle of the Chan school desire, from afar, to widely propagate the transmission of the lineage, so as to join with the eminent worthies and men of outstanding insight.
"To unify the spirit-altar within the vast void—could the profound mind of the Elder indeed have reached such a state? It is surely so.
Furthermore, the spiritual seclusion of the mountains and waters of Chuyang increasingly enhances what our Saintly Ancestor did in years past when he cast aside his weapons to discourse on learning."
For two hundred years, the successive sagely rulers have acted to broaden the people’s strength and provide them with rest and nourishment;
you, Master Weng, will surely use your pure karma to stem the drifting waves of decline and cool the flames of vulgar customs.

Thus, to say that Weiquan is merely a place for the younger son to enjoy leisure and suit his nature is to glimpse only its outer periphery without having yet entered upon the Master’s profound and subtle depths. I, Shan, am not clever enough to express this fully.
I venture to stand in the lee of your virtue, wishing to borrow the remaining years of my life to realize the single awakening of the Golden Immortal.

I only fear that after begging for water, my teeth may become parched, leading to regret at a later time; I pray that you, O Elder, will not be sparing with your instruction but will provide a detailed edict for those on the path of delusion. I respectfully rely upon the carving of this compilation to express my aspirations.
Written with deep respect by Sun Mingshan Maochengfu of Moling in the middle month of autumn, the Renzi year of the Wanli era.
